The Vanishing of Ethan Cater is a story that follows Paul Prospero, a detective with a paranormal ability to communicate with the dead, who travels to Red Creek Valley in search of a missing boy named Ethan Carter.
What stood out to me about this game immediately was how non-linear it was. It does not provide you with any hints, instructions, or hold your hand at any point throughout the story. The Vanishing of Ethan Carter encourages you to explore it's entirety and piece the story together yourself. It's a refreshing change of pace since it lets you absorb the games beautiful atmosphere and figure things out for yourself.
Without spoiling any of the story, I will say that it is engaging enough to make you want to play to the end to find out what happens. The games plot revolves primarily around dealing with the supernatural and has a very somber undertone to it.
The dark undertone of the story goes hand in hand with the games atmopshere. The game is visually stunning and has some incredible detail. Everywhere from the claustrophobic areas to the wide open landscapes, I think if there's one thing anyone takes away from this game is how stunning and photorealistic it is.
In terms of gameplay, it is pretty simplistic. While you are free to explore the game in any fashion you desire, you will come across various puzzles and dealings with the supernatural that require a certain tact in order to progress through the story. There are a couple puzzles that forced me to reevaluate my approach, but they werent pressingly difficult and didn't break the pace of the game.
There are only a couple negative things I can say about this game is how short it is. It took me just under 5 hours to complete and to get all the achievements. I got the game when it was on sale for under $10, and I found it to be a suitable price for a game that is as short as this one is.
The other complaint was the optimization. I would say I have a slightly above average rig, and there were parts of the game that felt kind of choppy, despite my attempts to adjust the settings. Granted it wasn't game breaking as much as it was a slight annoyance at times. It did not hinder my ability to play the game.
That being said, the game is very well made overall. While The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a short tale, I would still highly recommend this game.

Granted, the Vanishing of Ethan Carter was among the best scenery graphics I have ever seen.
But then there is a puzzle in the mine that has a game-breaking bug that makes it NOT able to be completed. After the initial animation, it never transitions you to the next map. It doesn't even teleport you anywhere. It simply sits there with the animation looping forever, until you press Ctrl+Alt+Del. The only way around it is to put the game to windowed at 800x600 until you reach the next scene. And even after nearly a full year, the developers have STILL not fixed it.
And to make matters worse, the Developers specifically stated that pre-orders would include special features that would be EXCLUSIVE to pre-orders, and then Release Day came along with the addition of The Collector’s Edition DLC, which was all of the stuff they stated was going to be EXCLUSIVE to the pre-orders.
So for Developer dishonesty to their customers, and for not bothering to fix game-breaking bugs, this game gets a Fail grade from me.

I'm quite impressed with the depth of this game already, being that it's alpha. You are the founder of a software company who can produce a huge variety of softwares--anything from computer or console games, to OS, antivirus, game engines or audo/video tools. After putting almost 17 hours in I'm only "10 years" into the game. <--you can customize the rate of time flow like everything else.
The really amazing feature of this game is that you can choose to micromanage basically every aspect of your company, right down to hiring employees, accepting contracts, and distributing the work among teams--or you can choose to automate a good portion of this, hiring "lead" staff who will take over HR and project management duties. Likewise, you can choose to keep your company small and "humble", taking up only a small amount of space and resource, or you can grow it into a mega corporate monster that sprawls and impressively large map.
This is the most in-depth game of it's kind that I've ever played and I'm extremely excited to see where this game goes with future updates.
It does currently suffer from a serious need of background music and more decoration options, though.

EDIT 2016-09-07: Much content and game play mechanics have been added since I last played back in February, I'm loving it all over again! All the changes have been nothing but good in my opinion. The game is more complex (in a good way) and it feels like it takes longer to reach "the end". Seriously, no complaints - other than I wish it was finished so I could be playing an even better version of this game!
OP:
It is definitely a full-on simulation, I love it! The irony of playing a game about developing software that is itself a piece of software being developed is also amusing (can't wait to see some more real-life 2D/3D art). However, after playing 54 hours in a single game I will probably not play it for a while until more content is added and/or changes are made to gameplay. I reached a self-declared point of endless monotony in the game far earlier than I expected to. It felt like 'The End' of the game. But then, what I find monotonous may be an enjoyable continuation of a simulation to others.
Granted, I played this game on the Medium/Normal difficulty - the alternatives being Easy or Hard - but I would hate to experience Easy. All said and done, I love the game and it was definitely worth the $14 I paid for it. At this point it's just a simultion that "peaks" too early in my opinion, but I have faith it will be improved significantly as it approaches official release.

With just about 9 hours of gametime, I decided to write a review.
I was quite unsure in advance if this game would have a little more deepness, compared to, say, Game Dev Tycoon. But then, I told myself what the heck and gave it a shot.
I don't think it would be fair to compare this and GDT. GTD is a ton of fun with some subtle memories for some gamers from the dark eighties, like I am. But Software Inc is different. You would have a lot more administrative stuff to do, and less detailt development work. Which at first plain suXed, but then again, hey, you run a company, you are not a simple game dev'er.
If you understand the game mechanics, it's quite easy on "easy" and "medium", I hope it will be more challenging on "hard" though, but I haven't tried that yet.
Undoubtly, Software Inc is highly addictive, be it for building an awesome company HQ, be it for that one uber operating system. Also, it's addictive if you are into micro management stuff!
Only thing is: you will need to be into simulation games. But then, it's great fun to play.
I am keeping away from the Cons, as this is early access and I am sure the devs will change stuff until the release!
8/10, there's so much potential in Software Inc! If you are undecided: go and grab your copy and support the devs.

I like this game and I love the premise. I personally like the fact that its very complicated since it makes it more of a brain exercise.
However starting a game is very difficult. The default starting cash is $10,000 (you can change it). The real estate for your first office will cost you half of that. Then you have to pay a crap ton of money for the licenses for your project. I personally found it convuluted that you had 20-30+ operating systems to choose from, all very expensive to acquire licenses. Completely blown away that there were no Open Source license options when starting out, especially since the whole point is to "start lean" and grow into a larger company.
The controls are a bit weird. You use WASD to move around the map and UP/DOWN/LEFT/RIGHT to operate the camera. Personally my natural reaction is to click on the ground and drag around until the camera view is perfect. The developer should change it to this way because WASD+arrows+MOUSE is too much functionality to handle when you are also dealing with a very complex UI.
If I gave it more of a chance I would probably like it more. I love the concept and 80% of the execution is there. I actually prefer it to stay complex as it is because it differentiates it from the other game tycoon games.
My suggestion is to start the game as a loner in a garage, since that is easier to handle rather than throwing all of these resources at the user from the get go. My $0.02 and I'm glad I could provide an early access review.

If I had to rate this like I do my books, I'd give this a 3 (out of 5) I think.  I played it a couple different ways, to sort of see where my character (I named her Tsunade) could end out.  Having played several otome games before this wasn't that hard to navigate to avoid the "bad" ending(s)...if there were any.  While the story makes little coherent sense (you can't legally bury a body the same day the person is found dead...and you definitely can't also read the will the same day), and the characters come off a bit two dimensional trope-y, I admit to wanting to keep trying.
I will say the writer distinguished the guys well enough that when presented with an option its ridiculously easy to figure out what would boost their feelings towards you or not.  With the added option of skipping dialogue you can blow through several of the routes fairly quickly once you get the flow of the story.
Still for a free game it was a nice way to kill some time.  I'll likely return to it to see if I can get all the endings, and the Blooper reels are amusing (and in some cases illustrate just how much post-work went into cleaning up the dialogue tracks).  The artwork, while not strikingly gorgeous is easy on the eyes.  And the music inoffensive, something I greatly appreciate.

Imagine a combination between GTA, Prototype and Internet Memes (including the popular one and the obscure or dark ones). This game doesn't bring a lot more to the table compared to it's predecesor with several big exceptions: you have super powers and a different story.
The story maintains the wacky and diverse style Saints Row has, making it quite entertaining to go through it if you do not expect something super serious or normal. The challenges can be challenging sometimes, as their name suggests, but in rest most of the stuff are pretty much the same like before, same style of missions, same city, same guns mostly, ofc, all adapted and a bit improved here and there to the new (actually almost the same) changed world in this version.
Super powers is the second selling point, they make any vehicle obsalete (unless you do plan to travel slowly and overly exposed around the city) on one hand, but makes pretty much everything else a lot more fun, giving you liberty to move around the city and over it with ease, not to mention quickening the travelling from one point to another. They also give a nice addition to the combat, a sort of Bioshock-ish feel to it, with a nice varriety of powers.
Of course, due to the high liberty you get in the game, things might break sometimes, there are some intentional "bugs" here and there, but sometimes you might stumble upon actual bugs that might make the game unplayable at times (it happened to me several times in the DLC missions), but that is usually quite random and rare thou.
Final words:
just like any other Saints Row game, in my opinion, this is a lot more enjoyable if played with someone else in co-op,
the soundtrack is amazing just like in the previous game.
despite using pretty much the same engine and most of the elements from the previous game, it does ask for a bit more resources to run well.

TL;DR 8/10
A Story About My Uncle is a nice and short 2-3 hour adventure game. The story isn't deep or well developed but the movement mechanics fully make up for it.
You play as an unnamed nephew searching for his uncle Fred, but theirs a catch, your uncle is at the end of a fantasy world of his own creation. It's now your mission to navigate this magical world using a suit fit with a grapple gun and later on rocket boots as well.
Visuals: 8/10
The game is graphically nice looking at distance and even mid-short range the graphics are still nice. However, if you get near the NPCs in the game they don't look so hot.
Movement:10/10
This games movement mechanics are flawless. You can so smoothly run, jump, grapple, and rocket you could spend hours just messing around seeing what you can do. It's very clear 99% of the developers effort went into perfecting the movement and map design.

It's pretty buggy, though. Cyborg tanks will sometimes spawn on screen (sometimes wedged in rocks too) and instantly sound the alarm. Sometimes you lose all control of your character. Sometimes the camera decides to take the day off and go for a walk without you. Sometimes your strategems will decide the nice open field you deployed them in isn't clear enough, and instead decide to deploy on top of you instead.
And then there's just some poor design choices, like when an enemy tank spawns right next to the objective and drives onto it, instantly destroying the objective before you could possibly do anything about it. Or the way enemies off screen can sound the alarm before you can see them. Or the way the UAV and all-terain boots (arguably two of the most useful pieces of gear in the game) are locked behind DLC.
But in the end, it's fun. It will probably infuriate you every now and then because of how buggy it is, but it's fun nonetheless.

I have to start with a caveat. Yes, I recommend this game BUT, and this is a big BUT, only if you really enjoy obtuse puzzles, lots of non linear exploration and interesting supernatural mysteries. The game is gorgeous and tells a pretty cool story. However I admit I used a walkthrough for all but the most simple of the puzzles in this game, namely the chronologies where you assemble timelines for murder mysteries you come across. However the puzzles aren't the most difficult part, it's FINDING the puzzles or even knowing you're solving a puzzle in the first place that gets really difficult. It's entirely possible to reach the very end of this game and not be able to finish unless you have solved every puzzle in the game, making it entirely possible to force you to back track through the ENTIRE game to find what it is you missed, using a basic map as a guideline.
I ultimately don't regret my time with this game as it does have a very clever story and good atmosphere. However I only recommend it to those who enjoyed titles like the old Myst games. The first thing this game tells you is that it does not hold your hands. And oh man they are not kidding.

I began to write a pros & cons list, but realized these are all pretty subjective features. So read 'em and decide for yourself if they're pros or cons
-Fast to learn. Nothing really too difficult in the way of UI or systems.
-Damn near impossible to master. There's plenty of systems that offer great synergies with different ships and crew members to create almost everything
-RNG. Roguelike shines through in the design: If things go wrong, they usually go catastrophically wrong. And all it takes is one bad encounter and you might never recover.
Is it worth the asking price? Definitely. I have over 60hrs clocked in, and still a handful of ships left to unlock. And I've read up on the mechanisms required to open them, so in theory I know how, but the gods of RNG haven't smiled on me yet.

This is a free visual novel with an admittedly corny name and more unhelpful joke reviews than I can count, so I wasn't expecting a great game out of this when I downloaded it. I'm a huge fan of visual novels and of dating sims in particular (or any game that features dating; Harvest Moon, I'm looking at you), so I decided to give it a try to see if I was pleasantly surprised.
And I was. After having beat the game more than once at the time of this review (the first playthrough will take the player about three hours, while additional playthroughs can be much quicker due to the convenient "skip" feature that allows you to experience different storylines from the different decisions you make without having to reread the bulk of the story, only that which is changed), I can say that I would have happily paid for this game, and I am admittedly frugal to a fault, so that's hard for me to say. This was the first game in awhile where after I beat it, I sat there wondering, "How can I support this developer? How do I give this woman money?" Through some digging in the game's options, I found a link that will allow you to support the upcoming sequel if you so wish, which is something I am seriously considering.
Seduce Me the Otome features a storyline that is interesting in its entwining of the world which we know and that of a fantasical demon realm complete with magic and otherworldly beings, many of which you can romance. I knew based on the screenshots above who I wanted to romance first, but I was surprised to find that ALL of the bachelors were unique, interesting, and charming in their own right. Each character is so distinguishable from the others that multiple playthroughs grant you completely different stories and backgrounds that add to your overall understanding of the world and its characters. While the protagonist can be subject to a couple of klutzy moments where it oh-so-conveniently leads to a romantic moment, I found that this wasn't overused to the point of being annoying, and she is strong and confident in her own right. I was surprised to feel right at home when I could tell my character to use the phrase "F**k off!" to an antagonist rather than blush and let the men handle it, because games like this usually have fairly weak women characters, and thus they are unlike any realistic women I personally know and are therefore unrelatable. This was a breath of fresh air.
In terms of content, the storyline was interesting (romance and otherwise) and built a world in which I would fully like to explore deeper, both through additional playthroughs and further games. This is a game meant for teenagers or older. It does have some violence (never shown) and uses curse words, but not to a fault, and you'll find no fan service that takes away from the maturity of the situations characters find themselves in. This game respects its characters and their relationships; while you may make the decision of whether or not to bed the character you pursue (and again, this is fully up to you), it is tastefully done. The emphasis in this game is on the emotional bond between two people-- not the limited physical connection, and thus, I found the relationships developed in this game tended to stick in my mind as stronger and more important than others.
Lastly, I want to commend the developer for tackling mature themes, and not making relationships shallow and based on attraction like many other games. This game isn't afraid to make its characters endure trauma and have resulting fears or personality changes based on such, and that is the reality of life. This isn't a dating sim where you give a date the right piece of food and they like you more; no, this is a mature visual novel for adults, and I couldn't have enjoyed it more.
Overall, the positives to this game vastly outweight the negatives to the point that the scale is broken in full favor of one side. I found very little to complain about. There were maybe three or four typos I came across during my time in the game thus far. I would have liked a few more intimate scenes (conversation-wise, between two interested characters). Through multiple playthroughs, the physical intimacy scenes can be repetitive even over several characters, though some do change. Also, there are romanceable options between women and men, and women and women, but no men and men. Your character is, by default, a woman, so this is to be expected; though I am a huge fan of male/male romances and would have liked the option. It also would have been nice to be able to romance more than one character and to eventually make a choice (or even have both love interests confront each other). All of these things do not even come close to overriding the positives, however (and some come down to simple design decisions, of course), so with that said, I would give this game a personal rating of 9/10. It is nearly perfect for what I look for in visual novels, and I will support any future visual novel projects this author decides to publish.

Solid gameplay, a nice little story and superb, free-flowing platforming. The pace is as fast or as slow as you want it to be, the soundtrack is very well suited to the environments, which themselves are eerily beautiful, and the story is simple and clear, providing a superb backdrop to the game. The levels are very open, and you can pick out your own route across the environment - it doesn't feel at all constrained. The challenge increases naturally throughout the game, and it's very satisfying to learn how to use the new abilities and gameplay features in series. There are also hidden extras to the main story which add that extra dimension to the game's feel.
It is, however, a very short game - I completed it in 3 hours. As it's a story-based game, I feel like going back and playing it again would rather miss the pont - there wouldn't be that same sense of discovery. A such, replayability is pretty low.
I bought it on sale at 66% off, making it £3.39. At this price, I wouldn't hesitate to recommend it to anyone who likes good, solid platforming, or a nice, simple, beautiful story-telling game. At full price, you'll have to make your own decision.

My only annoyance with this game was the technical bug some people experience at startup (see forum), but I solved that in just a few minutes by fiddling with the graphics settings. Also the spinning camera gave me motion sickness, so that's something to keep in mind if you're sensitive to that sort of thing.
Some reviews have called this game a glorified walking simulator, and sure, it is pretty linear and the puzzles aren't particularly difficult. But it does also have elegant gameplay mechanics and multiple story layers that made me eager to keep playing and unraveling the mystery. If you like immersion and moderately paced, contemplative storytelling you'll probably enjoy this game. If you go in expecting tons of jumpscares and action... well, you won't find them but you might enjoy the game anyway.

TLDR; If you're thinking about buying it, just go ahead - it's money well spent.
If this looks like the kind of game you like to play then you will thoroughly enjoy it.
It's very well drawn - when outside the whole city is rendered (hence the non-basic graphics requirements) but I also think it's really well optimised as runs at comfortable frames per sec on a GTX 660 1.5Gb on medium settings.
It's actually a first person shooter game - but you deal with the environment (lots of climbing/running/jumping and zombies everywhere) for quite some time with only melee weapons. This doesn't detract from anything - it adds to it. By the time you have a gun you've probably already learned how to avoid or demolish the odd Z or two, so they become easy meat with your new found weaponry. Other, more intelligent/tougher enemies however, lead to a further challenge.
There's lots of gameplay here. You get better at parkouring your way around the city, smashing a few Z's with melee or learning how to use the fairly extensive list of unlockable (RPG style) skills from different trees with practice, so it's totally a skill based game. There's a full, unadulterated story with plot development, etc, and shedloads of side quests that will take hours upon hours to complete - many of which give you useful items so aren't just there for the sake of it.
Day/night cycles, with the change of difficulty and pace add greatly to the overall feeling. After surviving a few nights outside you start feeling "boss" and get comforable with milling around with infected during the day. Almost over-comfortable in some instances..
I don't really regard weather as a game-changer but having a lightning storm kick in at night - the strikes and their vivid illumination breifly highlighting a shambling horde around me as I'm tring to sneak up to a particular enemy - really adds atmosphere in a memorable way.
I haven't played a lot of games recently in general, and don't often write reviews, but this game has captured my imagination and brings together different concepts (and genres I guess) in a seamless, quality environment where none of the aspects seem "pinned on" or shoehorned in / afterthoughts.
My friends and I purchased it on sale for about £17 and it's fairly safe to say is one of the best games I've ever played. I am therefore happy to give it a massive thumbs up and consider it worth every single penny we spent, and then some.
One buddy described this as the complete evolution of Left for Dead (or L4D2 on crack, as it were) and it's a pretty good analogy - it does totally feel like the devs have dragged the zombie boshing genre forward a full decade.
It's now over 2 and a half years old but content is still being added; should tell you something.

From what I was briefly able to determine, gameplay on this game is on par with all other recent Lego games.  However, I never got past the opening bit due to a fatal flaw they've apparently been building into the Lego games recently - Lego Batman 3 suffers this same flaw.  It is not possible to play this game properly single-player, at least in some cases.
The game starts you out with a normal screen, and you can begin fighting, breaking things, and collecting studs right away.  However, your second character does not follow you any more, and as soon as you move too far from them, the game switches to split-screen, leaving your second character behind.  Actively adding a second player, and then dropping out, temporarily corrects this problem, for a handful of seconds, before the game split-screens again because your second character does not follow you.
I have only seen this issue on newer Lego games, but it happens on several of them.  I don't understand why it's an issue when games even as recent as Lego Hobbit work just fine, but without them fixing the problem, this game is next to unplayable.  Refunded, and would love for the developers to fix every single game that suffers this issue.  Until then, absolutely not worth buying.

I am a HUGE lover of visual novels and dating sims, and I am quite the master of them.
This one was just the right amount of raunchy and the right amount of sweet.
It wasn't disgusting at any point, and for a free novel? It got DEEPER than most of the ones you have to PAY for.
The creator of this I definitely admire.
The artwork? Astounding. The music was enchanting.
The pros:
Artwork was incredible
The characters, although some called them stereotypical types, added an interesting but lovely take on this game
The script was not half bad, and was almost flawless.
I found myself wanting to play through ALL of the endings. It was captivating.
Cons:
The dialog although differentiating for each character slightly, was all in all almost the same.
I feel as if it should have varied with the different personalities.
The "scandalous" scenes were all practically exactly the same, which lowered some of the excitement factor, and did not feel as personalized to each character as it should have been.
Overall I thoroughly enjoyed this game, and crave more.
I'd give it a 7 out of 10, maybe an 8. It was beyond great for a free steam game, and it AMAZES ME. I would love to personally get to know the people who worked on this, because they deserve some pats on the back for this work!

So many reviews have been posted already as this game is hardly new anymore, but I will give my 2 cents anyway.

I have bought this game for the single player aspect only, because thats what I liked about CoH 1. So I am only basing this review on the single player aspect and therefor I will completely ignore all the negative reviews about the tons of DLC's for multi player here on Steam.
I have (am playing) played the main campaign and the Ardennes campaign.
What I among other things loved about CoH 1 was the (relative) freedom you had to complete the objectives. You were given a main objective and sometimes a secondary optional objective and then you could build a base and slowly build up defences and expand your territory on the map. There were multiple paths and directions you could take to take over territory.

In CoH 2 the gameplay is really restricted, even units like engineers can't use their capabilities until the pre-scripted story 'yada yada' unlocks their function in the battlefield. The game now constantly tells you what to do, how and where you should advance and what weapon you should use. You even get shiny hologram markers on the map that tells you exactly where the developers wants you to go.
I have broken the gameplay several times already by not doing what the developers expect me to do. On multiple occasions I have found spawn points of the enemy AI at sectors I could overtake, but apparently was not meant to overtake. I litterally saw the enemies spawn at a static location out of thin air every x amount of seconds. I builded static HMG nests around the spawn points and they kept dying the moment they spawned on the map lolz.

The campaigns are really designed for speed RTS, unlike CoH 1. Generally the developers expect from you that you advance on the map as fast (and dumb) as possible, while I like to take it more slow and strategic and fortify capture points before I advance further. Not playing the game by how the devs designed it leads to all sorts of gameplay issues. Biggest issues are the main oblectives that are timed and forces you to rush and play kamikaze mode instead of playing a 'strategic' game.

Some of the missions/objectives felt a bit like CoH 1 and I could play it the same way, but the majority of the time I felt hand cuffed, and rushed, and spammed by AI spawns during gameplay and on rails by a narrow developers mind that limits me to a certain gameplay approach.

The pathfinding of the AI also has not improved, or even may be worse now. Ordering AI to travel from A to B leads the AI directly through enemy fire. You really have to babysit the AI now and order them from corner to corner otherwise they will walk into an anemy tank or HMG fire.
A lot of the time there are also pre-scripted friendly AI infantry on the map, that keep advancing and dying. You see them walk right into HMG fire. They litterally were scripted with a static path to walk into enemy fire... you see a hundred dead NPC AI lying in a row on the ground. They behave like lemmings.
I also could go on about the UI and graphics etc (which are okay), but I will leave it at the gameplay aspect as that what matters the most to me.

CoH 1 is an 80/100 in my opinion so I think overall CoH 2 (single player) is a,
Barely

Company of Heroes 2, the sequel to the famous first COH is in my humble opinion a 'interesting' game but is it all that and a bag of chips?   Well whether or not a game is good is subjective to the individual and what exactly your looking to get out of a game.
The Good:
- Modding Support through the Steam-Workshop offers all manner of mods, unit skins, decals, Player made maps, and more all for free and easily aquired with the click of a button.
- Unit Diversity.  A counter for every move and with over 31+ Commanders to choose from per faction as opposed to the original COH with just 3 Doctrines to choose from per faction,  Each army has a distinct theme from focus ranging from Heavy Tanks, Specialized Infantry, Artillery, Aircraft and more!
- Enviroment Matters.   COH2 offers unit bonuses for taking cover behind pretty much anything,  Destructible enviroments mean that a wall or house can be blown away to create new avenues to flank your opponent!   Weather can freeze your troops to death in the cold blizzards or slow them down as easy targets when they get stuck in deep-mud.
The Bad:
- DLC,  Sega is rather heavy about DLC.  For example that fancy Skin you want for your tanks?  Or want a Tiger Tank but don't own the commander that offers one?   Gotta buy them.   DLC ranges from 3 to 5$ (prices vary on your region) but this can be mitigated both by the fact that COH2 is frequently on the Steam Sales where you can get the DLC for as cheap as 1$  or just download a Mod from the workshop that offers them.
- The Single Player Campaign.   I have mixed feelings about the campaign.   The Soviet Campaign (which is free) was dark (which is IMO good) but the characters were boring,  I felt no passion to empathize with characters and the mission objectives were generic and rather basic,  What you would expect from a RTS.....   SEGA fortunatly learns there lesson when they introduce the American Campaign "Ardennes Assault" Giving us more interesting characters and unique mechanics for a Story,  making the campaign into a RISK or Total War style where you only have limited resources to conduct the entire campaign.   Unfortunatly this absolutely amazing Ardennes Assault campaign is DLC:  10$ on its own,  5 or 3$ during a Steam Sale.
- Vanilla Gameplay is Boring,  Game ballance is about as fair as Starcraft,  but just like Starcraft that same  rock/paper/scissors can get boring.  IMO Get a realism mod from the Steam Workshop such as Spearhead or Wikinger just off the top of my head.   The All Units mod can also appeal if you don't want realism & don't want to buy the DLC.
- Axis vs Allies.    This should be a common theme,   however where  the Allies are diverse between the Soviets, Americans, and the British.... the Axis are just Germans with a east & west theme.  SEGA has rich options to choose from between nations like Vichy-France, Italy, or Japan and yet they have been reluctant to pool from it despite showing they can with units such as the Ostruppen pooled from the various nations that were absorbed into the German Army.   COH2 has great potential if only they would do more then just present Nazi-Germany as the only overarching villain.
In conclusion,  COH2 is not a game for everyone,  I'd reccomend it only to WW2 Enthusiasts who want a plethora of options to choose from, and I would highly reccomend players wait for the Steam Sales (COH2 g oes on sale extremly frequently),  The game's not worth full retail price.  Bu with that said I find boundless enjoyment out of this game and still play it even today as my fallback enjoyment.

"Well, it's free" is turning up in a lot of these reviews and yeah, that's one reason for sure. Grab it just for the voice acting bloopers and you won't have wasted the time you spent downloading it.
It's an interesting little story with each ending revealing another chunk that other endings don't reveal. The art is fine. The writing isn't quite polished, I'd say high school level or enthusiastic middle schooler writer level (been there, done that). There was just some awkwardness and poor word choice either for connotation or totally not meaning what the writer thought they meant but it's not cringeworthy. The intimate scenes are still fairly hot despite the amateur writing. The MC can have a varied personality based on your choices, which is refreshing.
The boys, as far as you get to know any except whichever one you go for (if you even go for one of them; you can get with the girls too), are the usual architypes: quiet one, smart/sophisticated one, cutely boyish one, shameless flirt, and finally, the "bad boy" i.e. a s s h o l e. Unfortunately, the last one is done in a way I just hate. When girls say they like "bad boys" they DON'T mean they want a guy who treats them like s h i t unless they're alone with him and he reveals his secret sensitive side. Other feminists have gone into better explanation of why this is not good so I won't repeat them.
I was annoyed that a huge section of story branches gets cut off if you make the seemingly arbitrary choice between going out with your friends or staying and fixing up the house with the boys (there's a part later where you can take food to one of the guys, and if you went out then you simply can't find any of them. I think this part should give you a second chance to connect with one, unless the creators wanted to punish you for going "oh thanks for doing all the work while I go out with my pals, suckers").  I really wish there was an option to get to know each of the boys a bit before picking who to persue. It would fix the somewhat frenetic pacing too.
Save often and make use of the "skip" function to fast-forward through the stuff you've seen already and you shouldn't waste too much time on the replays. Also, there's a guide to each ending so you don't have to fumble through if you don't want to.
Another peeve is that some of the responses are timed, others aren't, there isn't really much warning when they start GETTING timed, and the countdown bar is almost completely transparent. I would prefer no timed sections (especially the ones where there are something like ten choices to read through and choose one of before the time runs out) but at least make your countdown bar visible. I whiffed the first choice in one conversation not realizing it was counting down until the choices disappeared and the conversation moved on; only then did I see the barely-visible countdown bar.
The voice acting wasn't bad but I feel like it took me out of the story or made me too self-conscious at points so I just turned it off. Like I said before, though, the bloopers are worth the listen.
Overall not as good as something like Magical Diary but for a freebie it has plenty of merit, give it a shot.

♥♥♥♥ this game.
This is a dating sim, right. A dating sim. The lowest chain in video gaming industry. It is not supposed to have such a good writing.
It's not perfect writing, mind you (except Matthew and Diana, their character writing is perfect, in the game's standards.) But it's much, much better than whatever you'd expect from this game when reading through the introduction.
And you can go lez, too (the review which mentioned it was the one that convinced me to download it).
Pros:
+ The protagonist is annoying, shy stereotype only if you want her to be. She is kind and all, but she sure as hell can fight and argue - if you choose to, of course. I really like her.
+ Two of the good endings are aromantic ones. In fact, one of these endings is my favorite in the game.
+ A different part of the story is revealed with each route. Story is that big.
+ Good character and backstory writing, and while some characters don't have much to provide, some of them are much more than you expect that you may end up screaming "this is a free dating sim game, who gave you the right to go THERE" to the screen. In my personal opinion, these "deeper than you would expect" characters are Matthew (my male favorite), Diana (my favorite demon), and Damien (though you'd expect that from him, given "silent type" cliche.) Andrew and Suzu (my favorite humans) are fun and almost realistic characters. Sam is not too bad either.
+ All characters have different sides, expect two - who are so unimportant they don't even help the plot despite having more screen time than your parents. Spoiler:
+ The only character who falls in love with you is whom you choose to get close with. Meaning, no unnecessary rivalry.
+ Brothers are brothers first and foremost, and they care about each other deeply. This is combined with the previous pro, because what I've said in the previous pro means that just because you've fallen in love with one of them, brothers for years won't start fighting for your affection. I really appreciate that this game has avoided that.
Cons:
- It's not really a con, since this is not a game from professional developers but a free dating sim, but choices often don't have an impact on dialouges or characters' perceptions on your personality, unless they are main choices (but like I said, this is no Life is Strange, so it's not really a con.)
- I did praise character writing for being much better than what you'd expect from such a game, but James and Erik really don't offer you anything you wouldn't expect from them at the first glance.
- You can't keep the incubi AND end up with Diana or one of the incubi.
-
- I have praised the "brotherhood" between the incubi, but you don't see them interacting much. You can only guess their dynamics.
- Suzu and Naomi don't even act like seperate characters if you choose a route with one of the demons, even though they have pretty much opposite personalities. They come and go as a set.
- The protagonist's strength is completely ignored if you end up with one of the incubi - she becomes no different than any protagonist of an ordinary dating sim.
- Incubi endings are way too cheesy (even Matthew's, my favorite male character's ending, felt way too cheesy for me.)
Verdict: It's free, and if you are bored like I was when I downloaded it, it's worth wasting some time. The more you have doubts it's better, because the lower your expectation is the better the game feels. It is simple, but a fun story to learn about. (You can go lez or aromantic, what else you want?)

Ever wanted the opportunity to go back to 1980 and create your own software development company? Probably not, but that doesn't mean that you shouldn't do that.
Software Inc. is a game in which you can start with next-to-no money and work your butt off to make the biggest and best pieces of software on the market - including Operating Systems, Game Engines, Games, and more. You start out with a solo developer (who you can customise and name, likely after yourself) and who's stats you can adjust to make them better at things like programming, design, art, marketing, etc...
Once you've built your first office using a system that's simultaneously more simple and more complex than building in The Sims, you're good to get working. Fast forward a few successful releases and you're likely going to be looking at hiring and managing different teams of staff, each of which you can have specialised in one aspect of software development. Personally, I enjoy splitting one team in to three teams, each part specialising in the three aspects of software production - Design, Programming, and Art.
As your bank balance grows, your company grows, the land you own grows, and your buildings will grow. You can start with a room, and eventually own and fill the space equivalent to several city blocks, all because of your successful software company - and this really is just scratching the surface of the game. You also manage company insurance, you can buy and sell stocks, you can sabotage other (computer controlled) companies, buy out companies, buy and sell intellectual property, and much more.
And this is all just in Alpha 7.

I have bought this game for the single player aspect only, because thats what I liked about CoH 1. So I am only basing this review on the single player aspect and therefor I will completely ignore all the negative reviews about the tons of DLC's for multi player here on Steam.
I have (am playing) played the main campaign and the Ardennes campaign.
What I among other things loved about CoH 1 was the (relative) freedom you had to complete the objectives. You were given a main objective and sometimes a secondary optional objective and then you could build a base and slowly build up defences and expand your territory on the map. There were multiple paths and directions you could take to take over territory.

In CoH 2 the gameplay is really restricted, even units like engineers can't use their capabilities until the pre-scripted story 'yada yada' unlocks their function in the battlefield. The game now constantly tells you what to do, how and where you should advance and what weapon you should use. You even get shiny hologram markers on the map that tells you exactly where the developers wants you to go.
I have broken the gameplay several times already by not doing what the developers expect me to do. On multiple occasions I have found spawn points of the enemy AI at sectors I could overtake, but apparently was not meant to overtake. I litterally saw the enemies spawn at a static location out of thin air every x amount of seconds. I builded static HMG nests around the spawn points and they kept dying the moment they spawned on the map lolz.

The campaigns are really designed for speed RTS, unlike CoH 1. Generally the developers expect from you that you advance on the map as fast (and dumb) as possible, while I like to take it more slow and strategic and fortify capture points before I advance further. Not playing the game by how the devs designed it leads to all sorts of gameplay issues. Biggest issues are the main oblectives that are timed and forces you to rush and play kamikaze mode instead of playing a 'strategic' game.

Some of the missions/objectives felt a bit like CoH 1 and I could play it the same way, but the majority of the time I felt hand cuffed, and rushed, and spammed by AI spawns during gameplay and on rails by a narrow developers mind that limits me to a certain gameplay approach.

The pathfinding of the AI also has not improved, or even may be worse now. Ordering AI to travel from A to B leads the AI directly through enemy fire. You really have to babysit the AI now and order them from corner to corner otherwise they will walk into an anemy tank or HMG fire.
A lot of the time there are also pre-scripted friendly AI infantry on the map, that keep advancing and dying. You see them walk right into HMG fire. They litterally were scripted with a static path to walk into enemy fire... you see a hundred dead NPC AI lying in a row on the ground. They behave like lemmings.
I also could go on about the UI and graphics etc (which are okay), but I will leave it at the gameplay aspect as that what matters the most to me.

CoH 1 is an 80/100 in my opinion so I think overall CoH 2 (single player) is a,

Company of Heroes 2, the sequel to the famous first COH is in my humble opinion a 'interesting' game but is it all that and a bag of chips?   Well whether or not a game is good is subjective to the individual and what exactly your looking to get out of a game.
The Good:
- Modding Support through the Steam-Workshop offers all manner of mods, unit skins, decals, Player made maps, and more all for free and easily aquired with the click of a button.
- Unit Diversity.  A counter for every move and with over 31+ Commanders to choose from per faction as opposed to the original COH with just 3 Doctrines to choose from per faction,  Each army has a distinct theme from focus ranging from Heavy Tanks, Specialized Infantry, Artillery, Aircraft and more!
- Enviroment Matters.   COH2 offers unit bonuses for taking cover behind pretty much anything,  Destructible enviroments mean that a wall or house can be blown away to create new avenues to flank your opponent!   Weather can freeze your troops to death in the cold blizzards or slow them down as easy targets when they get stuck in deep-mud.
The Bad:
- DLC,  Sega is rather heavy about DLC.  For example that fancy Skin you want for your tanks?  Or want a Tiger Tank but don't own the commander that offers one?   Gotta buy them.   DLC ranges from 3 to 5$ (prices vary on your region) but this can be mitigated both by the fact that COH2 is frequently on the Steam Sales where you can get the DLC for as cheap as 1$  or just download a Mod from the workshop that offers them.
- The Single Player Campaign.   I have mixed feelings about the campaign.   The Soviet Campaign (which is free) was dark (which is IMO good) but the characters were boring,  I felt no passion to empathize with characters and the mission objectives were generic and rather basic,  What you would expect from a RTS.....   SEGA fortunatly learns there lesson when they introduce the American Campaign "Ardennes Assault" Giving us more interesting characters and unique mechanics for a Story,  making the campaign into a RISK or Total War style where you only have limited resources to conduct the entire campaign.   Unfortunatly this absolutely amazing Ardennes Assault campaign is DLC:  10$ on its own,  5 or 3$ during a Steam Sale.
- Vanilla Gameplay is Boring,  Game ballance is about as fair as Starcraft,  but just like Starcraft that same  rock/paper/scissors can get boring.  IMO Get a realism mod from the Steam Workshop such as Spearhead or Wikinger just off the top of my head.   The All Units mod can also appeal if you don't want realism & don't want to buy the DLC.
- Axis vs Allies.    This should be a common theme,   however where  the Allies are diverse between the Soviets, Americans, and the British.... the Axis are just Germans with a east & west theme.  SEGA has rich options to choose from between nations like Vichy-France, Italy, or Japan and yet they have been reluctant to pool from it despite showing they can with units such as the Ostruppen pooled from the various nations that were absorbed into the German Army.   COH2 has great potential if only they would do more then just present Nazi-Germany as the only overarching villain.
In conclusion,  COH2 is not a game for everyone,  I'd reccomend it only to WW2 Enthusiasts who want a plethora of options to choose from, and I would highly reccomend players wait for the Steam Sales (COH2 g oes on sale extremly frequently),  The game's not worth full retail price.  Bu with that said I find boundless enjoyment out of this game and still play it even today as my fallback enjoyment.
love it

I don't quite know how they got there, but Relic & Sega managed to pull back CoH2 from the brink of a major RTS let-down - and get old CoH players (like me) - back inline.
The core issue I think was with the vanilla CoH2 release. It featured the well documented Eastern Front struggle between the Germans and the Russians in WW2. As savage and tragic as that campaign was (from both sides) - it didn't necessarily make for a good RTS game.
Frankly, the Russian side was boring. It used units that unless you had some specific interest in that arena of WW2, meant very little. Worse, the developers seemed to take the stance that there were endless streams of Russian infantry cannon fodder to take on the German might. While there may have been some historical truth to that - again, it didn't make for a good RTS game. Added to that was the awful, awful 'freeze-factor' where your troops had to maintain a proximity to a camp-fire, otherwise they would freeze to death. The final nail in the coffin were the system requirements. Despite having a PC that easily surpassed the recommended spec for the game, CoH2 ran very poorly indeed.
CoH2 was initially a MASSIVE disappointment for me. Having put in around 500 hours into the original game, including completing the excellent campaign modes several times over - CoH2 just left me cold. The base building that was such a central, yet small part to CoH had now simply been left in as a game function. It was a legacy addition - as your new units crept in from the side of the screen, with little bearing on the building that they 'should' have spawned from. The buildings also looked (and still do) - very weedy. Like ramshackle constructions rather than a dedicated factory for producing units and machines of war. Gone were the little turreted Germans atop of buildings from the Fortify Perimeter of the Axis Defensive Doctrine - ones that provided the ultimate last-ditch defence and reminded me in a fond way of the Sensible Software classic - Mega Lo Mania.
CoH2 was uninstalled - and for quite some time. I purchased the occasional DLC, retried it, but the old demons and natural anti-bias against the game that I had built up, quickly made me remove it from my hard drive, yet again.
More add-ons came over time. The Ardennes Offensive was added, as were the new units of the US Forces and the Oberkommando West. Still, the game didn't drag me back - even when strangely I decided to purchase the British Forces DLC (why buy expansions for a game that you don't play? :P). I gave in several weeks ago - CoH2 had been out for a considerable amount of time and Windows 10 was now installed on my PC. A recent update patch came on the update list, so I decided to give CoH2 one last try....
I chose the British Forces - as they were never a favourite of mine in the original game and I wasn't expecting much anyway. A quick-fire skirmish resulted in my win over an Easy German side. I retried it - this time alone against two AI and I won again. The familiar paper-scissor-rock mentality of using units started to come back. Not only that, but Relic had added some immensely useful shortcuts within the game and being on Steam, the Greenlight community was in full swing.
My all-time favourite map from CoH of Achelous River was faithfully recreated and freely available for download. Knowing that map intimately, allowed me to take time and try out different units and combinations in the new CoH2 front-end. More of the game made sense - and more importantly, it began to flow.
Since then, I've fired up the Ardennes campaign and I’m thoroughly enjoying it. It's different, subtly so against the benchmark set on the previous CoH campaigns (Opposing Forces itself is a example of RTS structure genius) - but it still ticks all the relevant boxes. The attack/defence balance is never too far away - stretching your probing units to dangerous limits, or conversely, setting up the perfect defensive kill-zone. Do you churn out units en masse, or reserve and protect small concentrations of highly skilled units?
It's taken a while, but CoH2 is certainly back on track with the Company of Heroes franchise. Currently, all RTS games have to acknowledge what CoH represents and has achieved. Even if you have no interest in the WW2 setting, from a game mechanic and progress position - give it a try.
All I will say to Relic or whoever may read this for CoH3 is......
- Where is the Pacific campaign of the US and Commonwealth forces against the Japanese?
- Please, no more Russian sides - UNLESS you bring CoH3 up to a fictional WW3 backdrop

Given all of the recent franchises and IPs that the Traveller's Tales series has acquired over the years. This is definitely the Lego game you should play out of any of them. The Lego games have become very repetitive, recycling through same game play mechanics continously through the series. While Lego Star Wars: The Force Awakens doesn't mix up the standard formula too much, there are some surprising new gameplay mechanics that make this game a lot more enjoyable by a long stretch, such as the shoot outs and spacrship battles. What's more, if your PC isn't all that powerful, this game looks incredible on low end hardware. While I was at first skeptical about this game, it has proved to be excellent value for money, I purchased it with the season pass for less than £7.
If you have played the original Lego Star Wars games or are just generally a big fan of Star Wars, I strongly recommend this title, the fan service is unparalleled.

There is something with Lego games that they just surprise you each year. The Force Awakens is yet another movie liscensed lego game, but it really did surpass my expectation, and surprised everyone who enjoyed it. Many people believe that improving the graphics and visuals of lego games are not possible, because they would still look the same in terms of their blocky visuals. TT Games and TT Fusion have once again surprised us all and have delivered a much needed update to their usual lego formula complete with brand new mechanics, gears of war-esque cover based shooting (in SOME sections of the campaign,) and absolutely gorgeous visuals, especially for a lego game. I will never grow tired of the unique style of which these games are created in by seamlesly mixing realistic textures and visuals with the blocky style of lego. Out of all the games I have played and that I own I can honestly say that the Lego genre is one of my absolute favorites. The music, the exploration, the comedy, the creativity, the easter eggs, the endless number of side-quests, both short, and long, easy, and somewhat challenging. In terms of all those traits, factors, and wanting to achieve full relaxation after a hard day at school, or work. The Lego games are the titles for players that search for that. I am a casual player that looks for great gameplay, great optimization, great soundtracks, and to become fully imerssed within the worlds, and universes of my favorite film franchises. Despite each of their titles having the name of one specific film, they always include levels, quests, and campaigns from each film in the respective franchise or saga. Even though it says "The Force Awakens" do not expect content from the clone wars, rebels, the freemaker adventures, and the ot to be left out. I always become fully involved in these worlds due to how lively they are and how extremely interactive everything is. With the combined visual styles of realistic textures, the great story telling, immense creativity, humor, easter eggs, iconic sounds, iconic images, beloved sountrack, massive amount of content, and the large amount of interactivity with the environments, and people alike I always become so imerssed that I forget I am playing a lego game. For any casual gamers, Star Wars fans, and people just looking for hours of fun, and relaxation this is a must buy, as well as the other titles if you love the other franchises as well. Lego Avengers can be left out, to be honest. Lego Tfa is my favorite lego game and my second favorite star wars game that I own, next to battlefront 2, and I very much hope that TT will continue to make these titles for each upcoming star wars, marvel, dc, and other franchise films in the future, especially rogue one, and the last jedi. Scarif would be incredible to explore as well as playing with Luke, and training as rey. This is a review for lego tfa and the lego genre in general. There are so many titles that I might as well just right an overall review on one page. :) The clone wars, rebels, freemaker adventures, and some ot content is available through the season pass, but you should not pass up the chance to purchase it when it goes on sale.

Being fairly new to the VN genre, I didn’t know what to expect when I started playing Seduce Me so I was pleasantly surprised by my experience.  The graphics are well done, the story is imaginative and full of fun surprises and the voice acting is spot-on perfect.  I had a lot of fun playing the various scenarios and even with the repetition multiple play-throughs still found enough new content to keep things fresh.
That said, the text could have used an editor’s once-over as there were several typos and errors.  Also, some of the recycled panels didn’t make a whole lot of sense in the different scenarios in which they were used.  The art was changed but in many cases the words were not, robbing several plot-lines of depth and some of believability.
All-in-all however I feel the pros outweighed the cons in the cute and entertaining entry into the VN genre.

This was a really fun game that I enjoyed a lot, but I thought the game was very short.  I was originally hesitant about reccomending this game due to the length of the game, but it seems like I completed this game with almost unnatural speed, so this game might be worth the price for other players (especially completionists).
I spent 2.50 on this game, and I usually think a game is worth the cost if I play at least an hour per dollar spent.  I am a compulsive buyer, so if a game bores me, I tend not to play it very long because at this point I've collected a lot of other games I could play instead.  That being said, if this game was not on the Summer sale, I do not think I would have been very happy paying the full price (currently $13) for this game.  Most people seem to spend about 5 hours on the game to complete the main story.  I'm not really sure how I completed it so fast, maybe my experience playing Just Cause 2 and helped.
Also, if you are worried about the play time, there are achievements you can try to get.  They seem to be pretty hard and I didn't achieve a single one while playing, so they would probably give a couple hours of gameplay.  I did not decide to attempt to get the achievements because I did not feel like replaying the game.  This is not to say that the game wouldn't be fun to replay, I just have a lot of new games from the Summer sale now, so I would rather play them.
The story was pretty good.  Some parts were kind of cliche, but I thought the very end was kind of sad.  I did not really like the narrators that much, but they weren't aweful.
All around the gameplay was amazing.  The super jumps were really cool.  The grappling hook was a lot of fun, but I did not like it as much as grappling hooks from other games, such as Just Cause 2.  There was something that left me a little unsastisfied when using it, but I can't exactly figure out why.  I think my problem was I would have liked the grappling hook to pull quicker.  This might be a little bit of a spoiler about the last item in the game, so if you don't want to see it skip to the next section.  The very last items you get are rocket boots. They are really cool, but I wish you could use them longer before the game ends.
I thought the people models weren't great, but other than that the graphics looked really nice.  When I showed my brother the game, he didn't think the game was an indie game due to how good the game looked.  I also think the level design really added to the visual aspect.
This game is really fun, and my only big issue with it is the price.  If you see this on a sale, you should definitely get it, but if it's not on sale I would wait until it gets put on sale, but I don't think it would be a bad idea to pay full price for the game, it really is enjoyable.

Metro 2033 Redux is a pretty solid fps.  It's story driven and in that regard has a feel that reminded me of The Chronicles of Riddick: Butcher Bay (which is high praise). In the "hub" areas people are just milling about, talking, adding an atmosphere of boredom and destitution.  The gameplay is mostly well done, the weapons all feel good and (booya!) you've got 4 shotguns to choose from.  Thankfully, the late game weapons all felt appropriately powerful.
While this is touted as a horror fps, unlike other horror games, you have strong capability in dealing with said horrors.  The guns are all pretty weighty and customizable, while looking the part of post-apoctalyptic doodads.  Your main enemies are mutant-type creatures or evil humans bent on dominating the remnants of mankind.  All deserving of shotgun spray.
My only real gripes are the level called "Defense" and the voice acting on children.  Defense is utterly unfun.  You have small, fast-moving enemies that crawl out of the walls and often attack you from behind (think headcrabs, but faster).  On top of that, the game nerfs a specific aspect of your control so that now you are fighting these cheap enemies at a further disadvantage from lack of complete control. On top of which (!), you are forced to listen to some atrocious voice-acting.  My advice is to just run through this area as fast as you can, without dallying.  And those children are obviously just voiced by some low-rent adult actors.
Another annoyance is the preponderance of ripping control away from the player, especially late-game "mind-altering" experiences (think Max Payne dream sequence).
Aside from those issues, this game was really enjoyable to me.  I'm a big fan of first-person games where your hands aren't only for implementing death, but also for opening doors and picking up objects, and just generally making me feel like I'm actually interacting with this world.

This is a fun little puzzle platformer with a good mechanic: You use different colored light for different effects. Green = making platforms appear (in pre-designated places only), blue = slow down time, orange = blow up walls, yellow = reverse gravity. You only have max 2 powers at a time so it's easy to keep track of them and switch between them, which at times you need to do with split-second precision.
The difficulty curve is very fair (until the boss level. More on that later). On earlier levels, the checkpoints are spaced very frequently so you don't have to repeat much until you're used to the mechanics. Later, they get further and further apart until you have to do three or four sequences of puzzles in a row without a checkpoint, which can lead to some frustration after you FINALLY beat a difficult section, only to be killed immediately afterwards because you didn't know what to expect. The boss level takes this idea to THE EXTREME. There are hardly any checkpoints in the final level, meaning you have to do LONG, complicated sections that take pinpoint precision, dying frequently, then when you finally get past that section, something new kills you. There's a counter at the end of levels that tells you how many times you died. I'm not an amamzing platformer, so I was averaging somewhere between 15-30 deaths on any given level. The boss level was in the hundreds. It's grueling, and I decided to look up a walkthrough to see what I was supposed to do in the end, which I hate doing.
I think the game has pretty good replayability, since there is the counter for your number of deaths, there's collectibles to get, and there's a "Best time" to beat.
The art is good; each level is a different background color, with the foreground being silhouetted like Limbo, making a really nice aesthetic. Music is atmospheric and pretty good, though I didn't notice it half the time with all the platforming distracting me.
All but boss level: 9/10.
Boss level: 1/10.
Overall: 8/10. Definitely worth it if you like puzzle platformers like Limbo.

Like many indie platformers,
is constructed around a gameplay gimmick. In this case, it's the ability to collect four gems that each grant your character a different power, such as the ability to walk on the ceiling, break through rock walls, etc. The catch is that you can only hold one gem in hand at a time, and the power it grants only lasts for a few seconds before it has to recharge. So you'll have to carefully time your use of each gem, and moves that require you to combine the powers of two different gems (like breaking a rock wall near the ceiling) will have you working that quick-swap button with precision. Meanwhile the terrain is sprinkled with spikes and lava pits because, well, platformer. There's also the occasional enemy to avoid, and your character has no way of attacking them; this is a jump-and-dodge game through-and-through.
The TL;DR on
is that it's not the most innovative game in the world... but it ain't half-bad, either. The visual design is striking (if derivative), the stages are well-constructed, and the difficulty level is pure Goldilocks: neither a cakewalk nor a ragequit-inducing,
style wall-puncher. The whole thing lasts about 5-6 hours, which is quite a reasonable length for a $7 game. Most importantly, it's consistently fun to play through. I don't recall ever switching it off in frustration, or leaving it aside for a week after growing bored with it. It's not an essential purchase by any means, but it makes a solid entry into any platforming fan's collection.

You Have to Win this Game is a quality 2D platformer at an unbeatable price. Free.
Here's a Quick Look video I did of the game after “winning” it. Have a look if you want to see the game in action, or just read the in-depth review below for something more concise. (Please note I did this video before it was released on Steam, which simply means it only shows the original game and not the much-harder, remixed version you can select at the beginning)
To begin, I'll say this game is a classic platformer in every sense. You jump from platform to platform all the while dodging spikes, energy balls, angry crabs, and anything else the game throws at you. Yet while you may not be able to kill anything, you are able to acquire power-ups like activating ghost blocks, double jumping, and jumping off walls to navigate the map easier. There are even checkpoints littered everywhere so when you do die, you can instantly respawn and try again as many times as you wish.
But don't be fooled. Although you may not have any lives (except if you're doing YOLO or the cat, you crazy person), the game is challenging, especially when you're gunning for optional moneybags to collect. You'll probably die multiple times before nailing the pattern down to pass to the next screen. But thankfully it never feels frustrating due to the instant respawn that's always nearby. It's the game's forgiving nature that allows you to constantly want to beat what's stopping you. And I can safely say that every time I did fail, I just dismissed it as my own fault and kept at it until I beat the obstacle. Which is truly the mark of a good platformer.
The game also has a nice, retro visual style. I enjoy how the game acts as if you're playing a classic game on an old TV. It really put me back in the mood when I was just a kid playing my NES. Now while I realize that some people may not have experienced or liked something like this, I really do think it adds to the game because it successfully mimics the era where games used to be like this. It simply gave me nostalgia all over. But hey, for those that don't want it, you can easily turn it off in the options menu.
Now let's talk about a few of the game's flaws:
*There's no music. Some awesome chiptunes really would've made this game shine. Instead all you get is silence
*It's really short. It'll only take about an hour to “beat,” more if you collect everything and explore
*No story. You just thrown into it not knowing what the heck you are or what you're doing. Personally, I don't really mind it not having one since games like Mario never really had much of story either, but some people like to have some purpose other than beating the game. And no, the clever title doesn't count as a reason =p
That's really all of the negatives I could think of. The game simply does its job well, especially so because of how it leads you where you need to be without holding your hand. There's no maps, quest markers, or waypoints telling you where to go, just like most classic games. But somehow I always wound up where I needed to be even when exploring just for the fun of it. Sure, the game liked leading you to places you couldn't do anything in until you got a power-up, or even trolling you by making you do platforming again for trying to take an easy route, but I always regarded it as a discovery that brought me one step closer to the end.
So to sum this game up, it's simply a joy to play. You don't get many free games as good as this one. So if you have some time to burn or are bored, pick this up and have a blast. There's even a NG+ for those like me who missed stuff on their first playthrough.

Saints Row IV is fun. Lots and lots of fun. Developed by Volition and published by Deep Silver in 2013, this mindless action-adventure third-person video game focuses on crazy open world craziness. Taking Saints Row: The Third and adding super powers and an alien invasion is as cliché as it is fun, mainly because the game never takes itself seriously, and I guess that’s the charm of it. It knows it's completely bat♥♥♥♥♥♥crazy and over the top, but that doesn't stop it from enjoying itself.
The game starts with a quick prologue set right after the events of Saints Row: The Third, where The Boss, Shaundi and Pierce are assigned to take out Cyrus and prevent a nuclear missile from hitting Washington, D.C. After killing Cyrus, but letting the missile go off, The Boss has to reach the missile and disarm it. Four or five years later, The Boss gets elected President of the United States of America. But it isn’t long until an alien race invades Earth, and kidnaps The Boss and the rest of the crew...
The gameplay is exactly what you would expect from a good sequel. Saints Row IV improves pretty much every aspect of the past games in the series.
The weapons are a big part of Saints Row, especially guns. Saints Row IV took the already existing weapons and upgrades, and added to it, bringing new weapons of mass destruction, awesome new skins, and new craaaaaazy upgrades. There are tons of new guns that are super fun to use, like the dubstep gun, that shoots explosive wub wubs, or the abduction gun, that lifts people into the sky, and makes them disappear, but by far, my favorite gun to use is the 'Merica.
The 'Merica weapon is a combination of 1 LMG, 1 SMG, 1 Auto Shotgun, 1 Heavy Pistol, 1 Minigun, 1 Rocket Launcher, 1 Flamethrower and 1 GIGANTIC Combat Knife. All of that, in one badass weapon.
The superpowers were actually first introduced in a mission in Saints Row: The Third, and that was easily the best mission of the game. So, with that in mind, Volition decided to make a sequel with a big focus on superpowers.
There are 8 powers in total, 4 active and 4 passive, each with their own upgrades.
The best power and upgrade is the DFA nuke upgrade, which can devastate entire areas with the blast. Wall climbing a skyscraper, to then drop and fist the ground so hard causing the nuke effect to go off, killing everything around, while leaving only ash floating in the air, never gets old.
Customization is a big part of the Saints Row series, but Saints Row IV didn’t add much to the already existing customization of SR: TT. The car upgrades and customization are the same. The character features and customization are all the same, apart from a couple new hairstyles. The tattoos I’m pretty sure are all the same too, and they all suck. The only real differences are the clothing stores, and even those appear to be very close to what they offered in SR: TT.
How is Saints Row as an open world game? Well, just like the previous Saints Row, there are TONS of challenges and activities to complete, but this time they are actually FUN. There are also a lot of places to explore, and with the addition of the super jump and the wall running, exploring was never this easy or this fun. City takeover is still present here, but this time instead of taking down gangs, you’re against badass aliens.
If you ever played Saints Row: The Third and wanted more, than this game can overfill that space. If you never played SR: TT, but played any GTA and wanted it to act more childish, then this game can be for you. If you never played any of those or similar games, all I can tell you is that Saints Row IV is a damn great game. Extremely fun gameplay and plot, and an amazing time waster. Get it on sale, or in the Saints Row bundle!

This game had an enormous amount of potential. The basic grappling and movement mechanics are amazing, but the game feels severely rushed and cut short. The early stages have excellent pacing and aesthetics with clever variations on using the grappling and movement mechanics. There is even a fun "boss fight" near the beginning that requires timing your movement so you aren't seen by the boss. But inexplicably (other than the game being rushed), there are no other boss fights in the game. There is a fun endlessly-falling-platforms section, but I don't consider that a "boss fight" since there really should have been other sections like it with some variation.
The rushing becomes increasingly apparent as the game wears on because you mostly end up either repeating more of the same tricks or doing the same thing but with more difficulty. Requiring the same tricks with increasing difficulty is not necessarily bad but it should be interspersed with new ideas and other content. The end game just becomes a grind of doing tricks without much exploration beyond finding the necessary surfaces.
The end game also suffers from what appears to be a lack of design and testing. Sometimes you can easily and obviously skip things that would otherwise be difficult. Yet other times you have to go through a rapid and convoluted series of precise actions to just barely reach the target.
The game is also very short. I wasn't in a particular hurry, yet I beat the game in 2.7 hours. If the game were longer, and the quality from the early game carried over to the end game, I would recommend the game. However, I can't recommend the game as it is.
It's a nice game, but extremely brief. Might be worth it if it's on sale for $2-$3, but wouldn't recommend getting it at MSRP.
