Please take any criticsm I have with these caveats.
The initial impressions of this game had me interested to get this game on a sale based on its short length. The mechanics looked fun and unique, and the story seemed full of wonderment.
Sometimes I really do like the narrative-focused games that run around 2 to 3 hours. More polished storytelling and gameplay segments for a reasonable price is what I look for in these kind of games (Portal 1 and 2, Thomas Was Alone and TRI: Of Friendship & Madness).
And within the first thirty minutes, I was enjoying myself. Then after stopping after shortly an hour and a half to see how much of the game I had completed, I asked myself just what was I really getting out of this game.
Once you get the intial set-up and the gist of the gameplay mechanics (grappelling and power-jumping), the game doesn't seem to progress to anything more challenging or does anything different to offer variety with the mechanics.
Although there are sometimes small deviations in the paths you choose, you still feel like the gameplay has only one solution and you are trapped within a corridor.
A similar problem I have had with games like Magnrunner Pulse and QUBE is that the puzzles are scripted with only one solution. It's not a matter of using your powers to solve a room; the puzzle is doing everything in the correct order to reach the end.
Besides the story-bits, the optional seismographs are lackluster; they're not elaboratively hidden in the levels, and they don't provide much to you other than a few unlockables fpr achievements.
Even though the environments make you feel like there's a whole world to explore and absolute freedom at your disposal, there was nothing to set me off-course or extra challenges for choosing to go one route over the other. A corridor with a skybox canvas in disguise.
Much like the environments, the story also feels like something made much bigger than it actually is.
Your Uncle Fred went missing months ago, now you wander in this dimension with some small clues about where Fred went. He was some entrapenour scientist/inventor who became obssessed with his creations and they took him to another, magical world he inadverently created.
Good idea for a story, but not enough for this game. And there's not enough of motivation for the player to care.
There are some optional story-bits that flesh out characters like Mad Maddie and her relationship to Fred or of the protagonist and his attachment to his uncle from one of many adventures. Moments like these are so few and far between the experience, and some of which are hidden as details on the walls as notes, that you might overlook them entirely.
But other than these small glimpses of a narrative, I didn't feel any attachment to the protagonist. That's the failure of the narrative being given towards the player; the question I kept asking, "Why should I care about this uncle of yours? He sounds like a farce."
Here you have the narrator saying how awesome his uncle is and recalling some part of the in-game story in past-tense (so he obviously comes back home). I couldn't really get too attached to someone who keeps telling me how awesome his uncle is.
I'm more interested in my invovlement: What am I, the player, doing? Why should I care? What makes me invovled in the plot when it's been done already?
Perhaps it wasn't the story itself but the delivery of the narrator that drew me away. He is far too monotone without any reason to be--the guy has an uncle who creates jetpacks and alternative dimensions!
Maybe the narrator is supposed to be a blank-character that makes you want an uncle like Uncle Fred. Or perhaps you are the son/daugher of the narrator dreaming up the story about this uncle. (I'd believe that interpretation).
But it's not just a lackluster character that ruins the story. The world itself raised more questions that were never answered. Why is everyting in this world floating islands? Why did Salamanders evolve into people (yes, I know they were transported here in a hidden story-bit by Uncle Fred when he took in those eggs) but what led to their cognitive evolution?
Maybe I am not supposed to ask these questions. Or maybe I'm left to imagine the answers. The problem is nothing from the characters or the world made me grow any attachements. Only in the visual presentation.
For example, you stop by the Salamander village for the first sign of Fred. You don't really talk to anyone other than Mad Maddie, and then you  get their crystal from the elder. Off you go again to find Fred . There's simply not enough time to spend there to grow attachments to any character or place in a game where that should be the focus of its time.
Lackluster despite all the care put into the game.
If this game was a proof of concept to flesh out a future game, I would be happy because there is the potential for something amazing in its mechanics and for the game to bring out a charming narrative.
The game, if it ever gets a sequel, needs to remember the golden rule for stories, "Show, Don't Tell", because then we might be able to immerse ourselves in wanting to find our uncle in a strange world rather being told to find him. (Maybe some harder obstacles/challenges too.)
But above all for any narrative-focused titles in the future, the game doesn't need padding for the sake of artifical length; let us immerse ourselves in the world you create at our discretion as the player. Let us discover these worlds; let us discover these bonds we create; let us learn through our involvement why we care for something.

Oscura, the apprentice lighthouse keeper, has accidentally destroyed the Aurora Stone, sending shards across the Driftlands and plunging them into darkness and danger. It’s now up to Oscura to find the shards of the stone and restore light to the Driftlands before the creatures of the dark can destroy it. Fortunately, the accident has fused Oscura’s hand with glowing fire, enabling him to wield powers altering anything the light touches. Each level challenges your puzzle-solving skills and reactions in this modern adventure built upon the time-honoured mechanics of classic platformers.
Features
Master the Light: Along your dark journey you’ll find four different powers, each designed to help you through the Driftlands. Destruction, Construction, Gravity and Time are yours to command. Master each unique light power in your dark journey through the Driftlands.
Discover the origin of our accidental hero: Oscura wasn’t always the Driftland’s trusty lighthouse keeper. And he didn’t always have his flaming hand. Taking place before the previous Oscura games, Lost Light reveals where our hero’s journey began and the fate of the original light house keeper.
Old school platformer meets new school design: Taking inspiration from classic platformers such as Super Mario Bros, Oscura Lost Light combines these elements with a modern design aesthetic.
Use your wits: The Driftlands aren’t for the feint hearted and Oscura’s not a fighter. You’ll need to out-think and outwit creatures such as the Lost Ones, Shagrims, Bewinged, Grymfus, Cursed Skulls and more. Just as challenging are the puzzles you must solve if you wish to survive.
Confront Evil: Just when you think you’ve succeeded by collecting the shards of the Aurora Stone, you’ll need to face the ultimate challenge and restore the Lost Light … but beware … Mavro the Lord of Shadows awaits. Only by defeating Mavro can you save the Driftlands.

When it comes to platformers the movement mechanics need to be good, this game delivers well enough.
That doesn’t mean you won’t die… a lot, but the checkpoints are usually not that far apart so you will not be stuck at a particular point for too long.
That all changes when you reach level 20 or so (out of 22 I think), that’s when the fun stops and frustration takes over. At that point it seems more about luck than skill and I was just hoping that I would make it to the next checkpoint before some  moving circular saw chopped my head off, again. You also die as soon as your character touches some water.
and you’re dead.
I really like the look of
, there is plenty of animated eye-candy to look at while you are dying. The music and sound effects were also fitting, and the game moves along at a nice pace.
It’s a shame about the last couple of levels, I really enjoyed the game up to +- level 20. I would call
up to that point a good solid platformer.
Run around, jump (and double jump), reverse gravity, slow down time, and dodge a hell-of-a-lot of lasers, boulders, gears, and other way too sharp objects.
It’s not an original game and it doesn’t have to be, just enjoy it for a couple of hours and move on to the next game.

tl;dr: recommended when on sale.
Pros:
* Puzzle platformer with some interesting mechanics and generally well-designed levels
* Nice shadowy aesthetic (I'm biased here)
Pro/Con:
* Short: took me only about 5 hours to complete (disregard hour record, I was offline), and I'm not a particularly fast gamer.
Cons:
* Has a very annoying edge case bug - it is possible to get stuck inside / on the edge of certain configurations of platforms, and because there is no option to go back to the last checkpoint, the only resort is to replay the whole level.
* May be very frustrating: Most of the gameplay parts that frustrated me had to do with low skill at precision platforming. However, in several places I've had to replay the same checkpoint dozens of times purely because of bad luck, which is worse. Also, one of these involved dodging something with absolutely no warning right before a checkpoint, effectively doubling the amount of tries it took to get through the area.

I had never written any gaming reviews before but this had to be done.
Firstly I'm not a serious gamer and pretty average in English but I'm writing this down for my own satisfaction.
So this is my experience of Metro 2033 and Metro Last Light Redux:
Well, as I said I'm not a serious gamer and never played any game for eight hours straight. Until today.
When you find yourself glued to a game for eight hours you know you're experiencing something amazing and surreal (The only breaks I took when I felt the need to relax myself from the emotional roller coaster that the games were putting me through). Firstly this is not a fancy game. You won't be able to jump rooftops, ride horses or grapple and beat the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of your enemies with swords and fancy Laser guns. The games provide you with a real humanly experience in an unearthly and mysterious environment. The games are about survival. Its about what you will do if you are put into such an environment and trust me you would have done the exact same things which Artyom (the protagonist) did throughout his journey. The games will put you through the exact same emotional trauma which Artyom experienced. You'll be so engrossed while playing that you'll feel the 'need' for survival yourself. I often found myself gaping in awe or cheering in joy literally ninety percent of the time. That's the level of engagement you'll feel while playing Metro and that's where lies the success of the games. Metro will suck you inside. You'll forget everything and keep playing, you'll keep try to find out what happens next.
Putting you in an imaginary world full of deadly monsters (and The Dark One) and engaging each and every nerve and the emotional epicenters of a gamer into it throughout the journey? Not so easy. But Metro has achieved that flawlessly. There was not a single moment in the game where I felt bored or felt the things happening in the game are part of some fantasy novel written by Dmitry Glukhovsky. This felt so REAL

Based on a Russian novel by Dmitry Glukhovsky, Metro 2033 is set in post-apocalyptic Moscow. After nuclear devastation ravaged the earth and skies, the people of Moscow retreated into the sprawling underground Metro system in order to survive, building tattered towns at various stations throughout. The world is populated by mutants, dangerous anomalies and a number of supernatural occurrences. In the midst of this strange setting, players take control of the young Artyom and guide him on his quest to deliver an important message to a neighboring station. He'll fight a ton of generic enemies in order to get there, with a few surprises along the way.
The atmosphere is the most enjoyable aspect of this title. The gameplay, unfortunately, is the area where Metro 2033 suffers the most. When the game works, it works nicely, but that's not always the case. The stealth sections, for example, are incredibly frustrating, as the enemies don't always follow consistent rules. If you miss a passing guard with a silent throwing knife (or perhaps wound them without killing them), every guard in the area is not only immediately alerted, but they also know your exact location. The "gray area," where the guards are looking for you, doesn't really exist in this game.
These stealth sections almost ruined Metro 2033 for me, but luckily there are only a few notable ones that need to be overcome. If you can get past these obstacles, the rest of the game will be less frustrating.
Metro 2033 is also a fairly glitchy game, as I found myself getting stuck on fences and walls, as well as fighting an unintentionally invincible enemy that couldn't be killed. Another unusual glitch is when you try and replace the filter in your gas mask. The animation of swapping filters will play, but the filter is not actually changed.
Other players might be more frustrated with how unfriendly Metro 2033 is for beginners. Although there are plenty of basic gameplay tutorials, there are a number of systems that aren't explained well. The first time I set foot in a station market and attempted to trade currency, I was totally lost. The developers just don't give players enough context (whether intentionally or not) and that can be a bother for newcomers.
Metro 2033's greatest strength, on the other hand, is in its atmosphere and setting. Developer 4A Games has done a fine job creating the world and populating it with interesting sights and sounds. Crawling through dilapidated sewer pipes, riding down eerie train tracks and trudging through the cold wastelands of the surface are all examples of what this game does right. Although the overall atmosphere of Artyom's journey through the Metro encouraged me to keep playing, the story itself is occasionally clumsy. This is mainly due to the characters, who don't have particularly strong personalities (besides Bourbon).
At its heart, Metro 2033 is a standard FPS with a few interesting ideas built around it. The gunplay you'll find in the game is typical fare, as you constantly run and gun, with a few sidesteps in between. Artyom can only carry one gun from each class of firearms (pistol, automatic and heavy), though he can also carry a small assortment of throwing knives and explosives. The unique elements come into play when you examine the gadgets and gizmos outside of Artyom's basic arsenal. One of his most essential tools is his gas mask, which must be worn on the surface due to the poisonous air. Players must be careful, however, as the gas mask's filter must be swapped out constantly to keep Artyom's air pure. And if you make the mistake of wearing the gas mask into battle, there's a chance it could be damaged and will need replacing.
You're running out of time.
There are other great touches to the otherwise normal running and gunning, like the universal charger which must be cranked to power Artyom's headlamp and night vision goggles. Players can also bring up Artyom's journal mid-exploration, which lists current objectives and also has a built-in compass which points in the direction they need to go. Also charming are the game's pneumatic weapons, which must be pumped in order to be fired.
All these gameplay mechanics, along with the Russian setting, serve to make Metro 2033's atmosphere enjoyable. The survival horror elements also work well, forcing players to conserve ammunition and move carefully, building tension while sneaking through environments. But these positives are seriously hampered by the stealth gameplay and technical problems.
The Verdict
The game's atmosphere and unique design choices will make it a worthwhile experience for some, but Metro 2033 suffers from a number of issues (poor implementation of stealth, recurring glitches, etc.). Fans of post-apocalyptic stories should consider giving this a shot, if they can tolerate the aforementioned setbacks.

For the most part I really enjoyed this. The level design is a real return to form for Traveller's Tales after a few missteps (The Hobbit), and the retelling of The Force Awakens has the classic humour we have come to expect from the LEGO games.
However, one issue that has long dogged this developer remains front and centre in this title: unbelievably frustrating bugs. To be clear, I'm not talking about inane mishaps such as clipping and such. This is key points in missions - the ones you need to progress - not triggering. Playing through multiple levels in the game, both story and free-play, I had to quit/restart, losing the past half-hour or so's progress, all because a door wouldn't open / a build wouldn't appear, etc. This got to the point for me where it simply wasn't worth wasting my time trying to find all the collectibles, or replay story missions, when there was the chance my level progress would be wiped thanks to the broken game. Traveller's Tales have never been known for stellar PC ports, and the song remains the same here. I had real trouble getting the game to recognise my Steam controller. Restarting multiple times until the game recognised the input grew tiring, especially when you consider the time length of the games' opening splash-screens.
I limped through to seeing the credits roll, but this will be one of the first LEGO games I don't go back through and 100%. The bugs are simply not worth it. If you're looking for a good LEGO game, check out Lord of the Rings, or Marvel Superheroes. If you really need the LEGO and Star Wars combo, the fantastic Complete Saga and Clone Wars are on Steam too. The Force Awakens is a really solid entry, but if you find re-doing chunks of missions over and over in the hope the game doesn't bug out on you as tedious as I do, it is probably not worth your time.

True, it is and was buggy as hell. True, the graphics are antiquated. True, the combat system is lacking. But then again, few other games offer this kind of flair, something between noir and pulp fiction. It feels like the 90's - in a damn good way.
And then, there's the main storyline. Starting in the run-down Santa Monica, you get through LA's downtown, the legendary Hollywood and Chinatown in pursuit of a mysterious Sarcophagus. While this "ancient evil" thing may sound bland, it becomes quite the opposite, as surpringly many people are interested in it.
VtM:Bloodlines is a RPG classic and despite of its numerous flaws, deserved its place on the Walk of fame.

There's one follower who rides on your back, a frog girl named Maddie who is the stereotypical tomboy who gets sent home by the stereotypical village elder and (surprise surprise) sneaks out to help you on your quest.

75% off -> less than 2€, okay Steam, you got me !
I - DO - NOT - REGRET - ANYTHING (Don't get me wrong, I regret things, so many things. Like "no need to heal, let's just hit that f*cking bird with a... Am I.. DEAD ?! A bird freaking two shots me ?!". Those bad decisions I regret, but from them I've learnt how to survive)
You don't have proper towns to visit, proper NPCs to interact with, but the game doesn't really need it.. it's a fighting simulation, the menu let you go across shops anytime you want/need between fights, you can talk with NPC but no major things are at stake, the humour whatsoever is really much appreciated in my opinion.
My advice : buy the game, get comfortably numb and BE PATIENT.. The learning scheme is kinda like that : Play -> Die + learn -> Play again -> learn -> Die anyway -> Ragequit -> Play with more knowledge and more determination (like, 1h later, I'm not that much of a tryhard-guy though and I played it again and again, because that game wants to be appreciated, it has so many things you'd love..)
Be patient, that's how I made it though.. don't try anything in a zone you're not 10+ levels above the highest recommended level.. and don't try to fight bosses, you'll have your fair share of stressful bosses by following the storyline only, and I came to the conclusion that those bosses you encounter are a real pain in the neck..

This is my first game review on steam, mostly because even though I use reviews in my own decision making process when it comes to buying a game I'm rarely left with the urge to try and persuade or deter anyone from taking a chance on the game themselves. Software Inc is like many other early release games in the sense that it's not a finished product, but in my 30+ hours played so far I have yet to encounter any bugs that makes this game unplayable. What makes this game so much different than other early release games is that the developer is still constantly working on it and is providing updates almost every week. I remember struggling pretty hard to get started, but once you get the hang of how the game works its very manageable and fun, and as someone who has played other games of this genre I think Software Inc holds its own.
The reason I think that people should try this game, and why I decided to write this review is because of the developer's commitment to this game. This is a game that is constantly being tweaked and changed for the better, the developer is entirely transparent about those changes and welcomes the community feedback about what could make the game better. This is a chance for players to watch a game actually grow and evolve, as well as a chance to support a small developer whose actions have very clearly shown that they take pride in their work and have made a commitment to this game and its players. If you enjoy games of the business management / tycoon genre I would strongly recommend it.

Cons:

2) Too linear - you can kind of do things out of order, but nowhere near as "open" as advertised
3) If you're going to copy story tropes, copy good ones - uses a couple of *really* cliched plot devices
4) Too much traveling for such a short game

I said the discovery mechanic was creative, and it is, but it's still too close to the "hidden object" mechanic that has washed over the adventure genre and turned it into a puzzle genre.
I don't think it actually has any replay value. Look for it at $5 or so. The graphics and music are *really* beautiful.

A pretty decent platformer. It has elements of Glare, Giana Sisters, Teslagrad and Limbo in it and it is especially satisfying when you manage to pull off a good double power combination. The powers are responsive and can be used interchangeably even when mid air. The only flaw of the game is the jump mechanic which is not nearly as responsive as it should be. Nevertheless, this tame has a great aesthetic and overall good mechanics. The game is relatively short - it took me 2 hours to beat, but the experience feels complete and unrushed. On balance, I would say that Oscura is a relatively easy platformer, for those used to games such as blood of the werewolf, super meat boy or giana sisters, but it is a fun experience and as such i would definitely recommend.

Oscura seems like an interesting approach to platform games, the first few levels are enjoyable and you can test the concepts introduced in each level like slowing down time, reversing gravity and so on. Problems begin to arise once that sensation fades away, every level is very similar and the routines are repetitive. The same can be said about level design, it's dull and uninspired, changing the colour of the background every five levels does not make it feel like a whole new experience. Besides, the studio behind the game tries to imitate concepts seen in games like Limbo, Super Meat Boy and other platforming classics. The ending result? Not good.
In addition, the character design is also very poor. Oscura as a character has no soul, we see him die multiple times and I can assure you that you will not feel any empathy towards him. The supposed "story" behind the game is abysmal so if you have read that this game has an interesting story, I am sorry but they are trying to fool you, believe me.

Metro redux is a phenomenal game. The game is built around the metro books, so there is a rich vain to tap as far as story. The world and atmosphere is very engaging, and really does a lot to put you into the main characters. The english voice acting does, at times, leave something to be desired. Overall, it isn't by any means bad. Visually, even by todays standards, the game is absolutely gorgeous. The sound design is really well done, from the guns to the ambient noises heard through the dark tunnels, to the bustling of folks at each station, the sound really immerses you into the world. Gameplay is great as well. Honestly playing this silent protagonist, it felt very similar to playing the original half-life. And what I mean by that is the game design and the world around you is what drives the plot forward. It's through good game design and a well developed environment that you learn about the world and how to interact with it. It's really well done.
This may not be for everyone, but I played on the hardest difficulty. I did this because I was recommended to do so. The game doesn't become unmanageably difficult, as most games would be on this level. Instead, it felt like I played the game exactly how it was meant to be experienced. I really felt like I was trying to SURVIVE in this world. Drove home the narrative for me. Speaking of immersion, playing on this difficulty also completely removes the HUD, so you really feel it. Some actions aren't very obvious so checking out this tip guide for some actions would be useful, as tips are removed from the hardest difficulty since there is no HUD.
All in all the game is absolutely fantastic, and I would definitely recommend it.

There are few games that feature a grappling hook mechanic, fewer still are ones that are in first person and 3D, allowing you to feel the rush of chaining together multiple grapples together freely. A Story About my Uncle is a short, whimsical traipse through a well realized world that features a grappling hook and 3D platforming. There were a few moments that I truly felt I was fully in control of my actions as I used the multiple movement mechanics to blast through the world around me.
There are some pitfalls however, as there are images on the rocks that you can grapple to and while they aren't necessarily 'lock-on' mechanics like for example in the newest Devil May Cry, it still feels unnecessary as you are still allowed to freeform grapple around the world for most of the game. The ending also felt stilted as it features a lengthy 3D platforming area where you are simply running around and combined with the icy environment it takes place it, the game prevents you from grappling to most of the world. This felt like the antithesis to what the game was conceived to be, and my deaths here felt unfair and undeserved as the floaty movement that helped push the early parts of the game forward were now throwing me over a platform and plummeting to my death.
Overall though, the story and core mechanics of the game are enough to recommend this quaint indie title, especially at the current offer (£1.99).

A really well done game but can be a little annoying to get into considering the odd formatting and texty nature of the tutorials. After that the game is more expansive and an improvement upon Game Dev Tycoon (may not be the best reference point but that's what I'm going with). The game offers a nice progression system in terms of the time and the advancement of technology and the range of products that you can develop. Moreover, there is an understated stock system that lets you interact with other companies. Once you really get going, the stock system becomes a joke as you can buy out other companies without any effort. There are contracts to be had with other companies, but they aren't really worth it. The expansion of your company can go almost as long as you would like unless you play in the city. SanctuaryRPG is a rogue-like adventure with an emphasis on charmingly goofy writing and a surprisingly detailed combat system hidden beneath a primitive-looking interface. It also has a catchy and enjoyable soundtrack.
The central gameplay loop
seem monotonous, albeit instantly familiar:
1. Kill things.
2. Level up; find randomised loot.
3. Repeat, watching your numbers increase, until you can take on the boss of the current Act.
4. Kill the boss.
5. Proceed to the next Act and repeat.
(This is occasionally interrupted by inconveniently dying, cursing at the screen, and rolling a new character—or, on Softcore difficulty, respawning with 0 gold and 0 EXP. Also, there are a few side activities that produce EXP and loot with varying amounts of player effort, but they are of course only temporary distractions from the main loop.)
But hey, if the game were only as boring as I just made it sound, I wouldn't be recommending it. So, here's why I'm addicted to this silly and engrossing game:
1. The combat system instantly grabbed me. Chaining attacks creates combos, which raise the multiplier for your ult. You can (and should) reposition yourself to put distance between you and the enemy, to break their guard, to dodge an attack with a lead-up, or to thwart their missile lock-on. Oh, wait—they ensnared you? Cut yourself free. They wounded you? You'll have to heal or you won't be able to reposition as effectively. They poisoned you? Too many poison stacks and you'll go blind. And there's so much more to it than I can describe here. It's thrilling; looking at the combat screen and entering commands, I can't help but feel like a wizard.
2. The music is surprisingly good and goes beyond what one would expect from a game with these visuals. The battle themes in particular are stuck in my head.
3. The writing and enemy design ranges from silly meta humour to lightly engaging adventure-drama. I want to see what stupid random event will pop up, just as much as I want to see what happens next in the (semi-)serious story.
To give a more personal testimonial: I got someone hooked on this game, despite his dislike for typing and reading walls of text. The combat gameplay and the music won him over. That's a real triumph in my book.
Go ahead and give the demo a whirl!

There's an insatiable drive to tell stories in The Vanishing of Ethan Carter and the stories told therein are of intrigue and surrealism. With the likes of H.P Lovecraft, Edgar Allen Poe, and Stephen King (just a few that come to mind) influencing this supernatural story of a young boy's wild imagination taking the player along a captivating journey to uncover an unanticipated truth shrouded in darkness and mystery. Young children always seem to find themselves the epicenter of the most bizarre and surreal stories and Ethan Carter is no exception. The game places the player in a world that isn't as poignant and serene as it appears. Ethan's vivid imagination leads him down a dangerous slope strewn with mystery, cultist fanatics, strange characters and an insightful P.I (Paul Prospero) trying to make sense of this most unusual job he's taken on to find the missing boy- presumably his last case.
A title that will be a real treat for those who are fans of engrossing and methodically driven stories in games. Contained within the story is a great deal of atmosphere building between game-play sections so expect to spend a sizable chunk of the game walking through a stunning, idyllic countryside whose rustic atmosphere oozes with an impending sense of dread that looms over the bright, orange hue of the game's horizon. The Vanishing of Ethan Carter's narrative and design is beautifully enigmatic in a way most games usually don't set out to be in the modern gaming market- at least in the AAA sector anyway. It's a captivating game with just enough strangeness contained within the narrative to elevate it above an otherwise dull experience that may not be for most, but will definitely satisfy some in a unique way. Will you discover the chilling secret behind The Vanishing of Ethan Carter?

I'd like to share with you a short mission log. My, first mission to be exact. *shudders*
Mission log 01: Bug territory.
So I had decided that when purchasing the game that i'd convince my friend to buy and play the game with me.
Regrettably, I was successful..
We began by making comments to eachother about how cool the mission select interface was because you were actually inside of your ship in real-time selecting a mission to run on the galaxy map and then dropping into the thick of it! cool huh?
Well, that's what we thought.. we were so, so wrong. *shudders*
We began with a distress call from one of the "Bug" planets which had become in danger.
We orbited the planet, climbed into our drop pods and we were on our way to the bug hunt!
After landing on the planet's surface we had no need to aquaint ourselves with the controls as the game had already given us this pretty cool boot-camp esque experience as a tutorial upon logging in, and so we set off to the nearby "SAM Site".
Upon reaching the "SAM Site" we began reactivating the consoles and that's when we noticed the "Bugs"..
They were small, crab-like drones if you will.
We gunned them down with no hesitation and that was it.. We finished reactivating the consoles and had no trouble from any other bugs, which seemed odd.
And so we proceeded to the next objective which was the retrieval of a "Black box" which must then be delivered to and outpost.
Easy enough huh? well.. I found what was left of the previous carrier and proceeded to take the "black box" and began walking toward the outpost, with my friend in front to defend me from those pesky crabs.
The planet's surface was volcanic and had many treacherous drops into lava and so he had to tread lightly upon the ash-strewn surface.
We were almost at the outpost when something happened.. something that changed me forever.
We proceeded onward with my friend infront of me, my friend had been playing around with the dive mechanic and joking about by shouting "get to cover!" for no reason at all.
He, huh.. he ran ahead and shouted "get to cover!" and leapt onto the ground a few feet away from me..
There was a magma vent right next to him.. I had to watch as my fellow helldiver was encoated in volcanic material and dissolved infront of me.. screaming. My fellow helldiver, my friend.
And so I just called in another pod and he was back because the game works like that..
We killed some bigger bugs, one of which was able to plant it's tendrils into the floor and pop them out of the ground to assault you, and that was it.
Time to go to extraction! and only one death!
We proceeded to the extraction site and activated the beacon, calling the dropship to our location.
However, we had to hold out for a minute whilst the ship arrives, which is fine. Who doesn't enjoy a good firefight eh?
We held back the alien horde with automated turrets and strafing runs until at last the ship was arriving.
The relief that we were finally going home! it was overwhelming!
And so we ran to the ship as it was docking and were crushed by it in the process.
> GG WP 20/10 Would get flashbacks from a fictional war in a videogame again.

HELLDIVERS is a 4 player co-op "twinstick" shooter. It was originally released on PSN (Playstation Network) and received positive reviews. Its PC port is no exception, and is a wonderfully fun action game to enjoy alone or with others. Although the true fun of the game comes from 4-player co-op, when you can tackle harder missions. I would place it in the "party game" and "couch co-op" categories.
The game takes place in the local galaxy, in a distant future with space travel. Humanity resides on "Super Earth", as a very technologically advanced race. Humanity has united under one super-power, that believes strongly in democracy, freedom, and liberty (space murica'). During our expansion we have come to war with 3 races; Bugs, The Illuminate, and Cyborgs. All with their own reasons and backgrounds for going to war with us.
The main goal of the game is to push back and defeat each race, and conquer the galaxy in the name of Democracy. There is a large galactic map where you help fight the war and push back each race, and eventually eliminate them from the war. This is done through Influence points, which is gained by completing missions, higher difficulty missions give more Influence. However, they can push and fight back as well. If the players lose battles the enemies can retake sectors, and eventually lay seige to Super Earth. If Super Earth is lost the war is over, and the players lose. In either scenario, victory or defeat, a new war is started afterwards. The cycle then repeats.
Friendly fire is enabled which leads to some frustrating, and hilarious, moments. This forces coordination, checking firing lanes, player skill, positioning, and caution. The game is based as a twin stick shooter, and can be played with a controller. However my fellow PC users do not worry, the game plays absolutely fine with keyboard & mouse. It's a solid PC port with important PC features such as: Text Chat, VOIP, and Steam integration.
The game's difficulty scales from 1 - 12. 1 being the easiest (Dive in the Park), and 12 being the hardest (HELLDIVE). As you go into higher difficulties more enemies appear, and more difficult ones with them, but the rewards grow too. One key to playing the game is to keep moving, as the enemies will never quit coming. Patrols alert their allies, thus calling in more powerful enemies. It is imperative to kill these patrols quickly before you are spotted. You can likewise avoid patrols entirely, stealth is an option though difficult. Playing online can make it frustrating when one player is hanging back and not moving with the team, preventing everyone else from moving forward; the screen is locked, and all 4 players are stuck on it.
Fighting on planets earns XP and new items for the players to use. These items are called Strategems, which are drops the player calls in during missions. These can be anything from an airstrike, a heavy machine gun, a sentry turret, landmines, and even tanks. Be cautious though, these drop-pods can crush you and your allies (and enemies too!). There is character customization, althought it is light. You can change your outfit, cape, and select a gender (female is slightly skinnier looking, it doesn't affect gameplay). Expect your character to shout plenty of liberty, freedom, and democracy lines and puns, which gives a good laugh.
Overall the game is a fun action romp that will make you laugh, keep you focused, and have a good time. It's best played with friends, or people online. Solo players may find it difficult to unlock all the items, and do higher difficulties by themselves.

There isn't much difficulty, and the hardest part of the game is figuring which collectibles your missing, or why some achievements are not activating. This game is the easiest of all the starwars games I have played. Some of the "side missions" are tricky too, especially the races (if you are using a keyboard like I was). The "added" side mission content is good, with a couple of small side-story missions on each "hub world" which each have lots of content, yet a lot of the missions are similar to others on other hub worlds.
This game is made for people that watched the films, as much of the story is not explained, missions are stitched together with cutscences and "intermission" levels. Talking about cutscenes, they are well animated and funny will make you laugh at least once.
There is not much new from other games. The terminals have been changed up, being mini-puzzles of their own (you can get a "powerup" to remove the puzzles later). The character customiser has been made easier to use.
There is not much replaybility apart from getting 100% aswell as all steam achievements which I managed to achieve in ~55 hours of gameplay, with most of that being me replaying missions to get collectibles, and doing side missions on hub worlds.
If your a fan of lego games, and starwars, you will enjoy this game.

I really wanted to like this game, but it's just disappointing. I have a number of problems with it:
First, the problem with making a Lego game (which have always been full of content) out of a single movie is that you get tons of filler. There's a level that's literally about getting the Millennium Falcon ready to go to the Starkiller Base, just going around looking for missiles and wookie cookies. And let me tell you, it's not exactly an exciting one.
Second, I know humor is subjective, but I really don't enjoy it in this one. It's this Tumblr/millennial humor I don't really get despite technically being a millennial myself. I think there's one joke that actually made me laugh in the entire game, but for the rest of it not even a smile. The jokes are bad and the voice acting feels akward.
And talking about voice acting, this is my first Lego game with it instead of the mumbling and babbling, and now I get why most people don't like it. it's not only unfunny and akward, but it also kinda defeats the point of the game itself. Lego games are puzzle games for the most part, so it really bugs me how the characters feel the need to tell you constantly what it is you're supposed to do, even when it's painfully obvious, through the entire game. Yes, Rey, I know BB-8 can use that thing. Yes, Han Solo, I know that's a job for Chewbacca. And so on.
And the last thing is that the game is pretty buggy, sometimes you destroy something that's supposed to drop pieces for you to build, but it doesn't. Other times some characters you need get stuck and you can't get them out. Sometimes the game freezes and you don't know if it crashed or if you just have to wait. Sometimes it does crash and leaves you looking at your desktop like an idiot. The game has checkpoints, but you still end up having to replay a lot of it because it barely works.
It's not the worst game ever, and the gameplay itself is decent enough. But between the subjective problems I have with it and the fact that it could crash at any moment, playing this game wasn't an enjoyable experience. If you're doubting whether you should buy it or not, I wouldn't recommend it, specially at full price. If you really are determined to buying it, go ahead, I guess there's a somewhat good game hidden behind the bugs and the cringy humor.

Long Review:
"A Story About My Uncle" is a great game. The mechanics are fun and interesting, the visuals are beautiful, and the story is intriguing. While I don't know if I would pay the full price for this game, I got it during the Steam Summer sale and it was well worth the $2.50 I spent. While I enjoyed it overall, it is a bit on the short side and is honestly a little too easy for the majority of the play through. Unless you spend time trying to get all of the achievements, you'll be able to run through this game in 3-4 hours; I also did this while finding all of the optional story objects, completing Maddie's game, and finding a majority of the Collectables. Most of the achievements are difficult to get though, a nice touch considering how many games give achievements for simply completing a level. There are also certain mechanics that are introduced that I wish were either more challenging or simply used for longer durations. The Eye Serpent that you face at the end of the Chasm is easy to avoid and poses no real threat, and nothing like it is seen for the rest of the game. The falling boxes and stalactites which appear during a portion of the Ice Cave level appear briefly and could provide an extra challenge which isn't really exploited by the devs. All in all, however, this is a fun and interesting game and I would suggest giving it a try.
Short Review:
Pros:
-Fun and interesting game mechanics
-Beautiful visuals
-Great voice acting
-Intriguing story
-Challenging achievements
Cons:
-Short, only 3-4 hours
-Not all that challenging
-Certain gameplay elements aren't used to their full potential

Save your money, buy the original CoH, and download the FREE Eastern Front Mod. The developers of the Eastern Front Mod took the AI from that game and actually fixed it to the point where the units use real strategy instead of blatant cheating like in Company of Heroes 2. CoH 2 AI will just call in smoke attack, after smoke attack, after smoke attack - cooldown time be damned! But there is no real strategy or adaptability. (FYI - smoke attacks are special ability artillery/bombing attacks)
The only thing worse than the AI is the fact that this game really didn't do much to improve over the first. The pathfinding is still as terrible as ever and there aren't any sort of squad formations, which if included, would limit the amount of units that get killed when the computer calls in smoke every 20 seconds. These are two basic things that games in the late 90s were able to accomplish, so it boggles my mind how CoH cannot incomproate it! On top of that, I cannot think of anything added to CoH2, except for maybe line of sight and the ability to jump over sandbags that were actual improvements over the first.
Last but not least is the fact that you actually have to buy so much DLC, which is just a slap in the face to anyone who is an early adopter. "Oh, I see you paid $50.00 for our base game, here - spend another $20.00 five more times so you can get what should have been included in the original or offered at a significant discount for those who bought the original." Instead, they just have more and more bundles for people who haven't bought the game yet.
Once again - save yourself the time, money, and frustration and skip this game. Buy the original and download the FREE Eastern Front Mod. You can thank me later.
(Edited for grammar and to state that I donated $25.00 to the Eastern Front Developers because they actually EARNED my money.)

This is an amazing, gorgeous, thought-provoking game through and through. Some people have derided this as a "walking simulator", but that's only partially accurate as in there are many things that you don't need to find or experience in order to reach the end of the game. As such, it's only a "walking simulator" if you play it that way.
Although the game was designed to be a "no holding your hand" type of game, this is both a benefit and a drawback. Not knowing what was going on led me to completely walk past two of the optional story pieces and almost past a third until I decided to watch one of the developers' videos. Only then did I realize that those things that I briefly looked at were actually puzzles that needed to be "solved". Again, they're not mandatory, but it still left me with a "well, you could have at least told me about the first one" feeling. That, however, goes against the "no hand holding" implementation.
The main reason for the game is the story, which was fascinating to watch as it unfolded. It never fully explained what was going on and even the ending leaves room for some interpretation, but it kept me roped in with wanting to know what was going on. One section with jump scares that required stealth in order to stay away from a "ghost miner" felt very clichéd, but that was the only real negative with respect to content. Coming in at only a few hours, I found the story to be engaging and the comments about "walking simulator" to be slightly disingenuous.
Additionally, this game looks GORGEOUS in stereoscopic 3D. (Water effects should be disabled, though.) The game is drawn in such a way that there is plenty of "in front of the screen" action, particuarly when walking through forests and especially when walking through the flower-covered glade near the end of the game. These section come alive in ways rarely experienced when played in 3D. If you have an NVIDIA card, I highly recommend turning 3D on when playing this. Just be careful of those jump scares, because the 3D is effective!
It's a short game, but it's gorgeous and it's well worth the time as long as you can appreciate story over gameplay. You will likely be thinking about the ending for many days after playing it.

This is a fun little game that takes its cues from classic Treasure action games for the Genesis (Gunstar Heroes, Alien Soldier, etc.). Here's the thing, though: while Noitu Love 2 is inspired by those games, it does not play like them at *all*. Firstly, Treasure games are known for their flawless action game controls. This game, on the other hand, is a bit clunky to handle. You use WASD at get around and the mouse to attack...there's no controller support, which is just odd when you consider that the game is inspired by console titles. The mouse attacks don't always work that well, and sometimes it feels like you're just clicking as fast as you can and hoping that it's doing something. Secondly, Treasure games are known for their gameplay variety. Noitu Love 2 mostly just has you racing through short, linear stages, clicking the left mouse button as fast as as you can. You don't get techniques or skills as you progress: you simply click, click, click, and click some more. There's a stage where you fly around with a special beam weapon, but it's not different enough to break up the repetition of the rest of the game.
If all that is true, why am I recommending this? I'm making it sound like it isn't a very good game, right? Well, despite Noitu Love 2's drawbacks, it's still pretty cool. I bought the game for about a dollar when it was on sale, and I feel like it was money well-spent. It's a great diversion if you're burnt out on open world epics and you just want to kick back and have a retro-style action experience. There are a lot of cool, creative bosses (the TV camera boss was my favorite), the music is solid, and the art direction is awesome. All the sprites look great and they have so much personality and character. The story is nonsense, but that just adds to the frenetic, funny spirit of the game. You've also got some decent replay value here; you can unlock new characters with their own playstyle, which lets you mix things up a bit (one of the new characters is *very* different, but I won't spoil it for you), and you can try out the game on harder difficulty settings, do high score runs, etc.
So yes, it's a mindless, slightly janky mouse click simulator, but it's a *fun* mindless, slightly janky mouse click simulator. It's basically a Flash game on steroids, but it's a *fun* Flash game on steroids. I was blown away when I realized that Noitu Love 2 was almost entirely the product of one person...the gameplay itself might be quite simple, but the thought and effort that went into the game's style is truly impressive. If you have any affection for 16-bit action games, Noitu Love 2 will make you smile. Just don't go in expecting something on the level of Treasure classics and you'll be satisfied.
Oh, and one more thing: the game is short. You can easily breeze through the entire thing in one session on the normal difficulty level. But, as I mentioned, there are some nice replay possibilities, and short length of the game doesn't make it any less fun.

Noitu Love 2: Devolution is a short and sweet sequel to an older platforming game featuring a new movement and attack system that incorporates a mouse-controlled targeting reticle and keyboard keys. Compared to its predecessor, NL2 is a faster and busier game with enemies practically flooding the screen at times, their attacks ceasing only when you manage to progress to the next checkpoint.
Every stage manages to have its own theme and gimmick such as chaining beam attacks or inverting gravity and you get to “practice” with each theme versus enemies and mini-bosses before fighting the stage boss, who typically uses a combination of the things you learned earlier. This makes for a very smooth learning curve that even a novice gamer will be able to pick up on quickly.
Sadly, the one thing lacking in this otherwise perfect gem is length. Since many of the stages encourage you to rush forward, it’s very easy to end up breezing through this title in less than 90 minutes. It’s still a really fun 90 minutes though, and a great deal for such a low price.

Oscura Lost Light is a platformer with some platforming puzzle elements
in it.  The game runs smooth and solid, and the platforming is intense and keeps
you attention throughout the game.  The controls are basic, though I would have
appreciated having the option to rebind the special powers keys, as it would
have made my gameplay more efficient.  This did not, however, take away from my
enjoyment of the game.
You play as an apprentice lightkeeper that accidentally plunges the land
into darkness, and are out on a quest to recover the lighshards and bring the
light back.  The story is enough to keep you interested, but not so much that
it takes away from the platforming elements.  The game has a par time
goal, which
adds to the replayability, though I would have liked to see a leaderboard, as
it would have been beneficial to the competitive aspect of the game.
The platforming is well done and very well fleshed out.  The game is
great for moderate to experienced platformers, though it never felt
unfair.  There
were some challenging areas and some tricky parts, but the checkpoints are
balanced and set at decent intervals.  The game knows that you are going to die,
but it doesn't punish you for it by sending you back large distances.  The
mechanics and level design are constantly remixed and consistantly add new
challenges that keep you in the environment.
The atmosphere is beautiful, the platforming is challenging, and I
never felt like the game was wasting my time.  I enjoyed playing this game,
and it is an easy recommend.

HELLDIVERS is a 4 player co-op "twinstick" shooter. It was originally released on PSN (Playstation Network) and received positive reviews. Its PC port is no exception, and is a wonderfully fun action game to enjoy alone or with others. Although the true fun of the game comes from 4-player co-op, when you can tackle harder missions. I would place it in the "party game" and "couch co-op" categories.
The game takes place in the local galaxy, in a distant future with space travel. Humanity resides on "Super Earth", as a very technologically advanced race. Humanity has united under one super-power, that believes strongly in democracy, freedom, and liberty (space murica'). During our expansion we have come to war with 3 races; Bugs, The Illuminate, and Cyborgs. All with their own reasons and backgrounds for going to war with us.
The main goal of the game is to push back and defeat each race, and conquer the galaxy in the name of Democracy. There is a large galactic map where you help fight the war and push back each race, and eventually eliminate them from the war. This is done through Influence points, which is gained by completing missions, higher difficulty missions give more Influence. However, they can push and fight back as well. If the players lose battles the enemies can retake sectors, and eventually lay seige to Super Earth. If Super Earth is lost the war is over, and the players lose. In either scenario, victory or defeat, a new war is started afterwards. The cycle then repeats.
Friendly fire is enabled which leads to some frustrating, and hilarious, moments. This forces coordination, checking firing lanes, player skill, positioning, and caution. The game is based as a twin stick shooter, and can be played with a controller. However my fellow PC users do not worry, the game plays absolutely fine with keyboard & mouse. It's a solid PC port with important PC features such as: Text Chat, VOIP, and Steam integration.
The game's difficulty scales from 1 - 12. 1 being the easiest (Dive in the Park), and 12 being the hardest (HELLDIVE). As you go into higher difficulties more enemies appear, and more difficult ones with them, but the rewards grow too. One key to playing the game is to keep moving, as the enemies will never quit coming. Patrols alert their allies, thus calling in more powerful enemies. It is imperative to kill these patrols quickly before you are spotted. You can likewise avoid patrols entirely, stealth is an option though difficult. Playing online can make it frustrating when one player is hanging back and not moving with the team, preventing everyone else from moving forward; the screen is locked, and all 4 players are stuck on it.
Fighting on planets earns XP and new items for the players to use. These items are called Strategems, which are drops the player calls in during missions. These can be anything from an airstrike, a heavy machine gun, a sentry turret, landmines, and even tanks. Be cautious though, these drop-pods can crush you and your allies (and enemies too!). There is character customization, althought it is light. You can change your outfit, cape, and select a gender (female is slightly skinnier looking, it doesn't affect gameplay). At first sight, my impression about this game was that it was crazy difficult. From the very beginning, there's no easy tutorial and you get directly into a deadly fast-paced combat without having even been told where to find a gun. Even at easiest difficulty. Then in the next fight you discover that on top of that your ammo can disappear very fast. But finally, after a few levels, it gets better. You learn all the tricks, take advantage of maps which allow more sneaking, and abuse of free heals and the many reloading points. You also end up realising that what is maybe the main gameplay element of this game, compared to other FPS, is how many puzzles you have. You really have to listen at what the characters tell you, they usually won't repeat but they often give hints you absolutely need to understand to solve the puzzle. The alternation of puzzle solving, slow sneaking, rushing through irradiated areas, fast-paced combat and scripted events make it a pleasant game, where you're not easily bored with grinding. The general atmosphere is rather nice too, and the darkness of the tunnels puts you under permanent pressure.
However, having read the book, I'm not convinced by the adaption of the story. The editors have chosen to describe the story of the same main character, Artyom, using some names the reader is familiar with, but they have changed all of the content. Many choices have been done with the understandable ambition of putting more action into a story which didn't have that much shooting, but in order to reach this objective they have really sacrified too much from the original story. Even if you read all the notes you can find, the game version of the story is very poor compared to the book. The book was not the best book I've ever read but still it had some depth. A lot of thinking about visions, some almost philosophical parts, many historical and political references, considerations about religions, racism in Russia, and so on. Most of it has disappeared from the game, now it just looks like a dumb action movie. I would have prefered if the makers of this game had kept the book history intact, and decided to tell us another story instead, not Artyom's story but a spin-off using another character (for instance young Uhlman). It's what have been done by Metro: Last Light, which uses the book's atmosphere but doesn't follow any precise book (although Metro 2035 is being written, afterwards).

I really really wanted to like this. But I found it frustrating. There seemed to be more "cutscenes" where you lose control of the character to watch the scene take place than there was any actual gameplay. The loading screens lagged and lagged. There is no real explanation on how the weapons/ammo seem to work, or how to buy ammo etc. I mean, you can figure it out, but its not obvious.  It is very scripted and linear to the point where there is almost nothing to do and when you do happen to do something, it seems to have little or no consequence on the outcome. Or at least, it felt that way in the short amount of time I spent playing. Even at the start when you are told to head to the platform and to grab your gear and not forget anything... the cut scene grabs your gear for you! Couldn't even grab my own gear from my own room.
The combat system is a bit off too. imo. Reloading takes so long that you can be hit and felled in the time it takes, and it takes a lot of ammo to actually kill something. I don't know. Maybe I'm just spoiled on more recent shooters but it just seemed like even though I was aiming at something directly in front of me, I wasn't doing any damage. The people I was with didn't seem to be getting injured or dying at all either. And surprise, they always did damage and killed what was in front them quickly. Sigh.
Then there is the way the story moved along. Its basically walking down corridors and then shooting stuff in an open space. Walking down more corridors and shooting more stuff in more open spaces. There is more walking than shooting. And a lot of the time the person you are with hurries you down a set path even though it looks like you can explore other random corridors, but you aren't really given a chance. Don't get me wrong. I understand this is not an open world game and that is has a linear story, but there is linear gameplay and then there are walking simulators. This feels more like it falls into the latter category to me.

Flix and Chill is a short quirky dating simulator for 99 cents. I thoroughly enjoyed the 68 minutes it took me to complete the game. It has a good sense of humor and will make you smile.

Flix and Chill is a dating sim where you play in 5 dates, 4 new dates and the original one, wher you try to hook up with the other person. Each date is not that long as you chat with your date and play minigames, depending on which date it is. The choices you make will decide whether or not you will successfully take the other person to another date. This may be choosing an option or doing a minigame.

For $1, Flix and Chill will be able to pass the time. Any computer would be able to run this game with no problem. Each date does not take more than 30 minutes or so, but if you want to get all the achievements it can take up to 4 hours. I certainly recommend it.

I recently started and finished The Vanishing of Ethan Carter in a single sitting, and was thoroughly impressed the entire 4.2 hours it took me to fully complete the game.
Although very short (and possibly too short for the full price of the game), TVoEC offers a simplistic yet incredibly engaging game. Taking inspiration from early 20th century weird fiction (namely H.P. Lovecraft, as expected), the story revolves around a private eye on a mission in an isolated village to help one "Ethan Carter". While playing through the opening segment, it seemed quite similar to Dark Corners of the Earth (also available on Steam, but broken as all hell) - being dumped in a disturbing setting with next to no guidance, only to figure everything out for yourself. This minimalist style of gameplay definitely works in the game's favour, as it seems to allow for a more immersive experience. There is no HUD, health bars, maps or quest icons. You have the WASD keys, the mouse, and your own two feet.
Gameplay revolves around solving various puzzles, and entering the minds of those deceased to see memories shortly before their deaths. It feels slightly cliche, but isn't too over-the-top like you might expect. The game's story is unravelled through these various puzzle sequences, as you explore the village in which the game is set, learning of the characters and their relationships with one another. It's definitely not an in-depth story, but it is very engaging.
Where TVoEC really shines is in its atmosphere. From the very first minute of the game, the atmosphere of this game almost smacks you in the face with how incredibly immersive it is. The stunning environments, beautifully-composed soundtrack and occasional narration from the main character provide an incredible feeling of isolation as you make your way through an empty and run-down village. It's almost unlike any game I've ever played, and has to be played to fully understand.
I picked the game up off the Humble Store for $6.66 (coincidence?) and felt very satisfied with my purchase. For the RRP of $19.99 it may seem like a bit much for a game that can be finished in a few hours, but for anything ~$10 or less it's definitely a must-have for fans of mystery, horror, and weird fiction.

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter may well have been the most visually stunning game I've ever played. The experience is enhanced by the terrific job done by the voice actor playing Paul Prospero - you, the protagonist - as well as a music score that knows when to leave the background and sting you when the time is right.

Gameplay-wise, it's a first-person puzzle game-slash-visual-narrative in which the puzzles blend seamlessly into the story. You are a detective looking to solve a mystery. Piecing things together is your life's work, so here's an example of a perfect marriage between narrative device and game mechanics. User interface is simple and unobtrusive, interaction cues popping into view only and only when they're absolutely necessary, most of the time leaving the screen entirely available for the tasty pieces of eye candy the game throws at you.
All in all, an intense albeit short experience which I emphatically recommend. Indeed, upon reaching the end of the game (which should take between 3 and 5 hours, depending on how often you stop to smell the flowers), unless you've got a heart filled with sand, you're bound to feel the game's emotional toll. Truly a thing of beauty.

WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW BEFORE YOU PLAY:
This game is beautiful and I like the puzzles, but 2 hours into it I learned I had no clue how to play it and could not figure it out from the options, etc. So here's what I've learned so far about the game mechanics that you need to know before playing (no spoilers):
1. When a word comes up multiple times like a floaty question, slowly look around until all the words overlap to form a single word. It will then flash you into a "scene" that shows what you're looking for and it will be in that direction. If you do not do this, the item won't appear. I walked past a crank like 7 times without it highlighting because I didn't know about this mechanic. Don't even ask me about the rock. Afterwards, it's actually pretty cool and makes you feel a little more psychic (plus you can actually play the game the way it's meant without giving up or resorting to walkthroughs).
2. You have an inventory. It doesn't come up. You can't call it up. Things are just pocketed and then pop out when you need them to do something. Therefore you can forget what you're carrying. But don't worry, #3. will help with that.
3. When you leave a mystery area, the thing resets if you didn't complete it. That means things go out of your hidden inventory and back on the ground if you picked something up. Portals come back to their original state, etc. So if you want to start the little area over, leave and come back.
4. Holding Shift while you move makes you run. Holding Ctrl while you move makes you crouch.
I'm sure there's more. I've only been playing a couple of hours and was totally confused and broke down to see a bit of a walkthrough and realized these mechanics. Back I go to trying it without, because I like the challenge and actually role playing as a detective rather than walking through. Sounds like this game is short with the walk through so the time to figure it out will give me value in the game and satisfaction of "solving the dissapearance"
If anything else weird pops up that is a mechanic instead of a story piece, I'll post it here.

Half Life 2: Episode One while a very short game it is still a great 'short game' to be played. If you want more juicy details check out my Half Life 2 review for more information.
Anywho. Let us get the elephant out of the room. This particular episode tries a little bit too hard at what it wants to be. Is this still an action adventure game? Is it a science-fiction horror FPS? The reason why I say this is because unlike in Half Life 2 where the sections are spread out. The "chapters" jump from one genre to the next with really no breather for the player. And I guess you can say it's because of the "intense" circumstances of the story. But still, Episode One could've used more chapters to spread things out rather than just cramming it all in.
The story obviously takes places just hours after the events of Half Life 2. The overall goal is to get out of City 17. That's basically it. You get some "new" 'plot questions' in this particular game. But these 'plot questions' won't be explained until Episode 2. And even then, the new plot questions you encountered in this game and in the next episode won't be REALLY answered until (Half Life 3) <- Lol.
I recommend this game. But! And this might be a hard pill to swallow. But, I think Episode One and Two should've just been in the ACTUAL Half Life 2 game rather than spacing the game out. It might've been because of budget or giving players a breather. If that's the case then they should've made Ep 1 and Ep 2 into purchasable expansions rather than actual 'full games'. I recommend buying the Orange Box rather than the games seperately btw.

I'll amend this later if I need to, but first impressions are mostly good, so far.
Story - This is by far the weakest part of the package. Over-dramatized BS where everyone tries way too hard to out-macho each other. No funny beats that I can recall, which makes it monotonous. Even the weapon descriptions are preening and begging for you to think they're cool like you're the first seventh grader with boobs. The prologue makes sure you realize going in that you're nobody special, noob. A character does actually call you noob. Aside from all that forehead slapping, I kinda hate when the main character's motives are obscured. Didn't know going in whether I was a good guy or a bad guy. Still not entirely sure, and it feels like one of those things they plan on toying with the entire game just so they can pull a big ol PSYCHE from 25 years ago. Voice acting is pretty bad all around, but I'm sure the script wasn't the easiest to work with. Main character isn't awful, but he's very unremarkable.
Sound - Atmospheric music, some of it quite nice and helps build the tension. Growly, gurgly zombie noises, almost constantly. Main character's grunts during combat and parkour get the job done, but it would have been nice to have an escalating sense of pain and panic when he's getting close to death. Hard to see my health sometimes, and the way he grunts, I just figure I'm fine. Sometimes I'm not fine. Which leads me to:
UI - Nothing special, but nothing too intrusive either. I could stand either a larger health bar or some more indicators to let me know when I should be worried about dying. Hard to tell sometimes if it's my blood or zombie blood spattered on the "camera lens". I do appreciate the Tao Feng-style skeleton view and the audio cue when a sweet stun happens. Menus aren't too fiddly. I can usually get where I need to go with 2-4 button presses. Took me forever to realize the bars at the top were two separate XP bars for Agility and Power, but I blame public school.
Gameplay - Meat and potatoes. And good thing, too, because this is the sole reason for my recommendation. Combat is fun and imaginative. Not quite Dark Souls levels of animation priority, but not too far off. The combat stamina takes some getting used to, and means you can't just wade into a horde of zombies swinging a pipe wrench around like you're Lu Bu. Talents seem to add some interesting options, including dodge rolls and dropkicks, which are as fun as they sound (especially off bridges). Different weapons feel different, especially the crafted ones. Speaking of which, crafting is fun and fleshed out, but doesn't overstay its welcome or become the focus. Blueprints are pretty simple 2-5 ingredient recipes that can be cobbled together right there in the pause menu, no "workbench" or anything required. Parkour is fun, and the main character has an incredible knack for suddenly having his forearms attach to whatever surface is at eye-level when Morpheus tells him to free his mind. Running and parkour stamina doesn't seem to have a meter, at least not one I've seen in my 4 hours. Sometimes dude just gets winded and has to walk for a bit, but once he's powerwalked for a second, just goes right back to running without having to hit the sprint toggle key again. Kinda nice.
Night time deserves its own paragraph, because it's a different game. Well, it's the same game, but you gotta play by different rules. You get used to being all Dovahkiin during the day with your fancy shock pipe and slashy wrench, but at night you better put that thing away, stay down, and shut up. Super Zombies called "Volatiles" come out at night, the stuff of nightmares what could cause a grown man's sheets to carry yellow stains the rest of their days. It's like some sick ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ crossed the Nemesis T-type and the Predator. Ever played any Commandos or Deus Ex? These guys got vision cones you can see on your minimap. And the first time you step inside one is the last time you'll wanna go outside at night. It's darker than a gothic wardrobe, and they give you this dinky flashlight so you can see what's about to kill you. Don't bother fighting them, either. I went straight to papa Google after my first encounter to show him where the bad man touched me, and I learned you CAN actually kill one... in a UV light trap... with an assault rifle... and the maximum amount of bullets. For one kill. Four hours in, and I don't even have a pistol yet.
But in all seriousness, it's a really tense and fun stealth-style system that rewards you with a nice fat Agility XP bonus for shaking your pursuers GTA-style. Also, all XP is doubled at night. Still not enough to make me care. I'm goin to bed like a normal person, thanks.
You can see from the videos that the game looks great too. Personally running it on a 970 and getting 60. I did turn off film grain and motion blur, but that's only because ♥♥♥♥ film grain and motion blur. It's worth the normal asking price, but I picked it up on sale for like 60% off or somesuch.
But hey, four hours in, so grain of salt.

So what's its saving grace? Paradoxically, level design and writing. There's inimitable atmosphere and sense of purpose in Bloodlines' dingy motels, sleazy nightclubs, the occasional haunted manor and their throughly twisted inhabitants. In essence, Bloodlines is like Torment's goth cousin from 3Dville, and it's awfully hard to find another story-driven cRPG worthy of such a praise.

I'm a huge fan of Dating Sims and Visual Novels, so imagine my excitement when I found this on Steam. It was free, so of course I had to try it! And man, I wasn't disappointed!
First of all, while there are indeed some things that could use a little touch up (the art was sometimes a little off and I spotted some typos) but overall it was pretty great! AND IT IS FULLY VOICED. Let me repeat that. All characters (except the player character, but since that is basically supposed to be 'you' I'm glad that one wasn't voiced) are voice acted while speaking to you. I really liked the voice acting! I could gush about that all day.
The story was pretty neat, I liked how the plot unfolded when trying all the different routes to get the endings and the characters managed to leave an impression on me while doing so.  While trying to unlock all the Gallery pics you do have to go through the same dialogue a few times, but there’s a handy dandy skip button that automatically stops when you reach a new line of text you haven’t seen before! Saved me a lot of time trying to unlock everything. (I can’t leave Visual Novels without trying EVERY SINGLE OPTION, so this worked really well for me!)
More pros are: You can romance your female friends, the player character is not a helpless damsel-in-distress and THE THEME SONG IS SO CATCHY. I always listened to the ringtone until it stopped playing before picking up because I like the song that much.
The only real thing that I missed is that I couldn’t romance the hell out of Malix. I kind of seriously fell for him and his crazy cackle. *weeps* Oh well.
Conclusion: Play it if you’d like a nice free Visual Novel with cute characters and on point humour.

This game is a roguelike. Things get challenging, and there are no savepoints. All this I knew going in, and I was fine with that.
But you can get absolutely screwed on certain scenarios, and the game can become unwinnable. The game is too luck-based and doesn't have enough emphasis on skill. When things are going fine, it's fun. When they aren't... it just feels cheap. I'm fine with losing, or games being challenging, but when it feels like I did everything right and the game cheated me, then I have an issue. That's what it feels like to me.
Anyone considering this game is probably alright with it, and that's fine. I just want to let those on the fence know that this game is more losing than winning, and it won't always feel fair. If you need to it always feel like your failures are your fault or you're averse or failure, this is not one for you.

This is a lot like a old old old game called "Free Enterprise", which was basically the same premise. This game, however, takes the simulation factor up a notch. I have nearly called into my real job, just to stay home to oversee the design phase of my pretend OS.

Should I re-tile the bathroom floor? I think so. Should I put the server farm in the basement? Yeah, why not? Should I fire Susan, because she hates the company founder and can't even effectively market a simple audio tool? Most definitely.
This seems like it would just simulate the bad parts of working in a cubicle farm, but I cannot stop refining my strategy when I'm not actually playing. I'd whole heartedly recommend this game. Look at the negative reviews, and you see a bunch of people who played for 15 minutes, couldn't figure it out, and trashed the game play. This game deserves a higher level of player. Perhaps that is you.
