An incredible experience.
I didn't know what to expect from this. The trailers weren't exactly gripping, and I wasn't aware that there was much more to it than just some parkour. There's a world, here, though. An intricately crafted one, full of surprises. And a narrative with the kind of warmth you'd expect only from a talented author. It's foreign and exotic enough that it may throw those with limited tastes off, but I found it an incredibly comfortable experience.
In a world where everything is about dramatic, stone-faced grimdark brain rot, overly dramatic negativity, nihilism, or just being a sociopath/murderhobo? This is a bit different. How often does your entertainment make you smile? That's the magic, here, and it's what I look for in my games. When I think of games that have made me smile, I look back on titles like Portal 2, Ori & The Blind Forest, and Gone Home. Yes, very separate titles, but with everyone straining themselves so hard to be Mature (not mature, that's something entirely different, and more in line with this game, interestingly enough) that they probably look like they have constipation?
It's different. It's nice. It's a representation of what you should like about humanity. It's creative, it takes your inner child by the hand and drags it through a world of wonderment and awe. If you're like me and this world hasn't chewed up and spat out every last shred of humanity you have, you'll smile. You'll smile a lot. And you'll be happy.
It's worth it, just for that.
This isn't your usual game, no. If I had to describe the mechanics as anything it's probably Mirror's Edge by way of Spider-Man with a sprinkling of Portal 2. Considering how much I enjoy that method of travel, I had a blast. It's got that sort of pull to it, the desire to explore the experience, understand it, and master it. It's thoroughly engaging, but not in a
sort of way. It's oddly more cerebral than that. Yes, it requires reflexes, but it also dares to challenge you to think a bit, and that's where I feel the mild Portal 2 sprinklings flavouring it. It's a joy to just
in.
You'll like it, it's as simple as that. Unless you're a cynical beast, devoid of any emotion, and you actually enjoy every story being nihilist with a miserable ending, filled with suffering? You'll love it. I mean, I'm not that. And since I'm not that I end up just rolling my eyes at most of the 'entertainment' out there. You'd think we were all crazy, backstabbing sociopaths. It's cathartic to have something like this, something that's just this different.
It's a story. It's a
story. It's a story... told well, to a child, about wandering through an alien world in power armour that grants super powers.
It's the story your inner child has longed to hear.
Fun, easy to get into, and short. Worth the price.

At least forty-three times better than the movie. However I feel as if there are a lot less levels than the previous games, and the game places too many restrictions on you at points (no free-play/character toggle in hub areas until you complete the main mission arc). Gameplay is superb though, lots of onnovation. Sadly the game has a major downfall in the total lack of vehicles apart from a single AT-ST in the tutorial mission and a couple super-slow and super-useless animals throughout the game.
Pros:
- Great gameplay
- Good voice acting
- Classic LEGO humour
- More background story than the movie (some missions exist that tell events that the movie didn't i.e. how Han Solo got the Rathtars)
- Responsive attack animations
- Good sound
- Works superbly with controller (I used a wired Xbox 360 controller, and everything was great. Good vibrations from breaking bricks and getting damaged etc, and controls are well set out).
- Lots of minigames in the hub areas after finishing campaign and side missions
- Character creator is a lot more diverse and specific than previous games.
Neutral:
- New combat system that ocassionally happens where you get thrown into a cover-based on-rails third-person shooter. Look up some gameplay to see what I'm talking about.
- Easy but smart puzzles
Cons:
- No vehicles
- Few missions
- Confusing hub layouts
- No central area to access all the unlockables etc
- Repetitive puzzles
- Overpriced (worth 30 USD at max, currently it's at 40 USD. Get it on♥♥♥♥♥if you can't afford it, otherwise get it on special).
- Game is not made for keyboard setups, let's face it. However you can change the controls to your liking in-game. I just don't feel like the movement fits well with a 4-directional input scheme. If you have a joystick it might be worth trying out.
tl:dr
8.5/10

The Best Star Wars Game Ever Made: SWBF2
Star Wars Battlefront II is possibly the best Star Wars game ever made. It has all the features you could want in a shooter: a good story, good missions and gamemodes, and good gameplay in both singleplayer and multiplayer modes. As this game is fairly old now, multiplayer has since been terminated. Don't let that inhibit you from buying it though! The A.I. in this game are not to be trifled with, and the continuing production of mods for this game (imho) better than EA's Battlefront.
Pros:
Extensive single-player
Lots of maps and gamemodes: Campaign, Galactic Conquest, Instant Action
Easily modded (you haven't played this game right until you've played it with the "Battlefront: Extreme" mod
Vehicle combat: Dominate on land and in space
Hero mode: play as your favorite jedi/sith characters
Capable A.I.
Endless supply of new maps via mods
Hours of fun
Cons:
No more multiplayer
The class unlocking system (though this can be taken care of with a mod I'm sure)
Unlike the original battlefront, this game does not have much by way of air combat (like starfighter v infantry and vv)
Conclusion:
This is a great game to buy, even if you have no intention of modding it. If you were dissappointed with EA's Battlefront lack of singleplayer modes, this is the game for you.

The Saints Row series is just a zany parody of open-world sandbox games, that manages to improve upon its own formula and personality after every iteration. For me personally, it's one of those games with no real reason to play, but neither is there any reason not to.
Burnt-out playing your favourite MOBA or compet CSGO? Then this will be a nice break from more serious games. If you can find another person to co-op with it will be a blast, as you accidentally kill each other with horse♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s and kick each other out of moving vehicles.
In terms of the actual game, it's a souped up version of Saints Row 3, with all the character/vehicle customization, janky mechanics (increased tenfold in co-op) and over the top storyline that only serves to fill your screen with increasing amounts of enemies and game elements.
It's the type of game that really influences the cookie-cutter "meme/10" steam reviews because of all the random content in it.
e.g.
>Saw X
>Did Y to X
>Ate a Z and became X, and got Y by V
10/10 game

Thanks to the developer and publisher Fireproof games for creating another great puzzle game for me to enjoy.
The Room 2 is basically a continuation of the first amazing game. The difference in the sequel is instead of being locked in a room with changing puzzles, you will time travel to different rooms to solve a puzzle which unlocks a door to escape. The rooms are near photo realistic and the attention to the smallest detail is what makes the The Room series rare in the genre.
There are 6 chapters in the Room 2 and each room can take up to an hour depending on your reluctance to use the hint system. Some of the rooms you will explore include a cave, labaoratory and a pirate ship. As you enter a room there are usually 3 areas that you will be tasked to solve. The Rooms signature gameplay of finding a hidden compartment to open another compartment, to find an object to solve the puzzles is front and center again. Veterns of the first game will find some of the tricks from the first a lot easier but a lot of them are still cleverly disguised. Luckily the hint system(optional) is perfect as it offers 3 hints to each problem while never exactlly telling you the answer. On most occasions when i did use a hint, the first was more than enough information needed to proceed.
The Room series so far is never been about the the puzzles per se as they are pretty simple and straight forward but its about using your eyes, exploration and trying to find that hidden door, twist of a hinge, or looking under a drawer for the next piece to the puzzle that is satisfying. The attention to detail, amazing enviroments and complexity to these objects is why the series is unique, successful and one of the best.
After completing the game i asked Fireproof games when the Room 3 was coming to Steam and their answer was "We hope to bring it to PC in the future but no immediate plans" :(
Positives
Photo realistic enviroments and puzzles
Attention to detail
Hint system
Every puzzle was different and satisfying to complete
Perfect laptop/couch game
Negatives
Story continues to be an afterthought
Wish you could freely walk around
Sometimes not knowing when an area in a room is complete

The Room was a great success.  It had satisfying puzzles of just about perfect difficulty that were wrapped into a central construct of an ever changing box.  Basically a puzzle box toy on steroids.  However, a crucial factor was the atmosphere that the game created, especially in the second half.
The Room Two takes these core elements and builds on them to make a sequel that outshines its predecessor in just about every way.  The puzzles have shifted from a box on a table to a series of rooms, and the puzzles now span several objects and areas in each room, making them more interesting and intricate.
To me, the mood and atmosphere of the game are where it truly shines.  It's darker than the previous installment, much to my pleasure, and the expanded nature of the environment allows the developers the space to create vivid locations.  The fact that the puzzles are woven into the level design (rather than a thin pasted-on decor) makes it all the more involving.
The game provides a rich experience, and hopefully we'll see its sequel in PC form.  Given what has been achieved here, I have high hopes for that one.

Overall, I definitely recommend this game if you enjoy puzzle-type games, escape rooms, old point and click puzzlers like Myst, etc.
Hopefully they'll bring The Room 3 to Steam soon.

I'll amend this later if I need to, but first impressions are mostly good, so far.
Story - This is by far the weakest part of the package. Over-dramatized BS where everyone tries way too hard to out-macho each other. No funny beats that I can recall, which makes it monotonous. Even the weapon descriptions are preening and begging for you to think they're cool like you're the first seventh grader with boobs. The prologue makes sure you realize going in that you're nobody special, noob. A character does actually call you noob. Aside from all that forehead slapping, I kinda hate when the main character's motives are obscured. Didn't know going in whether I was a good guy or a bad guy. Still not entirely sure, and it feels like one of those things they plan on toying with the entire game just so they can pull a big ol PSYCHE from 25 years ago. Voice acting is pretty bad all around, but I'm sure the script wasn't the easiest to work with. Main character isn't awful, but he's very unremarkable.
Sound - Atmospheric music, some of it quite nice and helps build the tension. Growly, gurgly zombie noises, almost constantly. Main character's grunts during combat and parkour get the job done, but it would have been nice to have an escalating sense of pain and panic when he's getting close to death. Hard to see my health sometimes, and the way he grunts, I just figure I'm fine. Sometimes I'm not fine. Which leads me to:
UI - Nothing special, but nothing too intrusive either. I could stand either a larger health bar or some more indicators to let me know when I should be worried about dying. Hard to tell sometimes if it's my blood or zombie blood spattered on the "camera lens". I do appreciate the Tao Feng-style skeleton view and the audio cue when a sweet stun happens. Menus aren't too fiddly. I can usually get where I need to go with 2-4 button presses. Took me forever to realize the bars at the top were two separate XP bars for Agility and Power, but I blame public school.
Gameplay - Meat and potatoes. And good thing, too, because this is the sole reason for my recommendation. Combat is fun and imaginative. Not quite Dark Souls levels of animation priority, but not too far off. The combat stamina takes some getting used to, and means you can't just wade into a horde of zombies swinging a pipe wrench around like you're Lu Bu. Talents seem to add some interesting options, including dodge rolls and dropkicks, which are as fun as they sound (especially off bridges). Different weapons feel different, especially the crafted ones. Speaking of which, crafting is fun and fleshed out, but doesn't overstay its welcome or become the focus. Blueprints are pretty simple 2-5 ingredient recipes that can be cobbled together right there in the pause menu, no "workbench" or anything required. Parkour is fun, and the main character has an incredible knack for suddenly having his forearms attach to whatever surface is at eye-level when Morpheus tells him to free his mind. Running and parkour stamina doesn't seem to have a meter, at least not one I've seen in my 4 hours. Sometimes dude just gets winded and has to walk for a bit, but once he's powerwalked for a second, just goes right back to running without having to hit the sprint toggle key again. Kinda nice.
Night time deserves its own paragraph, because it's a different game. Well, it's the same game, but you gotta play by different rules. You get used to being all Dovahkiin during the day with your fancy shock pipe and slashy wrench, but at night you better put that thing away, stay down, and shut up. Super Zombies called "Volatiles" come out at night, the stuff of nightmares what could cause a grown man's sheets to carry yellow stains the rest of their days. It's like some sick ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ crossed the Nemesis T-type and the Predator. Ever played any Commandos or Deus Ex? These guys got vision cones you can see on your minimap. And the first time you step inside one is the last time you'll wanna go outside at night. It's darker than a gothic wardrobe, and they give you this dinky flashlight so you can see what's about to kill you. Don't bother fighting them, either. I went straight to papa Google after my first encounter to show him where the bad man touched me, and I learned you CAN actually kill one... in a UV light trap... with an assault rifle... and the maximum amount of bullets. For one kill. Four hours in, and I don't even have a pistol yet.
But in all seriousness, it's a really tense and fun stealth-style system that rewards you with a nice fat Agility XP bonus for shaking your pursuers GTA-style. Also, all XP is doubled at night. Still not enough to make me care. I'm goin to bed like a normal person, thanks.

But hey, four hours in, so grain of salt.

Wow, what a game. I don't want to waste your time, so I'll try to keep this short and sweet.
Story: I liked it! It isn't the most amazing story in the world, but it is far from boring.
Side quests: They fit in VERY well with the flavor of the enviroment. They also can impact your game, whitch is something I wish more side quests in games would do.
Movement (Parcore): I have never, ever seen a game master parcore like this game did. The movement is amazing, and you will fall in love with it.
Weapon balance: This topic is too often overlooked. Games will provide melee weapons, but as soon as you get a gun you never have to use that baseball bat or sword agian. Dying light puts a cap on how much ammo you can carry for each weapon type, and ammo is just hard enough to come by that you'll opt to use your melee weapons. Not that that's bad though! Melee weapons are one of the best parts of Dying light! You can stun your foes, shock them, set fire to them, send them flying with fart bombs.. Wait, really? Yep! Speaking of which...
EASTER EGGS! Dying Light's devs are the KINGS od easter eggs! You will find OP weapons, hidden caves, and even a Plants vs Zombies minigame if you look hard enough!
World Design: Fantastic. There are 2 main zones: First, the slums. It's very slum-y. Then a little into the story you unlock an equaly impressive map called "Old Town". Fast travel between both places is easy, and not at all frustrating.
And last but not least, DLC's: They are not needed. This is what I love. Some games you are missing out without the DLC's, but in dying light they add content, but the game is the same enjoyable experience without them.
My overall rating? 9.4/10. A true masterpeice.

This is a game unlike most others.  It eschews accessibility in favor of being at times deliberately obtuse.  It is truly "oldschool" in a very real sense rather than simply appealing to the "8-Bit" aesthetic.  I think those of us that like the game most were probably those that played text-based adventures in glorious monochrome.  Or played countless sessions of Legend of the Red Dragon on ancient and likely now extinct BBSes.  Or engaged in awkward roleplay at 3am on some forsaken MUD out there.
If you understand any of that at all, then this is the game for you.  You are also probably like me, getting old, and seeing a game like this helps you convince yourself the things you enjoyed in yesteryear are NOT in fact entirely irrelevant!
If, on the otherhand, you didn't understand any of that but still have an appreciation for ASCII art, catchy beep-boopy music, and grind heavy RPG mechanics, then you too may find this game worthwhile.  Whippersnapper.
All of the gameplay consists of entering (mostly one character) commands as highlighted on the current screen.  At first, most of this will be simply an encounter crawl, a series of battles using a handful of attacks and abilities.  Combat is turn based and text heavy.  You need to pay close attention to both your own and your enemy's condition, and carefully chain together your attacks and simultaneously avoid the power attacks of your enemy.  There is a very definite rhythm to it all, and you can die very easily if you don't master it.
As you progress, you will unlock an increasing amount of side-activites and quests.  These involve running a tavern, expanding your player home, mining iron, crafting gear, arena battles and random dungeons, among many other things.  However, despite the number of activities the end result is mostly about gaining gold, XP, or a RNG item reward.  Speaking of RNG, I hope you like it or at least tolerate it, because this game uses it
.  As a result, it pays to invest points in a few different weapon proficiencies as it can be difficult to come across a good weapon of the one specific type that you want.
Apart from the ASCII graphics, which are fairly attractive but also not the best I've seen, there is also a very complementary soundtrack that is very retro-inspired without being too chip-tuney.  If you have a sweet tooth for nostalgia, prepare your mouth for cavities.
Last, but not least, is the humor of the game.  There are plots and sub-plots to unravel, but most of that is lost in the extremely silly and "le random" type of humor in the narrative.  I actually found it pretty amusing for the most part, but boy oh boy am I tired of seeing the word "potato".
Although this game gets "Overwhelmingly Positive" reviews, and despite the fact that I recommend it myself, it is actually
for everyone.  I personally love it as a throwback to mostly forgotten games of the past, for the ASCII art, for the fun assortment of grinding activities, and even for the heavily potato-based humor.  However, I can easily see all of those things being negatives for another person.  One man's potato is another man's radish, or so the old saying probably goes.
For my part, the only thing I really felt missing is a solid multiplayer aspect.  Most of the great BBS door games of old were heavily competitive beyond simple leaderboard rankings.  It often entailed a lot of direct PvP, raids, and even things like ship combat and kingdom warfare.
I'd love to see a sequel to Sanctuary that kept the single-player grinding and expanded upon it with competitive multiplayer activites.  That would make the game a true Yukon Gold, rather than the more common Idaho Russet.

Today I finished the entire storyline and oh my god was this game so so so worth it. The graphics are beautiful, even on a mid-range older gaming laptop I still got upwards of 55 fps steady. The storyline is incredible and has the capability to make you feel a real connection to the NPC's that you venture through the tunnels with. The weapons and mechanics are amazing; even on "normal" difficulty ammo is still precious and treated as such, gas masks are vital and rare to come by (I think in the entire storyline I only came across ~10) and most creatures, even the weak ones can kill in 2 or 3 hits. The voice acting and cutscenes are just spot on but overall what made me desire Metro for so long and finally purchace it with money that took me quite a while to scrape together; was the eyecandy value. Graphically, (in my opinion) Metro trumps just about every other game in its category and just goes above and beyond in so many aspects. Even how the monsters and demons are rendered is breathtaking. Each time they appear; its genuinely terrifying because the atmosphere the game projects is just that good. This game immaculately cuts the fine line between easy to pick up game, and gritty realism.
The only dislike I have is that on some earlier parts of the map, its possible to break the barriers and clip outside the render range. Other than that, 0 complaints. Buy this, its worth every penny and more.

If you like story, First Person Shooters, Fallout, Russia and/or Vodka; this is the game for you. As you could probably deduce this game is a story driven FPS set in a post-apocalyptic Russia. It is very well made and I highly recommend it too any gamers out there looking for a good quality single player experience. Not only that but there is a ton of replay ability. While you are forced to follow the same linear story every run through; there are different game modes you can play it on. The first of these game modes is "Survivalist Mode", which limits the amount of ammo, money, health, etc that you receive throughout the game, making it ultimately harder and more stealth based. On the flip side there is a game mode called "Ranger Mode", which give you more ammo, weapons, money and health which makes for an easier more action pact adventure while also making the possibility of stealth much harder. To go along with each game mode there are 4 separate difficulties you can play on either of the game modes and using the power of permutations, there are 8 different ways you can set the difficulty of your run through and almost a limitless number of ways to play through it.
One thing I would recommend you do before buying this game is wait for a major steam sale, due to the fact that the game will fall to about 3 USD compared to its 20 USD normal cost. Also the A.I is kind of derpy at times, but try and this some slack.

A short, yet powerful little game. It keeps you interested during its entire duration. Things never get boring, since you are constantly getting new content during the entire game. There is no grind, no padding, just action. Not to say that the game doesn't tone it down a little once in a while, it masterfully keeps the interest curve well balanced. You won't get fatigued by too much action too long, yet at the same time there is no risk of getting bored. Some parts may be simple traversal, but even then you are assaulted by enemies just often enough not to feel safe.
The art and music are excellent too, the soundtrack could easily have been sold as an extra, but instead it's downloadable free of charge. As for the art, it has an unique style that fits the game and is easy to read, yet never gets monotonous.
The story isn't anything special. It has a twist or two, but if you are playing a game like this for the story then you are doing it wrong. It's a fair excuse to have an awesome time and nothing more.
The difficulty is just right.
Overall, if the trailer video didn't instantly win you over then there is no point in trying the game, you just don't "get" it.

Helldivers is a pretty good game, honestly. It feels fair - albeit unforgiving - most of the time. You'll laugh, cry, and swear your♥♥♥♥♥off with your friends and random players alike. With team damage always on and a horde of bugs chasing you down, times are rough and an interesting situation is sure to arise!
Helldivers is polished, neat, and above all else FINISHED. It's a fairly original concept that feels fresh and exciting. It has interesting mechanics and a huge amount of customization.
The game is not really "gated" by dlc, per se - but you'll definitely want the stratagems and abilities they bring. That being said, though, the game is more than playable without the dlc content. The dlc more-or-less just allows a single player a bit more freedom in the types of missions they can take, such as the use of satchel charges versus a rocket launcher with a co-op reload mechanics for example.
One of the coolest parts about Helldivers, (Aside from the small price tag.) is that everybody who plays contributes towards the galactic campaign of Super Earth - your homeplanet - to conquer alien planets which inhabit three distinct races, all of whom want to expand and take over Super Earth. You genuinely feel as if you're part of something bigger when you play Helldivers, and get the feeling of being one soldier among many.
Overall I think Helldivers deserves a cool 8.5/10. Sure it's fun and original, but sometimes the game begins to feel stale when you get good enough to solo the hardest difficulty without even being spotted once. The limited number of randomized objectives really becomes apparent when you have ten or eleven objectives on a single randomized map.

obviously this is the second 'the room' game and it's just as great as the first one.
if you have ANY interest in puzzle games then it's impossible to go wrong with either games of the series.
however there are subtile differences in the second game. instead of usually one insanely detailed object you have a whole room with multiple but still very detailed objects to investigate. that's neither better nor worse, it's just a little different.
at the same time the game offers a little more story and a darker and more  mysterious feel. while this adds a lot of immersion you will still be able to enjoy this game without getting scared or anything.
the presentation of the game is one of a kind. the graphical detail is just amazing. and it has to be, after all you can't have people investigate objects at a nose's distance and insult their eyes with crude and mushy graphics.
like before you are looking for actual objects. you are never forced to go on one of those overly annoying pixel hunts. for example there's a panel of wood that looks slightly different than the rest of the surface. or you see four knobs and one is shaped a little different.  maybe an ornamentation that is not quite symmetrical. suspicious stuff like that.
i finished the game in 4 hours and it was great fun. like before i would love to see some more rooms as dlc.
sadly there aren't any but for 5 bucks it's perfectly fine.
and again be warned: DO NOT overuse the help button!
you will spoil your own fun by speeding through the game and you will regret it in the end. take your time and enjoy. this is gaming slow food and not yesterday's pizza warmed up in your microwave.
if you have zero patience and you want instant success then this is totally the wrong game for you.

Currently I have just clocked in 17 hours as I write this review.
Firstly I would say that if you are into tycoon games this is a must buy and is hands down my favorite tycoon game for the year, it has been a long time between the last good tycoon game and this one I must say.

Software Inc is an absolute master piece and is only going to get better, when I first watched a "lets play" of this game it was by accident and my first impressions were a little negative based on the current state of the graphics but damn I was wrong and after watching a few videos I was more and more intrigued and really started to warm up to the purchase. It has taken me this long to get my head around the core gameplay as there is a bit of a learning curve but nothing that should prevent you from playing at its full potential.
The gameplay and mechanics have a great amount of depth and work well together and the game is super stable. The ability to build a software company from the ground up is the key nature of this game. You'll build your first office to get started and before long you are running multi stories and building server farms, then there's the employees that are another key aspect. there's not a great deal of objects in yet but what is there is functional and customizable to your chosen color palette(s). Building is pleasurable and the ability to build what you want is huge which brings me to the map size, I would say you will have a hard time filling it especially considering you can go up 10 levels and down 1, the map is massive which gives you free reign to do as you please. I'm hoping to see updated graphics and new objects and styles for customization in future builds.
Now to the core gameplay which is developing software, marketing it and supporting it. There are a number of options for you to choose, maybe an Operating System? (this can take a long time to make) or perhaps a visual program that's linked to a few different OS's? There are different features within your software as well that you can choose to add or not. Put your best design team into action and get that puppy to the development stage, the more time you put in the better the quality, smash the bugs or do half and have your support division take on squashing them as they come up after you've released. Now market the hell out of it until it's not worth it anymore and watch the dollars roll in. Maybe take on some contracts early game to get some funds to kick off that killer program that will launch you into the business world. Once you get your head around multiple teams you could plop down a reception and get paid to develop, design, support or market other companies software. Don't forget to get that server room up and running to help support your online distribution store or for compiling your new code and tackling bugs easier. Maybe you could develop an online OS that requires a server that's running 24/7?
The options in this game are amazing and I haven't seen depth like this in a tycoon game for a number of years, if your on the fence then check out some game play videos on Youtube and check it out. I would say just go ahead and grab it, the price is actually much less than this game is worth for sure.
Oh did I metion the mods that are available and easy to install? Well they add new software development options such as Mobile OS, Web Browsers, Forums, VOIP servers. The list is long and once you get your head around the game I would recommend starting a new game on hard with mods and see how you go.
This game is still in development and can only become exceptional, the tycoon aspects of building a software business are massive with great management aspects all so.

Software inc. is the best simulation game out on steam at the moment. i hope to see more updates and progress the game further and add new items and features. i dont under stand the insurance part of the game, but otherwise great game support

I got these games on a sale a while back and just got to them.. While i would expect it to be longer if I had payed full price for it, I am very impressed with it given what I payed. Its mechanically very similar to Bioshock (i.e. the environment primarily tells the mostly linear story, with scavengable journal entries, and you can use currency to customise your weapons), but the environment and atmosphere are excellently done. Today I finished the entire storyline and oh my god was this game so so so worth it. The graphics are beautiful, even on a mid-range older gaming laptop I still got upwards of 55 fps steady. The storyline is incredible and has the capability to make you feel a real connection to the NPC's that you venture through the tunnels with. The weapons and mechanics are amazing; even on "normal" difficulty ammo is still precious and treated as such, gas masks are vital and rare to come by (I think in the entire storyline I only came across ~10) and most creatures, even the weak ones can kill in 2 or 3 hits. The voice acting and cutscenes are just spot on but overall what made me desire Metro for so long and finally purchace it with money that took me quite a while to scrape together; was the eyecandy value. Graphically, (in my opinion) Metro trumps just about every other game in its category and just goes above and beyond in so many aspects. Even how the monsters and demons are rendered is breathtaking. Each time they appear; its genuinely terrifying because the atmosphere the game projects is just that good. This game immaculately cuts the fine line between easy to pick up game, and gritty realism.
The only dislike I have is that on some earlier parts of the map, its possible to break the barriers and clip outside the render range. Other than that, 0 complaints. Buy this, its worth every penny and more.

If you like story, First Person Shooters, Fallout, Russia and/or Vodka; this is the game for you. As you could probably deduce this game is a story driven FPS set in a post-apocalyptic Russia. It is very well made and I highly recommend it too any gamers out there looking for a good quality single player experience. Not only that but there is a ton of replay ability. While you are forced to follow the same linear story every run through; there are different game modes you can play it on. The first of these game modes is "Survivalist Mode", which limits the amount of ammo, money, health, etc that you receive throughout the game, making it ultimately harder and more stealth based. On the flip side there is a game mode called "Ranger Mode", which give you more ammo, weapons, money and health which makes for an easier more action pact adventure while also making the possibility of stealth much harder. To go along with each game mode there are 4 separate difficulties you can play on either of the game modes and using the power of permutations, there are 8 different ways you can set the difficulty of your run through and almost a limitless number of ways to play through it.
One thing I would recommend you do before buying this game is wait for a major steam sale, due to the fact that the game will fall to about 3 USD compared to its 20 USD normal cost. Also the A.I is kind of derpy at times, but try and this some slack.

The Adjucator had one mission: Make it to the federation base with vital intel. Manned by Captian Chris Philips, Weapons expert Jill, and Ship's Engineer Borman, they embarked on their journey.
Before reaching their halfway point, the nebulous Slug Homeworlds, they hired a new Weapons Expert: Krussy. Jill became the Shield technician after some quick training videos, albet a very clumsy one.
Finally the four of them reached the Slug Homeworlds. They proceeded carefully, aware of the dangers of the nebula. Unfortunatly, they weren't careful enough. They were ambushed by pirates, who hacked and shut off their oxigen. The crew fought valiantly and managed to destroy their enemy, but there wasn't time to repair the oxigen before Philips, Jill, and Borman all suffocated. Krussy was the only one left, the captain of a crewless ship.
He could've left. He had no obligation to continue. The ship was his. But after watching his friends die, gasping for air on the ground, he had to complete their mission. So he took up the controls and engaged the FTL drive. Alone.
He made it out of the nebula and into Rock territory. He had fought at least ten ships alone, but finally he made it to a shop to repair and restock. There he met an Engi known as Rebekka. Rebekka was a pilot by trade, and after listening to Krussy's tale she decided to offer her services for a one time payment of 50 scrap. Krussy gladly accepted, desperately wanting to get back to being a weapons specialist.
It wasn't long until they were out of one rock sector and into another. The Rebels were on their tails and they had to move. Things were going much smoother in battle now that the ship had a proper pilot and Weapons Specialist but it was sorely undermanned.
All was...relatively well until they encountered a strange sight. A Mantis ship had been defeated by Rock pirates and the Rock ship seemed docked to the Mantis one. The Rock ship turned toward them as soon as it noticed their presence. They powered their weapons to engage the Rock pirates and they were ready to fire when they heard the sound of a teliporter in their ship. The Rocks had salvaged the Mantis teliporter and were using it on them! Krussy set the weapons on autofire as Rebekka lept out of her chair to make it to the door control room. Krussy rushed across the ship to join her as she opened the doors that the boarders were in to the cold heart of space. Unfortunately the shield held the atmosphere, but even rock can't survive in an area with no air.
But rock is resiliant. They smashed door after door, looking for the crew. What they found instead was the Oxigen supply to the whole ship. They destroyed it in seconds and moved on.
Krussy and Rebekka knew what had happened when they noticed the air began to thin. They didn't have time to repair the supply because the Rocks were pounding on the door to the Control Room that they were in. Rebekka closed the doors to space to prevent more air from excaping the ship before the Rocks broke in, and then the battle began. Thankfully the Rocks were weakened from their extended period in an airless enviroment, but they still could hit hard. Krussy and Rebekka won, but only barely. They had to repair the oxigen or they would die, but the oxigen was in the section of the ship that they had opened to space. They would have to try to repair it before they ran out of breath.
Outside the port window they watched as the rock ship blew up to the autofire of the weapons. It was a beautiful sight, and possibly the last one they saw. They both took the deepest breath they could, and plunged into the room with the oxigen supply. They tried their hardest to get it back online, but it takes a long time to repair such a thing. Before long, the Adjucator had two more suffocated bodies laying in its depths.
This was a game I actually had. FTL does this thing where tragedy isn't frustraiting to you but instead makes you care more deeply about the characters you have in your care. I really wanted the lonesome Krussy to succeed, knowing it wasn't even his mission he was trying to complete but the mission of his crewmembers. FTL has its problems, yes (mainly its relayance on chance), but its a very well done and impactful game.

This game could've been one of my favorites and it looked GREAT, but if this game were a circus act, it would've fallen down in seconds, why? because what does this game and cirrcus acts need to do well, balance, this game doesn't have that
First lets go over the nice things about the game, which to be fair, it does have nice things
Soundtrack-Its soundtrack is simple yet catchy, a  jazzy/classic/piano style hybrid of music, with the same flow as Cook Serve Delicious (In terms of the soundtrack itself and pace)  to compare music (gets hectic at the right times, and gets you immersed
Good Controls and overall good mechanics-For the most part the game's mechanics and ins and outs seem simple to understand, but difficult to master, as thats the vibe I get from the game, and thats a good sign for a challenging  rouge like "simple looking, but complex and deep on the inside" for lack of a better term
Where the game falls is how the mechanics are actually IMPLEMENTED AND EXECUTED (Big letters=emphasis btw) which in turns creates a domino effect causing balance issues
Here's the rundown
You have a time limit to complete objectives, such as rescue trapped people, turn off power,. then put fires out, or just put all the fires out. During this, you also need to manage your water and fire extingusiher "foam" for lack of a better term, as there are two types of fires, "normal" which use water to put out, and electric fires from machinery/devices (i.e. a computer, pop machine. generator etc...)  which takes a fire extinguisher
But the problem is, you can pass out and lose a life if you are around fire too long, which in my opinion is EXTREMELY unbalanced and almost DEFEATS THE PURPOSE of the game, (I get it being a firefighter can actually cause things like this, but with video games you don't always need to be 100% accurate as long as the games fun)
Not to mention, you constantly have to look for water resources or foam resources to refil your water or extinguisher which are particularrly located at random rooms on the map, all while being on the clock and worry about the possibility of fires "re-growing" and spreading around again
This is where balance is a problem, you either pass out because your rushing for resources to complete the objectives in enough time, or  your trying to stop fires from re-growing and other fires end up consuming the building or distract you from other objectives, not to mention all your resources get used on one "patch" of flame
A better way to balance the game could've easily been modes (a more relaxed mode, one without a time limit, an endless mode etc) NO PASS OUT METER (It's more a foe than a game mechanic) and power ups
Think of it this way, to compare, how hard would Mega Man be with no health or ammo power ups except a few big ones at each part of the stage, and you'd be timed
That's this game's problem
GREAT CONCEPT AND EXCELLENT IDEAS
Jumbled/rushed execution  and bad balancing, the game simply asks for too much in so little time
Pity, becase the game had EXTREME potential and I was very excited at first ):

I thought this might be an interesting variation on all the monster bashing of the other twin-stick games I've loved (Nuclear Throne, Binding of Isaac Rebirth, A Wizard's Lizard), but... somehow it feels /grim/. Innocent victims dying on you. Bodies littering the floor. Fire overwhelming you from all sides. And no break from it--no enemies with motivations--just a primal natural force destroying everything in its path, and never stopping. Never letting up. When your enemy is a natural force, and the logic of its progress is so often hard to make sense of, you get a game that feels fatalistic. Your mileage may vary, but this is how the game hits me. If the fire mechanics were rebalanced, maybe it would feel like less of a losing proposition, and it would be more fun to pick up the fight.
That's not the only dealbreaker here. The right stick moves both the camera AND the direction you face/aim. I'm not sure what's behind this choice. It confused me, at first, even making me think there was no true aim independent of the direction you're moving. I got a little more used to it, but I never enjoyed the way the character controlled.
I really dig the idea behind this game, and my hopes were pretty high. It's actually kinda nice that it's not kill, kill, kill. But--on the other hand--fighting one faceless enemy that pops up at random again on the other side of the room after you make a little progress...? The fun factor was low for me.

I cannot believe I was on the fence regarding whether or not to buy this game.  This game is great.  A few items to consider:
1)  If you do not like chaos, this is not the game for you.  I have died upon initial landing on a world due to another player landing on top of me.  I chuckled, then chortled, then gufawed.
Another time, we are fighting off 200 units of the Illuminate, we are half way home, then a player joins us, lands on top of my son, and suddenly our defense collapsed.
2)  Can some players solo very difficult challenges?  Sure, but the focus of the game is the coordinated mayhem of playing with a group.  I play with my 2 boys on a single machine.  Online play is seemless, but that is the focus of the game.  I do some solo drops to test out weapons, etc., but the fun is to be had with other players.
3)  You can complete all mission objectives, but unless at least one player leaves the mission in the shuttle, the mission will fail.  That 200 creep defense mission I mentioned before?  It took us about 10 tries to get it right.
4)  The screen is locked, you are not totally omniscient.  You cannot join a team and go Rambo style to another objective, you must stay with the team.
5)  Online play is seemless.  I play a lot of MOBAs and have not played as much lately due to lag.  This game is seamless.  I have yet to see as much as a stutter on screen.  Great job by the developers.
6)  I would suggest unlocking equipment rather than buying the DLCs all at once.  Part of the fun, to me, is grinding towards that next shiny weapon.  Figuring out how to use in it a fight.  Most weapons seem to be balanced (although I am no where close to unlocking everything), the Scythe works great against the bugs, but is poor against the Illuminate.  The basic AR is a solid gun, but you need to fire in bursts, not on full auto, etc.
7)  Expounding upon the Rambo statement, if you run through a mission heedless of enemy patrols, you will die.  And you will die again.  And again.  And again, or until everyone has their reinforcement stratagem on cooldown, and you will each die one final time.  The last one, mere seconds before the cooldown on reinforcement comes back online.
Unlike games that have great systems, but lack cohesion overall, I feel this game is greater than the sum of its parts.

I started out playing Helldivers on PS4, and this game was honestly one of the reasons I picked up the console. I was thrilled to see it released on PC and couldn't resist grabbing it here too—and at full price, which is a rarety for me and that alone should speak volumes as high praise.
Know that this game really shines when playing with others. It works as a single player game but can be very challening. However, when you have a full complement of players it's at its best. However, nothing holds a candle to being knee-deep in bug guts with close friends. Helldivers is a shining example of the reason you play games with friends. Everything in the game is leathal to everyone else I've laughed plenty of times when a friend's drop pod lands right on me squashing me instantly like a bug, or he accidently steps on me in a mech leaving me a stain on his big metal foot.
The game harkens back to one my favorite games, Alien Swarm. Alien Swarm was a free game released years ago here on Steam (and is still available). Helldivers is a true spirital successor that game and incorporates the chase for new cool gear and leveling while battling hordes of rentless enemies.
The missions have diverse and creative objectives that don't easily tire. The arrow seqeunces used to call in support objects and interact with missions are a neat innovation and trying to correctly enter them to diffuse a bomb while enemies are bearing down on you is a fantastic thrill. Tension rides high as you are the last one standing, running crazy knowing that the sucess of the mission rides on you finding a spare five seconds to enter in a key combo to respawn your teammates and save the mission.
Helldivers has a great Starship Troopers and Warhammer 40K vibe with a healthy dose of humor. The art is wonderful too, with diverse planets and enjoyable vehicles, weaponary, and enemies.
I highly respect the approach to selling the game too. If you're uncertain, you can lay down $20 and easily get your money's worth with the game. All of the base content will make you a solid contribution to a team. Paid DLC unlocks more cool options for the game but isn't strictly better than the content that comes in the base game. This is pass number #1 of my review of "The Vanishing of Ethan Carter". I'm going to break this up into a few different categories.
Graphics: Some of the best I've seen. Beautiful environments that seem close to photo realistic. Truly remarkable. HOWEVER this seems to be a pretty poorly optimized game. I run the game at a constant 60 FPS however I get an almost unbearable "micro-stutter". I have went through hours of forums and tried several different methods; editing the ini, turning on / off smoothing etc. Nothing seems to help. Sadly I feel like this is unacceptable. When you buy a game you shouldn't have to spend hours editing .ini files trying to make it work.
Sound: Wonderful melodic soundtrack is married with well done (if a little underutilized) voice work. Can't complain on this end at all! Well done.
Story: I haven't beaten the game yet (mostly because I have spent so much time trying to make it work); however the story is very intriguing and reminiscent of a Lovecraftian tale! Certainly keeps the momentum going. Can't wait to continue.
Overall thoughts: I'm currently giving this game a thumbs down. Not because I don't think this game isn't great; it certainly is; potentially could go down as one of my favorites. However the amount issues are insane! Launcher didn't work, controller didn't work, constant stutter and audio locked a low volume. All of these issues are fixable (except for stutter as far as I'm concerned)  however you have to waste WAY to much time making this work. It's a bummer these issues bring down such a remarkable game. I'll edit this review once I finish the title.

Okay. I'll try to get the most out of my review to make it as understandable as possible. (EDIT: SPELLING AND GRAMMAR)
The voice acting was good enough. Not perfect, but it was a great addition to the game that made it a lot more inmersive.
The story was interesting and thrilling.
Great range of possibilities, different endings, and all of that.
The art was fine. Enough. Not HuniePop quality, but enough.
The voice acting, altough good from some of the characters, (Suzu, Jason, Erik, etc), some others were a bit too weird to be taken seriously. (Both devils being the ones in my mind) Also, the protagonist desperately needs a voice actress. It totally killed the inmersion that every other character has an actor and she did not.
The story felt rushed. And a lot. It could've been a lot longer and it had several characters that could've been a great addition, only if they were developed a bit more.
The art, although not perfect, was fine. Enough. There were certain parts were the bodies were just weird. (I'm looking at you, undershot of Diana)
I feel the thing that definetly must be taken into account in the next installment (being sure that there will be, "Seduce Me 2: The Demon Wars") is that the story must stop being a girly fantasy of hot demons and lesbo desires and actually take itself serious. And I think this Issue has a lot to do with the writer, Michala Laws, as I saw in her Tumbrl that se was a
inexpirienced writer/artist and needs to work a lot to improve on her artsy ways. (I know this got personal but trust me, I've been were she is, and I mean it when I say that she needs to put her pride away and accept that she actually needs improvement). More character development, (an example could be Lisette, K, or Andrew) And WAY more background troughout the story (Again, making every scene longer and more in depth)
So, all in all, I enjoyed the game a lot, for a free game, I really got more than I was expecting. Because of this, I'm really struggling to pick a side, recommended or not recommended.
But I'm a good guy, so, knowing that this is a free game and I enjoyed it, It stays on recommended. 6/10.

I originally watched TB's 15 Minutes of Game on this and thought I would enjoy it. Happily for me, I was right.
This game is the perfect mixture of easy mechanics but hard gameplay, I like dying by my own stupidity instead of not understanding the controls/mechanics. Don't get me wrong, there's a bit of trial and error when you first arrive at a new section of the game - most notably the lab. Just know that green fire = hose, green gas = extinguish.
I love the cheery music/art style, I'm a fan of the non-pixelated cartoon look in games (Spelunky has a very similar 2D version to this look). I think it's easy to look at it and think oh it's not that hard. Yes it's hard, don't get it if you don't want a challenge. Or are okay staying in the Office levels forever. I think the contrast between difficulty and theme is interesting and works.
One thing I would have added was the possibility to save and quit your progress at the start of each level. I understand you can start at the beginning of each section, but you are at a disadvantage not having access to the shop in the early levels and multiple achievements require a full playthrough. I want to be able to play for a while, save, then start up again right where I was. To avoid save scumming the developer could make it a one time only save. I think it would add to the longterm replayability of this game since it takes about 45 to an hour per playthough.
Overall I love putting out fires, the music is cheery and somehow doesn't grow old despite being fairly repetitive. I would get this on sale though since all but the most obsessive will probably only put a few hours in before getting frustrated/bored.

The levels are procedurally generated, slapping rooms together in different layouts, which is a plus for newness each time. Each of the different zones has a diferent feel to them. On each floor that contains the electrical type fires, there's a power room where you can shut down the power and nullify them all as being "electrical fires" so you can just put them out with water. Unfortunately every fire spews out fireballs every other second directly at you. I want to say literally, but it might be every

Half-Life 2: Episode One begine right where Half-Life 2 ended, and continues the story of Dr.Gordon Freeman in City 17, however, this time, the priority remains to escape the city following the events of Half-Life 2.
With updated lighting and AI for deuteragonist Alyx Vance, and expanded usage for the Gravity Gun, Half-Life 2: Episode One continues Half-Life 2's usage of advanced graphics, physics, music and writing to create a game that is both rich in gameplay, plot, and emotion. Like its predecessor, it uses training techniques to allow for a more fluid experience, and utilizes the game's physics engine to a full. With excellent performances by its cast, it's able to greatly explain the story of Gordon and Alyx escaping City 17.
With an excellent soundtrack composed by Kelly Bailey, the game becomes even more action packed, and the act of blasting zombies in an infected hospital with a shotgun becomes far more enjoyable, and the scene of fighting infected Combine soldiers in the underground becomes more threatening.
The game also includes Developer commentary in the form of a commentary mode that allows the players to listen to the developers' thoughts on everything from map design to character and scene writing, and includes all variant of Valve Employee sharing their thoughts on the game.
If I had to say I had any issues with the game, I'd have to say that it's fairly short, while Half-Life 2 is around 12-15 hours long, Episode One is around 5 hours long. That's not to say it's a bad game for that, though, as the story and game runs at a certain pace that allows for it to be enjoyed to the fullest; Replaying the game with the knowledge of how short it is doesn't damage or reduce the enjoyment of playing it, as Valve injects a great deal of fun into the game so there aren't many moments or time that is wasted, and every minute is used to its fullest.
If you enjoyed Half-Life 2, and want more, I greatly suggest you buy the
Steam bundle, preferably during a Steam Seasonal Sale. The bundle consists of this game and every other Valve-released Half-Life title, and is an essential for a fan of Half-Life.
Don't call yourself a Gamer if you didn't play Half-Life.

This was a pretty stellar exploration game. You play as Paul Prospero, a sort of psychic detective hired by what is presumably a dead Ethan Carter to investigate his disappearance and a number of murders in a small mountain/lake/mining town.
The dynamic for revealing the pattern of each murder and finding certain clues was really cool. Basically, each piece of evidence allows you to peek a little bit more into the past until you finally unlock sequences of memories that, after putting them in the proper order, reveal what happened for each murder/disappearance. However, that is still just a small part of what this game is about. As you find pieces of stories Ethan wrote, you often unlock other sequences that end in reveals that further send you along your path of investigation.
Attention to detail is important with this game. There are subtle cues that let you know sort of where to look or what you might have missed. These largely take the part of weird flashes in the distance. You can also easily find yourself wandering around wondering what to do next, but overall, once I grew familiar with the game and started to take note of the cues, my experience was far more straightforward. Of course, by that time, I had spent plenty of time enjoying the amazing graphics this game boasts. The game is truly beautiful, and attention was spent giving everything the little details that really breathed life into this game. From little nests to birdstains and moss on rocks, weather worn surfaces, and so on, this game really nailed it on a visual level. In this regard, it boasts similarities to Dear Esther, for example, but in a far superior fashion.
The music was also excellent, and ofttimes completely creepy. You start wondering when some crazy creature is going to jump out at you or some beast is going to start gnawing on your body, lol. Really, really atmospheric music that adds to the mystery and sometimes tension of the game.
As far as the story itself, it was also really well thought out. At the end, you kind of have to chuckle a little bit even as you feel completely saddened by the revealed source of everything that was happening in the game. The whole time, it keeps you guessing a bit, and then once the final reveal happens, you start having personal revelations akin to having watched the Sixth Sense for the first time (in that all the seemingly disparate events all tie together at the end and seem obvious in retrospect).
I found this to be a thoroughly enjoyable experience and one I can easily recommend to anybody who loves games (and especially exploration/mystery type experiences).
I give this ten "solved murders and creepy piano runs that sort of make you jump" out of ten.

The succubi route however, deinitely has enough in it to make an entirely seperate game, and it'd be totally awesome if there was a spin-off with more succubi routes, but that probably won't happen.
The human routes also leave something to be desired and end way faster than the demon routes. The game IS meant to be truly supernatural , but I almost wish those routes didn't exist because they're so lackluster.

I've played other otome with at least slightly more diversity. For a game that's trying to do something unique, they really failed me on that part.
Overall, I wouldn't really recommend this, but it's short enough that if you want to play all the routes, it won't take you 10 years to get through all of it.

+ The Blooper reel is also fantastic and hilarious and I suggest giving it a listen. Can be found in "Extras" on the menu. You can tell they all had such a good time with the game and that makes me happy to know the love that went into this game.
+ Good story. Not super intricate or original, but it was fun and it was entertaining. Same goes with the writing of the characters. There were cliches, but they were the good kind, not the bad, and I found most of it endearing rather than annoying or over-used.
+ I spent 3 hours on one route which is a decent length for an otome. Not the longest, but certainly not the shortest.
+ Good amount of choices which are helpful in developing the story. You get to choose exactly who you want, and how you want your MC to be. Probably in the overall story the choices weren't amazingly important, but there's 22 endings so who knows?
+ Did I mention this beautiful bundle is free? Because it is. So if you're poor, get on this immediately.
- No voice acting for MC. It broke immersion when it was her turn to speak when everyone else can. A voice for her would have helped conversations flow better. Despite this, I understand why she did not have a voice, for people to identify with her more and also to make it easier for branching choices that you select. Unfortunately, while a silent protagonist can work in games such as Dragon Age: Origins, it really didn't work for the game here.
- The art style is simple. Not fantastic. There are problems with proportions and characters can often look strange. The backgrounds were sometimes not even art, but real pictures. These things don't bother me much and really didn't ruin my gameplay, but everyone is different and good art is important to a lot of people, especially in a VN. If you were looking for outstanding artwork, this isn't the game for you. It is still nice to look at. Not the worst i've seen by far.
- Music doesn't seem to loop often. Often I found there were random silences where it felt there should have been music.
- Mallix's (Is that his name?) motivation for hating the guys didn't seem clear to me. Not sure if it was explained and i'm dumb or it's explained in another route, but I cannot figure out why he was after the guys. Because he was a devil? Not enough for me. Needed more focus on his character.
Overall, it's a good, entertaining, free-of-charge time. It was cute. I blushed once or twice. There was definite seducing.
8/10 would get seduced again.

Summary (for tl;dr readers):
I love this game! It's innovative yet keeping within the core practices of old-school roguelikes. Play it for at least 10-15 hours to truly appreciate it. 9/10.
Pros:
-Beautiful ASCII art
-Wonderful soundtrack
-In-depthmechanics and gradual learning curve
-An old-school roguelike that is not a clone of Angband/Nethack/ADOM
-Funny
-Good crafting system
-Solid RPG elements
-Good replayability
Cons:
-It could do with some more content and rebalancing
-The story is a bit lacking
-The encounters (events) can get a bit too random
Possible caveats (i.e. things you might either love or hate):
-Absolutely unforgiving (in non-softcore modes)
-Repetitive combat (it's a design choice, but it can get frustrating)
-The community is rather small
-Very different from Angband/Nethack/ADOM, and somewhat less in-depth
-No new-school roguelike progression (a la Rogue Legacy), but progressing in the game will unlock new options
-It has a weird obsession with potatoes
Detailed review:
Sanctuary RPG is an ASCII roguelike that does not follow the steps of Angband/ADOM/Nethack, so if that is what you are expecting you might be disappointed. The exploration is done via menu choices, rather than moving your character around a map, and so is the combat, dialogue, and pretty much everything else. The immersion is achieved, instead, through some rather stunning ASCII art, an absolutely outstanding soundtrack, and various interactions with enemies and NPCs. The game mechanics, and various menus, are complex enough to keep things interesting throughout the game, but not so much to become overwhelming; this is also achieved by new features, skills, and areas becoming gradually available as your character levels up.
If what you are missing, however, is the unforgiving nature of old roguelikes, then look no further. Sanctuary RPG looks deceptively friendly at first, with its light humour and digestible chunks of text, but the moment you get distracted or overconfident, you're dead, no mater how overpowered you felt ten seconds ago. The game is rather difficult to master, not because the underlying mechanics are complicated, but because you have to be very careful with all your decisions, just like in any old roguelike worth its salt. I have played it for over 20 hours and never managed to get past act 2. For those looking for a less frustrating experience, the game also has a softcore mode, with reduced loot drops and no permadeath.
As some reviewers have mentioned, the combat does get a bit repetitive, again, like in any old-school roguelike, and that is exactly how most of my characters meet their untimely demise: I get distracted and miss a crucial step to heal or use an ability. This is a design choice, I believe, and one I understand and accept, however much it frustrates me to lose my precious wizards to it again and again.
Some of the text could do with a spell check, but there are no major grammatical mistakes, just a couple of sentences here and there that sound a bit odd. As much as the content has grown and been improved over the last year or so, I would love to see more dialogue choices for the NPCs you meet in every adventure, as those get a bit old after a while and lack depth. I also feel that some of the randomly generated loot needs a bit of a rebalance, but that may also be a design choice to prevent characters from getting too strong too quickly.
I think my main gripe is with the small size of the community that plays this game. It is very difficult to find guides, and even the wiki is barely there. As such, it is rather difficult to compare strategies with other players. Many players seem to abandon this game after a few hours, which I think isn't anough to fully appreciate it. And while it is fun, and in-theme with the old-school roguelike vibe (I didn't have walkthroughs for Angband back in the 90s!) to discover the game by trial and error, sometimes it also gets a bit frustrating.
All in all, however, I truly love this game. It's balanced, it's fun, and it's unforgiving in a very familiar way, while also being surprisingly innovative. If any of its elements appeal to you, you can't go wrong for that price, give it a chance. And get the soundtrack too! :)

If you’re like me there was a part of your childhood where you wanted to be a fire fighter. It’s one of the most common career ambitions among children around the world. And why wouldn’t it be? You get to save lives, be a hero and of course the chicks always dig the man in the uniform. It’s not until a little later in life that we realize that the goal isn’t as realistic as what we would have hoped. Our dreams dashed because it’s either too difficult to become a firefighter or the reality that you’d be putting your own life in danger too regularly scared the living daylights out of you and you reassessed your position. But now there is a way that you can live out your childhood dreams and be a firefighter. You’re still putting your lives on the line but this time its the virtual lives of the character that you play. That’s with Flame Over one of Laughing Jackal’s games on Steam and our first of three of their games over the next three days.
At it’s heart Flame Out is a top down shooter that has been designed in the form of a fire fighting game. The levels almost play out as puzzles whereby you need to determine whether you need to hose certain areas with water or extinguish them with foam. The game plays out as a real fire would for example foam is the only thing that will put out electrical fires. The game isn’t easy but it’s an enjoyable challenge that will have you learning its systems relatively quickly. I do recommend that you first playthrough the tutorial and understand the basic gameplay concepts and mechanics. It’s a different enough game that it really should be mandatory otherwise it’s likely that you will find yourself dying quickly and often when it comes to the legitimate levels, of which there are 16, in the game.
I was a big fan of the game’s presentation starting with the music and the comic stylistics of the graphics. It’s loaded chock full of charm that will take your breath away. When gameplay does get underway after the cool introduction it puts you in head first. It’s not easy from the beginning and you should take this as a sign of things to come. Other than just putting out and extinguishing fires you will have to do your job and save the myriad numbers of civilians that are spread out throughout each level. You need to do this concurrently to putting out the fires because each time you do you are awarded with an  extra minute of time to complete the level.
The physics are pretty spectacular in the game as well. You’ll think that you’re on top of the fire and then holy shitburgers something you had forgotten about has shot a fireball restarting the blaze somewhere else. Thus you’re going to want that extra time I just told you about because fires will restart seemingly at will unless you’re super careful and Super Blazed. The blazing trail of destruction left by the fireballs will have you raging but will also aide you in becoming a better, smarter player. In that way the game asks a lot from your gaming ability but once you do learn you’ll feel as though you’ve grown as a player not only of this game but of others as well. I believe it takes a good game to do that.
This is one of those games that people will cry ‘rogue-like’ and where Total Biscuit’s discussion video about gaming terms he’d like people to avoid fits right in. Yes, it’s brutally difficult. Yes, it has some of the trademarks that would fit the genre but at the same time I wouldn’t classify it as a rogue-like. What I would classify it as is a bloody good game that you should at the very least try.

Whether I would enjoy Helldivers was a question that lasted the fifteen seconds it took me to deploy from my ship to a mission. I inexpertly chose to helldive in the middle of an objective – a SAM site I had to reactivate in order to help the war effort against the Bugs – and what that meant was the moment I came out of my pod I was swarmed by crawling insects, desperately trying to bludgeon and fire my way away from them before activating. I survived, because democracy must be brought to everyone.
Helldivers is a game version of Starship Troopers, to explain the sentence above. You are a highly armed, entirely disposable marine from Super Earth, whose job is to spread freedom and democracy to the melee-centered Bugs (yes, that’s how they’re called), the tech-heavy, shield-using Illuminate and the also heavily armed Cyborgs. You do this by killing them by the thousands with guns aptly named ‘Double Freedom’ and ‘Patriot’, all the while screaming one-liners like “FREEEEDOM!”. Other references to Starship Troopers abound in the introductory cinematic and the dialogue you can have with the other military personnel aboard your ship, though there’s no plot-depth to speak of – there’s a war and you need to win it.
From your hub you will upgrade your weapons and stratagems, change your perks and, of course, customize your clothes (Helldivers evidently wear capes, because why not), and once all that is done you can choose which enemy you’ll face and what planet you’ll helldive onto. The war effort is essentially a cooperative one, as each of your and other helldivers’ actions on a front add points to a bar that, once full, will allow you to besiege the enemy’s home planet and terminate him for the remainder of the war period (or if you allow them to push the front, they will besiege your capital planet and you shall need to defend it).
The missions themselves can be carried out by one to four people, with more helldivers equaling more and tougher enemies, and get increasingly hectic with both amount of players and mission difficulty. Arrowhead’s past with Magicka is clearly here: from the frequent friendly fire – you’ll often shoot your friends to death or deploy exosuits and turrets on top of them, spelling their demise, though they won’t be stuck in boredom for too long, as you can quickly and easily re-deploy them – to the key combinations that you’ll use to call in a wide range of stratagems, from fly-by shootings and tactical nukes to shoulder-mounted flamethrowers and motorcycles.
The objectives of each mission are varied and intuitive, and you’ll see yourself having to use your abilities in different ways as you defend an area for a set amount of time, escort a group of friendlies to an extraction point or search a small field for ordnance you need to disarm. The means to carry out these missions also increases greatly as you gain experience and research points, not only unlocking new weapons, stratagems and perks but improving said weapons and stratagems to further flesh out their uniqueness. I found the progression system to be particularly good, as I never felt like I was playing to progress, but rather progressing as a consequence of playing – the variety of enemies, planets and their hazards (from frozen wastelands and boggy swamps that slow you down to volcanic regions that spew fire) and tools to deal with them means you have to alter your loadout according to necessity, as each faction plays differently and is susceptible to certain tactics and weapons.
While it isn’t particularly good-looking, with relatively simplistic graphics implemented (likely due to its presence on the PSVita), Helldivers is far from an eye-sore, and once you’re in motion – deploying bombs and in gunfights – the lack of detail becomes hard to notice. The sound design, on the other hand, is superb: meaty sound effects and visceral noises play appropriately according to who you shoot and what you shoot them with, each weapon having a distinctive and recognizable sound that ramps up according to its firepower.
Helldivers is a simple game, but what it does it does well. With little down-time within and between missions you’ll constantly be in the thick of combat, praying that neither foe nor friend kill you, laying down democracy at whatever rate of fire your weapon has. A quick to join and easy to use multiplayer interface means your friends and strangers can easily drop in and out of your games, no hassle involved, and while you can certainly enjoy it alone Helldivers shines when
you and your buddies help each other, frantically trying to stave off hordes of enemies before making a heroic escape on the dropship. And remember: it doesn’t matter if you’re panicking, don’t ♥♥♥♥ing friendly-fire me with your rocket launcher.

Where do I start?
Pros

~ The characters have their own abilities and obsticles in gameplay that is just assigned to them e.g. Finn with his gas mask, Rey with her staff, etc.
~ You can walk around the whole millineum falcon, need I say more?
~ I LOVED walking  and exploring StarKiller Base and Jakku
~ Graphics are actually really good for a lego game
~ The actors have actually voiced their characters from the film which is soooooooo cool! Daisy Ridley as Lego Rey is so calming and adorable
~ There are added (canon) lines in the game that are not present in the film but in the novelisation which is one of my favourite aspects.
~ The film's soundtrack is played throughout gameplay
~ The characters actually talk to you and help you along the way
~ There are special levels where you get to play in the perspective of Kylo Ren and the first order.
~ Sassy Lego Kylo Ren with his perfectly conditioned hair and beauty spot ;-) ....and his DARTH VADER BEDROOM AND SHOES?!
~ ....Lego Rey....just when I thought she couldn't get anymore adorable
~ It is super easy to get 'True Jedi' which is the best hahaha
~ I love how you can match characters in a party together.
~ There are so many characters you can be.
~ The achievements to this game are hilarious, especially the one where you have to destroy things as Kylo Ren
~ There is so much to do in this game for just one movie, it is honestly so awesome
~ Lego Maz is so tiny and cute
~ I bought the season pass and I can play as Anakin aswell as my badass girl Ventress!!
~ The return of Stormtroopers in pools, yeahhhh!
~ I GOT CHEWIE A BUNCH OF WOOKIE COOKIES! <3
CONS
~ The crashes. They haven't happened that much for me but when it does, it is really annoying because it exits your game suddenly without warning. I had to do one of the Space battles FIVE times as Poe because of it.
~ BB8...okay look, he is cute and all but the amount of times I had to use him in EVERY SINGLE PART OF THE GAMEPLAY IN STORY MODE annoyed me SO BAD. Every time I realised I had to use him again, I was rolling my eyes and sinking in my seat of frustration and bordem.

~ Versing various bosses such as Kylo Ren and Palpatine was just TOO DAMN EASY! All you did was press ONE BUTTON multiple times, I found myself cringing at how easy it was.

If you ever dreamed of an action-arcade game where LMB is pretty much the only control, you might enjoy this game. The enemies, bosses, and how they interact with the environment are really the highlights of the gameplay. However, one minor setback is that there's no "Restart level" option, which is something that has become expected in similar arcade-based games.
I wouldn't say the bosses are Nintendo-hard, but they are pattern-based, which can be a bit of a jump from the button-mashing that the game establishes. The game basically forces you to restart from checkpoint when you die, so even if you were doing well in a level and get whooped by the boss (which isn't always easy to predict), you'll still end up with a D grade. It's like taking a course where all the assignments are straightforward, and suddenly the instructor gives you a pop quiz with totally new material worth 50% of your grade.
Apart from this minor complaint, there is little else wrong with the game. I would recommend it for everything it does right -- the simple cathartic pleasure of beating things up, the music, graphics, and the style-over-substance story (which actually works in a game like this). If you enjoyed the demo, then you wouldn't be doing yourself a disservice to pick this one up.
