Game runs great too.

So I dumped 6 hours into the game, crashed and burned several times, and now ended up with a $550M in cash and $1B in stocks.
The early parts of the game are very well developed with a good balance of macro/micromanagement. I think the game just needs more polish since many of the interfaces are extremely clunky. I despise those silly radial menues that are so hard to control. They remind me too much of Castle Story.
I also think there is serious feature creep. If I was making this game in the game, it would be a medium scope game with recommended 5 developers being written by a single dev. Stuff like distribution and project/hr management are really good ideas but the amount of code required to make them functional/useful/interesting would far exceed the scope of this game.
Here's some more of my opinions/advice for the developer
-I don't think a UML minigame is medium priority, more low priority.
-Need way better server management system, I mean come on you can't be seriously asking me to manually place 200 servers
-Need better furniture management system, I mean come on you can't be seriously asking me to manually move 200 servers
-IT requirements are too low. I have a ton of servers all managed by one IT guy who works only 4 hours a day.
-AI companies are really weak, by year 4 I was worth double any other company in the game
-There's an opportunity to develop a really cool financial system - play Railroad Tycoon II to get a feel of what I'm talking about. The current system is a bit lacking.
-I don't think loans scale up. The max I could ever borrow is 100K.
-Salary management is a massive hassle. I find myself just hitting accept & close every time because manually going through 50 employees is not worth the 5K/month.
There's a lot of other stuff but the main point is that the game is already pretty fun, don't ruin it with features you can't implement right that will crash/bug out the game.
Congrats on going full time, I envy you.

This game is about as good as first person platformers are gonna get. The controls are tight, and the movement is very fluid. Some of the puzzles can take a lot of deaths to figure out, so I wouldn't recommend this game for the easily frustrated. I swore more than a times while playing it, but it was never the game's fault, I was just trying to brute force through the game instead of finding the correct path.
Most of the game centers around the grappling gun mechanics and that's where most of the challenges come from. It's a lot of fun flying through the air, and taking multiple paths to get to the same destination. Though I did have occasional trouble telling the difference between large objects in the background and small objects in the foreground. The game is reasonably forgiving with lots of checkpoints and I feel like the game gives you quite a bit of leeway when it comes to some of the momentum puzzles. The character animations were a little clunky at times, but the background scenes and stages were absolutely gorgeous.
I'd recommend this game if you enjoy games like Gone Home and Dear Esther, but wished that a couple minutes in you could swing around at hundreds of miles per hour like Spiderman.

Flame Over is cheap, decent fun in the vein of Human Entertainment's "The Firemen" for SNES (though with a much lighter sense of humour).
The good:
* Easy grasp gameplay
* Good replayability
* Novel core concept
The bad:
* A camera rotation system that adds nothing to the game, save low key annoyance
* Low quality AI (including fire AI, which considers rooms at the end of a hall "nearby" for the purpose of throwing fireballs)
* Some issues with gameplay refinement (The same amount of water is more or less effective depending on how you aimed the stream. It takes some calibration to learn how to apply your tools)
Overall, it's pretty good, but the little details will nibble at your enjoyment. And, this may be personal preference, but the slapstick angle of the game doesn't work as well as the much more serious and heroic tone of it's spiritual predecessor "The Firemen" (which, if you enjoy this game, is well worth your time to buy/emulate/whatever. It's better, if not nearly so replayable).

First, I have a piece of advice for the people who complain that the zombies are too hard:
AIM.
That's one thing I love about this game.
Want to knock that zombie down so he doesn't get back up? Slide into him and kick his legs. They break and he falls over. Or he falls and busts his head open and insta-dies.
Is that zombie carrying a weapon?
Aim for his hand or chop his arm off.
Have an electrified weapon?
Toss some conductive liquid onto the zombie and fry him like a toaster in a bathtub.
Most of these complaints are people who played a few minutes or hours of the game and have tried hacking away at a zombie with a butter knife. Find a few good materials. Craft something fun. The developers made a TON of fun weapons to craft and their killing/maiming effects are phenomenal.
I love this game because it genuinely gets me spooked: that under-the-skin type of scary where you just need to turn the game off for a few minutes because the girl on the radio just reminded you the sun's about to set.
The sun dips to the horizon.
There's a bone-shattering scream.
The birds all fly away.
The only light visible now are the burning barrels and burning cars.
The wind blows a can across the sidewalk.
A text box appears:
NIGHT IS COMING
Most fun I've had with multiplayer in a long time. Be sure to say "Watch out!" 100 times before anyone actually watches out.

This game is just awesome to me...... though it has it's shining moments while having moments I think could be tweaked. So let me get started by saying I do love this game, though probably not as much as I love Nameless. Now on to a real review.
CONS: The voice acting for the females could use a lot of work. I have sensitive ears so I had to skip over them a lot just so I wouldn't wince. That being said I did love the male voice acting. Could use some older sounding guys for father figures though. The fathers {Both MC's and the boys'} and MC's grandfather came off a little too young sounding.
Some of the art was a bit off putting. I noticed it most with Damien and James honestly. The others art was pretty good though it could use a little cleaning.
Dunno why Lisette was even in game, considering she took no part in everything other than to pick on the character. That being said I think I would have been more ok with her if she had been tied to Malix some how. It would have made her part make a bit more sense in the long run.
I kinda have to agree with others that the writing did seem a bit repetitive. I would have liked to have seen at least one of the guys question the MC after her confession, just to make it seem more realistic. That being said the guys having such varied personalities was a good start to that, with James being so serious, Erik so flirty, and so on. I beleive a few tweaks could have made the game slightly more enjoyable.
PROS: The fight scenes...... Like seriously I can't write a fight scene to save my life but the ones written for the guys were just perfect to me. And the fact if you call for one of the two youngest one of their older brothers take their place was a great way to deal with them not being the ones beside you.
Not all the VA was bad at all. In fact what pulled me in was Erik introducing the game. As I said before I only had an issue with the high pitch of most of the females and with how older men sounded too young.
I do like the fact you can pick how you want to commit, whether to be seduced or to just be held. It shows a respect for both the MC and to the guys.
OK this is the main selling point to me honestly and most might disagree....... THE HERIONE ISN'T A DELICATE FLOWER! Seriously, while I adore Dandelion and Nameless, the herione is always some delicate flower who needs the guys. In Seduce Me the girl has a backbone, cusses out her enemies, and even though she is only a frail human stands up to Malix and Diana. We need more lead characters like this, that even though they fall in love they have opinions and a backbone to stand up for others.
All in all yes I would recomend this game. So what if the art style is a little wonky and the girls a bit too squeaky? The story is great, the MC isn't some shy wilting flower, and the writing{while repetitive} is actually really decent.

I've seen a lot of people complain about the quality of the art. For a free game, I felt the art was fine, and I thought the voice actors did a decent job as well. However, the writing was pretty awful. The entire story felt like an uneditted slab of fanfiction written by a fourteen year old girl. The details were too wordy, repetitious, and nonsensical.
I also felt like the main character (you) had zero development and were forced into a rather adolescent personality. In the beginning, the writer tried to give you choices to tease out a "unique" personality, like which friend to side with or what food to select, whether to pick a fight or not... But that quickly ends and you just turn into an angry teenager. The glaring and fury that went on was borderline ridiculous. I understand it's a VN and freeware, but it's not that hard to write a few extra paths of slightly varied dialogue to flush out a few personality types... Not to mention that the writer kept having the main character come off as surprised whenever a guy showed his attraction or love for her. Every... single... time. It made me feel completely stupid. What? He's shoved his tongue down my throat a few times and I don't know he's attracted to me? He said he loves me three times and I'm still wide-eyed with surprise? Am I operating on three brain cells or what?
I also felt like the romance developement was too limited and moved way too quickly. It was unfocused, as well. One minute it's about your relationship with your grandpa and family, then being threatened by devils, then toyed with by a rival, but the familial relationships were never resolved, the plots were more important than the romance, and the romance in general was just filler between major events that unrealistically happened in the span of four or five days. And that's fine if the point wasn't the romance, but that's really what the game was supposedly about, and that's what the ending sure emphasized. And the branches themselves, while numerous, were not unique enough to justify replay. It was the same silly story filled in by tiny tidbits with a different guy. Even the choices you have to win them over are the same. Steal a kiss or don't, barge in and defend him or don't, say you love him or don't.
All in all, it just felt very immature. Props for ideas, I guess? I mean, whatever she intended to do was cool, but she didn't actually do it. Play it, don't play it - it doesn't matter. You'll lose like 3 hours following one path, which is not a big deal. But you won't get anything out of it save for mild disappointment.

Half-Life 2: Episode One - the next part of the popular series Half-Life, released in 2006. The developers at Valve decided that creating a full extension would take too much time, suggest us to eat the game pieces, making the system episodes, allowing you to produce more games. It's hard to tell if it was the right decision.
The game continues exactly in the place where we stopped in the finals of the second part. The reactor of the Citadel blown up, but its core is still not stable and eventually detonate undermining the entire city. Gordon and Alyx have to slow down the response of the kernel and try save the residents of the city. And to save ourselves...
The game comes out two years later, offering us plunge once more into the history of the universe Half-Life. However immersed we are literally down to his knees, after which the game ends quickly, showing us the gripping trailer for the second episode. This part of the series has become more dynamic than its predecessor, but ends so quickly, do not have time to fully enjoy the game. After two years of waiting, we get a little more than a three-hour campaign. Why it seems that we are playing in a full game, but rather a small addition.
The gameplay has remained virtually the same. Like a dashing start, where we are using the gravity gun throwing soldiers of the Alliance in different directions. In this part fights with zombies and mutants became more. So it was somewhat unusual to play with Alix, which accompanied us almost the entire game. While AI has been improved even more. Our partner shoots, climbing over walls, when the enemies approach too close, you might even strike with his legs or butt. Often comments on different situations and makes the tips in some places.
There are a couple new enemies. Added HDR, which was later moved to the second part. Plus was improving the artificial intelligence and character animation.
This episode is like its dynamism, however small the duration of the game and lack of any features, don't allow to put the game a higher score.
Rating: 8/10
(Русский)
Half-Life 2: Episode One - следующая часть популярной серии Half-Life, вышедшая в 2006 году. Разработчики из Valve, решив, что создание полноценного продолжения займёт слишком много времени, предлагают нам кушать игру по кусочкам, сделав систему эпизодов, что позволяет выпускать игры чаще. Трудно сказать, было ли это решение верным.
Игра продолжается ровно в том месте, где мы и остановились в финале второй части. Реактор Цитадели взорван, однако его ядро всё ещё не стабильно и со временем сдетонирует подорвав весь город. Гордону и Аликс предстоит замедлить рекцию ядра и постаратся спасити жителей города. А так же спастись самим...
Игра выходит спустя два года, предлагая нам окунутся ещё раз в историю вселенной Half-Life. Однако окунаемся мы буквально до колен, после чего игра быстро заканчивается, показывая нам смачный трейлер второго эпизода. Данная часть серии стала более динамичней, по сравнению с предшественником, однако заканчивается настолько быстро, что не успеваешь полностью насладится игрой. После двух то лет ожиданий, получаем чуть более чем трехчасовую кампанию. Отчего создается впечатление, что мы играем не в полноценную игру, а скорее в небольшое дополнение.
Геймплей остался практически таким же. Понравилось лихое начало, где мы используя грави-пушку раскидываем солдат Альянса в разные стороны. В этой части схваток с зомби и мутантами стало больше. Так же было несколько необычно играть с Аликс, которая сопровождала нас практически всю игру. При этом AI был улучшен ещё больше. Наша напарница метко стреляет, перелазит через стенки, при подходе врагов слишком близко, может даже ударить с ноги или прикладом. Часто комментирует разные ситуации и делает подсказки в некоторых местах.
Появились пару новых врагов. Так же добавили технологию HDR, которую впоследствии перенесли и во вторую часть. Плюс были улучшения искуственного интелекта и анимации персонажей.
Данный эпизод понравился своей динамичностью, однако малая продолжительность игры и практически отсутствие каких-либо новвоведений, не дают поставить игре более высокую оценку.
Оценка: 8/10

Short version:
The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a short game. Completion time can range from 4-6 hours depending on the players. The graphics are downright gorgeous. The soundtrack is beautiful. The puzzles as mentioned are logical, but they are also short and few. The narrative feels a bit jumpy at times, but given the context of the story it can play out no other way I suppose. There's only one solution to the ending, so there's practically no replay value unless you are the types that enjoy exploring games and looking for more easter eggs or other narrative devices you may have missed. $19.99 is a tad much for a mystery game that's under 7 hours, I advise waiting for a sale.
Long version:
The very first thing the game tells you is that it won't hold your hand and explain the game mechanics to you. I'm usually anti forced tutorials, but this one could've done with some explanations to start with. I'm introduced to a detective named Paul Prospero, I'm on my last case and I'm looking for a young boy named Ethan Carter. Oh gosh, I accidentally found a Plot Thing. The game prompts me to hold Left Mouse Button to interact with it. Ok. I'm holding my mouse for a good 20-30 seconds, why is nothing happening? Sod this, I'm going to look around some more. Oh, more Plot Thing. Hold Left Mouse Button again. Hey, this time there are more things happening. I guess I need to find more Plot Things for actual investigations? Turns out this train of thought was correct. Still not the best way to start.  The game could've at least dropped some additional hints or prompts. Minimalism or no minimalism.
The actual puzzles of the game, thankfully, are very logical. So there isn't any stupid adventure game logic of rubbing random things from your inventory with Interactive Environment C and hope fire somehow happens. You are a detective, you find clues and you piece things together and draw logical conclusions. You just have the additional perk of seeing things magically happen in the past as well, otherwise we can't progress with the story.
The game paints a very unflattering picture of the characters in tVoEC. I came in, totally oblivious and eager to learn more about this case I'm on. Yet I keep finding these terrible stories and even horrendous murders as part of my investigations? Why am I playing this game with utterly unlikable characters whom I wish they will all suffer a terrible and  painful fate? Then I get to the end, and everything clicked. into. place. Ah. Now I see. It all makes sense. Now I see why those puzzles have such stories attached to them. They all point towards one thing. I see there's actually a reason the story unfold the way it does. Somehow at the end of the game, all the frustration and annoyances I've felt with the story all bloom into something else. It's not unexpected. I've seen endings of such type happen before. But this was done well and there WERE buildup towards this ending that I simply didn't examine deep enough. The ending could've happened differently, but this was more than adequate and satisfactory. I was tempted to give up midway due to that one annoyance in the middle, but thankfully didn't. Said annoyance did nearly kill the game for me though. Take your ooga booga booga and go elsewhere please, that was jarring and pointless.

Sanctuary Plays like a single player MUD.
If you ever wanted to dip into text based online games but find them intimidating or to rapid paced, this is a much slower, more friendly RPG introduction to ASCII textual adventures. Set your nostalgia back to the 80s because Sanctuary returns us to the days of IBM floppy disk playstyle, but adds all the swish new techniques of today's slickest MUDs.
The RPG elements are top notch and more often than not innovative over today's AAA games. The character class combinations are incredibly fun. The system is easy enough to understand, so one is never bogged down with endless cumbersome keyboard commands. The controls make sense, are to the point, displayed on the screen and turn-based, so you can learn at your own pace. The risk factor makes the game feel very realistic and often even frightening. Charming townspeople and chilling dungeons alike await intrepid adventurers. The music is wonderful and worth buying as a DLC. It evokes feelings of old Nobuo Uematsu fantasies with lots of crunchy nintendo blip goodness. The graphics may seem simple, but they are incredibly complex and beautiful. Just try to draw these yourself! Every monster and treasure is well rendered in ASCII and better than 3D graphics in this case, as it allows the player to imagine a fair amount of the world as well.
Crafting is great. Quests are enjoyable. The fightng is damned fun. The limit break system is dynamic and carries over across battles. Stored TP can then be used for difficult battles, opening up with that devastating special attack. That's just one small example of how complex the battling is. All the while, it never gets hard to control, overwhelming, or confusing... but don't go thinking this roguelike holds yer hand, it does not. The player is soon plunged into a world of danger & excitement. I fear for my characters' lives. Their experiences feel very real.
Black Edition is wicked & well polished. Worth buying again.

Metro 2033 Redux is a heart-wrenching, terrifying classic. I have not even finished yet (I am a big majority of the way through, however) and this is easily one of my favorite games of all time.
Based of the book 'Metro 2033', it gives it an even better sense of realism as you spend a lot of your time lurking through the Moscow maze of an underground metro. You are given a brief chance to learn the game, however the more-complicated things are addressed, and you are literally rolled into the post-apocalyptic, mutant-inhabited hell that is Metro. There is no turning back, and the fate of neo-Russia and humanity lies within a dogtag you carry to Polis.
You will have a teammate to help and guide you when you want one, however I hope you do not get attached easily. You will be alone in the dark with only 50 rounds when you don't want to be (seems like a lot of ammo at the time...). After running out of bullets for the seventh time (and scores of times to come) you will STILL ask yourself, "How in the name of Stalin will I pull through this, comrade?" Every shot counts. This game beautifully and 'benevolently' forces you to not dwell when you are on the surface, and you have to basically jog through buildings, scanning the decayed concrete ground and bodies for rounds, notes and MORE FILTERS while your pre-War gas mask filters are burning like fuses. Oh, did I mention the F***ING WATCHERS? Yes, they and the demons ("b*tches" -Uncle Bourbon) will ensure you sprint through the city ruins if up-to 20 minutes of filters aren't enough of a challenge for you. Also, the game seemlessly keeps you as the main character in the game by making your lack of speech not awkward, unlike other games (the script flows very well, even when you are being talked to, basically).
There's not more I can really say; this game is 9.9/10 and I'm very much looking forward to finishing it and starting Metro: Last Light Redux. One last thing: You will be speaking in a Russian accent for days to come. Embrace it, and push on through the grimy, dangerous tunnels, comrade!


Despite their seemingly miserable setting, both Metro games are in fact fun, diverse shooter-adventures, and the remastered 2033 does a good job of smoothing down the original's rougher edges at the expense of some of its brutal personality. Getting both in a single, enhanced package is a great way to discover (or rediscover) the Moscow Metro's unconventional charms.

Noitu Love 2 Devolution is a retro side-scroller beat-em-up game with Metal Slug-esque graphics. Unfortunately, the game is both incredibly simple and incredibly easy, and not worth your time.
Story
The game’s story makes no sense; it involves some bizarre time-travel plot which isn’t really time travel… it doesn’t really make any sense, but it doesn’t need to and really isn’t supposed to.
Gameplay
The gameplay is very simple and is at the heart of the game, but unfortunately is also terrible. You control an on-screen reticle with your mouse, and by clicking, you attack to that spot, if there is an enemy highlighted. You can also hold down your mouse button for a charge shot, jump, move side-to-side, or do a dash attack or spinning jump attack. In the end, while these attacks are theoretically meaningful, most of the time you’re just running to the right, frequently using dash attacks to get through the stages faster to fight the bosses… where, mostly, you just wait to do your thing, or sometimes just straight up attack them as fast as possible, depending on the boss. Many of the bosses don’t require any strategy, while others require a little strategy but not very much.
Ultimately the gameplay is very unsatisfying, and there is very little “meat” to it – the game requires very little strategy and very large amounts of mindless clicking. There is some enemy variety, but most of it is fairly meaningless as strategy has little meaning with the game’s control scheme, and most of the ordinary enemies are both trivial and easily bypassed. Even the bosses mostly are not very interesting, with only a very small number requiring any sort of real strategy. On the whole, the game feels far too simple and straightforward, like you are only there to click to attack a large number of times.
Graphics
The game does a fine job of emulating the era it is trying to emulate; it isn’t particularly beautiful, but it isn’t ugly either, and it is significantly better than a lot of the 8-bit pseudo-retro graphics indie games floating around the market.
Final Summary
Noitu Love 2 Devolution is not worth your money, but more importantly, it isn’t worth your time. You will derive more satisfaction out of doing most anything else.

Ok this game's awesome.
I mean, everything's completely old and we've seen all of this tons of times.. but can we speak about the idea?!
Basically this is the most classic tower defense you'll play - enemies come in waves, they have a pre-drawn route and if they reach the core you get hit on your health; hence you have to put towers in fixed places, you can upgrade them and they're all different for what concerns firing speed, type and so on.
But the whole setting isn't the usual fantasy or medieval thing, but it's hard rock. Yeah, you have to defend a hard rock stage and your towers are actually different types of sound amplifiers and speakers.
I found everything brilliant, really.. never thought about such an idea xD
And the game is funny, graphics and mechanics are very simple of course (the game costs less than 1€, so of course it's an indie issue) but very enjoyable, with a good difficulty curve and an awesome array of amplifiers/towers to upgrade and defend your rock festival xD
I've been to thousands of concerts so maybe this influenced me a bit ahah :)
You also have many of the most important features in tower defense games: special skills, speed up button, call enemy wave early and so on.
So for being an indie game it's really entertaining and new for its idea!
I saw lots of negative reviews that to me have little valid points. It's a game made by a single developer, so of course it has its flaws.. but for 1€ it offers a great tower defense experience.
Obviously, mainly if you're not used to this genre, the game can be repetitive.. even the best tower defense games if you want to 3-star every level get repetitive.. this game hasn't that variety but hey, fixed spots in which you can place towers are a feature of more than a half of the tower defense category and it's not a bad thing to me. Just look at the Kingdom Rush games, or even Cursed Treasure which has fixed spots for mana recharging and such, Idk, it's not a bad thing to me. Highly customizable tower defense series like Gemcraft can be boring for other aspects maybe, but I mean, again, it's a one-guy game here.
A negative thing that I could point out is that actually the music is quite boring and you may expect something way more entertaining for a game based on music on its premises, but I play most of the games muted and listening to other things so yeah I couldn't enjoy the soundtrack, it's a downside but who cares in the end.
I'd really recommend this game, of course it comes after dozens of other ones in this awesome genre but still it's a positive addition for us :)

Probes, the Matrix, puns, references, sing alongs, and an at times overwhelming sense of power. What's not to love? Bounding through the streets, sending anything in your path spiraling through the air, jumping over buildings, slamming into the ground from rediculous heights... What a rush. Saints Row IV is not a perfect experience by any means. It crashed a few times, you quickly become so overpowered that your chances of dying are miniscule unless you fall asleep on the keyboard (I didn't buy any of the damage resestence or health perks until the end of the game and only died a couple times), and some of the characters in your party have very little development before becoming largely inconsequential. But it's fun. It's a lot of fun. Easily one of the most overall enjoyable experiences I've had in an open world like this. Your powers are fun to use, and you'll find yourself not bothering to get in a car most of the time cause you can run much faster than you can drive. In a series that started out as a GTA ripoff, yes, you'll probably not get in a car very often. I know, how far the series has come, right? Let's not fool ourselves, this series has spun way out of control into coo coo territory, but it's mostly to the game's benefit.
Plot wise, it's pretty simple but gets the job done. There's few surprises once you're numb to the chaos. You gather your friends, take over the town, and then fight the big bad. Several of your friends are amazing and some of them are just kinda, you know, there. They exist. Some characters end up being throw away summons with little novelty. But you won't care, because you'll be laughing and kicking alien butt and feeling like a badass. The DLC scenarios were good, too. This game makes you feel good, what more do you need to know? Best third act I've seen in an action game, loved the ending and even the credits.
I can't recommend this enough. Set aside your desires for realism and ride this crazy train.

A quick and dirty review while this game is on sale:
GET IT!
This may look suspicously like a mobile title, but it isn't at all. (not even available on mobile) It also looks a bit better when you're actually playing it.
If the premise looks interesting to you and you played a certain SNES fire game and always wanted something more this might fit the bill. It offers a lot of challenge and variety and the fact that the levels are randomly generated add a lot of replayability to this game. The game basically plays like it looks. You have a fire hose and extinguisher. Hose for normal fires and keeping the fire from spreading and the extinguisher for electrical/chemical fires. There's also items like water bombs and you have to rescue people, cats and a stuck up lady that won't leave unless you find her purse, kill alien specimens, clear out a bank vault, etc. This is a very arcade-like game and you only have a couple minutes to finish a level, with an extra minute added per rescue. People and cats die fast and fires spread fast so it's rather chaotic and stressful at times but you can upgrade as you go along to help bring the difficulty down at times.
It's dastardly difficult and very unforgiving at times but it's definitely skill based and not hard for the sake of being hard. This game surprised me and is well worth the purchase at any price, let alone sale.

It’s kinda like mirror’s edge with zombies. Sometimes weak dialogue stemming from the story being based on the game, and not the game being based on the story. Some of the acrobatic stuff doesn’t seem realistic (can avoid fall damage if you land on trash, I.e. assassins creed). It can get very repetitive (somehow only hulking black men worked at power stations, and they all carried rebar), especially looting. A lot off buildings are the same, both interior and exterior. Saving NPCs doesn’t feel like saving people- they give you a little reward and run off, never to be seen again in the story, or even incidentally in safe houses. There’s a good deal of silliness that makes it hard to get into the grim atmosphere (throwing stars, drop kicking zombies, etc) that seemed to be designed as a conversational piece for friends (duuude that was totally wicked)
That being said, game is still worth buying and playing. Visually appealing and intuitive mechanics. Nice user interface and skill trees. Fighting zombies is pretty difficult and should be avoided, which feels right. The panic is real when your plan doesn’t work out and you’re struggling to get away. Would likely be fun with friends or online, but I haven’t tried it yet.
If you can suspend your disbelief in some aspects of the game, you’ll have a good time.

I really think Techland should just stop making games... You'd think they'd learn from their mistakes in Dead Island...
The biggest problem that game had was a map filled with boring side quests, the completely illogical gear system and a story that I actively try to suppress from memory.
Lo and behold, the exact same design flaws exist in Dying Light. The exact same annoying gear system, where every time you die the world resets but your gear doesn't. It's like an evil (and poorly designed) Dark Souls, the game just gets more and more difficult as you try, but instead of fairness the game just laughs at you while it takes away more and more tools to solve the problem:
"Oh you died, bad luck! By the way you used up all your bullets in that last attempt, so good luck attacking with melee only!"
"Oh no you died again! Don't worry, you're about to respawn and you can try again. Oh by the way you've used up all your medkits so try not to take any damage ever!"
"Dead again? Don't worry, third time's the charm! Although you've broken all your good melee weapons now, so I guess you'll have to do it without medkits and that random knife you found in the garbage. Have fun!"
Then there's the side-quests. If I ever meet the person who designed these quests, I'm going to slap them in the face. When you've already got an system that hand-holds you with objective markers, you may as well go all the way. Just point out where the item is so we can run to it while fighting off zombies. That'll allow the game to maintain a fast pace with a focus on combat and action. Don't just give players a vaguely worded goal and objective area, forcing us to wander around in search of whatever it is you want us to do:
"find a car battery" "How, I can't open up car hoods and search it"
"grab 3 cans of paint" "You've only marked an entire block, and haven't told me where I should be looking"
"Search the area" "Search the area for WHAT."
It doesn't help that the whole reason to be doing these quests, the story, isn't very interesting. None of the characters you meet are well-written or memorable, the goals they give you are generic fetch quests 90% of the time, and all-in-all it never feels like these people care about the effort you're putting in. You spend 2 hours running up and down the map, fighting zombies, and opening crates to find 3 bottls of alcohol, and in the end all you get is a short thank you and a small  boost in xp. Hooray...
(Yes, sometimes they also give cash rewards. But the economy in this game is a joke so there's really no point in getting an extra $1000. Especially when you're already sitting on $23 000 with nothing to spend it on)
TLDR; Don't. Not even on sale. The bizzaro gear system, the bedtime-lullaby writing and quite frankly horrendous quest design will make sure you regret the purchase, even if you find some moments of fun.

I originally got this game because I thought it would be something fun to laugh at with friends.
I started playing it on my own just to see what it was like, and I was genuinely surprised.
The voice acting is quite good, especially for the incubi, as well as the two main antagonists, Malix and Diana. You can truly feel their emotions through each line.
The artwork is nice, not the best I've seen for a VN, but I still like it.
I would say it has a lot of replay value, given the different paths you can take. I have only completed the game all the way through once, so there is still quite a bit of it I haven't seen.
The character development is good, you get a feel for each character's personality type. Though of course, each character also has many secrets hidden away so you get to learn more about them along the way.
The story is pretty straight-forward, but that isn't a bad thing. It's easy to understand and it's fun, so I like it a lot.
The game itself has two arcs, one focusing on Malix and the other focusing on Diana. (At least those were the arcs for the character I pursued, I don't know if that changes depending on the character you choose.)
The length of the game isn't that long, but it isn't too short either. You can play through it in one sitting if you have the time. I prefer longer VNs, but this one does what it has set out to do without taking too much time. Then again, if you decide that you want to go through each character's story, then it will be longer and give you your fill.
One of the only things I dislike about this game is the abrupt ending. The ending itself (at least for the character I chose) isn't bad, but I felt like it could have lasted a little bit longer. Like after you get rid of Diana or whatever you choose to do, I feel as if there should be a little bit more time after that for just you and the character you pursued. But that's just in my opinion. All the loose ends get tied up and then it's happily ever after.
Once again that is all just in my opinion, but if you're looking for a nice story with drama, romance and humor, I would suggest this. It has many different types of characters and a unique storyline!

A visual and narrative masterpiece. I spent the first couple of hours just roaming around trying to figure out what to do or what was going on. The inital stages of the game feel very slow. There's no intro, no map, no objectives. You are left alone in a semi open-world (essentially a village and surrounding area) trying to piece together together a series of strange events.
The user tags define this game as 'detective', 'psychological horror", and "puzzle." I would say that it's more of a first-person atmospheric walking narrative with some mystery elements. A few pointers if you decide to give it a go:
1) Do not use online walkthroughs until you are ready to move on to a new 'zone' (usually designated by new scenery, a new cutscene, or a change in music). While you're in a zone, explore every nook and cranny. It's a beautiful game, so explore it.
2) I only figured out around the 3-4 hr mark that I could run ('shift' key). Made my life a whole lot easier getting from point A to B.
3) Don't let the strange 'fantasy-like' cutscenes throw you off... they will all make sense in the end.
4) Play the game through in its entirety. It took me ~6 hrs from start to finish (including a quick run-through to find some achievements that I missed in the first playthrough). The ending may seem a bit confusing, but there are some awesome "Vanishing of Ethan Carter Explained" websites out there that help make sense of it.
Picked it up on sale, and it was definitely worth the money. Really was a great experience.

Not only do the play differently, some more than others, they can also change how you and the world around you interact with one another.
Another thing to remember, though abandoned by dev and publishers it has been supported heavily by the community. With a host of user friendly mods that not just add to the game but also fill in some of the things the devs didn't get to.

I don't know why this game gets so many positive reviews. The only thing to recommend it is the basic design of the combat system, which is decently solid. The rest of the game plays like a satirical take on Free to Play games. That is, the whole game is variations on the theme of "make the player waste their time jumping through UI hoops to earn tiny incremental rewards." Just about everything in this games takes at least 6 button-presses more than it should, maybe so that it can provide the illusion of variation in gameplay where there is none.
Pros:
+ Decent basic combat system.
Cons:
- Designed to make you press as many buttons as possible to accomplish as little as possible.
- The whole game is just one giant grindfest. Even non-combat activities are designed to to take many pointless steps.
- Insanely linear. No exploration. You just select "Continue on in plot" from the menu.
- Permadeath starts EVERYTHING over from the beginning. This wouldn't be so bad if you didn't waste so much time building stuff up every time you play, all for only incremental benefits.
- The "humor" in this game is so random it's not funny, with some exceptions.

After putting about 20 hours in, I can safely say that I would recommend this game to a friend that enjoys tycoon/management type games.
What I liked:
- There are not many management games on steam these days that give as much customizing options as this one, you can really build your company wall-by-wall, desk-by-desk, development team-by-development team.
- The beginning of a game is great because there are so many options for income. It's fun being creative and trying different ways of getting your company off the ground.
- After having a scroll through the news, it seems this game is updated pretty regularly and just gets better and better.
What I'd like to see:
- MUSIC! I appreciate all the little sounds (the typing of the keyboard, the birds chirping, etc), but it gets really dry without any music. I suggest something relaxing, something along the lines of the infamous Minecraft soundtrack.
- The user interface is good for the most part, but there are still some small problems that are fine at first but get very frustrating with repetition. Many of these problems occur because of a lack of information when you need it and the player needs to backtrack through menus to find it. Players get really specific in the discussion board when they address these problems, let's get them fixed!
- I find that the interest on insurace is a bit too high later in the game... I got to a point where I'm making millions, yet my reputation is low, my workers are unhappy, and my products are not the best... I have so much money that I can buy out every other company that even begins to try to make a product. Quite hilarious... but boring once it gets to that point.

It’s kinda like mirror’s edge with zombies. Sometimes weak dialogue stemming from the story being based on the game, and not the game being based on the story. Some of the acrobatic stuff doesn’t seem realistic (can avoid fall damage if you land on trash, I.e. assassins creed). It can get very repetitive (somehow only hulking black men worked at power stations, and they all carried rebar), especially looting. A lot off buildings are the same, both interior and exterior. Saving NPCs doesn’t feel like saving people- they give you a little reward and run off, never to be seen again in the story, or even incidentally in safe houses. There’s a good deal of silliness that makes it hard to get into the grim atmosphere (throwing stars, drop kicking zombies, etc) that seemed to be designed as a conversational piece for friends (duuude that was totally wicked)
That being said, game is still worth buying and playing. Visually appealing and intuitive mechanics. Nice user interface and skill trees. Fighting zombies is pretty difficult and should be avoided, which feels right. The panic is real when your plan doesn’t work out and you’re struggling to get away. Would likely be fun with friends or online, but I haven’t tried it yet.
If you can suspend your disbelief in some aspects of the game, you’ll have a good time.

I really think Techland should just stop making games... You'd think they'd learn from their mistakes in Dead Island...
The biggest problem that game had was a map filled with boring side quests, the completely illogical gear system and a story that I actively try to suppress from memory.
Lo and behold, the exact same design flaws exist in Dying Light. The exact same annoying gear system, where every time you die the world resets but your gear doesn't. It's like an evil (and poorly designed) Dark Souls, the game just gets more and more difficult as you try, but instead of fairness the game just laughs at you while it takes away more and more tools to solve the problem:
"Oh you died, bad luck! By the way you used up all your bullets in that last attempt, so good luck attacking with melee only!"
"Oh no you died again! Don't worry, you're about to respawn and you can try again. Oh by the way you've used up all your medkits so try not to take any damage ever!"
"Dead again? Don't worry, third time's the charm! Although you've broken all your good melee weapons now, so I guess you'll have to do it without medkits and that random knife you found in the garbage. Have fun!"
Then there's the side-quests. If I ever meet the person who designed these quests, I'm going to slap them in the face. When you've already got an system that hand-holds you with objective markers, you may as well go all the way. Just point out where the item is so we can run to it while fighting off zombies. That'll allow the game to maintain a fast pace with a focus on combat and action. Don't just give players a vaguely worded goal and objective area, forcing us to wander around in search of whatever it is you want us to do:
"find a car battery" "How, I can't open up car hoods and search it"
"grab 3 cans of paint" "You've only marked an entire block, and haven't told me where I should be looking"
"Search the area" "Search the area for WHAT."
It doesn't help that the whole reason to be doing these quests, the story, isn't very interesting. None of the characters you meet are well-written or memorable, the goals they give you are generic fetch quests 90% of the time, and all-in-all it never feels like these people care about the effort you're putting in. You spend 2 hours running up and down the map, fighting zombies, and opening crates to find 3 bottls of alcohol, and in the end all you get is a short thank you and a small  boost in xp. Hooray...
(Yes, sometimes they also give cash rewards. But the economy in this game is a joke so there's really no point in getting an extra $1000. Especially when you're already sitting on $23 000 with nothing to spend it on)
TLDR; Don't. Not even on sale. The bizzaro gear system, the bedtime-lullaby writing and quite frankly horrendous quest design will make sure you regret the purchase, even if you find some moments of fun.

Its a good game, it is. Its fun to play and is different from the rest of the games out there, but it has one MAJOR flaw which makes it basically unplayable to an extent.
You see, there really is no save mechanic. Well, no good one anyway. In order for you to save the game, you must DIE. Yes, you read that right. You have to die to save. If you simply get to the next level and quit, everything will be wiped and you must start again. If you die, your level progress, and ONLY that is saved. Your hearts, time, upgrades, EVERYTHING is wiped and you must start again.
I've tried for thirty minutes to get past a single stage of the labs with just the basic loadout, and i've failed. Every single time, i've failed. So in order to beat this game, you must:
A) Play through the entire game in one sitting (Roughly 3 hours of playtime)
OR
B) Beat the first level, die, and start from the second level.
AND ON TOP OF THAT, if you are given no useful items from the shop, you gotta, you guessed it, START OVER!
Actually, thats a good name for this game: Start Over.

In many more words, this game is funny, moving, real, it pushes the limits, and you can't help but want more. The dialogue is really good and I love how the game centres around a guy who is obviously going through post traumatic stress.  Having grown up an American with 3 cousins and an brother who are FDNY firefighters and members of the FDNY Emerald Society Pipes and Drums, I am impressed with the personalities of the characters, the situations, and the whole game overall is just so real.
Flame Over brings a mixture of comedy and drama and it works perfectly, with the characters and art style using dark humour to hide how significantly the events of 9/11 have altered their lives. Blaze Carruthers the main character, who has, among other things, a drinking problem, a drug problem, a marriage that has fallen apart, and survivor's guilt is probably one of the more interesting characters in gaming whom I think we can all relate to in many dimensions of his life and personality. All in all Flame Over is an amazing game that is a powerful meditation on post 9/11 society and a tribute to the hard work and service that firefighters do every day.
5/10

Just shy of 100 hours of play time and after getting all of the Steam achievements I finally think I'm ready to write a fair review of this game. Needless to say I enjoyed it quite a bit. There were several things that I disliked throughout my play time, but with as much as the community has contributed with their experience I was able to get through all that the game had to offer.
We'll start with my dislikes; There wasn't enough information given about the in game items from the developer and I actually had to contact them directly multiple times to get accurate describtions. Furthermore the in game shop was never designed to prevent items that you've already bought from showing up again, and there's nothing stoping a player from accidently double purchasing something he or she already has. The upgrade store where you spend your tokens is only available when you have enough tokens saved up to buy an upgrade, but this mechanic wasn't exactly transparent to myself or other players from what I've read on the forums.  In my opinion it would have been better if they made the shop visable from the menu at all times even if you didn't have enough tokens to buy an upgrade. One of the most annoying mechanics in this game involved fireballs spawning when you open a rooms door. The NPC's in the game were seemingly randomly placed within rooms, and more times then I can count I would open a door and hear the sound of a fireball immediately spawn further in the room and then later find a dead NPC that was instakilled by said fireball. This mechanic is by definition anti-fun in that there is absolutely no way to counter play it and it made one of the achievements quite difficult to get. I must have prayed to RNGesus a thousand times before I was actually able to make it through a complete run without losing an NPC that way. On the topic of NPC's they are slower than your character and when they get too far behind they just stop moving, which is a much smaller issue, but still quite annoying when you're trying to herd six of them to safety and little Jimmy refuses to pick up his feet and move.
Okay okay, on to the good; The random level generation makes the games replayability great. The power boost gained from store items feels very signifigant (Super hose!!) and makes a run much more rewarding. Though very repetative, the music is actually quite catchy and I like it. The cartoonish artistic style is also very cool, and I think it adds allot to the fun of the game. I'm sure there's more, but I feel like I'm dragging on so I'll just end by saying that I highly recommend this game and I hope the devs get a chance to address the issues I've experianced.
P.S. Dance With The Devil on PC; Clear level two, spray shop keep in face with extinguisher and steal items, clear level 3 and then 4, goto shop in level 4 and shop keep will tell you that you won't steal from him again, wait for time to run out and meet Satan.

Flame Over is a very difficult roguelike where you control firefighter Blaze Carruthers as he faces alone a whole big building on fire.
Easy to pick up but very difficult to master Flame Over is very good but, perhaps, a bit too hard for the average gamer.
-charming art style
-the various level are quite detailed and sport a good variety between stages
-the fire is appropriately difficult to extinguish as it'll try its best to expand either by getting on objects close to it or producing fireballs and flame walls that can quickly engulf a room again
-having an health system and a timer adds to the sense of urgency and gives one more level of challenge
-there's a good amount of permament upgrades plus special items you can buy at a merchant during your run
-from stage 3 onwards it gets fiendishly difficult, so much that it can easily turn into frustration
-sometimes the fire can spread so quickly, even from a single small flame, that it feels unfair
-as in many roguelikes the random generated floors can sometimes give you a run that's too easy or too hard, depending on their layout
-opening a door to a new room only to see a fireball killing a civilian or a cat in one hit, without even having the time to react, feels a tad unfair
-some permanent upgrades feel a bit underwhelming
-the game saves checkpoints for each stage you clear but you'll soon realize it's a bit useless due to the fact that you'll start with no special items: this means you'll either have to replay the previous stages to gather money and find chances to buy them again (which can get repetitive) or try and tackle a difficult stage with no special items (meaning it'll be very hard and often frustrating)
Flame Over is deceptively cute and funny in its presentation, but behind this seemingly light-hearted game lies a very tough roguelike due to its difficult gameplay and some design choices that add even more challenge.
It's pretty fun for the first two stages once you get the hang of it and the demanding gameplay makes for some engaging runs but from stage 3 onwards the difficulty ramps up quickly and it'll take quite alot of retries to get through: sadly the checkpoint issue I've mentioned beforehand makes the gameplay a bit dull and repetitive in the long run as there's only so many runs one can stomach before frustration and boredom start to set in.
I'm giving this a thumbs up cause Flame Over is indeed a good roguelike with lots of charm and good gameplay but do keep in mind that I feel it's too hard for the average gamer: if you love a tough challenge and have the patience to try run after run go for it otherwise just go for something easier.

Initially, this review was going to be negative and not reccomend it.
The start of the game, is not exactly endearing.  It is very difficult to get immersed in what is happening, and the fact that you play Gordon Freeman again (yes, I know he is the
protagonist of the series, but he is just that - the main one).  I felt that this was the perfect opportunity to play as Alyx, or Barney again.  Someone other than Gordon, indeed, I was more of the mind that this game would have been more interesting if it had changed tact, and the purpose was to find Gordon after the events of Half-Life 2.
Either way, going through the opening chapter of this game was tedius.  Mind-numbingly so.  It was not enjoyable, it was not great storytelling and it definitely did not flow well.  Alyx as an NPC Mary-Sue that offered constant exposition became annoying very very quickly.  This issue with Alyx would only continue as the game progressed.  Too much emphasis was placed on doing things in a buddy-cop fashion, but without the laughs associated with that genre.
The game didn't get too much better for a while.  The reliance on the game to pair you up with Alyx had many of the same issues that you got with Half-Life 2 and the squads, they would constantly get in your way.  And Alyx would do that with a repetitive glee that could only be described as malicious.  I also found that this game seemed buggier than Half-Life 2 in that you could get caught on so much more debris.
The game also has a predisposition to clunky gameplay, revisitng many of the poorer elements used in the series, such as platforming and un-inspired puzzles.  But at least you can still shoot things up with the SMG, Pulse Rifle and Crossbow.
However, the game did start picking up once you got to the final chapter and met up with an old friend again.  I believe that this sequence and the final mini-boss fight at the end were the saving grace of Half-Life 2: Episode One.  They raised the score of the game enough for me to recommend this game.  Unfortunately, though, whilst it tips the scales on the fun side, this game did not enhance the lore of the series.
3/5 - only get if on special.

So I've never written a review before, but I had to for this game.
I'm a huge fan of adventure/exploration/puzzle/etc games such as Myst, The Longest Journey, stuff like that, so I thought this game was friggin' fantastic. If you're looking for lots of action and killing things and such, go play something else. Long story short, if you like the same games as me, get this. Long story: I'll just break this into sections.
Graphics
10/10 This game is friggin' beautiful. Look through my screenshots for some maxed out graphics pictures. Everything is turned to high with view distance maxed as well, totally worth it! No lag either. Peoples' faces are a little weird looking, but I suppose that's because they have a weird face, not because the artists suck. Everything is seriously beautiful, just look at the pictures.
Sounds
10/10 I like games like this to have kind of minimal background noise, and this game has plenty of music, sound effects, and ambient sounds to keep it busy but not take away from the game itself. There were definitely sounds that added to the feel of the area too, creepy animal noises in the woods, rushing water, creaking boards in houses, wind, etc.
Gameplay
10/10 The controls are crazy simple: WASD to move, Shift to run, CTRL to crouch, Left Click to interact, Right Click to zoom (which I only used like twice), Q and E were used to scroll up and down between selections. The gameplay itself was much harder. It tells you right in the intro "This game will not hold your hand," and that's not an understatement. There were key parts of the game that I literally missed because it tells you almost nothing about doing things in order or where to go next. So be prepared to either look things up or use your damn brain! The puzzles were interesting, not too hard, although some of them were very easy for me. Lots of walking, lots of very interesting narration, exploring every corner of everything to find everything. Definitely a game for me!
Replayability
6/10 If you're one of "those people" like me who finds everything there is to find on the first playthrough, you're probably going to have about as many hours as me (8.5), give or take a bit. Once you beat it and find everything, there's really no point to play it again. However, despite the almost disappointing length and lack of replayability, it is more than worth it.
Story
10/10 This story was intense, it was involving, it tugged at my heartstrings, it made me mad, and it made me cry (only a little). Now, I'm one of those people that gets almost too involved in everything I do, so I tend to feel significantly more towards fictional characters. So maybe you won't feel the same as me, but its worth a shot. Still an outstanding story, whether you cry or not.
Overall
100/100 Just buy the damn game.
Also, if you played this and liked it, give Among The Sleep and/or Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons a try. Both emotional and amazing exploration/adventure kind of games, though very different. I played them out of Steam, otherwise I would write reviews -.-

What I enjoyed most was the "no hand-holding" approach the devs took. You're put into the game and have little to no guidance. You have to discover stuff on your own. It reminds me of the original Mist.  First-person, atmospheric and story-driven.  The game has creepy supernatural elements and a sound track that builds tension and anxiety throughout the game.  Although seemingly peaceful,  you never feel safe.   The dev's approach to puzzles are refreshing.  There is a rationale behind each answer  (e.g. there are no combine every item in your inventory with every item) and there is never any hand holding for the player.  They just drop you into the semi-open world and you peice the clues together in at your own pace.   It's relatively short, but with satisfying ending.

The game has many elements that are very attractive but is relatively short and the story is not very deep. The graphics are very attractive and allows exploration of an intricate abandoned mountainous mining community. The mechanics for reconstructing a crime, murders in this case, are interesting. I found that the process for searching for clues could be in some cases seem very arbitrary, sometimes I had to go back and forth over the same area many times, even with the aid of a guide to find a clue.
As mentioned in other reviews, the story is Lovecraftian. My experience with well-developed stories in this genre is that as understanding grows, the world becomes increasing bizaare, disturbing, and horrible. In order to work, though, you need to  have characters you care about. The shortness of the game and the particular view of the world you get (the last moments of ghosts) limit the depth of character development.
At $19.99 I won't recommend the game; too short and not enough story depth. But for $10.00 I'd recommend it. The developers are skillful and they have interesting game mechanics that could serve well in the mystery/detective genre.

First of all, for those who are wondering, the game IS playable (But don't expect much more than 25FPS if you're running my old setup which I mention below) well under the minimum requirements. About 60 hours of my playtime were at the lowest settings with 20FPS, running a GT730, an i5, and 16GB of DDR3 RAM. After I upgraded to a GTX1050Ti, the experience is smooth, amazing, and beautiful at ultra graphics. Anyways, on with the review.
The game is priceless, long after the story is over. I would still pay $80 for this game.
If roleplaying is your thing, you will without a doubt find that in this game. While I feel like the weather doesn't change enough in-game (It does, and there are several types, too!), it does change and is perhaps the best way to set a mood I have ever seen in a game. The feels like a completely different one when you find yourself hiding behind a car at midnight from the volatiles, versus the sunny mornings spent parkouring and looking for crafting materials around the map. This game seems to do it all right, and with the free DLC drosp coming this year and the next, it seems like they're only doing it better and better. Occasionally, you'll find some BS moments with the runners and their attacks, but for the most part they're fun and easy to decapitate.
For people who play only for gore, intense combat, and storymode, you'll find most of that here, though gunplay is something that feels neglected by the developers (1 shot to the head with one of the best pistols in the game doesn't kill a zombie until you're firing from point blank, and even then it's unreliable). Melee combat is masterfully executed, with loads of hidden weapon blueprints and modifications for you to discover and make. There are lots of pointless statue collectibles if that's you thing, and many hidden letters for those who like a little more purpose in their collectibles.
Now, the most fun of this game, in my opinion- night time. Night time in this game is just as described earlier- it feels like you're in another game, and this one isn't just zombie survival. It's survival horror. More often than not, un the early game you'll find yourself crouching behind cars and trying to sneak past the heavy-footed night hunters and their freaky mouths (Find yourself in their grasp and you will get exactly what I mean).
If horror isn't your thing, then daytime will be your domain (You can sleep through nights). You'll enjoy bashing zombies' heads in with all sorts of pipes and sledgehammers, or slicing them up with machetes and knives. Throwing weapons is an important skill to unlock if your stealth game isn't as strong. This is because the game doesn't provide you with many stealth tools, precisely to add to the risk factor of it- the only convenient (and it can be a lifesaver) stealth ability you can unlock is the camouflage yourself with zombie guts, which is a smart one for wading through the hordes that you may occasionally find.
I won't analyze the entire game's mechanics, but believe me, if you want a zombie game that will make you truly feel like you are surviving (probably until you get reckless at the higher levels because you begin to become quite powerful), this is it. I'd tell you to try it out for the two hours and refund it if you don't enjoy it, but truth is you'll find that the 2 hours will pass way quicker than you anticipate.
Plus, Dying Light at 60% off? That's a total steal!

Company Of Heroes 2 brings a new campaign, new multiplayer maps and units, new co-op modes, more explosions, more units on the field, and deathly winter combat, all presented with the gameplay that made the first such a hit. It stays true to its roots while bringing in enough new, compelling content to make it worthwhile.
The sequel to one of the best strategy titles out there, Company of Heroes 2 lives up to its predecessor. The game focuses on the Eastern front of World War II, and during the campaign the player takes on the role of the Russians. It's a slow-paced RTS, with a big emphasis placed on unit placement and having troops stay behind cover if they want to survive.
Each unit is a squad of troops, rather than just an individual. The strength of the squad is based on how many soldiers are alive. This system lets their be hundreds of soldiers in the game, but the player only has to focus on a dozen squads or so. Squads can be refilled with new men at headquarters, or conscript troops can be assigned to fill in missing ranks. At a given time a player will control anywhere from five to twenty squads, which doesn't seem like it would be that hard to do, but it can be hectic to keep everyone moving and alive.
The utterly fantastic campaign is among the best I have played in a strategy game. Missions are varied enough that different tactics have to be used to win each one. There are some defense missions that are so hectic I had to constantly readjust my troops to face new attacks coming from all sides. One mission takes place in the snow, and you have to prevent your troops from freezing to death by moving close to fires, or keeping them inside.
Another one of my favorites involved hunting down and destroying a Tiger tank, which I ultimately accomplished by luring it into a series of mines I placed as a trap. There are 14 missions in the campaign, and each one takes between 20-60 minutes to complete depending on the difficulty and how terrible you are at playing.
All of the new mechanics fit well with the Eastern Front setting. Lots of soldiers will die, and CoH2 does a brilliant job of making it expensive to lose troops. Conscript troops can be cheaply deployed quickly, but these soldiers are ill-equipped to survive for long. They are best used to replenish the ranks of more valuable units, and then sent off to the front lines. As units are built they will often shout out, "Need a suicide squad?" Taking over an enemy territory will certainly require you to sacrifice a lot of men, and sometimes you'll have to do it knowing you won't be able to replace them easily.
I was always faced with some form of a choice with each unit. "Do I have them run in and face certain death, or do I hold back and wait for a better opportunity?" Better opportunities don't always come, and sometimes the only way to win the battle is to lose a fight. Wounding a tank is ultimately more valuable than a squad of infantry. The cold weather adds to this dilemma of having to choose to lose expensive units, since having them out too long can cause them to freeze to death. Even if they survive a fight, they can and often will die in the cold soon after. All of these calculated decisions are heavy to deal with, and the game's atmosphere and mechanics make sending every squad to the front lines a hard choice.
Alongside the campaign, there is the "Theater of War" mode which includes a series of co-op and single-player missions and scenarios. This mode is meant to provide more battles along the Eastern front that don't tie in directly to the campaign. While right now all of the battles focus on the year 1941, Relic has stated that it plans on adding more content later.
The scenarios are tightly-focused missions revolving around one aspect of the war that year, and they are some of my favorite missions in the game. Company of Heroes 2 shines the brightest for me when I have three squads and keeping them alive is insanely hard. The co-op missions are large-scale battles that pit players against a computer opponent; the rest are simply single-player missions that use the multiplayer maps and have a computer opponent.
There is a competitive multiplayer, of course. It's what gave the first game such a long life, and it's just as solid in the sequel. It plays out the same as in the first game, either with players fighting over control points or simply trying to demolish each other. This time around there are all new maps and units, which is enough to make me want to play the same style of game. If you are a classic fan of the series and you're only interested in the multi-player, it's hard to say if you'll find enough here invest in this if you already played the first. It's more of change than the Call of Duty series has every year, and people still play that like crazy.
No matter what your style of play is, there's a ridiculous amount of achievement, unlocks, and progression to keep you in the game. There are 366 Steam achievements, which is just absurd, but if you play often it's nice to know there will always be something you haven't done yet. Your in-game profile, which is tied directly to Steam, will gain levels and as you level up you'll be able to customize your army with different units, abilities, and even custom skins.
Company of Heroes 2 brings the classic gameplay of the original game into the modern era. It has all of the familiar mechanics while embracing new technology to make everything look and respond better. The physics are very realistic, and just about everything can be destroyed. One mission had me defending a point from oncoming Germans, and I kept getting flanked by them crossing a bridge. On my third attempt I had the crazy idea, "What if I blew up the bridge?" and I sent over a team of engineers to rig it with explosives. The first round of Nazis was met with a surprise, and the bridge was no longer a problem.
All of the cover can be destroyed if the other guy has a big enough gun. Hiding behind a fence might be great for stopping bullets, but tank is going to destroy the wall and everyone behind it. Standing on ice is a really bad idea, since if enough weight is applied, it will break. As things get destroyed, soldiers can take cover in holes in the ground or behind rubble, broken tanks, and even corpses. After a long match the middle ground will often be demolished, filled with the effects of war. This evolving battlefield makes Company of Heroes 2 stand out from other strategy games, and I have a feeling it will make any other game without this level of physics feel fake.
Company of Heroes 2 is an excellent real-time strategy game. The campaign is challenging, varied, and true to the setting of the war. The atmosphere is intense and filled with bass-rumbling sounds, and an orchestral score that provides the perfect background. It's visually impressive, yet manages to run at a smooth frame rate. All of the matchmaking and multiplayer systems are tied into Steam, so you don't have to log in twice to play the game; everything runs flawlessly.
I was worried that the campaign would be weak and everything would be focused on the multiplayer, but I was happy to be proven wrong. The campaign turned out to be my favorite part, and with the added content from the Theater of War mode, there is a lot of game even if you don't want to engage other players. The amount of content is generous, going way beyond the normal six-hour single-player campaign and multiplayer formula that most games use today.
Overall,It's one of those games that can suck you in for hours and keep you constantly engaged. Company of Heroes 2 is shining example of what an RTS game should be: a mix of classic mechanics with new features and technology.

Probes, the Matrix, puns, references, sing alongs, and an at times overwhelming sense of power. What's not to love? Bounding through the streets, sending anything in your path spiraling through the air, jumping over buildings, slamming into the ground from rediculous heights... What a rush. Saints Row IV is not a perfect experience by any means. It crashed a few times, you quickly become so overpowered that your chances of dying are miniscule unless you fall asleep on the keyboard (I didn't buy any of the damage resestence or health perks until the end of the game and only died a couple times), and some of the characters in your party have very little development before becoming largely inconsequential. But it's fun. It's a lot of fun. Easily one of the most overall enjoyable experiences I've had in an open world like this. Your powers are fun to use, and you'll find yourself not bothering to get in a car most of the time cause you can run much faster than you can drive. In a series that started out as a GTA ripoff, yes, you'll probably not get in a car very often. I know, how far the series has come, right? Let's not fool ourselves, this series has spun way out of control into coo coo territory, but it's mostly to the game's benefit.
Plot wise, it's pretty simple but gets the job done. There's few surprises once you're numb to the chaos. You gather your friends, take over the town, and then fight the big bad. Several of your friends are amazing and some of them are just kinda, you know, there. They exist. Some characters end up being throw away summons with little novelty. But you won't care, because you'll be laughing and kicking alien butt and feeling like a badass. The DLC scenarios were good, too. This game makes you feel good, what more do you need to know? Best third act I've seen in an action game, loved the ending and even the credits.
I can't recommend this enough. Set aside your desires for realism and ride this crazy train.

Do you like Mischief Makers? Do you like Gunstar Heroes? Do you like Alien Soldier? Do you happen to enjoy highly-rasterized cult classics with fast movement and faster combat (Treasure games)? If you answered yes to any or all of these questions, then pick up Noitu Love 2. Each one of your punches and kicks resonates with that distinctive crunch and pop that calls pixel art games home, while an unrelenting lo-fi keyboard soundtrack and and screen-filling explosions whenever anything blows up (there's hardly a moment where something isn't blowing up) seal the aesthetic deal. It's very satisfying when all's said and done. Good game for speedrunning if you're into that, too, since the entire game is built on that very concept.

Tons of beat-em-ups mistake damagesponge enemies as a difficult game, but really, it's just tedious. Noitu Love 2 is a great study in game design, and it's a lot of fun. Recommended~

An adorable, and very fun roguelite twinstick shooter where the only enemy is fire, and a ticking timer.
Pros:
-Replayable, with random map layouts, random upgrades, and random amounts of people/cats to rescue
-The mechanics are solid as a rock, and work very well
-Controls are tight and fluid, this is a necessary point because this was originally a PS Vita game
-Very optimized, I never have any framerate issues whatsoever
-No upgrade feels underpowered, or overpowered.
-It's satisfying to see an entire room engulfed in fire, only to watch it slowly be extinguished
-The game is very cheap, when I first bought it it  was ~$7, which was cheaper than a meal at Wendy's
-Being a rogueLITE, the game isn't especially hard, and can easily be beaten once you get enough upgrades, making it rather relaxing to play.  It's still challenging, though, and I still find myself dying more often than winning.
Cons:
-Some upgrades are 100% necessary to get a decent time.  If you don't have the large water tank by stage 3, you'll have to refill your water tank somewhere (sometimes the only area where you can do so is the beginning of the level)
-There's no description of what power ups do, not even a glossary.  The fact that the game is relatively unknown means that the wiki page (if there even is one) contains zero to little information
-There's no FPS cap option, so if you don't like playing with Vsync on, prepare to be maxing your video card as it renders 400+ frames per second
-The fire extinguisher feels very weak, despite the claim that it "puts fires out faster" than water, it doesn't prevent the fire from spreading, so you end up using far more extinguisher foam than you would water.  Not to mention the foam can disrupt your vision, making it difficult to see where the fire actually is (double dangerous when the green fire comes into play)

If you expect a puzzle-solving "adventure" with clever graphics, a superfluous but well-presented storyline and some unexpected twists and turns, then you'll like The Room Two. I certainly did.
The attention to detail is outstanding, as were the textures and lighting effects used throughout the game. Not surprising, perhaps, given that the available scenes (or chapters - seven in total) are limited to one room or setting each. But small can be beautiful; a point well made by the Fireproof team, who have succeeded in conveying The Room Two as the labour of love it most likely was.
Most of the puzzles progress logically (to my mind at least) and often simply require you to find yet another hidden compartment in a piece of furniture. It can be quite satisfying when you do. Only on a rare few occasions did my enthusiasm fade enough to consult a well-structured hint menu that guided rather than pushed me to the next discovery.
A quick mention of in-game sounds, which again are top-notch and help to build tension towards the end of each chapter. And of the sheer inventiveness on show here, that at times had me mutter "wow!" under my caffeinated breath - never a bad sign.
For a fiver, The Room Two proved great value for money and left me with a warm enough feeling to write this. And I didn't even have to kill anyone. So if you're the puzzling type and enjoy a good-looking game that doesn't rush you, this may well be one for you.

The game has many elements that are very attractive but is relatively short and the story is not very deep. The graphics are very attractive and allows exploration of an intricate abandoned mountainous mining community. The mechanics for reconstructing a crime, murders in this case, are interesting. I found that the process for searching for clues could be in some cases seem very arbitrary, sometimes I had to go back and forth over the same area many times, even with the aid of a guide to find a clue.
As mentioned in other reviews, the story is Lovecraftian. My experience with well-developed stories in this genre is that as understanding grows, the world becomes increasing bizaare, disturbing, and horrible. In order to work, though, you need to  have characters you care about. The shortness of the game and the particular view of the world you get (the last moments of ghosts) limit the depth of character development.
At $19.99 I won't recommend the game; too short and not enough story depth. But for $10.00 I'd recommend it. The developers are skillful and they have interesting game mechanics that could serve well in the mystery/detective genre.
