Of course, this is mostly due in part to how static the environment is. There' no major particle effects from super violent gameplay. This game is 60% walking simulator. So almost all of the beauty of this game comes from just walking around and admiring the amazing lighting, hi-def textures, and great atmospheric music.
What gameplay there is though, is truly original. I love the supernatural detective powers of Paul Prospero, your character, and how they tie into the gameplay mechanics. Pure poetry. Such a great game mechanic which I can't go into detail about because of spoilers so I'll say it's just about the highlight of the game.
All of this being said though, there were two things about this game that really rustled my jimmies.
1. The character models are uuuuuuuuuuuuuuugly

There really is no excuse for this. Since The Astronauts put so much work and effort into making the landscape so gosh dang beautiful (and it really did take my breath away, so many screenshots), it would make sense that people would pay a lot of attention to the details of this world. So of course people would pay EXTRA attention to the character models who are more important to the story than the environment. Unfortunately  they just look so terrible in comparison to the environment it's a really jarring juxtaposition that isn't welcome.
They all look like wax sculptures that were left at a couple degrees higher than recommended. On top of that, the facial rigging makes their mouths move in all sorts of disgusting ways that really breaks the immersion. Their eyes are also not separate from the rest of them so they never blink and they always look straight ahead.
2. The acting is rather sub-par
I'm not just talking voice acting either, the way the characters talk to each other as well as how the animations were "directed" seem really awkward and contrived. It's like watching a cheesy Scyfy movie. This could just be the bad character models doing this and the acting would seem fine if they weren't so ugly,
If you really find this so hard to believe I'll even post a cropped screenshot here of Ethan with as little spoilers as possible:
First off, his eyes are WAY too big and his mouth is so warped it looks like someone stitched it shut.
I still highly recommend this game for any atmospheric game lovers and walking sim lovers. The terrible character models aren't enough at all to counterract how great this game is overrall.

Ever since I played Myst back in the 90's I have craved a game that would allow me to explore every nook and cranny it has to offer. In fact I've played many first person shooters hoping to satiate this need for exploration. With these I have always been left with an emptiness afterwards, a result of the fact that there is an "S" in FPS rather than an "E" for exploration.
Finally a game that does away with that "S." The Vanishing of Ethan Carter presents us with a gorgeous world designed to be savored and explored. A gorgeous and creepy world. Damn those 2 things blend nicely. The breathtaking vistas compel you to explore the other side of every hill and see where every bend in the road leads, but the haunting soundtrack adds just enough apprehension to keep you on edge as you explore.
If you, like myself, are craving an adventure game that transcends the point and click variety, consider giving this game a go.

Note:  This is a spoiler free review, as such you might find the review vague.  That is an unfortunate side effect of being spoiler free.
Synopsis in 10 words or less:  Its Dear Esther with bad puzzles.
I had high hopes for this game, and was ultimately very disappointed.
Regarding the graphics:  Pretty average.  Nothing special and nothing we haven't seen before.  I give the game kudos for being very photogenic, as there are plenty of nice locations and venues for landscape screenshots.  However, since the gameplay so often has you looking at the ground or nitpicking over objects you really will begin to notice that a lot of the environmental texturing quality is inconsistent.  I also noticed that pretty much the only visual filtering they used was sunbeams during the first few minutes of the game, and during the short yet enjoyable phases when following Ethan's writings.  The rest of the time the visual effects were static or just... more sunbeams.
Regarding the narrative:  Let me put it this way; the premise is not what the game really is about.  Granted, the first hour or so feels pretty good, but then things start to get... well there is a noticable drop in quality.  Its as if for the first hour they were trying to make a game based on the original premise, and in the second half of the game they suddenly scrapped it and changed writers, but JUST BARELY managed to get a coherent story out for the end.  However, it was RIDDLED with plot holes, fridge logic, and hand waves.  It feels like a series of random events happening one after another in no real coherent pattern.  I do give them points for actually finishing the story and making a (barely) coherent narrative, but its the sort of thing that sneaks up on you on the last minute or two of the game and makes you go all "well that felt pointless and empty."

Regarding pacing:  Horrible.  Level design noticably decreased in quality during the course of the game.  At first, a lot of things were close together and there was environmental abiance after triggered events, such as distant rolling thunder over the mountains and the sky becoming overcast and such.  There is also a veeery interesting story by Ethan in the beginning.  GOOD!  However, that all just goes away after the first hour.  After that first hour, you can tell the developers tried to "lengthen" things by making a lot of space you could walk around in that was utterly empty and devoid of anything, especially between locations.  Like I said, its like they lost half their staff and needed to get out a game or something.  The worst part is that the gameplay encourages you to look in every nook and cranny because if you don't you'll probably miss something.
Regarding the Gameplay:  I'll be honest, an adventure game that doesn't hold your hand is an interesting concept but ultimately all this game does is prove that it makes for a frustrating experience.  What the game did well during the first hour or so was the feeling of exploration; the valley was big and interesting, with abiance and texture.  Buuuut that came to a grinding halt since you realize pretty quickly that the game is completely linear.  There are a lot of times when it is clear what you are supposed to do but you have no idea where something is, and many objects are placed so they blend in perfectly with the scenery (hense the immense amount of time staring at the ground and walls).  The game mixed two things together which simply don't go well together; linear experience where the only way to progress is to solve the puzzle, yet the puzzle involves finding something.  Okay, but the game doesn't give you any clues to where those things could be.  In other words, most of the time you will be wondering around aimlessly, without clues, trying to find the next thing to do in the game.  Its a lot like Dear Esther gameplay wise, with some puzzles thrown in with utterly no explanation on how to do them, and (at least after the first hour) instead of a stunning visual journey it just ends up as the same dirt corridor lined with rocks and pine trees, and houses that turn out to be a lot less interesting than they could be.
Regarding the sound work:  Average.  Music was forgetable but not unpleasant.  Pretty much all the same sound bits are recycled throughout the game, there is not a lot of variety.  Most of the sound effects are within the ambiance.
Regarding the Characters:  Utterly and completely forgetable.  Nobody in this entire game stood out, at all.
Replayability:  None.  The game's strongest point is being exposed to it for the first time and the feeling of exploration encountered in the first hour, after that it gets dull and boring and repetitive.  After getting kicked in the gut with the narrative at the end, replaying the game would just be a painful, predictable, slow experience.
Value:  I wouldn't pay more than $3 for this game, the $20 price tag is ridiculous.  All things considered, this game has virtually no content.  The only reason I have 7 hours on this game is because 2 of those hours were AFK time, and the rest of that was just walking around to every nook and crannie trying to find♥♥♥♥♥♥  I'd say the actual real gameplay in this game is a little over an 1 hour, the rest of the time you will be just trying to find stuff.  So, 1 hours of real gameplay, 4 hours spent searching for♥♥♥♥♥♥ and 2 hours of AFK time.  Not worth $20 in any sense.
In summary:  The premise is not what it seems.  Everyone in this game is forgetable, everything about this game is forgetable.  Its like Dear Esther (walk through the park type game) except added in frustrating gameplay and it literally just stops drops its strongest point, the visuals and the ambiance, after the first hour.  So you might have fun for an hour, but after that hour its just a boring, frustrating game.  This game is definitely not worth $20, and if you want a similar yet much better game go play Dear Esther (its free too).

It is clear that the only people who still play this game are people who have only recently gotten into this game, and the hardened veterans of yesterday's Company of Heroes 2.
I have over half my time in this game into the Soviet Union, who have been both the most and least powerful faction, and are now sitting somewhere in between.
I will spare you the details, but this game has always, and will always need balancing. That is with most competitive, asymetrical RTS games though.

This is probably the most fun Rogue-like game you will ever play. I think the challenge is what makes this game so great. Disregard the hours that Steam shows ive played, that is just on my new PC. I bought the online humble bundle and probably played around 200 hours throughout my senior year high school classes. Even with so much time spent playing, this game will still bend me over, and it doesn't use lube.
Ok, now to the gameplay mechanics.
The Ships.
- The unlock style of the ships is amazing. Can't beat the boss with a ship to get the next one? Then just figure out the random events that will unlock the ship. Even with there being 10 ships (8 of them with 3 variations, 2 of them with 2 variation), each ship's play style is unique and requires different strategies to be successful.
The Weapons
- The different kinds of weapons also cater to the individuals play style. From Missles, to beams, to lasers, there are so many different combinations that work well together depending on the ship build. Even the best weapons aren't too overpowered, they are balanced well so that there is no "Guaranteed Win".
The NPCs
- Each race has specefic advantages, and disadvantage, which means a healthy mix is suggested. And through the extra long and tough games you may find yourself becoming attached to your crew members. There have been tears shed when a faithful crew has met an early demise.
The all powerful RNG
- The unpredictability of this game is probably the most important feature. Literally everything is dictated by the RNG. And believe me, you can be having your best game yet and out of nowhere the RNG will literally crap on your hopes and dreams.
Conlusion
- I hope I have convinced you to buy this game, because what else are you looking for in a single player game than:          ------Unlimited replay value
------A challenge level so high you will have an aneurysm at least once
------Seriously do you need more reasons than I have already given.

Hmm, how do I review such an awesome game... There's so much to talk about...
*Warning, this is very long, mate*
~Mechanics~
It's like all other Lego games in most ways; you go through the story of the movie the game is based on, destroy things and Lego studs pop out, you use them to buy characters and vehicles and upgrades (most commonly known as "Red Bricks").
There are some things that set it apart a bit from other Lego games though.
:Graphics:
The game has really good graphics. The shadows and textures and water and all are really good. It runs smooth and all the places look like from the movie.
:Missions:
This game has missions (y'don't say). Missions for Scavengers, Resistance members, First Order members, Bounty Hunters, translator droids, and general missions for anyone. You have to be one of those folks, then accept the mission. They're fun to do, and once you've completed them all you can redo them.
:Hub:
The hub in this game is many smaller hubs. There's a pretty good sized hub on each planet, D'Qar, Takodana, Jakku, and Starkiller Base. There are missions to do and characters to buy in each planet-hub.
On D'Qar is the Resistance base, it looks just like from the movie. The character creator and place to buy Red Bricks (upgrades) is on this planet.
On Takodana there's Maz's Castle (or, the ruins of Maz's Castle...) and the lake and a few small islands.
On Jakku there's Niima Outpost, the village the First Order attacked at the start of the movie, and a large area of desert with crashed Star Destroyers and X-Wings and Tie Fighters from battles both long ago and recent.
On Starkiller Base there's, well... Starkiller Base xD There's control buildings, the big platform from wich General Hux gave his speech before firing the Starkiller, out in a stone area where you can't get to there's Tie Fighters lined up and ready, and there's the snowy forest in which the battle between Kylo Ren, Finn, and Rey took place.
~Storyline~
The storyline is just like in the movie, but with Lego humor added. The only thing I don't like is they make the First Order act rather silly... But it's Lego, so eh, that's what Lego does. You play through all the iconic events as Rey, Finn, Poe Dameron, Han Solo, Chewbacca, BB-8, General Leia Organa, etc...
On buyable DLC levels you can attack the Resistance as Kylo Ren and Captain Phasma of the First Order (personally, my favorite levels). Kylo Ren and Captain Phasma are included in the game already though, the DLC I'm referring to just adds one or two levels from the First Orders POV.
There's Steam achievements as well, something I always love. =D (I don't have them all yet, shhh...)
~Characters~
The game has the most characters to play as of any Lego game I've ever played (and I have nearly all of them xD ). There are 293 playable characters (not sure if that includes my DLC ones) from every Star Wars movie; prequels, trilogy, sequels, and The Clone Wars. There are many versions of some characters as well, with different outfits, weapons, and abilities as they acquire them in the movies storyline, e.g., you can play as Rey as she is when you first see her with just her salvaged quarterstaff and Jakku desert clothes, then there's a version of her after she receives the LPA NN-14 blaster from Han, and then a version when she gets the lightsaber. And all versions have different/edited outfits (some may be ripped/dirty), it's quite amazing.
:Character Creator:
The character creator in this game is probably the best one I've seen so far. Every time I get a Lego game I always run as soon as I can to check out the CC. It's a big thing for me, I like the creator to include many body pieces and weapons and things so I can make my own hero or create a character they didn't add to the game.
TFA's character creator is great. It includes all body and weapon pieces in the core game (except capes ;^; and it doesn't include DLC pieces, sadly, even after you've bought the DLC), allowing for lots of customization.
The custom minifigure characters all act the same, they act like Luke Skywalker I believe, not too bad. Can be a boy or girl custom character without looking really odd. I don't like it
when the default "acting" for custom characters is silly. ( I wish you could choose who they acted like... *coughcough* *hinthint*
In Lego Pirate of the Caribbean all custom minifigs acted like Elizabeth Swann... Really prissy and silly. And they sounded like Jack! That character creator was really bad... It had maybe 6 different pieces to choose from... But I'm not here to talk about that game.
What are some other Lego game character creators like you say? That is a good question, for another time... ;)
In TFA's creator you can also create a custom BB-8 or R2-D2 style droid (however, on the R2-D2 style droid the colors on the "head" piece are stuck as gold and blue, even if you change it it reverts back, a small annoying bug :/ ).
In character creator conclusion, the only complaints I have with TFA's CC are:
1. There are only six total "human" custom character slots. My sis and I play the game together so we each have only three custom character slots. I wish there were more "human" ones, the droids aren't as customizable or fun to create and play as.
2. Only one character has a cape, a white one. It's color is unchangeable and no other custom character can have one.
3. Only one character sounds like a girl when jumping/doing things (not that bad, just mean the majority of your custom characters have to be dudes).
4. You can't choose the acting of the character. So if you want to make an alternate version of Kylo Ren, he acts like Luke instead of himself... You should be able to choose how they act. Seems like it wouldn't be too hard to implement...
But other than those things, it's a great creator. (Can you tell character creators are one of my favorite parts of Lego games, haha xD ^^^ )
~DLC~
Seven (7) of the DLC packs add characters from previous Star Wars movies and new and upcoming movies (Rogue One, I believe).
These packs are:
The Empire Strikes Back Character Pack
Droid Character Pack
Prequel Trilogy Character Pack
The Clone Wars Character Pack
The Freemaker Adventures Character Pack
Rebels Character Pack
Jabba's Palace Character Pack
Four (4) of the DLC packs add new levels.
These are:
The Phantom Limb Level Pack- During the process of C-3P0 and a number of other droids trying to escape an acid planet, you learn the story behind how C-3P0 got his new red arm.
Jakku: Poe's Quest for Survival- Poe Dameron is trying to escape Jakku, with the help of Naka Iit and Ohn Gos. This is after Finn leaves their stolen Tie Fighter wreckage, believing Poe to be dead.
First Order Siege of Takodana Level Pack- You are Kylo Ren and a Stormtrooper of the First Order, storming the shores of Takodana and leading the assault on Maz's Castle.
Escape from Starkiller Base Level Pack- After crash landing on the surface of Starkiller Base, a pair of Resistance pilots, Lieutenant Wendy Wright and C'ai Threnalli (along with a droid, R3-Z3), must escape the planet before it explodes.
I bought the game November 29th 2016 and first played it December 1st 2016. I completed the game on February 7th 2017. It took me (and my sis playing with me sometimes, she co-op'd with me) about 87 hours of gameplay, with a bit of just running around the hub/levels and exploring.
That's about all, I suppose. Get the game to explore it all. ;P

* I'd give this game an easy 10/10, but for a rather weird "global war" mechanic it has that I find detracts from the game. Every game you play contributes to an on-going global war which is fought on 3 fronts, against the 3 main enemy types. If one of those fronts is conquered, that enemy type is shut out of the game completely until the war ends. In practical terms this can mean 1/3 (then 2/3) of the game's content can be locked away from the player for days on end (wars can take 20+ real time days with one front being won on day 12, so that's 8 days with 1/3 of the game unavailable to you). So be warned. I think it's a really bad mechanic in an otherwise simply amazing game.

Helldivers is a great game. (Maybe spoilers?) It's simple, it's got some clever gameplay traits, unique and varied enemies, weapons and items are punchy and clever, and and it's just plain fun. Bouncing around the map hitting any objective you can, fighting back to back with your teammate, holding out against hordes, and scrambling to the shuttle; it's a rush and it's fun, especially on the higher difficulties. Stratgems are very interesting and are really a compelling game mechanic. Rather than carry a bunch of useables and such like, you have to call these support items. They're not just there for to use at any time. Calling in an airstrike, an APC, a weapon, ammo, what have you, it's always a tactical decision. A constant debate I have is at the start of a mission, should I call in an ammo drop, when I'm only going to use one ammo box out of the two. Should I save it for later when I've drained some ammo, although that may leave me high and dry deep in enemy territory. I also love the universe the game is set up; it's not greatly elaborated on, it's not a story driven game obviously. But it's pretty clever with the way the NPCs quip or the descriptions for enemies or certain entities, and the constant sarcastic yet subtle digs at democracy by BEING a democracy. It's pretty clever and funny, and it always gets a chuckle out of me. However, I feel like the game slows down once you get over level twenty. You kind of stagnate. It takes forever to level up and most of the stratgems and weapons are unlocked by that point. Upgrading them is a nice goal but its a tedious process. I think a better decision than releasing a lot of DLC right off the bat which consisted of a few outfits, weapons, stratagems and such, should have been to incorporate all of that DLC into the game as unlockable items, which would have made the game more packed full of natural content. I decided to get the game with all its DLC just so I wouldn't useless when playing alongside others who have DLC. Other than that, my biggest issue with Helldivers, is the single player, in that it doesn't have one. Look it really nags me as someone who enjoys a game with a balance of single player and multiplayer (leaning towards the single player) when a game advertises that it has Single Player but in reality it just plonks you alone in the multiplayer world. That's not single player. The game had a lot of potential for a single player, seeing as how the self-mocking democracy Super Earth thing was really polished up could have created a dynamic story in which the player character discovers that his or her patriotism is being exploited to engage in galatic imperialism. But instead it just has you alone in the game world. Which can be a nice challenge; a Helldiver by yourself is quite the (AWESOME) experience. But again, it's just a personal thing when a game says it has single player and really doesn't. I don't distaste Helldivers all that much for it really; it's base value is twenty bucks, which is how much a multiplayer only game should really go far. I hold it against games more like Titanfall, which was like sixty or seventy dollar game that was only multiplayer which really goes nowhere. Helldivers is worth the price though! No mission is the same and the challenge always ensures you'll have fun. :)

Flame over is a game where you are a firefighter, going through the different floors of a burning building. The floors are randomly generated, making every run unique. Each run through the game gets you coins and possibly upgrade tokens, which allow you to buy improvements making the next run a bit easier. Sometimes a level also contains a store allowing you to buy items that will help you along the way,
Equiped with both a water tank and an extinguisher, you have to carefully manage your resources as you are fighting the fire. Water will work on all fires, but if you don't also extinguish electrical fires, they will flare up again.
The game has both a time and a health system. If either runs out, you will die. The timer or health don't reset between levels. By rescuing people and cats you gain extra time and health. On top of that, you might receive a mission from one of the survivors. completing these mission will earn you upgrade tokens.
Sadly the upgrade system is somewhat pointless, since  a lot of the upgrades apply to items you can buy when you come across a store. These store are so rare however, and the items you can buy are randomized, so most of the time you won't have access to the items you upgrades with your tokens. It makes the upgrade mechanic mostly pointless.
I had great fun with the game at the beginning. There is a tutorial level and 4 more  area's, each compromised out of several floors. The first two areas are great, but once you hit the lab area, the difficulty ramps up in such a wa that progression is hardly possible. After dozens of tries, I have yet to clear a single floor in the Lab area. The game went from pretty fun to incredibly frustrating.
In the end I wouldn't recommend it. Without a better upgrade system and a better scaled difficilty system, the game feels lacking

Let's just get this out of the way right now: I love this game.
There is something about roguelikes that I love. Except almost all of them try to be copycat versions of another game. Rarely does a game try to actually do something unique! So what makes Flame Over so different? Is it because you're slogging through a dungeon/space station fighting enemies, drinking potions that you aren't sure could kill you? No.  Nothing like that. You're fighting an enemy. That enemy is fire. Electrical fires and regular fires. There are flame overs as well as fire that spit out embers which can set other things alight!
You're a fireman aptly named Blaze. The game takes place at Infernal Industries. There are 4 levels with each level containing 4 different segments. These are procedurally generated floors consisten of cooridors and room setpieces. The fire is random. Some rooms are ablaze with several people in them.
You try to rescue people, and cats. There is also Miss Ion who won't leave until you do some task for her. She lost her purse, she needs you to find and post the secret documents, she needs to to enter the vault and secure the valuables, or she needs you to back up the servers. There are other things, but I won't spoil that here. You can level up, Blaze, by completing these tasks. You are awarded some coin as well to purchase upgrades. People give you bonus time and cats give you bonus hearts. There is also a shop where you can buy temporary upgrades. Perhaps the best ones are the super hose and the large water tank.
So what makes this game so fun? There is just something enjoyable about putting out fires. It isn't so much that I feel like I'm helping people or the cats that are in the building. It's just that it changes every time. This doesn't get old. No fire is the same. I have played lots of Roguelike games that tend to do the same thing as the others, this doesn't do that.
Of course, it isn't a perfect game. Like most roguelikes you get good runs and terrible runs. Sometimes you'll run out of time, others, you'll have more than enough time and this is needed for the later levels. If you die and manage to get back to the level that you died, you can regain your old items. Of course, this doesn't apply if you select a level that you died on. Sometimes you don't get the chance to save people. A fire will spit some embers or a flame over will happen and they die instantly. Unless you have a resucitate them, they remain down, once they are dead you lose 10 seconds. This is somewhat unfair since there is no way to get items other than the random shop. You can find extra time and money though.
Also, when you run out of time Death will chase you around the map. Which is a bit funny. You can actually manage to drive death away if you can get people through the fire exit.
There are some things that I would love to see in this game. I would love to see an infinite mode where the time limit is removed. Also a time trial mode to see how many rooms you can clear in a given time. I would like to see more variety in the people you rescue, more women for instance. I think that the upgrade system needs a little tweaking as I was easily able to max everything out after just a few runs. Not necessarily just make things more difficult, but add a few more perks. Maybe this is something that can be made in the sequel?
There are a few other suggestions. For example with the electrical fires. You have to flip the main breaker to remove power, however, this doesn't change any of the lighting nor does it remove power from the servers that you're supposed to back up. These aren't major issues however. Perhaps once the fire is out the timer can stop? Sometimes you'll clear the map and be at the farthest point from the door. Having rescued everyone already, you have to trudge across the map to clear the level.
One other very minor complaint is that the game doesn't constrain the mouse to the window on a multi-screen setup. In fullscreen, this makes it possible to glitch the game out by accidentally clicking outside of the window and then the renderer gets confused/broken. A save and resume would be nice as sometimes if you're having a really good run, you need to take a break and it would be great if you could just resume at the same "level" that you were.
The music is catchy and jazzy if a bit repetetive, however, it does get different mixes depending on the level that you're on it also speeds up in the same way that Super Mario Bros. did when you were running out of time. Overall the sound is good. It would be nice if maybe the people could cough more than once after initially entering a room. Also the cat makes no sound to let you know it's there. There is a strange music levels problem from when you are in the main screen to when you play a game. In game it is much louder than in the main screen. You can turn off the sound of the coins and the feet.
There are a good number of items hearts, stopwatches, hoses, water tanks, extinguishers, axes, masks, night vision goggles, and other things that can help you through your task.
The camera is funky, but works. You can rotate it with the middle mouse, if there is a key to set it back to default, I haven't found it. It would have been nice to just have a hotbar for the various power ups and then we could use the number keys to activate them.
Fully rebindable keys is a nice thing to have although the defaults are just fine.
In closing, I have very little negative things to say about this game. The game even provides advice: Don't rush it. Take it one room and cooridor at a time. I haven't mentioned the graphics, but it's very cute. Laughin Jackal, You done good!

This game's novel approach to difficulty makes it unusually engaging. This is not a game you will sit down and complete in a single game. Make no mistake, this game is CHALLENGING and you will fail, repeatedly. But nor is this game inordinately punishing in the vein of an actual roguelike such as NetHack. A large part of the progression comes in terms of your own personal skill and strategy, which will develop over multiple play-throughs.
There aren't many games about firefighting, and this one does it in comic, challenging style. It deserves more players.

Flame Over:
~~~~~~~~~~
Your name is Blaze, you are a solitary fireman who is armed with a hose, axe, water bombs and foam. Your objective is to put out a raging fire that spread from an office to a factory (Levels) as soon as possible and make your way to the exit in time.
In each level, you will be able to save people and escort them to safety. Each soul saved will be rewarded by 1 additional minute. Save cats, your favourite pets, and you will be getting additional health each time you do so and let me tell you, Blaze needs as much health as he can get! Do not forget to search rooms as you can find some valuable items, like the watch which give you a bit more time and others.
With each level you beat, the difficulty increases. Remember that whatever time is left when you finish a level, it will carry to the next one and that will be the time your will have to clear the new level.
You will earn money by putting out flames. Sometime one of a trapped person will refuse to follow you to safety because they have left something behind. Recover the items for them and be rewarded with a token. REMEMBER, PEOPLE YOU SAVE EQUALS ADDITIONAL TIME! Upgrade your perks if you accumulate enough money and tokens.
In terms of game play, it is absolutely marvellous either with the gamepad or mouse and keyboard. The graphics are great and the soundtrack is SUPERB! This game is extraordinarily addictive but with a soundtrack like this, it becomes insanely addictive! $11.99 well spend!
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Great graphics
-	Controls are easy to master
-	Addictive and fun to play
-	Challenging
-	Achievements
-	Trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Can be a tad too challenging at times
Just get it! It is a brilliant game!
9/10

Blending top down ‘squirt ‘em-up’ action with Roguelike RPG mechanics, Flame Over features fast-paced fire-fighting thrills, randomly generated levels and 4 deadly game zones.
Guide fire-fighting hero, Blaze Carruthers, in a race against time and near-certain death! Squirt, splash and spray your way through all 16 floors of the deadly Infernal Industries building, combating ferocious fires in a red-hot adventure that changes every time.  - Recommended!

Flame Over is a procedurally generated roguelike title about being a firefighter. It reminds me of Sega Saturn’s Burning Rangers, except you get a top down, almost twin stick shooter format with two modes of putting out fires. Water puts out flames, and foam puts out stubborn sources of fire. You also have to watch you oxygen while you rescue people and return them to the starting point. You can find power ups and upgrades, or just buy them from the merchant who decided opening up shop in the middle of a burning building made sense. Whatever, just go with it, putting out fires is fun and the random nature of the game means you can play it a bunch before getting bored. Grab a controller, the keyboard isn’t recommended.

If  you have read the store page, and watched the trailer, you will know what your in for. basicly your goal is to put the fire out, recover as many people and cats as you can, and make miss ion happy (that kinda is the only painful thing about the game) being a "rouge inspired" game mechanics wise. its unlikly that two runs will be exactly alike. however I do feel this game has understood what makes this kind of gameplay good and addopted it to the firefighting gameplay.  while its not with out its flaws, its a very well focused game that knows what it wants to do
the actual gameplay is great because it gives you the rules upfront. this is a race to the 16th level, (of which each 4 represenets a zone, with a set style) on top of that, you have a few diffrent tools to work with up front (as in your not compleatly weak to everything from the start) not that its not hard. but its not unfair from the start. when you first spawn in a level, the timer is stoped until the green door is opened, giving you time to check the map, see whats in each area of the map.  while this game has a kinda awakred camara, the green door gives off a glow even off screen so you can find your way back to the exit with out needing to look at the map all the time.  the time limit is really there to keep you moving and is the major threat in this game, fire will not do damage to you, until you sit near it for too long, and as such, it punishes you for rushing into a deep blaze (though sometimes you need to to get civs out before they die) the other main form of damage is the overheateded doors which you will know because of the fire at the base of them, if you open them, they expload on you. usualy there is at least one cat per floor so you can get hits back if your decent enough.
where this game gets hard is as follows. when time runs out, the reaper shows up and chases you around the level, if he hits you, its game over. though you can still get your loot back if you make it to that level in one run. but while its posable to dodge him, most new and even experanded players would rather have more time on there clock.  civs and cats die very quickly, if you get the defibulatior items, its posable to revive humans, but, you can only do it twice, after which they are dead. cats can no be revived if they go down, not that easy to see them ether.  in a room with fire, when you enter, only then do the other charators start taking damage, but there is a coughing sfx to make sure you know there is someone there, cats might have a small sound effect, but I cant here it. the game drops 10sec for every person you let die. no penetly for cats as well all know they have more lives elsewhere.  there are also electrical fires which are used to force you to chose between going for the plug box, or going elsewhere first. while you can put them out with the foam (not the water) it often takes a while, and many times its easy to put all but one out, then have a random fireball set all of the electric fires back alight, which makes everythign take so much longer. thankfully once you hit the fuse box, all of them dissapear
miss ion and the progression system, she is a npc who like others can die, however until you do her mission (terible I know) she will not follow you, each mission on the floors she appears on are always the same. (floor 1, one red bag, 3 5 files and post it in the red post box, 5 find the valult and loot it. however once compleated, you get a min and a half of time then and there, and she dropes a ion token, collect them so you can unlock more perks
the game has around 7-8 perks, aside from the first one, you need a set number of ion tokens to unlock them, then you can spend some  of your money to upgrade them up to 4 or so times, most of these really help you out in small simple ways. but. they really dont add that much to the game out side of giving you a reason to do the miss ion quests. if I had to say there was any bad points to the game, its that the missions are trivial and annoying, as all your doing is moving around near objects and pressing f. but at least its not interfearing with the game play at all and can be done fast. I am sure some people like it more then others. its never needed, but it can help.
the games difficulty goes up each stage set by not only getting slightly larger, but also expanding the size of the fires in each room. every 4 levels changes the theme (1-4 is office, 5-8 is ex rooms, 9-12 is the lab, 13-16 is the factory) each zone adds more flamable material, thigns which spread fire in more dangrous ways, as well as the 3-4 zone adding extra hazzerds. this makes it very hard to beat all of the levels, however you will be able to start at any stage if you want. once you have gotten to it once.
the soundtrack is for the most part really good, though each zone has only one soundtrack, when you get low on time, it changes to the panic form and stays there until you at least get one min of time on the clock. the theme of this game is amazingly fun, being very uk. I do find the audio to be very good with the exception of the looping on the spray for both foam and water. it tends to have weird pauses instead of being continuis fully, however these can be fixed. for a indy game its pretty well done though it has bugs.
the only downside is that there could be more room types. and the difficulty goes down alot on the early areas with pratice. to the point of sometimes feeling trival. and often most rooms are not that hard. however, there will always be that one room which is a jerk to you. and I do think that a bit more work could be put in to make the map generator a bit more consistant.
the developer is active on the forums, there was a day one patch which did make the game better, and its clearly a soild product. i can recommend this game to people who want somethign that works, and plays well. as always check the forum and do your reserch, watch a video or two to get a good idea about how it plays and if you will like it or not.
I give this game a b+, very solid, while still having room to improve.

This is one of my favourite games. To be honest the title of this games does not sound that interresting and the graphics might be a bit outdated (but still very nice in my opinion), but it's really worth it to take a closer look at this game.
The story is being told like a bedtime story. The character you play, tells his daughter the story about his journey when he was searching for his missing uncle and discovered a different world.
You'll find a suit invented by your uncle that lets you jump high and far through the scenery. Also included in this suit is some kind of grappling hook that you can (or better have to) use to swing through this new world (and to use this, is SO MUCH FUN!)
So now you start your journey, discovering this world on your way to find your missing uncle.
The playtime is really short. I finished the game in about 3 ½ hours.
And if you don´t fall in the ground as often as I did, you can finish it much faster. But you will fall in the ground very often ;)
Like I said it was a lot of fun "flying" through this world, but there are many places where you don´t see where to go next at the first time. So when I was wondering where to go next, what I did was to jump in a direction and try if I can grab a rock or something else nearby. Aaaand.....what a surprise.....I fell in the ground ^^ But even if you see where the right way is, it´s often not easy to follow it. That can get a bit frustrating after trying the same thing over and over again.
But this is the only thing that makes this game difficult, because you don't have any enemy to fight. And that's a good thing in my opinion, because that way you can really enjoy discovering this beatiful world and the feeling to "fly" through the air.
So would I recommend this game?
YES, absolutely.
BUT: Considering the playtime of only 3h - 4h I would wait for a good discount to buy it.

half-life 2: episode 1

Intro
One of the first ever let’s play series I did for YouTube was Valve’s staple Half Life 2. While I wasn’t as awestruck as some fans of the series, I can appreciate that at the time of release that game would have been revolutionary, combining simplistic intuitive controls with incredible storytelling that was mostly accessed through cues in the background. Recently I headed back to City 17 to continue my adventures with Dr Gordon Freeman and companion Alyx Vance in pursuit of more headcrab zombies, quirky puzzles and of course any more information concerning the ever-elusive G-Man.
Graphics & Aesthetics
Now it has been a good while since I played Half Life 2 from what I remember it looked great. Not mind-blowingly spectacular by any means but certainly utilitarian, Valve are very good at dark rusty kind of textures that we say plenty of over the corner of the game. Speaking of dark, this title featured quote un quote dark sections much more heavily than its forebear, often plunging you into complete blackness and surrounding you with zombies - I found myself relying on the flashlight much more than usual. The lighting effects that we are given are perfect for their role, and the occasional sparks and energy blasts we see are nicely convincing. While we don’t get any of the beautiful panorama shots present in Half Life 2, it does definitely feel like effort has been put into the small spaces we see, and I don’t begrudge the designers for that choice.
The game ran almost flawlessly on my system at 1080p and a butter smooth 60fps, and really is not taxing at all. I did encounter a few bizarre microstutters at some points, this maybe happened three times over the course of my playthrough, but nothing crashed the game so there’s that.
Details on items and weapons look great, as do the models, it’s pretty much identical to Half Life 2 for all intents and purposes. I do think that these titles will start to look dated in the near future, but in 2015 we’re still at the point where everything looks just dandy to me.
Sound
Now the sound design with this one was very interesting to me. The ambient musical tracks present in the game are extremely quiet and unintrusive, which does add to the starkness of the whole thing and increase the sense of isolation. Occasionally however, during lengthy combat segments, the volume really ramps up and we’re treated to very loud very fast passages, and I wasn’t as keen on this, as it really does become overwhelmingly noisy, particularly when trying to see what’s going on or use sound to determine the location of your next target. I can see what they were going for here with this dynamic disparity to establish a mood, but it could have been pulled off a little better by taming things down just a little bit.
The sound effects and voice acting are great as per usual, a real strength of the series. I must commend Merle Dandridge here, the voice of Alyx, as while she is the only speaking role that accompanies you throughout the whole game, her delivery feels extremely organic and I was highly impressed. The ominous moans and whispers of the zombies is as blood-chilling as ever, particularly during the very dark sequences, and the weapon sounds you’ll hear while dispatching are nothing short of sublime. Valve really take a no-nonsense approach to sound effects that I appreciate, and for some reason the one that stands out to me is the crossbow. The dull thunk that accompanies seeing an enemy slump to the floor is so satisfying.
Gameplay
Now as we all expect it’s fairly standard FPS fare when it comes to gameplay. I love the smoothness of camera pans whether using a gamepad or mouse, as it’s little things like this that help keep you immersed. Movement is fine, a very stripped down affair, apart from some small issues that I had when trying to jump into vents or other small spaces, the navigation of which plays a larger role this time around.
Speaking of which, our lovely companion Alyx Vance travels with us over the course of this adventure, and feels much more like a true partner, dishing out damage to combine forces and scaling obstacles as well as Gordon Freeman himself. While she’s a more-than-capable bullet sponge, she can actually die, so don’t let her take on all the zombies by herself, okay? She starts to panic in pitch darkness, and you’ll have to use that trusty flashlight to pierce the blackness and illuminate the oncoming hordes.
Simple logical puzzles also return from Half Life 2, but do note that the challenges are both fewer in number and arguably much simpler. There is nothing new on offer, more of the same kind of thing we’ve seen before, perhaps tighter if anything, less open to novel problem solving. In any given room it’s usually extremely obvious what to do once you’ve explored, and not much is required of the player in terms of grey matter. Not that that’s a bad thing of course, I really didn’t mind the lack of difficult logical problems, but if you were expecting the same degree of nuance as before, you won’t get it here I’m afraid.
Ollie’s Verdict
So, this game currently retails at £7.99 on Steam, and for that price, I’d definitely say hold off for a sale or buy it as part of a larger bundle. I got about 3 hours out of the main story, so it really is very short, and while it’s a great experience, don’t pay full price for it.
Who is this for? It’s for people who’ve played Half Life 2 and want more, that’s really it. If you haven’t done that, you likely won’t understand a great deal of the plot, so make sure you do that first. It’s another adventure in the Half Life universe you love, nothing more, nothing less, but a highly enjoyable experience overall, however brief.

Really fun game that seems to take a lot of cues from Crackdown, rather than from Grand Theft Auto. While the last game in the series (Saint's Row 3) was a lot more in line with the others in the series and the whole open world gang/car theft genre, this one instead imbues you with a plethora of super powered abilities. Such as super speed, the ability to jump miles up into the air, as well as a glide ability that basically is as close to flying as you'll get in this game. So you won't hardly ever (if ever) use your vehicles like you would in past iterations.
That's not to say it's a bad thing, especially since I find this kind of super powered gameplay a lot of fun especially for fans of Crackdown, but fans of past Saints Row games might find this one the odd one out in the franchise, seeing as how this one has the most drastic changes to gameplay out of all of them.  I still had a lot of fun with this title, but people who are expecting more of the same from the past 3 games will be in a pleasant surprise with this one. Would recommend.

Bring back Lego games. No voice overs, please.

This game belongs to an era that sadly was never meant to be. It is an RPG whose design diverges sufficiently to the norm of the era (and even onwards) that remains an unique piece worth checking. Character development doesn't occur via experience points at all, rather every assignment you finish grants you Skill Points, which you can then choose on what to spend (categories broadly include combat, stealth, sorcery, social, merchant, compuer hacking, among others).
There are classes divided by a set of available vampire clans, a few of which have some notably interesting traits, including for example that Nosferatu clan members are so hideous that they must remain out of sight of all humans all the time, moving through sewers and hidden passages. Dialogue is superbly written, and the semi caricaturesque character design grants them a huge array of facial expressions rarely seen even today.
Game is not perfect, and its development was rushed due to Executive Meddling, which left the very last section of the game poorly done in contrast to the beginning and middle parts. While there are some excellent fan patches that iron out most bugs, some design choices just can't be changed without some hardcore reengineering.
Nevertheless, this is an excellent game RPG fans should check.

As an RPG fan of all genres (western, japanese, action, etc) Vampire Bloodlines is my own personal favorite. Vampire captures that dark sort of gothy 90s feel perfectly, and is an incredibly immersive experience. If you get a chance. play the game only at night with high quality headphones.
It isn't without problems, like all great RPGs. Namely, a number of bugs that makes the game near unplayable without propper patching. But if you're willing to do a little extra work (15-30 minutes tops) you'll be rewarded with one of the very best experiences and stories gaming has to offer.
Vampire is probably one of the last games of this style, coming out between the 90s and 2010s, it's an RPG that has the 3d immersion of current games with the depth and complexity of early RPGs. Even the Witcher, which is vaunted up as a paragon of storytelling, hasn't reached the kind of writing you get in this game. Which isn't to say that this game throws heavy mature philosophy at you like Planescape. And it doesn't have the extreme violence or sex of the Witcher. It isn't even as massive as Skyrim. But it doesn't need to. It's a tightly wound self contained experience.
I also suggest first time players try the Malkavian race, which no doubt every single other person who's played this game would recommend. And add some fun mods the more you play it. Although, honestly the fan made patches by wesp add so much content that it's always a joy to come back year after year to find all new content that's subtly been added. Or minor tweaks to certain quests and cutscenes.

TL;DR: Short, but I liked it, and it's a challenging game unless you have good teammates.
A lot of the DLC equipment you probably won't use, except for the helmets/ capes/ armor. Usually the most viable gun options are the tanto/scythe, justice, breaker, and rail gun. You'll see most people running around with these.
You start off at lv.1, and work your way up through the varying difficulties of planets for either bug, illuminate or cyborg. Levelling up nets you weapons and a few perks, successfully completing planets gets you strategems like mechs, turrets, etc..
It's fun and amazing, until you beat all the planets.
Generally you beat all of the planets and races, around the time you hit lv.16-18, by which time you realize that it requires a LOT of experience to level. A LOT. Then you think "Oh, I'll just grind planets lv. 10+ for a few hours". You then realize that few people know how to do these levels without alerting every scout, and then they pack on the fun by forgetting to bring adequate anti- armor supplies. You end up running around the map with no way to kill big enemies, constantly ressurecting your pals, with one objective left.
If someone tells you to get in a vehicle on a illuminate planet that is lv9+, shoot them and blow yourself up. It's what would have happened anyway.
Then it's decided that you grind lower levels. After a while this gets boring, and you realize that most weapons are almost useless at planets lv8+, and some are exceptionally good at killing your teammates. Many many times people have turned to shoot a scout, and instead hitting me point blank with a shotgun.
Unless you're willing to reset your progress every so often to keep things fresh, I'd say that there are about 30-40 hours of really nice gameplay until you hit the wall of high exp and no more gear to get.

It's a good thing this VN was free, in my opinion.
I will say a few things constructively that I didn't enjoy with the game.

*First, this game with all of it's paths is extremely short. Even with the bonus content, and bad endings - it was easily completed fully for me within a few hours.
*Some of the lines require proof-reading as grammatically, they do not make sense. There were a few sentences that absolutely lacked grammar. Which made it difficult to read.
*Some of the sound clips do not loop properly leading to me actually turning off the sound effects as it was annoying to read for parts of it. Also some of the voice clips weren't recorded properly either leading to some unintended distortion.
*The artwork really could use some work here. Anatomically most of the faces in this are distorted in a way that is unappealing (eyes that do not align properly, clothing that doesn't sit right, the male body/torso construction, While one can argue that it's related to art-style, I would disagree and say that even if you have a specific style, It's still important to understand how the human body moves/changes shapes with different directions.
Also Some of the shading doesn't make sense with light direction/scenery in the CG's. The "adult" cg's weren't done very well either, while maintaining a "innocent/seductive" theme it should be important to study human anatomy at the very least. There were a lot of issues here with the art.
On the pros:
*It was a fun premise for an otome game, and I liked the background of the story/the world setting, although with such a short story it left a lot of openings and plot-holes to add character/world development it was still interesting on a base level.
*You can name your character whatever you wish and have it not effect the game's story, as they make use of the MC's last name, or "her" instead of saying the name. Which is a good touch.
*All of the characters are fully voiced in English, minus the MC. Which is a good thing. The only thing I did not like about this is that some of the characters were extremely annoying to me due to the voice actor in question. Some of the lines were delivered without any emotion which gave a cringe-feel to their paths, others just had a really high pitched "not cute" fake-cute voice, which would have been more interesting had the voice been lowered and more natural.
I would still recommend this if you're bored but as far as VN's go, I've played much more enthralling ones, with a price tag attached. Given that this is free however, it's not that terrible.
It's a shame there weren't more interesting lines used and difference in character paths aside from one or two differences a lot of the romances are copypasta. So - I'd say that it's good, not great.

Much of the game is wandering around the absolutely beautiful landscape looking for clues. There are only a small handful of puzzles, but the few substantial ones are very enjoyable. While I was wishing I had more to actually do, the beauty of the presentation, the story and smattering of puzzles made the game worth playing. At 4-6 hours it neither wore out its welcome nor felt too short for the type of game it is. I think if you enjoyed the other two games I mentioned The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is worth a look. Having a little more 'game' to it may also make it worth playing if the thought of wandering around examining things doesn't turn you off too much. As a whole I'm happy with the time I spent with it. What to say about this game that probably hasn't already been said. Probably not much, so I'll lay out my words all the same. I enjoyed this game quite a bit. It's what Dear Ester wanted to be and failed in doing so. Yes, it is mostlky a 'walking simulator', game interaction mostly taking you from one story scene to the next; but where this game does it right is in how you're able to interact with the story elements. I loved the detective work parts, finding the various items, putting together how the sequence of events went down and finally getting to sense the story that happened in that area. (I want more games with this feature)
So points to 'The Vanishing of Ethan Carter' for telling it's story and allowing the audience to interact with it; to feel as if they're experience it. And I really do like that the game doesn't hold your hand. (Perhaps a little detrimental, at least in one part. I got lost and hadn't the faintest idea where I was suppose to go next)
As for the story itself: It's engaging. I can't speak too much on it, least I spoil it. It's very good though. Tense and suspensful. In one part, it was downright creepy and overall a sorrowful one. The music works very well with the game, haunting you as you walk through the forests, tense when you're exploring the crime scenes.
The game is also amazingly beautiful to look at. Lighting is perfect, the game feels organic, as it should: You are looking at nature through most of the game. There's a sense of loneliness, isolation as you wander the Valley, seeking answers.
I would highly suggest this game, but it is more of a walking-simulator then a proper game. It is not, as I said, a game where you're immersed in action, but more so that you're experiencing a story and you get to investiage how something happened.
Overall Rating: 9.9/10.

I was intrigued by the very first words upon starting up this game - it doesn't hold your hand.  It almost comes across as a challenge and it was one I was keen to take up.  To begin with I made my way through the game without too much trouble.  I even discovered some aspects that were apparently easy to miss the first time around.  Eventually though I after spending well over an hour wandering around I began to get frustrated.
And that's the biggest problem with the game.  Actually knowing that there was a puzzle in front of you.
Generally they weren't that taxing to solve once you came to that realisation.  It took me playing for 2-3 hours and the use of a guide to work out that I actually hadn't completed several sections of the game - but I had no way of knowing that.  In hindsight, I realise now that the very first encounters do allude to methods that need to be used further on.  It was just too subtle to pick up on.
Visually the game is stunning.  I found myself stopping regularly just to take in the surrounding scenery.  It actually looks and feels like a living breathing world.
The music is mostly understated but suits the unfolding story perfectly.
The game isn't long.  I played through the entire thing in around 5 hours but my playtime was definitely reduced by the use of a guide at certain spots.  Normally I try to avoid external help as it detracts from the experience but in this case the lack of guidance within the game warranted it.
So if you're looking for something short and challenging with an interesting story to discover then I'd recommend giving this a look.

The roguelite genre is becoming a rather busy place as of late, with all sorts of entries satisfying the various niches and cravings that a fan could possibly desire. This one however is a rather unique and notable entry because the foe isn't something that you'd come to expect, namely - fire. Sure, fire might be an incidental or environmental hazard, but it's not every day you're going to be donning the uniform, putting on a nice shiny helmet and getting your hose out. (Make of that what you will). Here you play a rather cartoony firefighter, based in good ol' London, tooled up with bottles of foam, an axe and water, and it's his job to go charging in to various toasty environments and make things not so burny.
The civillians (Which remind me of the Xbox avatars) and cats you must rescue equate to precious extra minutes and lives, and time here is given out at a rate which means you have to keep moving fast, fast, fast. There's no time to dawdle and take in the scenery, it's a case of zoom in to the room, clear out the worst of the fire in the most efficient manner possible (without taking too much fire damage), use foam to clear out any electrical fires. And on to the next room, if you need to rescue anyone, you time it so you can get them back as you need to refill your water and foam supplies. This is a game that really punishes you for sticking around, as the moment you run out of time, the grim reaper may elect to show up, and if he catches you, that's an instant game over.
This brings me onto the difficulty overall. This game is harsh, as in - "Do the tutorials a few times, then repeat the first few levels until you've got the hang of it" harsh. Because the fire has been programmed in such a way that it will spread if areas that are burning are left untended, and will spit out fireballs that can catch on areas and start up new fires once more, it's very easy to not douse a room properly and before you know it, a room that's "Mostly done" becomes a room full of fire, and you'll lose 20-30 sec having to re-do your work. It pays to be thorough in each room, but without sacrificing too many of those precious seconds.
You're given three hearts (lives) as a means of recovering from mess ups, either from taking too much fire damage, or opening a door that's on fire, or similar misdemeanors. It's
to use up a heart simply by straying into areas which are too hot for too long and then having the fire pop up behind you, turning a safe area dangerous, educational in a sense in showing that fire is unpredictable and a roaring blaze needs to be treated with respect, but in game terms, it means you'll be losing lives almost as often as you'll gain them at times. The only thing that keeps you from running out of lives by say, floor 4 are the cats you save, which keep you alive and ticking over.
Thankfully the game does get easier with repetition, cash can be poured into firefighter upgrades which improve drop chance, lengthen rescue revive times, and generally improve the overall hardiness of your firefighter. The roguelite metagame means that in the long term once you've picked up some equipment from one of the shops as you play, and once you've some upgrades in the bank, things smooth off and you'll be making steady progress, getting further and further.
The graphics are consistent and cartoony, and well presented, everything is easy to see and on a pad at least, controls are quick and easy to manage, this is important because quick reactions are fairly vital to not losing your lives in a hurry. The music is equally cheery, though how long before you reach for the "mute" button on it will be a matter of taste, the sound effects are well into the "functional" category, they work, that's it. Not much more to say. What I will give credit for is that the fire spreads and gives a glorious bright display when you open a new room, it can be quite livid and hateful when it wants to be, it's not some horrible bitmap, it feels like proper, angry fire.
It ticks the roguelite boxes, with proc-gen levels, with a persistent upgrade tree, with equipment that makes life easier that you can get during the course of your run, and the game is pretty fun. It's very competent, and the theme helps make it stand out from what is now becoming a very crowded genre. It's not quite among the greats, but as they'd say t'up norf : "It'll do."
Verdict :

Flame Over is a rogue like, firefighting, twin stick shooter that has you play the role of Blaze Carruthers as you fight your way through 16 floors of a burning building of various levels, putting out the fires and trying to save civilians and cats. The game has a very simple premise, but because of it's simple premise, you can find it quite addicting. Controlling Blaze can be a bit of a struggle at first, since you move him the left stick and rotate the camera with the right (Like a normal video game) but pulling either of the triggers will make you aim with the right stick instead of rotating the camera. Since this means you have to stop using the fire extinguisher or the hose just to turn the camera, it lead to time wasting, but that's not necessarily a bad thing since time is always counting down regardless of what you are doing within the level, so it leads to a few decisions making in which you can decide either to save this person or leave them because you are running out of time.
The civilians and cats aren't there just to fill empty space and add urgency to your mission (Though it does do a good job at making the game more intense) they give you bonuses if you save them. Each civilian you save grants you one minute of extra time which is very crucial to progressing through each level and floor. If you do end up running out of time, the grim reaper will spawn within the level and hunt you down and kill you the moment he touches you, adding another sense of urgency. Cats, on the other hand, give you a heart of each one you save (Maximum of 5) which is your health and it carries over through each floor and level. You don't have to save everyone, but with each person you let die, takes ten seconds off your remaining time.
There are two different ways of fighting the fire, one is a fire extinguisher which is used to put out fires on electrical equipment (Phones, computers, vending machines etc) but can become useless once you turn off all the electrics at the generator that is in each level somewhere. A second way is your hose, which is what you'll use the most, since it has decent reach and sprays water quite effectively. Lastly, you have water bombs, which you can throw and will splash water in a large area and douse the fire. Both the fire extinguisher and the hose will require water, so you will eventually run out and need to refill at either a water cooler, drinking fountain or at the entrance of the level. Water bombs do not require a refill, instead, you'll have to either find them or buy them at the shop.
Obviously, the fire itself is the main issue, not just because its a fire (Duh) but because of how it spreads. The game promotes realistic fire spreading but that's not entirely true. The can fire can sometimes spread from one object to another like a real fire does, but it has a habit of materializing into a ball of fire and flinging itself across the room or into the next, sometimes leaving a trail of fire till it lands. Unfortunately, it seems to purposely aim for you only when it becomes a ball of fire, making it a bit annoying to deal with.
As a firefighter, Blaze seems have a low tolerance to heat and fires. Each room you enter that has a fire within it, can lead to a gauge appearing around him symbolizing how much heat he is taking. Once it is completely full, you will lose one heart from your health, which means you have to move away from the fire before the gauge is filled. Not entering the room however, doesn't raise the heat gauge, meaning you can stand outside the room and spray water in without risking your health.
It may not be the best looking game in it's graphics but it's artistic design and measure make it stand out and look unique, as something that is graphicly impressing can have boring gameplay, but a game that has a specific art design that suits it can make it more appealing.
The AI however are another problem within the game. With every person you save from the fire, you have to lead them to the entrance of the level to save them. However, they don't follow a direct path, instead, the follow you exactly, leading to them running into walls and objects and getting stuck.
At the end of it, it is very similar to Spelunky in it's design. It's challenging, addicting and quite fun, with that sense of urgency to each level as you try to save everyone while getting rid of the fire as you race against the clock. For a cheap little game with an interesting design and cartoony style graphics that make it more appealing, it's worth the asking price for hours of entertainment and content.

You dont see the whole story, it wont say it to you in black and white, but it leaves just enough to be understood, with so much to be interpreted that if you want to put the thought into it, (or just cheatingly check its forums) you'll have that much more understanding and appreciation of it as a game.

Excellent platformer! Truly beautiful environments to fly through with some very tight and well executed controls.
Graphics - Amazing! Art direction is really good. Environments are beautiful and inviting and glow with light. Quite spectacular. Also ran quite well with no problem keeping the framerate up at 60 on max everything which I find helpful for platforming.
Story - Not really that great. Voice-acting is also so-so. The narrator who speaks the most is actually the worst voice acting in the game. Serves as a justification for the excellent platforming.
Level Design - Almost entirely excellent. There are only a few parts where you have to wonder which of a couple paths to take and only a few where it takes a while to discern where to find a path.
Difficulty - Not overly challenging. I am not a very good at platformers and clocked in at about 6 hours with only a few areas with numerous repeat deaths. Of those I only found one area to be actually frustrating vs. challenging. There are a few spots where it seems like you have to go too far before the next checkpoint, but most checkpoints are after around 2 sets of actually challenging maneuvers.
Controls - This is really a big part of the game. The controls are very responsive and work really well. You really feel (with a nice big monitor in a dark room) like you are hurtling through the air almost wildly out of control at times barely escaping death but touching down to safety. It is one of the more exhilarating experiences I have had in a game.
Overall, excellent game and definitely worth the few bucks this will run you.

Sanctuary Plays like a single player MUD.
If you ever wanted to dip into text based online games but find them intimidating or to rapid paced, this is a much slower, more friendly RPG introduction to ASCII textual adventures.  Set your nostalgia back to the 80s because Sanctuary returns us to the days of IBM floppy disk playstyle, but adds all the swish new techniques of today's slickest MUDs.
The RPG elements are top notch and more often than not innovative over today's AAA games.  The character class combinations are incredibly fun.  The system is easy enough to understand, so one is never bogged down with endless cumbersome keyboard commands.  The controls make sense, are to the point, displayed on the screen and turn-based, so you can learn at your own pace.  The risk factor makes the game feel very realistic and often even frightening.  Charming townspeople and chilling dungeons alike await intrepid adventurers.  The music is wonderful and worth buying as a DLC.  It evokes feelings of old Nobuo Uematsu fantasies with lots of crunchy nintendo blip goodness.  The graphics may seem simple, but they are incredibly complex and beautiful.  Just try to draw these yourself!  Every monster and treasure is well rendered in ASCII and better than 3D graphics in this case, as it allows the player to imagine a fair amount of the world as well.
Crafting is great.  Quests are enjoyable.  The fightng is damned fun.  The limit break system is dynamic and carries over across battles.  Stored TP can then be used for difficult battles, opening up with that devastating special attack.  That's just one small example of how complex the battling is.  All the while, it never gets hard to control, overwhelming, or confusing...  but don't go thinking this roguelike holds yer hand, it does not.  The player is soon plunged into a world of danger & excitement.  I fear for my characters' lives.  Their experiences feel very real.
Black Edition is wicked & well polished.  Worth buying again.

This is an incredible game.  It's an inexpensive puzzle game that is expertly crafted.  It's a few hours long, not quite twice as long as the first Room (which is wonderful as well).  The approach is slightly different, with a greater focus on interacting with different objects in a small space and inferring when to bring an object from one 'station' to another part of the room and use it there.  The graphics are updated a good bit from the previous game, and there's more impressive particle effects and animations and interludes, more cut-scenes, all that sort of stuff.
There's more of a horror æsthetic but not to a degree that it would be troubling for most people.  There's one scene in particular that may put off someone that is very against the whole horror thing, but it's not an extreme sort of thing.  Personally, it was one of my favourite aspects of the game, this whole creepy, mysterious atmosphere.  It was like all the best atmosphere of classic Resident Evil and its puzzles, but with gameplay that is exclusivley puzzles and where the puzzles are infinitely more complex than Resident Evil's.
They do have a timed hint feature that can be turned on and off, so if you think it may too hard for you, probably not.  The hints start out small and get bigger over time, and you have to click on them to see them.  It's very well done.
There was an elegance in the first game that is eschewed in favour of intricacy here.  Neither is bad.  personal preference I suppose.
The story is told in notes, and frankly, I don't think it's incredibly well told (same as the first game, more or less).  But that is the last thing on my mind when I play.  Everything else is just too engaging.

Now that I have 150 hours into the game I can probably write a review. The game is still early access but is still being developed fairly fast by a one man band and he has a full time job to boot. If you are looking for polished graphics and audio, then this game is not for you (so far).
It's a simulation of you being a software developer/guru. You run your company on one of 3 difficulties. There is mod support too.
Gameplay can be found on Youtube but some of the videos are of some pretty early versions of the game.
What's in the game so far: pathfinding is really good but there is some improvement that is being made, ability to hire, train   (through education or leadership skills) and fire (but there is a penalty for this) workers, bonus items for your workers including managers( called lead in this game), better chairs, room decoration, food and coffee, toilets, windows, lights, heating and air conditioning, servers for control management as well as for web store and online game servers,  software contracts and other jobs(deals) through a receptionist feature, multi-story building (up to 10 stories) and a basement. Recent addition is polygon rooms. There is also an automation feature too!
You get to control the quality of the software you produce at the expense of more time developing and programming. There is also reputation in the game which can influence how your customers perceive you. There is a stock market.
When creating software you can choose to sell to the market, give it away (open source) or use it in-house (this may change shortly so you can use in-house then sell in the marketplace).
Weaknesses: As stated above, graphics and audio leave a lot to be desired but in my opinion are fine as they are. The financial system could be better. I am not a fan of the stock market nor of the financial reporting system for expenses. I did not note above but there is insurance for your employees too!
Overall, I highly recommend this game if you like building and management games. Oh, did I mention Mods? Well, this game can be modded too!
