Noitu Love 2: Devolution is an absolutely smashing (pun-intended) hidden action/indie gem. It features some fantastic mouse controlled gameplay with tons of robots to smash up and plenty of firepower to do so. To be blunt, every single bit of this game is absolutely fabulous.... the boss battles are challenging but fair, the pixel-art style is gorgeous, the level design is awesome, and the music... is great!
Really, what better could you possibly ask for out of a $5 game? Granted, it's not all that long with the base story, but I found myself completing the game many times with the variety of unlockable characters available to you and the multiple difficulty settings. Too easy? That's okay, the game is more than happy to crank up the difficulty for you... no matter how experienced you are, there's always something fun and challenging for you here. Beat your previous score on the levels, shoot for an A ranking, or even just something as self-imposed as trying to go through the game without taking any damage.
For those few saying the combat is "Boring"... did you even go through the OPTIONAL tutorial available to you? There's many different attacks you can use, not just the simple punching up an enemy to bits one... (although even that is great fun) and the other two characters you unlock after beating the game in various ways each feature their own unique attack and movement styles... it's all great fun, so you really need to give it another go.
To anybody debating about purchasing this game, just go ahead and do it! It's well worth the money, one of the best games you could buy at this pricepoint.
As for me... I'm just hoping they make another sequel! :D

I personally feel that they could have combined Episode 1 and Episode 2 into a single game, considering how short both were to Half Life 2. Still a great game, though.

The
episodes were meant to be a foray into a new method of game development. Instead of spending several more years making Half-Life 3, Valve would release smaller iterations over shorter spans of time, which would also let them refine their work as they went. Coming out two years after HL2, Episode One was a relatively understated success, with improvements made in AI and the Source engine taking the technical spotlight.
It's not nearly as long, dealing primarily with the aftermath of HL2's finale, but in the process avoids the drag that game sometimes suffered from. There's a decent variety here: the first third of the game only gives you one weapon to work with (albeit a powerful one), the second third is almost survival horror, and the final third is a roaring return to Combine-destroying action.
You're partnered the entire time with Alyx Vance, who is thankfully more helpful and humorous here than annoying, and it's with that you realize that Valve also meant Episode One to be an exercise in character development that did more than just have you stand around for 5 minutes every time an NPC opens their mouth. The game is largely a success in that department too, and Valve's signature stealth brilliance in writing manages to make her not only cool, but human.
If you're reading this, you probably already own it, but if you don't (or do and haven't played it for some reason) and were a fan of Half-Life 2, I'd say go for it. At the very least, it's a good bookend between its predecessor and its more outstanding sequel, Episode Two.

Dying Light offers players an open world filled with loot and zombies to play around in that offers a large array of quests to complete and weapons to use. The story is alright, as much as you can expect from a zombie game, but I actually really liked the characters. The main character Kyle Crane is voiced by an extremely talent voice actor, Roger Craig Smith. I think he did an exceptional job here along with the script from the writers. He reacts very realistically to the situations and says often what I'm thinking which is awesome. The story is very linear, you're unable to alter the story in any way or make any choices, but Kyle Crane always makes the right decision in my eyes which I'm really glad about. Moving on, the graphics are great and the music is good enough. The gameplay is really solid. It's very impactful and satisfying using both melee and ranged weapons. I'm not a fan of gore, but the effects of slicing and dicing zombies with a wide array fo melee weapons, is gruesomely satisfying (does that even work?). The game has a really awesome drop in and drop out multiplayer which is great for playing with friends. There's quite a lot of variety in the skill tree which can change the way you play. Now literally one of the BEST things about this game is the Parkour system, you can literally be Spiderman swinging between buildings with your grappe, it's insane. It is immensly enjoyable jumping and swinging between buildings, climbing almost everything and moving where ever you please.
Now some negatives, well, they're more just me nitpicking, because I think this is an excellent well designed and functional game, these are just some things that annoyed me personally. I really dislike the whole lose xp on death thing that you have in ARPG's (Path of Exile, Titan Quest) and it's also used here. It makes dying really frustrating, especially since many deaths are not really your fault. At first I hated the low durability and the fact that after you repair a weapon a few times you have to scrap it, but as I kept going I noticed that I was always getting more weapons than I needed, making it much more tolerable. Lockpicking is an okay mechanic but it's massively overused here. Like 60% of boxes and many doors need you to lockpick them, and believe me, there's a lot of boxes. I just find it very tedious and frustrating, I decided to just use a mod to remove lockpicking which enhanced my experience tenfold. Okay, guns... There's loads of awesome melee weapons to mod and use, but there's practically no guns. I understand this is a melee focused game, but come on... there's like 1 shotgun, 2 rifles and 2 pistols. That's it... Looting is awesome in the first half of the game but in the second half I literally started just leaving everything because I was overflowing with resources and money, which really started to make the game boring to me.
I can't really comment on the multiplayer experience as I couldn't find a game. So maybe keep that in mind if you're looking for a multiplayer experience.

If you played any door games in the past, such as Trade Wars, Legend of the Red Dragon, Tele-Arena, and various other games played on BBSes, or later MUDs in the beginning of the internet, then do yourself a favor, and buy this right now, you don't need to read further.
I'm such a person.  I played lots of door games, had a BBS myself, and been active on various BBSes for a good number of years, starting with a 2400 baud modem and going all the way up to 56k, then broadband.
I saw SanctuaryRPG suggested to me, and as soon as I saw the store video, saying this was Steam's first ASCII game, and saw the very nice ASCII graphics indeed, I was sold instantly.  I didn't looked up the reviews, nor checked the forums, I didn't even expanded the more info on the game.  I just bought it.
So when I tried it, I had the biggest surprise of my life... this game is pure genius.  Only with a text game you could come up with such a brilliant, deep, very deep, combat system.   Yeah, you heard me right, this text game has better combat than all graphic games out there.  And yet, you see nothing of the combat itself.  I won't spoil it, but it's real good.
Don't be fooled, its no rogue-like in the common sense, you aren't a letter on a grid, and move one square at a time, with enemy moving after you.  This is played more like traditional door games.  Not MUDs tho.  You don't move with directions.  The rogue part is the permadeath, tho you can play softcore.  But I highly recommend you play the way its intended, classic with permadeath.
The chip tunes soundtrack is very good and totally fit the game.

I am a massive fan of both Star Wars and Lego. I've played Lego Star Wars I-III, Lego Indiana Jones I+II, Lego Harry Potter I+II, and several others, and I have always loved them. And in fact, I loved the 30 minutes that I was allowed to play this game. You know, right up to the point where it decided that the controller I'm using isn't good enough to let me continue. I made it to the hub world. That's it. I then had to "launch BB-8" using some booster pad, and it was only then that I was informed that I needed multiple joysticks on my controller in order to continue. "Okay," I thought, "I guess I'll just use keyboard and mouse, then. I don't want to, but at least it will let me progress."
Or, you know, no mouse support.
I am now at a point where I have already dropped $25 to get this game and all of its DLC, and now I need to spend an additional $20 on a controller that will actually let me play it. I am currently contemplating whether that purchase would even be worth it.
If you have the right controller, then by all means, have fun with this game. It's as good if not better than the games that preceded it. If not, be aware that even if you buy on sale, you'll have to spend nearly twice as much as advertised in order to actually play the game.

I played this for over an hour and that is time I will never get back, because as there's no manual save and despite finding a whole load of stuff and entering one of the buildings, I didn't hit a single automatic save. Whether I do it all again now or come back later after finding a save point I'm still faced with the fact that when I've done it it probably won't be saved, and I face I don't know how many more examples of my option being do it all again or leave the program running. I should live so long.
Would it have been so difficult to give us a configurable quicksave button or to automatically save whenever we achieve something? Definitely not. Clearly the programmers aren't incompetent which means they made a conscious decision to leave this huge gaping flaw in this otherwise cool looking game.
It seems like pure bloodymindedness, like once they'd seen how cool and pretty it is they decided that they should also judge what the right and wrong ways to play the game are. It seems I fell on the "wrong" side, but I was just exploring. They've made this huge beautiful environment and they expect us to just rush through it to hit the savegame points before we get bored or run out of (real life) time – How does that make sense? They haven't decided the right or wrong way to play the game – They've shown us the wrong way to make the game. They've got my money, but hopefully it's not too late for you.

Pros:
- This may be the most beautiful landscape I have ever traversed within a game. The attention to detail is phenomenal and you really do feel like you are walking through a painting. Considering the short length of the game, I'm actually quite surprise how much detail went into the landscape. You will spend a great deal of your game taking screenshots of the scenery
- The story is chilling and compelling and is one of the better ones that I've seen in a game
- The paranormal murder puzzles are a unique story telling device and were easily the most enjoyable aspect of the game.
- Voice-acting and character design were good and fit well with the serious subject matter of the story
- A few of the locations offered a genuinely creepy vibe and one in particular offered a downright jumpscare
Cons:
- While it looks quite large at first, the game world is actually remarkably small with hidden walls and natural barriers blocking any travel over a stones throw off of the road. Part of me was thankful for this, however, as finding the puzzles would have been near impossible had you actually been able to travel everywhere you could see.
- For the most part, the puzzles (especially the last couple of murders) are fairly weak for an adventure game. They seemed to serve more as a storytelling device than as a traditional adventure challenge.
- The game is surprisingly short with less than a dozen or so largescale puzzles. Considering the unique and successful execution of the murder puzzles, it is a shame that the game only lets you play with this feature a few times.

Do not let the ASCII art turn you off, this game is really amazing. The art is honestly very good for ASCII, and the minimalist style allows for greater focus on the solid combat mechanics that make up the core of the game. As well, you will immediately notice the incredibly high quality chip tune inspired sound track, which is also allowed greater brain share as the graphics are less attention demanding during combat and dialogue.
There are 6 classes which all interact with the basic set of commands available differently. Barbarians heal while doing damage better than other classes, Wizards put up Barriers that increase their defense and offense, Rangers shoot and stab things to death while nimbly avoiding damage, etc...
On top of this, there is a vibrant meta-game layer in which you can own a bar, build a house, become a master crafter of various items (this system is VERY well done), go to the Colosseum and use the Arena (fight for crafting materials), explore Portals (fight for great loot), and do Ranked Matchmaking (fight for Skill points).
If you can deal with perma-death, this game should not be passed up. Fights tend to be fair and you will realize quickly what you're doing wrong after the first few deaths. It does have a mode where death is not permanent as well, though, if that is really a deal breaker for you.

I am a massive fan of both Star Wars and Lego. I've played Lego Star Wars I-III, Lego Indiana Jones I+II, Lego Harry Potter I+II, and several others, and I have always loved them. And in fact, I loved the 30 minutes that I was allowed to play this game. You know, right up to the point where it decided that the controller I'm using isn't good enough to let me continue. If you have the right controller, then by all means, have fun with this game. It's as good if not better than the games that preceded it. If not, be aware that even if you buy on sale, you'll have to spend nearly twice as much as advertised in order to actually play the game.

If you like any of the previous LEGO star wars games, you'll enjoy this one too. Basically the same formula except with more characters and features. The first negative I can think of is that since it is only based off of the one film, it feels like the games story mode is a bit stretched out, with less variety of playable characters then previous games. That said, the fact that they got pretty much the whole cast back to do more lines is really awesome, allowing for better integration between the game's humour and the source material.
I will say that I personally have not come across any bugs or crashes yet, so the issues that a few people are reporting are not ubiquitous.
I also have not even bothered trying to use mouse and keyboard, since i gave up on using them in LEGO games ages ago. If you have a controller, I fully recommend using that.
The only other negative i can think of is that, unlike in previous games, notably the complete saga, in which all the characeters are iconic, or at least recognisable in some way, a huge number of this games large characeter grid are completely unknown to me, even as a massive star wars fan. The DLC character packs help reduce this a bit by adding additional established characters from the previous films and both animated TV shows, but the level packs mostly add obscure or possibly made up characeters that tend to be slight variations of others in the base game.
Overall, its a LEGO game, and that means obsessively smashing everything you see, collecting every red and gold brick, and unlocking every vehicle and character. In general I'd say it improves the standard formula of these games adequately, and is an enjoyable experience to pass the time. I only wish that there were more iconic characters in the game, however i understand that since it is based on one film, it is predominantly going to draw from that one film. The positives outweigh the negatives however, and I fully recommend this to any star wars fan, of any age.

I am a long timer lego player and love the lego games and always try to play them to 100%. Right off the bat I want to say I'm very happy with the original voice lines the actors from The Force Awakens did for this game. They didn't say anything amazing but the fact this lego game had its own dialog from the actors themselves was a huge point of pleasure playing this game. The game also looks amazing, scenery and characters look great, its still a lego game but it looks crisp.
Now on to the negative part of the review.
This is the first lego game I've played on the PC and I'm not sure how other games have worked but the keyboard controls for this game were difficult and awkward to use. I had to use a controller to play this game comfortably, not a big complaint though as I have a seperate controller, but for users without one it might be difficult.
I am upset with the constant level breaking bugs. Critical items disapear as soon as you build them, if you fall off devices stop working the way they should, characters are randomly inside the roof or walls. I have to restart the level for all of these and it is very frustrating when you work hard to complete a level 100%. This game has had more bugs and problems than others I've played.
The gameplay is fun, but I'm sorry to say it suffers from the lack of force powers. Previous star wars games were very fun with the use of the force and the creative ways the game incorporated it. It isn't the games fault so much as the movie has little force use at all, but even after acquiring force users and playing free play your force use is limited to shaking and breaking things, nothing more than that.
The side missions can be fun, but for the most part its just running your head against a wall for a gold brick. The carbonite classic character feature is a waste of time. I have to collect the carbonites, then take them to the Alliance base to open them and unlock the character? Just give me the character token, don't make me open 30 something carbonite boxes in a row and take up 10 minutes of my time.
Overall I ask myself what was I expecting? There are lego games that cover multiple movies that are filled with great game play but this movie just wasn't something that could have been made into a fun lego Star Wars game. It wasn't bad but it was a little boring and unremarkable.This combined with the large amount of bugs and other mentioned issues is why I am giving it a negative review. I will still continue to try to get 100% completion, with luck I won't reach my limit of level restarts before then.

Hot off the heels of
, this direct sequel picks up where the last left off. It follows both in story and gameplay to deliver more of what made the first one great: manipulating all manner of improbable mechanical contraptions to win your freedom.
- Sharp, high-resolution graphics. Has settings to support low end, too.
- Ambient music that fits the mood and is never intrusive.
- A hint system that you can disable at your own pace
- The creative touchscreen inspired controls are back, and are a breeze to use
- A variety of locations, unlike the first installment
- Quite short. 2-5 hours tops.
- Virtually no replayability, since the puzzles and solutions are all the same.
- Being a direct sequel, it largely is more of the same, so if you're looking to be amazed, you might be disappointed that there aren't too many new ideas in this one.
- The next to last chapter isn't a room or puzzle at all. I believe it is there to set up the ending, but it really serves little purpose.
In case you aren't familiar with
, the story follows you, the unnamed protagonist, in search of a vanished researcher who was chasing after the legendary element "null." You are stuck in a series of rooms, all belonging to different places and times.
brings this short tale to a conclusion, but it's still a delightful time if you enjoy working with your hands. The game involves "safe cracking" all manner of mechanical wonders to try to escape the room. What makes it particularly unique is that it was one of the first on mobile devices, so it has a realistic feel, since you need to turn keys, flip levers, and so on, using touchscreen gestures.
If you're new to the series, do pick up the original first, although it is not necessary to enjoy this installment. And much like the first, I still recommend picking this up on sale. It's quite short, and there's no variation to the content on replay, so much like a fine wine, savor it while it lasts.
If you are reading devs, please bring Room Three to steam as well. Fullscreen PC versions bring it much more to life.

Even for someone with no programming background- this game is by far the most fun tycoon I have ever played! The feeling of being ablee to create every single aspect of your company from the server rooms, to the furniture, to the placement of computers, lounges, etc, and the vast range of software you can create with different sizes and features as the years go by.
I spent 11 hours straight playing this game, and started from a tiny one-room shack to a three story warehouse with fully furnished and decorated workspaces, three lounges, two meeting rooms, and a server room with over seventy servers. My most recent Operating System had been rated Outstanding, and  was close to 100% coverage in the world. I had a distribution channel with multiple physical stores all over america (or so i'd like to think.)
Pros:
+endless replayability
+customization of almost every aspect of the game
+complicated but fun financial features
+furniture and decorations, for those creative and artistic
+realistic needs of employees (bathrooms, fridges, coffee, nice looking surroundings)
+employees sometimes don't get along with eachother (that's realistic!)
+employee ages
+tons of different software production options
+tons of different features for said production options
+great graphics (imo) and hilarious animations
Cons
-features unlock only as time moves on (research teams in the future, maybe?)
-marketing is too easy (you only need, like two marketers for a company of 26 employees)
-assigning furniture to people is hard (you have to wait for them to sit on the furniture first)
-assigning a specific profession to a room is hard
this was a great game, and I'll keep enjoying it. Buy it!

I can most aptly characterize The Vanishing of Ethan Carter using its own words 'This game is a narrative experience that doesn't hold your hand'. To me, it's almost like a lovechild of Alan Wake and Dear Esther, combining brilliantly dark writing (reminissant of Edgar Allen Poe) and stunning life-like visuals (even well-textured foliage!) into an unforgettable masterpiece that shows the genre is still very much alive.
The Vanishing of Ethan Carter explores ideas of broken souls, the human condition, a child's imigination and, apparently, vanishings.
As I'm always fond of in games, there were some splendidly odd sequences (namely the space segment), yet nothing felt out of place. Every scene and aspect worked and flowed well.
And I must comment on the sheer atmospheric genius - everything feels so alive, but you feel so alone. Yet with a lurking sense something or someone is waiting for you. The music compliments the atmosphere design perfectly, provoking emotional response and, not gonna lie, it gave me goosebumps.
A beautiful metaphor and a loveletter to the genre.

I can't even begin to describe the feelings I have toward this game. It's simply at the top of its genre. The atmosphere and world design is absolutely incredible. The inspiration from the old weird pulp magazines connects with me in ways I'm unable to communicate. Art can be subjective, but honestly I don't think I could be friends with someone who couldn't agree that the atmosphere and art in this game isn't beautiful.
The feelings I had playing this from beginning to end reminded me of my childhood and things I know I can never get back.
The story set up is nice, the side quests are passable but I give them extra credit for having a direct connection with the main story. There's little negative I can say of this. I won't lie though: I picked this up on special because the normal price tag is highish, but honestly I'm pretty tight and I consider anything over 8 euros to be expensive. I'd like to compare it with Murder: Soul Suspect, which is valued at $29.99 and in my opinion that is way over priced for what that game offers, despite it giving around 7 - 10 hours of gameplay. Ethan Carter has half that and yet its full price tag of $19.99 just seems so much more worth it, purely for the atmosphere alone.
Art is subjective, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is not. Welcome to USSR of Hugo Zombiestalker. Liking this game is mandatory, or you'll be sent to the gulags.

HELLDIVERS:
~~~~~~~~~~
This is a special news broadcast from Super Earth!! Ladies and Gentleman, Super Earth is under attack! Yes, we reached out of space and discovered 3 other galactic civilizations and our initial contact was friendly. Now in 2064, we have to defend Super Earth from 3 fronts! Fortunately we have the best military units in the galaxy and you know who they are . . .  the mighty Helldivers; thank God for that!
Helldivers is an action twin stick shooter / online co-op game where you play a soldier in the famous Super Earth military unit “HELLDIVERS”.  You have to prevent Super Earth from being destroyed by three very interesting intergalactic races (Bugs, The Illuminates and Cyborgs) by taking over regions in the galaxy and by successfully defending them from their counter attacks.
When you first launch the game, you will go through a quick but thorough tutorial which give you a very good understanding of what you have to do in combat. Then you will hit the main spaceship bridge where you will be able to choose missions, weapons upgrades and the excellent “Helldivers encyclopaedia” with plenty of content.

Head up to the Galactic Campaign table; from there you will be able to see the war fronts and choose which race you would like to fight against, or just join another group in battle. There are lots of variable missions; some will be to eliminate a specific number of enemies, some will have several objectives to achieve before you go to your extraction point! You will face an infinite number of enemies in each map and your team will be using all available tricks under their sleeves to extract themselves safely.
Some of the tricks are: the “Stratagem” (which are additional gizmos you can call upon), ammo drops, defence turrets, strikes, vehicles and more. You will find samples lying on the ground; make sure to collect them as they will go towards your research points. Collect 10 samples and you will get 1 research point. Each time you level up, you will own an additional research point which you will need to upgrade your weapons and stratagems. One thing I forgot to mention is to be really careful who you shoot, as friendly fire is always on! Plenty of “Oops, sorry mate!”

If you successfully achieve your mission (objective and extraction) you will be given XP and great rewards depending in which region you fought in. Rewards could include new stratagems, weapons and more.
The graphics and animations are fabulous and the game runs brilliantly.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Great graphics
-	Fun and fast gameplay
-	Plenty of enemies – 3 different races
-	Number of upgrades and equipment
-	Different levels of difficulty (1 to 12)
-	Up to 4 player online co-op
-	Achievements
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	No trading cards
My goodness, I am hooked on HELLDIVERS! Just a splendid game!
10/10

A disappointing tower defense game. There is no choice in creating paths, very few locations to build towers, and little variety among the towers available. Over the course of the game, you do not "level up" in any way. You do not unlock new towers or improve your towers. You simply play on new maps with the same towers. Lastly, the towers always seem to target the enemy closest to them, rather than the enemy furthest ahead, so they often do a little damage to several enemies without killing any of them. There is no way to adjust the towers' targeting behavior. Other than the soundtrack, there is very little that is distinctive or excellent about the game, and there are plenty of other games that do the same thing better.

CoH1 was one of my favourite games of all time. That game was supposed to change RTS games, but unfortunately didn't.
CoH2 keeps the core of CoH1. I didn't like the changes at start but when you get used to it and re-master the game you realize that its still very good, just different, and not by that much.
for those who didn't play CoH1, this is a game that keeps the classical RTS elements: resources, units queue, tiers, but also adds realistic elements of Combat, that suprisingly, make the game so much better. The Cover system gives every tiny element in the game a strategic value, because engagements that involves infantry completely rely on your ability to find the best Cover (With optimal distance for your unit abilities, and correct direction for the fight). The Coer System is also Dynamic- and covers can be destroyed or created (for example, a destroyed tank is a great cover)
Tanks in this games are, well, Tanks. They are big, Destructive, and you can shoot them with rifles all day for no result at all. They are also very expensive and can take high damage if you hit them from the right direction.
another system is the 'suppression'. Infantry don't only cause damage to each other, but with the right tools, and with clever flanking, you can make the enemy infantry lay low, even when outnumbered.
CoH2 adds the 'true sight', which makes flanking easier and deadlier. there also nice additional elements: new destroyed vehicle smoke will block the sight for a short while.
there is also freezing system, which IMO is totally useless for gameplay, and doesnt work on multiplayer anyway because its dumb.
and of course, the resources system is smart and forces you to fight on the entire map. while the fights in other games (C&C for example) happens mostly on bases, in CoH you fight on the entire map, all the time, and rarely attack the enemy base directly. It is also designed in a way that gives player in disadvantages the tools to fight back, so battles will never not be decided until they are over.
tl;dr
Pros:
*Cover System
*Supression System
*Realism that benefits gameplay- I found myself using tactics I learned in the army as a combat soldier to win engagements.
*Different from the classical Rock-Paper-Cissors for games like StarCraft. All the Anti-Tanks in the world won't help you if the enemy tank suprise you by coming from an unexpected direction, and manouver it well enough.
*Luck is important- but still isn't. Like in real combat, the game intruduces statistical-weapons, like mortars for example. While other games try to keep the game deterministic, this game let luck have its effect, but a game won't be decided by luck (usually) because it is long enough in order for everyone to get their chance.
*Game is still supported and there are matches to play. Right now you don't need to wait to find a match (even 3vs3 or 4vs4), and the game is still supported (because some people still pay), which is the reason I left CoH1 int he first place.
Cons:
*Its not pay to win, but payment does have some benefits.
*High price. CoH1 is purchable on steam for 7.5$ only, with all expensions included.
*Balance issues are still common. there are however attempts to fix them
*Crappy AI, and pathfinding
*Boring Campaign, that teach you nothing about the game.
*Very sharp learning curve. I don't know if I could stand it if I wasn't familiar with CoH already.

Perhaps the best movement I have experienced in a First Person game. The parkour is generally very smooth, and the camerawork is super immersive, especially in the most precarious situations. The co-op is pretty seamless, and it's a lot of fun to run around a zombie apocalypse with your friends.
It's also a great zombie survival game, as the enemies are challenging, but generally you can pick and choose your battles, however not to the degree that you get to just run away when things get tough. In my opinion the zombie survival aspect of this game does the best job I've encountered in balancing difficulty and variety, in that there is enough of both. The side missions and challenges are pretty fun (keeping in mind that they are just mechanics by which you can grind XP). The day/night mechanic is very cool, and keeps things interesting without being cumbersome (you can just sleep to the end of either day or night if you want to play during the other).
The story is okay, and I think the ending was kind of weak, but that's not really why I play games like this. The story does a good enough job of having you explore Harran, which is about all I ask from it. Honestly, it's a cool way to get to know the world and then it ends, which is nice because then you can freely explore. The gear/skill progression is great, and you're constantly learning new ways to destroy zombies before you're done enjoying the skill you learned previously. The variety in terms of weaponry, agility, and combat skills means that combat really does not get stale, and there is plenty of room to advance the awesome ways in which you wreck the undead.
I haven't played The Following yet, but from what I understand it basically takes this already great survival game, moves it to the countryside and adds an upgrade-ready vehicle to the mix, so I am pretty excited.
CONS: I don't like that you lose so many survivor points when you die, because I finished the story under-leveled for The Following so I have to grind to get there. Granted, that is because I'm not very good at this game, and the way to level up is to just play the parts of the game that I enjoy, but it's still annoying. Fall damage is too high. I have died way too many times from minor falls when I had no option but to jump down. I know this is likely more "realistic" but you're fighting zombies for crying out loud.

As of this review, I have only played the prologue and it was amazing, If you enjoy zombie games AT ALL, and I mean if you get even a small bit of enjoyment from zombie games, buy this and play this, you won't regret it.

A lot of the "puzzle" often derives to noticing a switch in a certain spot or identifying that two shapes go together.  Further, somtimes the puzzles felt more like a step by step errand more than a quandary (as in, the next step wasn't much of a mystery). The tone is ominous and supernatural.  I don't think the game is meant to be scary, but there were times my imagination ran  a little wild, and I was left cautiously wondering what would be thrown at me next.  With the puzzle gameplay and the atmosphere, I was reminded quite a bit of Amnesia: The Dark Descent.  So, if you liked the puzzle aspect of Amnesia, but didn't like your heart leaping out of your chest and your pants needing to be cleaned, you will probably like this.
Ultimately, my main complaint is the game felt quite short, and a touch unfilfilling by the end.  However, I did put a solid and enjoyable 4 hours into it, and the game sells for $5.  I got the game on sale, but even at $5, it's hard to argue this isn't worth $1.25 per hour of entertainment.  You defeinitly get bang for your $1.25.
If this was longer, I would say this is a B+, possibly an A-.  As is, I'd go with a B.  I am looking forward to the Room 3.

I played this game a long time ago. My CD was defective so I never got to finish it. As years went bye I forgot almost all about it, even the name of the game, except for one thing: the diplomacy was just hilarious. Then I found the game here by chance and sure thing went ahead and got me a copy. The diplomacy, as I recalled, is hilarious indeed. But more than that, might be the best diplomacy feature I've ever seen. It's not an afterthought as in many games or just something to declare war or peace or trade stuff as with many other games, there is an strategy you must understand for each thing and each race, so is complex. But the most enjoyable thing are the many choices to banter between you and the other aliens.
Now, what is this? Very old fashion turn-based strategy game. Heavy, and I mean heavy micro-management. If that is not your cup of tea, stay away. Second, the combat is just moving troops to an enemy territory and wait for the outcome the next turn. No control whatsoever. So if you like the combat aspect more than anything, also stay away. You like awesome graphics?... same, don't bother.
Nevertheless, there're plenty strategic choices and a lot to learn to play this right. There's a rather huge research tree and several buildings and units. There are several unique features exclusive to each race, so what works for one is not the same for others. Moral and economy are big factors too. There's a single player campaign and it is huge. 42 scenarios, most of them long, 6 for each race. Hours and hours to spend. Be aware it is a little bit weird cause once you finish one of the race's campaign, it just kick you out to the main menu, so you must go to the campaign menu and chose another race and do the campaign for that. They are all connected to the final goal, but there's no indication of that. So yeah, weird. I saw no bugs and runs flawlessly, except for the rare times the screen freeze and you have to do the manual reset. Nothing big. For these old games I use my Vista PC, so dunno about performance issues for much modern systems.
I do recommend this game, is very entertaining. But, as I said before, also there are plenty things that many players would not overlook due to the game's age and very old school mechanics and features.

It was cool to play as three different characters, each with their own backstories and combat traits unique to them. I thought the whole endless dungeon crawler became repetitive over time as I completed each character`s story one after another. I thought we`d actually be able to explore the kingdom of Ys in this game but it was just a tower structure with endless dungeons one after the other. Regardless, the game does a great job of introducing the characters and the story behind the goddesses as well. I thought it was really well done and one of my favorite Ys games.

First off, if you've played any of the STALKER games, I guarentee you'll enjoy Metro 2033.
The wonderful thing about Metro more than anything is its atmosphere. It maintains the constant dread looming over everything as people scratch out a measly existence years after nuclear war in the metro tunnels beneath Moscow. The characters are interesting, getting small but satisfying helpings of their lives as you make your way through the metro tunnels in order to find some way to save your home. Along the ways you'll be treated to Russian horror in fine detail. A decent above the bar stealth system, good combat and situations that will leave you sweating as you fend off mutated animals, bandits and factions of people still fighting long after the war ended.
Pros:
-Movement feels like it has weight, gives a unique feel to the game
-Atmosphere is evrything here
-A modest amount of good characters you encounter through your journey
-The Redux has excellent graphics, in spite of some taxing areas on your fps
-Guns feel good here, they have their uses in situations and finding rare weapons can be rewarding
-Rewarding exploration of levels with plenty of nooks and crannies to search out
-Good selection of difficulties and a survival mode for a real harsh experience
-Secret but provoking alternate ending
-Excellent replay value
Cons:
-Game is a bit taxing in some areas, even with anti-aliasing turned off
-Different armors were removed in the Redux version (heavy armor and light armor)
-It's a bit short, pushing just over seven hours on normal difficulties
-Enemy AI is kind of dumb
-Frames per second can be choppy in certain environments
-Stealth system doesn't seem to have much of a reward
Overall, this is a very good game worth it's playtime, especially if your into survival-horror or just a good story heavy shooter. If you do get it, I recommend getting it bundled for the $30(USD) because the second game, Metro: Last Light is just as good as Metro 2033.

HELLDIVERS:
~~~~~~~~~~
This is a special news broadcast from Super Earth!! Ladies and Gentleman, Super Earth is under attack! Yes, we reached out of space and discovered 3 other galactic civilizations and our initial contact was friendly. Now in 2064, we have to defend Super Earth from 3 fronts! Fortunately we have the best military units in the galaxy and you know who they are . . .  the mighty Helldivers; thank God for that!
Helldivers is an action twin stick shooter / online co-op game where you play a soldier in the famous Super Earth military unit “HELLDIVERS”.  You have to prevent Super Earth from being destroyed by three very interesting intergalactic races (Bugs, The Illuminates and Cyborgs) by taking over regions in the galaxy and by successfully defending them from their counter attacks.
When you first launch the game, you will go through a quick but thorough tutorial which give you a very good understanding of what you have to do in combat. Then you will hit the main spaceship bridge where you will be able to choose missions, weapons upgrades and the excellent “Helldivers encyclopaedia” with plenty of content.

Head up to the Galactic Campaign table; from there you will be able to see the war fronts and choose which race you would like to fight against, or just join another group in battle. There are lots of variable missions; some will be to eliminate a specific number of enemies, some will have several objectives to achieve before you go to your extraction point! You will face an infinite number of enemies in each map and your team will be using all available tricks under their sleeves to extract themselves safely.
Some of the tricks are: the “Stratagem” (which are additional gizmos you can call upon), ammo drops, defence turrets, strikes, vehicles and more. You will find samples lying on the ground; make sure to collect them as they will go towards your research points. Collect 10 samples and you will get 1 research point. Each time you level up, you will own an additional research point which you will need to upgrade your weapons and stratagems. One thing I forgot to mention is to be really careful who you shoot, as friendly fire is always on! Plenty of “Oops, sorry mate!”

If you successfully achieve your mission (objective and extraction) you will be given XP and great rewards depending in which region you fought in. Rewards could include new stratagems, weapons and more.
The graphics and animations are fabulous and the game runs brilliantly.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Great graphics
-	Fun and fast gameplay
-	Plenty of enemies – 3 different races
-	Number of upgrades and equipment
-	Different levels of difficulty (1 to 12)
-	Up to 4 player online co-op
-	Achievements
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	No trading cards
My goodness, I am hooked on HELLDIVERS! Just a splendid game!
10/10

Like a few other Arrowhead games, Helldivers is a "coop" game where you can "accidentally" kill your teammates. Another element that Magicka fans will recognize are Stratagems that require a sequence of button presses to execute that will give players ammo resupplies, reinforcements, additional equipment, vehicles, turrets, and all manner of airstrikes.
Pros:
+ It's Magicka in spaaaace
+ Despite friendly fire, it feels like there are more opportunities for real cooperation
+ Varying loadouts provide playstyle diversity
+ Galactic campaign that progresses through everyone's contribution
Cons:
- No crossplay with PlayStation players
- Matchmaking feels broken, there are more on-going games than the browser leads you to believe

I haven't played a LEGO game in a while and was kind of itching to play one. The Force Awakens scratched that itch well enough.  The LEGO game formula is still enjoyable when experienced in moderation.
Traveler's Tales added a few new twists since last LEGO game I played (cover shooting being one of them - had a laugh at that), but nothing that really drastically changes the gameplay versus the prior games.  That's ok, I still have fun with the very basic puzzle solving and button mashy combat in these games.
One new element (to me at least) is side missions on hub worlds - but these are all pretty tedious.  They mostly boil down to time limited checkpoint races or performing short tasks recycled from the sort of tasks you perform in the story mode levels - both of which are exceptionally easy and repeated many times.  Repeating these tasks outside of the context of playing a level just feels like busy work to pad out the play time and I don't think the game needs it.  I got my money's worth from the story mode - though was compelled to do the side stuff anyway because of the obsessive completionist in me.
On the bright side, I was pretty impressed by the graphics, even though they're only representing LEGO figures, they're quite detailed and look almost photorealistically believably as toys come to life at this point.  Also they got the entire principle cast of the movie to record new lines for this game, which is pretty amazing.
I did experiencing some crashing, somewhere around a half dozen random crashes over the course of 30 hours of play - which is not too bad, but the game has one of the most obnoxiously long, unskippable (by any means) startup sequences I've ever seen, so that certainly didn't help lessen the annoyance of getting back into the game after a crash.  Obviously fixing the crashing would be best, but even if it was fixed, a skippable intro still the only major thing I'd wish was different about the game.

Company of Heroes 2 is the second installation of the ever popular Company of Heroes RTS series. The game offers superios graphics, animation, but perhaps not gameplay. There are new units, tanks, artillery and aircraft to explore along with new maps for you to fight it out on, but many gamers have displayed their distaste to this installation of the famous CoH.
The gameplay runs about as smooth as an RTS can. Constantly seen in the top 3 RTS' in terms of popularity, Company of Heroes has an intense reputation to live up to. We can't take away from it, the gameplay standards. Having a large scale battle in the middle of the battlefield with bullets, shells and artillery strobing the screen is simply satisfying to any gamer.
The graphics are incredible, as long as you can run the game on high or ultra. The same goes for the sound. The game allows for an ambient experience, and you will definitely know that you're controlling armies in the midst of war.
The campaign offers an enjoyable experience for any fan of RTS. The missions are satisfying, well produced, and genuinely give a sense of fulfillment to the player. The campaign is overall well designed, well narrated, and subtitles are available (which is always important!).
The game offers a skirmish gamemode, which can be replayed as many times as you want. Play the game your way, and without a doubt, the game will have the upmost replayability.
Of course, multiplayer battles are available if you wish. The matches vary from casual to competitive depending on your opponents, but without a doubt, the multiplayer is satisfying to play to all RTS fans.

One of the quintessential turn-based strategy games of the 90s. Deadlock II is basically Deadlock with an expansion pack, so not much new here if you've played Deadlock - but a few nice nice fixes and additions.

Edit: 6/15/17 - I have SUCCESSFULLY made this game work with windows 10 (this will require a patch) and played a multiplayer game between a windows 7 computer and a windows 10 computer (which may require a VPN). Instructions on both these items are below the review.
ORIGINAL REVIEW:
This game has fantastic strategic depth, and is a very good single-player game.  As far as mechanics, it is a 4x game where several alien species land on a single planet, and then battle it out for global domination.  You build up your colony, expand and colonize additional areas, build an army and fight with your enemies.  Fairly simple at its core, but what makes it special is that this basic formula is done just right.
Each species has its own unique abilities and traits, and each really has very distinct advantages.  Even the humans, which in most games is the "average race" has very special abilities that no other race has, including a berserk ability for infantry, and very high taxes and trade.  Re-lu begin seeing the whole map, and so they know the composition and strength of enemy forces long before the assault has begun, and they can subvert enemy morale with their spies, leading to riots and much destruction of property.  There is really no average race, which is nice as a change of pace.  Each race also has a major penalty associated with it, such as with the Re-lu, weak military units and defenses, or with the humans, extremely expensive military maintenance.  There are 5 other races with equally interesting advantages and disadvantages.
The arguably worst feature of this game is the battles themselves.  You can watch them, but you have no control, and units often move around the battlefield in odd ways.  There is also some degree of luck involved because units have "accuracy," i.e., they just miss sometimes.  Nevertheless, the automated battles means you can focus on the more strategic elements of the game, rather than the nitty gritty tactical, which speeds up games substantially.  Personally, I don't mind it.  But if you are looking for Command and Conquer, this is simply not that.
The tech tree is functional, and depending on the map type (mostly land/mostly sea) and world type (alien, earth-like, volcanic, etc.) you will need to adapt your selections.  This is a refreshing change from games where you always research the same techs, no matter what.  You can still sort of get away with this in singleplayer, but you must adapt in multiplayer to have any chance at survival in a competitive game.
And this brings me to multiplayer. In full disclosure, I have mostly only played 1v1 matches with the non-steam version, so I can't make any guarantees with the connection capabilities of the steam version.   I use Hamachi (free) to make the TCP-IP connection function. But wow is multiplayer wonderful.  I have played dozens of extremely close games, and you really feel the tension build as forces maneuver around the seas or make surprise land assaults with illegally purchased Skirineen Veterans.  Or subvert your morale... or poison food at just the wrong moment...  Or blockade you cutting off much needed food and energy to your colony (starvation and powered down defenses).  The point here is that there is substantial strategic and tactical depth here that really shows in multiplayer, and to me this makes multiplayer the best part.
And another thing is that even after years of play, I am still discovering things I never knew.  Did you know that submarines have special abilities?  Did you know you can maximize taxes on every colony on the Cyth from turn 1 with no penalty because of their unique static morale ability to generate a ton of cash from the start?
I would almost say it is a game that is deceptively simple.  Something that can be easily learned, but hard to truly master.  If you've never played it, I highly recommend it.  If you have played, I hope to see you in a game.
Just a warning, I have been unable to make this work on Windows 8+, so be wary if that is your system. Edit: Now I have, see below.
WINDOWS 10 Compatability: To make the game work in windows 10 you will need windows 7 direct draw capability which is no longer included in windows 10.  Follow these steps:
1) Go to
2) Download ddrw.zip
3) Extract the ddraw.zip to your Deadlock 2 main directory.  By default, this will be located at: C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\SteamApps\common\Deadlock2
4) Locate the Deadlock.exe, right click it, and go to compatability.  Ensure that you select Windows 7 compatability and also run as administrator.  Apply these changes.
If you double click the exe the game should now play normally.
MULTIPLAYER: Deadlock 2 cannot utilize Steam's standard multiplayer system, however, you can still play multiplayer using a VPN (or virtual private network) such as Hamachi (which is currently free).  To use Hamachi Multiplayer, you will need to download Hamachi, set up a room, and have the other players join that room BEFORE starting the game.  Have the host note their specific IP address in case of difficulty joining.  This will be noted right next to the power button in the hamachi window.  It will read something like 25.167.103.101. Then, host a game of Deadlock under the TCP/IP connection protocol.  Once the game is hosted, have all other players select join a game under the same TCP/IP protocol.  If they are unable to find the game through a general search, simply have them type in the IP address. Players should be able to join the game.  Once all players have joined, simply start the game.
FINAL NOTE ON MULTIPLAYER:  Do not load a multiplayer game from a manual save file.  You will need to load a game from an autosave only.  Currently, a bug exists in that if you load a game from a save file rather than an autosave, the game may change populations, tech queues, and other items which could drastically alter the balance of the game. This however, does not appear to occur when loading from an autosave. This game is just phenomenal in multiplayer, so give it a shot!

I played Ys: Oath in Felghana a few years ago and absolutely loved it. Seeing the similarities with this game I decided to pick it up, and while I wasn't disappointed I also wasn't nearly as impressed as I was with Oath in Felghana.
The game takes place all in a tower with numerous floors. The floors have different themes, but they're still floors in a tower. As a result the game doesn't really feel as grand in scope as Oath in Felghana. It feels like a long day, which I guess is the intent going by the story, but somehow it just lacks that same feel of a big journey that I tend to enjoy in games like this. Oath in Felghana took you from mines to volcanoes to mountains to castles, and the varieties of enemies and bosses complemented that. There is still variety in bosses and enemies in this game, but it just doesn't feel nearly as expansive.
There's also a sort of eye-rolling quality to the story that Oath in Felghana didn't have. Maybe this is because I played through as Yunica, but the "oh I'm so inexperienced" shtick got rather annoying pretty quickly. Maybe this is also due to the tower theme, as over the course of a long day she went from totally inexperienced to besting legendary demons of unimaginable power. There are two other characters, one of which is unlocked, and they may not have had that same annoyance factor, but I couldn't really get up the desire to play through the game again.
Which I guess leads to my personal biggest point in the comparison to Oath in Felghana, which is that I replayed Oath 3 times moving up through the various difficulties, whereas this game I picked the hard difficulty, played through once, and couldn't summon the interest to play it again. I enjoyed the one playthrough, but it just didn't stick with me and keep me wanting more like Oath in Felghana did.
Based on all that, if you had to pick one Ys title to play, don't make it this one - go for Oath in Felghana. But if you loved Oath and want more, this game might not wow you in the same ways but it will still satisfy.

First off, if you've played any of the STALKER games, I guarentee you'll enjoy Metro 2033.
The wonderful thing about Metro more than anything is its atmosphere. It maintains the constant dread looming over everything as people scratch out a measly existence years after nuclear war in the metro tunnels beneath Moscow. The characters are interesting, getting small but satisfying helpings of their lives as you make your way through the metro tunnels in order to find some way to save your home. Along the ways you'll be treated to Russian horror in fine detail. A decent above the bar stealth system, good combat and situations that will leave you sweating as you fend off mutated animals, bandits and factions of people still fighting long after the war ended.
Pros:
-Movement feels like it has weight, gives a unique feel to the game
-Atmosphere is evrything here
-A modest amount of good characters you encounter through your journey
-The Redux has excellent graphics, in spite of some taxing areas on your fps
-Guns feel good here, they have their uses in situations and finding rare weapons can be rewarding
-Rewarding exploration of levels with plenty of nooks and crannies to search out
-Good selection of difficulties and a survival mode for a real harsh experience
-Secret but provoking alternate ending
-Excellent replay value
Cons:
-Game is a bit taxing in some areas, even with anti-aliasing turned off
-Different armors were removed in the Redux version (heavy armor and light armor)
-It's a bit short, pushing just over seven hours on normal difficulties
-Enemy AI is kind of dumb
-Frames per second can be choppy in certain environments
-Stealth system doesn't seem to have much of a reward
Overall, this is a very good game worth it's playtime, especially if your into survival-horror or just a good story heavy shooter. If you do get it, I recommend getting it bundled for the $30(USD) because the second game, Metro: Last Light is just as good as Metro 2033.

From the Swedish indie developer Joakim Sandberg, comes Noitu Love 2. The digit appended to the end of the title begs the question "is there a Noitu Love 1" and yes there is. It's available as a free download on his website
. Noitu Love 2 is a throwback to the golden days of arcade games. Reminiscent of games like Metal Slug (sans the quarter consumption) this game is a very face paced and it won't leave you bored for a second.
The artwork is exceptional and each level features all new environmetal art and unique enemies. There are also loads of unique minibosses (usually around two to three a level).
Sadly there is no USB controller support for this game. It seems that the develop really had the keyboard and mouse in mind when designing this game. There doesn't seem to be any way to change the keybindings either. If you don't like the default controls then I am afraid you are out of luck.
With only seven levels the gameplay can be very short, especially considering the levels go by quickly but there are unlockables that give the game a fair bit of replayability.
If you're looking for a gratuitous fast based action scroller then I recommend this
Score: 8/10

I enjoyed this game overall and I'm glad I was able to experience this story. That is the long and short of how I felt about this game; not to say that it didn't have problems, but I'll get into that.
You play as a paranormal detective investigating "The Vanishing of Ethan Carter"; hence the title. You find clues about him through solving the murder mysteries of his relatives. As a paranormal detective, you have a special skill of seeing exactly how they died, and where Ethan went, by solving each killing. As you progress through the game you find out more about the family members, and Ethan himself through papers you get from solving each mystery. Think of a Myst-lite crossed with murder investigatons... and that is more or less this game honestly, it isn't much broader than than that.
Speaking of Myst, this game is very heavy on exploration and immersion. However, the puzzle aspect of Myst is slightly lacking in here for this to be a perfect comparison to Myst. Not to say this doesn't have puzzles, there are quite a few in here, but they aren't as difficult or... as usually obscure, as they are in Myst. Which to be honest, i'm pretty happy about since I was able to get through the game without a guide. (I did use a guide for one of the achievements though).
This game is very short and sweet, and I was able to complete it in an afternoon. However, its length felt appropriate, not bloated or too short, I'd compare it to a nice desert and wine that follows a main course meal. That being said I have some "minor" complains about it.
My main complaints about this game are are:
1.  There are multiple parts where you have to ride an elevator up and down SlOWLY, ride some sort of locomotive SLOWLY, or just having to go through really slow areas. Not only multiple parts, which I can be fine with, but you potentially have to go through them multiple times. Not only that also, but elevators stay on the floor that you left them on, and then you have to wait while they SLOWLY come back up, and then having to wait while they take their time on going down. I HATE that we still have these parts in games, we have maps now for games with fast points. WE HAVE THE TECHNOLOGY TO FIX THIS. Which brings me to point-
2. There is no map in this game. Now I can hear people saying that having a map would break the experience of being fully immersed in this world. Those people might be right, but me breaking my keyboard in frustration brings me out of  games faster than having a map would.
That is all.
3. I experienced a couple hiccups in the framerate, my computer could be at fault, but I saw where other people were complaining about this also.
Other than that, this was overall a very good game. I'd recomend it to people who enjoy love, happiness, and puppies.

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a very mysterious adventure game in an absolutely stunning environment. You are a detective who is to find a boy who has been missing. This game does not have a lot of game to it, and is very much a narrative focused experience, which I'm a huge fan of. The music really sets the tone together with the very high quality graphics and beautiful, well-crafted environments with immense mountains and lush forests. I especially liked the timing of the music, which really set the tone just right for every part of the world.
By solving puzzles you unravel a series of very mysterious and macabre tales in the world. The puzzles aren't very difficult, but finding out what the puzzle actually is is a lot more challenging. I somehow managed to skip the first 2 puzzles and just walked straight by them, only to complete them at the end. I was simply not aware of the fact that those were puzzles. The game can feel a bit pretentious with its whole "not holding hands" at times, and can scare away newcomers to games.
Other criticism I have is that, while the story is nicely told, it's not in every part of it. The character art, voice over and development really pales compared to the setting making it very hard to empathise with them. Furthermore, there are some very cheap jumpscares in the game that I thought were utterly unnecessary, and in adventure games I nearly always find inexcusable.
In the end the story itself also doesn't have much of a lasting appeal even when so masterfully told, which is a problem I have with most of the games in the genre. It's however probably still my favourite game of 2014, and a huge recommendation.

Company of Heroes 2 is the second installation of the ever popular Company of Heroes RTS series. The game offers superios graphics, animation, but perhaps not gameplay. There are new units, tanks, artillery and aircraft to explore along with new maps for you to fight it out on, but many gamers have displayed their distaste to this installation of the famous CoH.
The gameplay runs about as smooth as an RTS can. Constantly seen in the top 3 RTS' in terms of popularity, Company of Heroes has an intense reputation to live up to. We can't take away from it, the gameplay standards. Having a large scale battle in the middle of the battlefield with bullets, shells and artillery strobing the screen is simply satisfying to any gamer.
The graphics are incredible, as long as you can run the game on high or ultra. The same goes for the sound. The game allows for an ambient experience, and you will definitely know that you're controlling armies in the midst of war.
The campaign offers an enjoyable experience for any fan of RTS. The missions are satisfying, well produced, and genuinely give a sense of fulfillment to the player. The campaign is overall well designed, well narrated, and subtitles are available (which is always important!).
The game offers a skirmish gamemode, which can be replayed as many times as you want. Play the game your way, and without a doubt, the game will have the upmost replayability.
Of course, multiplayer battles are available if you wish. The matches vary from casual to competitive depending on your opponents, but without a doubt, the multiplayer is satisfying to play to all RTS fans.

Alright. So this game is really nice. Developers really got that catchy vibe going on here. The moment I entered the game menu I understood that I am going to like this game. The music is moody and mysterious, gives a lot to the game's atmosphere. I would even consider this game having a bit of a horror touch to it (story line which is written in the letters/notes found on every level of the puzzles develops an uneasy feeling). Every level of this game is really well created. Whenever you think would be the end of the level it gets a new piece of a puzzle in front of you and that is another thing to solve in order to progress. And it's mesmerizing how in-depth every puzzle was created. One object can have like 10 things to solve before you move on to another. Progressing further through levels will increase puzzles' difficulty and eventually it will get really hard but still keeps you going and wanting for more even if you get stuck to one thing for quite some time.
So, if you're into puzzles, this is that Nr. 1 game in the list to go for. I absolutely give it 10 out of 10. 5 euros for this kind of genius puzzle-engineering? This is my first review on steam. I'm writing it because I really enjoyed playing the series. The Room Two is, as the first part, a great puzzle game with a tremendous atmosphere (I enjoyed the second part more because they added these small horror-like cutscenes and the overall feeling was darker). I can absolutely recommend this one to everyone interested in puzzle games.
Still there is room for improvement.
In my opinion the puzzles were easier than the first part, maybe because I got used to the type of logic, but often I found myself just moving levers or shifting around pieces with only one option to go. I liked the new game mechanics (the crossbow for instance, but also having to solve several puzzles in each room), but they were not really challenging. Often the camera focussed on the next part of the puzzle, which made the whole 'solve a bit here then switch there'-thing a bit useless.
Coming to the level design itself: I enjoyed the changing surroundings and the story telling (letters + environment), but who thought that the typewriter part in the tarot level was a great idea? Doing it once was okay, but why did I have to repeat that task like five times? Puzzle games are easy (and often boring) once you know how it works, so please don't design the game already that way.
I found the hints to be rather useless, hint one often told me what I already knew (you have this new strange looking thing in your inventory which you didn't use yet, you might need it wink wink) while the last one gave me the solution and the second one was either like the first or like the third.
Last point: camera movement. How comes that for the detail views the camera movement is normal but for the whole room perspective it's inverted? It's a minor detail, but it gets really annoying over time.

This is a rogue-like game which allows only one play-though per life and it sometimes seemed the most unfair and biased system. Somewhere in the pain of loss you decide it's not worthwhile to help those in distress, it's not worth stopping every bandit raid, and using your body for science wasn't that great an idea after all. You may have thought you were the biggest gun in space, but you'll be lethally humbled by that inevitable bigger gun who punches holes through your ship effortlessly. No good statement ever follows after "not to be racist" but, it'll be beat into you quickly that all races suck in their own way equally and specializing in one is a terrible idea. And finally --Space-- don't mess around with it, simply put. Between asteroid fields, plasma storms, solar flares, and the never ending vacuum, you will know with out a doubt that you are not the Captain Kirk of this universe (though you may be just as doughy).
This game is punishing and I love it. This is what a space game is supposed to be. There's no take backs with loaded save games, there's no pandering to you because you're the user. It plops you straight in and you have one chance to save the fleet from the rebels. I don't often experience the thrill of joy that I experience when I finally had my first victory.  Defeating the end game capital ship was most satisfying as it crumpled away into the void of space. At least, until I realized that I was so desperate for a victory, I had lowered the difficult to easy and even then it took a forgotten amount of attempts to achieve. A single play-though may take 30 minutes to an hour from start to finish, but that's assuming you get to the end game capital ship. You will be destroyed many times before then even after everything was going your way. You had all the weapons and systems you want, more cash than you can spend, and full health to boot, but you get to some lower rank pirate ship and it all comes crashing down because you were simply out classed. After recovering my controller from across the room I went right back in a tried again.
The game seems impossible at times, but there's a strategy being formed slowly with each failed attempt and that final success is most gratifying and seals the deal that this is phenomenally crafted game isn't like the rest of the rogue-likes out there. It's well balanced, addictively simple, and there is a heavy focus on choice. Highly recommended distraction from those bigger game titles. It's worth more than that for me, but that's how I specifically ended up playing the game.

FTL is an excellent space crawler game that features many unique events, encounters and locations that makes every playthrough fun and exciting. The premise of the game is jumping from beacon to beacon, each containing an enemy ship, store, distress signal, or random event.
First let's talk about the events. There are a wide range of different events to keep you interested, such as blocking ally ships with your shield, sending crew down to investigate, or even a trap. The most interesting part is that an event could pop up with the exact same choices twice, but these choices don't neccessarily have the same outcome, which adds to the randomised aspect of the game. Although choices can be risky, blue choices that relate to a certain installed system or crew member will almost always result in a successful outcome as you are using a special abilty earned through your playthrough.
Next, the combat. The combat in FTL is mostly controlled by two systems, weapons and drones. Missile weapons can slip past sheilds to damage the enemy hull or systems. Lasers on the other hand require multiple shots to temporarily break through sheilds to damage the ship. Ion weapons can disable whole systems for a few seconds but do not damage the hull. Drones are also a very useful aspect of combat, they can be used to repair your ship, fight intruders, disable enemy drones, attack ships and more. But FTL's combat also relies on some of the more 'passive' systems. Having a pilot and a manned engine will allow you to evade, decreasing the chance of being hit. Turning the oxygen temporarily off or opening airlocks can put out fires without crew getting burnt. A manned camera room let's you see inside enemy ships. It is a very well rounded off combat engine with many aspects to consider, and it is really satisfying once you get the hang of it.
The last aspect I want to talk about is ships, systems and resources. At the start of every playthrough you can choose a ship (only one is unlocked at first) and configure it's layout. Each ship comes with different systems, races and drones and more can be bought through stores or events later on. Each ship has it's own challenges that unlock different layouts for the ships. Another ship or layout can drastically change the way you play, from a multimanned ship with a high tech clone bay, or a ship that runs entirely off drones. Each race also has it's own benefits such as immunity to fire.
FTL is a great game that can keep you engaged for hours on end, great buy, would reccommend.

There have been a lot of indie games jumping on the retro bandwagon, but often taking the worst elements of ancient games to heart. Noitu Love 2, though, really does feel like a lost Treasure that was somehow unearthed... in more ways than one, because it echoes the older games from Japanese developer Treasure. Unlike other games of its sort, you don't ever "power up", but instead get all the tools and moves you need from the start and can just focus on kicking butt. It's also well-animated, and the 16-bit look doesn't look lazy at any point.
It's a bit clunky in the control area - it's designed for keyboard and mouse deliberately, and there's no controller support. Though it does things you couldn't do with a controller, WASD will always feel inprecise. It's also only available at the default resolution (if you care about that sort of thing) and it's rather short, though unlockable bonus characters extend the play somewhat.
Still, I think it's one of the few games that distills the fun of old console games without being weighed down by their tropes.

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is quite honestly unlike any video game I've ever played before. It really wasn't what I was expecting and it's hard to decribe what I mean by that. It's often bewildering, sometimes strange, but it's always intriguing. Yes ok so it's played from a first person perspectvie and you have walk about looking at stuff to find those all important clues and like any mystery game there are notes and letters just dropped on the ground for the player to discover. Familiar game mechanics? Of course they are, but in this game they do tell a fascinating supernatural story and are definetly not filler or collectibles.
You play the game as Paul Prospero 'a supernatural detective' and I imagine him as a cigar smoking, fedora wearing type not unlike Columbo, but I don't want to put images in your head. Anyway you've been summoned via a handwritten letter to Red Creek Valley by Ethan Carter, a young boy who appears to be in some kind of trouble and it is clear that he is going to need your help and to do that you'll need to don that fedora and do some investigating.
As you examine the clues you find in the game world and interactive with objects Propsero’s inner thoughts are displayed on screen. Subtle clues to help you gather evidence and fit the pieces together. Find the correct order and the events are played back in supernatural film-reel style with a blue filter that act as cut scenes progressing the story.
A point to note is that the game makes it very clear even before you start out on your journey that "This game is a narrative experience that does not hold your hand." That means there are no quest markers, no maps, no golden Fable-esq trail to follow. Just your own noggin to guide you. There are just a few clues to discover in the game world and you must explore, explore and explore. The world is a very beautiful place though and you'll frequently find yourself stopping just to admire the view. It would be unfair to just praise the visuals as the the musical score is equally beautiful, but also subtle and haunting, fitting perfectly with exploration and discovery.
If you are into narrative experiences with lots of exploring required and a thought-provoking backstory to encourage you forward then you will definitely enjoy The Vanishing of Ethan Carter.

As a demonstration of how little gameplay is required to make an engaging 'game'  Ethan Carter scores. It's moody, creepy and full of atmoshpere.  Helped by superb graphics (I would imagine you'd need a fairly hefty GPU to make the most of it) and a large roaming area.
That said, you are largely along for the ride.  You do a LOT of wandering around looking for the few objects that advance the game;  there is no interaction with anything outside that required to progress, there are few puzzles and in that respect it's not as interesting as the Sherlock adventure i played a month ago.
It's quite short too.  If you get bored with not finding an object and resort to walkthroughs you could be done in less than 10 hours.  I can't see there being much replay value either.
While it's on offer it's worth a punt but I'm glad I didnt pay full price for it.
In a nutshell, it's a story that plays out in front of you.  From what I've heard the ending leaves you asking more questions than it answers, too.
Pros; great graphics, atmosphere, kind of investigative nature
Cons: price tag, user interactivity, replay value, all a but sparten (if you like that sort of thing), better mystery games available.

A great puzzle piece story wrapped in a dark sticky macabre blanket. Stunning visual displays- bonus.
Vanishing of Ethan Carter unfolds  as a mystery game  should. It allows the player to immerse themselves into their enviroment and surroundings without making it too monotonous or difficult to the point where you lose track.
You 'want' to explore and be able to find the next clue or hidden section of the map. The crisp stunning visuals make a great time just walking around, trying to discover an area you havnt been, or an item you need to find.
As the game states in the beginning 'it does not hold your hand' when it comes to completing the story or anything for that matter. You teach you how to go about piecing the puzzle for each mystery/scene back together, which can be challenging and maybe frustrating for some, but its a good element to this game, and makes it more rewarding once complete a scene.
There is no map, no quest maker or directional help, inventory or hud assistance. It leaves alot to the imagination, but majority just takes some logical thinking and diligent exploring, making sure nothing is missed.
The story is good and gripping enough, with metophorical narration filling alot of it. At some points i was a little confused, but it all ties in eventually.
Id definitely recommend this game just for the free and ungated play syle, letting you play at your own pace, and really getting into the detective sprirt and making you think, and search and ponder.
Didnt want to spoil too much of the story, but would say it is has a slight Alan Wake feel, mixed with some Silent Hill eerie'ness nestled in a quiet countryside town etc, The graphics alone make you feel like you're there living it.
