A fun game but with horrible historical inaccuracies.
The Stuka G1 and G2 were the variants that used the 37mm cannons. The G1 was first available in early 1943 but in this game you can use it in earlier dates. That isn't all, it also has the fire rate of the german 20mm cannons, are you kidding me? The 37mm cannons had a very slow fire rate but in this game they fire as fast as the 20mm cannons.
The MG 42 first saw service in 1942, there's a reason is called the MG 42, but in this game you can see them in 1941, couldn't they at least put the MG 34/39 in the game for the 1941 missions? And for skirmishes the MG 42 as an upgrade? Seriously.....
Last but not least, the worst of the offenders. The German uniforms. The German uniforms in this game are fictitious at best. Green uniform with yellow cap in the Eastern front? And the cap doesn't even have an eagle, come on..... Who the hell designed the units in this games? This is their second WWII game and they still have no clue of how things actually looked like.
I could be here pointing out all the historical inaccuracies this game has but it would take me all day and I would end up writing a testament.
Now the game has become a buff and nerf fest, making it even less realistic and for the sake of ''balance'' some units will be over performing while others will underperform so if you want an historically accurate game this isn't for you.

That means Gordon and Alyx must return to the place they tried to escape from in order to stabilize the reactor and escape from City 17 along with the help of the remaining survivors of the city. I had more fun than I thought I would with this one. It plays like a stealth game, digging for treasure while trying to avoid being spotted and killed by the variety of spirits that haunt each graveyard. Some puzzles and mazes are thrown in, along with the optional goal of collecting keys from each stage that unlocks the final graveyard of the game.
You get a "mission briefing" at the beginning of each stage where the grave robber (YOU!) and his companion discuss the main score that you have to get at each graveyard to complete the level, along with some silly dialog that eventually leads to a bit of story later. You can go for the main goal and get out, or you can stick around and try to clear the entire graveyard for completion purposes and to get that special key I mentioned earlier, once you collect the map pieces from graves to find it.
There are a handful of enemy type in the game, and you'll get a tutorial on each one as you encounter them in the game. The Bride's my favorite enemy for her disturbing scream and determination to kill you once see spots you.  You also get a hard mode where enemies will randomly spawn as you remain in the level and you only get one life instead of three. I still have a few achievements to get, but the game took me around 4 to 5 hours to complete on Normal.

Very good WW2 Real-Time strategy game, with more unit movement and defensive structure based building then base building.

There are none resources that can be "gathered" but are acquried via capturing resource sectors whitch provide fuel, manpower and ammunitions. Gameplay is HUGE with the long campaing smaller separate missions in mission packs and when you are done with that there is the multiplayer with so many players and mods and maps taht you wont even have time to try them all. This is not a game. This is art, pure art. Each second of this game involves its player with amazing graphics and sounds through a very peculiar and unpredictable story. And as any piece of art, its meaning is difficult to be seen and guessed. Each player may have his own interpretation of what truly happened on Red Creek Valley and each player may be affected by it differently. I myself cried on the end when I realised what happened.

Vanishing comes very, very close to a Walking Simulator. There really isn’t a failure state, your actions don’t really affect the game in any meaningful way and the game expects you to experience a lot of it. The only influence you have is exploring the world of Red Creek Valley, solving the puzzles and, by extension, the mystery Paul Prospero is here to solve. Oh right, that’s the guy who you’re controlling and hear monologue as you explore the valley. So, you'll walk along at a fairly steady pace (there's a reasonably faster sprint as well), drink in the atmosphere while you search for clues of Ethan's whereabouts. All the while discovering that there's something creepy and sinister beneath the surface.
Red Creek Valley is divided up into multiple areas, each containing a major puzzle or two for you to solve. Puzzles, for the most part, boil down to finding all the objects within a given area and figuring out how they all go together. The music playing in the background will clue you in on whether you’ve left the given area very subtly. Which is helpful because you’ll never need to leave an area in order to solve that particular puzzle. There aren’t any random items on the other side of the map that you have to find. It should be noted that it isn't required to solve these puzzle areas in any particular order, they can be done at any time. Outside of soaking in the sights and experiencing the strange events going on, there’s not much else to do. However, I always felt like I was involved. There wasn't any boring section I felt forced to walk through. It might help that Red Creek Valley appealed to me. Being able to see the burned out buildings, the rusted train cars and nature reclaiming the area, it really intrigued me. It's a feel of history and decay that Vanishing goes out of its way to really sell to the player. It feels like a real place and it’s setup like a real place. I think that helped me enjoy the game more.
The atmosphere ate away at me. Slowly, creepily, I would sometimes jump at my phone beeping at me. It’s insidious how this game gets into your head. It makes you think something will jump out, scare you half to death and eat what remains of your sanity alive. Spoiler: that doesn’t happen. Except for one area, I’ll explain below. This isn’t a hardcore scare title like Amnesia: The Dark Descent. It’s far tamer by comparison while holding its own. I was often thinking that some dark fantasy creature such as Cthulhu was behind the scenes. It was amusing when that theory was half confirmed. The game will do its best to unnerve you. So long as you let it.
There’s only one section of the map where jump scares are present. It’s in a mine and they sort of warn you that it’s coming. Sort of. And it’s mostly optional unless you want a 100% completion rating. At least, I’m fairly certain its optional. The scare is when you’re running around in a mining maze, searching for clues to open a large door in the center of it. In this area, is an undead miner who’s been cursed. While you’re walking around, if you hear a telltale noise you should immediately turn around and go the other way. Otherwise, BOO. You have to start from the beginning of the maze.
Optimization wise, this game leaves a bit to be desired. You will need to tweak your graphics options to get the best performance as running everything on high will drag the performance down hard. I noticed that Anti-Aliasing and Texture Filtering were the big performance hogs. Oh and there is constant texture loading, which will cause your game to “stutter” frequently as it loads them. This is a problem that affects a lot of computers and it’s immersion breaking. Additionally, if you’re not running a 16:9 resolution, the game will letterbox/pillarbox. Which I find to be frankly inexcusable for a native PC game to be this way. I can’t figure out why the devs didn’t scale the resolutions properly, it’s not like the Unreal engine can’t do it. PCGamingWiki has a installable solution to fix this as well as grant you multi-monitor and ultra-widescreen options. Additionally, while there is a proper Field-of-View slider in the options, (70-120) it crops the image in order to do it. Overall, while the game does run/scale well (and it does so long as you tweak about in the settings), the remaining problems are less excusable. Also, saving is only done in chunks so you might revert some of your actions when quitting and reloading.
I gave the Redux edition a quick run through and they seem to have fixed a lot of the problems the original game had. The micro-stutter is completely gone, there's no more pillarboxing as the resolution scales and performance generally seems to be better, if more taxing on machines. Saving is now done every time you act now too. FoV is still a crop effect but I'll let it be. There's also a bunch of tweaks and visual improvements added that you probably won't notice. There's no story difference between the two editions so if you can, play the redux. If that's too taxing, play the original. Kudos to the devs for doing this for free.
The atmosphere and mystery makes for a compelling experience. While it does have a lot of adventure/walking simulator aspects to it, it still keeps the player involved the entire time. The atmosphere of a decaying rural area known as Red River Valley is simply intriguing. The psychological horror just works so well. Jump scares are rare but there’s something that eats at you the entire time. When finished, the game will leave you with more questions than answers though not in the “find out in the sequel” sort of way. I should note that the characters are rather cliche but when I consider the ending, it works and feels intentional. Visually, the game looks superb and the audio is top notch. If you're looking for a fun mystery/exploration through a decaying rural area, give The Vanishing of Ethan Carter a go.

Walking in the dark,damp tunnels of post-apocalyptic Moscow subwaysystem and shooting mutated monsters with home-made weapons is far more impressive than you would imagine.Metro2033 was a fantastic novel——but the game was even better.The redux version has definitely satisfying graphics and doesn't need much hardware.I'm having fun with my ancient AMD HD6770 and only 4GB of RAM.Anything better than that should be able to run this game with little difficulty.
在黑暗，潮湿的莫斯科地铁通道里行走并用土制武器干死怪物是个极其让人印象深刻的经历。地铁2033本身就是个很棒的小说，但游戏比小说还要更好。重制版刻画的后启示录莫斯科具有相当不赖的画质，而且硬件要求也很低。我4GB内存加上神卡HD6770都能流畅，所以说优化简直太棒了。
The story of 2033 is intense and moving.You are just a nobody in the Metro when an alien race called"the dark ones"hit your home station hard.To save your friends and families,you set out to the largest station in the whole metro to seek help——and to learn the truth.
地铁2033的故事线紧凑而激烈。你只是地铁里的一个无名小卒，但名为黑怪的奇异生物袭击了你所在的车站。为了拯救你的朋友和家人，你动身前往最大的地铁站寻求帮助，但却在一路上渐渐揭开了真相的面纱……
The gameplay is really two-wayed.It can be a hardcore FPS like Insurgency (if you choose to play in survivor mode)or it can be a casual spray' and pray' like COD(if you play in spartan mode).A huge amount of details awaits you no matter which way you want to play it.I strongly suggest you to play twice, once in each mode.
游戏体验走了两个极端。如果你玩的是幸存者模式，那么弹药很有限，敌人也很强大，玩法更偏向硬核。不过要是只想放松一下，斯巴达模式就很好。这个模式子弹和补给都多得多，不用时时刻刻担心有枪没弹的尴尬。不管选那个模式都能体验到2033的魅力，不过我建议两个都来一遍。
One of the best features this game had was the moral point system.You are awarded with moral points if you do the right things——a coin for the beggar, medicine for the sick, listening to people and watch the beasts to understand the world better,etc.If You get enough points,you will have a chance to choose a different and better ending(which is another reason I suggest everyone to play this game twice).I can see that 4A Games is really trying to make us understand more of the 2033 world instead of just shooting everything you see. I appreciate them for this.
这游戏的亮点之一是道德点数系统。如果你做了好事你就能得到一些道德点数，比如说给乞丐钱啊，听别人说话/多逛几个地方了解你所在的世界之类的。如果结局的时候你道德点够的话你可以选择一个不一样的结局，这也是什么我建议大家都玩两次。4A Games确实是想让我们了解一些关于地铁世界的东西，而不是一路无脑打打打。我不得不说他们干的不错。

(WARNING: This review contains information that you will be safer not knowing. Also don't read it if you want to find it out yourself, i.e. spoilers)
Confessions of a HELLDIVER:
I don't know how long I'll be able to leave this review up. The things I'm about to type out will most likely make some very powerful people very angry with me. Thought-policing is right around the corner, maybe already here, so, hey, maybe they're already on their way to publicly execute me. They'll probably court marshal the comrades I dive with, too. I'm sorry.
But someone needs to stand up for Truth, Liberty, Freedom, and Democracy. Not as we know those concepts now, but as our ancestors knew them.
Let's call this war we're fighting a game from now on, because that's what it seems to be to our "elected" officials.
In this game, we HELLDIVERS are literally dropped from orbit into the middle of hostile alien territory. Our training beforehand consisted of getting mortally wounded by a robot so that we could learn to get over the blood loss and get back on our feet, among other horrific things.
As dangerous as these aliens are to us, they are generally no more dangerous than we are to each other. We don't have special guns that magically don't hurt our allies, and while precision in those situations was part of our training, it wasn't extensive enough. I'm proud to say I've had only a few friendly fire incidents that resulted in a death, but I've seen more than my fair share. Most of the time it's an accident, but... Let's just say not every HELLDIVER is mentally stable. The media has the audacity to report these incidents as either acts of mercy to save them from a more horrific death, or in some cases the execution of enemy sympathizers. Heck, sometimes they blame it on "mind control". These are lies. Take it from someone who's been there. The Truth is, and the media doesn't want you to know this... Most of us are just inexperienced kids; not the heroes they make us look like in the commercials.
Oh, and we also have to watch the skies when we're calling in supplies or getting reinforcements. Those pods do NOT land softly, and take it from me; getting crushed to death is unpleasant and gruesome. (If the gore bothers you, there is a setting to filter it out.)
But I'll be completely honest with you. As horrific as it was, I enjoyed being a HELLDIVER. I felt like one of the lucky few. I joined up a little less than halfway through the war, and I got to see the swarms of bug enemies, had a short tour of the mysterious Illuminates, but mostly tested myself against the heavily armored Cyborgs. My other buddies who joined were with me, making sure I was getting qualifications for more weapons and supplies without too much incident. I took part in the defense of one of our off-planet capitals, and even assisted in the final push against an enemy homeworld. The war was over soon after that, and I was commended for it with a nice set of clothes and a bright blue cape (plus a shiny achievement).
During the ceremony, I wondered what was next. We'd wiped out the enemy, hadn't we? Does a HELLDIVER belong in a peaceful galaxy? On my ship, I had some time to think about what I was a part of. I happened to notice a console I hadn't used before, one that supposedly had information about the enemies I had faced and helped to defeat. What I read was... disturbing to say the least.
According to reports, we didn't wipe out any of our enemies.
It was discovered early on in our assault against the Bugs that their bodies rapidly decompose into precious fossil fuels. When we captured their homeworld, HELLDIVERS were no longer allowed to warp to that quadrant of space. The reason why is because our scientists were there, working on turning the Bugs into a renewable fuel resource. They were keeping alive the Bugs that I fought against, the ones I watched tear apart my friends, so that Super Earth could continue to fuel its death-bringing machines on death itself.
The conflict against the Cyborgs began due to a terrorist attack on Super Earth itself, wherein a Cyborg, one of many who denounced himself from our dystopia, detonated himself in a crowd, killing several. Those in charge decided that meant the entire Cyborg race had to die; all because of one possibly mentally ill individual, an extremist. But again, instead of actually wiping them out, we brought "Democracy" to the Cyborg homeworld. How? By installing voting machines on their planet. The voting machines you're used to seeing, if you don't use your home computer, you know. The ones that ask you your political preferences and then put in your vote for you depending on which candidate best matches your answers. The Cyborgs had the choice to either vote or be executed. A surprising percentage chose death.
We started invading Illuminate space when it was suggested by an official that a race that technologically advanced would surely have weapons of mass destruction. I found a charred old book that had a similar incident from many years ago, but I can't remember the details... I digress. The reports have since been deleted, due to the inevitable emergence of a new conflict against all these races, so I don't recall if there actually were weapons, or if there was simply the means to make them; in either case, Super Earth seized the technology to create "peace-keeping weapons capable of destroying planets".
As I mentioned, not too long after I read the reports which were too thinly-veiled with our own brand of propaganda, another war began against all these races. They broke free of our clutches and it all began again the same way as before, like one of those old time-keeping interfaces.
I learned all of these things, and I'm sure I'm not the only one who knows. I'm sorry to say that, as a HELLDIVER, I'm incapable of saving Super Earth from the clutches of managed democracy. I go where they tell me to go, and shoot what they tell me to shoot. There is some leway in precisely where I go and what I shoot at, but nothing I do will end this cycle; only serve to perpetuate it. I can only hope that this message gets out, and that those with the patience to read it will do what little they can to change our dystopian society into what it's meant to be; that the words Freedom, Truth, Liberty, Peace, and Democracy will no longer be perverted, and that perhaps someday we will live in balance with our neigbors in the stars. Meanwhile, I will do all that I can to protect you and your families from the consequences of our leaders' brash decisions.
But none of that was my confession. I shared no information that any other HELLDIVER wouldn't know if they took the time to read it. I guess perhaps I may be accused that I should be more patriotic, more loyal to Super Earth and its ideals, and this because I shared my true feelings about our military endeavors, but that wasn't my confession either.
I confess, despite the fact that we may not really be the good guys... Being a HELLDIVER is fun as hell, and I highly recommend it.

Sigh...what a disappointment.
The trailer looks promising, with a unique color palette aesthetic and interesting enemy sprites. The gameplay seemed to mix old-school arcade shooters with modern bullet hell titles.
While Red Death does offer gameplay like that, it's incredibly shallow. Enemy design is limited, bullet patterns are predictable, the framerate drops to a chug every few seconds, the music is dull and listless, and there are only three levels. It took me about 20 minutes to get to the end of this game.
And the worst part? The writing, oddly enough, as you'd think the writing in an arcade shooter shouldn't matter. But as the game attempts at presenting a narrative throughout the levels there's nothing you can do to skip the spelling errors, grammatical errors, egregiously unnecessary profanity, and stupid story. Does Lovecraft really need to be shoved into everything? No.
For $0.50 I guess I can't complain too much, but if I found this in a real arcade, I'd pop my two quarters in once and never come back to it.

Indie game, style shooter in scroll or bullet hell. It seems simple but inside it hides a great potential and shows that the developers put all their efforts into it.
•Scoreboard of the highest score always present at the top of the game.
•It is very addictive, you will always try to beat your best scores.
•Good music and sounds that remind of several retro classics.
•Option of '' Guide '' where all the controls are shown.
•The controls are super simple. Only two attacks and movement arrows.
•Option to mute the sounds of the game if they are annoying. (I do not recommend it, it makes you enter more into the action).
•Option to switch between window mode and full screen mode with the F key.
•Very funny achievements that will make you smile once in a while.
•Visual and conceptual art well done. The HUD looks very good, it is very comfortable and intuitive. Very nice visually.
•Power up's and improvements that you can collect during the adventure.
•Many different enemies.
•The bosses are original and all have attacks that differentiate them from others.
•It can give you hundreds and hundreds of hours of fun trying to beat your record.
•A single game mode.
•Advanced difficulty, you have to have experience in this type of games to be able to take it well.
It is a game that I recommend to buy if you are a fan of the ''Bullet Hell'' style, I do not recommend it at all for those who want to enter the genre or those who are not so good (I repeat, its section of difficulty It is very high). It is not an ''Air Strike'' but it is not left behind either. It has a price that is incredible, and I think it should be worth more, for all the content it brings and the hundreds of hours it can give us.

This game just feels right when you are playing it. Alone or with a group its easy to lose yourself hours on end taking control of planets throughout the regions. Randomly generated levels that give you new maps and objectives every time you load a planet on your ship keep things feeling fresh. I was doing helldive max difficulty maps with a friend and we were making it with only a little bit of trouble stopping us, but then we load up a map that is small and every objective is practically touching towards the center of the level. I lost count of how many times we died until we beat it.  Different maps  can sometimes put you in a tight place in the game. You could find yourself dying alot on an easy or medium level if its generated difficult. On top of the excellent levels that will keep you feeling fresh every game you have three alien factions to fight in this game. This offers different strategies you will need to discover on your own to find the best ways to beat levels against each alien faction. The most dangerous thing in the game that is going to kill you most of all is your own squad mates and if your clumsy maybe you'll kill yourself every now and then. Full friendly fire throws an amazing spin into this game and really calls for teamwork if everyone is planning on beating the mission. You will probably die a lot in this game when you are first learning the way of things, but its okay that is what makes this game so much fun. This is a fairly hardcore game at times and its going to call for your full attention in some maps. Live and learn, then live again...and well...learn. This game offers so much whether you are a solo gamer or a person that likes to play with others. There is no story so much as a meta online PVE campaign that consist of picking regions in space, picking planets to conquer for Super Earth(your faction) and eventually making it to the home worlds of these aliens and trying to end their exsistence in the galaxy. All progress forward is measured by missions completed by yourself as well as every other player online. Solo and multiplayer matches all push the bar forward towards the next region and eventually the enemy homeworld. When all enemies are knocked out of the war the war ends and the game recycles itself to a new war. Every new war is based off the previous stats from all players. So if everyone wins a lot in the war, eventually the game will increase how much xp the progress bar needs online to unlock further regions. If players can't push the progress bar it will slowly decline and push back towards Super Earth then it becomes a defense game and if players can't push the aliens out of Super Earth the war is lost, and humanity is defeated and a new war recycles. I would say alone the average gamer playing purely solo will probably play 20-40 hours in less they absolutly fall in love with this game as many others have been recently. People that love to group and play solo will probably range much higher in the amount of hours this game offers. The description says 100s of hours, and I believe it. This is an easy game to step into, and as you play further and try out harder locations it becomes even more addictivly fun and complex. At the asking price of $19.99 this game is a must buy for anyone who enjoys sci-fi shooters, fast pace strategy, and accidently killing your friends.

Vampire: The Masquerade is a decently well-known role-playing system that I was not familiar with before playing Bloodlines. However, for a new player like myself to jump in without any prior context, Bloodlines does a great job of establishing the fiction of the world of Vampire.
What is most impressive is the game's way of forcing a "vampire mentality" on you. The Masquerade is a system requiring vampires to keep their existence secret from humanity, and this sometimes means having to kill innocents in unfortunate circumstances. By not doing so, you risk the lives and foundation of all vampire society.
Bloodlines is an open-world modern RPG/adventure, allowing you to take quests while following a main story narrative. For a game released in 2004, the graphics aren't half-bad, and the character expressions/facial animations are actually rather impressive. Be aware that some odd unofficial patching needs to be done to make this game work on modern systems.

I couldn't tell you how much I love this series. Ever since I've played Ys VI, I've been hooked. Oath in Felghana drew me in with it's fast-paced and action packed RPG gameplay.
This game is no exception, and was well worth the years it took to finally get an English translation. I have to say, I'm not disappionted.
The main thing that sets this game apart from the others was the inclusion of 3 playable characters (before Seven made the party system). Each of these characters play different enough from each other, and each of them are just so much fun to play.
Playable Characters: Yunica is as close to the familiar gameplay that started with Ys VI, with strong melee and straightforward magic attacks. Hugo is a ranged spellcaster with interesting magic attacks. Then you unlock the Claw, who uses fast melee with a powerful boost mode to go with it (you'll understand when unlock him).
The Gameplay: This game is a fast paced 3D platforming Action RPG style game. The combat is fast, brutal, and some enemies will require more than just hacking and slashing to beat. Learn your movement and attacks, and you should do just fine. There is some exploration, but nothing too big, so you shouldn't get lost. The controls are pretty simple and fluid, but I do recommand a controller.
The Presentation: The presentation pretty good, even if the enviroments aren't the most impressive looking. Then again, graphics can't sell a game completely. After all, a shiny pile of crap is still a pile of crap. The character artwork looks nice too, and the visual effects are nice to look at as you slaughter your way through monsters.
The Music: As to be expected from Falcom's own in house rock band, the songs are blood pumping rock songs. Each song will get you pumped to fight all manner of monsters, be it a set of mooks or a massive boss. The Ys is legendardy for this, and this game has it just as good.
The Story: As far as plots go, they're pretty alright. Ys has never really been known for complex or deep storylines, but it's decent enough to keep you interested in the characters. I'm not gonna say much, because why would I spoil the plot? Thankfully, the plot is fast enough that you won't be spending too much time on the dialouge, so you can get right back to the action.
The Difficulty: There's plenty of options here for anyone to enjoy. You can take it easy on lower difficulites like Easy or Normal, or go straight for a quick death on something like Nightmare or Inferno mode.
Extra Modes: Even if you finish the Story mode, you still have Time Attack, a Boss Rush mode, and an Arena mode with some extra goodies to get from playing it. Arena Mode is where most of my hours after the Story Mode was done.
In Conclusion: This game is simply wonderful. It's well worth the price and will give you plenty of enjoyment for hours. The only problems you may find is that the platforming can be a little problematic at times, but nothing you can't deal with. Overall, I recommand this game and any of the other Ys games you can find on Steam.

Here is the short and sweet: This is a surpisingly enjoyable game. Buy it.
- SanctuaryRPG is RPG in its core form. You get right at the stats, drops, and builds that makes RPG... RPG. No fancy UI interfaces get in the way. It is in the title of the game. RPG. RPG. RPG.
- Feature to turn off dialog exists if you find it too annoying.

(You can turn off perma-death if you want. It is more exciting with it on, and the drops are better. Recommend you do classic to start with.)
- Pacing is up to you. Play casual or play hardcore.
This game isn't perfect, but the downsides are so minor there is no reason to mention them.

A damn fine game. I'd call this the true evolution to classic computer text adventures. It's just loaded with so much to do and it presents those things to you a little at a time so you don't feel overwhelmed at the start. Not to mention the music is absolutely stellar. It couldn't possibly be any more fitting.
The battle system is really interesting. In most RPG's your best tactic is to just use your best spell or ability and spam attacks until the enemy is dead. This game is different in that you have several meters you need to keep track of and you're given a multitude of special attacks to perform to either ramp up your meters or spend it all on devastating blows. You use certain attacks in a sequence to unleash combos, filling up your meters, your health bar, and laying down the hurt at the same time. You're given multiple combos you can perform, each having their own uses. You will also need to keep track of when you need to shift spots or defend. The enemy telegraphs charging attacks, giving you enough turns to ramp up your defense or get ready with heals. They can also leave your guard wide open, forcing you to reposition to gain footing and get your defense back. These are just the standard methods of battling for all classes. Each class gets extra abilities to go along with this to compliment all their playstyles. Seems like a lot but it's something you get used to quickly. The game is especially good at dishing you new things in small doses to make sure everything you learn sticks and you don't get overwhelmed with knowledge. A great example of teaching a player how to play your game that every game developer should practice.
The people making this game are very, very talented. Show them some support, do yourselves a favor and get this game. If you love a good, hardcore RPG then this game is definitely for you.

This is a stunningly beautiful adventure game played from the first person perspective. I did a mistake by calling such a game an FPS (see my Stanley Parable review) so in order to avoid the ranting of other gamers let's clarify that while it does resemble that particular genre it does not have any weapons at your disposal.
You do not fight, you do not have boss battles, you do not even have levels to complete. You just walk in a vast, wonderfully crafted world and you are completely free to go anywhere you want to. You play a detective who arrives to the fictional area called Red Creek Valley to find a missing boy, Ethan Carter.
You can inspect objects throughout the game and you also find several dead bodies. The idea of every "section" of the game it to find out how the people in question were killed and by whom. Once all items / objects are found / inspected, you can utilise your sense ability which enables you to reassemble the murder from the various "memory" fragments given. Once the chronological order is selected properly you can move onto the next piece of mystery.
I can't say enough how good the graphics are in this game. The atmosphere (thanks to the accompanying sound effects and music) is just excellent and it makes you stop and look at your surrounding area several times. And the game lets you do that - there's no time limit and no way to die and reload. You are free to complete the mystery at your own leisure.
Oh, yes, and while the game has excellent graphics it does run very well - I have to admit, though, I encountered some occasional stuttering which various forums seem to confirm. Hopefully, one patch will fix this as it is an underlying issue irrespective of the hardware you have for the game.
To summarise: Ethan Carter is an interesting, new take on adventure gaming. In my opinion, it is a rather unique and wonderfully done software that - and this is important to highlight - may not be to everybody's liking. However, if you liked Dear Esther, Gone Home or Stanley Parable you may just as well enjoy this one.

I was making my last stand, severly wounded and lying on the ground, blood oozing from my hole-ridden armor, firing my pistol between my legs with my last magazine as the hordes came running at me.  I had almost given up.  Then a voice came over the comms, telling me the extraction shuttle had arrived to take us away from this hell.  There was hope.
And then the shuttle landed on me.  I was instantly hooked.
I don't play twin stick shooters, but I bought this on a whim after hearing some positive coverage on it.  The sci-fi is clever and funny (like Starship Troopers, but so much wittier), the graphics and effects are satisfying, and the gameplay itself is incredibly fun and can be oh-so-derpy in the best way, especially with four people playing.  The community is very friendly (I've only played with random players so far).  I hear this game is much easier to play with a controller but I've been able to play just fine with good ol' mouse and kb.  As far as a port goes, the developers have done an excellent job and I must say, I'm very impressed.  And again, this is not a genre that I ever thought I'd enjoy... and I'm addicted.

Easily one of the best games I have picked up in a while. It is great with friends, and if you don't have any friends, there is a solid community that welcomes new and veteran players alike.
The combat is fluid and easy to learn with a variety of weapons to satisfy your every need! Not to mention the variety of tricky enemies, each with their own combat tactics. Another cool feature is the ability to select planets based off of your desired difficulty level, each planet with it's own environmental features that you can use to your advantage, or even get killed by.
Now...get this in your head very quickly. You will die. A lot. You will have supply drops crush you, friendly fire shred you apart, and surprise anal gangbangs brought about you via the bug swarms (it isn't as bad as it seems...you will get used to it). My point being...don't get frustrated! Enjoy yourself and the comedic mishaps that are destined to happen with each playthrough!
Another thing you should know is that this game is NOT pay to win. The DLC consist of mostly cosmetics and a couple of weapons. But if I am going to reccomend one DLC pack, it would be the Terrain Specialist pack. It gives a fantastic perk that eliminates harsh conditions impairing your movement.
All this being said, I highly reccomend this game. It is full of fantastic combat that will leave you thirsty for more on every playthrough, and it has a phenominal community to back it.

Vampire: The Masquerade is a decently well-known role-playing system that I was not familiar with before playing Bloodlines. However, for a new player like myself to jump in without any prior context, Bloodlines does a great job of establishing the fiction of the world of Vampire.
What is most impressive is the game's way of forcing a "vampire mentality" on you. The Masquerade is a system requiring vampires to keep their existence secret from humanity, and this sometimes means having to kill innocents in unfortunate circumstances. By not doing so, you risk the lives and foundation of all vampire society.
Bloodlines is an open-world modern RPG/adventure, allowing you to take quests while following a main story narrative. For a game released in 2004, the graphics aren't half-bad, and the character expressions/facial animations are actually rather impressive. Be aware that some odd unofficial patching needs to be done to make this game work on modern systems.

Red Death is a Sci-Fi space shooter, produced by Indie Panda Games, and released by New Reality Games.
In this game, you are commanding the ship RED-001, with no mission told, or any aspect of how the games works.
There is no tutorial, and the game throws you in with the hope of the player knowing how to quickly understand the controls.
In the Guide Menu says that the spaceship can only be hit on the center circle of the spaceship; this can lead into some risky and successful battles, but also the feeling of "injustice" as some bullets go exactly through the player model.
Through the gameplay contains Normal Enemies, Special Enemies, Mini-Bosses, and Bosses.
The text that exists during the gameplay (Contains not-so-friendly works) are impossible to disappear without pressing Escape or Enter, leaving again the player in a state of looking randomly for the right keys to make the action.
After playing some hours, you will get Arcade Mode.
There is no Multiplayer/Coop and there is no CheckPoints.
The Game's visuals are a 8-bit space sci-fi theme. Its pixel arts are very simple, and shows mostly one or two colors in every sketch made.
In the Menu, there is a "Guide" menu, where shows the controls and its purpose, in the keyboard, and in the controller, and the only options available being: the Fullscreen/Windowed Option (F) and Mute Option.

CoH2 is a great game. As a squad-based RTS, you won't find a better game, perhaps but CoH1. It preserves its focus on storytelling, the controls and the scale, and also adds a multitude of new features like the climate. Not only the AI makes the player nervous, but also the lack of resources - every decision counts and you are going to cope with your own errors. Thus as a strategy game, it is the top level.
The WW2 eastern front setting is brutal and challenging. The game doesn't follow the "Private Ryan"-like idealized narrative like the first CoH, but confronts the player with the historical ambiguity, presenting a story of a soldier being pressed from both the Nazi enemy and the Communist regime. So, while you could be satisfied with nearly perfect game mechanics, you also have a food for thought.
However, while offering a magnificient content, the game presents itself very cheaply. The first thing you see when you start the game is an advertisment - a bright white banner presenting DLCs. You don't even have the obligatory "Options" tab in the main menu - an "In Game Store" seems to be much more important, while there are numerous ways to access it, e.g. through the inventory or buttons on the banner. You have the system of "commanders" from the first CoH, but you can't build up your own ones - you can buy them. Alongside the skins, decals etc. The effect is following: you have a plenty of choice without any real meaning. In CoH1 or DoW2 every commander/hero makes a difference for the playing style; here, it is a mere decoration.
You don't feel like in a strategy, but rather as in a supermarket. When starting a skirmish, you have to click through the number of maps which aren't available as long as you don't buy the DLC. One even feels relieved when the Nazi hordes crush through his minutely prepared defences, because at least then he isn't annoyed by the overpresent Sega's attempts to sell you a DLC.
Shortly, I just want to play with some tanks, why all that ad??! I do believe that many of the fallen Soviet soldiers weren't very deeply indoctrinated in the Communist ideology, but this game doesn't honor them much by falling into the other extreme.
Buy it. just Buy it. you will not regret. I really hope they make like a modern COH one day.

I’m not a fan in which the way the game is sold in piecemeal the way it is. With that said however, the game is truly solid in my opinion. If you’re a fan of RTS and like WW2 this is definitely the game that will fit that bill and it does it very well.
It has everything you’d expect from a AAA title to good graphics, sounds, gameplay, good control setup, unit variety and now at this point in time, the number of factions (on release it only had two but now five if you opt for the DLC Western Front Armies and British).
At the time of this writing, the game is coming close to 20k reviews with a mostly positive rating which really speaks volumes on how this game is. While I could balance my review to talk about the graphics, sound, gameplay, etc... etc... something 20k other reviews have pretty much covered in depth at this point I wish to cover why I think this game has become so appealing.
This game is genius in that it offers something for all walks of RTS players.
If you’re the single player type whether casual or seasoned, this game has you covered. It offers the traditional campaign with difficulty settings and if that’s not enough you can grab additional mission packs. You can also skirmish vs the AI you can even team skirmish vs the AI so that you can enjoy larger battles all without ever having to play with another human.
If you’re the super competitive type this game has you covered as well. It has the usual 1v1 complete with rankings. There are still tournaments held to this day, the last being hosted on twitch with $5k in awards a few days ago from this writing. It also has team vs team modes so that you and your buddies (or random players) can play against opposing teams.
And the real beauty of this game is that it even offers something in between.
Don’t like being super competitive but enjoy playing with others? Well this game again has you covered as it also provides a co-op skirmish with other online players against the AI with whatever difficulty setting suits you. When going through the list of games you can watch that are currently being played, this mode in addition to 2v2 appears to me at least to be one of if not the most played.
I felt it important to really give props to Relic Entertainment for remembering that there are different types of players and providing an avenue, mulitple even, for those players to fully enjoy the game. I felt it important because it’s something some other developers seem to have forgotten some time ago.
You know I may gripe about the price but in all honesty I got over 1000h in and I’m still playing so even if you didn’t want to wait for a sale then just pick it up. Casual or hardcore, you’ll most likely get a ridiculous amount of playtime out of this.

This is one of those games that is hard to recommend. It has it's moments where I did enjoy myself, but I had to swim through frustrating game design to get there. Every major battle is either a quick time event or you are stripped of your gear and left to fight with what you are given. It took a long time for me to start to enjoy the combat, due to extremely weak weapons with low durability and lack of character skills. Once you level up and get some decent skills and weapons, things start to look up.
The game is split into two areas, the slums and sector 0 (nice part of town). The parkour works much better in the second part of the game while in sector 0. The way the slums are layed out, it is harder to find running and climbing areas. I really only enjoyed my time in sector 0. The slums are a grind and is the first half of the game. So between the area you start in and the poor weapons and skills, it is more punishment than fun. I was about to quit so many times but kept going back hoping it would redeem itself. It sort of did, but not nearly enough for me.
The parkour worked well enough in the last half of the game, right up until the end where you have to run through an obstacle course to make your way to the end guy. Every time in the game that requires you to jump to a ledge, it feels like a 25 to 50 percent change that you will actually grab it. I died so many times falling to my death because I did not grab a ledge. And after several tries, suddenly it just worked. I am pretty sure I was doing the same thing every time. There were entire side missions where you need to climb a long ways up and falling means death and starting a long ways away to try again. I ended up dying about 12 times before passing on those missions. Just not fun.
I played this as a single player game, and maybe it would have been a recommended game as a coop experience. As a singly player experience I would not recommend it.

Ys Origins is the 3rd game released on the "Napishtim" engine of Ys games, accomapnying Oath in Felghana, and Ark of Napishtim, but takes place before Ys 1 and 2, the first games in the series. I strongly recommend playing Ys 1 and 2 before you play Origins, as much of Origins is a complete retread of 1 and 2 to the point where it feels like a modern retelling of the story, for purposeful reasons. While the description of the game describes it asa "Metroidvania", it has ery little to do with the genre - there's very little backtracking save for 2 specific parts of the story, and the use of new skills is almost entirely 'going forward', rather than unlocking new parts of previosu content.
Ys Origins takes place 700 years before Ys 1 and 2, and tells the tale of three adventurers, Yunica, Hugo, and a 3rd unlockable, as they scale the Tower of Darm searching for the Goddesses, who have gone missing from Ys. Yunica and Hugo's stories are slightly different, and the game is short enough to where playing them both (and then the 3rd character, for the "Canon Story") is something that can be accomplished in about 20-25 hours of game time. If all you care about is the story, my recommendation is to play it in the order of Yunica -> Hugo -> 3rd Character, all on Very Easy or Normal, depending on your skill. If you're an achievement hunter or looknig to 100% the game, be aware that you'll be beating the game a minimum of 6 times, with 3 of those being on the hardest difficulty level, Nightmare. You'll also be doing side arena challenges and grinding them for extra, non story related, content. There's little reason to play difficulties between Very Easy, Normal, or Nightmare in my opinion - one for just experiencing the story, one for a standard challenge, and one to tear your hair out.
The art style and presentation is much the same as the rest of the Ys series: A bombastic, anime-styled tale full of dramatic adventure and magic, backed by orchestral and rock music that constantly keeps the game running at a full throttle energetic pace. Each section of the tower is themed with a new, vibrant tileset, so climbing the new sections of the mega dungeon feels different aesthetically. Returning fans of the series will find the game runs so much common ground with Ys 1 and 2 that oftentimes you'll know how to solve a puzzle or sidequest just from the presentation of it. The instant you get the Blue Necklace, you know what it's used for, and as soon as you see the Dreaming Idol, you know you're looking for something to slot into it, and so on. It's full of pleasant callbacks, as the entire game takes place within Darm's Tower, and on some level, feels like a modern remake of the second half of Ys 1.
Combat is still breakneck paced, and runs off the engine of the previous games. For those unaware, the Bump Combat system of the early Ys games was replaced by a button mashing swift attack and magic combo system, with no directly usable healing items. Healing items drop from killing enemies, as do strength, defense, and MP regen buffs. EXP earned also increases the longer your combo goes, and so combat entails you mad dashing from room to room, constantly hammering and crashing through foes to keep up your combo and buff meters. There is also a "Boost System" that ups your character's defenses and their magic powers, but doesn't directly buff their attack, making using it a matter of skill more than button mashing. The game works to keep you constantly engaged, and it accomplishes it magnificently. As you go through the game, you feel powerful, as skills level up and your own ability to plow effortlessly through mobs increases. The game also features SP you use to level up abilities outside of direct XP, things like decreasing MP cost for spells, increasing the boost meter recharge, increasing resists to statuses, and so on.
The two characters differ, both in story presentation and in combat. While the basics of the story are the same, the characters accomplish different goals, and NPCs are seen in a different light based on who you choose. The 3rd unlockable character's story is different in its entirety and features new bosses and content not seen in the other paths. Yunica Tovah is a magic-less knight who fights with a battleaxe (and later a Greatsword), similarly to Adol, the protagonist of the other games, and those familiar with Ys will find she's an easy fit. Hugo Fact is a magician who handles like a walking shmup character, firing blasts and lasers, sacrificing speed for range. His abilities are slighlty less straightforward than Yunica's, but having a spammed range attack option that pierces enemies in a Ys game makes the game so much easier it almost feels like cheating at times.
Bosses continue to be highlight encounters of the series, and test your pattern recognition and reaction speed in equal measure. I did not play on Nightmare, and have no desire to, but there are a few bosses who I can only assume would be absolutely maddening to go through. Yunica in general has a harder time with bosses due to being melee, and due to her block mechanism being a timed parry rather than an easy to put up forcefield - but it's not much of a difference, and you quickly find that Yunica can go completely hyper aggressive, using her guard parry to allow her to constantly stay in a boss's face with no fear whatsoever. In general I would say the expanded repertoire of the game makes the bosses in the Napishtim Engine games easier. I have not played Oath or Ark yet, so I unfortunately can't compare to those games, but from what I hear, those two games are more difficult in boss terms than Origins.
All in all, a story that explains the "Origins" of the series, coupled with a sterling presentation, and consistently fun, engaging gameplay, the Ys series continues to impress. It should be at the forefront of any action gamer's list to play, if they haven't already. With a wide range of difficulties to accomodate all skill levels, and a relatively short playtime per story, completing and learning everything is well within the grasp of even non-hardcore gamers who might otherwise be put off by the series' somewhat legendary difficulty levels among its more rabid fans.

Quick Summary – Atmospheric First Person Shooter in a post-apocalyptic world. This means scavenging, fighting off mutants, and stealthily avoiding bandits whenever possible. As a “redux” the game has been remade using the Metro Last Light engine and runs smoother with better graphics. The Steam version of Metro 2033 already included all the DLC for the game, but some of the Steam achievements have been changed/removed.
You play Artyom, a young man living in the Russian Metro (kind of like a vast subway system) 20 years after a nuclear apocalypse. The world above is a radioactive wasteland where humans cannot survive even a few minutes at a time without wearing a gas mask. The tunnels and cities (metro stations) that the few thousand surviving humans inhabit are dirty, cramped, and occasionally attacked by mutants hungering for that tender human survivor flesh. Half of the enemies you encounter will be humans though, whether they’re unaligned bandits or from rival city stations (communists, Nazis, etc.) Beyond all this, a new threat has appeared in the tunnels that guns and bombs can’t fight.
Metro 2033 uses a regenerating health system where the screen turns red as you take damage, and if you avoid damage long enough it goes back to normal. However unlike Call of Duty, this healing takes a relatively long time, which might be impossible during a raging gunfight or swarm of mutants, so you’ll need to use med kits for quick recovery. If you’re a run and gun player you can get through the game relying on quick reflexes and the various weapons you find lying around, but if you’re a stealth player, you can avoid about 75% of the fighting in the game by sneaking around and doing silent takedowns.
Something that the game does NOT explain to you is that like the original Metro 2033, the Redux has a “morality” system where you can gain moral points by performing certain actions such as finding the corpses of long dead humans, finding hidden ammo stashes, sneaking undetected past enemies, etc. You can lose moral points by killing enemies unnecessarily or not following directions, etc. The only thing morality affects is the game’s ending and you have no way of knowing how well you’re doing until almost the very end. I remember playing through Metro 2033 about 3-4 times and I never saw the “good” ending. You pretty much need to follow a game guide to accumulate enough moral points.
If you’ve played the original Metro 2033 and are wondering what the differences are, here are a few notable ones:
+Better graphics
+The game is split into 2 main “modes” Spartan and Survivor (less ammo available). There really isn’t much noticeable difference between the two, honestly. Ranger Mode (more realistic gameplay) is still available as a “difficulty” but no longer has Steam achievements tied to it.
+There are now “safe boxes” and corresponding keys half hidden in most of the game’s levels. If you find the keys to unlock the boxes, you can accumulate a lot of money, way more than you’ll ever spend. I ended the game with over 1500.
You should buy Metro 2033 Redux if:
+You enjoy stealth elements, but also like to shoot it out occasionally. Unlike games such as Dishonored, if you get “caught” in Metro you can blast your way through fairly easily if you’re a decent shooter player. It just feels cooler if you stealth your way through (and you get moral points).
+You like post-apocalyptic atmosphere with “horror” elements similar to the STALKER game series (mutants, radiation, psychic phenomenon).
+You want 100% Steam achievements without “too much” effort. No need to play hardcore mode or grind 100 hours.
You shouldn’t buy Metro 2033 Redux if:
-You don’t have spare money and already played the original Metro 2033. The story is unchanged.
-You are afraid of mutants/spiders/communists breaking through the walls and getting you.

Somewhere between walk-'em-up and adventure game,
blends the best elements of both.
The atmosphere.
people who like their walk-'em-ups with just a tad more gameplay.
received a lot of buzz in the indie-sphere, and rightly so.  It also has its detractors, and I can understand why.  There is just enough game here for it to be unequivocally a game, unlike other narrative-driven walking simulators like
and
and thus, like
- another gamified stroller - Ethan Carter left itself open to criticism focusing only on the game elements.
Now don't get me wrong, the game elements here are brilliant.  You are a supernatural investigator who stumbles across murder victims, hunts for clues using your psychic sense, assembles them, then gets to see little still poses of the victim and their murderer assembled around the scene.  By tagging them in the correct chronological order, you get to view a cutscene that explains what happened.  This denouement is masterfully done.  The process of stumbling across and then piecing together all the elements of the crime is entertaining, and doesn't break your immersion in the tense atmosphere the game is building by forcing you to involve yourself in mindless tasks or fiddly interfaces.
But while these murders drive the narrative, the crime scene investigation definitely plays second fiddle to you just walking around this town.  I think the balance is just right, but for those who like more game in their game, the short running time combined with the few instances of this interesting mechanic equals not much game.  And I think that's a real shame, because the beauty of this game is in the way it artfully places you in a plausible scenario dealing with increasingly implausible elements that all have such gravity because the scene, the mood, the atmosphere are all so engrossing and so foreboding.
The one criticism I do have is that that one wonderful mechanic is not explained.  It is barely referenced that you have this extra sense, and how your window on the past expands by assembling clues is never mentioned at all.  It doesn't help that the very first scene you encounter, the one where your powers are introduced, is completely atypical, lacking a body or any clues to assemble, and using a different visual to literally every other instance of the sense that occurs the entire duration of the game.  As far as communicating mechanics organically through gameplay goes, that's a cardinal sin.  I feel like the developers have heard this complaint before, and have inserted a warning up-front that the game does not hand-hold as a defence against this criticism, but if you find your players are googling "ethan carter touch not working" so frequently that google autocompletes the search three words in you've not communicated well enough.  And that's a real shame, because having to backtrack to redo the puzzles you didn't realise were puzzles kinda breaks the flow of the narrative and takes you out of the game.
I do want to especially call out the jump scare section.  Ethan Carter is that rarest of beasts: a horror(-ish) game with an effective and appropriate jump scare.  Half way through the game, when the tension has been built and you're starting to get a sense that these are more than just mundane murders, this terrifying section comes out of nowhere, with no warning, and is genuinely terrifying.  Not just shocking or unexpected, but
.  The fact that this section was managed so well is all you need to know to be sure that the whole game is subtle and intelligent and very expertly crafted as an experience.
And it's beautiful, as all walk-'em-ups must be.  Unlike
's saturated surreality,
is delicate, and wistful, and melancholic, but every inch as artistically gorgeous.  Take frequent scenic screenshots and you will be set for desktop wallpapers for a good long time.
As a piece of Innsmouth writing, it is utterly on-pitch in its length and narrative progression.  If you're a fan of the understated horror of actual Lovecraft, rather than the Cthulu monsterism that has taken over the horror genre, this is a perfect experience for you.  It's not a long game, but it is exactly the right length.
That said, I do hope there will be a sequel.  The set-up in terms of mechanics and theme here makes that perfectly possible, and it would be a real shame if we didn't get to play with this system again.

This game made me seriously consider buying a PS4 back in the day. Overall a very fun and fine game. Criticism on my part can be limited to the following points.
1. The very restricted movement due to the small area covered by the camera. This is a central drawback of the chosen format to focus on local coop (but 20-30% more vision/room would have helped a lot).
2. Overall mission-play can become repetitive. They fought of a lot of fun little objectives to do, but the objectives don't affect the general play on the map. If the objectives would have had an effect on the entire map, other objectives, enemies etc. it would have created a multitude of situations, instead of the now barebones 1.move to A 2.finish a QTE 3. move to B (repeat).
3. Enemies sadly also fail to create fundamentally different experiences. Yes, a race might be focused on melee and another might have access to lots of heavy armor - but the Scout-mechanic (which is the most fundamental part of the game) works the same for all the races. Other factors of comparatively limited importance (mostly to which weapons or equipment is most effective). Also, spawning of enemies is sometimes weird and obvious.
4. Prepare to suffer loss of motivation or boredom when you are out of the beginning phase of the game (and no longer are given new fun or weird equipment very fast) but are not yet good enough to play the difficult missions (especially when playing in a group).
5. That some races are not available after defeated is ok - but that the corresponding unlocks are unavailable is BAD. It is a serious annoyance that overshadows all other factors of the global war. (Serious mistake from a game design perspective).
Edit: 6. Forgot this point. Partially quite weird weapon balancing (mostly on the primary weapons). This wouldnt be that hard to fix but I don't expect them to work on this. Since it is a coop game it is annoying but not destructive to the experience.
Consider these points, but also that it was on the most fun games for me in recent memory.
Edit: I also gifted this game to multiple people out of principle. So take the above points in perspective :)

This is a an above average, budget-priced bullet hell game that could be great with just a few tweaks. I've only beaten the first three bosses and played for less than an hour upon writing this review, so my opinion may change over time.
First, the balance. The laser is ridiculously over-powered. Or perhaps, rather, the other weapons are under-powered compared to the laser. It takes mere seconds to beat a boss with a double laser, vs. about 50 times longer (literally!) to beat the same boss when you don't have the double-laser combo... and the first time you're hit, you lose both lasers (plus your overdrive damage bonus)! This feels too punishing as it basically turns the game into a challenge to get the two lasers, then see how far you can make it without taking a single hit. It feels too all-or-nothing. I think the balance would be better if your ship only dropped one laser--not both--unpon taking a hit, and if the non-laser weapons either did a bit more damage or the lasers did less.
(UPDATE: After giving this some more thought, I don't think increasing non-laser weapon damage is a good idea as it would make the non-boss enemies too easy to destroy. I think a better approach might be to grant each boss roughly half as much health (so that non-laser weapons are more effective) but compensate for this by drastically reducing the damage done by the laser--probably cutting it in half as well. This way, the laser or double laser won't cut through boss stages in mere seconds, yet players that lose the laser(s) will still have a hope in hell of defeating a boss without one.
Second, the dialogue. Use of the word "sh#t" in the dialogue, along with the fact that the voice-over seems to say "sh#t" instead of "ship" every single time you gain an extra ship, makes it appear as if the dev is a giggling 8-year-old obsessed with bodily functions. Then there is the use of the f-word in the dialogue. I'm not opposed to cursing in games, books, or movies, but  it should serve some function. Here, it neither enhances the characterization (which is practically absent to begin with) nor addss any grit or realism. It just comes across as juvenile and amateurish. It also means that my kids can't play the game until they're older. I hope the dev takes out the cursing because it detracts from an otherwise fine game by making it appear more amateurish than it otherwise might, based on the otherwise fine presentation, polish, and gameplay.
Third, the game does not display your score when you die. It takes you back to the title screen after you click through a couple lines of dialogue, and then it displays the high score. It would be nice if the game showed you your score when you die. I would expect this to be an easy fix. While discussing the score, I'd like to commend the dev for keeping the score total low and reasonable rather than in the zillions of points like in some bullet hells. The latter approach just makes it harder to make read the score and, thankfully, that's not a problem here.
The gameplay, apart from the aforementioned weapon balance complaint, is tight and fun. The ship's control is very good using an XBox 360 controller. The amount of slow-down when using focus mode feels just about right and makes it much easier to dodge bullets while sacrificing some rate-of-fire. This trade-off also feels just right. Overall, I'm very satisfied with the control.
There is a good variety in enemies, mini-bosses, and bosses. The boss stages and bullet patterns are fun and interesting, if not revolutionary. The graphics are simple, yet crisp and appealing, and I never once lost track of my ship in the swarm of enemy bullets, despite the fact that there was a lot of red on the screen at one time. The sound effects are sparse but functional, and the level designs are satisfactory if unambitious. There isn't much story, but this style of game doesn't need one. I'm glad that there isn't more dialogue to click through, actually, because it would only detract from the game's good sense of pacing and momentum by interfering with the action. The amount of dialogue felt just right. The little plot twists, as revealed by the bosses, were a fun and welcome surprise.
I commend the dev for choosing a $0.99 price point. I've paid $4.99 for games that are less polished and less fun.
Overall, I recommend this game to anyone with an interest in bullet hell games who isn't expecting the next CAVE- or Touhou-style  masterpiece. For the price, the game is reasonably fun and appealing, and it offers a good amount of challenge. I'm looking forward to spending more time with it as well as trying more games from this dev.

I posted a video "quick look" on Steam based on my playtime so far. Below is the text transcript of that quick look.
YouTube Quick Look:
Welcome to Red Death: a budget bullet hell-style vertical scroller on Steam that serves as a prologue to a series called "Project Starship." I'd never heard of or played either of these games prior to sitting down to record this footage.
In Red Death, you step into the shoes of the highly saturated Phillip J Fry look-a-like over on the left - or more accurately, this near microscopic spaceship in the bottom center area of the screen. The premise and execution of game mechanics are both pretty simple: dodge red stuff with the control stick, shoot with the a button.
I haven't played a ton of bullet-hell games - or maybe more accurately, I've never been very good at them. I should probably preface everything that follows by saying that not only did past experience with the genre ring true while playing Red Death - it reminded me just how much suck I'm capable of exuding when sat down in front of a game like this. This game is difficult. I checked around online and it seemed like other people were saying so too - so I can at least cut myself some slack knowing I'm not alone.
Now, from my limited perspective - let's talk about the greatest strength of Red Death: the price. This game is $0.99 as a base price on Steam, and it's even on sale for 20% off at the time of this recording. There are far worse ways to get rid of a dollar. This game is fun. It's simple and easy to jump into, and you'll have a lot of fun playing through the first level over and over like I did - only to be rewarded with a crazy first boss fight that will demand some deep concentration.
The enemies, in my limited experienc, have some variety to them and I really particularly liked that when I destroyed an enemy, all of their on-screen projectiles exploded at the same time in a cloud of points to drive my high score up.
Now, let's talk about a pro that evolved into a con during my playtime with Red Death so far. At first, I was mentally praising Red Death for being high-contrast. It can be argued that more detail in bullet-hell backgrounds usually means low-contrast and added difficulty keeping track of the player character - or at least I'd say so. Here, I felt it was really easy to tell what was going on with the pale teal backgrounds and the vibrant red that seemed to protrude out of the screen. But then... more red was on screen. Slowly, the backgrounds started to have red seeping into them. Enemies started putting the "hell" in bullet hell. It became really tough toward the end of the first level to distinguish where I stopped and thousands of red bullet orbs began. Sure, this is probably at least a little bit expected based on the genre alone. This many moving parts is bound to make your head spin after a while - but I couldn't help thinking just one more color could have helped set apart the helpful and the harmful. The redness of the ship was a huge benefit to my eyes at the beginning, but at the end it made me almost cross-eyed.
I really greatly enjoyed my limited time with Red Death. I played for about 45 minutes so far and wasn't able to clear the first level in that time. This boss fight was usually the first place I even lost a life during each playthrough, so it should be noted that the difficulty spikes quite a bit. Regardless, I think there's enough gameplay here to recommend Red Death at the current price point. The aesthetic is still cool - if at times a little impractical and the gameplay mechanics are simple, but solid. Whether you're a fan of the genre or not, what you get here is pretty fun for less than a dollar.

because we had the promise of a new next-gen Battlefront game and they completely flubbed it. Now I know that may not sound like it has anything to do with this game,but what I want to point out is that I didn't play Battlefront 2 again until 2014,after I bought EA's Battlefront I thought to myself,"It's amazing how a game that came out ten years ago can have the same great sound design and while the graphics aren't super amazing now they don't need to be,the game came out TEN YEARS ago." My point is,if you are going to play a game with the heart and soul of a Star Wars game play this one. This game launched with WAY more content than a game claiming the same name ten years later,and while the gamespy servers are shut down,third-party devs keep the online community alive and well,and there are still alot of fun and cool mods out there for the game. If you can't or don't want to play this game online than I still urge you to buy this game,because even just booting up the campaign,galactic conquest,and the multitude of modes in instant action makes this game worth your time.If any game designers read this,and I seriously doubt any will,This is how you make not just a single-player/online shooter,this is how you make a Star Wars game. Nothing short of a fantastic improvement on the original. The addition of a proper story to the Single Player campaign is quite welcome, but also well thought out, and there are a few maps that you can only get to play by going through the single player. Space battles were added to the game, with air vehicles like xwings, etc being taken out of the land based levels as in the first one the levels just weren't quite big enough to allow for any strategic value to be gained by flying around. Unfortunately although it is a fun element, it quickly becomes repetitive and is probably the one glitchy point of the game, by glitchy I mean that its rather intermittent as to stationary turrets bothering to fire at you and next to impossible to dodge on some occasions, whereas other times you could shut your eyes and not get hit, even if you opened them and tried to fly into it. That aside it was still a step in the right direction. The other addition to the game is heroes characters ranging from Obi-Kenobi and Mace Windu, to Boba Fett and Han Solo, not to mention Yoda. The heroes are simple enough to use, but can easily turn the tide of battle, and in the hands of a master can mean total annihalation for a side. The only drawback to the heroes are that some seem to be a bit pathetic, but all in all its another step in the right direction for the Battlefront series. If you liked the first one, this is well worth the purchase. Ignore the bad reviews here people, if you like Star Wars this definately one of the good games in the franchise. Battlefield in the Star Wars Universe, who cares if its a ripoff, it makes for good gaming, not to mention the last good game in the battlefield series was the Desert Combat MOD for Battlefield 1942.

CoH2 is a great game. As a squad-based RTS, you won't find a better game, perhaps but CoH1. It preserves its focus on storytelling, the controls and the scale, and also adds a multitude of new features like the climate. Not only the AI makes the player nervous, but also the lack of resources - every decision counts and you are going to cope with your own errors. Thus as a strategy game, it is the top level.
The WW2 eastern front setting is brutal and challenging. The game doesn't follow the "Private Ryan"-like idealized narrative like the first CoH, but confronts the player with the historical ambiguity, presenting a story of a soldier being pressed from both the Nazi enemy and the Communist regime. So, while you could be satisfied with nearly perfect game mechanics, you also have a food for thought.
However, while offering a magnificient content, the game presents itself very cheaply. The first thing you see when you start the game is an advertisment - a bright white banner presenting DLCs. You don't even have the obligatory "Options" tab in the main menu - an "In Game Store" seems to be much more important, while there are numerous ways to access it, e.g. through the inventory or buttons on the banner. You have the system of "commanders" from the first CoH, but you can't build up your own ones - you can buy them. Alongside the skins, decals etc. The effect is following: you have a plenty of choice without any real meaning. In CoH1 or DoW2 every commander/hero makes a difference for the playing style; here, it is a mere decoration.
You don't feel like in a strategy, but rather as in a supermarket. When starting a skirmish, you have to click through the number of maps which aren't available as long as you don't buy the DLC. One even feels relieved when the Nazi hordes crush through his minutely prepared defences, because at least then he isn't annoyed by the overpresent Sega's attempts to sell you a DLC.
Shortly, I just want to play with some tanks, why all that ad??! I do believe that many of the fallen Soviet soldiers weren't very deeply indoctrinated in the Communist ideology, but this game doesn't honor them much by falling into the other extreme.
Buy it. just Buy it. you will not regret. I really hope they make like a modern COH one day.

I’m not a fan in which the way the game is sold in piecemeal the way it is. With that said however, the game is truly solid in my opinion. If you’re a fan of RTS and like WW2 this is definitely the game that will fit that bill and it does it very well.
It has everything you’d expect from a AAA title to good graphics, sounds, gameplay, good control setup, unit variety and now at this point in time, the number of factions (on release it only had two but now five if you opt for the DLC Western Front Armies and British).
At the time of this writing, the game is coming close to 20k reviews with a mostly positive rating which really speaks volumes on how this game is. While I could balance my review to talk about the graphics, sound, gameplay, etc... etc... something 20k other reviews have pretty much covered in depth at this point I wish to cover why I think this game has become so appealing.
This game is genius in that it offers something for all walks of RTS players.
If you’re the single player type whether casual or seasoned, this game has you covered. It offers the traditional campaign with difficulty settings and if that’s not enough you can grab additional mission packs. You can also skirmish vs the AI you can even team skirmish vs the AI so that you can enjoy larger battles all without ever having to play with another human.
If you’re the super competitive type this game has you covered as well. It has the usual 1v1 complete with rankings. There are still tournaments held to this day, the last being hosted on twitch with $5k in awards a few days ago from this writing. It also has team vs team modes so that you and your buddies (or random players) can play against opposing teams.
And the real beauty of this game is that it even offers something in between.
Don’t like being super competitive but enjoy playing with others? Well this game again has you covered as it also provides a co-op skirmish with other online players against the AI with whatever difficulty setting suits you. When going through the list of games you can watch that are currently being played, this mode in addition to 2v2 appears to me at least to be one of if not the most played.
I felt it important to really give props to Relic Entertainment for remembering that there are different types of players and providing an avenue, mulitple even, for those players to fully enjoy the game. I felt it important because it’s something some other developers seem to have forgotten some time ago.
You know I may gripe about the price but in all honesty I got over 1000h in and I’m still playing so even if you didn’t want to wait for a sale then just pick it up. Casual or hardcore, you’ll most likely get a ridiculous amount of playtime out of this.

Cons:
- Customization (which is along the lines of how your character looks physically, building textures, and furniture) is somewhat limited at the moment.
- The game can get boring if you do set the 'days per month' option at the max amount of days, which is 8 days per month.
- The game may or may not lag a little when there are more people on the screen. All depends on how your rig is set up.
