10 hours of gaming later, and here's my inital thoughts on Software Inc.
Pros:
+ Addictive
+ Art Scheme
+ Endless Amounts of Opportunity and Fun. You can start off in the 80's and become a company like Microsoft, or start off in the modern era and struggle to compete with the major names in the market. The possibilities are very large, and each playthrough brings different cards to the table with randomly generated stuff and things.
+ Dynamic Stock Market
+ Reputation System, has a few kinks here and there, but still, its there.
Cons:
- Glitchy, Clippy, 90's-esque Graphics. If you NEED amazing graphics, this Alpha is not for you.
- Slightly unbalanced difficulty settings.
- No music? Minor, but definitely something I enjoy having in a game that takes HOURS at a time to play (D:)
- Super. F***ing. Needy. Employees. No. Really. Expect to deal with, "I NEED TO PEE, THE BATHROOM IS RIGHT OVER THERE, BUT INSTEAD OF GOING TO THE BATHROOM, IM GOING TO ASK FOR A RAISE." a lot. Cheap, dirty ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.
- Overall, a lot of improvements/fixes/adjustments to be made (that's why it's an Alpha :D)
If you're into strategies and want to get behind something new, innovative, and extremely addicting, then you've come to the right place. Although there are still PLENTY of bugs at this stage, the developer seems rather set on game development, even if his abilities are limited. Take those twelve bucks you were going to spend on Junk Food to support a great game. :D

Software Inc. is a The Sims less then but more eager to be more cousin. When I say that I mean imagine a game where your Sims can have a custom job and live in a custom made office with your own staff and everything. So far I was able to sample the game enough to get a fair and accurate review of Software Inc. and I have to say... its different.
I made a boss named the Canadian Devil and the business Pay2Win Inc. I first didn't understand how the staffing worked but I played a few game developer clones and quickly found my way around although I had to restart a couple times. My first mistake was making 2 rooms one with a kitchen and one the main office but found out that you can only have one team per room and so I stuck my advertising team in the kitchen with the bathrooms, the team would call in sick then quit after two months reporting to news that well I was the Canadian Devil not letting them pee and eat. Then I realized every project I started took six to eight months to just get the bare minimum and have the reviews say "surprise Pay2Win made yet another bad product." and only sell 50 units. I finally found out that you can take on jobs for other businesses to earn some quick and more effective cash however sending staff to school seemed like more of sending them to Las Vegas for a week.
Overall the game delivered what it said it was but there's 1 glaring issue that should be addressed minus the 4x timer sometimes makes the time go faster and the workers stay at 2x but the lack of a good tutorial to show players what does what and why. Don't get me wrong I still recommend this game but I recommend it as a fun "The Sims at work" type game for now. I'll keep this review updated.

I like this game quite a bit, there are much better MMORPG's with the same non target style but you don't come across as many as you think. Some pros are:
- The Aforementioned action style combat rather than tab-targeting system
- There is item enhancement and auction house (ala Archeage, WoW, etc)
- The PVP aspect of the game (May be a problem for many people but that's why the PVE server was made)
- There are quite a bit of classes to choose from (gender locked with certain races like demon gets top and bottom male and middle female, and humans get top and bottom female and middle male, so it sort of evens out.
- Quite a good amount of people for a slightly new MMO
- The skills are a bit less then most MMO's but they are easy to get as you can get most in about 3-5 hrs
- Enemy's are fun to fight and the game is quite difficult (depending on the class you choose
- You don't have to grind much unless your going for lvl 40 (good luck) really quickly
- PVP is great due to the aforementioned action style combat
- The download isn't so much so great to try out for a bit
Even thought I say it's a good game, it's got quite a bit of cons
- Graphics are not as good as most new MMO's (I don't care but some people do)
- High lvls can spam kill newbies depending on their moral compass
- The server is pretty stable but I ran into a few server glitches and some 10 second disconnects because of the server
-  I ran into a few bugs ( one including when I started the game Fluffy got stuck inside the wood of a carriage) but not that many
- Some spelling and grammatical errors
- Many things you can buy but not "Pay2Win" (Mostly cosmetics and mounts but there are weapons.
I like this game and I am still playing it, as long as my internet holds up :(. I seriously recommend you play this with a friend because you can team against bosses and dungeons, do quests, and you will run into many pvpers on your journey so having more than one person will usually grant you your win, or intimidate your opponent. I recommend it and I will hope to see you out there :)

I used to play text adventures back in the 80's and early 90's and SanctuaryRPG really brings me back.
Sanctuary pays homage to a time when these great games totally relied on your imagination and that alone.
The game is extremely deep and there is a massive amount of depth in character and weapon customization.  The best way to play is classic (permadeath).  I find that if you play with respawning enabled, the game just isn't as fun.
SanctuaryRPG has a really great soundtrack as well!  Lots of text games didn't have soundtracks and it really adds to the experience.
A glorious return to the days of Zork, Adventure, Jigsaw and more.  There really is a lot more going on in SanctuaryRPG than any of these older games, the massive amount of depth is actually quite impressive.
A quality experience for sure!  Great work guys.

NOTE: I immediatly wrote this review after my first Playthrough of the game so I have not experienced much.
I had read about this previously (before steam release) in PC gamer and I thought I would love it as I do like me some classic Rogue or Stone Soup and I was right.
You dont have a top down view of where you are and move around with strange keyboard controls like most ASCII RL games. It plays more like an interactive text game (like zork for example) but with less freedom and knowing where you're going more instead of spamming north until something interesting happens or waiting whilst thorin starts singing about gold.
The combat system looks really complicated and it is, you have starting moves, linking moves and finishing moves. You're meant to use a starter then a linking move and then a finisher unlocks which you can use for extra damage or something. there is also relocating so if an enemy is about to charge you or something then you can relocate and the enemys charge cancels. There are also rage attacks but I have no idea how it works.
This game is packed with references to fantasy/Sci-FI films and games Like the lord of the rings, the game also seems to have an unhealthy obsession with potatoes (seriously the second weapon I picked up was a potatoe staff). and the game makes me laugh in normal conversation with the NPC's saying stupid things or breaking the fourth wall. Once during some "Mountain Exploration" I came across some "Random Onions" and my options were 1) boil 'em 2) mash 'em 3) sitck 'em in a stew Which was a hilarious nod to lord of the rings (well I found it pretty funny at least).
The soundtrack is pretty good and it made me feel weird actualy like I was tripping out or something and I couldn't help feeling disconnected from everything but the game immersing me in its rather ridiculous world.
The ASCII art of the different characters is really good too even on the enemies the same jumbled letters, numbers and symbols put together are different each time and I even saw a skeleton that looks like Megadeths mascot "Vic Rattlehead" although I don't know if that was intentional (Megadeth is a Thrash Metal band that was famous throughout the 80's and 90's).
Overall the game is really good although i'm probably biased because i'm a sucker for roguelikes.
I score the game a solid 9/10 If you like good storytelling and strange monty python/deadpool humor then this is a must buy.

Let me start off with saying I own Ys III for the SNES but other than that game of the series, this is my first time really sitting down and playing an Ys game.  I am someone who loves games such as dark souls to sword of mana and this game feels a little like both This game is great if you like any action-RPG elements, but it does have some kinks and gimmicks that are a little off puting at times.. I will keep this as short as I can and layout the pros/cons and give a summarization.
Pros:
-The graphics in this game are great with lots of detail in most areas
-You will level up fast and find that enemies will never be to overpowered
-The music in the game is fantastic and will usually not get too dull
-Bosses are great, fun to fight and great music with them too
-The story is decent although a little cliche
-New players to the series will feel welcomed and don't need to play the others to understand whats going on
Cons:
-Collecting all ore in order to power your weapons is necessary, bosses will be to strong if you miss 2 or more later in game
-There are some cheap deaths in the game such as having a certain item equipped will kill you instantly if you don't already know about it, or a certain boss will be able to trap you (unfairly) and you will take massive damage with no way to regain health during the fight.
-The game doesn't give that well explanations on what items do and whether you need to equip them or not in order to use them (some are passive with no explanation of it)
-Mid to late game you will start to see enemies from the early game that are just stronger than before (hp and strength,  some aquire new moves too)
-Weapons are pretty bland and basic for Yunica, not sure about the other two characters.
Although I go into detail about the cons, I found that I really liked and enjoyed the game and will continue to play it with new characters to see what the difference is between them and update this review once I have done so. I do also plan to play the other games of the series because I do love this type of gameplay/story. For now I will rate the game a 8 out of 10. Although I found that there wasn't much variety in the weapons and even though there were some cheap deaths, the game kept me engaged and not want to quit for hours at a time.

I'd say this is the best Ys 6 engine game we have on Steam, as far as gameplay mechanic goes. It has (I think) the most bosses, it also has the best bosses, its dungeon is really well-designed for the most part, and the action got even further refinement from Oath in Felghana. There are two problems however. Having three character is nice, but having to play three times is not nice, especially when considering the dungeon design stay more or less the same. And when that third and hidden character's story is the "truth," it means you have to play it at least twice to get the actual story.
So it actually comes down to how much into Ys you are. I do not recommend this to people who are going into Ys for the first time; it's not a good reflection of how Ys series actually work, because it's a game entirely based on dungeon-crawling. Not only that, the storytelling is more similar to Trails series than Ys series (same scenario writer), so you have to be fine with crap-ton of dialogues.
If you like Ys 6 and Felghana, you can just play it once as Yunica to feel satisfied with its mechanics, because it's one hell of a tight ARPG, but really, the game wants you to have played Ys 1 and Ys 2 before playing this. The level design, story, characters, background music, they are all designed around the fact this is a prequel to Ys 1 and Ys 2, and the game doesn't shy away from making that connection.
But to be honest, if you've played Ys 1 and Ys 2 and have fond memories of it, Ys Origin has such a good story that gets to you in so many ways. There are so many subtle connections to Ys 1 and Ys 2, and a lot of them add a lot of emotions to those games retrospectively. You get to understand its lore better, a few of its characters better, and you get to understand why and how things came to be when Adol first got washed ashore on Esterian beach in Ys 1. It's dependant on whether you have played those games or not, so it's not recommended to everyone, but if you have, this is a must.

DLC REVIEW
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Its beeen a few months since the release of the game and the DLC content has started to role out, all the packs that have released so far are just character packs and dont add much to the game.  For the most part im not really impressed with these packs but anyways, here's my thoughts on the DLC so far...
Empire Strike Back Pack - 6/10
Cool characters from one of my all time favorite movies, han solo in his hoth uniform is awesome but the best character from the pack is the prototype Boba Fett character!
Prequel Trilogy Pack - 3/10
Having the Darth Maul character from the clone wars is pretty nice and over all im not to fussed with the character selection, unfortunately that is all washed away with the inclusion of..... him.
Freemaker Adventures Pack - 3/10
Watched a few episodes af this mini series after I saw the DLC in the game, mainly just for kids, dont care too much for these characters, the inclusion of the playable Hutt is nice though.
Jabba's Palace Pack -  6/10
This pack not too bad, Finally being able to play as Jabba turned out to be a slow and sluggish experience (should have expected that).  Great to see my favorite character of the franchise Bib Fortuna in the game... De Wana Wanga!
Jedi Pack (Season Pass Early Access Bonus) - 4/10
Cool inclusion of a few of the Jedi from the Order, Mace Windu is always an awesome character to have. Not much else to say really, most of the levels are better suited for non lightsaber battle so these character arent too useful, still, they're a decent inclusion to the list.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Overall my current verdict on the released DLC is, 'useless', 'no real reason to have them'.  If you havent got the season pass yet you're not missing out, although its a nice little inclusion to the character roster most of these new additions aren't realy needed, if they were released closer to the games releade date they might have been more usefull but after having these packs release after having completed the game is a little bit of a let down as I havent had a use for them. Some of these dlc characters should have unlocked special areas in levels or maybe unlock extra powerbricks, I feel these characters are just being added for no real reason other then to just have them.  Im just hoping the level packs release soon and change my mind on the season pass as a whole.
The reason I havent brought up the Vehicles is because they serve no real purpose and are not that interesting compared to the base game vehicles.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Overall Score for DLC (as of 29/8/2016): 3/10

From the moment I saw the trailer to this game I was hooked. Rapt. Pierced through the heart by the harpoon of mystery and dragged beneath the turbulent waters of unfathomable horror, and I enjoyed every white-knuckled second of it.  I'm not going to spoil anything for you, but from what I can say about the story, the protagonist, Paul Prospero emerges from a tunnel, through a portal into Red Creek Valley, and things just get weirder from there. While I'm not one to gush about visuals and atmosphere of a game, this particular game manages to take superlativeness to a whole new level when it comes to looks and atmosphere.
The setting, the fine details had me on my toes literally from the first minute, and had me asking a lot of questions come the end of the first 'sensory' scene. The kinds of questions that gnaw at your sense of comfort and stability, eat away at your confidence in the mundanity of reality. I particularly loved the way the game handles its doses of startle and fright, getting the dosage in that sweet spot that makes your stomach backflip whenever you hear the strings twang or the sound of an otherworldly moan. One little segment of the game in particular scared me in a way I haven't been since the original STALKER, and to a far better degree might I add. Until today I have never dreaded the thought of being in a cave underground as much as I do now. I am scarred for life and I have never enjoyed the experience more.
There are only two drawbacks to this game that I can think of: The first is its length. Entirely forgivable given the amount of work that has clearly gone into making the game. The second is the way the game's progression can be obfuscated at times. While a horror game is rarely enhanced by extra degrees of handholding, surely a game with such wonderfully written narration and oodles of interleaved details in all of its backstory could tell us how to use Paul's abilities through his own words, and maybe, just maybe, make a few of the more difficult items/doors/buttons/etc. a teensy bit easier to find?
But other than those two tiny things I have yet to enjoy a single horror game more than I've enjoyed this interactive story. Worth every penny you pay for it.

This game is great fun! I grew up playing text based rpg's, and this game takes those old games to the next level!  SanctuaryRPG has interesting fight mechanics, a great sense of humor, good/catchy chiptune style music, a wide veriety of enemies, and a high enough difficulty level to keep you coming back.

INTRO
Sanctuary was an impulse buy for me because I have a weakness for ASCII art and keyboard controlled games. Like many of my Steam purchases, I was fully prepared for this to entertain me for a single play session and to be quickly forgotten. I was not prepared for how immediately engaging this game would be.
DIFFICULTY
I continually feel rewarded by the frequent leveling and item drops. I was never in any doubt that my character was growing increasingly more powerful with every action taken, and I've never felt the need to grind levels or gear. Despite this being true across my playthroughs, the game never allows me to be careless. Any encounter could easily result in my death which, in Classic mode, is permanent. For me, there is a perfect balance between reward and challenge in this game.
GAMEPLAY
In addition to advancing the story, there are various side tasks that can be performed often, but not constantly, including crafting, management, fetch quests, and battles. I did not ignore any of these since they provide experience and offer a nice diversion. I'm not sure if the core gameplay might become a bit monotonous if I ignored all of these side tasks.
LENGTH
I have not succeeded in beating the game yet, but I'd estimate that an average, successful playthrough would take 2-4 hours depending on familiarity with the game mechanics and progression. Keep in mind though that this estimate is based on the assumption that I've made it to the final encounter of the game.
STORY & WRITING
It's too soon for me to accurately say, but the story seems to be entirely linear. This could be considered a negative to some due to the game's length and permadeath feature. A softcore game type is option, but this seems to prevent unlocking some game options. In my opinion though, the story is very well written and there likely would have been a quality drop if it had been branching or randomized. The flavor text that is included with battles and other interactions has been entertaining and varied enough to me to keep me looking forward to reading it.
SOUND
I appreciate the retro-inspiration and found the music to be very, very enjoyable. Sound effects are about what I expected, though there are situations where a battle end sound effect seems to be missing, which briefly takes me out of the experience.
REPLAYABILITY & VALUE
Once I beat the game, I'm not sure if I will immediately start playing with a new class or if I will move on to another game, but I know that I'll have enjoyed every hour spent during that playthrough and would gladly pay $7.99 again if I had to do it over.
Update on game length: I completed Act 3 in about 3.5 hours as a Barbarian. I assumed this would be the end of the game. There is an Act 4, but it felt more like post-game than a continuation. I, admittedly, did not live much longer though, so it's possible that I just didn't progress the story yet. I ended up dying during "Ranked Matchmaking" at the Colosseum.

Around about a year ago the 'original' SanctuaryRPG was released.  I downloaded it back then (it is freeware) and fell in love with it.  Black Edition (paid now) adds more content, better art, more races, more class perks, mercenaries, faction system, etc.
This is a turn-based rogue-like RPG with surprisingly deep content.  Combat requires you to always pay attention.  Is the enemy getting ready to charge you?  Are you snared?  What sort of special modifiers does this enemy have?  What debuffs have I got & can I get rid of them (is it worth it)?
There's a few different places for combat to take place, too.  You can just be out in the fields encountering enemies, pressing forward with the story, in one of the 'randomly generated' dungeons from the Colloseum or taking part in ranked matches in the colloseum.  I'm not really far into this edition, so there might be more later.. Who knows.
Besides combat there are other things to do!  You can take over a bar and serve the patrons to try and get gifts, spend cash to upgrade it & draw more patrons, get cheaper beer, etc.  There's a sort-of house building mechanic where you can gradually upgrade your camping ground to a hut, shack, cabin, etc.  A great crafting system that reminds me of the system in Final Fantasy XIV.  Plenty of amusing 'events' that take place!  See a syringe on the ground?  Yes, you have the option of picking it up and injecting yourself.  Come across a cow?  You can kiss that thing.
The caveat of this game is that it is entirely text.  All the art is ASCII art (and it's great) - this means it's definitely not for everyone, but I HIGHLY recommend everyone at least give the freeware version a shot (this might just be a demo now.. Google for it), and if you like it.. Pick up the Black Edition.
I highly recommend this game, but am willing to admit that it is probably not for the majority of gamers.
Addicting gameplay- felt somehow similar to Mirror's Edge (which I loved). Highly recommend.

Vampire: The Masquerade: Bloodline has too many subtititle in its name, yet it proves itself worthy of all of them.
You play as a vampire. As the game is a WRPG, you can choose you vampire race ('bloodline'), history, and stats. It's set in LA. The overworld is quite small, and confined to a few hub worlds. It clearly isn't a completely polished game: some stuff seems short, pathways that should be there not present, iffy combat. The game was rushed out.
With that said, it still oozes charm and charisma, like it's a Toreador Vampire. The Voice Acting is fantastic; the story draws you in; the dialogue is genuinely gripping for the most part, as if written in a novel or a TV programme, not the cheesy stuff you expect from games. The facial animation reminds me of L.A. Noire in places. Obviously not as advance technologically, but they're wonderfully expressive all things considered.
All in all, this game is a great WRPG. It's easily the best WRPG I have played. It draws you in a lot.

Helldivers is a top-down twin-stick shooter with 4-player coop from Arrowhead Game Studios, the same studio who brought us Magicka. It released on PC recently but doesn't have cross-coop with the Playstation platforms with the exception of the persistant galactic war influence contributions.
Maps are procedurally generated from a variety of terrain tilesets including snow, forests and deserts.  The game features a galactic map on which the Helldivers community has to defeat three alien races to win the galactic war. To defeat an alien race, players must push through the enemy's territory all the way to their homeworld, where you are given 48 hours real-time to successfully fill an invasion meter. There are around 15 different mission objective types in the game - ranging from activating SAM sites or capturing territory - and different missions will give you up to six of them to complete in any order you want. Each enemy race has a couple of race-specific objectives to make things a bit different.
Enemies spawn infinitely during a mission as long as you keep getting detected by the many patrols that roam the map. It is possible to fully stealth your way through any mission with judicious use of the minimap and careful planning. At the end of every mission, you have to call down a shuttle to evacuate your team which takes 90 seconds to arrive and remains in place only for 30 seconds. During that time you will be fighting off waves of enemies as they attempt to stop you evacuating. Don't miss the shuttle as it costs you XP. XP is only awarded for completion of mission objectives, being evacuated, and having a low death count. Every player's performance is added up and each player is awarded the same amount of totalled (not averaged) XP.
The multiplayer lobby is the bridge of your ship, which you are able to walk around in and access the armoury console, the galactic campaign map, and the Helldivers encyclopedia. Missions are started by climbing into the ship's drop pods. People can drop in and out of your match whether you're in the lobby (via bridge teleporter), or mid-mission (via drop pod). They can drop out at any time and it won't interfere with the mission.
Friendly fire is always on and there is no option to disable it. You can be killed by your own supplies as they are dropped in from orbit, too. Hell, you can be killed by the rescue shuttle at the end of the mission if it lands on you. You will die many, many times in this game. In order to be respawned, an ally has to call in a request for reinforcement. Yes, you can kill a teammate when you spawn if they are under you. Expect many, many deaths.
This game is basically the Starship Troopers game you always wanted but never knew. The humour in it is very tongue-in-cheek, gleefully satirising the concept of spreading democracy through war. Helldivers is highly customisable in terms of your character's loadout, and there are some cosmetic customisation too.
You will notice there is a lot of DLC for Helldivers too, but don't be put off by this - the DLC is by no means required to make you better at the game. The DLCs feature weapon or strategem side-grades and cosmetics in the form of helmets/armours/capes with one or two holding small quality of life upgrades that are nice to have but are by no means mandatory.
Overall Helldivers is an excellent co-op game and one of the best twin stick shooters I've ever played. If it weren't for the Witcher 3 being released this year I would name this my GOTY hands down.

Lego Star Wars- The Force Awakens is a joy to play. Weather your a fan of Star Wars or just the Lego games, there is something for everyone.
I never really tried the Lego games until a few years ago when Lego Marvel Heroes came out.  It really took me by surprise how much depth there was to the game, and how it wasn't just for kids. 30+ hours later and 100% completion and I was willing to try anything else the Lego games could throw at me.  When The Force Awakens game was announced I was delighted as I am a big Star Wars fan.
The game itself is a series of hub worlds with a few levels on each. You could probably get through the campaign in about 12- 16 hours, but if your going for 100% it's more around 30 hours.
The levels are bright, wonderful and full of the usual Lego charm that leave you smiling from ear to ear. The source material is held in high regard, and there is lots of fan service. The levels are a good length, unlike the very short 5 minute episodes offered by DLC.
I enjoyed every minute playing the game, seeing the 100+ characters and many vehicles they had to offer.
The only downside to the game was that i encountered a number of bugs that forced me to replay some levels a few times. This probably added an hour or two to my total time with the game. They may have been patched now, as I played mainly during the week of launch.
I can't really say the season pass is worth it as it only adds 3 short levels that are about 5 minutes each and a few extra characters.
I recommend this game to anyone willing to give it a chance, Star Wars fans, Lego fans, young and old- give it a go, and may the force be with you!

With only 4 hours in I feel like i have barely grasped the game in depth. It took me a few tries to figure out the mechanics and to have a game where I didn't go bankrupt.  Here is a small pro/con breakdown:
pros;
-Feels like a class tycoon game, start from the bottom and work to the top
-Has a plethora of in game tasks to keep the player busy, from managing teams to seeking out contracts to complete all the way to building up your offices to expand for more employees.
-On the other spectrum, it also has a "Sims" feel meaning you can literally build new rooms/buildings for more space, place equipment & furniture, each having direct impact on your firm.
-The interface is aesthetically pleasing to the eyes and is easy to interpret.
-Spreadsheets & numbers for the statistic-savy folks.
-In game stock market including loans you can withdraw for more cash on hand to do whatever with.
-And by the looks of it many many other features i haven't yet experienced.
Cons;
-Albeit the game is in alpha, there is still glaring room for improvement.
-Graphics/Audio are by no means on a AAA standard, so if you are wanting some crazy high-resolution ultra HDR direct x90000 quality graphics, move along. (This isn't really a con for me, i don't care about graphics or audio for these types of games).
-Some finicky in game mechanics could use some fleshing out such as how effectiveness & happiness numbers really work.
-A few graphical glitches but do not have an impact on gameplay.
One last line,
This game has so much potential, a fellow Dane appears to be the primary (or only?) developer for this title, and so far he/she is off to a great start. I will continue playing, and will follow development closely.

If you don't want to read:
Pros:
-Very enjoyable characters
-3 different playable characters, with completely different character mechanics AND unique storyline for each character!
-Beautiful storyline, such that I just sat and stared at my screen when it was over and contemplated life
-Variety of difficulty modes - bosses gain new moves and effects at higher difficulties, not just increased stats
-Nightmare Difficulty is REALLY hard (nice for those like me who are tired of really easy games)
-Combat system is very strategic and engaging, and you will need to pull out all your moves at various stages in the game
-Quite possibly the best soundtrack in any game I have ever played, INCLUDING FINAL FANTASY 7, 8, 9, AND 10 (though 10 especially would be close)
Con:
-Unfortunately you can't skip dialogue. Not a huge deal if you're just doing "regular" playthroughs, because each story is pretty unique and there isn't much overlap. Where this gets annoying is if you're going for the Steam achievements where you have to beat the "unbeatable" bosses, because you have to reset the game every time you fail and go through the dialogue again, because dying doesn't trigger "retry" option.
Ys Origin is one of those games that I wish I could go back in time and experience all over again. I picked this gem up a few years ago on a whim, and wow. W-O-W. From the combat to the characters to the classic-but-heart-wrenching story, this game delivers on all fronts. The story is beautifully unveiled, as you can play through with three different characters (one unlockable after beating the game with either one of the starting characters), and each one tells a different story, so you have to beat all three playthroughs to get the full story, and there is a special last boss that is only available on the secret character. (as well as a special ending sequence) What makes this great is that each character plays completely differently, so in addition to having new story content you have a completely new playstyle to learn, which especially affects the boss fights. Personally I chose axe-girl (yunica) --> mage (hugo) --> secret character, and I would recommend playing through in that order, because Hugo is a little OP so you spoil yourself if you start with him, and the secret character reveals all the secret details of the story so it's best to do last.
From the moment I picked the game up I couldn't put it down, grinding my way through 3 nightmare playthroughs (yes I'm insane), and completing the challenges for beating the bosses that are supposed to be too hard for you to beat. (You know those bosses that are supposed to kick your♥♥♥♥♥in the storyline, where you're supposed to beat them the next time you fight them? Well you *can* beat them for a steam achievement, although it only changes a few lines of dialogue, and they are FRIGGEN HARD). I had many moments on my first playthrough that had me screaming and raging at the screen as I started my 15th, 20th, or even 30th attempt at a specific boss. I chose nightmare mode to be challenged, and it doesn't disappoint. But even with the frustration of getting my @$$ kicked repeatedly, the combat was so good, and the story was so engaging that I kept coming back for more.
One thing that I think is very cool is that the bosses actually gain new moves and effects as you increase the difficulty, rather than just stat boosts. I only played on nightmare but if you want to play through on a lower difficulty first, the fight will be different when you up the slider, which is excellent design.
The game was so good that I instantly went out and bought all the other Ys games on Steam. Unfortunately, I fell a little bit TOO in love with the characters in Origin, and was saddened that I wouldn't be able to play them again in the other games (because Origin is set 700 years prior to the rest of the series). That combined with the fact that I was uncertain if I wanted to play the (very) old Ys1&2, but not wanting to play the games out of order, meant I didn't end up playing any of the others! At least, until now. I can gladly say that I have started the series back up, having completed I and am currently almost done with II, and am enjoying them very much. So I thought I would come back and write a review for the game that sucked me into this amazing series, and here we are! Hope everyone enjoys it as much as I have.

"Let me tell you a story of the beginning.....Of Ys"
Set 700 years before the events of Ys 1 and 2 we venture to the destroyed world of Ys by an unknown force of demons.
Days pass as the remaining survivers atop a floting island that they sent to escape the scorge of demons on the earth known as "Solomun Shrine" the 2 Goddesses that watch over the people of Ys Reah and Feena have disappeard along with the source of magic in the world of Ys "The Black Pearl"
A group is dispatched to search for the godesses on the earth but are soon separated by an unknown force that attacked them on the way down from a tower that showed up out of nowhere.
Shortly after regrouping the search party begins to climb the mysterious tower in search of their godesses only to find much more afoot the tower that awaits them.
Unlike most Ys games where you plays as the title character "Adol the red" Ys origin gives us 3 different characters all together to play as.
Yunica Tova: A young girl and Dauther of the Captain in Gaurd command that protect the godesses, She wields a small battle axe and is a "less mobile" Adol if you are familier with the other games.
Hugo Fact: A mage in search of his missing brother and seeks to achieve great power, He wields "The Eyes of Fact" making Hugo the first Mage character to be playable in an Ys game as unlike Adol or anyone else he uses projectiles to fight from long range.
Toal Fact: Hugo's older brother and was once a commander of the Gaurd for protecting the goddesses, Now a half-demon Toal's Action's seem questionable at first as he as sided with the enemy to achieve great power as well...or does he? (Unlockable only after beating the game once as Yunica or Hugo, Note: His story is the actual cannon to the series)
Ys origin uses the same Ys engine that began with Ys VI and later improved in "Oath in Felghana" and as its own game and prequel story it holds quite well. Areas are broken to floors as you are climbing up the tower but variety exists as each floor as its own theme (Water, Sand, Fire ect) and its not just going up stairs upwards as they spice of the areas giving you places to explore for goodies and what not. However despite the variety in areas unlike other games in the series Origin is very linear in where you can and can't go to with only a very small bits of Exploring later down the line. There's also not that many Intresting characters to meet as most of them are either from the search party or the Villains of the game limiting the feel of a living world like previous games.
Despite those small down parts Ys origin is still fun and challenging game like all other Ys games in the series.
One small problem that kind of annoyed me is the Checkpoint systume. unlike the two eariler Ys games using this engine (Ys 6 and Oath in Felghana) if you die in an area/room you will restart from the start of that room and you can go back to a previous area if you are low on HP however Ys origin doesn't do that and instend your only means of checkpoints our the Goddess Statues that let you save the game/buy upgrades.
Which means if you died a along ways through an area without getting to the next Statue its all the way back to the previous one, And while you can Teleport back to one at any point to save any progress you made (I.E points or Key story items) you still have to go all the way back to the last point you got to which on later Difficulties can get on your nerves sometimes.
But if you've played any Ys game before and tried to beat it on Nightmare mode you should be pretty used to the pain and suffering by now. :P

Not as good as its predecessor, but still not a bad little game. Runs much smoother than the first room, and travels to more diverse locations. That being said the puzzles have been dumbed down substantially, so instead of having a rewarding experience of deducing things yourself, it's more of a "can you follow simple orders" simulator. Find the keyhole shape that matches the key in your inventory, put the circular piece into the circular hole. The simplicity of it all does make it much faster paced, for about the same length game (2-3 hours).
The hint system is obnoxiously fast in this one- you'll be dropped into an area with multiple things to check out, and before you're even done with the first one, the hint indicator will be binging on screen, before you've even assesed what is a puzzle. It's a minor complaint, but an annoying one, especially when the first game got it right.
Overall, I've bet you've spent $5 on worse things. Hoping that the third game in the series is designed more like the first one, but with the clean presentation/optimization of the second.

This review focuses on the singleplayer aspect of the game only.
As a fan of the first part of the series, I had to get to 2nd one (during a sale).
I finished the campaign in under 20 hours (and played several missions twice). Most missions had no real sense of danger to them or they only had a forced time limit to hurry you along. The story told by the game was quite 'nice' .. or let's say interesting. Almost none of the missions felt like real battles (like in CoH 1), most of them were about cleaning out a city with barely any enemy iniative and/or resistance.
So the story was okay, the missions helped in understanding what was going on in the protagonists' heads. But from a RTS standpoint, the mission were at best average. (No, increasing the difficulty does not help. I tried.)
Now that I've finished the campaign, I noticed that there is a price tag on the 'Ardennes Assault' campaign. Full price! REALLY? I visited the store page, read the reviews ... Nice, another DLC hidden in the DLC and another 'average at best' campaign with recycled material.
The sum it up: if you're looking for a singleplayer experience, get the first CoH. The second one will either cost you a lot of money or disappoint you.
PS: Again, singleplayer view only. Multiplayer seems to be another cup of tea because the game is obviously made for long term multiplayer engagement.

Short Review:
Bad successor of the first game.
The first company of heroes had the main game and 2 Add-Ons, which could be played as stand alones.
Comapny of Heroes 2 however released a ton of DLc's and Add-Ons, making the game a money milking machine to gain maximum profit, instead of providing the best experience to its players.
You can buy extra skins, commanders, campaign packs, Armies, Perks...[the list goes on].
Many of which grant you quite an advantage above your enemy. (i.g. producing tanks in seconds, making it possible to spamm your enemy with tanks -> very easy tactic to win the game in early stage)
The variety of "pay extra" parts make this game absolutely unenjoyable to me. While i got the game pretty early at which not so many addons were available i still got annoyed by the paywalls.
The new engine used for CoH 2 is imho worse than the original one and takes away a part of the feeling related with the series. The hp, aiming and pathfinding system is bad (applies only to you, not to AI) making the game feel sluggish and unfair when playing against AI opponents.
Overall - not recommended. If you are looking for an arcadish 2nd World War Strategy Game, either go for Company of Heroes 1 (plus addons) or try out the a little bit more demanding Men of War series.

Sphere III: Enchanted World is a pretty average MMO all around. The graphics are dated, but it has pseudo-action combat for those curious, you target with a crosshair and use left and right mouse to use primary abilitys (that you set) and then the number keys as ability keys like MMO standard.
To go into a little more detail, character creation begins with race and class selections, there are 4 playable races to choose, dwarf, human, elf, and demon. Currently only humans and demons are selectable. I am not sure if elves and dwarves are locked because they are unfinished and unimplemented yet, or if they are some sort of bonus you get for something. Class wise there are 9 that I remember, the classes are gender locked. The 9 classes are Barbarian, paladin, warrior, ranger, monk, assassin, sorcerer, priest and necromancer.
Currently I am leveling an Assassin, so far throughout the demon starting zone my experience has been solid, dated, but definitely decent.  Overall I feel that Sphere 3: enchanted world does not do very much different from MMO's that were out 5- 10 years ago. It does however manage to keep what made many of those MMOs decent. I would recommend it to anyone who is a fan of classic MMO's

I'll get the most obvious thing out of the way first by stating unequivocally that as of the date when this review was written,
is the most gorgeous game in existence. The last time I remember seeing graphics that I almost couldn't believe existed was in the summer of 1997 when they began advertising the pre-rendered FMV cutscenes from
. There is - quite frankly - nothing to even compare it to graphically at the moment beyond simple stylistic examples, of which the closest competitor might be
.
The soundtrack is very good for setting the vaguely-unsettling mood that drives the plot of the game at a nice, unhurried pace. While none of the tracks are overly thematic - you won't be whistling the bridge song tomorrow afternoon - they're finely crafted and handsomely performed.
The gameplay itself is essentially a walking simulator mixed with an extremely easy point-and-click adventure game; in other words, nothing to write home about but effective nonetheless. Mechanically, the entire purpose of the game is to uphold a beautiful story, a function that is served amazingly well, in part because the mythos itself is so grippingly bizarre in a Cthulhu-like way.
My final verdict is that the game is essentially flawless for what it is and what it set out to be; a great many AAA development studios could learn a thing or two from looking at
.

Youtube could save my intelligence there a bit, so I was able to solve the problem, thanks to youtube, but I was smart enough to know where to find answers when you need them, so that doesn't make me that stupid.
I am now heck who knows how long into the game, saved a few additional puzzles and all I can say is, to be honest, I have no idea. So let me list the Cons and Pros.
By the way, if you are a COD or BF fanboy, I think this game is nothing for you, you are able to throw a hand grenade into a lake at one point for no reason, that is all about the action you will get up to my point.

SUMMARY:  Must-buy for RPG fans.  An easy-to-play, surprisingly complex and deep humorous RPG with a retro text-graphic aesthetic.  A bargain at the price, it provides plenty of challenge delivered with humor.
SanctualyRPG is probably best summed up as "far more than it seems."
At first it seems like an attempt to do a retro RPG, with graphics consisting entirely of text characters and simple controls and character management.  Very quickly you realize this game is the very summary of "more than the sum of its parts."
Characters?  Well you pick a class and races, and then level up various attributes and skills.  However the traits, the attributes and skills you chose, have a variety of effects in game.  They're even more pronounced when combined with equipment.
That Equiment?  There's armor, shields, charms, and a variety of weapons with assorted randomized traits and stat boosts.  You're never quite sure what you're going to find or make, and surprises abound.
Crafting?  Oh, you'll get plenty of that.   You'll collect and salvage various resources to make weapons, armor, and more.  You even unlock more crafting options over time, giving you more to do back at camp.
Camp?  You get a camp to start with, and are able to upgrade your home, mine, and of course make items.  When you're done you can leave to visit other areas in Sanctuary.
These other Areas provide plenty to do, from shopping to visiting a library to fighting in an Arena or in procedural dungeons.  They even have a few surprises.
Oh and there's actually a story behind all this.  Often silly and loaded with potatoes, sometimes gruesome and sad, and always driving you forward.  It even comes in acts so you know how far along you are.
This, you'll note, is even before you get to adventuring.
Adventuring is pretty simple - go to an area, something random happens, and occasionally a secret area or exploration option will appear.  Youi'll usually meet monsters, but also can find yourself accomplishing various silly tasks or finding treasure.  Though you may have to climb a statue or dance with a golem to get it.
Combat is a combo-based and status-effect based system.  Building combos unlocks more attacks, and status effects can provide vital differences.  You can build up powerful attacks, and acquire more and more abilities over time.  Juggling them in proper order - and the proper sequence to handle various enemies - is of utmost importance.   You have to pay attention to a variety of factors, and most combats are pretty involving as your HP, statuses, and MP fluctuate with choices.
On top of all of this there's different difficulty levels and unlockables, so the more you play, the more there is to do.
The entire package is a fun, addictive, clever game that I'd have happily paid twice the price for.  If you like good RPGs, want one you can play for a few minutes or for hours, and have a sense of humor, go for it.  Buy it.

I'm really torn on recommending or not recommending the game.
It is a great game that simply shouldn't be a rogue-like. Deep combat, huge amount of RPG goodness like classes, crafting, customization, skills, discovery, exploration, and a deep narrative. So much to do. So much love in this game and the DOS-like interface is hardly noticeable. The game is very, very immersive and you grow attached to you characters. The game is deceptiely deep.. literally not one dull moment.
There is a lot of content in the game. A full playthrough could easily go 10-15 hours.
Therein lies the crappy part - this game is a 1-death permadeath roguelike. Some enemies are very very strong and sort of "come out of nowhere"  and two-shot you (often after a wave of trivial fights). Your characters die rather... unceremoniously... and you get nothing from their deaths.  It's not like other roguelikes where the game is short enough to where it's alright, or you have sort of an "HQ" through which dying at least allowed some sort of gain... you start from square one.
There is a "softcore" mode... but each death in this mode reduces global item drop rates. That just isn't fun. So much of the game is collecting items and managing them... not an inspiring or fun way to play the game. I don't count that as a decent softcore mode - each time you die the game becomes less fun and more tedious.
EDIT: I WAS WRONG ABOUT SOFTCORE MODE! Each death DOES NOT drop global drop rates. Rather, global drop rates are dropped just once.. at the beginning of the game. Not as harsh. THAT SAID - the reduced item drop rate still is a "punishment" mechanic for choosing an easier difficulty. Further, softcore mode just feels... lame. You die and instantly come back and can enter that exact same fight with a single keypress. In other RPGs with a save system, you at least have to "go through the dungeon" or something similar. There are some stakes on the line for dying - you'll have to climb to the top of the mountain, or whatever. Softcore mode removes the stakes entirely. The game has two extremes - a completely inappropriate die-and-restart-the-entire-15-hour-game, or absolute-0-consequence-for-dying. Neither are compelling to me as a player. Game would be perfect with a Final Fantasy style in-between.
Also, I know people say "yeah, hard perma-death... that's the fun! that's the point". But I don't know. It doesn't feel right for this game. It's so deep... there is so much joy just from the RPG elements. The game replays every narrative scene on playthroughs.... you slowly unlock gameplay elements EACH playthrough... it's like the game wasn't MEANT to be a roguelike. You end up banging the spacebar through story sequences you've already seen. You end up saltily unlocking skills and gameplay elements that you already have intimate knowledge of ("You've unlocked crafting - here's hw you craft" after having been a craftmaster last playthrough). I feel like the developer jumped on the roguelike train on a game that didn't need to be a roguelike.
The result of the harsh roguelike set-up with a simply ANNOYING and UN-FUN result is that you grind grind grind to make sure you don't die to an encounter that catches you off-guard. You make your character OP. Still, you may die to a surprise insanely powerful enemy... but maybe not.
All this bad stuff said - the game is great fun. Well worth 5 dollars. ESPECIALLY if you like challenging rogue-likes and are slightly masochistic... GET THIS GAME. If you just want a great RPG... maybe look elsewhere. This game will frustrate you for being a great RPG that deletes your save when you die.
3/5 (5/5 if not a rogue-like)

The Kings' Crusade is a crime against gaming. I really wanted to like this game; it's set in an interesting time period, features cool historical figures and looks good on paper. However, all that you will take away from this game is that it is more broken than my dreams, is savagely unbalanced and is about as fun as amateur surgery.
The main meat of this game is Total War-style RTS battles. However, where the Total War franchise manages to create suspense, challenge and fun, Kings' Crusade creates frustration, sadness and glitches. The battles themselves are plagued by poor troop-control mechanics (which is to say, they are as unbelievely slow-moving, have barely any formations and run away to attack the enemy at random). This combines with the insanely over-powered enemy to create a massively annoying experience. Take the second mission for example: the Saracens for some reason receive 2 missile launcher squads (I'm not even kidding). These boys will rip through your janky troops like Uncle Phil on a Christmas turkey - and all you can do is sit there and take it like a champ because your troops run at 2 mph and have a mind of their own.
The game's biggest crime however is how broken it is as a piece of software. When I first fired it up, the screen was streched out of proportion and this couldn't be remedied through the in-game options. After managing to sort it out through wizardry, I went on to the play the game only to find that there is a near universal crash after the first mission. Though I found a work-around by trawling the forums like a peasant, the game still crashes at random once you get beyond the incredibly boring first mission, rendering all the time you watched your goons crawl painfully across the desert pointless.
Bonus burns: the voice acting is absolutely terrible. For some reason the Pope is American and sounds like he has a mouth full of golden syrup. Also, although I've spent a few hours trying to get this turd to work, it says I've only played for 6 mins. Another sign of a well-polished piece of software.
All in all, I really did want to like this game, but it is a disgusting mess and is probably the reason why the Crusades failed in real life.

HELLDIVERS is best described as a mix of Magicka + Alien Swarm + Irony.
Got your attention? Well, let me explain some bits here:
Magicka is definitely to be found in the raw backbone of the game (4-player with single player possible, dark humor and a harsh take on the "subject") and where Magicka was a tongue-in-cheek take on norse mythology with world eating snakes (easy kill for a meteorite, who would've thought?) and lots of friendly fire in the hectic of battle or out of boredom, HELLDIVERS has you and up to three friends drop into a combat zone to spread democracy and liberty among hostile alien aggressors.
And of these there are numerous! No storyline you can easily wander along anjoying the sights, it's almost always a run through territory crawling with enemies (sometimes literally) and they're always ready to drop some heavy, unfriendly blokes into your group.
Alien Swarm saw you and up to three friends follow the story of an infested colony, trying to rid it from crawling space bugs. The levels were gorgeous and the story pieced together through audio logs scattered in the levels.
You had your pistol and some main weapon, be it a flamer, grenade launcher, shotgun or whatever.
It's a good example of dedication to crafting nice levels and lots of little details that pop into focus when you play the second/third run. Since it's still free on steam: Go and give it a try. You most likely won't regret it and if you do: HELLDIVERS might not be the right game for you.
But that crafted story was also one of the downers: You played the same time and again. Sure, updates/mods allowed for other stuff but even these were the same after a while.
The first run was always tense and some trigger happy moments led to accidental team kills, the second was easier because you had a rough idea where the enemies would pop up and the third became a definite been-there-done-that run.
HELLDIVERS is different in that each player is contributing to the overall campaign, the War SUPER EARTH is fighting against the Bugs (which by PURE incident turn into bio fuel on death, totally not the reason to fight them and keep the industry going!), Cyborgs (which want liberty of the single being and think man & machine could work in the same body. Everybody knows that the managed democracy is the best way for humans to live in prosperity and liberty!) and Illuminates (which are a total threat to SUPER EARTH because they don't want us to have their advanced tech and also they're producing WMDs to eradicate humanity!).
Now, these missions are generated on randomized maps, with the outline of the combat zone hardly ever the same (apart from arena fights where you have to kill a certain amount of enemies to teach them a lesson!) and on these maps you get an area that might be using the same models of rock outcroppings, bunkers, cyborg AA emplacements, battlements, wrecks and the like but these assets are always rotated differently, so that you won't see two in the same orientation soon. I played 47h now and I haven't.
Controls are responsive enough with either Mouse & Keyboard or controller though in some cases you can clearly notice it was made for controller with twin stick and d-pad controls.
Your trooper moves fluidly, diving for cover in the direction he's facing (that often saves your behind, if you remember it) and generally shooting where he's looking.
Shooting? You'll do a lot of that and with a load of weapons. Aim to get a crosshair (otherwise your cursor is invisible) and unleash a salvo of slugs, blasts of shotguns or laser beams.
Because... if you don't shoot the enemy patrols will notice something's wrong with you, you not being a six-legged bug/heavily implanted mind-linked cyborg/descendant of jellyfish and signal for backup to ... cleanse that problem.
This backup -depending on the mission difficulty- might consist of some simple worker drones (boots up and stomp 'em out!) up to tanks (argh, another one? We're running low on AT ammo here!).
And that is the moment where the real fun starts.
See, every HELLDIVER starts his/her mission with a pistol (which can become quite a capable tool to dish out democracy), a rifle of one sort or another, one perk (an always-active item of equipment like incendiary grenades or a cooldown reduction for your stratagems) and four stratagems. These are marvelous.
They can be anything from an ammo drop to recoilless rifles vs armored targets, grenade launchers, artillery barrages, auto turrets, napalm, cluster bombs, mechanized assault suits (bad if you think they look like Warhammers Dreadnoughts) and many more.
These equipment drops can themselves be used as a weapon. Because, you see, they're dropped from a Hellcarrier in orbit. And they drop fast. And are heavy. And don't really brake before hitting the ground...
Anything standing under or next to them takes damage. A lot! No matter if it's your comrade, your teams APC or a bug Tanker: They're squished. Add to that the ability to upgrade them between missions and you go from "cluster bomb to take out infantry" to "laser guided bunker buster with side munitions to clear the area". Or for rifles from "the second shot goes in the same direction" to " four shot salvo dead center".
Overall, HELLDIVERS is a lot of fun thanks to the friendly fire incidents that are often times hilarious; the backstory that's brilliantly deliverd by NPCs (nice voice acting there, too!) and the Encyclopedia on the Hellcarriers; and the satisfaction from completing a stressful mission against the odds, evacuating all HELLDIVERS just before the shuttle is overrun.
Matchmaking is as fluid as you can wish for, just step on the teleport pad on your carries bridge and select a mission on some world and difficulty you like, short moment later: BLAMM, you're dropped into combat.
It might not be the right thing if you can't handle satire and are from the best damn nation in the world but even then:
Ignore the story, come for the shooting.
And the explosions.
And the laughter when another well meant and poorly placed artillery barrage takes out not only the enemy but your team...
Sure there's stuff they could've done better, like a planet rotating under the Hellcarrier to bring the later missions required to "liberate" it in sight, but the way it's now (left side with the Hellcarrier in geosync orbit and part of the planet with mission markers in the corner below; right side for mission details) you can select where to start.
Want to keep the mission with "Assassinate cyborg leader" for the end? Sure, go for it. Command thought it should be number 1, but it's your choice where to drop first and wreak havoc.
And maybe more than one climate zone per world. That'd make for a nice difference in appearance. Right now it's a Star Wars universe: desert worlds, snow worlds, jungle worlds, city worlds... but no variety. If it's one climate, that's it for the whole globe.
But that might be asking too much from a very fun, light take on guns-blazing-democracy.

Ys Origin is a highly entertaining ARPG that let's you slice, smash, and burn your ways through demons floor after floor. The first Ys game as far as the lore background of the series is concerned, Ys Origin takes place several hundred years before the events of the first game and portrays several issues that have only been mentioned by name or entirely left in the dark in the previous Ys games.
In the game's main mode, you can choose one of two (later three) heroes to reach the top of a mysterious demonic tower in pursuit of two goddesses. Though the game mechanics and the tower itself are identical for all characters, each plays a bit differently - Yunica is a fairly tough melee fighter with useful area of attack special abilities, while Hugo is a range-centric mage with a strong standard attack and largely defensive skills. The third, unlockable character finally is goes full rogue, being capable of dishing out lots of damage in close combat yet also sharing Hugo's fragile nature.
Unless you plan to start in nightmare mode right away, the difficulty of the game generally is reasonable. Trash mobs typically do not pose much of a challenge unless you are seriously underleveled (and this problem can be solved with a bit of grinding), but the boss fights more than often will take you multiple tries to find the right strategy. Fortunately, this rarely becomes frustrating, not to the least because the game's fantastic soundtrack is one hell of a motivating factor.
Story-wise, the game is okay-ish. Though Ys Origins does answer lots of questions propped open by the earlier games, two of the three playable character follow the old "THE POWER OF FRIENDSHIP(tm)" plotline, with daddy issues galore. Ys Origins certainly has its moments, the plot will become fairly predictable if you've ever played a JRPG before
Despite of its minor flaws, Ys Origin still is a more than decent ARPG and one of the better parts in the Ys series.

Ys Origin is an action RPG, with a hack and slash styled battle system. There are 3 playable characters, the 3rd being unlocked when you clear the game the first time with either of the first two characters. Each character has a very specific playstyle. Gameplay consists of your typical RPG fare: battling monsters while exploring your surroundings. In Ys Origin, you are tasked with exploring a giant tower that extends to the heavens. The tower is broken up into segments, with each segment offering a different environment to do battle in and explore. They are varied enough to where sometimes you forget you are in a tower and are instead traversing a dungeon located elsewhere. At the end of each segment (and sometimes in the middle) you are presented with a boss. The end of each segment is always a screen-filling boss, and these are the most fun parts of the game, each requiring some strategy to defeat.

Short Review:
Bad successor of the first game.
The first company of heroes had the main game and 2 Add-Ons, which could be played as stand alones.
Comapny of Heroes 2 however released a ton of DLc's and Add-Ons, making the game a money milking machine to gain maximum profit, instead of providing the best experience to its players.
You can buy extra skins, commanders, campaign packs, Armies, Perks...[the list goes on].
Many of which grant you quite an advantage above your enemy. (i.g. producing tanks in seconds, making it possible to spamm your enemy with tanks -> very easy tactic to win the game in early stage)
The variety of "pay extra" parts make this game absolutely unenjoyable to me. While i got the game pretty early at which not so many addons were available i still got annoyed by the paywalls.
The new engine used for CoH 2 is imho worse than the original one and takes away a part of the feeling related with the series. The hp, aiming and pathfinding system is bad (applies only to you, not to AI) making the game feel sluggish and unfair when playing against AI opponents.
Overall - not recommended. If you are looking for an arcadish 2nd World War Strategy Game, either go for Company of Heroes 1 (plus addons) or try out the a little bit more demanding Men of War series.

The first game's puzzles felt like they were left for you by a quirky scientist, this game's puzzles feel like they were left for you by a devil worshiping cultist. The atmosphere in way too dark and evil in comparison to the last game, in my opinion; it makes is feel hard to take serious. The light hearted mysteriousness of the first game fits the little puzzles extremely well and I hoped that I would get more of this in this game, however the disturbing imagery and downright frightening nature of the visuals in this game made me feel uneasy.
Also, I much prefered the compact puzzle boxes from the last game over the room scale puzzles in this game. The puzzle boxes felt like you were advancing towards a goal and every layer that you peeled away was satisfying and fun. However in this game the puzzles get extremely overwhelming and often extremely repetitive and boring. The game puts so many little important things in little dark corners that the camera has trouble getting to, and half of the "puzzles" in this game are just levers and switches that get to be extremely annoying very quickly. I found myself rushing through the end of the game waiting for the hints because I couldn't bother to stay invested.
One improvement over the first game is improved framerate on physics based objects such as opening lids and swinging levers, as these things in the first game would look jittery and ugly when let go of, however the controls are still just as awkward, only made worse by the constant back and forth between corners of each room.
I love The Room One so much, but this sequel left me with a very sour taste.

In this review I'll cover some common aspects like the gameplay, graphics and other noteworthy things about this game. This is all from my personal point of view and experience. I usually don't write negative reviews unless I actually care at least a bit about a game I played. Either way I'll probably get bųllshitdownvoted anyway. I read some reviews and saw the rather high positive rating on Steam, which leads to believe I'll just be a black sheep amongst many, but nevertheless, not every game is suitable for every person.
Dying Light is a first-person zombie survival game in an open world. Set in Roam, a city infected with zombies, you're on the hunt for Antizin, a medicinal suppressant against the Harran virus, which eventually turns humans into the infected. Everyone in the holdout The Tower needs it, including you.
This right here is my main reason to dislike this game, the gameplay. While I don't think it's
flawed, in the end I just decided to give up on Dying Light because of it.
So you can freerun and loot. Both are things I enjoy in games, like in Mirror's Edge and the Fallout franchise. While I didn't have much issues with freerunning, I still find it a bit slippery. Often times the character does things against your will or seems to just "forget" to grab a ledge.
The looting is where more of my annoyance lies: it simply feels unrewarding. You keep finding melee weapons and crafting items. It sounds nice and using consumables is fun but it's a rinse and repeat process that wears on your mind rather quickly. And everything you find is just weak, which I'll be covering soon. Even the lockpick system is just off. It's ripped straight from Skyrim and Fallout and is way too easy. Even the hard locks I often find myself using just 1 lockpick, while I have like 90 left. The rewards in the chests are also not that remarkable. Never a gun or ammo, just more and more melee weapons that fail to dent even common zombies.
Now we're on to things I truly disliked in Dying Light: the combat. Shortly said, you are weak. Even when carrying weapons like axes and machetes, they barely do more damage than blunt melee weapons. For just one zombie it can take up to 5-6 strikes of a fire axe, which is just plain ridiculous. I find myself knocking zombies over and stomping them for an instant kill much and much more than actually whacking them to death. You'll exhaust yourself trying to kill zombies with weapons while jumpkicking and stomping them works better and takes nothing from your stamina. This really just makes little sense.
And seriously, screw those big zombies with the sledgehammer. I've exploded propane and gas tanks on just one, threw like half a dozen of molotovs and whacked its head about 20 times with a sledgehammer and yet he stood. And what if you do manage to kill him? His rebar hammer which is way too heavy to use effectively and only a minor sum of cash, which is as good as killing two common zombies. You often have to kill them in order to progress with an area.
And just a minor pet peeve next to having almost no ranged weaponry and ammo for such, you see everyone else carrying guns, at least the good guys. While you are the hero and get bad stuff. Wouldn't they just stop and think, "maybe we should help him and kit him out?". You don't even get a starting gun. Only melee weapons...
One last annoyance is Virals and Rai's men. They keep dodging your attacks, tank all your hits and drive you nuts, but once they're on the ground you can simply stomp them. With Virals you can even just climb on an object and wait for them to climb there too and just stomp them. TL;DR: the stomp is OP, the rest is UP.
Not much to say about these. They work and it's always great to acquire a new skill to fool around with.
One thing, the Lucky Repair skill. I have not
had it work. Every time I've repaired a weapon it has consumed a repair charge. And this issue dates back to Feburary 2016, which is not a good sign development-wise...
Let me just slip in a few more things that don't work: flares and the UV light. Zombies ignore it completely. It doesn't do a damn thing.
The graphics look good and it runs well on medium-high end PC's. I did have some rather annoying frame-drops which were not the fault of my PC setup. Overall the game's okay on this area and is pretty to look at. The environment looks great and the city is fun to explore.
While apparently the OST on YouTube is diverse and well-made, in-game I find myself droning at the same boring tracks over and over. The OST on YouTube is a lot better than what you get in the game, strangely.
It's difficult to really explain these as on the surface and on the store page, everything about this game looks great. The soundtrack seems great, the gameplay looks awesome and everything else just looks really exciting. However, upon actually entering the game, you might just be disappointed with everything, like I've been. I enjoy zombie games but this would not be one of them. It feels boring and repetitive.
It's not a horrendous game at all but damn, this was a rather boring experience for a game that I really looked forward to to play with a friend.

Downloaded the demo for this thinking, "Oh it's yet another dungeon-crawling roguelike. I'll try it out but I'm sure I'll get bored of it soon." After nearly 5 hours of playtime on just the demo, I grudgingly (and happily) have to admit that I couldn't be more wrong. This is an interesting and excellent game that reminds me of what would happen if Zork, Aniwey's CandyBox, and Kingdom of Loathing made a freaky three-way lovechild that has a bizarre obsession with potatoes.
PROS
+ Fun and engaging retro-esque gameplay
+ Demands your attention during battle, unlike a lot of turn-based RPGs where you can just autoattack your way to victory
+ Quirky and goofy sense of humor
+ Really good music
+ Potatoes
WASHES
= Challenging and punishing, like most roguelikes seem to be. I find this enjoyable personally but be warned!
= ASCII graphics. I don't mind much personally since they're fairly well done, but YMMV.
CONS
- Heavy RNG reliance and it often bites you in the butt (example: I'm playing a Paladin. One of the class "perks" is you deal 25% less damage unless you have a Heavy shield. After about 2 hours into the game, I've found dozens of Light and Medium shields but no Heavy!)
- Pretty dense information-wise, definitely has a bit of a learning curve. Doesn't help that the official wiki is pretty sparse on some details.
On the whole: Extremely engaging for any dungeon crawler looking to delve back into the "good old days" with a little text-based romp. Very, very good for the price.

Having grown up in the 90's, I was spoiled on 16-bit graphics, and later, polygons. I didn't even know ASCII was a thing until I started getting into roguelikes in my teens, and even then, I had to use tilesets for games like Rogue and Nethack just to comprehend what I was seeing. Some games, like Dwarf Fortress, have remained arcane to me even after hours of video tutorials. In short, ASCII graphics were something I either liked games
of, or an obstacle that prevented me from enjoying games I'd otherwise like.
Days ago I'd have laughed in your face for suggesting I'd be charmed by this graphical style one day... Particularly because years of struggling with it had made me bitter. It had become a sign of desperation to me in modern indie games; the last bastion for a dev team short on artistic talent. I saw it as an easy out. A flaw. A design choice always made when the pressures of time, money, or ambition precluded other, better graphical styles.
SanctuaryRPG: Black Edition is a turn-based tactical RPG with, as you've probably guessed, ASCII graphics. Naturally this means that most screens in the game are represented by text, (usually white) on a black background. It's my opinion that this is innately annoying to look at for hours at a time, but SanctuaryRPG have made several smart design decisions that make it tolerable, (at the very least) even to the harshest detractors of text-based graphics.
For one thing, ASCII games are notorious for often being visually cluttered. In some genres, like grand strategy, this is practically unavoidable. But SanctuaryRPG, being predominantly a turn-based, menu-heavy RPG, includes a great deal of negative space in every screen. Even better, most of the time the positive space is taken up by nothing more than competent, charming, and not at all visually taxing ASCII illustrations that vary in colour, plus the omnipresent menus beneath them.
Obviously if you're not a fan of turn-based RPGs the menus can be a turn off, but as someone with a bit of experience in the genre I can say with confidence that SanctuaryRPG's menus are quite easy to understand and navigate. And when they're not, you can type a question mark in most screens of the game for some clarification. Also, and this is kind of a weird observation, the devs take a great deal of care in not forcing you to remember your character's details. Usually if you can take an action that draws on your character's traits, the game will inform you of the relevant trait in parentheses at the end of the option you can select to perform that action. You'll rarely have to look at your character sheet in-depth, making gameplay much more kinetic and less prep-heavy than it otherwise would be.
Now, I know I've gone on about the graphical style of the game quite a bit... But if I do, it's only because I know how skeptical I was before purchasing - and I want to bully other skeptics into doing the same. Because underneath its divisive ASCII exterior lies a truly fun and fulfilling RPG. It doesn't just set up the main quest and inexolerably push you toward its conclusion; it gives you
. You can engage in random events, fight in an arena, dig for minerals, craft equipment, fight sets of procedurally-generated enemies, do sidequests, join factions, have awkward conversations with NPCs, run a bar, improve your camp, read books, be followed home by a potato, and more! And some of the minigames associated with these activities are surprisingly robust.
Unfortunately, this wouldn't be a review without outlining some things I take issue with in the game; thankfully none of them are too bad. For one, even after the tutorial I found conducting combat a little confusing. Some of the less traditional RPG battle concepts, like moveset swapping, knowing when to heal and when to finish a combo, fully understading your meters, and the *HUGE* list of enemy traits are hard to get down at first, and the subtleties kind of have to be arrived at through trial and error. Also, there are no combat animations or anything, so tossing a fireball as a mage is about as visually interesting as swinging a sword; which is to say, not. Thankfully the classes are differentiated greatly by their traits, so it's still very worthwhile to try on different hats... Not that you'll have much of a choice playing in classic mode, because you're almost certainly going to die, and will NOT want to level that barbarian up to 20 again.
So, in closing, I would say that SanctuaryRPG is not only a great game, but the only one to ever cure me, (if only temporarily) of my bias against ASCII graphics. If that's your last sticking point when it comes to buying this game, at
try the demo, (available on the developer's site) and see if you enjoy the gameplay. If you typically enjoy challenging turn-based RPGs with a great deal of content outside of the main storyline, this may just be the game for you. If you like all that and don't mind harsh penalties for character death, this is almost certainly the game for you. But don't take my word for it; research! Do enough digging and you'll find the lovely, impassioned devs behind it all, who clearly believe in their product and have infused it with quality to match. And if that isn't the best argument for taking a chance on this game, I don't know what is!
Oh, and did I mention that the game is chock-full of oddball humour? Didn't feel right to list it with the pros or the cons since it's such a subjective thing. I like it, though. :)
