Pros:
- Very nice fighting system: you can't just spam your preferred skill until the enemy is dead, but you have to actively respond to his attacks and pay attention to his bonus stats.
- Has a lot of humour in it. (a lot of potatoes as well)
- The music really fits with the ASCII-images
- This game proves that flashy graphics are not needed for a good game.
- You're not just limited to fighting enemies, but you can also craft, run a tavern, dance naked and do unmentionable things to potatoes.
- Exploring all of your options is rewarded.
Cons:
- The game can sometimes get grindy: all of a sudden you'll need X items to progress the main story.
- What I really miss in this game is some sort of backpack, no matter how limited. Most of the time it is pretty clear whether you should keep your current item or replace it by a new one, but in some cases (like with weapons that do extra damage at night) it really depends on the situation. A backpack would really be useful in such situations. (Note: there is a backpack in game, but it is only used for crafting mats and such, not for equpable items)
All in all, this game is really worth your time and money.

Pretty basic at its current state. Graphics are plain, but I don't normally care about graphics in the first place so it doesn't bother me. It is quite funny to see the animation of your employees, it is like they are just hitting their keyboard very hard.
The game is unique for its type. It is a lot better than Dev Tycoon or other related games by far. There's more to do and you aren't limited on what you can do. Expand, hire employees, manage, make servers, connect servers, make Software for your company and many more features. There's a ton of management in this game too, which is great.
Tutorials are buggy and a few systems could use some touching up. It has its bugs, but what Early Access game doesn't?
The main problem I came across was, is the game is too easy. Given 1 hour of my played time was reading through the tutorials and learning how the game works. However, once you get your skills up (Marketing mainly: which doesn't take long) for your employees, money is too easy to receive. Of course that means you can expand further and try to dominate your competitors. I created an OS with just two employees (recommended was 7 team members) and I received over $950,000 in revenue, after that I still gained over hundreds of thousands every month until it finally stopped. I now have over 2 million dollars.
I'm just pointing out that this game should be more challenging or at least more time consuming to get up to that amount of money.
The other portion of the game I don't enjoy is you constantly have to keep fast-forwarding (don't have to but normal speed is super slow if you don't). Perhaps if the game values and progress worked at a different speed you wouldn't need to fast-forward so much.
In due time this game will get better and I can't wait to see the finish product. I'll still play regardless to dominate my competition as the most successful company in the game. I still recommend this game regardless of what I wrote, especially at the price it is at because there is a lot of features in this game, currently. I'll update my review when improvements to the game occur.

This is an amazing game. Nearly infinite replayability. I end up playing a run through of this game almost every week, it's always there looking at me, calling for another victory. I don't know why but whenever I play this game I often end up making something hilarious and fun out of each run no matter how screwed over I am for the final boss. For example this one run I had hacking and non hull damaging small bombs and I used them to target the enemy's oxygen systems and starve them all of oxygen. Even though I was screwed over for the final boss I still had fun. Being able to enjoy the game no matter how bad a run in this game is going is the reason why I like this game so much and why I recommend it. It is something I've rarely found in other games. In a lot of other games, take League of Legends or something as an example, if you're screwed over then the game is never fun, but it is not always so in FTL.

By now you probably already know what FTL is, but just in case, this is a strategic game where you pilot a ship across procedurally generated star systems and deal with random encounters along the way. Your goal is to stay ahead of the advancing rebel army and reach your own army in time to warn them of the coming attack. Along the way you'll need to gain enough power (by upgrading your ship and crew) that you'll be able to successfully defeat the enemy flagship at the end.
There are some hidden secrets and missions that will allow you to unlock a lot of new ships and variants on old ones. Additionally there are a lot of cool mods out there on the interbutts that introduce new equipment and game modes. Check out some videos to see the flow of the gameplay. If they interest you at all then FTL is definitely worth owning.

I got so afraid of this universe right on top, because it really knows how a mistery story should feel in a dynamic, interactive and personal medium as video games are. It has such sensitive aesthetics. The game pulled me so easily towards its mysteriousness, that it took me some time to realize the structure in wich it had been developed (both in level design and narrative terms). As the most impressive strenght of the game, the "unobjectiveness" between crucial moments, surrounded by the level design and sound styles, made it possible for me to develop not only a personal and thoughtfull sense of the story, not only to rise questions about what was presented to me and what would still come up, but, mostly, I didn't felt the sense of urgency, so common in video games. "This game is a narrative experience that does not hold your hand", it says in the beginning. And they mean it, wich is loveble,  When you know what you have to do, right after you've just finished doing something that you, not so long ago, knew that you had to do, there is no space for the player to participate. One can only fulfill the needs that have already been defined by those who created the game. But the freedom from condescending objectivity was what made possible for me to create and appreciate the whole experience.

Short version: The game is great if you like randomness and challenge and don't mind using keyboard input. This game is not so great if you don't have a full keyboard and numpad.
First, let me say that I absolutely LOVE SanctuaryRPG, and it's Black release is just wonderful. The project started out free (as in beer) and has since moved to a paid (Black) version.
The actual navigation of the game is basically non-existent. You have locations that you can choose to enter, but there is no "map" to speak of. The combat is interesting enough, but the real fun is in all of the randomness and volume of options. Everything is a die-roll in the background. Enter a location, die-roll determines the event / baddie. Kill a baddie, die-roll determines the loot. Perform crafting, die-roll determines the actual item. And on, and on, and on.
And all along the way, you're presented with options that change your experience. Agree with this pamphlet you just found? Your alignment just changed slightly. Solved this puzzle? Here's a sidequest that might kills you. Killed a boss? Here's a subtle customization option. I've been playing SRPG for about 3 months now (free then Black), and I've only used one class. There's a HUGE amount of gameplay variation available.
The graphics are actually very well thought out, and there is tongue-in-cheek commentary to be found in the ASCII art. You won't get a chill from seeing moonlight glinting off the water as the breeze blows through shoots of grass, but the graphical approach works well to pull off a consistent aesthetic and feel.
Now here's the caveat: you really should play with a full keyboard plus numpad. The experience is clearly tailored for a left hand on A-S-D-F and a right hand on the numpad. With this setup, the game plays smooth and the design works. If you play with a laptop, though, the fun diminishes somewhat, and if you try a touchscreen keyboard, the fun disappears.

Strangely enough, the closest comparison to SanctuaryRPG in my mind are Disgaea games despite the fact that they look and play completely differently. The reason is that both of them have made traditionally maligned grinding experience in the center of attention, and created a good game out of basically making numbers go up while going through thousands of battles.
It helps that the battles themselves strike a good balance between mindlessly repeating one winning strategy and making the player spend hours on each battle. The battle system is flexible but simple enough to get you in the sort of relaxing concentration state. Sometimes it's not very far removed from slot machines, but here you won't waste your inheritance away.
There are some things that are bothering me (things require too many keystrokes, there are some one-hit KOs remaining, the beginning gets boring after a while, some components of the game seem underutilized and some overutilized) but they're mostly minor and/or personal preference. I've enjoyed the game even if not every untimely death of my character.

Sanctuary is a loot-fiend's wet dream. Weapons, shields, trinkets and more, just about every fight you get that odd looking loot emblem and then the suspense. Will it be an upgrade or just another item to salvage into crafting components? Visiting the town and crafting, pouring ale for your tavern customers, reading something from the library for an XP boost. There are a lot of things to do in this text-based adventure. I haven't beaten the game yet but I keep coming back to it. There are several starting characters and races with the ability to unlock even more. The combat commands are simple (just press a number or a letter) but the complexity of it still baffles me after hours of play. Every few levels they add another layer to the combat with another option. Bottom line - For the price you get a lot of game.

The engine may have aged, but the game itself is great and still puts some more recent attempts in the genre to shame. Think FPS/RPG in a darker, spookier version of L.A.; similar gaming style to Fallout 3, S.T.A.L.K.E.R, Deus Ex: Human Revolution, Red Dead Redemption, etc. Well worth whatever paltry price it is being sold for these days.

Poor design choices mire an otherwise strong core concept to make a game that is "meh". Not terrible, but it just doesn't pop out and make you want to play it.
I've had my friends compare this game to another top down old-hand alien shoot-em-up, Alien Swarm, and let me tell you: My friends are full of♥♥♥♥♥♥ Alien Swarm is the superior game, even if it lacks mission variety.
For one, Alien Swarm lets you move more than two feet from your mate's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. The fact that the camera is centered on the rough center between you and your up to three other very similarly sized and colored companions, and zoomed out so you are all somewhat small anyway, means that you will lose track of who you are and, when you try to dive out of the way of an attack that you thought was going to hit you, the actual you dives into an explosion because you were halfway across the screen from where you thought you were. Even if you can overcome that hurdle and actually function like a proper human being (which, let's be fair, I am not because I tend to err on the side of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥), everybody else in your squad won't: Unless you have friends who you trust, never, not ever, not once, play online. Always assume that you will get gargleblasted by either the enemy or your teammates because someone couldn't shoot the sniper who was off-screen or someonw thought they were someone else and shot their friend with a rocket.
Additionally, in Alien Swarm, your character faces your pointer at all bloody times: Helldivers decided it would be a spectacular idea to throw this out a window, and have your character's direction determined by your movement key inputs. What this means is that, if you are running away from an enemy and want to shoot them, you have to turn around, aim (which slows you down) and then start shooting: By this point the enemy will have caught up, with all his mates, and started turning you into a Super Earth Brand Human Shishkebab, every time. It also means that you will miss-throw grenades consistently, since the crosshair only appears while aiming, and that means more dead teammates. Even if you don't use explosives, your teammates will die anyway because your dumb♥♥♥♥♥thought it would be a good idea to pre-fire while sweeping towards your target with the LMG and someone who wasn't in your line of fire previously wandered into it because they thought they were another guy or because they took one too many confusion bolts to the face. Oh yeah, and that LMG I mentioned? It's a great weapon in my opinion, except for the fact that until you get the last upgrade for it, it immobilizes you while aiming. Yet, you can't upgrade that specific weapon to that specific level until you unlock an arbitrary laser cannon weapon, which I believe is an unlock you get from completing planets: This means you might not see it, or might not be able to get it, for a while if you're unlucky. Unless it's a level up reward, but I haven't gotten enough levels to know, so take this part with a pinch of salt (because I am well salted by now, I can spare you some).
While we're on about upgrades, I like the system: Completing missions works towards conquering planets, and conquering planets gives you rewards, generally an unlock. This means that, with a friend or two who knows what they're doing, you can unlock a freaking mech in your first hour of gameplay, and then spend the rest of your time tearing it up inside of said mech right after you drop it in and crush one of your mates with it because he wasn't paying attention. In addition to the planet unlocks there are also level up rewards, cosmetic armor and main guns, and the weapons do offer some variety until you realize that some suck and others are outright better, even when comparing upgrades. Certainly, they all have some level of viability against certain targets, but... Well, we'll get to that problem later. As for how you upgrade your call-downs and shoot sticks, you wander around the map picking up science bits to unlock research points with every ten. With each upgrade generally only costing 1~2 research points, you can upgrade stuff pretty quickly, which is nice. You can upgrade it even more quickly if you purchase the DLC that gives you a UAV drone that shows you where all the science on the map is, of course, because greed is the path to evil and all developers have proven money is more important than integrity by now. This is balanced somewhat by the fact that most of the DLC weapons and goodies BLOW MASSIVE CHUNKS, but still.
Now, comes on of the main mechanics of the game: The War. The universe is broken up into a lot of quadrants around Super Earth, your home and native land, and these quandrents branch off into three paths towards enemy homeworlds. Three different alien types means three different enemies to fight and familiarize yourself with, from the heavily shielded and psycho-blasting Illuminant to... Well, actually, I haven't fought any other races, because there's on enormous, glaring, huge♥♥♥♥♥problem with The War: Once the community has beaten back the enemy to their home-planet and conquered it, they are no longer a threat until the end of the war. That's right: You kill the enemy off and I can only assume The War is reset when all prospective enemies are dead. At the time of playing the community had whipped the♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off of every other race except for the Illuminant (and the home-planet of the "cyborgs" was avoided by me and my friends, since I was new to the game), who are hear-tearingly frustrating due to their shields, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t one-hit KO snipers (who wouldn't be a problem if you could keep track of who was who in the midst of all the shiny, particle-effect, laser-wall laden chaos) and floating, chair-bound, Halo-Prophet-Rip-Offs with psychic control-reversing powers. Keep in mind that I haven't even FOUGHT on higher difficulty levels because me and my friends wanted to work my level up and get me some experience before I did: The highest mission I did was ten, which was literal hell on earth. You trigger one patrol and start fighting it, and then another three invisible ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s pop up behind you and trigger additional spawns, with seven more invisible ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s showing up to sound more alarms and trigger more spawns until you are awash in a sea of squid aliens and laser walls that block your movement and shots but in no way hamper the enemy. It's "fun" in the same way jamming a hot poker into your eye is "fun": Not at all. There are ways to avoid fighting, which is nice, but they are finnicky at best because the focus of the game isn't on it: Stealth? In my shoot-em-up? You bet your♥♥♥♥♥it feels tacked on and menial.
What I'm saying is, there's a lot to complain about, which outweighs the good by a hefty sum. Certainly, it's fun at times, and I joined at a bad time for variety seeing as I can't fight anything else but the Protoss, but come on. My friends have defended the poor design choices, saying that they are intentional and that this game is supposed to be like Magicka, which these devs also made, where murdering your friends was your top priority and completing the story was a secondary objective.
Horse ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
This is not a game where it is fun to die constantly to your enemies and then your friends. It's a more serious feeling game, driven by success and unlocks: Magicka felt like a joke and that made the death less impactful because you hadn't just wasted a half an hour of everybody's time trying to complete the same bloody mission so you could get an unlock. Also, Magicka didn't penalize you for death really badly: You just start over and do it again. In Helldivers, dying too much docks you an experience bonus, which makes it even more rage inducing when you maybe could have gotten it but a teammate railgunned you in the back at the last moment because they wanted to "save" you from an enemy two feet in front of you while you had a shotgun.
tl;dr buy at your own risk

A very good game in the same vein of Mad Games Tycoon.  It's not yet at MGT's level, but it's definitely got the potential to catch up and surpass it.  There are still some bugs/improvements needed, but it's already incredible.  I can't wait to see what the finished product is like.
Pros:
Managing teams is just complex enough to be fun without being overwhelming.
Being able to grow the building size, rather than moving as in other games allows for more "organic" growth of the business, you can look back and kind of trace your steps, which is pretty neat.
Managing the hours the staff and cleaning crews work is pretty fun, making sure no time is wasted.
Cons:
- At times employees get stuck, and it can be hard to locate them.
- Employees can at times have too much difficulty finding restrooms (and other things effecting happiness.)  I found my buildings requiring far more restrooms than would make sense in the real world.
- The room building leaves something to be desired, new rooms have to be made outside the existing walls, or must be made all the way across a room (rather than making a room from a square quarter of an existing room, you have to make a wall from the north wall all the way to the south wall, instead of north wall to middle of the west wall)
- Not yet much customization with office items, I suspect that is coming though, this is being written just 9 days after the EA release.
Despite the cons, I promise you, this is an amazing game already.  If you're a fan of business sims, definitely pick it up!

This game is good, but those who want a "Software development tycoon" game, look elsewhere.

Ok this is a very weird review for me to make because I don't think this game is bad. In fact I think this game is quite good for the right audiance.
In fact part of me likes the game and its charm. Yet I always feel that games need negative reviews in order to give people a more balanced idea of what it is being offered here.
Basically the best way I could describe the game is: What if you could build a software development factory using automotons that were fueled by coffee? and that has its appeal, it is up to you to make the best possible layout to give you the best possible results in *beep* Insert product #246 here *beep* and building your entire floorplan to make sure that your robots bump into other robots less often.
Now because your workers are robots of course your products are also made robotically. *Beep* Making Videogame #34, inserting GUI, Inserting 3d models... *Beep* basically all software is made out of lego blocks so to speak you just attach different features onto a product and the game tells you how good it "potentially" is and even how "innovative" it is (because robot). You then craft the product by working on it until it is of sufficient quality. They will even hammer it out on a keyboard as if they really were robots (and I am not convinced they arn't)
THIS is what I think the game excels at. If this makes you want to get the game do so now!
But in terms of being a software tycoon it will not satisfy. The products feel like they don't even exist within the game universe and the game has an odd way of spoonfeeding you information that you should infer yourself (How innovative a product is) as well as not telling you upfront what information you would want to know (Who is buying your product). Thus after spending a long time on what might me your magnus opus your overall attitude towards it will probably be "Ok, I guess it was made".
As well because the people are all robots and software is made of legos the whole "I am doing something creative and intellectual" aspect is kind of lost. When a game is just a list of features with "stats" on how "good" and "Innovative" it makes it, it stops feeling like a game.
Don't get the game for the wrong reasons, I hope this helped you get a bit more of an educated idea.
It's like Game Dev Tycoon meets The Sims, and it's deep enough to keep you hooked. You'll start over a few times getting the hang of it, but it strikes a great balance of difficulty and reward.

I'm sure people have said this better than I have in the last however many years this game has been out, but I'll put in my own two cents.
If you're a fan of a little absurdity, this game is awesome. This franchise crossed the line, drew a new one, and crossed that one, too.
Pros:
+Mechs? Aliens? Matrix ripoff? Ships? This has tons of the elements that go into making a great sci-fi game, just without the space opera story to go with it. Because what this game does is it takes that story and then mocks it relentlessly.
+Superpowers. Of all the superhero games I've played (and admittedly, I've played relatively few), this has the best implementation. Which is weird, because the superpowers SHOULD have been a hilarious add-on to the Saint's Row franchise, and yet it felt fluid and intuitive, the way superpowers should feel in a game!
+Story. Seriously, just accept the absurdity of it and you'll have so much more fun.
+Wooooooooo dubstep gun.
Cons:
+Gameplay: can get stale over long hours of play. You can only kill an alien by destroying its genitals so many times in one sitting. But really, that's what happens with basically every game so... yeah.
+"Open" World: it never really felt that open to me. Which may have been the point (it makes sense in-universe) but still, I felt kind of constrained throughout the game.
+Saint's Row Third was better: not really a con, but SRThird was just so good in every single way for me. SRIV tries its best to emulate, but it's clearly an imitator in certain aspects. Your relationship with the other Saints is slightly distant at times, and you don't get the huge gang fights that you did in SRThird.
Honestly, if you were even slightly interested in "GTA on LSD", I'd suggest picking it up. You'll know if this is your type of game before the return period is up!

+Great environment, scenery and music

+Easy to run - very accessible for people with older rigs

+Open-world PvP
-Currently only 2 playable races which have gender locked classes
-Outdated graphics and animations might be offputting for some people
-Traditional fetch, kill and loot quests
-Character customisation is limited
Now, I will be updating this review as I play more of the game but so far I'm liking what I see. The main downside to this game is that you'll have to be an old-school MMORPG player to really appreciate the game (WoW Vanilla, EQ era). I think the game has potential, and the positives mostly outweigh the negatives. Outdated graphics don't bother me and the combat is pretty satisfying and you have plenty of skills to choose from. Questing is typical of an MMO which is something I've gotten used to. Art direction is great and there's some really nice looking areas. Hopefully they'll remove gender locked classes and polish animations and stuff like that in the future.
I wouldn't listen to all the hate the game gets until you try it out for yourself, and you'll most likely enjoy this game if you're a hardcore MMO fan.

This game is truly something new and original. It brings much more to MMORPG genre, then most of the popular MMORPGs since WoW.
This game is not about core classic MMORPG mechanics - such as doing quests, grinding mobs and passing through dungeons. If it's what you like about MMOs - this is not the right game for you.
The most important thing about S3 - is PvP and metagame, connected with it! Grinding mobs? Suddenly demon attacks - and you're dead and lost some of your money to attacker. Trying to make it to teleport - and you're dead again. On a third try carefully, stealthly crawling to teleport through jungle. Demon saw you, but you were quicker - and you're in human city, asking for help against demon. Now you're back in area with some high-lvls helpers. They're killing demon a couple of times, getting all gold back. Then you're on revenge expedition to demon lands.
In this game you don't lvlup for nothing, you lvlup to survive. And when you kill your first demon/human in an honest PVP fight - this is an achievement to charish and remember.
This game - probably unintentionally - offers something, that no other MMO has - awesome metagame with hardcore PvP. This game is not about graphics or doing quests - it's about survival, friendship and rivalry.
Totally recommend to mature hardcore games, who tired of standard wow-clone mmo experience, and wants some new and unique experience.

Even though I haven't finished yet, this game is outstanding by delivering everything I expected from it and a bit more. Like Steam cards :P . In Garry's Mod you can have this grappling hook crossbow which also shoots arrows which seemed a lot of fun if there was a map where it were useful. This game is as if someone played with that and tried to make a proper videogame about it.
The game tries to immerse us in a bedtime story context to which it pays quite attention to detail. When you press the "Exit to Desktop" button, it has the father figure (the narrator and, supposedly, player character) suggesting that maybe it's too late to keep telling the story and we can continue next day. Usually people complaint about child actors, but this game doesn't bother me in any way about it. Plus, there is piggybacking involded. You know... like that level from Metro2033... But piggybacking with an EXOSKELETON!
Some levels require a good framerate to get thorugh properly, but even then, the game is very tolerant on which route or methods one takes to complete the level. So, there's quite a room for mistakes most of the time.
I could critique the fact that sometimes there seems to be terrain collision issues, but quite minor ones. Maybe related to my computer being really slow. When hitting the head  on ceillings, I could glimpse outside of the level and if I forced the character moving through terrain the screen would start shaking as when you press the mouse for powered jumps.
There is also a problem in conveying the Crystal's game mechanic. There are crystals on later levels that grow from walls and ceiling which can be used to refill the number of grapples available in mid-air. Problem is that I would spend a lot of time failling to use them repeatedly until it became frustating. It turns out that you can only use these crystals while the grapples aren't depleted. So they can be clicked when there's one grapple left, but not if your out of grapples.
I'd like to add about something that I found really inspiring in this game which is very interesting to try in future games. There are characters which use a weird writing system. So one of them travels with the player and translates some inscriptions. But when that character leaves, she lets you know (if I recall correctly) that their writting transcribes easily to real world writting, so it is let up to the player to remember how the translations work to be able to read further inscriptions. I'm sorry to tell that I failed this challange as I thought that the writting was fictional and didn't bother to pay attention to when it was being translated. It's unusual for a game developer to trust the player's intelligence so much!

Metro 2033 Redux review
Metro 2033 Redux, is a remake of the original Metro 2033, which came out 6 years ago.  It is a survival horror stealth game with an amazing story and world.
Metro 2033 is a game set in the Metro.  After world war 3 evolves into nuclear warfare and eventually atom bombs being dropped only a few thousand people remain. You take up the role as Artym who after a small section eventually sets out to save his station in the metro from an oncoming threat of The Dark ones.  The Dark ones supposedly have been driving people mad, killing others and are threatening the very existence of his station.  Although the story may seem run of the mill the best part of the game happens to be the dialogue.  The first time I played through it I was rushing through it because the story didn't seem interesting whatsoever.  The second time though I decided to slow down and listen to whats happening around me.  The coolest part of this game happens to be how immersive it feels.  Never has a game got me to just sit there and listen to what two guards have to say to eachother.  Usually in most games they say some dumb dialogue but the writing made me think of them as 2 people not just targets.  Other times they would talk about shortcuts and then when you go look there would be things there as they said so it felt like you were really in a world.  Optional dialogue is what makes this game so impressive so slow down and enjoy the world.
As for the combat well, it's boring and uninteresting unfortunately.  The stealth isn't very good either.  So in some chapters you are trying to get behind enemies which you can either kill or avoid them.  You can also knock out people but it's really cumbersome as you have to walk up press action key and sometimes it doesn't respond.  The funny part is you can literally have people be shooting at you and you can knock them out. There is also no way to lean. Although majority of the time will be stealth sometimes you are forced to fight the beasts that roam the tunnels.  These are the worst parts of the game as you have to fight off hordes of enemies with some crap guns.  The enemies don't seem to go down, sometimes you can shoot them with a shotgun 3 times and they still don't die which can actually get you killed.  So you have to aim your shots at their heads.  Humans also have this issue too if you chose not to stealth pass them.  One of the problems I had with this game is on my first play through I was upgrading weapons but then realized I had wasted so much money as upgraded weapons show up throughout the game dropped by the many enemies.  Another problem is that the weapons have no stats so I have no idea if weapon a is better then weapon b, it doesn't even tell you what ammo they take before you buy/pick it up.  Unfortunately since you have to fight the beasties you are forced into it and I just wish it was more informative.
Metro 2033 Redux is sadly not a very good game but is one of the most immersive games I've played.  As for the horror in the game it's a bit weird.  Throughout the first bit of the game it's moderately scary, but mostly tense as you don't know where the enemies are coming from.  It eventually hits a peak at a really eerie section but after that it really just stops being scary whatsoever.   It just evolves into this game that isn't scary but very tense, always keeping you on the edge.  There are also a few story elements that disappear only to reappear later it just seemed very odd.  The world of Metro 2033 is also very dark and depressing, it doesn't feel like the most inviting place but it's correct to the idea of living underground.
I definitely recommend this game but not as a game more as an immersive experience.  If you want a game with good gameplay there are many others but most of those games will not make you feel like you are in another world.

So I am pretty sure this is my first review ever, that's how good this game is.
Usually I am a fairly passive gamer when it comes to being involved in a community. Don't talk much on forums, don't review and I have never really tried to actively provide input and suggestions to the developers when it comes to early access games. This game changed all of that for me.
First thought on your mind is most likely; "But it is another Early Access game and too many past ones have burned to the ground". You're right, by this point so many people have been ripped off over silly development stalls and a lack of promised content. You have a right to be and if that is a position that you can't be budged from read my review and just wait, keep an eye on the game's development, watch videos, and ask players the questions you want to know about it. The developer, username: Coredumping on steam, is extremely active and responsive on the forum which is where I will start my review I suppose.
I haven't ultimately owned the game long but in about two and a half weeks (maybe less) I have put in over 50 hours XD this game is so addicting. With that said I have already talked with the developer on the forums on multiple occasions addressing bugs I had stumbled into and some small imediate suggestions I had. All of these conversations were wonderful, I felt "heard" (would it be feeling read in text forums? o.O) and I also felt like he seriously cared about what I had to say. He is very open with his project, almost all his current goals and development directions are listed on trello
. This kind of transparency is nice as a player and supporter of his game and another reason for you to support it if this game interests you enough.
Now the game.
Like I said earlier this game is addicting or as my friend said, "This game is f*cking coke!" Be warned though, there is definitely a learning curve to running a successful long term game. I personally like this as it makes the game more rewarding to play but others may not. There is also a decent amount of content for early development, especially compared to other early access games. I would suggest watching a video for most the basic mechanics and game options but I will give you a rough overview. You get a personal character who starts a business. Hire employees, manage their salaries, educated them, and try to make the best selling software. You get to completely build and customize your Office (obviously within the limits of how he codes the construction mechanics). The building mechanics are a bit clunky and can be a trouble at times but there is a way to work around most of it's limitations with some experience at it. I am sure he will improve it as time goes but one thing for example is a second story (no matter how wide the dimensions of it's lower floor) can only have enough "structural support" to hang over one square messurement. Progress in the game feels pretty nice so far. One "day" is a month on the game calender and he has already stated he will have a time bar option to make one "day" be a week on the game calender with four weeks to a month. The game starts in 1980 unless you choose otherwise and as years pass new software and tools become available. Characters and Softwares have various details, traits and skills (characters only). The game is a bit limited on a variety of furniture/tools but stuff like that should be towards the end of alpha developement. I personally have also not come across any game-breaking bugs.
Modding: I am personally not a modder but this game as inspired me to learn a tiny bit to make some mods for this game when it drops. Right now modding is very limited to changing the values of certain mechanics and adding new companies, senarios and software. The future of modding for his game seems very appealing, he plans to have modding accessible in-game and very user-friendly. This is a huge plus in my mind as a supporter of the game because it shows that the developer understands that not only is the content he adds important but player driven content is also extremely important and he has a plan for that already.
If this review has interested you in the game even the slightest more I highly recommend watching a few videos and asking some questions on the forum. For 12 dollars this game is already very impressive and shows massive potential for a final product. Or just wait and watch it :) if I am not mistaken the game will be 12 dollars on release as well.

I've always been a fan of tycoon games, ever since I was little, so when given the opportunity to review Software Inc., I didn't even think twice. And after a "few" hours of playing it, I don't have to think twice before recommending it to any fan of the genre, and even to those that aren't so familiar with it.
Without any further delay, I present to you my review of Software Inc..
Let he who has never thought about developing some sort of software throw the first byte and I shall compute it.
Software Inc. is a game that allows you, the player, to develop your own software, while competing against AI companies that can easily go bankrupt, or simply bought out (I'm looking at you Microsoft!). From choosing your company's name, to the year you wish you start, you'll have a wide range of options to customise your character, and surely even more in the future. You won't be able to start a gigantic company from the get-go, so you'll have to work hard and complete some side contracts while developing your company's first software. And after developing that first piece, you'll just find out that the critics tagged it as crapware.
Once you get the hang of it, you'll find out it's incredibly fun to develop your IPs, whether you choose to develop an AntiVirus IP, a Games IP, or even an Operating System IP, and just when you're about to release that latest piece of technology, your thoughts will be: "Ok, just one more and I'll go to bed." Trust me, it won't be just one more.
Sure, the game isn't perfect. Even simple changes could make the game more enjoyable. But that's why it's Early Access, and that's why the developers are so active around the forums. Software Inc. is a true gem.
Considering it's an Early Access (EA) game, I've decided to add a "Neutral" category, for details I consider important, but not gamebreakers, and could easily improve the gameplay if attended.
Considering most of the "Cons" I had in mind were already mentioned by the developers as something they're planning to fix, this list will be somewhat short, and I'm sure it will be even shorter after a while. I will, however, still list some that I feel are in bad shape, despite being mentioned by the developers.
I'd give it a
, which could easily increase to a 9, and even a 10, with further updates and some more balancing. I've no doubt that, if attended to, it will be one of the best, if not the best, of the genre.

I'm sure people have said this better than I have in the last however many years this game has been out, but I'll put in my own two cents.
If you're a fan of a little absurdity, this game is awesome. This franchise crossed the line, drew a new one, and crossed that one, too.
Pros:
+Mechs? Aliens? Matrix ripoff? Ships? This has tons of the elements that go into making a great sci-fi game, just without the space opera story to go with it. Because what this game does is it takes that story and then mocks it relentlessly.
+Superpowers. Of all the superhero games I've played (and admittedly, I've played relatively few), this has the best implementation. Which is weird, because the superpowers SHOULD have been a hilarious add-on to the Saint's Row franchise, and yet it felt fluid and intuitive, the way superpowers should feel in a game!
+Story. Seriously, just accept the absurdity of it and you'll have so much more fun.
+Wooooooooo dubstep gun.
Cons:
+Gameplay: can get stale over long hours of play. You can only kill an alien by destroying its genitals so many times in one sitting. But really, that's what happens with basically every game so... yeah.
+"Open" World: it never really felt that open to me. Which may have been the point (it makes sense in-universe) but still, I felt kind of constrained throughout the game.
+Saint's Row Third was better: not really a con, but SRThird was just so good in every single way for me. SRIV tries its best to emulate, but it's clearly an imitator in certain aspects. Your relationship with the other Saints is slightly distant at times, and you don't get the huge gang fights that you did in SRThird.
Honestly, if you were even slightly interested in "GTA on LSD", I'd suggest picking it up. You'll know if this is your type of game before the return period is up!

is an absolutely rock-solid action RPG with a ton of play depth, multiple playable characters, and difficulty levels that make meaningful changes to the gameplay (rather than just modifying damage dealt and received). Even absolute neophytes will be able to clear the game on Very Easy, but every time you go up a level, you have to learn new attack patterns and new ways of dealing with them. The only drawback to the difficulty levels is on the Nightmare difficulty, which pulls the nasty trick of nerfing the XP and SP given by mobs, and turns the game into a long, dull grind.
The game opens with two playable characters, and there's a third to be unlocked later. There is also an "extra" version of each of the characters with slightly different abilities, an alternate outfit for Yunica, and an unlockable "arena" mode that pits you against waves of mobs, complete with online cheaterboards if you're curious who can tweak Cheat Engine the most effectively. That's quite a lot of content!
Plot-wise, the game is set in the ancient history of Ys, long before the original
This means that
is the only Ys game not to feature Adol Christin as the main character (he can be unlocked as a bonus character in the arena, but not in story mode). Instead of Adol, the main characters are important members of the priesthood of Ys, as they seek to contain the spread of demonic energy that's destroying their world. If you're familiar with Ys (particularly the original two games, available on Steam as
) there will be lots of material here you'll recognize, but the game is perfectly playable without any Ys background at all.
It's hard to go wrong with
if you like action JRPGs. There's a lot of play here, and it's a good introduction to the elder statesman of the genre.

If you still confused with some plot and background story of
even after finish playing both.

Short Answer: This game is a high speed and precision dance between you and each and every boss, with a soundtrack to match.
Long Answer:
This game uses speed and precision in one heck of a balancing match. On one hand, the characters and fights never last more than a couple of moments.
On the other hand, (on the higher difficulties) if you mess up at any point, it's back to the save point.
On the other hand, (on the lower difficulties) every fight feels like a race to the finish, only barely sqeuaking through errors.
Only on the highest difficulty did I feel the NEED to grind, and... being completely honest here... the highest difficulty is definitely something I'm only doing for the achievements. Normal mode is enough.
Special note to the devs here though. I bought this game because of the demo. Not only did that demo get me to buy this game, but through this game, I've become a fan of pretty much all of your works that I've found.
I just wanted to say thank you for the demo that got me into a phenomenal series, and a phenominal developer.

Ys Origin takes it's stand as a prequel to the following games before it: being Ys I, II, etc. I've never enjoyed such a vibrant set of characters before; each with their own unraveling stories AND abilities. Mastering the mechanics is some sort of joyous experience that only proves itself further when you go into boss fights. You'll be frustrated and tired of dying, but with those tight controls, well thought out music compositions, and charming graphics, you'll always come back for more.

Even though I haven't finished yet, this game is outstanding by delivering everything I expected from it and a bit more. Like Steam cards :P . In Garry's Mod you can have this grappling hook crossbow which also shoots arrows which seemed a lot of fun if there was a map where it were useful. This game is as if someone played with that and tried to make a proper videogame about it.
The game tries to immerse us in a bedtime story context to which it pays quite attention to detail. When you press the "Exit to Desktop" button, it has the father figure (the narrator and, supposedly, player character) suggesting that maybe it's too late to keep telling the story and we can continue next day. Usually people complaint about child actors, but this game doesn't bother me in any way about it. Plus, there is piggybacking involded. You know... like that level from Metro2033... But piggybacking with an EXOSKELETON!
Some levels require a good framerate to get thorugh properly, but even then, the game is very tolerant on which route or methods one takes to complete the level. So, there's quite a room for mistakes most of the time.
I could critique the fact that sometimes there seems to be terrain collision issues, but quite minor ones. Maybe related to my computer being really slow. When hitting the head  on ceillings, I could glimpse outside of the level and if I forced the character moving through terrain the screen would start shaking as when you press the mouse for powered jumps.
There is also a problem in conveying the Crystal's game mechanic. There are crystals on later levels that grow from walls and ceiling which can be used to refill the number of grapples available in mid-air. Problem is that I would spend a lot of time failling to use them repeatedly until it became frustating. It turns out that you can only use these crystals while the grapples aren't depleted. So they can be clicked when there's one grapple left, but not if your out of grapples.
I'd like to add about something that I found really inspiring in this game which is very interesting to try in future games. There are characters which use a weird writing system. So one of them travels with the player and translates some inscriptions. But when that character leaves, she lets you know (if I recall correctly) that their writting transcribes easily to real world writting, so it is let up to the player to remember how the translations work to be able to read further inscriptions. I'm sorry to tell that I failed this challange as I thought that the writting was fictional and didn't bother to pay attention to when it was being translated. It's unusual for a game developer to trust the player's intelligence so much!

I was unsure about this game. I've never really played any ascii type games, except when I was too young to remember them, but I thought I'd give this one a go based on all the positive things people have said about this game, and I am 100% glad that I did!
First of all, there is so much to do, so many little quests, bounties and even the management of the tavern if you play your cards right. All of the random encounters, hilarious and often nonsensical slices of humour thrown in here and there really make this game feel so much fun. You'll find dialogue such as "A potato has decided to follow you around." to something terrifying funny like "The worm defecates in your ear."
The ascii art work is very polished and looks as though it has had a lot of love put into it. It's charming and simple.
The gameplay, from character creation to the immense replayability and even the combat system, reminds me of one of my favourite games of all time: Tales of Maj Eyal, it has that similar feel of even if you lose, you just want to start over and try again immediately, which is an essential element to the rogue-like genre. Starting over in this game doesn't feel like a chore, because it's different each time and every character you play. There is so much loot which really is part of the glue that holds everything together, making every run through a unique and challenging experience.
The combat system is very intuitive and unique. There are a whole bunch of different skills and combos which makes the combat a real edge of your seat sort of affair, but if you play your cards right, and you take your time and are meticulous with your decisions, it will leave you feeling incredibly satisfied after a challenging fight.
Overall, I have yet to discover anything negative about this game, I love every feature and every bit of text is a delight to read. For an ascii game, it is more engaging than a lot of the games in my library, I recommend it 100%!
Also, do not be fooled by the early access sticker, because this game is very polished and clearly a very loved project by the incredibly talented developers. My hat's off to you guys!

Metro 2033 Redux review
Metro 2033 Redux, is a remake of the original Metro 2033, which came out 6 years ago.  It is a survival horror stealth game with an amazing story and world.
Metro 2033 is a game set in the Metro.  After world war 3 evolves into nuclear warfare and eventually atom bombs being dropped only a few thousand people remain. You take up the role as Artym who after a small section eventually sets out to save his station in the metro from an oncoming threat of The Dark ones.  The Dark ones supposedly have been driving people mad, killing others and are threatening the very existence of his station.  Although the story may seem run of the mill the best part of the game happens to be the dialogue.  The first time I played through it I was rushing through it because the story didn't seem interesting whatsoever.  The second time though I decided to slow down and listen to whats happening around me.  The coolest part of this game happens to be how immersive it feels.  Never has a game got me to just sit there and listen to what two guards have to say to eachother.  Usually in most games they say some dumb dialogue but the writing made me think of them as 2 people not just targets.  Other times they would talk about shortcuts and then when you go look there would be things there as they said so it felt like you were really in a world.  Optional dialogue is what makes this game so impressive so slow down and enjoy the world.
As for the combat well, it's boring and uninteresting unfortunately.  The stealth isn't very good either.  So in some chapters you are trying to get behind enemies which you can either kill or avoid them.  You can also knock out people but it's really cumbersome as you have to walk up press action key and sometimes it doesn't respond.  The funny part is you can literally have people be shooting at you and you can knock them out. There is also no way to lean. Although majority of the time will be stealth sometimes you are forced to fight the beasts that roam the tunnels.  These are the worst parts of the game as you have to fight off hordes of enemies with some crap guns.  The enemies don't seem to go down, sometimes you can shoot them with a shotgun 3 times and they still don't die which can actually get you killed.  So you have to aim your shots at their heads.  Humans also have this issue too if you chose not to stealth pass them.  One of the problems I had with this game is on my first play through I was upgrading weapons but then realized I had wasted so much money as upgraded weapons show up throughout the game dropped by the many enemies.  Another problem is that the weapons have no stats so I have no idea if weapon a is better then weapon b, it doesn't even tell you what ammo they take before you buy/pick it up.  Unfortunately since you have to fight the beasties you are forced into it and I just wish it was more informative.
Metro 2033 Redux is sadly not a very good game but is one of the most immersive games I've played.  As for the horror in the game it's a bit weird.  Throughout the first bit of the game it's moderately scary, but mostly tense as you don't know where the enemies are coming from.  It eventually hits a peak at a really eerie section but after that it really just stops being scary whatsoever.   It just evolves into this game that isn't scary but very tense, always keeping you on the edge.  There are also a few story elements that disappear only to reappear later it just seemed very odd.  The world of Metro 2033 is also very dark and depressing, it doesn't feel like the most inviting place but it's correct to the idea of living underground.
I definitely recommend this game but not as a game more as an immersive experience.  If you want a game with good gameplay there are many others but most of those games will not make you feel like you are in another world.

I played and beat the first game of The Room so this review is mostly going to be centeralized around the improvements and differences between the two games and the specific pros and cons of this game on its own merit.
I deeply enjoyed the first The Room game. It was very exciting, it roused my curiousity, it was charming to flip little switches and twist little cogs. The premise of the game was to open a vault which contained a box with many secrets within. Each level focused with one "box" and one box only. Everything revolved around that one box and everything was related to the opening of that one box. Now while in some levels this could be considered kind of true in The Room Two. The game steps back and creates and enviroment and various "puzzle stations" for you to explore.
To some degree, it's pretty refreshing and fascinating. You have these gorgeous rooms to explore, each with its own distinct theme and little gimmicks. While on the other side of the spectrum, I felt like it lost some of the charm in-which I found the original The Room to be so bewitching, that I just had to solve every new puzzle.
To start, sometimes I felt like the levels were a little too long, because it felt like 2-3 levels in one level. With constant switching between tables and finishing puzzles on various tables, it felt a little lackluster in reward and slightly exhaustive. Along with that sensation comes the notion that you may not actually be fully done with a station.
See. Because you can constantly revisit tables, you don't always essentially believe you are done with it because not only is this a game that hides little knobs on objects, it's also a game that does, in fact ask you to revisit a table just to find one more piece even though you are relatively confident you have reached completion with a station.
So because of that, I started to feel like there was a little too much switching between "Stations" in the levels regarding puzzles and it kind of killed my buzz of curiosity. Because in The Room One, there was all these little switches and levers exclusive to one box and it was very fun and interesting and satisfying. Whereas this one felt more like pulling a bunch of big levers around the room and when the game wanted you to home in on something and find a tiny switch it could get very confusing because you are not fully acquainted and knowledgeable about the box or station like you are in The Box One. Where you knew everything that's happening and hasn't happened on the box. Where your eyes could pry over the box in glee looking for any out of place section that could unlock more secrets.
This game presents very detailed areas which could hide a lot too quickly and there was too much. It was easy to get lost and it was tiresome to find direction when there's so many areas to explore for miniscule details that I would have to meticulously pick through just to find it. I ended up having to rely on the hints a little too much and I didn't quite like that very much.
However there is some new factors brought to The Room Two which I thought were nice. The levels, along with being distinctive. Felt adventurous. I felt like I was taking on the role of an adventurer. Journeying deeping into the rooms that await ahead. Along with many relics and excerpts and signs of progression made along your path. There was some kind of thrill you'd get from exploring the various stations to proceed ahead in these spacey rooms.
Along with the new rooms, comes along with something less precedent in The Room One. Horror! Ohhhh boy does this one have a lot more horror! It's not the type of horror where monsters pop out of you. It's more like the sense of dread of something will happen at any moment. This game keeps up a solid theme of horror throughout which I kind of admire as the The Room took on a new tone from the amiable nature of The Room One since you venture into a place of menace and supernatural. However you should prepare for a few creepy things to suddenly happen, fair warning.
All in all, I personally prefer The Room One, though I don't think my distaste for this game necessiates a dislike, I rather think that it just wasn't my cup of tea in the end. I think that the issue with the "look for a tiny button" spread across 3-5 different work stations is something that should be panned out and is something worth nothing. But in total, this game is pretty good and enjoyable and I think people who enjoy a bit of adventure and exploration in their puzzle games may enjoy this game. This one's more cinematic than the first one, and that's quite alright.
As for final notes, I think the game's lighting is a bit too dark and it can be quite hard to see things you're working on/with. I'd advise to turn up the brightness in the game a bit.
And I wish there was more lore behind each room you enter. Aside from notes from your companion who's lost in the rooms, from what I see there isn't a tie between rooms in letters you find. It'd be nice if you could distinctly read books and journals to find more lore in places the notes and letters you find take place in.
Anywho, thank you for reading my review, I hope it helped you in making an informed decision on whether you wish to purchase this product or not. I recieved this product as a gift from a friend since I was a fan of The Room One. Thank you, and have a good day.

Super interesting game, still in development and it needs a lot of work, but the developer has a very good sense of design and the mechanics are already very deep. Game has huge potential already, and the dev is extremely responsive to bug-reports and feature suggestions.
You can:
- Take software contracts for quick cash but with steep penalties for failure.
- Run your business into the ground and lose the game.
- Take out loans to stay afloat.
- Start your own software projects, choose from a number of different types (games, game engines, OS, tools, anti-virus, etc), choose the OS(s) to build it for, choose the tools you use to make it.
- Release your product in an unfinished, broken state, but hype it to hell and make a bunch of money anyways.
- Market your software to increase awareness and marketshare
- Interview employees at a cost, choose one with the skills you need and a personality that plays
well with your other employees.
- Educate your employees on the various skills (there are a ton) and make them better.
- Negotiate wages and lowball your best employees, it's so realistic!
- Make it Open Source if you hate money (or want to handicap your competitors)
- Make it In-House to keep it all to yourself
- Build an office and keep it clean and working. Make sure it's quiet, clean and comfortable to keep coders happy.
- Buy servers to run your network based programs, and keep your Source Control repos on to keep your projects safe.
- Trade in the stock market
- Curse when your employees call in sick on the last day before the work is due.
- Choose your distribution channel, or start your own if you've got the infrastructure. Charge money for mods and start a firestorm. (not really, that's crazy)
- Tons more
There are a couple negatives atm, like blah graphics and animations, a couple bugs and weird behaviors, not very many options for purchasing furniture or decoration right now, and game pace that's just slightly out of whack. But the dev is hard at work and is constantly listening to the player-base on things that need to change or improve, and I really expect that most of these issues will be resolved before long. Definitely worth a try, I do this all day at work and still want to play this game when I'm home, for some reason.

2. RPG aspects and DLC.  There are magical items and other skills for you to upgrade your units, and the DLC has legendary and supernatural units.  I don't mind this, it adds a bit of spice to the game, but some of the historical wargame enthusiast reviewers don't like this aspect as much.
Cons:
1. Campaign is not great.  You basically just unlock a series of maps, eventually seizing Bagdad as Richard Lionheart, and then reverse the process as Saladin.  There are some decisions to make along the way, but they still don't add up to what I would call a 'dynamic' campaign.
2. DLC units do not appear in multiplayer.  If not for the multiplayer, the game would be a throwaway once you complete the campaigns.  Unfortunately the DLC units are annoyingly absent from the custom and multiplayer battle roster - a pity.
3. BUGS.  There is a runtime error that has been widely reported, and supposedly this will not be fixed for Win7 64-bit systems.  I played through the whole crusader campaign only to not be able to complete the last battle.  Very disappointing indeed.
4. Can't save battles.  The battles, being on very large maps, also take a long time (over 30 minutes of real time).  They can't be saved mid-battle.  That is all.
I cannot recommend this to a casual player, but if you really like historical RTS and want a different perspective and style than the Total War series, then you might find this title interesting.

Cons:
- Relic doesn't care
- Vanilla unmodded CoH 2 is ultra arcadey and silly, think Dawn of War 2, but with germans and russians
- Has a winter mechanic which was a big sell, but which actually doesn't matter because the AI doesn't even care

- Plagued with various bugs, both big and small that Relic knows about and ignore

- Relic doesn't care
- Has a campaign that's pretty much half finished and filled with fillter skirmish missions

- AI is mentally challenged, gets bonus resources, can see all your units (even hidden units) and often breaks completely
- Relic. does. not. care.
- Progression system that the game once had, was replaced ages ago with a 100% RNG system called "War Spoils", in which everyone - including the losers, and people who didn't even do anything - randomly get awarded random items, ranging from skins, to faceplates (lol), to commanders, victory strikes and bulletins of all kinds (what this actually means is that you will have 800 duplicate common "+3% faster IR light turret rotation" bulletins and tons of duplicate commanders), it doesn't matter if you are good or not, pray to RNJesus that you ever get anything good out of it.

- Relic deliberately holding mod tools back and releasing them one by one instead of in a bundle like in the past, in order to milk as much money out of the game as possible with DLC
- Oh also, METRIC S-TON of DLC, they even have an ingame store where you can buy individual commanders and skins and faceplates, jesus christ!!
- Relic talks big about "caring about the community", and "listening to feedback", etc, but not once have they actually really listened to us about things that matter. They don't acknowledge us, they don't respond to anything on their own forums, they don't tell us about their own community events for their own game even, or listen to the overwhelmingly bad feedback about things like War Spoils, etc.
They literally DO NOT CARE anymore and are seriously only out to milk the game as much as possible.
So what IS the verdict on this game??
Like, buy it by all means, but for the love of god do it on SALE (except for Ardennes Assault).
The mods can and WILL defenitely carry the game for you if you have some friends to play with and tolerate the asinine AI, it CAN be fun, but don't expect god knows what kind of amazing product or experience here and be prepared for disapointment and broken dreams.
Maybe one day, when Relic finally decides that they are done trying to squeeze money out of us and breaking the game even more, we'll get the full mod tools and then the healing can begin.

The Force Awakens offers what you would expect from any other LEGO game - it's short, easy but enjoyable experience for all ages. The plot follows the newest Star Wars movie almost 1:1, you will visit all locations from the movie plus 3-4 extras (battle of Endor from Return of the Jedi is a game prologue plus there are 3 unlockable short missions). The animation is on a good level, there's usual great sense of humour and lots of easter eggs to find, game can be enjoyed by you as well as your kid, you can play solo or in coop - so far so good.
But let's now go to weaker points.
Voice Acting - it's obvious that devs will not hire the whole cast of hollywood blockbuster as voice actors, it's common practice for video game characters to be voiced by different actors, but here some choices are weird at least. For example Rei, who is a teenager, sounds like an old lady, not even close to original character. For anyone who's seen the movies quite a few voice actors will make you feel strange.
Port - the game is ported poorly and you will encounter many port-specific bugs. For example it launches by default in 720p. Each time you alt-tab game will return to 720p and you got to go back through options menu (no mouse support in options so a lot of clicking) to change it back. Also if you decide to invert flight controls, each res change will reset this change. If you decide to play in windowed mode your window will always be 720p, you cannot make window of any other size etc. None of these bugs is gamebreaking, but they all add up to lessen the fun you have from the game.
Boring replayability and lots of grind - game itself is 7-8 hours long, but it unlocks you only 20-25% of collectibles. Here lies game replayability - replaying missions with different characters you can use their different skills to unlock more and more of new stuff. Sounds amazing, but sadly in fact it gets very boring very fast. How it works in practice is that you choose a new characters for free play, launch mission, mission pays the same every single time and just in few spots you use new characters to do some stuff which you were unable previously. Then you pick another characters once again and do the same. Rinse and repeat. You play the same easy content 95% of time, spend 30mins on a mission just for 2 mins of new content, then you do the same thing again with another character. Another problem is that some unlockables are placed in autoscroller parts of mission giving you basically like 0.3-0.5 sec to get them. So you play a mission for 30min, fail to get unlock, so you have to restart the mission over and over again (30min each time) hoping this time you will not screw up this 0.5 sec section. Not only boring but frustrating as well.
AI - tends to bug quite a lot - have seen my AI companions commit suicide a lot, and each death costs you score, so if you target score attacks I strongly advise playing coop only.
Price - it is basically the most expensive LEGO game so far. LEGO games are expensive in themselves - ~20$ fow 6-8h game. But here we not only get 30$ base price, Deluxe Edition 10$ more but even Season Pass. In total it's a 50$ for a game that lasts for 7-8h of first playthrough and only very few people will be willing to stick with it to unlock all. Many people may consider 30-50$ a lot for such a short game.
OK, We've complained a little, so now to good things :>
Like I said - story is awesome, full of great humour that will make both adults and kids laugh. It also stays true to original material and is complete, which is good considered some LEGO games had problems with it in the past (looking at you Hobbit!).
Gameplay is quite fresh compared to other LEGO games.You can divide it into 3 elements - one is usual LEGO gameplay - easy adventure game with very basic 2-keys combat and puzzles which most of the time ends up with "automatically build something with lego bricks" - nothing new here. Second part is cover-shooting sections - and it's the weakest part of the game I must say. It's very boring, offers you next to none freedom and feels just like a waste of time. Still it's something fresh in LEGO games. But then there's flying sections - and boy are they good! I wouldn't mind if whole game consisted just of them. They are very fun, offers a lot more than simple ground combat (U-Turns, barrel rolls, normal shooting, torpedos, flying away from homing missiles, big variety of combat areas and enemies and so on and on). It's easilly the best part of the game, which is good, because I can forgive weak shooting in Star Wars game, I can even forgive very weak lightsaber fights (luckilly there are only 2 of those), but good space combat is a must!
All in all the game is quite good, offers some replayability (well a lot of replayability but mostly boring one), but suffers the same problems as other LEGO games. If you are LEGO games fan, SW fan or looking for a game you and your kid can play together both having great fun - this one will be a good choice, but not for a full price. Wait for a sale.

A true throwback to the era of text-based roguelike games, this title should satiate any need you have for text-based dungeon crawling and monster murder.
*** I used a stemkey provided by the developer for review purpose ***
Gameplay: 7/10
You start off creating your character from a base class, begin ASCII customization of your appearance and information, watch the intro and you're off to scour the murky depths of a textual fantasy world. Why'd you milk that ghost? Why are you completely naked?! If you've ever played a text-based roguelike you'll be familiar with how the game executes and if not, be prepared for an immensely thorough and funny gaming experience.
Graphics: 6/10
You wouldn't think graphics in a text-based game could be much but... The ASCII art in this game is incredible for what it's medium is. Even the animation is awesome. The ability to accurately convey the art of the genre and actually be enthralling and interesting is amazing.
Sound: 10/10
Easily my favorite part about this game is the chiptune soundtrack. The music is plentiful and mixed. The sound effects are perfectly adapted and timed. There are so many rich and warm tunes it immerses you right into the game like you wouldn't believe. I hope they release the soundtrack for this game on Steam too.
Overall: 7/10

Probably not the best review, this would be my first game of this kind, text based/ascii art game. But for what it is, I think it does well. The ASCII art is actually rather endearing and as you put more time into it, you'll begin to look forward to getting a certain item popup, or dreading meeting a really powerful enemy as your character's life is on the line every time.
The music matches the style, "retro" but in all the best ways. There were very few songs I disliked.
The humor can be hit or miss but there's a lot of little references to popular media that I think many will appreciate.
Combat while it has a simple interface, can become rather interesting as you level. You MUST pay attention to on screen cues or you will get punished in the worst way. It isn't a game that you can just idle the same buttons, at least until you are sufficiently strong.
The first area won't be that exciting, but if you make it to the second area, you'll meet a lot more npcs which will also help you level, unlock more powerful abilities, and so on. It can actually become a bit too much if you try and manage your time between adventuring, going on npc fetch quests, messing around in the colosseum, making armor, serving drinks, etc.
Warning though, if you are a "fair player", stay away from using auto combat. Certain combinations of negative statuses on your character can confuse your CPU self making it make bad decisions (continously trying to heal or reposition when it cannot instead of breaking free from a snare) which leads to your character's demise. This may be adjusted in the future as this is an early access game, but at time of writing, this warning is accurate.

Although this game could be played seperatly, it does continue the story started in The Room, so for the full experience, I suggest you play that first.
As with the first game, this game is rather short, one could finish playing it in roughly 3 hours, depending on your puzzle-solving skills. Hints are included, but can be disabled from the options menu for an extra challenge. For the price it is currently selling at, I strongly suggest you buy both The Room and The Room Two. Even at full price, I would personally say this game is still a good deal, although the decision is up to you whether you think 3-ish hours of puzzle is worth it.

Super interesting game, still in development and it needs a lot of work, but the developer has a very good sense of design and the mechanics are already very deep. Game has huge potential already, and the dev is extremely responsive to bug-reports and feature suggestions.
You can:
- Take software contracts for quick cash but with steep penalties for failure.
- Run your business into the ground and lose the game.
- Take out loans to stay afloat.
- Start your own software projects, choose from a number of different types (games, game engines, OS, tools, anti-virus, etc), choose the OS(s) to build it for, choose the tools you use to make it.
- Release your product in an unfinished, broken state, but hype it to hell and make a bunch of money anyways.
- Market your software to increase awareness and marketshare
- Interview employees at a cost, choose one with the skills you need and a personality that plays
well with your other employees.
- Educate your employees on the various skills (there are a ton) and make them better.
- Negotiate wages and lowball your best employees, it's so realistic!
- Make it Open Source if you hate money (or want to handicap your competitors)
- Make it In-House to keep it all to yourself
- Build an office and keep it clean and working. Make sure it's quiet, clean and comfortable to keep coders happy.
- Buy servers to run your network based programs, and keep your Source Control repos on to keep your projects safe.
- Trade in the stock market
- Curse when your employees call in sick on the last day before the work is due.
- Choose your distribution channel, or start your own if you've got the infrastructure. Charge money for mods and start a firestorm. (not really, that's crazy)
- Tons more
There are a couple negatives atm, like blah graphics and animations, a couple bugs and weird behaviors, not very many options for purchasing furniture or decoration right now, and game pace that's just slightly out of whack. But the dev is hard at work and is constantly listening to the player-base on things that need to change or improve, and I really expect that most of these issues will be resolved before long. Definitely worth a try, I do this all day at work and still want to play this game when I'm home, for some reason.
