is built on what is possibly the best ARPG engine out there, featuring fast and tense combat with responsive controls that requires a little strategic thinking.  On top of that, the graphics manage to be impressively beautiful while retaining excellent system performance.  The plot's pretty good, too - about as straightforward as you'd expect in a game like this, but I think the character development carries it, and the fact that there are three slightly different versions of it (one of which is unlocked by clearing the game once, has you initially fighting
the other protagonists, and includes additional plot revelations) improves replayability.
I do feel, though, like Falcom made a mistake with the difficulty levels and achievements - many mistakes, actually.  For starters, SP (points for buying ability upgrades) gain rates are tied to difficulty level, and some upgrades are so exorbitantly expensive that getting the related achievements is only feasible by playing through and farming on the lowest difficulty level, which is so easy as to be boring.  That's not the really crazy part, though.  The crazy part is the extra outfit for one of the characters - let me say that again: it's just an alternate sprite, and an achievement to go with it - that requires beating the game at least 6 times, including 3 on nightmare difficulty, plus spending a lot of time in Arena Mode.  Even if you just want to fight the unlockable optional boss, which I kinda do, you'll still have to do the 3 Nightmare runs and the grinding in Arena Mode.  Now, I do have to give Falcom credit for making the higher difficulty levels challenging in ways that are a little more creative than damage dealt/taken adjustments.  I already mentioned the SP gain rates (I think EXP is also affected to a lesser degree), and your special abilities have longer cooldowns, but the most noticeable difference is in the enemy AI: on higher difficulty levels, enemies will attack more frequently and aggressively, with bosses in particular saturating their lairs with hazards to your health, making the game not just more difficult, but also more exciting.  Unfortunately, though, your chances of surviving still come down to experience level.  A single level gain makes the difference between a boss fight you have absolutely no hope of winning and a boss fight you can probably clear with your character just barely still breathing if you practice a few times.  Upgrades, of course, help too.  And, remember, farming is slower on higher difficulties.  What this means is that a Nightmare playthrough is basically a long, tedious grindfest punctuated by occasional intense boss battles.  It doesn't help that all the dialogue, which ordinarily I'd appreciate, is all unskippable, and there's sometimes a lot of it immediately before a boss.  I had been planning on getting as close to 100% completion as I reasonably could (Caress of Steel?  Ha, ha, NO.), but having beating the game once with each of the three characters, including one Nightmare run, and cleared all but the last arena stage multiple times, it's gotten too repetitive, and I'm kinda sick of it now.  Uninstalling for my own sanity.

Game Title: Helldivers - 35 hours
Review Date: 12/20/15
I felt like playing a simple slaughterhouse with friends that might provide some laughs and awesome last stands. This game didn't disappoint in that aspect.
I never really liked the idea of shared camera's in games, seems like a significant step backwards in gaming to me, personally, but I figured I'd give it a try anyways.
After about 20 hours of gameplay, I had fun doing missions, unlocking new gear, hearing my character talk about liber-tea while slaughtering aliens because... reasons.
Sadly, for a game that has 2-3 "expansions" or content updates... whichever they call them... It's really lacking in content that keeps you playing. I've honestly lost reason to continue playing other than helping others with random missions for the sake of it simply because I've obtained everything I'm interested in or that I need in the short time I played it.
I honestly had to go to wikipedia to even find out what the actual background story of the game was. Disappointingly, there really isn't much of one to be found.
If the 8 lines of text the entire plot of the game is written on is a bit long for you, TL;DR: Hyper democracy, brainwashed Earth fighting aliens because they need to be fought because reasons...
Good plot by the broadest stroke possible, I suppose... Can't say it helps the game at all. Maybe Helldivers 2 will explain more.
Combat in concept works perfect and is going to be typical of any top-down shooter. Simple point, aim, slaughter gameplay mixed in with having to keep in mind factors like friendly fire and resource drop pods potentially crushing you or your friends is a fun concept.
However, the execution of these concepts are held back by things like shared camera view between FOUR other players... This is 2015, it's the internet, this is a EXTREMELY impractical idea.
Between the randomly generated terrain and objectives in missions the game offers varied enough maps to give you a unique experience in every mission you attempt.
That said, there is a bit of a let down in the enemy AI that you spend the entirety of it fighting. The game offers twelves levels of difficulty for missions, but after about level six or seven you've already seen everything there is to see. It's nothing exactly game killing but in a game where you literally repeat mission after mission fighting the exact same aliens it will get old fast.
There's a variety of gear to unlock depending on your play style. Sometimes you just can't find a use for stun mines compared to normal mines... Regardless, there's enough unlockable content to keep interest for several hours if nothing else.
This is a shining example of graphics not being the sole thing that determines your game as a big hit or financial flop.
Graphics are second to gameplay, always, no excuse, ever. It's a game, not a painting. We all love pushing our computers but if its gameplay suffers because of wasted effort on things like 4K textures or other non-sense then you clearly aren't trying to make a game.
Graphics range from textures to models, general environment, shading, color palettes, etc. This game was never intended to be big on graphics and they clearly didn't waste time trying to pander to people that complain about them. That said, the graphics *ARE NOT BAD*.
Models are interesting and unique, textures fit the world, gear, monsters and player characters perfectly. The environments you fight in are unique and offer different ways to play while looking beautiful and lush or dark and intimidating.
I love the sounds in this game. The weapons sound as powerful as they are, airstrikes, bombs and nukes are threatening, explosions make you want to clear out and the aliens all have unique sound effects to make them stand out.
Also, who doesn't want a nice cup of democratic liber-tea?
This is obviously the biggest disappointment for a game like this. When your game relies on repeating the same/same-ish content literally every 10-20 minutes and you don't provide enough variety in things to do different then you end up getting bored relatively quickly.
I can't say the game isn't worth its pricetag because of this but if I went strictly on the guidelines of 1$ = 1 hour of entertainment then between my purchase of the game and 3 DLC totaling to 30$ USD... I had to actually force myself to play to get that value out of it simply because I got bored so quick.
If you intend to buy this game as something to spend hours on like you would in something like the witcher, mass effect, gta V, etc, then you'll probably be disappointed. Fair warning.
Overall, this game honestly feels like a time killer phone app such as angry birds or other games of that sort. It doesn't make it bad, but at the end of the day it is just a time killer.

I really, really, really wish I could recommend this game.  Actually, I kinda do (see the bottom for my update after managing to finish the game).
Let me start by saying that, if all you are looking for from a LEGO game is a chance to play through the story and see Tt's humurous take on The Force Awakens, you won't be disappointed.  It's fun, and pretty, and probably the best LEGO game so far as far as mechanics and variety are concerned.  It really is pleasure.  In particular, the new voice recordings and audio from the cast is a treat to listen to.  There are also original adventures featuring ancillary characters and background that was mentioned in the movie but we haven't had a chance to see before now.  It's a curious question to wonder "is this canon?" because each of the new stories has a solid foundation in the new canon, but are obviously told in TT games' unique style.
So, if you want to drop $50-60 on a game that you will absolutely have a blast playing for the 4 or 5 hours it takes you to work your way through the main story and perhaps the side adventures, don't hesitate!
If, however, you are like me and you play LEGO games as a completionist and you'd like to get to 100% unlocks, with all red bricks, gold bricks, "True Jedi" on every level, and all character and vehicle unlocks, well, prepare to be frustrated.  This game is FULL of bugs.  Here are just a few that I have encountered:
* My save game inexplicably reset after the first 6 chapters of story mode, showing 14% completion but forcing me to restart from the beginning and play through the first 6 levels over again.
* Numerous video and sound glitches.
* A Microfighter race on the D'Qar hub that simply will not start, no matter which character or vehicle I use, preventing me from getting the last gold brick on that hub (even across multiple restarts of the game).
* A bug in the "Battle of Takodana" free play level that does not trigger the TIE fighter sequence during the "cover" battle near the start of the level and so your characters remain trapped in cover, unable to advance through the level.
* Tried to interact with a door that could be cut open with a lightsaber only to have the character freeze and become unusable (thankfully the problem fixed itself when I switched to the other character and continued playing).
* Several instances where "multi-build" objects could not be destroyed and I needed to exit and restart the level in order to build the different configurations.  This never prevented me from advancing in a level, but did prevent me from obtaining collectibles.
Keep in mind that I finished the main story two days ago, and I've encountered all of these problems in the first few hours after trying to work my way towards 100% completion.  One bug I figure I'll give up on and wait for a patch while I work on other stuff, but now I've encountered several that prevent me from collecting minikits and bricks to move forward.
If the game is patched soon to fix these bugs, i wouldn't hesitate to recommend it.  It's fun, and by far the most beautiful LEGO game to date.  But right now it simply is not worth the $50+ to play a game masquerading as a AAA title that has only a few hours of gameplay before you encounter game stopping bugs.
UPDATE: After letting the game sit in my library for a few days, I decided to fire it back up.  I was able to slog through and get 100% completion as well us unlock all of the Steam achievements the game has to offer.  As a result, I'm flipping my review from a negative one to a positive one with some caveats.
It's still a buggy mess.  This is not helped by the fact that many of the quests for gold bricks that you will find in the hubs offer little or no guidance about how to complete them.  Some of them do!  You pick up a quest and you'll get a trail of blue studs that lead you to your objective.  Others, not so much: you're left standing at the quest giver with no idea where to begin.  Some can be completed in the immediate area; others require you to travel a fair distance; others fall everywhere in between.
One particularly annoying "feature" is that you can't view the map while you're on a vehicle, meaning that you need to dismount, open the map to find what you're looking for, and then hop back on.  Another map-related bug means that trying to set waypoints only sort of works...there usually isn't an indication on the map of where your waypoint is, but usually when you close the map you'll have a trail of ghost studs to follow.  Another is that quest markers will flash back and forth between checked and unchecked as you move the map around.  Think you already finished one quest?  Nudge the map a bit and it may show up as checked!
The combination of progress-halting bugs and quests without any kind of useful information regarding how to complete them means that I gave up on quests more than once, assuming the game had bugged out, only to return later and find out that I'd just missed something or hadn't looked under the right rock.  It's pretty bad when a game is so buggy that it's easier to believe that it is broken than that you're missing something.
But, it is possible to play all the way through.  Yes, it still bugs out from time to time.  Yes, sometimes you have to try the same level or quest 3, 4, more times before it finally works.  Yes, it crashes to desktop without warning.  But it's still a fun game, and with enough patience, you can get through it and see everything.
I'd still recommend that most people wait until WB/TT gets around to patching it, but that day may never come.  If you have patience and are a LEGO and/or Star Wars fan, it may be worth giving it a shot.

First of all, I've played the orginial Company of Heroes a lot. I had around 200 hours into the original Company of Heroes game (not reflected in steam hours due to me having it played a pirated version with friends untill I finally bought the game a few years later on) which I've been playing from time to time on an amateur level for around 4 to 5 years. That being said, I'm just the average player in Company of Heroes.
Now, I have conflicting thoughts about Company of Heroes 2.
THE BAD:
- Poorly optimised:
This is a big issue, I'm running this game on an i7 2600k processor with a gtx770 graphics card while the game is installed on an HDD, (mid-tier pc). Loading times are crazy, even if you have this game stored on an SSD, your opponent might not have done the same so you will still be forced to wait untill both of you have loaded in.
The framerate is also terrible, I first played this game on 'recommended' settings and noticed my framerate going below 60 a lot. In the recommended settings everything was pretty much changed to normal, the game on normal settings looks even worse than the original CoH (sarcasm.. or is it??). So I tried max settings, to see what it would look like. Strange enough after I've maxed out the game (a part from AA, set that on 2x) I surprisingly had a higher FPS, wait what?
- User interface:
The user interface is a mess, all sorts of icons of different colours and artstyles everywhere, they are not fitting together plus common usage of extremely ugly colours.
The visual assistance in the maps also looks terrible when it comes to territory control, each flag has a circle around it with a colour which represents the team which is holding it, but it also has another outline which is indicating the border between said point and other points. This makes it look messy, should have stuck with the orginal Company of Heroes design when it comes to that. The minimap is also extremely bad, it's hard to find units on there.
- Boosters
Now, I used to be a Counter-Strike player, I'm extremely font of the idea of only offering cosmetics for money, nothing else. A game should also be extremely balanced and both sides should  have the exact same chance to win if they would have the exact same amount of skill.
This game rewards you with playing by giving you boosters every now and then, which means they are rewarding good players with perks such as having a tank deal more damage, or infantry having more accuracy. Cosmetics is what it should stay at, never reward players by making them even stronger, their experience itself should make them strong enough already. Sad part is that you can even BUY these boosters together with commanders and other things.
THE GOOD:
- Still has most of the great mechanics and concepts from the original Company of Heroes, they have made a few changes here and there, such as having green cover while infrantry is walking next to heavy tanks etc. Really great improvements in general a part from a few things which I've mentioned here above. The multiplayer system is also pretty decent, you can earn XP for winning and losing matches, you can unlock cosmetics and slight boosts, the cosmetic part is fine but the boosts are absolutely not, e.g commanders and the other assets which slightly improve a select amount of things. (e.g riflemen have 3% more accuracy).
- The matchmaking system is pretty great, I've played multiplayer a few times, usually matches me up within 30 seconds against a player of similair skill. Had a few mismatches a few times but that I don't mind.
- Nice visuals if you can run it, eventhough it's poorly optimised, the game looks decent on max settings. Really gives me a kick sometimes when I call in an airstrike with lets say rockets to take out hostile light armour.
My common sense is telling me I shouldn't enjoy this game due to it's way of making money and poor optimisation, but this is all outweighted by the good old Company of Heroes legendary gameplay mechanics.

To call this game an RPG is a simplification. It's not like any other RPG I've played because the combat system is so different.
The combat system with Bard's Tale, early Wizardry, Might and Magic, etc. relied on choosing party options and then executing a round at a time. Eye of the Beholder/Grimrock types use a real-time system feel for combat which can be exploited with common strafing techniques. However this game is an interesting combination of both. It features a pause mechanic allowing you to interrupt the real-time combat and monster AI that denies strafing. The result? A significant tactical challenge to any RPG lover.
After a clever introduction, the game becomes frustrating. (Admittedly I overcomplicated the game by insisting no-one ever gets knocked unconscious, forcing me to spend far too long in combat). The monsters knock you out apparently easily. There is no map available for a period of time (again a challenge I took on myself), forcing you to learn the dungeon layout. The skill tree is not dramatic. And it doesn't seem to get any easier as you go.
However, the effort is worth it. The result is a game that is genuinely taxing and more complex than it appears. The dungeons are actually well designed. Each has its own flavour and there is nothing gimmicky. The puzzle rooms are not taxing but there is a multi-level puzzle that I found too hard without hints (even that puzzle is not mandatory). The classes and skill trees are nicely balanced, with a clever option to allow you to change classes with no penalty. The levelling both for characters and monsters is such that you never pull ahead - each combat requires focus. You have the option to knock down the difficulty if you like but that would have hurt my pride too much. There is also plenty of information about the combat power of each character so you can make good equipment decisions.
The monster graphics are clean. The audio is sufficient and the spells are fine. It's not a visual feast but I never felt disappointed. Finally, the ending made sense of the journey, enough to make me keen to try again with a different setup.
The game is not without its flaws. It does grind slightly around the later levels but not too much because the skill tree becomes interesting at that point. I advise against challenge games (by all means leave automapping off - the game works fine that way - but don't forsake the little Wizard's eye window). There are a few spelling mistakes. Combats tend to go on a bit long, especially the bosses. I played the Mercenary level which I would now move beyond - I just felt insulted when it said monsters were less than 100% toughness. Listen to the warnings at the start about the game difficulty!
Overall this is a game I'll remember because it required concentration, persistence and intelligence to overcome it, rather than grinding, with a clever finish.
Completions: 2.

Ok I had taken down my previous review, which was negative, after one of the Developers contacted me, for which I was grateful, giving me a few hints. Like, what I did not know at first, some difficult puzzles are optional. So, I fought on up to Level 14, but, alas in this new review, my negative statement must remain.
While I like the idea to reviv classic dungeon crawler and I accept this is a lower budged product, at the end of the day the fun must outweight the pain, and at this point it simply didn't.
Beyond level 10 or so, the hints what to do are really becoming tiny and the buttons you have to find, the pressure plate in what order become so tedious, that I found myself walking back through the cleared empty tunnels in the same level literally for hours. The problem is, the level design is quite bland, and I would by all means accept that (I bought much simpler looking games and enjoyed them), if there was not hours of walking, looking, just trying to find a grey button on a grey wall in a grey and dark enviroment. And when grey and brown make like NINTY PERCENT of what you see all the time, I simply could not bear it anymore.
Alas, there is too less incentive in the game to keep playing against the "finding the right button at the right wall" issue. The very thin story, and there just isn't much to see just make the frustration way too high. I already have automap on and the lowest difficulty and I still find walking hours through cleared dungeons at this level mind numbing frustrating. Just one level before I had spend two entire days using teleporters in the right order, and with the corridors all looking the same, I open up the map like every 10 seconds EVEN with minimap on.

To be clear, this is a middle thumb rating. I decided to put it "up" rather than "down" because I prefer to encourage this type of dev and game rather than the usual crap we are used to see coming out these years.
Now, this game ....I love and hate it.
I love its genre since the first PC games I played 20 years ago were Eye of the Beholder serie, Lands of Lore etcetc so the nostalgia kicks in rather fast whenever I see one of those games being made. The dungeons are well done, the secrets well hidden. Its beautiful enough and by that I mean that you dont need more than this in this genre if you ask me. Its just perfect the way it is.
I hate it because of the combat. Unlike most games of this type, combat is offered to you in a semi real-time "skills with cooldown" way making it very much more combat oriented than lets say Legend of Grimrock. You simply cannot move around, dodging the enemie's attacks. On paper, it is fun but in reality, the way it has been implemented and the fact that items are randomised makes it more of a pain than anything else.
Let me explain : The "recommended" party is, of course a Tank, Healer and 2 DPS type. There are different core class which you can choose from but basically, you have a heavy tank, dodgy tank, HoT heal, Protector "direct heal" healer, mage types and ranger or assassin for DPS. The combat implements Threat, which your Tank has to keep if you hope to survive the most basic fight. The thing that pains me is how cubbersome keeping the Threat is in this game. For the tank to properly keep aggro, he has to use his -very- limited "taunt" skills. If they fail, youre dead. To fail your taunts, you have to miss, hit slower, hit for lower damage than your DPS, hit for lower damage than you heal, start a fight with the enemy group having anyone other than your tank targeted by default, etcetc. What this leads to is a tank that fails to do anything BUT use his taunting skill the whole fight. Either that or purposely make your DPS or Heal deal less damage. Also, since you would think that for a tank, you have to increase his HP, Armor, Dodge etcetc, youll have a tendency to put on the side his other stats like "hit chance" or "w/e gives more damage" but if you do that, youll either miss your taunting skills, which will then not taunt anything and be useless, or do so much nothing in damage that the mob will just go back to your other teamates the next attack. When it happens a few times, its ok, you try to be more careful, but when it happens every single fight, that you fight more against your own tank than the actual enemies because he never can keep aggro, it becomes tedious and simply not fun anymore. I dont find it normal to have to build my tank more "DPSy" but more squishy simply because there isnt a good balance in aggroing skills.
Anyways, the game is still very good and worth getting. This was my issue on this title from the start when it came out and still now after coming back to it to finish it.

Absolutely awesome game. A better
game than any of the official ones.
Basically, the game lets you command your own little starship with your own little crew, made up of whoever you damn well please to make it out of. It's not an all-humans club, either, as various different races such as the Engi, the Mantis, the Rockmen, the Zoltan, and the Slug can be enlisted into your crew, each species having their own unique trait that can aid you in your travels.
The game often gives you freedom of how to go about your mission, either, by giving you a variety of different situations to tackle throughout your journey. A mining ship is being attacked? You could either be the hero and save them, or you can decide for yourself that it's a waste of resources and time and carry on. A slave trader threatens to kill you unless you give up one of your crew members? You can either fight, or do as they say.
The starship battles are also quite fun, too. Granted, the action isn't super-fast-paced, so if you're looking for something like that this may not be the game for you. However, the battles
interesting in the fact that you need to manage your resources, your people, and your attacks. What room should you aim for on their ship? Who should be stationed where? Should you use a torpedo to breach their shields, or not?
There's a lot more I could say about this game, but all you really need to know is this: If you're looking for some immersive, strategic sci-fi gameplay, then pick this up now.

Ys Origin is a good game. It's worth every bit of money I spent on it. But it's not perfect. There are some flaws with the game that prevents the game from being great.
1) The story
-If you've already played Ys back in the golden age of the Super Famicom, you'll probably appreciate the story in this prequel. But if you never played them, chances are you'll be disappointed with the story. It's very cliche and predictable. Even worse is the story for each characters. Long story short, each of them aren't parallel with each other.
2) The difficulty
-Hard games are good and welcomed but the difficulty in Ys Origin is borderline cheap and unfair. Basically, the higher difficulty means enemies have more health, takes less damage and deals more damage to you. It pretty much boils down to grinding enough levels by killing the same enemies over and over again, just to inflict damage more than 1 to the enemy. That, and finding power-up item to strengthen your weapon because if not, the later stages becomes nearly impossible. Unless you're a masochist or have a lot of free time, just play it on normal or easy.
3) The gameplay
-It's fun enough for a few hours, especially after getting all abilities but it get pretty old as you play. Equipment, stats, abilities, items, etc are all streamlined and simplified. You'll be begging for more complexity the more you play. Almost no exploration or secret locations to discover, a few unneeded platforming and a non-existent puzzles to solve.
I'm giving this a thumbs up simply because it succeeded in giving me a brief moment of enjoyment.
RECOMMENDED        : For Ys fans. If not, buy this during a sale.
NOT RECOMMENDED: Player who seeks more complexity than slash-fest J Action RPG

It's a satisfying hack and slash game, but keep in mind, this is not a title for the intellectual gamer. I'll start by explaining what I don't like before what I do like.
(IMPORTANT - This game is not worth $19.99. Get it when it goes on sale.)
The writing is horrible and the game treats you like a baby that can't figure anything out on your own. For example, I entered a zone on the 12th floor that would quickly drain my HP simply by being there, forcing me to leave the area. When the character said that it felt like an evil sound boring into her head, I checked my inventory and saw the silver harmonica given to me by one of the goddesses. I figured "No brainer right? I just got this thing, so obviously this is the solution."
I go back into the zone and try using the harmonica, but it doesn't work. And not in the context that the character tried using it, but failed. I mean I went to use the item and got the equivalent of Prof. Oak saying "Now is not the time to use that."
No, you have to call somebody outside of the room, listen to a conversation, and have the character say bluntly that "Hey, look at this here harmonica. I'll betcha that will solve the problem." So now, I don't feel like somebody who used reasoning to deduce the solution to a problem. I feel like my hand is being held. (And yes, I know that the harmonica still doesn't technically work even after the conversation, but it still serves the purpose of progressing the game.)
And again, the writing is fanfiction levels of god awful. Maybe if the writing were better and didn't look like it was tailored to pre-teens, the story could possibly be decent. But with writing like this, there's no way any adult could enjoy it.
---
As for the good things about the game, despite not being the deepest combat system, it's very fast paced and feels extremely satisfying. I've played the game for about 6 hours now and I'm still not tired of the button mashy combat. Enemies spit out tons of resources after being defeated, giving that packrat portion of our minds a constant tickle.
My favorite part of the game would have to be the boss fights. Unlike other aspects that treat you like a child, these boss fights are pretty brutal. I'm playing the game on hard mode, and I've had to go through these fights at least 10 or so times before coming away victorious. I love that there's actually room to strategize in these fights. Like a giant centipede that drops poison time bombs from its destroyed body parts. Do you try your best to methodically clear out the bombs, or do you continue assaulting the boss and hope to outlast them? And while you do have the opportunity to go back and grind out some levels to make it easier, these bosses will still command all of your attention.
Overall, I don't believe the game is worth the asking price of $19.99. If the writing were better and if the zones actually had secrets and left more room for exploration, then it would be a no brainer. As it stands, Ys Origin is a fairly straightforward hack and slash that is very good when you're actually playing the game, but suffers when anybody opens their mouth. Again, get it on sale for sure. Around $4.99 is more than acceptable.

1. The Machinegun Noise/Endless Gunshot Loop in multiplayer
From all the reading I've done (and it's been a fair amount because I used to play the game a lot), this was a server/latency issue.  Nothing worked fixing disc versions of the game.
With the Steam version, there is a fix that I've seen work.  In game, you disable all voice options.  Mute yourself, mute other players, turn off all in-game voice chat features.  And you enable vertical synch/Vsynch in the options menu.
With those fixes in mind, I've still run into the machinegun noise loop a few times, but it'll be after hours of play, not seconds of play.  The end of a match will reset it anyway, so you'll only have to tolerate it briefly.
2. Occasionally Tactically Unsound
This game came out before MOUT was as much of a thing outside of the military, room-clearing wasn't as big of a deal, and all the lessons learned from modern conflicts hadn't made their way into games yet.
As such, if you're used to "slicing the pie" and going support-side shoulder to minimize exposure when moving into a danger area in real life (whether you're an IRL operator or just a paintball/airsoft ninja), you'll find that it's behind the times.  Or if you just prefer to give the least possible exposure around a corner while not adhering yourself to a wall... which would put it behind games like ARMA & maybe even Operation Flashpoint.
You'll also find that the "stick/unstick to walls" animation takes a fraction of a second to run, so there's a little bit of learning curve getting adjusted to utilizing it and getting killed vs exploiting it.
Also if you're a gun nerd, you'll have to ignore that some of the guns are mislabeled (SCAR 17 (H) is treated like a 16 (L), etc.), and performance between guns that have the same barrel lengths and the same ammo and that have identical ballistics in real life are treated like different things, and things like reloads that may be slower than IRL counterparts, and guns that accept only one "accessory"... because optics magically limit magazine size.
-
Overall, as a multiplayer shooter, even with having to workaround the machinegun noise loop bug and firearms enthusiast complaints, it's still fun.
For somebody totally new to the game, keep in mind it's almost a decade old and so the story mode has long since been eclipsed by modern AAA games and their massive plotlines.  The storyline plot is somewhat linear, but where the game shines is the terrorist hunt single/multiplayer maps, especially set on realistic difficulty.
The enemy AI alternates between incredibly clever and staggeringly stupid, where you may have some patient enemy wait for you to make a move and then get the drop on you, and other times you'll have them keep coming through the same door over a stack of bodies you've just slain so they can all get killed like lemmings.  Either way, it keeps you on your toes.

This game is an amazing adventure through the old World of Darkness, suitable for anyone regardless of experience with the tabletop roleplaying game. For those interested in that, I'd like to note the world in which this game takes place has been rebooted in a new game, and the current analogue to Vampire: The Masquerade is called Vampire: The Requiem. Some terms and ideas still exist, but the very feel of the world and the themes of the game are wholly different. TL;DR: A very decent and fun Lego game, but not without its faults.
SPOILERS FOR THE FILM "THE FORCE AWAKENS" AND THE GAME AHEAD -
The Pros:
- Kylo Ren. Immensely fun as a playable character.
- New gameplay features that make the game vastly different to its predecessors but still keeping the old Lego Star Wars spirit - such as the new taking cover mechanic, manipulating Lego piles for multiple objects and the use of multiple weapons e.g. with Rey - you get a lightsaber, blaster and staff by the end of the game.
- Fun story campaign that doesn't get too repetitive or boring
- Space battles - They remind me of Star Wars Battlefront II. Very fun and engaging, especially in the trench runs of Starkiller base where you are dodging and diving in the snow.
The Cons -
- Lack of good old fashioned lightsabering. I appreciate that much of the Force Awakens doesn't feature lightsaber fights but going a good six levels with only a blaster in a Lego Star Wars game gets a tad boring after a while.
- Stretched out plot - much like the Hobbit movies, I felt that the developers had little in terms of story to go on here and so dragged out the plot of the Force Awakens for ten levels when it could have easily been four or five. A complete saga style game with episodes VII, VIII and IX would have been better I feel.
- Disappointing boss battles - There weren't many lightsaber duels in this game, and the ones that we did get were dead boring. Particularly the Kylo Ren battle on Starkiller base at the end, where you can't hit Kylo at all and instead have to run around him until he jumps at you, at which point you mash your keys and then hit him once, before having to do the waiting game again. Dull.
- Bugs. Currently, the game crashes and glitches a lot. It's not fun.
In summary then, it's a very fun and interesting Lego Star Wars game that is different enough from its predecessors to not look like a money grab. New gameplay features are excellent, but I think that this game would have been better as a Complete Saga game released when all the new Star Wars films are out, with only four or five levels each for episodes VII, VIII and IX.

I liked this game enough to write a guide for it.
It's a dungeon crawler. Everyone has their opinion of the genre, and if you don't like it, then this game probably won't make you change your mind. But if you DO like dungeon crawlers, then give this one a shot. It has real-time pausable MMO-style combat (tank, healer, damage dealers, aggro management) with random loot.
There is a surprising amount of depth in character development. Each of the 4 base classes (warrior, rogue, healer, mage) has 3 specialties with each its own set of talents. Most of them offer 2 different ways to play the specialty and that's not even considering the fact that you can invest in the other 2 specialties' talent trees too. That's a lot potential combos. The game even lets you fully respec to redistribute talent points and even change specialties, not infinitely, but enough times.
The game has several quality of life features such as automapping and highlighting of items that you can turn on or off to make your experience as modern or as old school as you want. You can also lower or increase the difficulty at any time. Combined with respeccing, this makes it very difficult to make the game "unwinnable."
It took me 3 playthroughs and many hours of just poking around to explore the game to my satisfaction and write the guide. For the price, that's pretty good deal, especially compared to all the AAA games I bought at much higher price points and from which I got many less hours worth of enjoyment.

Easily one of the best dungeon crawls I have the pleasure of owning.
Great game, decent storyline, fun exploration with tons of secrets, nice mix of monsters and puzzles, tons of character class customization, interesting locations, and loads of fun.
Developer is very hands on and has updated the game three times since I have owned it each time enhancing the product allowing more customization for relaxed, casual, and hardcore gamers.

Very good Dungeon Crawler variant: it adds to classic tile by tile action an interesting MMO component based on the tank, healer, and damage dealers party concept.
I personally don't like MMO... but this original choice mixing the two things together is very well done.
The game has also good gfx and audio, and level design is varied, and much better than many other titles of this kind (f.e. you have also multiple floors with bridges etc. on the same level with minimal backtracking and some well balanced puzzles). Skill trees and specializations are there too... Gameplay is also accurately tuned and you can configure EVERYTHING to customize difficulty (even by monsters class!) for a more classic dungeon crawler action or a more RTS oriented one.
Supports also modding and is multilanguage.
Great, constant support from the developer.
Final question:
Is it better than Grim Rock? Yes, in many aspects and especially for gameplay, even though GR may have a bit more polished gfx/sound.

Clearly a lot of effort has gone into making this game. Lovely graphics but repetitive, boring combat. Overall I recommend it, but only just, you must have a lot of patience.

FoDG has the right mix going for it. I can tile dodge effectively, the monsters are levelled nicely and also are placed/grouped in the right areas for fighting or running.  As should be the case with this style you gain just enough to get you through, dumping obsolete gear as you upgrade (i'm not sure if each level has a special item, if not it should).
I haven't used any bows or throwing weapons ingame yet, so not sure if they are present and the monster spells  clip the walls and score against me, maybe thats just my copy ?? not sure.  Nothing major.
All in all a solid game, i like it alot and i would buy a FoDG 2.

First of all. It's a good game. Really.
I find it perfect for the ones, starting their journey with dungeon crawler genre. It offers everything that this genre consists of and adds few twists. You can customise basically everything, from difficulty level to the amount of monsters, their hp, and behavior. You can play paperlike mode or use all newschool features like minimap. And the thing that is unique in crawlers - holy trinity class system with fight style inspired from MMORPGs. Character development offers plenty of options.
Combat system makes this game truly unique but at the same time a little bit boring and repetive. You can treat fights like WOW raids sometimes but basically you will have to repeat the same things over and over. While it works well in MMORPGS coz you control just 1 character and all you have to do is to play your role, here you will have to play 4 at the same time. For sure its challenging (oh yes, it is) but like I said - sometimes it might be too much. Thankfully like I said, you can customize basically everything so you can have challenging fights but the enemies will appear more or less often. Its up to you to decide. And whatever you will do, EXP will remain the same (splitting).
Now the part for Dungeon Crawler fans. FIrst of all Grimrock. I would put this title on the same level as 1st Legends. The amosphere is less claustrophobic and at least for me, least immersive but still its on good level. The game uses similar schemes and mechanics. While 1st Grimrock was bad coz you could abuse moving during the combat, this game wont let you do anything like it. That's a plus. You will find secrets, riddles, bosses and resource distribution.
The game is not as good as 2nd Grimrock or the best dungeon crawler ever created which is Wizardry 8 but for god sake, this genre needs more good games and this is for sure one of them.
YOU HAVE TO PLAY IT if you are crawler fan.
YOU STRONGLY SHOULD PLAY IT if you are RPG fan.
YOU WON'T REGRET If you are looking for single player game with MMORPG flavor.

The "Open Environment" that "allows you to roam around and explore" is no such thing, in fact it is a cookie-cutter, one-way game without imagination. The puzzles over simplistic other than for the house which can is overly complicated and relies on cheating.
The game claims that it won't lead you by the hand, because they don't know how to develop a learning ramp for the user, which is steep but caps pretty quickly and doesn't develop further.
After all the hype, I was seriously expecting something great and instead I found myself with a 12 year old's creation, and no, the game wasn't created by the protagonist.
The characters are simplistic and one-dimensional, the main character has no feelings for anyone yet there is no indication otherwise of sociopathy. The graphics that depended on the artist's skills, bloated, ugly and unrealistic.
Overall, disappointing and a waste of good money. Cudos on knowing how to place previously designed rocks, tree or grass on top of one another. Un-cudos on the buggy environment that prevents you from jumping over a speck of dust blocking your way.
Beautiful environment, fun puzzles that build to a satisfying narrative conclusion.

Gameplay is actually quite simple, you pretty much just left click on your mouse to interact with the enviroment. If this game even caught your attention while browsing the store, you should buy this game. It is a very deep game and much more than a simple crime investigation. You play as Paul and not as yourself, it is that kind of feeling.
And now...Pros and cons
Pros
+Amazing graphics, can't tell the difference if you look out the window 10/10
+Very thrilling and exiting story, you can't wait to see deeper in the lives of the characters (haven't completed the game yet) 9/10
+It never gets boring. Pretty much the only thing you do is walk around and click on different objects. But your will to solve the mystery is what makes it fun and once again, to look at the amazing world around you is another reason to enjoy it 8/10

But don't keep your eyes focused on the cons because, as in all games there are cons. Don't sit at home and discuss with yourself whether you want the game or not because trust me, you do want this game.

One of the pitfalls of this game is that there's not much to do outside of grinding levels and experience for new agents. Players can join groups known as 'holdings' and it's basically a guild system where you can own starbases and customize them. I think you can even get ore from planets in your zone of control. But there's not really that much to do with other players so it's kind of a singleplayer experience...
The crafting isn't really deep enough to make you want to do it, though it is more effective to craft your items than it is to buy them.
Game might get better, but you could easily squeeze 100 hours or more out of this game so it's worth ten bucks even if it never recieves any other updates. You should buy it.

A friend turned me on to FTL a little while ago and at first I was sceptical.  Then I tried it...  And it is fantastic!
Pros:
1)  Pick your ship and customize it with rooms and crew to change how it works.  At first you'll only have one ship available but you'll quickly expand as you explore the galaxy.
2)  Several different races with different strengths and weaknesses make for a diverse team where everyone has a job they're best at.
3)  Crew actually have skills that level up for subtle passive bonuses, encouraging you to keep them alive.
4)  Shops around the galaxy offer a wide variety of weapons, rooms, and crew to add to your ship...  If you have the crdits.
5)  Star system map changes from game to game and each path has it's benefits.  Friendly sytsems may be safer but hostile ones may yeild different rewards or navigating dense star clusters can slow the enemy fleet.  Each system has it's merits!
6)  Dozens of different instances that let you decide how to proceed, engage the enemy or retreat to where it's safe?  Your call.
Cons:
1)  While there are dozens of instances and events you will inevitably start seeing the same ones after a while.  Some instances have varying rarity however so some you might not see for a very long time.
2)  Credits can be very hard to come by and you'll often be fixing your ship.  I recommend playing on easy your first time through so you can learn the game before lamenting on how broke you always seem to be.
The Overview:
FTL is a terrific game!  It definitely drew some inspiration from Firefly in it's feel (and one of the ships looks suspiciously like the Serrenity.)  It is however difficult with a final boss battle that is immensly challenging.  With the variety of ships and rooms you'll quickly find a style of fighting you prefer and enjoy.
I should be clear, this isn't a flight simulator, and it isn't first person.  It's a space sim with a top-down view of your ship and the enemy.  You control your crew and the power allocation to your ship's systems and tell the ship which targets to attack (don't forget to turn on the auto-fire!)  That being said each fight is pretty fast paced and requires you to quickly redirect your fire to target other enemy systems.
Between fights you'll be navigating a celestial map where each star is a different event that could benefit you or hurt you.  Sometimes having a certain crewmember or ship augment makes the challenge easier or lets you solve a problem that would otherwise be unsolvable.  As you travel the rebel fleet slowly takes over the system, forcing you further on.  This means your time to gather resources and visit stars in a system before traveling to the next one is limited, so every movement counts.
The balance between tactical movement among the stars and the fast paced action of ship-to-ship combat make this game a personal favorite of mine even though the ending battle is a brutal shootout.  The varying instances and number of ships to play with give this game a high level of replay value and will have you returning to the stars again and again.
Fly fast for the Federation friend, the Rebels are catching up.
Happy Gaming,

A sprawling, humorous adventure in the old style, beset by enough problems that it's better to save yourself from the frustration and forget about it. Lots of pretty decent voice acting, even if it's all hammy and silly, but few of the belly laughs of the Monkey Island games they tried to emulate, only with too much heavy sarcasm and not enough absurdity. The graphics are bright and shiny, the characters even occasionally have a bit of real-life spark to them, and there are a hell of a lot of puzzles to solve (plus a few fetch quests). When the occasional hilarious moments clicked, it almost made it all worth it.
My biggest problem with it was the utterly plodding pace everyone shuffled at, and with such a huge world, you could catch a nap walking between areas. With zero in-game tutorial, there was no way to know that a double-click made you run, until a puzzle near the end through was unsolvable if you didn't, so I had to go online and find out that the game screwed me. Combine that with terrible pathing, where you take the longest route and walk in circles to get to anything, and it was a dull, frustrating game. The horrible camera contributes significantly; they tried to make it as cinematic as possible with fixed cameras that turn with you, but half the time that just means you have to click every two seconds to keep walking. Some of the swooping effects are nice, but interfere with gameplay whenever you want to click on something while you're walking. The cinematic experience was kind of broken anyway, when everyone looks off into space while talking to each other and  uses the exact same hand gesture.
Compared to that constant irritation, the occasional insane puzzle (or insane chapter, as Amanda's seemed to be), and the expected heaping bugs that every adventure game has weren't as bad. They just meant I ended up leaning on a walkthrough at times to figure out what one thing I'd missed somewhere, and occasionally rage quitting for a few days when it crashed again.
I think I truly came to hate it when I found a good fix, and Jack said, "No, that would be the obvious solution. I feel like some challenge. Let's try it another way...."
Ultimately, I grimly finished it just because I'd already invested so much time, but it became an endurance that I wouldn't wish on anyone. A little polish would have taken the game into the timeless classic realm, but instead it ended up average and forgettable.

From the makers of Magicka comes an action-packed, challenging, and engaging twin-stick shooter where you're a soldier of Super Earth fighting off three alien factions in the name of democracy.
HELLDIVERS plays very similarly to Valve's free-to-play twin-stick shooter Alien Swarm, though this game has considerably more content to keep you satisfied and playing. Rather than being class-based, however, players have a choice of weapons and strategems to pick from to customize their character, including unlockable aesthetic gear.
Strategems are support items you call down to aid your team, such as extra ammo, automated gun turrets, and much larger weapons to swing around. They drop in pods shot from space, so you have to wary of falling supplies, otherwise you or your squad will get crushed.
As is the case with Magicka, friendly fire is always on, and some of the weapons you use hurt your teammates as much as they hurt your enemies; grenades and stray bullets will shred your friends' health bars and, as I mentioned, a badly-placed supply drop will reduce soldiers to bits. Fortunately, you can call in reinforcement pods to bring your comrades back from the dead. Just make sure you're not crushed by the pod.
The controls seem fairly tight and easy to get into, though if using a controller you should make sure your right stick isn't janky; aiming your gun with the right stick slows your movement speed drastically, so if your stick has a tendency to move in a direction you might be in for a bad time.
All of the missions seem to be randomly generated, so playing the same difficulty on the same planet may put you in a different battlefield, helping extend the play time. However, even so, after particularly long play sessions HELLDIVERS starts to feel a bit repetitive. This is eased somewhat by playing with friends, but it's still recommended you take a little break after awhile, otherwise you might start feeling burned out.
Being a big fan of both Alien Swarm and Magicka, I had very high hopes for HELLDIVERS being a fun and engaging twin-stick shooter. And I wasn't disappointed.

HELLDIVERS is a semi-RPG co-op top down shooter where the main goal is to spread freedom and democracy for your planet, Super Earth. You invade alien planets with your friends, slaughtering everything in your path and completing objectives for Experience and research points. You use these to unlock new items so you can more effectively slaughter everything in your path. All players are on the same screen at all times, making teamwork vital to survive missions. A lot of the items and gear encourages teamwork, like a medi-gun that heals other soldiers, as well as items that work better with two or more players.
Pros
+Encourages the use of teamwork to survive
+Difficulty between larger missions is at a decent scale
+Multiple ways to play the game, with no set classes
+Multiple enemy factions, as well as plenty of enemy types
+Objectives vary from capturing points to aquiring items and simply killing off enemies
+Global scale events that depend on players everywhere to complete
+Community is friendly and helpful (For the most part)
+Big homage to Starship Troopers, with little lines of dialogue added to further reinforce this
Cons
-Could be more difficult for a more casual gamer to simply pick up and play
-Certain difficulties are nearly impossible for solo play
-Can be difficult to complete global events if everyone is not working on them
Mixed
+-Friendly Fire is always on
+-Controllers are preferred over keyboard and mouse
+-Graphics are more for an arcade feeling
+-A nice selection of weapons and items that seem to not get used often
+-Later levels require a bigger grind to level up
Personally, the game is very enjoyable if you have people to play it with. It is worth the price.

Not only is the best Lego game I've ever played, it's easily one of the best Star Wars games I've ever played.
The Good:
1.  Larger and better level design
2.  We finally have actualy dialogue from the movie - no more of that grunting and groaning crap from the earlier games
3.  Lots of action, with improved interface and more varied puzzles
4.  Bricks used for puzzles can be broken down for alternate uses, and many puzzles require multiple steps in this regard
5.  Graphics are the best yet for a Lego game
6.  More diverse and varied gameplay overall - blasters, sabers, flying, and taking cover.
7.  The trademark humor is intact, but it seems held back - this is for the better and is much less cartoonish
8.  Most of the levels follow the movie (or at least relatively so) better than other Lego games in the past
9.  There are side missions that earn you gold bricks, etc.
10.  Flying missions handle better than the god awful Battlefront versions did.
11.  The game encourages more exploring and experimenting
The Bad:
1.  Intro Logos are not skippable - there are 3 just to get to the main menu (sorry, but I'm tired of everyone's logos).  And once you get to the main menu, no amount of key pressing will get you to the menu options any faster.  Grrr......
2.  Each level has its own opening crawl.  It's comepletely unnecessarry and no doubt anyone playing the game has already seen the movie so cut scenes should/would have this covered.  While I'm at it, changing from one location to another involves a cut scene showing ships in hyperspace which, after the first 200 times of seeing that, gets repetitive and is also not skippable.  And in Free Mode, the cut scenes seem to sometimes show the random character you have selected...or not.
3.  The flying levels towards the end are a little odd to control.  There is also a lot going on visually and there were times I felt like I was just shooting at whatever instead of applying any strategy, etc.
4.  Speaking of flying, the game defaults to a "non-inverted" flght control setup - you have to pause the game and select it if you want it - and you have to do this any time you restart the game.  Why that couldn't be saved is beyond me.
5.  The map leaves a little to be desired, especially considering how large many of the environments are.  Being able to zoom in while on location would have been nice.  There are also many locations that don't logically link up.  For example, in the free roaming hangar area of D'Qar you can redo the attack on Jakku from a terminal there - those two locations aren't even linked in any way, so that makes no sense whatsoever.
6.  Character swapping, especially in Free Play mode, is a pain.  There are so many characters, it's hard to even see them all.  Plus, multiple characters can have multiple versions (ie, say 3 versions of Rey) which are "stacked" in the same slot but the grid will cycle through each version.  When there are enough of these cycling at one time, it gets very confusing to look at, even on a large monitor.  Also, in terms of getting new characters added to your collection, there are a few spread out in various locations, but I wound up buying most of mine right from the collection "grid".
7.  I haven't experience any major glitches, but I have had a few CTD cases.
8.  John Williams is my favorite film composer of all time, but since the game will loop the same music over and over in most sections even I have to turn it off after a while.
Also....There is a small part of me that wonders why, with all the effort put into this game, that the developers couldn't have just made a full fledged normal (ie, non-Lego) version of this instead.  I think that's kind of a shame really...they could have easily done it, all the pieces (heh) were there.
Regardless...if you like Star Wars and/or the Lego games, grab this one for sure - it's defintiely a lot of fun.  Despite my nit picks, I really enjoyed it.

A fun short game where the funky and catchy music makes it all the more enjoyable.
What I liked about the game was that although a level is about 30 minutes long, it is divided into 5 checkpoint sections. You start off swimming around as your main character, but every other checkpoint you get to swim with an awesome vehicle that shoots and automatically regenerates health. This change of pace every two checkpoints keeps the game from feeling samey. I actually enjoyed these sections the most.
Another great thing are the collectibles. In your adventures you collect crystals to unlock pictures about the development of the game. Normally I don't care much for concept art, but this game shows quirky pictures of the development team with funny captions and a bit of an insight in the development of the game. I really enjoyed these.
I also really liked the hand-drawn art-style the game had to offer. However, at times it was a little bit hard to see if a section was actually passable or a wall. This is just a slight annoyance, but to me it was worth it for such a great style.
My favourite thing however, has to be the music. Every time I finished a level, I thought to myself: let's play something else. That was until I heard the music of the next level and decided to stay and play another one. The catchy guitars, amazing singing and grooving beats kept me nodding with my head almost the entire playthrough. The fact that different creatures add different sounds to the music is an amazing touch.
Negatives: At times, the control of the character felt a little bit too slow and unresponsive for me, especially when I used the "run" (or in the case of this game: swim faster) button. There weren't many spaces where I felt I could utilize this skill. However, when there are timers in the game, they are forgiving and you do not need precision swimming to get through most of the levels. The dash ability that you get usually gives you enough speed to make it to certain points in time, and the "run" skill is therefor not needed to finish the game.
Another thing that bugged me was that sometimes it was unclear if a path was a secret path with gems or a path to the next goal. This sometimes led to points where I realised I missed a secret, but was unable to go back and get it. It felt unfair that I had seen the path, but that it locked me out of that path for taking the "wrong" route. I guess this adds replayability, but I don't care much for it.
Overall I would say it is worth playing even if for the music alone! If you like funky, groovy music mixed with a little techno, this game is for you. Also, if you like an easy-going, casual side-scroller where you can just enjoy the surroundings and play through without too much effort, you'll like this one.

The Fall of the Dungeon Guardians breathes new life into the dungeon crawler genre by combining the mood and atmosphere of classic crawlers with a combat system reminiscent of games like WoW, Rift, and the Dragon Age series.
The result is a dungeon crawler with something the genre's never really had before -- dynamic, fast-paced combat that requires strategy and tactical adaptation, instead of the usual perfunctory attack and spell spam. In other words, combat is fun!
At first the game looks like standard dungeon crawler fare, and superficially the first few levels are reminiscent of Legend of Grimrock, with moss and ivy-covered hallways, portcullis barriers, levers, pressure plates and hidden treasures. But it becomes apparent early on that this is not Grimrock -- the puzzles are challenging but not obtuse, and there's always a logic to them that reveals itself if you look at them the right way. Unlike Grimrock, FotDG doesn't ask you to go pixel hunting, but there are still plenty of secrets, cleverly hidden items, and areas you can access only after unlocking them.
FotDG's strengths aren't limited to combat, boss battles and smart level design -- the game is exceptionally well-balanced despite providing three full talent trees chock full of abilities and enhancements for each class. It does a fantastic job of keeping you in the sweet spot where mobs and bosses are challenging -- no steamrolling and no feeling helpless during tough boss encounters either.
That balance is helped along by an intuitive gear and upgrade system with strong itemization for each class of character. FotDG uses the familiar green/blue/purple system to denote uncommon/rare/epic quality, items are either cloth, leather or plate, and the stat bonuses are self-explanatory.
Players who are coming from a traditional dungeon crawler background might need a short adjustment period to understand things like global cooldowns, talent trees, spell/ability rotations and the concept of aggro in real-time battles, but the combat system will be instantly familiar to anyone who's ever played MMOs or modern RPGs.
While FotDG puts you in command of an entire party of four, and you're responsible for managing the abilities and cooldowns of those characters, the combat features a pause button that allows you to stop, issue orders and queue spells/abilities, just like the Dragon Age games. It's a nice blend of features that combines the immediacy of real time with the tactical depth of more complex encounters.
I can't recommend this game enough, for fans of dungeon crawlers as well as fans of RPGs!

A friend turned me on to FTL a little while ago and at first I was sceptical.  Then I tried it...  And it is fantastic!
Pros:
1)  Pick your ship and customize it with rooms and crew to change how it works.  At first you'll only have one ship available but you'll quickly expand as you explore the galaxy.
2)  Several different races with different strengths and weaknesses make for a diverse team where everyone has a job they're best at.
3)  Crew actually have skills that level up for subtle passive bonuses, encouraging you to keep them alive.
4)  Shops around the galaxy offer a wide variety of weapons, rooms, and crew to add to your ship...  If you have the crdits.
5)  Star system map changes from game to game and each path has it's benefits.  Friendly sytsems may be safer but hostile ones may yeild different rewards or navigating dense star clusters can slow the enemy fleet.  Each system has it's merits!
6)  Dozens of different instances that let you decide how to proceed, engage the enemy or retreat to where it's safe?  Your call.
Cons:
1)  While there are dozens of instances and events you will inevitably start seeing the same ones after a while.  Some instances have varying rarity however so some you might not see for a very long time.
2)  Credits can be very hard to come by and you'll often be fixing your ship.  I recommend playing on easy your first time through so you can learn the game before lamenting on how broke you always seem to be.
The Overview:
FTL is a terrific game!  It definitely drew some inspiration from Firefly in it's feel (and one of the ships looks suspiciously like the Serrenity.)  It is however difficult with a final boss battle that is immensly challenging.  With the variety of ships and rooms you'll quickly find a style of fighting you prefer and enjoy.
I should be clear, this isn't a flight simulator, and it isn't first person.  It's a space sim with a top-down view of your ship and the enemy.  You control your crew and the power allocation to your ship's systems and tell the ship which targets to attack (don't forget to turn on the auto-fire!)  That being said each fight is pretty fast paced and requires you to quickly redirect your fire to target other enemy systems.
Between fights you'll be navigating a celestial map where each star is a different event that could benefit you or hurt you.  Sometimes having a certain crewmember or ship augment makes the challenge easier or lets you solve a problem that would otherwise be unsolvable.  As you travel the rebel fleet slowly takes over the system, forcing you further on.  This means your time to gather resources and visit stars in a system before traveling to the next one is limited, so every movement counts.
The balance between tactical movement among the stars and the fast paced action of ship-to-ship combat make this game a personal favorite of mine even though the ending battle is a brutal shootout.  The varying instances and number of ships to play with give this game a high level of replay value and will have you returning to the stars again and again.
Fly fast for the Federation friend, the Rebels are catching up.

Ah so about the game. Basically it's an RPG real time strategy game.
You are the Corporation. You start at level 1 leadership. Leadership level is your 'main level'.
You then get 1 agent from the start and you go and do tasks that accumulate experience. There are 4 skill trees of experience.
Crafting- Trading- Resource- and Warfare.
Doing crafting tasks gets you craft exp which I think it's about 10% of it goes towards Leadership exp, and then you use your crafting exp to level up the crafting skills you want. Same goes for trading tasks, mining and refining tasks, and combat tasks. All of them raise towards Leadership exp but at a small fraction. Get enough exp for a leadership level up and then you can hire another agent. This means now you can fly 2 ships! You'll hit this point like 5-20mins within starting the game if you follow the tutorial guidelines. You can 'fleet' them together so that they attack the same target and stick together.
What's really unique and cool about this game is exactly that, the fleets and multiple ship ownership.
Fleets are also 'parties' as you know from other MMO RPGs. Your ships share experience in a fleet. The ships with the most Skill Points from Agents [and I think the more advanced ones hold weighter exp-extract power too than say an equal amount of SP of standard skills] pull in the most experience and then splits that amongst the agents on that ship even further.
You can form a guild, in this game it's called a Holding. I'm in one called The Death Penalty with a few of my friends.
We're training up quite nicely. The leader can command 2 battleships. So far I can only command a Cruiser and 2 scouts.
And while there are some very nice people, there are some smug bullies too that pretend to be your friend or friendly.
Try not to let them drive you off the game. I hear a few groups like that have driven off a hundred plus new and intermediate players. There are a lot of constructive things you can do for leveling up and bettering your economy and skills while not entering into Red space where you can be hunted down.

Quick note prior to the review:  If you wish to play an older, but completely free version of SanctuaryRPG, head on over to
.  It may be an older version, but it gives you plenty of content to test and is very fun.
Now, onto the review itself.
SanctuaryRPG: Black Edition is a text based RPG based off the old classic RPGs, while also taking inspiration from many new-age RPGs and JRPGs.  Seeing as I'm a fan of reviews listing information about how the game is played and the strong points of it's systems, I'll explain a bit of it, and what I like about it.
Combat:  This makes up a lot of the game, and as such, is an important system.  Combat works on a turn based system using abilities and combos.  Select one of your attacks with the corrosponding number or letter key, press enter.  Simple.  There are 6 different classes, each with their own attacks and special abilities, which gives the game great variety on how you like to combat your enemies.  In addition, all classes have their own ultimate abilities which are charged based on the use of combos.  Ultimate abilities work much like you think they would, and each one has it's own advantages.  The game also features lots of status effects and enemy affixes, which can change the pace and strategy of the fight significantly.  There's also many other different types of abilities with their own special uses you will unlock later in the game and experience for yourself.
Events:  This game features random events you may find throughout your adventure.  Events will usually occur when you find a secret area, indicated with either an [8] or a [x] on the scene depicted in the menu.  Events are usually some random choice based event.  One such event might go as follows:
(A giant cow is blocking your path.)
[1]  Jump on it.
[2]  Kiss it.
[3]  Smack it.
[4]  Walk away.
Depending on which answer you select, there may be consequences or rewards ranging from being damaged down to 1hp, healed to full health or being rewarded with a random item drop.  There's a wide variety of events, some more humorous than others, and plenty of loot to get from them.
Crafting:  Yes, there's crafting, and the system for it is pretty neat as well.  Using different crafting abilities, and there's many more to unlock by leveling up your crafting skill, you need to fill the progress bar while also watching your durability, heat, and quality in order to ensure better stats.
These are a few of the systems inside of both the classic SanctuaryRPG and the new SanctuaryRPG: Black Edition.  I've played quite a bit of the classic, but only just gotten ahold of a copy of the Black Edition (Thanks again, Devs :D) and look forward to seeing all the differences and rebalances.
Overall, I'd probably rate this game a good 82/100.  If you're one to enjoy text based RPGs at all, you'll more than likely enjoy this.

Holy sh!tsnacks, get this game. If you have that craving to basically be a goddamn ODST and have the most action-packed funblast ever, this is the game to play!
Your experience will consist of starting off in a just-comedic-enough tutorial that it's fun, yet still pretty much teaches you everything you need to know. In game, you start on board the bridge of your ship, and you can choose which planets to orbit over (in one of three sectors, one per available enemy type). Victories are small, but there is a community driven victory condition for everything, meaning you're never truly alone. You choose your loadout and cosmetic badassification options, head on over to one of your four laundry chutes, and drop in to action.
Each mission has different amounts and types of objectives, varying from mine defusal to hostage rescue. You drop in, complete the missions, grab any upgrades you see nearby for later, then head to extraction. Sound simple?
It's ♥♥♥♥in not, m80.
This is the Dark Souls of top-down shooters. That has multiple meanings, however.
1) Very unforgiving. You can't take many hits before dying, and only get one revive on solo. Multiplayer you must rely on your friends to call in a backup if you die (think Magicka, since Paradox also made that game).
2) DIYOW. There's so many way to take on objectives. Blaze right the ♥♥♥♥ in and hope to God that you don't get gunned down and ploughed like virgin soil, or have one guy on each point watching for patrols while one guy does the objective. It's up to you.
Now, there's one mechanic that I absolutely love, and those of you who played Magicka will remember: FOCKEN' SPELLS AND ♥♥♥♥!
Not really, but sort of. See, the way you perform tactical drop-ins like ammo and vehicles requires holding down control and performing a series of keypresses in order, ranging in complexity. Company of Heroes 2 without any DLC is a traditional RTS. With DLC, it starts to change things up a bit. I honestly really like playing this game and right off the bat, recommend you give it a shot, now let me tell you a little bit about why.
+The Graphics are astounding. The visuals during snowstorms, of any and every terrain, splendidly done.
+The sounds are near-perfect. Just about everything sounds right. From the gunfire, to the explosions, to your poor infantry unit screaming in agony as he crawls away from his dead squadron, both of his legs blown off. Someone, PLEASE SOMEONE! Just the poor guy out of his misery already!
+A truly immersive experience in terms of animations and "impact". Every unit you kill or injure. Every base or building you destroy, everything just feels right. It's satisfying, terrifying, and depressing, all at the same time. The game pulls off playing with your emotions without even trying.
+The controls are done just right for every faction to play smoothly, gameplay is quality.
-Optimized JUST poorly enough to notice unless you're packing a $2000 dollar computer.
-No multi-GPU support. So you can't even make up for that lack of optimization.
-A typical boring and aggravating campaign. It starts out fantastically, don't get me wrong, but as you get further in it feels like less effort was put into it. Towards the end you'll be begging for it to be over.
-The most annoying marketing strategy I have ever seen. $40 for the game, $20 for the US and OKW (or $13 each separately). $13 for the British. And $40 for a US campaign! Not to mention $5-$10 for misc DLC. The entire game will cost you a whopping $143 full price. Stop charging us so much for extra content when you won't even optimize the content you already have.
The game's real hit game modes are its 4v4 PvP or PvE matches. Most of my 48 hours I've played upon writing this review were spent there, and I know yours will be too if you pick this game up. I give this game an 8/10. It's fantastic, but the lack of optimization and multiGPU support, plus the lackluster campaign and ABYSMAL marketing strategy knocked it down from being the best RTS I have played in a long time. I'd still recommend it however, but do yourself a favor. Unless you have money to spare, buy this on a holiday sale. Don't fall for Relic's greedy marketing strategy if you can help it.
