The game is not hard, the puzzles are average in difficulty, but there aren't many of them: approximately 30% of the game. The rest of the gameplay is exploration, which is very rewarding because of fantastic visuals. The story is mysterious and dark, but for me was a bit confusing. Gameplay is otherwise based on detective style. The soundtrack is beautiful ambient stuff, and brought back the feeling of wandering around the mountains in Skyrim.
Overall a very impressive game: strange, weird, dark, amazingly beautiful, with a fantastic atmosphere. Now, if you will excuse me, I am off to try and mod Skyrim to look like this.

TLDR:
Pros:
1: Super powers are fun.
2: Tons of collectibles.
3: Saints of Rage.
4: Some fun new features.
5: More challenging than SR3.
Cons:
1: Feels like an SR3 expansion.
2: Over the top gameplay & humor doesn't mix well with harsh & religious profanity.
3: Radio stations/songs don't get much use.
There's a lot to like about this game but at the same time there's a lot to NOT like about it.
The super powers are a lot of fun to use. You'll be using super speed so much so that you don't listen to the radio much because you won't actually be in a vehicle. It's kinda sad really that all those songs go to waste for the most part.
If you enjoy collecting stuff then there's a lot to collect. It's mostly these "power points" that you use to upgrade your various powers. There's about 1255 points to collect, along with some other collectibles scattered throughtout the city.
UNFORTUNATELY it's the same city from Saints Row 3, which brings me to the biggest problem with Saints Row IV, and that problem is that it feels more like an expansion to Saints Row III than an actual game. You're in the same city as the last game. It has the same clothing (but somehow feels like you have fewer options, since I could not recolor some things I could in SR3).
The next issue that sucks some of the fun out of this game is that it takes itself too seriously. One moment you'll be doing some over the top carnage and having lots of fun and there's all this cornball humor and then the next your character will go spouting religious profanity. If you want something to be funny then you don't mix it with religious profanity. Sorry but that's just a big no-no. Some other expelives (namely the F-word) are said a little too harshly and it just doesn't go over well. Maybe I picked poorly when I was picking my character's voice, because she seems to be the only one ruining the normally fun experience.
Some of the missions can be fun. In particular I enjoyed the Saints of Rage bit where you play a beat-em-up game styled like Streets of Rage and other similar fighters. The game converted my character to 2D quite well (not sure how they did that, but she looked great as a 2D fighter!). I wish the Saints of Rage had been used more in the game, rather than inserted as a minor distraction during a storyline quest. Speaking of quests, the game is a lot more challenging than SR3. You can't just accumulate a bunch of levels and money so that you're immune to everything. It helps a lot, but you won't be completely immune as you were in SR3. Also, a lot of missions will nerf your abilities, which helps the game's challenge level. Hardcore is actually more meaningful and fun in SR4.
Also, there are a few fun features like being able to summon a vehicle anywhere. It helps a lot too on higher difficulties when you're low on life. It's been a serious lifesaver.
As it is, I would only suggest buying this game if you can get it bundled with all the DLC for about $10 or less. Just don't be too disappointed and pretend that it's all a big expansion for SR3. If the game's default price ever goes down to $10 I will change my recommendation to a "yes".
Hopefully with SR5 they will tone down the seriousness of some of those voices for "The Boss" or even let you pick a mute option.. just for your character. Seriously tempted to switch to the zombie voice. xD

This game feels similar to Legend of Grimrock to me, since that's the main source of experience I have with this genre, except with less puzzles and a strong RPG focus.  But despite the similarities on the surface, there are enough differences that it stands on it's own. There's a strong focus on combat, and your party has several skills, with more added as you level.  Party members have designated roles.  Tank, Healer, DPS.  It's hard to keep up with battle in real time, so basic gameplay involves a lot of pausing battles to queue up your party's skills.  Quite different from the constant dancing around and slashing I did in LoG.
The dungeon you have to explore is massive.  I recommend turning on auto-mapping in the options, even if the game doesn't recommend it.  The floors are just too big to keep in your head.
Overall, it's quite satisfying.  The downside is probably that, even with the scenery changes and new skills, most people will eventually get tired of the repetitive gameplay and won't finish this very long game.  But you'll definitely get your money's worth before then.
If you want Legend of Grimrock, but with better combat (much more tactical) and less annoying puzzles, this is the game for you.

Don't let the look fool you, this game is kinda tough! If you're good with timing your moves right, it may not be, but if you're a little impatient sometimes, it can turn into a really rough playthrough. That being said, it's a fun, challenging game with some cool little puzzles as a result. The story's not much to write home about, but the art style and music are the biggest highlights of this game.
The developers managed to bring together a variety of musicians of all sorts (including Austin Wintory of Banner Saga and Journey fame), giving each level a nice, distinct beat to match the changing environments and increasing difficulty. Even more impressive is that the sound effects of the various objects in the game complement each song, making more challenging sections even more enjoyable as you experience the full form of the background track.
The gameplay itself is pretty straightforward swimming about, grabbing objects to open doors, swiping at enemies to defeat them or to hit switches in the environment. However, much of it is interwoven with following the rhythm of certain obstacles to solve puzzles by fitting into enemy movements and/or creating openings in moving obstacles to roll with the flow to get further along. It's not hard to figure out, but getting it just right can take a few tries, and it's pretty clever design to match with the overall theme of music embedded in the game from the soundtrack to the land of Symphonia's own little mythos.
If you want a lighthearted, charming experience, that doesn't over stay its welcome too long, I highly recommend checking this out. It's lots of fun, though I might recommend a controller. =)

TL;DR section: Wizardry, Eye of the Beholder, Dungeon Master, the new Legend of Grimrock. Rings a bell? Stirs some memories? Pick it up immediately. Otherwise read on.
Note: This review has been reviewed (ugh...) after completing the game on Mercenary difficulty. The time recorded was not all spent on the game, but I'd say it took me about 60 hours in total. Due to the difficulty setting, a fair number of save/loads were needed.
Aside from the usual aspects of grid-based dungeon crawler, the game is... weird. In an interesting way.
Let me say it first, some people compare this to Legend of Grimrock - and they're not exactly right. The look and feel are rather similar, but combat mechanics here are ways deeper. The puzzles here are a lot clearer (exactly as they should be by my impression) as well.
You feel like you're in control of a party of newbs just jumped out of World of Warcraft and into some outworldly multi-tiered dungeon. But you have to control all four of them alone. And that's where the ultimate use of a tactical pause comes very handy.
The balance overall feels very fine, your DD have to manage aggro carefully, and your healer has to conserve mana (unless you run with a druid). The balance of specializations looks a tiny bit off to me at the moment but respec feature comes very handy (albeit way too limited to really employ it as a way to modify tactics on the fly).
There's no front or back row (oh thank God for that), but as such there's no way to save your casters' arses other than careful aggro management.
The mapping feature is totally awesome. When you first enter the level, you have no way to map it. When you find the first map of the level, you get an automap showing where you've been up to the point. And with the second map (usually pretty well hidden, and not on every level) comes the full map with all secrets revealed. But it's totally your choice if you want to pick up one or both of them.
Ah yes, the loot is randomized, but not totally. You will always get items fitting your charaters in their current specs (but the questions of usefulnesss still stands). The best loot (Epic and Legendary) is always hidden from plain sight. The best possible dropped loot is Rare.
Overall, I totally recommend this game to dungeon crawler fans,
I only wish the dev opened up respec for free (at least on harder difficulties where it is a necessity sometimes). And please, disable respec in mid-fight :) It feels a bit strange switching your tank and DD roles in the midst of a heated bossfight.

Well, this be my first review... Dunno how to format it but i'll try my best
Story: The game has 2 normal endings but 1 true ending, giving 3 in total. While they of course vary, there are many things which stay the same in the story such as how each character progresses. At points this makes you believe you already know all the story and what's going on after one play through, but later on the story can completely take a twist for each character. Each story does start off pretty slow, especially if you go in without any prior knowledge to the Ys series, but once the plot thickens, it thickens good. It is pretty engaging and most the characters are quite understandable and likeable.
Gameplay: I suggest you play the demo itself. On higher difficulties it can be fast paced, manic, epic and overall very enjoyable. There are a few moments in the game mind you where it can be frustrating trying to defeat a boss or enemy, because some of them are just soo cruel on the insane difficulty!.. Each character have 3 abilites they unlock through the game, each of them have their special uses for puzzle solving but also for combat, the main problem I find is that you unlock these all of these three abilites around half way, leaving not much else to unlock except for one super move or a sort per character (Which is awesome but missable) and passive abilities.
One thing which did annoy me a lot though is how vague the game could be with it's in-game instructions. For example - if you play as Yunica the game will tell you about how you can use a descending jump attack, what it DOESN'T tell you until later, after soo many chances where it could have been useful, is that the attack is capable of stunning enemies, but since the attack does little damage alone you will probably spend a lot of time playing the game without knowing this gameplay element. Neither does the game explain thrusting or how the boost meter charges quicker when you have less health (Which is really essential to know for a certain task otherwise you could be waiting about for a good 30 minutes). Now, honest maybe it did explain some of these things in the game, but if it did, it obviously didn't make it's point since i'd completed the game twice without knowing some features...
Visuals and Audio: Uh... Well this is a sorta old-ish game now, so the visuals aren't all that great for the 3D? models. Weirdly though I find the special effect in game to still look top notch, flashy and cool. The audio is fine really, I haven't much comments on it except that the OST is pretty epic and great, especially nearer to the end of the game.
Overall: Since you can, I suggest you just play the demo first, it's a great game in pretty much everyway, there are a few moments which will make you pull out your hair but otherwise the experience as a whole is brilliant for the price.

Even with its focus on Dungeon Action/Platforming, YsO is by far my favorite adventure game and story amongst Falcom's lineup currently on steam.  The dialogue and localization is fantastically written, realistic, and invests you into characters without spoon-feeding you or succumbing to many of the usual JRPG tropes. Civilization V is not a new game.  On the contrary, it's almost seven years ago.  Its sequel, Civilization VI, has been out for almost a year.  Despite that, I find myself repeatedly coming back to Civilization V to get my 4X (eXplore, eXpand, eXploit, eXterminate) strategy game fix.  Having gotten back on a Civilization kick this past week or so, I plan to review Civilization VI before too long, but before I do, I thought it would be good to go back to the game that got me full-on addicted to the series.
Civilization puts you in the role of the leader of a budding civilization, having you build from a single settler unit and a warrior unit to - hopefully - a massive empire turning the world green with envy with your religion, culture, science, economy, and military might.  The base game includes 18 unique civilizations, each with their own unique units, traits, strengths, and weaknesses.  There are two major expansions that add an additional 18 civilizations along with a few more minor DLC packs that add another seven civilizations for a grand total of 43.  It's not just the in-game differences that make these civilizations unique but the detail that went into them; every civilization leader is fully animated and complete with lines of dialogue spoken in the leader's native tongue.  For example, when interacting with the Romans, you'll see Augustus, the first Roman Emperor, fully animated with lines recorded in Latin.  When interacting with the Aztecs, you'll see Moctezuma I (no, that's not a typo) speaking Nahuatl.  While it's not exactly a work of historical fact, obviously, as a history teacher, the amount of detail that went into the leaders and their presentation makes me absolutely giddy.
Civilization V offer five different paths of victory.  Of course, you have the tried and true domination victory in which you must crush your enemies.  As of the Brave New World expansion, you must control all players' original capitals including your own to achieve a domination victory, meaning that you could technically win through domination without actually wiping out a single civilization.  Leaving them alive, however, will obviously give them incentive to retaliate and rid their capital of your filth.  You also have the option of a science victory, requiring you to complete certain research projects, build, and be the first to launch a starship to Alpha Centauri.  Cultural victory involves making your culture so vibrant and desirable through various policy upgrades (that, in turn, end up influencing your Tourism) that other civilizations' citizenry all start to prefer your culture over any other.  Diplomatic victory involves progressing to the point where the World Congress is created and then develops into the United Nations.  From there, you must attain enough votes from your own delegates as well city-states or - if they have no sense of self-preservation - other empires to be elected "world leader" by the UN.  The last victory type is the time or score victory.  Unless this victory type is disabled, whoever has the highest total score by 2050 AD (that's turn 500 on standard speed) is the winner.  Score is determined by pretty much everything - gold in your treasury, units you possess, research you've done, territory you control, the number of cities in your empire, the population of your empire....it's an exhaustive list, but the idea is straightforward - the highest score wins.  Of these various victory types, cultural is probably the most obscure due to the less-than-straightforward relation between the culture that generates your policy upgrades and the tourism stat that actually triggers the victory.
My favorite thing about Civilization is that it can be as confrontational as you want it to be.  If you want to, you can start wrecking♥♥♥♥♥♥right off the bat.  If you're more into the empire building aspect than the empire conquering aspect like me, you can build up your empire relatively peacefully, maintaining just a defensive army (or no army) and focusing on science, culture, and city growth.  Diplomacy, while having some flaws in Civ V, allows for relatively peaceful interactions as well as confrontation with various trade options and a few different kinds of pacts you can pursue with other nations.  Making all of this better is the option of playing online with a mix of people and CPUs.  My favorite thing to do is play with a couple of friends and handful of computer players and - hopefully - keep a relatively cooperative, peaceful relationship with my human counterparts.  It's a lot like Risk in that there are some backroom deals going on but unlike Risk, avoiding confrontation is a perfectly viable option.
Civilization V was, in my opinion, the absolute pinnacle of strategy game perfection at the time of its release.  As my first "main" Civilization game (excluding the spin-off Civilization Revolution), it's secured both a very special place in my heart as well as the status of being my primary point of reference when playing any other Civilization or 4X strategy game.  While there are a few areas that I think could have been improved, it's still a definite masterpiece of strategy design.  The detail of the maps, the variety of strategic and luxury resources to claim and exploit, the diplomatic aspects, the number of different victory types, and the diverse array of civilizations from which to choose all make this game truly mind blowing when you stop and think about it.  If you have any interest at all in strategy games, I'd give this one a go.  With Civilization VI having been on the market for nearly a year, Civ V isn't too pricey these days, and it's still an amazing experience, and that's even before you take into account the various (and often hilarious) mods on the Steam Workshop that you can download.  Of all the games I've recommended, this is one of the most highly recommended, hands down.

When I bought this game, I didn't expect too much. Like may be it can kill couple of hours of boredom. Most reviews are of some grand praise but how actually this could be any good, YouTube videos quite meh, nothing amusing.
So without much anticipation I picked some girl with axe and started in nightmare difficulty. Control was good and responsive; there are some instruments in your arsenal on how to wreak havoc on your enemies. However, your enemies aren’t going to watch you kill them, some immune to this, some immune to that, some shoot barrages of projectiles, some charge without rest, some come in swarms, some bestow loads of status effects. All of them share one thing: they want you DEAD RIGHT NOW.
Terrain is quite simple, however made well in its simplicity: every zone have unique feeling about it, not like “I can watch landscape forever” of course, but certainly adds to game.
Music was to my liking, which does not necessarily mean that you would like it, but this game strong point is that tracks come in huge variety. Orchestra, piano, violin, harmonica, metal, electronic stuff – game has that all. If you played through whole game and did not like a single track that would be a huuuge “WOW!” from me.
Plot is not complex and has nothing unexpected in it but still makes you feel for characters. If you’re new to YS, it would make a nice introduction, so you won’t have “what’s happening?” feelings, if you’re veteran, some why’s and what’s would be answered.
So like I said, I picked girl with axe and started playing. Shortly I came across that guy – Velagunder, he is boss of first subsection. And he killed me… repeatedly… for six hours straight… WHAT THE F…?! I sure am not “high skilled” player or something, but I was able to finish battletoads, TNMT, contra, rollergames and such titles on NES in my childhood. What is this guy? He surely is enjoying watching me struggle, shouting angry words and writhing in agony. Six hours after he decided to surrender and I was like: “YEAH! DIE! YOU ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥!!! HA! HA! HA!” running around the house like an idiot. Great feeling of completion over some pixels dead body, really not what you would have often nowadays.
And what I would like to say all of this guy's friends share his hobby. This not much anticipated game gave me hell of a journey. May be not the best game I ever played, but one of most memorable for sure. I liked it so much, so I bought other YS games available on Steam, and expecting more to come. YS is great franchise forged for over 20 years already and doing great on delivering suffering and spanking to people.
In conclusion, if you’re YS veteran, I wonder why you haven't bought it already, YS Origin lives up to YS series standards in any way possible and if you’re new to YS whatever you like this game or not is up to you but it is sure worth a try.

It's a good game, and fun. Though Falls short of Valhalla, being looked down on by other immortal Steam titles with sadness in their eyes. Knowing what could of been but never was. What was so close to perfection but blasted to beautiful shattered bits as a baseball sized diamond dropped from a skyscraper. The on-lookers still seeing the beauty, of the many fragmented pieces. Knowing with enough time, and money (approximately $3 USD a piece) the shattered bits can be made whole again.
But that beauty that once was, can never be refound. The experience cheapened by the necessity of capitalism to remake what was lost. The on-lookers slowly fading away with each piece coming together, seeing only the malignant qualities of each crude augmentation. Scratched and marred by the experience the Frankenstein, in some places kept together with electrical tape (Pointless DLC) and some spots reinforced with Steel (OP DLC=Tank) now walks the streets with the plebeian Steam games. Making friends with Payday 2, Street Fighter X Tekken, and even Evolve.
Looking up at the halls of Valhalla, A shattered mess slapped together with financial aid, Helldivers mourns the loss of the days of old.
Told of them by his father (Halo 1) and his father's father before him (Doom) who sit mighty in Valhalla. Days where a complete product was put forward for the people to enjoy. Days where a gamer by his mettle and steel could win the day! Days when some challenges were too great for the weak, and mighty warriors arose to meet the challenge (Gamers). Days where the casual was given his toys, but the games for gamers did not cater to the weak! Days where you could not simply pay your way to the top, your financial status meaning nothing to the challenges before you. A heart of steel and the courage to go on was all a gamer needed.
*A single tear falls from Helldivers eye at this moment upon his reflection.*
Evolve having no fathers dose not understand the sadness, thinking his small fetid cardboard box is how life was meant to be. Street Fighter X Tekken knows those eyes, and starts to break down into an uncontrollable sob. Pulling out from his Gi a locket, one side saying Capcom, the Other a picture of Megaman X.
*quickly drawing his samurai sword Street Fighter X Tekken commits Harakiri on the spot*
*Helldivers quickly awakens from his thoughts rushing to the aid of his friend, Evolve slinks farther back into his box as partially congealing blood absorbs into a grounded flap of his make-shift home.*
Helldivers holds his dying friend one last time and ask why, as uncontrolled tears run down his face.
Street Fighter X Tekken just smiles back as his eyes go dark, blood frothing in his mouth as he tries to breath and speak. Through the foam he croaks his last words. Words that will echo eternally in Helldivers mind during his short life, and the mind's of his creators forever.
"We are dead dreams."

So I've just completed the game. Took me almost 8 hours, a significant portion of which I've spent running around, trying to figure out what I'm supposed to do next. Fortunately the graphics are beautiful and create an interesting atmosphere.
It's a relatively new kind of genre - an exploration adventure, similar to "Gone Home". You explore the world and solve a number of relatively easy puzzles while soaking in the sights and sounds. If you've played adventure games in the 90s then you're probably overqualified when it comes to puzzle-solving. Still entertaining though.
The story is a neat little supernatural mystery. It wouldn't really stand on its own (like as a book), but fortunately it doesn't have to. The atmosphere is achieved through well-matched graphics style, sound and little stories. There's a kind of horror that relies on atmosphere rather than jump-scares - for the most part at least. It makes the game more interesting and engaging rather than making you too scared to play it. Except for one part which might get a tiny bit uncomfortable and seems a bit out of place.
Technically the game is quite solid. The graphics are basically spotless (photographed textures, skillfully put together). Unfortunately Eyefinity/Surround doesn't work out of the box, which would have been nice for people with 3 screens. Also I don't like it when first-person games don't show your legs/feet. Player movement is very basic - you can walk or run and whenever you get to a steep slope / water / any place that might get you hurt, you bumb into an invisible wall. I haven't experienced any bugs.
The one problem with the design is the save system. I won't spoil anything by telling you that the game is made up of a few puzzles / murder mysteries strewn across the world, with each puzzle occupying a very small area. The game only remembers whether you completed a puzzle or not - incomplete puzzles will not be saved! Remember that when you temporarily give up on one puzzle and move on to the next.
I bought the game when it was on sale, like 9€ or so. That was a fair price for the experience, and I hope to discover more games like it.

Headlander truely is a great game and I had a blast playing it! The concept sounded strange to me at first: You're the last survivor of mankind and the only thing left of you is... your head!? In a flying helmet, ready to mount on robot bodies?
Well, that's the story - and more, of course. You have to fight your way through a large number of security guards to uncover the secret behind it all. Your primary weapon is the ability to take control of a robot after replacing his head with your own, which requires to get close without being shot. In return, you can make use of whatever they had to fight you, namely lasers and even bigger lasers.
Robots have different security levels, designated by their color, and security areas only allow access with sufficient privileges. This brings a tactical element to the game as you need the right robots to enter secured zones. It often isn't easy to bring the respective droid where you need it in order to gain access. Sometimes, this requires thinking, sometimes it takes dexterity or fighting skills to reach your goal.
There are also hidden rooms to discover and you often find technical improvements for your helmet in them (faster movement, more energy, new abilities, and so on). These rooms normally can't be reached with a robot, so they require you to fly using your helmet only. Altogether, I really enjoyed finding all of them and figuring out how to get there.
Fighting is rather easy and there are multiple ways to defeat your enemies. You can shoot off their heads and take over their bodies, you can destroy them with your laser or ram and beat them, resulting in an overload. Your laser beams reflect off walls (as do theirs) to shoot around corners and there are different patterns of laser fire, depeding on the weapon model (single, double, triple, fractal, and so on). However, when you destroy a robot, it will respawn some time later, so it's best to shoot off their heads and leave their torsos standing around.
The very best about this game is the whole presentation. It's like the modern version of a 70s sci-fi movie. Robots are much like people imagined them to be back then, with humurous AI, big guns, following some simple program. Also the graphic style is very clear and polished. It somehow reminds me of the new Star Trek movies trying to resemble the original look, but with modern CGI. Additionally, the menu and loading screens have an awesome retro touch, just like an old 8 bit Atari game (but somehow modern again). The music much reminds me of the Tron 2 soundtrack and adds a great atmosphere.
Here are the pros and cons in my eyes:
- Interesting story
- Great presentation
- Modern retro look
- Atmospheric soundtrack
- Good humor (I just say door AI)
- Excellent playability - responsive controls for keyboard / mouse AND controller
- Fluent gameplay at steady 60 fps
- Solid and bugfree (I didn't experience a single crash or any other issue)
- Borderless fullscreen window mode
- Moderate difficulty (mostly easy fights, nice riddles)
- Some challenging achievements
- Lift positions may require longer detours as you can't enter the lift from all sides in certain positions (actually the only thing that annoyed me a little)
- Being such a quality game, I wish it would be longer (it's not really short though, I completed it in 18 hours without rushing)

Put on those bell-bottoms, let your hair down, and let’s groove in Headlander, a game from the masterminds at Double Fine Productions, published by Adult Swim Games. I’m Weise, aka Thomas, and I’d like to invite you to join me in this retro-futuristic, side-scrolling, action-adventure game set in a world inspired by 70’s science fiction. Be sure to check out my other reviews on the channel and watch me live at
.
Welcome to the future, a utopia for humans, who have all gave up their bodies to live in robot suits that allow them to be immortal, free from disease, free from harm, and so much more. But they are NOT as free as they thought! The evil AI ruler of the utopia Methuselah has actually enslaved humanity and can control these robot-human hybrids.
You are humanity’s last hope, possibly the only person with an all human head, preserved in a futuristic space helmet that resembles the head jars from Futurama. You must land on various heads (hence the name of the game), taking control of the robots to move through the world and take down Methuselah, freeing humanity from her control.
When you start the game, you are merely a head in a helmet, able to fly around through a propulsion mechanism within the helmet itself. In a kind of RPG style, you unlock various abilities as you play through a skill tree menu which will allow you to do things like rip off the heads of robots walking around, have a higher durability so you take less damage, and much more.
Early on, you are introduced to a core gameplay element that almost acts like a light puzzle mechanic. Various security doors have color codes that will only open for guards of the same color. So for example, if you want to get through a red door, you need to take over the body of a red robot guard, shoot his phaser at the door, and walk through. There are security levels, so some higher ranked “colors” will allow you to pass through the lower rank ones as well. Through this means, you can progress through more and more of the world, completing side quests along the way as you continue down the path to save humanity.
Visually this game blew me away. Double Fine Productions did a fantastic job setting the theme of this as a retro-70’s futuristic world. Throughout your travels, you’ll come across disco dance parties, robots with afro heads, bell bottoms, and so much more. The 70’s disco theme is present throughout the entire game and is extremely fluid.
The detail in the phasers, the robots themselves, the environment and destructible cover elements is just perfect and I couldn’t have asked for more.
When you play Headlander, you are given a COMPLETE game that sets you in the world of this futuristic 70’s sci-fi environment. As mentioned with the visuals, the audio sets the scene perfectly from the start with a retro feel, that’s groovy and hip and makes you want to boogie.
Take that soundtrack and match it with great voice acting and you have a winning combination. Earl, the voice in your helmet that guides you throughout the game, was casted perfectly and the scripting and lines used are wonderful. Your character is a mute, but all the citizens, err, robot citizens, have their own voices as well and truly have some character behind them.
Finally, the sound effects are just great. Overall, they did an amazing job with the audio here. The blasters sound right, the destructible environment sounds right, ripping off the head of a robot sounds right, it’s just really a pleasant experience all around.
Replay-ability is really the only area this game is lacking. It’s a fairly short game overall, and even if you wanted to 100% the game with all the achievements, it can be done in less hours than some may prefer. But honestly, the quality over quantity phrase is key here for me. This game was very enjoyable from start to finish for me and well-polished.
The main replay-ability mechanic would be to complete the game with 100%, finishing all the side quests and getting every achievement. While this is fine, it really doesn’t leave much to come back for outside of just enjoying the mechanics of the game, and I do wish there was a little more to do.
Overall, I definitely suggest picking up this game, if not at full price, on a sale. To me, it’s worth playing through due to the high quality and polish of the game. Again, there is not much replay-value to be had unless you are an achievement hunter and want to 100% the game, but it is a very fun experience that played to my metroidvania nostalgia in a fun world that felt complete all the way through. As always, I’ll have all the relevant links in the description below. You can watch me play this and other great games live at
. I’ve been Weise, aka Thomas, and I thank you for watching.

Headlander is quite a unique take on the 2.5D side-scroller genre. By cramming the player into a head rather than a full character, the game opens up many opportunities for combat and exploration. Why destroy an enemy when you can just take over their body?
The level design in this game is quite good. There is room for combat, for puzzles, and for secrets. Everything is aesthetically pleasing and keeps one big theme in mind all the time, and that is 1970s retro-futurism. The game captures the style of the 70s perfectly and never misses a detail in its style. Along with its style, the game also maintains a humorous approach to some things which makes the game more enjoyable.
The writing of the game's story is also top-notch, Characters have their own interesting personalities and feel alive. The way the story develops deliberately leaves you aware of the present but completely confused about the lore, because that is the same way the character, a 20th century man awoken from cryostatis would feel like.
The drawbacks in this game are:
1. Backtracking is very common. For example, the player finds a locked door, so they need to go to a branching hallway and cross 5 rooms full of enemies to flip a switch after they flip a switch, they have to run back through all the five rooms with all the enemies re-spawned back in their places as if the player never touched them.
2. Combat is functional but not satisfying, instead it feels like a chore. The slow paced combat often involves standing in one place, shooting at an enemy, shifting a little to the side and then continuing the firing until the enemies are dead. WIth the constant respawning of enemies, this eventually gets annoying.
In conclusion,, this game is not legendary, and will not be remembered for decades. But, regardless of that, the entertainment value is really good and a purchase on sale is a really good idea.

Note: I am playing on a laptop with an integrated GPU (Intel HD 4300). The game is not smooth but it does run. For this type of game, a smooth framerate is not needed (although it would certainly add to the experience).

TLDR: If you like dungeon crawlers (as I do) this one is totally worth picking up. Its not as much of a masterpiece as Dungeon Master or Legend of Grimrock, but its still really good.
The plot - its your first day as a guard at a dungeon where the worlds worst inmates are kept. Theres a brief intro, during which you can create a character as you go down the elevator to your post, talking to a trustee of some kind. You can also skip the intro, and after viewing it once, Id recommend you skip it as you get much more control over the initial character's (the one that's "you") creation that way. Of course, something goes horribly wrong once you settle into your bunk for the night...First day on the job and something has happened. All the prisoners were let out and have fled into the tunnels around the dungeon complex. The fat a**hole warden assigns you to go get them back, along with 3 other guards. The dungeon must be attached to Undermountain or something...because the starting intro looks like you're going down into Black Mesa and this place is HUGE. Who goes "yeah, lets build a dungeon with the worlds worst criminals next to tunnels into god knows where". Apparently, these guys.
You have 4 char slots to fill, a tank, a healer, and two damagers. The races are basic fantasy, human, dwarf, elf, dark elf, and halfling. Theres also 4 classes Warrior, mage, healer and rogue. However, each class has 3 subclasses, which provides a slightly different take on that type of class. For instance, a healer Druid relies on strong HoT spells, a Priest has instant but weaker straigh heals and protection spells and a healer Necromancer's skills rely on pulling health from the enemy to heal. The subclass options are really cool. I like all the different options, theres pretty much a party for every playstyle.
One thing I really like is the Duelist - a Rogue tank that relies on speed and quickness to avoid being hit along with "threat boosting" techniques to tank. Thats way cooler than your stereotypical "brick in platemail" tank.
Combat can be confusing at first but is cool once you get the hang of it. Space pauses, like Baldur's Gate, and you can queue up to 3 abilities per party member. You can pause at any time, which is great and avoids the step dance annoyance of games like LoG (a great dungeon crawler in its own right). Abilities run on cooldowns like WoW or Diablo, and as your characters level, you get to choose talents from a talent tree to improve your arsenal of abilities. I just wish that when targeting enemies, the "red aura" around the enemy to show they are targeted was a different color for each player and appeared every time you paused. Its annoying to have to remember who was attacking where in the heat of battle, as all that it shows is a red glow over the enemy being targetted..
Graphics are good for the genre,  and sounds are your typical dungeon noises, bumps, sword clangs, spells firing grunts and so on. The writing isnt great, but Ive seen much worse. Hey, at least your characters talk amongst themselves, and really, people dont play dungeon crawlers for the dialogue. Its servicable, and (IMHO) its much better than crawlers with no dialogue at all.
This is a solid dungeon crawler, and Id recommend it for any fans of the genre. I love grid based realtime dungeon crawlers, and there hasnt been much decent to speak of lately in the genre besides the two LoGs. This one is totally worth it, and I love the addition of the "action pause" combat. I dont know how many times I got frustrated by LoG/LoG II because my disability prevented me from playing in realtime as smoothly as the game wanted me to, THotDG solves all that

It's a pretty solid dungeon crawler, and it's well thought out to capture a large audience. Beginners in the genre, such as myself, will find an extensive tutorial and pick a easy level of difficulty, allowing them to get going without frustration, while seasoned players can skip the tutorial and choose a much harder level (there are 6 level of difficulty if I remember correctly).
Of course you'll find most of the genre's commonplaces right there as you expect them - from the visual style to the types of objects, the gameplay mechanics, etc. This has caused some people to blame the lack of originality, but at the same time, had the game departed too much from these standards, people would have complained about it (or simply been turned away) as well. So I think the developer made the right choices.
All in all, a solid recommendation if you're attracted to dungeon crawlers, whether or not you're skillful at them.

I greatly enjoyed The Room, and I was looking forward to its sequel. I will say that while the storyline is much creepier than that of The Room 1, it raises more questions than it answers and leaves the player wanting to know more at the end. I think The Room 1's strength was its focused gameplay; The Room 2 is a little more disjointed and some of the puzzles seem to be a bit forced. At one point you have to charge several batteries, and the charging mechanism's fuse blows, forcing you to search for another one. You don't unlock anything new in the course of doing so; it seems to exist merely to create more busywork for the player--"go here and do a thing, now come back and do the thing you were trying to do in the first place." I want to solve puzzles, not change lightbulbs.
That gripe aside, it's a very fun game and immersive in its own way. While it's not as intensely gripping as the first Room installment, it retains the charm of the original in quite a few ways. I would say if you liked the first Room and you're not adverse to parting with the cost of a large latte, go ahead and buy this game.

Unlike the first installment, this one—for some reason—loves busywork, making you repeat the same puzzles (like the typing one) several times. Unlike the first installment, this one goes for a number of settings—that feel like completely separate levels. Unlike the first installment, this one tries a mystery/psychological plot, forgetting that the plot in a puzzle game of this type operates strictly on a "less is more" basis. Unlike the first installment, that gave you a single box each time, this one gives you a whole room, making puzzles feel more convoluted and game-y.
Unlike the clockwork meditation of the first installment, this one is merely a fine puzzle game. It's fun, but feels more technical than the previous one due to being aesthetically disjointed. A collection of levels rather than a single experience. It also goes after more direct horror.
It's good. I had fun playing it. I probably would have loved it, had I not seen the fine-tuned brilliance of the first installment—that felt more whole, had better puzzles, and had courage to be a focussed experience without unnecessarily increasing its scope.
Still, if you like the genre, you have every chance to enjoy this one.

A Story About My Uncle is a very decent game. The visuals in this game has landed it as one of the prettiest and dreamlike 3D games I've ever played. There are certain shots and levels that are so vibrant and colorful that you really can't help but appreciate the amount of work put into making the environments look so awesome. A game like this would be excellent on the Occulus Rift.
Platforming is the core gameplay, and it can be as fun as it is frustrating at times. The grapple beam, jumps, and boosts are exciting mechanics, especially with the scale of the world your make you way through.
That said, this -is- a first person platformer and there -are- definitely those sigh moments when you miss certain landings. But I didn't find it too difficult, and I enjoyed the ride far more than I was annoyed with it at certain points.
Story wise, it's not all that complex. That isn't a bad thing at all, and despite how linear it is, more narrative and story is available to those who take the time to explore and examine, and that's a major plus. There's a lot of heart in what it presents, and I thought it was really cute. Voice acting is okay/could be better, but it's not awful.
This is definitely a shorter game, and while that's nothing to really fault it on, I still feel like there was the potential to get more for it to get across than it did. The conclusion is nice, but it's a little too sudden for my taste. There isn't a whole lot of closure.
Still, I vouch for this game. It's fun, it's pretty, and it's a running blast through a dreamy world. Check it out when it's on sale.

Everyone talking about how GUUH SERVER NO WORK is forgetting the best part of this game--it's not the singleplayer, it's not the multiplayer, it's *coop* [mostly terrorist hunt].
The map design in this game is deceptively interesting in coop. Chokepoints and crouching terrorists with SMGs or Shotguns will kill you instantly, but if you're working in a team of 2 - 4 the game becomes totally different and many times more fun. You need to make careful use of incidental cover and suppressing fire in order to actually survive, and you have to flash/smoke and clear tough doorways [almost] every time.
The damage that enemies can deal means that you have to engage on careful terms, and it's actually important to log what weapons enemies have based on sound cues. Facing 3 guys with UMP45s at medium range? Great, solid easy engagement. Same range, but 3 guys with SCAR CQCs? Suddenly a lot more dangerous, as SCARs have more punch.
More importantly, the AI is deceptively smart. They'll flank you, lure you forwards with easy enemies, stay quiet so you leave cover, and more. The only hitch is that if you stay in one doorway and make noise, they'll continually walk through the doorway and die. This isn't super feasible except on a couple of maps, and it's the best way to grind. But don't--the game is so much more fun otherwise.
Let me summarize: Coop is fun because it's hard and you have to take it slow, unlike virtually every game released in the last 10 years. Small squad tactics are *actually feasible* because of the enviornment, and minus a couple of instances of 'he should've been flashed!' things usually roll along pretty well. Even when you've run the maps dozens of times, they're still capable of presenting challange because of how many open routes they provide.
When they get CD-Keys, it's $10, which is a steal without a sale. Give it a look!

One of the most original premises out there. Play as a flying head that docks onto robots exploring a metroidvania 80s themed future space station with groovy music and rad graphics? Sign me up! *Terms and conditions apply unfortunately.
The gameplay is unique to say the least. You fly around as a disembodied head with jets at your neck and dock into robots of various colors. The color of your robot determines where you can go in the level as there are gates that are color coded and only robots with access level of a certain color or higher can cross those doors and this is mostly where the metroidvania aspect mostly resides. You traverse the levels in search of the next access level robot to go through the levels that you know are gated and repeat until you unlock the purple(?) robots which unlock every single door in the game being the highest access level. You can also unlock various powerups for your head which allow you to boost when flying, suck more powerfully with your vacuum suck (???) and transform the robots you take over by giving them shields or making them into sentries or turrets.
Though the flying and exploration aspects of the game are pretty fun, the combat is not great honestly. The aiming on the robots is not precise and most of the time you'll simply shoot in the general direction of the enemies hoping to hit them. You have the option to aim but some enemies have some quirky hitboxes which mean you won't always hit them or hit them in places you don't expect. You'll also get caught in rooms that have been FILLED with bullet particles from various enemies shooting at you and their bullets bouncing off the walls which has lead me to many deaths over the course of my playthrough. You'll mostly want to keep pushing on to explore the rest of the game but this gets frustrating sometimes.
The graphics are SUPER trippy with lots of rainbow LSD-esque effects and wild colors. The bullets all leave particle trails that may sometimes overwhelm you. The detail in the levels is very well executed with the 70s-80s theme shining through on almost every room you'll explore. Suffice it to say, the art direction is one of the best parts of the game. There are also a LOT of attempts at dirty humour which are amusing at times.
There are problems though. The BIGGEST caveat when playing this game is the fact that it feels unfinished. There are only 2 major bosses in the game and when defeating the second one, the game ends ABRUPTLY. There's very little resolution and you'd find yourself wanting more of the game yet the only thing left to do is find any rooms you might have missed to get 100% completion. There is definitely a feeling that a lot of the areas in the levels were gutted due to restrictions in time or budget. There are 2 major exploration levels with one of them less than half the size of the other and one linear map which is essentially a path straight to the boss. The whole game takes about 6-8 hours to complete 100% including every single achievement which seems really small. The side missions are INCREDIBLY dumb and are simply "go here -> collect thigs/kill things" and there are WAY too few of them. I hope at some point the devs release the game with some dlc to fill the empty areas as was done with Ori and the Blind Forest.
At the normal price point, this may not seem worth it for a game that's just 6-8 hours of content. I bought it at 70% off and at that price it was DEFINITELY worth the cost. I suggest waiting for a sale for the game only due to the lack of content. Whatever you pay, the time you spend will definitely be an enjoyable one.

If you have just watched the Steam preview videos and are wondering if the game is any fun... it is!
Build a party of four, go explore, kill things, gather loot. Everything is set on a grid, but the game plays in real-time, though you can pause it at any time by hitting space. In combat this is more or less a requirement to keep track of what's happening.
I'm playing on Warrior difficulty (1 up from default), and there you really have to pick your battles. If you just burst into a room and charge the first monsters you see, chances are that you will get flanked by another patrol. Elite and Boss monsters really require some thought into how to counter their special moves.
There are 12 classes in the game, with 3 variations of 4 base classes: Warrior, Rogue, Cleric and Mage. Each class has a primary role in the party: the Tank-Healer-Damage trinity, though each class has different skills that can change how they fulfill their role. A Ranger is pretty good at dealing ranged damage to a single target, while a Man-At-Arms might be better at dealing melee damage to a group, and a Warlock is has more of a focus on weaking enemies with damage over time.
I like that there are some interesting class choices. For example: the healer in my party is a Necromancer, who suck the life out of his enemies to heal his allies.
For a game that was just released and developed by a single person, I am impressed with how well done and stable it is.
I've recorded some gameplay footage of the early game to show what the game is about:
Update 1, 3 weeks after my initial review: the developer has done a great job supporting the game after release. Bugs and balance issues have been resolved, and a lot of nice quality of life features have been added.
Update 2, another 3 weeks have passed: I have reached dungeon level 6, and the level design is still varied, with every level "feeling" different from the previous one. Every level adds a few new monsters to the roster, slowly increasing the variety and complexity of combat encounters. The game has definitely increased in difficulty, making it a pretty good challenge on Warrior difficulty (1 up from normal).

Please note the following points before reading the rest of my review:
- I haven't finished the game yet. I'm through slightly more than 50% of the Dungeon levels, which is probably a little less than 50% of the total playtime, since the first few levels were less complex.
- I have more playtime than I can reasonably have accumulated on release day. I've bought the game through the developers' shop and activated it on Steam a few days ago. I didn't receive a review copy but instead paid full price. So this review is by no means biased by having gotten something for free. ;)
Now that that's out of the way back to the game:
Gameplay:
First and foremost it is a grid based dungeon crawler that apparently draws significant inspiration from genre classics like Dungeon Master. There are no outdoor areas. The game (in contrast to for example earlier Might and Magic titles) is played in real time, meaning monsters will move and act even when the player doesn't do anything, but here an active pause function was implemented. This allows for a much more tactical combat experience than can be found in some other, more 'retro-ish' dungeon crawlers like Might and Magic X Legacy or Legend of Grimrock for example, where modern computer RPG features like active pause, hotkeys and quickbars where deliberately ommited to provide a gameplay experience closer to "the classics of old". Also in other regards there are nice comfort features that you could use. For example when you mouse-over a key on the map screen the place where you picked it up will be highlighted on the map. (EDIT: In my original review I mentioned at this place, that progress-relevant items like keys can potentially be almost invisible on the ground IF dropped in a very dark corner of a room falling close to a gap or stairs for example. This has since be fixed by a patch implementing an optional highlighting option for dropped loot, which can be switched on in the options ... just making the game even better.)
The only thing I'm not so sure about is the number of classes. Since I'm still in my first playthrough it's hard to say, but there are only four classes. Even though the skill trees are quite varied and for example the man at arms may be played as a damage dealer or a tank... For longevity I think some more exotic classes would have been nice. (To be fair however: The classes in this game are MUCH more complex than in other retro-ish dungeon crawlers and I guess balancing additional classes would be quite a bit of work ... but still, would be nice. ;) )
Visuals:
Overall the game provides a quite modern look while still reproducing the atmosphere in classic dungeon crawlers. If I were to compare The Fall of the Dungeon Guardians to other recent high profile grid based dungeon crawlers I'd say it's mostly on par with them, though if you are really looking at them comparing little details there might be a very minor lack of polish here. (One example would be: At the start of the game you go down to the bottom of the dungeon via elevator passing multiple levels and also some cross-bracings ... and that's where the edge of the platform merely clips brazenly through the cross bracings. ;) ) Once the intro sequence was over and I started playing I quickly got absorbed in the game to the point where I completely stopped noticing these miniscule hickups which are VERY rare anyway. The only thing that got a little bit 'more' negative after playing the first three levels was the lack of variety in wall textures within one texture set, which became apparent once I started spending more time searching for hidden switches, but I'd just say it's "noticeable, but not problematic". The different sets after clearing a few levels are very varied though and all are incredibly pretty and convey a very different atmosphere every time you change the 'area'.
Also the spell effects and illumination look very nice. It's just incredible when you play in a dimly lit room and rain down fire on an entire group of enemies, temporarily lighting up everything just to see the ash of your incinierated foes fall to the ground while the dungeon (and your room) returns to it original lighting conditions.
Sound design:
The sounds works very well with the game and overall the ambient soundeffects are very atmospheric and do a great job forming the overall positive picture.
Bugs:
The only one I'm still having right now is that 5.1 digital surround sound via HDMI (from an nvidia GTX 970) doesn't work, but that's a Unity thing: Search their developer support Forums and you'll find out that most developers ultimately "fix" the problem by using an original Creative Labs Soundblaster card, because the audio component of Unity just is very, very bad.
Two other minor problems I had were so little I might not have noticed them had I not deliberately looked for problems. One was fixed before I could report it and the other one was addressed by the developer right away, who by the way is very responsive and friendly.
Conclusion: (note: this is prelminary, since I haven't finished the game!)
The Fall of the Dungeon Guardians is a lot of fun. It's by no means an easy game, but it offers very comprehensive difficulty settings, which will allow the most casual of players to still enjoy the game while pure masochists will be served just as well. The atmosphere of the game quickly sucked me in. The representation of the deep dungeon and the sense of being lost in those tunnels ist just that strong and from what I've played so far I truly think it might just be one of the best grid based dungeon crawlers of the last few years.
(Also note that the game offers a map editor, but I didn't have time to check it our yet.)

My first impressions are good. This is as close as it gets to the original Dungeon Master experience I had on Atari ST back in the days - only with more up to date graphics/sounds/display. Obviously there's no AAA production values to be found here, but that's not what you come here for. You come for the thrill of not knowing what you're going to stumble upon as you roam through the dungeon, sometimes carefully planning your moves, sometimes indulging into leaps of faith as you dash through.
The ability to pause the game at any time makes the combat system both easier and more tactical - there's less of an urge to blow any damage right away, and more of an incentive to choose your strikes wisely.
You can save your game at any point, which diminishes the frustration of making a wrong move - to the extent that you saved before! Perhaps the real wrong move is in not saving regularly :).
I have only been playing in the easiest difficulty level so far and didn't receive life-threatening damage, so I cannot comment on the game difficulty yet. But there's a large amount of difficulty levels to choose from so I assume that you'll find whichever difficulty suits you best.

Yeah, I'll admit. I played it on easy. That doesn't mean it WAS easy. I died, time and time again. I eventually got to the point where I could consistently (maybe 60%) beat it, depending on ship choice and store luck. It didn't click with me, at first. I played it for a few hours, then put it down for a couple years. When I finally decided to invest the time, I found a rewarding game of surprising depth.
Each play is different, even with the same ship. Sure, there are modules you always want to have for the final boss, leading to similar tactics for that specific fight, but the interesting part (for me) was balancing progression strategy (getting to the final boss) with preparation for the final boss, itself. These are often conflicting goals, since a ship built for progression might not be any good at all for the final battle. I think that dynamic, right there, is what makes this game so intriguing to me.
It's not for everyone, though. If you just want to play a casual spaceship simulator, this will leave you unsatisfied. If you want to play "savior of the galaxy, against all odds", look no further.

FTL: Faster Than Light is easily one of the most entertaining (if sometimes frustrating) games I have ever played on Steam. It is simple to learn, but difficult to master, with engaging story events often driven by a wry sense of humor, nail-biting tactical combat, and a tremendous amount of customization and unlockable content available.
As a rogue-like, every game is different. You know generally about how strong enemies in each of the 8 sectors you'll fly through will be, but you have no idea what order you will come across specific resources - vital system add-ons, powerful weapons, additional crew members, all of which are eventually needed - or what specific hazards you will face on your way there. In order to deal with this, two things are required: 1, you have to cultivate a unique and flexible strategy for each ship you play, capitalizing on its strengths and your own personal playstyle to achieve the most desirable results. 2, you have to accept that you will still die a lot, no matter how confident you are in your skills, because it is a rogue-like.
But that's part of what makes it so engaging. Unable to revisit saved states, you have to learn to play the game better; and every defeat demands you to improve by sending you to an entirely new set of events and challenges when the game restarts. A typical game might go something like this: "Okay, I've got a ship with limited offensive capabilities, but an incredibly durable defense system. So, instead of focusing on upgrading weapons just yet, I'm going to upgrade sub-systems in order to improve my chances of winning a random event and getting better rewards that way. In a few sectors, I can turn the profit into a better weapon system, and pad my crew out as I go." Two sectors later - if you survive - you now have to make a new decision about what to prioritize based on how exactly the last two played out: "I didn't get as many crew as I wanted, but I did get a nice weapon. I think my ship can handle itself for the next sector, so let's save up some cash and try to hire a crew member at the next store." But can your ship handl itself? What if it is suddenly boarded - do you have a provision for that? Your crew count is awfully low, after all - do you hope that no such scenarios take place, or do you lose money you could spend on crew by investing in stronger blast doors?
The choice is yours. There is rarely one clearly correct answer, which is what makes you feel like you really are a desperate, desolate captain of a doomed crew trying everything in your power. The feeling upon victory of "Oh my god I can't believe I made it, this is incredible!" that one feels, as such a captain should feel, is genuine. The game makes you work for it and then rewards you with genuine relief and joy at your success.
I have sunk more hours than I care to admit into this endlessly entertaining and challenging game, and I haven't even tried it on hard mode yet. With the recent addition of an entirely new species, along with cloning, mind control, new weapons, new ship layouts, new random events and hacking drones, I doubt I will get bored for a long, long time.

I played this game in the course of a free weekend, I have not tried multiplayer, since I don't like the multiplayer experience per se, so there are only a couple of things I can point at.
I really love the sound design, and the pacing of the game - it's uncomfortable, loud, hectic, complicated… it's hell, and I suppose it's intended to feel like that. (well, that's what you get for signing up to defend Stalingrad, I guess)
The single-player campaign is either a sign of supreme storytelling or very bad game-design, depending on how much one likes the developer. Most of the time, the mission is on rails, just endlessly spawning enemies until you move to the next waypoint. At other times, winning a mission or losing it are literaly paces apart - no matter if your men make it to the strategic bridge in time, they all die - but when they almost reach the bridge, you win.
Generally, I don't like the feeling of being played by a game, but again - this could be a clever way to make one feel the ambivalence, brutality and unfairness of the conflict portraied.
Either way, I could not take more than two missions in succession - not only because the game crashed every two missions, but also because the tense atmosphere and the utter inability to make any difference really put a strain on me.
Bottom line is - this game isn't fun, it's intense, unfair, ambivalent and hectic. If you want to see games as art, it's probably a good portayal of the conflict.
Things I liked:
Great atmosphere.
Awesome sound design.
Customisation and Mod-support.
Nice campaign, compelling cutscenes, good storytelling.
Things I didn't like:
No Windowed mode - very annoying for multiscreen users.
Didn't find a way to configure controls - I'd like to scroll using WASD
Middle-click scroll is broken and frequently takes you random places.
Ambivalent and illogical mission design.
Completely on rails as far as I've seen it.
Inconsistant loading breaks, did not find a pause-function.
Cluttered and almost incomprehensible user interface.
The game is quite a upgrade compared to the original.
Creepy atmosphere, enteraining story, with a nice blend of desperate action.

Too big to run across, so they give you an offroad buggy to run over fields of zombies with.  I think the story in part 1 was better than part 2, but both stories were great. You can even slide down a pipe like Mario to play a Dying Light version of Mario, albeit very short, but still, its just one of the many crazy easter eggs that are hidden throughout the game.
They just started releasing 10 additional pieces of free DLC not too long ago because they realized that, like myself, others haven't stopped coming back to play this game cause its so fun.  As far as I know, however, it has been relative fluff so far.  Nothing substantial.  A few new monsters/enemies who are supposedly tougher and smarter.  I am hoping that one of them is something substantial, like a new map, new characters to deal with, new 20 hours of story.
And, like everything, lets get to the bad part.
There isn't a dying light sequel and its been years.  And they haven't mentioned anything in the works.  COME ON TECHLAND.
Good Night.  Good Luck.

The Room is a interactive puzzle game, a sequel to the first game, which was a hit, The Room, which was released in 2014. The Room Two's theme is more deeper, darker, scarier and more mysterious. I have played the first game, and I absolutely loved it. After the first game leaved me with a lot of questions that needed answers, i couldn't resist the urge to play the sequel. And I don't regret playing The Room Two, i loved it more than the first game.
Pros:
+Graphics were amazing and stunning. I specially loved the detail, those made the game look even more gorgeous.
+The Sounds were amazing. The sounds were very effective emotionally also. Specially when you advance to a new chapter, the sounds gave me chills down my spine, just like in a horror game. And the music at the menu is very relaxing and feels a bit mysterious.
+New puzzles, no puzzle were similar to the first game, which was very good indeed. The mechanics of the puzzles were more complicated, which i really liked it.
+The Story. The story is amazing, it feels like you are a part of it. Specially when "The Craftsman" writes notes to you. Kind of breaks the forth wall, at least it felt like it.
+The milieu is more complicated than the first game. You litearly go through space and time, which is cool.
+A very good game for it's pricetag.
Cons:
-After i played The Room Two and went trough the ending, I was still left with questions (I would give examples but I don't wanna give spoilers to new players). Hopefully the devs make a sequel to this game.
-The game was relatively brief. Make it a bit longer.
In conclusion:
The Room -series is not only a game, it's art. This, is something we gamers don't see everyday. The Room is very unique, and it has managed to pull me to the point i didn't want to stop playing, because i was deep into the story and the game itself, its addictive. I highly recommend this to everyone who likes puzzles and mysteries.
Final Rating: 9.5/10

FTL is one of those games you either love or hate. Or sometimes you love to hate it. Or hate to love it.
Overall, a really fun, difficult, cheap game with an awesome soundtrack and tons of replayability.
In FTL, your mission is simple: take your crew and spaceship through a series of hostile space sectors and defeat a Rebel Flagship to beat the game. However, surviving the trip to the final sector and destroying the Flagship is painstakingly difficult. The game has an insanely steep learning curve, and you will spend hours and hours just trying to survive.
There is a lot of info to process: various weapon systems, each with their own pros and cons, oxygen management, enemy boarding crews, shields, balancing power usage, making smart upgrades, which systems you choose to man with crewmembers, different crewmember races, and much more.
Despite the initial difficulty, you will quickly find yourself learning the ins and outs of the game. Progress is earned, not given, and nothing feels better than finishing the game for the first time. There is always something new to learn and to improve upon, and new ships and ship layouts are unlocked via unique quests and objectives - the game has tons of replaybilty.
Highly recommend.

The weirdest thing about Headlander is that you can't jump. Can you imagine completing a Castlevania without jumping? Bionic Commando didn't let you jump, but it had the bionic arm. There is no bionic arm in Headlander. There are short range teleporters, but otherwise your legs are simply for moving left and right. Except, at any point in time, you can pop your head off of whatever robot body you're currently inhabiting and fly around. I guess that's pretty weird too, now that I think of it.
In Headlander, you are a disembodied head. You have a little thrust rocket and not much else at the start. You progress in the game by attaching yourself to headless robot bodies with varying abilities. There's an experience point system, and you can upgrade your head's abilities. By the end of the game, you'll have more abilities than you'll know what to do with. The story kind of gets a little lost, but the gist of it is that you might be the last surviving human after everyone has uploaded their brains to robot bodies, but an AI named Methuselah has taken control of them and you have to stop him.
Headlander does this all within a beautifully realized 70's sci-fi style. Funk. Rooms with shag carpeting all over. An early area known as "the Pleasure Port", which is full of sexual overtones without ever doing anything get in trouble with a ratings board. Every enemy shoots lasers, and they bounce around the room. Trippy colors everywhere. Every non-combat robot body can dance. I didn't grow up in the 70's but it all seems very spot-on. It's a fun to explore world with a lot of what we expect out of a Metroidvania.
Where it loses some shine is that there's a real lack of enemy variety. It's mostly humanoid robots that stand still and shoot bouncing lasers at you. After you learn how to aim for their heads as a reflex, they don't offer much challenge. You also get the ability to pop the heads off of enemy robots while disembodied early on, which is a quick way to disarm them if you're not actively being shot at by other robots. There are a couple more enemy types that show up late in the game, and some with defense against having their heads immediately removed, but they're rare. It's also a fairly short game, but that's less of a complaint and more of a welcome sight that the game won't overstay its welcome.
However, beginning to end, Headlander is good, weird fun. There's a moment halfway through that I won't even begin to spoil that literally made me laugh out loud and it reminded me that these moments are what Double Fine does best, even if the gameplay has a few kinks. Headlander's a pick-me-up for a boring weekend.

I played this game in the course of a free weekend, I have not tried multiplayer, since I don't like the multiplayer experience per se, so there are only a couple of things I can point at.
I really love the sound design, and the pacing of the game - it's uncomfortable, loud, hectic, complicated… it's hell, and I suppose it's intended to feel like that. (well, that's what you get for signing up to defend Stalingrad, I guess)
The single-player campaign is either a sign of supreme storytelling or very bad game-design, depending on how much one likes the developer. Most of the time, the mission is on rails, just endlessly spawning enemies until you move to the next waypoint. At other times, winning a mission or losing it are literaly paces apart - no matter if your men make it to the strategic bridge in time, they all die - but when they almost reach the bridge, you win.
Generally, I don't like the feeling of being played by a game, but again - this could be a clever way to make one feel the ambivalence, brutality and unfairness of the conflict portraied.
Either way, I could not take more than two missions in succession - not only because the game crashed every two missions, but also because the tense atmosphere and the utter inability to make any difference really put a strain on me.
Bottom line is - this game isn't fun, it's intense, unfair, ambivalent and hectic. If you want to see games as art, it's probably a good portayal of the conflict.
Things I liked:
Great atmosphere.
Awesome sound design.
Customisation and Mod-support.
Nice campaign, compelling cutscenes, good storytelling.
Things I didn't like:
No Windowed mode - very annoying for multiscreen users.
Didn't find a way to configure controls - I'd like to scroll using WASD
Middle-click scroll is broken and frequently takes you random places.
Ambivalent and illogical mission design.
Completely on rails as far as I've seen it.
Inconsistant loading breaks, did not find a pause-function.
Cluttered and almost incomprehensible user interface.
This game is fun!

A Story About My Uncle is a platform game where you guide the protagonist through another, alien dimension in the search of his adventurer uncle Fred. You can take advantage of a power suit to navigate the five bizarre areas the story will take you to in the roughly four hours of gameplay.
The main beef of A Story About My Uncle is indeed Fred's power suit and the various moves you can pull off with it: you can jump to greater heights, sprint, resist great falls, dash in mid-air thanks to a pair of rocket boots and use an energy beam to hook upon certain surfaces and cover large distances. The game makes a good job and introducing the different mechanics gradually and offers a steady increase in challenge as you go on.
While the title does have a story of its own (and a rather good one at that) and introduces few characters to you, the interation with the NPCs is minimal (save for two major characters): what really drags A Story About My Uncle is the platforming and the tale is told mainly in-between the various sections. The game primary appeal is the scenary: the environment is especially rich in design and always plentifully detailed, reaching scenary porn more than once.
Apart from the main story, you are given a time trial mode and a hunt for collectables around the areas you visit, which unlock mainly cosmetic goodies.
A Story About My Uncle is a little gem of a game, both very entertaining to play and plesant to look at that. It's definitely worth its price

"Beatbuddy: Tale of the Guardians" is a sweet music and beat based game.
The level of adorableness of this game is too damn high. So let's take it from the top.
The environment is underwater. The beautifully made areas are hand painted, and filled with rock formations, plants, and cute sea creatures. It is all very pleasing to the eye, and generally forces me to smile throughout the whole experience. Also, the environment is not motionless, it is all vibrant, pulsating, bouncing, and swinging to the soundtrack.
The main character is called Beat Buddy. It's a small, blue, bubbly creature with big eyes, and... earphones. Whenever you stop to figure out a puzzle, he floats in the water bouncing his head and swinging his arm, like a real DJ. Did I mention it is adorable?
The game is basically an action-adventure with loads of puzzles, all focused around the music playing in the background. Each obstacle, element, creature has it's own unique sound which always incorporates nicely with the music, creating a beautiful, energetic soundtrack. From jazzy oldschool sounds, through clubby electronic, and even funky-rocky sounds.
While you can solve any puzzle and go through any obstacle without even turning the sound on, listetning to the soundtrack gives you an advantage. The beat, the sounds actually give you small tips and clues, when and how you should move to go through a challenge effortlessly.
The puzzles slowly progress from absolutely obvious to very complicated. It requires logical thinking, timing, and a good ear.
For me, the game is very relaxing. As I traverse the underwater environment, searching for my friends, hoping to save them.. as I bounce, float, punch my way through complicated labyrinths, I feel myself unwind. The music, the soft but vibrant colours, the sweet personality and feel of the game have a wonderful, positive impact on my mood.
So if you would like something gentle, soothing, and adorable. Something that will make you smile, but will still challenge your gaming skills, try "Beatbuddy: Tale of the Guardians". And don't forget to wear good headphones or turn your speakers up.
