TL;DR -
This game has a good premise, a fun atmosphere, decent puzzles and pretty lackluster combat.  I'd give the first half of the game a 7/10 and the second half like a 5.  If you're just looking for something new to try out for a bit then this game is worth playing.  I had a decent time with it.  If you have a limited gaming budget and only want the very best, I would definitely pass and look for something else.  Most of my enjoyment of this game was from the atmosphere/novelty of it, but that somewhat wore off after a while.
I'll probably sound pretty harsh in this review, but that's just because it's easy to pinpoint what I don't like about the game, and I think that stuff is worth mentioning.
THE GOOD -
The combat does not play much of a role in the beginning of the game.  When I started playing, this came off as a very charming little puzzle/exploration game (emphasis on exploration, not so much on puzzle) with a bit of light combat sprinkled in, and I thought it was pretty nice.  I enjoyed all the shag carpet nonsense and crashing my dong-rocket into the pleasure port (yeh that happens).  I enjoyed the sassy doors and general atmosphere of the game.  But it slowly moves away from this, and you will end up spending more and more time on the mediocre combat.
THE BAD -
The game feels a lot more combat-heavy toward the end and the combat is pretty weak.  You can take on different robot bodies, but most of them feel the same.  Trade in your orange body with an orange laser for a yellow body with a yellow laser!  I think one of the worst parts of the combat is that it was usually more effective to not even bother using a body, and to instead just float around as a head, removing the heads of everyone else.  IMO this *should* feel like a last-ditch effort, but instead ended up being my go-to method.  Even if you do decide to do it the "fun" way and use a robot body, it's usually fine to just walk at everything and mash the attack button, then pop into a new body whenever the current one dies.
The last big problem with combat is that the late-game enemies have way too much health.  I would sit there fighting something for long enough that I became convinced I was doing something wrong, and there was some kind of puzzle aspect to the fight that I was missing.  Nope!  Just had to keep shooting.  And shooting.  Without feedback that I am doing damage (health bar, red flashing, debris flying-- there are reasons that many games have this stuff!) I will start to wonder after I've been shooting for a bit with nothing happening.  Even in encounters that did have a health bar, I still felt that they just dragged on for longer than they should have.
It also felt like they kind of ran out of puzzly ideas after a bit.  Just rehashes of the old "bring this body from point A to B" or "shoot this thing at the right angle" that didn't have much meaningful difference from the last couple times I had to do it.  They even resort to literally having you play Simon (the old kids toy/game) completely out of the blue, which was about as boring as you'd expect it to be.
And finally, I encountered one game-breaking bug that made it impossible to continue without exiting to the main menu (maybe closing the game entirely, can't remember) and starting over again.  No progress was lost because of this.
So yeah, overall I'd say it was a positive experience, but it has some pretty major flaws that I couldn't ignore.  I think if I were not streaming the game when I played it, I probably would not have bothered finishing it.  I don't think the game is bad but there are just better games out there.  If I could choose something other than thumbs-up or thumbs-down to describe my opinion, I'd probably call it "lukewarm".

Headlander is a fantastic metroidvania title that oozes 70's retro-futuristic charm.
SERIOUS SPOILER, DO NOT LOOK IF YOU HAVEN'T COMPLETED THE GAME!

Never had played an Adult Swim game other than the goofy flash title from ages ago--Robot Unicorn Attack, I must admit I wasn't expecting much. What I will tell you now is how very wrong I was with it all. Head Lander is a simple, brilliant, GORGEOUS game to which I had the absolute pleasure in playing.
-The strong, silent type....of head-
The story is pretty simple. You're a head. A head without a body to be exact. One of the first things upon playing that you discover is that since you have no lungs, you're unable to speak as well. This puts you into one of my favorite heroic categories: The Silent Protagonist. You might remember such members of the month including Link from the Zelda series, Gordon Freeman from Half Life, or perhaps Chell from a little title known as Portal. In any case, when you have a game that chooses to leave you silent, it becomes apparent that the story is told around you in many different ways. In Head Lander, you've awoken after being cryogenically frozen only to find out the terrible Methuselah has enslaved human consciousness inside robots for some terrible plan.
The menus took me off guard not knowing what exactly to expect from this game in the first place. Instantly you feel you're transported into some super 70's sci-fi flick with the burnt oranges, sound effects, tracking lines and clever way it's all put together. Hitting play, you dive into these amazingly beautiful worlds, so easy to navigate from the perfectly smooth controls. You would think flying a severed head around would be difficult, but it's quite the opposite--and crazy fun. It's a simple puzzle game of opening doors with the right colours attached which means you have to plop your head on other robots walking around the place. This isn't limited to the citizens or soldiers either--cleaning bots, information bots, hell, opening doors a lot of the times means you have to plug yourself into some computer system. It's completely off the wall, and so well thought out.
-Try not to lose your head in combat-
The combat can be quite clever too. When you attach yourself to a robot that job is to carry a weapon, your abilities range with said weapon. Different colours are more tough than the last, or created more bounces with your laser beam. Since in a lot of the case of stealth or combat here is to line up a shot with your laser, you often end up playing a pocket game of Snooker just trying to shoot the other guy. If guns aren't your thing, you can usually just zoom up with avoiding the shots whizzing past and literally suck the head from your opponent right off rendering them useless. Guns blazing isn't always the best idea, but what I really like about this game is that it lets you try without penalizing you too much.
-Head of the class-
You even get a little talent tree to dump points for upgrades in so you can become a more, uh....efficient head. Around the levels, you'll find cheeky vents hiding which have upgrades outside of the talent tree. It doesn't take you long to really beef the little guy up, and quite appropriately the areas scale to all the extras you have. Instead of feeling like you're going into God Mode with it, (which I tend to get easily bored of when I'm allowed to do everything around the place) it adds to the complexity of the challenges as most abilities allow you to move from one area to the next.
It's funny, slick and amazingly entertaining. I honestly can't recommend this one enough. The concept is so out of left field that it works seamlessly. The gameplay is ace, the jokes are a good laugh, and the graphics are stunning. Just don't play it in front of little ones...they might start to ask questions as to why that robot is...uh...humping things.

A story about my uncle first came to my attention when I noticed two things from the trailer. It was a first person game without a gun in anywhere in sight, and  is that platforming? Usually when you mention Platforming,  you think of games like Mario, Mario, Mario, and Mario. Alright there's plenty of other platformers out there that aren't mario. Without mention mario again, there's Little big planet, supermeat boy, freerunners, Fez, Limbo, braid and "I wanna be that guy" take the cake for this generation of modern platformers. And fangames, can't forgot those.
Games like these usually get one simple idea in your head in the first few minutes. "I'm dying alot..." Skill is the one thing  games like these demand, and of course trial and error. Which is what most games lack now a days, inorder to help sell their products, and I don't really blame them, but doesn't mean I have to like it. I expected more from an indie title and  unfortunately this is where "A Story About my Uncle falls victim to right off the bat, with the first and second part of the story. The game holds your hand as you try to complete the next jump, making it rather unchallenging about going through the first few levels. The idea of a well structed level design is there, its just excuted poorly, making me think either it was because they were lazy or in a rush. Or perhaps it was purely intentional, Because in the last act and level of the game, things finally do become somewhat challenging which I'll get to later.
I'm a little kid again... thats what I first thought of myself as I was jumping and swinging around in the first few levels, but then the main characters narrative kept reminding that I'm in the past. I'm consstantly reminded that he's just telling a story to his kid inorder to help her fall asleep. The beginging of the game excuted my imagination as a kid fairly decent, only to be ruined by the questionable plot points in the story where things start to get a little ridicdious once you start to think about it, and the constant cut scenes where the main character starts talking, ruins and breaks the illusion that I'm playing as kid, when they could've just mentioned that part in beginging, only for me to forgot about it later.
The story is okay, nothing too complicated, it's simple and obivious by the beginging, and by the title of course. However towards the end, I felt alittle cheated as if I had gone through all that for a simple pat on the back, with some small uninteresting dialouge and being rushed home. Basiclly like having sex, and the person you're with telling you get off because they already finished before you and thus satisfied.
Now I did enjoy the game to a degree, it was admitly fun having the ability to reach long distances with this suit that grants you Tarzan parcoring abilities without the climbing portion. The game failsto change things up enough with  the exception of one or two occasions was this idea taken further, the potenial for an even more fun and enjoyable level design was missed, you can only jump and swing from rock to rock for so long, While the setting may change, the basic simple now jump on this wall, now swing off these rocks becomes too repetitive, where at least in other games, the frequent  challenging levels is what keeps me or anyone coming back. And it finally did, in the third act. So much I almost raged at certain parts, but I was also happy because now they finally make it harder, more difficult. and  rage indusing. I remember remember dying a number of times at one point where I was asking myself do I suck or is the game finally starting to wake up. It had earlier but died down.
You only fight one boss in the game, which was a breeze, but I loved how it finally through me off from the repeititve level design that I had to endure until then. I would've like to have seen at least one or two more bosses, but one could suggest the final act was final boss.
In the end I feel the game could've had more to offer, but it just offered below my expectations. The games has achivements and side challanging yourself scenarios, but I could myself ask to make things harder on my own without being asked or suggested to.  I really appericate the developers and the folks behind this game for their effort and I wouldn't mind at all seeing what they come up with next. Hopefully next time it won't feel rushed, and it'll be game I and many other will always remmeber.                         3/5

Perhaps a strange advice, but better do not watch the trailer for 'A Story About My Uncle'. Not only does it feature an annoying spoiler, it could also give the false impression that this game can be classified between such little gems as 'Dear Esther' and 'Journey'. After all, we see a story-heavy game, set in a beautiful world and introducing an unique gameplay-mechanic. Though  'A Story About My Uncle' is certainly amusing, in the end it cannot live up to these expectations.
Let us consider the story first. The narrator tells to his daughter a story about his uncle Fred, who had suddenly disappeared. In search of him, his nephew had to enter an underground world consisting of floating rocks. With some help of the frog-like creature Maddie, he had to traverse this world using a mysterious power suit with a grappling hook, which enabled him to jump and float from one rock to another.
This story however is a bit cliche at some times, but more importantly, it really never becomes exciting. There is not much of a hurry to find uncle Fred, as there are no clues that something is wrong with him. In the end, the plot is enough to drive the game forward, but it certainly could have been less dull.
'A Story About My Uncle' (despite its title) is therefore more a game you play for its gameplay than for its story. Luckily then, the gameplay is more exciting than the story is. It is fun to traverse huge caverns without touching the ground, making enormous jumps and floating from great heights, especially in the (sparse) areas where you can choose your own path. Due to some difficult parts, it is sometimes hard to come into a flow, but when this happens, it feels great.
The only real downside to the gameplay is that it offers too little variation. After all your moves are introduced in the first level, the gameplay stays more or less the same during the full 4 hours the game last (probably longer if you go for some fun achievements and hard-to-find unlockables). You do get some upgrades for your suit, but these do not change the gameplay much. I therefore would not have mind if the game had been an hour shorter, especially since the last level contains some tedious parts.
In the end, 'A Story About My Uncle' is still an amusing little game, which offers good value, especially when you pick it up in a sale. Just do not expect too much of it, and as I said, do not watch the trailer.

It's a fun concept, but ultimately very shallow. You and up to three others drop on a planet, complete a couple objectives, then extract, all while fending off waves of enemies. It's great for the first hour or so, but gets incredibly repetitive, as all the objectives blend together (effectively, dash to this location, then do a quicktime event, then dash to the next). As for strategic objectives? There's a galactic map where you choose to fight one of three enemies, eventually pushing back to that enemy's homeworld. The end objective is to win the three separate wars with "Community Event" assaults on their individual homeworlds. Unfortunately, the devs forgot to, y'know, balance that "Community Event." 48 hours to get 7.5 million points, when a group of 4 people can get about 12 points for the toughest mission, which takes ~20 minutes? Do the math; there isn't anywhere near the playerbase to support that. So, the "Community Event" fails, and we're back to an endless slog.
It's a cute idea, and has potential (especially given the Starship Troopers vibe they're heavily going for), but not worth $20. Maybe $5 on sale. Doesn't help that it seems to be a vehicle for distributing DLC, what with the bunches of special packs that give you overpowered weapons.

This game is, quite simply, extremely fun to play. It's not a particularly hard game, you just have to remember all the abilities you slowly gain to advance through the game. Normally with games that aren't hard I find myself growing bored, but not with Headlander.
The storyline is interesting and genuinely comical at times but at the end leaves many unresolved questions. Much of the story is filled out in text form, however, and I think many reviews that fault the story failed to seek out and read all the text that fleshed it out. It doesn't have the feel of a "we left this unresolved for a sequel" kind of situation, its just there are many questions left unanswered.
What Headlander does do well is ooze style and creativity at every turn, with a good mesh of retro themes and music coupled with absurdist sci-fi elements. Couple this with with solid gameplay and you've got a fun time to be had.
My biggest complaint, which really isn't much of a complaint, is that its a short game. Given that it started off being listed for $20, and its common for new games to go for $60(or, blech, more), I can't find fault in its brevity except for one thing... when the game ended I still wanted more. I would have gladly paid more for a longer game.

Recommending this ONLY for the gameplay.
You’re a head floating through space and need to defeat a robot who nicked everyone’s bodies. You help a resistance movement regain the bodies and reveal who you are. The story itself is intriguing to start with when you don’t know what's going on and you have to piece together the puzzle. However, I found the ending REALLY anti-climatic because nothing was resolved. That could have been forgiven if the characters were interesting but you don’t speak throughout the entire game save for 1 line. There are basically 3 characters which talk (majorly) and the resistance lady is just boring. The other two are used for exposition dumps rather than actual character so at the end, when the computer was going on about creation and humanity and blah blah… I didn’t care at all. I just wanted to finish the boss.
It’s a metroidvania style game where you have a giant map with rooms connected by doors which need security levels contained by bodies. You, having no body, can take anyones body and go through the door. This mechanic is good as it keeps the game from being a straight linear movement and instead gives it more exploration as you have to guide one body from one door to another.
You as a character have a shield to block lasers and a suck to pull heads off. Personally, I like this system because if you get tired of the laser shooting like I did, you can just eject and rip the heads of your enemies out and just screw it. The laser shooting is adequate for the job but having multiple enemies with multi fire can just fill the screen in confusing shoots everywhere and none of the shooting is what I would call engaging.
The main problem with the combat is the escalation. As your start, you steadily grow through the first 4ish levels as you unlock more areas. The lead up to the boss fight is this big actually fun fetch quest and has story tie in and visual themes that tie back to the boss fight. But after that point, you just end up repeating everything. You gain 2-3 more levels and see the same bases and same gameplay. Nothing changes. Plus, the whole ending is just one big linear sequence so the computer can monologue.
The upgrade system lets you upgrade stats and gain abilities through consoles (?) that you find all over the places and which are (thankfully) marked on the maps. But by the end, I had upgraded everything and still had upgrade points to spend. Plus, the shield and speed abilities are the only useful ones because the rest are just for combat which never got challenging or overly difficult.
Performance is absolute♥♥♥♥♥♥ The game looks retro but not pixely or cell shaded. But overall, I liked it. When it zoomed in for close ups it tended to look a lot less “good” but overall the visual style was good. But the performance was just all over the place. It would bounce from 30-60-75 all the time and the game is not visually demanding at all. It’s jarring in gameplay when you’re going down a hallway and you suddenly slow down a lot.
The game honestly felt rushed. I really liked it from start to the end of the first boss. But after that, it just stagnated and I got really bored doing the same thing again. The story was anti climatic, the gameplay never evolved, and the combat stayed the same. However, that initial period of marked exploration to find your way across a map is something I’m into enough to very hesitantly recommend it. If you’re not into that, I would really ignore this game.

Great game!
The concept of this game, in which you take over NPCs with your head, is slightly similar to Stick It to the Man, another game I enjoyed a lot.  But Headlander has a more polished presentation.  The headlanding mechanic also reminds me of the Oddworld games, with Abe's possession ability, although it's much easier and there is no traditional platforming (no jumping).
Like with other Double Fine games, Headlander immerses you completely in a bizarre world.  The art, soundtrack, writing, voice acting are all top-notch, and I love the retrofuturistic look.  It also seems like an open world, although you do unlock different areas as you go along.  It's easy to navigate and go back to get upgrades you overlooked or did not have the abilities to reach before.  Everything in this game is simple to understand in a way that allows you to just enjoy it.  There's never much pressure, since the areas you've visited don't lock you out as you play.
The gameplay is smooth and makes sense at every moment.  The chess area was my least favorite part, and it was still pretty fun.  The game is maybe a little short, but I think I only feel that way because I liked it so much.  But there are a lot of achievements, which give a reason to keep playing once you've finished the story.
A lot of the combat can be avoided, sort of, by removing enemies' heads rather than shooting them, but the actual combat is well thought out, too.  There are a few bosses; they're all of the type that you need to figure out a simple technique of some kind for each phase of a fight.
Overall this is a game that relies on thinking more than on reflexes, but although there are some cool little puzzles, including the boss fights, nothing is overly hard.  I can imagine some players considering this game too easy, although the difficulty was perfect for me.
Recommended to fans of classic sci-fi and/or puzzle platformers.  Actually, though, this is the kind of game that just about anyone could enjoy.

Metro 2033, and Redux makes it better. I first played this game when i was about 11-12 on my xbox 360 (I am now 17). The Russian aspect on this game as well as the references to The Red Line (Communist Russia) and the 4th Riech (Nazi Germany) make this game a joy to play, on top of the great story, atmosphere and place it is set in.
Good Stuff
+ Weapon Customization and diversity, an adequate selection of Guns are avaliable throughout the playthrough, but dont get put off by just recieving a revolver at the start, it has some serious firepower
+ Currency System: This is based of the Military Grade bullets that were produced before the Nuclear Warheads hit Russia, as there is only a limited amount of them they are valuable, though you can use them as a high damage boost if you must.
+ Interaction with different people can be interesting, you can listen to peoples stories about their life in the Metro or about recent events (Hint: Listening to most conversations gives you positive morale points which earning enough gives you the good ending (yes there are 2 endings i only learned this after like my 4th playthrough))
+ Surface exploration is probably the most thrilling yet horrifying high-lights in the game, constantly on guard and keeping for spare filters so you can *breath* on the surface through your *gas mask* keeps you on edge, also you Gas Mask can break while in combat so keep an eye out for replacements
Middle Ground
+/- Isolation: Was hoping for more of this but anyway, most the time during your playthrough of Metro 2033 both the first and Last Light you are with a group or Partner, only for maybe a total of 2 out of the 10hrs of game time you are by yourself. However when you are, oh boy are you in for a treat. The slightest sound or movement makes you jump and puts you on edge, making you paranoid, but like a said wish there was more of it.
+/- Acquiring Better Gear: Military Grade Ammo (The moolah or $$) is basicially useless, unless you want a damage boost. Why? If you dont spend any money, and manage to pull through about 1/5th of the story with your basic weapons (Up to Dry Station, thats a place you go to) you will start acquiring better ones *with attachments* off dead enemies, unless you want powerful guns early game, wait until you find better ones :)
+/- Mutant Combat: Most of it is pretty one sided, you shoot them they die, unless you fight demons, you will burn through over half of your stockpile and perhaps most of your filters to take one down, but...there is one exception the *Nosalis* if you start getting hit in its combo "You have to back out" since your getting stunned and for some reason they take no damage when attacking you (or so i have seen, i might just be complaining cause im bad)
Cons:
- Annoying Sway: There is once place where you pick up
after doing so, you are greeted with a heavy sway which makes it difficult to aim and look around, i understand his a kid, but his not that fat....is he?
- F**cking Librarians: The AI of these tough Sons of b**ches can sometimes work, they either attack or dont attack, and if they do, your burning through about 30-40 shotgun rounds.
Thats it, thats all my ranting done and complete, i hope this helps you decide if you should get it or not. Oh, almost forgot, yes i do recommend you get this 9/10 for me :)

I noticed this game when the developers released a demo, which I really appreciate - so if you're wondering if you'll like the gameplay, go check out the first 2 levels for free. Just don't expect the rest of the game to offer anything different. I did enjoy the demo; but made the assumption that the full game had more depth.
The gameplay is fairly standard for this sort of dungeon crawler, it's a real-time action game, so you walk around and you explore, kill creatures and pick up keys in order to level up and progress to the next level. The movement is simple and well executed, and the animations are smooth and swish.
Unfortunately the levels are extremely repetitive, to the point where most of them feel the same, and the selection of monsters very poor. There is a mini-boss guardian between each level, but they didn't seem to do anything special.  There are also only 7 levels to the entire game (repeatable on 3 difficulty levels), so it's really rather short. There's not a great deal of loot (only gold and health in game, and a very small selection of weapons you can purchase at each level start, no armor or skills or special abilities), and stats don't seem to make a whole lot of difference (and you can max them out by level 5 on casual). There are also no puzzles, and the mapping is standard and predictable, which unfortunately makes this game lack in much of the intellectual variety.
So, you get where I'm going with this, there's just not enough. It's just shallow. Not enough depth, length, variety or gameplay at all. What is there is done well, and I understand it's a £2 game, but it really feels like the entire game is a Unity demo or concept - and it just needs more more more of everything. Since the levels, monsters and environment lack variety, I was thoroughly bored by the end of casual (approximately 90 minutes). I have no doubt that the harder difficulties are much more challenging - but without any additional monsters, loot or mechanics, I just couldn't find any fun in a further grind.
If there is a mega epic battle around the corner, then the music ramping up in intensity and tone is great. However, the music in this seemed to be slightly confused, as on many occasions it got all excited over absolutely nothing, which really didn't help the tone at all. That wall I just walked into? Yeah, that's not a threat. Sometimes there would be no change in music (there are also no footsteps or noise indicators until you're being stabbed in the back by a goblin), which I suppose added an element of "jump scare horror" to the game when I turned around and realized three orcs were all up in my face.

I would really like to recommend Beatbuddy, but I just can't... at least, not fully. While it's got a lot going for it, I just can't get past how buggy it is. Although I did manage to complete it, it wasn't without some serious issues. Several times I got stuck in various ways that prevented further progress - sometimes it was a matter of a game event not triggering properly, and sometimes it was due to going some way the game wasn't expecting me to (apparently). I also encountered issues where the controls would just stop working for no reason. Restoring to the last checkpoint sometimes fixes the issue, but this is rarely the case. Most times, there is no choice but to start the level (or entire chapter) from scratch. Do you know how annoying it is to have 30-40 minutes of progress wiped out, have to start over again, and hope you don’t make the same game-breaking mistake again (whatever it was)? Let me tell you - it's really f%@*&g annoying. I ended up having to do that multiple times. And would you believe, as a final bug-ridden cherry on top, the very end of the game also glitched out on me as well? Well, believe it. So on top of all the other frustration I experienced just getting through the game, I didn’t even get to see the full conclusion of the story.
Now, putting all of that aside, what’s actually good about Beatbuddy? Quite a bit, actually. The hand-drawn layered 2D graphics look great, the controls are responsive, the puzzles are generally well-designed, and the music is decent. And that’s a good thing, because the music plays a large part in the gameplay - the environment works in time with the beat of the music, requiring specific timing to pass obstacles or solve puzzles. The first couple of hours are great, as the basic mechanics are introduced. Unfortunately, it starts to lose its luster a little bit after that, as most of the subsequent puzzles are pretty much variations on things you’ve already done several times. So you might start to get tired of it after a while (or maybe I was just burned out from having to replay several areas). I would estimate the overall playtime to be somewhere around 4-6 hours.
Overall, the game is not bad, and I enjoyed it while it was working properly. The frustration from all of the technical issues I had just ended up being too much for me to give it a full recommendation. If you enjoy action/puzzle sidescrollers, music-themed games, and/or games with pretty 2D artwork, it’s definitely worth a look. Just be aware of the potential issues. I suppose it could very well be possible that you'd encounter no glitches at all… but I doubt it (several posts in the Steam forums seem to corroborate my experience). At the very least, don’t buy it at full price unless the developers hire more QA people and/or release a patch that fixes the game-breaking issues.

This game throws away the majority of things that made the previous game great.
It forces you to have bots during coop who can glitch by running very fast against walls like Sonic the Hedgehog. The player can also run in place instead of leaning when using cover. AKs dropped from enemies can fire indefinitely (making it impossible to hear what's happening in game due to how many times it can happen and how loud the AKs are). Players are seen teleporting during level transitions. The main character's speeches with the bots are unnecessary and break the immersion. During coop, your partner shouts anything he does, from removing his suppressor to changing the combat mode of the AI.
Ubisoft somehow made the UI for the character customization worse than the first game by not adapting it for PC. On the title screen, it takes forever to spin your character when you drag your mouse on screen. You're not given access to every gun and outfit right at the beginning. Instead, you have to complete challenges (like shooting 10 bad guys at a long distance) that should be optional and then unlock what you want with points. Boxes can be found during missions that you can use to change your loadout and appearance. However, enemies can still come kill you while you're in the menus and the bots are useless to protect you. If you dare put the difficulty on realistic, snipers can eliminate you in one hit without clear feedback that you've been spotted.
The options are in a submenu named extras when they should be visible on the first screen. The game forces you to restart after changing the aspect ratio. You can only walk from toggling and it's barely noticeable compared to moving normally. The multiplayer is unstable and you might need to host multiple times until it finally works. The logo from Unreal Engine 3 is used on Windows' taskbar and the volume mixer instead of the game's logo.
You're forced to carry two main weapons + a sidearm. This is unpleasing from a realistic standpoint. All of your controls except movement are removed during story segments. Your name doesn't show up when you die. Instead, you're given the name of the story character.
The map and thermal vision look good. The gunplay feels nice like in Vegas 1.

100% voltado para cooperação entre o time, jogar sozinho é praticamente inviável. Ação frenética, com muita informação visual na tela entre tiros e explosões. Exelente som e trilha sonora que dão muita emoção ao jogo. A grande pegada de Helldivers está no sistema de fogo amigo (um tiro vindo do aliado doi tanto em você quanto no inimigo) e nas combinações do teclado, que são marcas registradas da Arrowhead Studios, também criadora de Magicka.
O vasto leque de possibilidades de customização, e a evolução persistente de sua conta mantem as coisas interessantes. Uma grande diversidade de atributos, armas, equipamentos e tecnologias que vão se tornando disponiveis conforme seu progresso. As opções táticas são diversas e abrangentes.
Não é um jogo leve. Nescessita sua total concentração durante suas breves partidas. É também bastante desafiador ao decorrer do avanço nos niveis de dificuldade. Dentro desta, achar uma partida com pessoas aleátorias e na dificuldade desejada se mostra rapido e facil. No entante, o jogo brilha em seu maior explendor, quando jogado entre amigos.
Estou muito contente com o resultado final que é um jogo extremamente divertido e bem polido. Bem balanceado e com uma infinidade de opções taticas e estratégias a serem executadas pelo time. Quando a equipe está em sintonia e consegue completar a missao, a sençação é positivamente eufórica. Por fim quero ressaltar o que jogo foi devidamente optimizado de forma que é graficamente bonito sem grandes requerimentos do PC.
Recomendadissimo!

If so, you'll find that this game has the same tongue-in-cheek comedy with an almost original Robocop-esque subtlety on overpatriotism and a government that has so many twists in it it can rival the #$%^ing Gordian Knot. However, we're not here to discuss social commentary, we're here for a random person's verdict on the game.
Objectively, the game runs superbly. The movement controls have tight responses and it feels like you're moving with actual friction as opposed to gliding around, the weapons are diverse and are as difficult to master as they are fun to use on your adversaries as well as the odd unwitting ally (Did I mention there was friendly fire in this?). The strategems, little goodies dropped from high orbit, can either aid you with the contents of it or kill you via crushing you, and don't think the enemies won't be obliged to smear your entrails across the ground. You may be scared at first from what I've just told you, but don't worry! You are not alone, and other players can jump in anytime to help you out of your spot of bother. I might also want to add that you can communicate to your brothers and sisters in arms efficiently without using voice chat.
In short, Helldivers is a hilarious, over-the-top Sci-Fi twinstick shooter that is the love-child of Starship Troopers and Arrowhead Studios, the makers of the Magicka franchise. It has transferred well on to the PC, and I am glad to say it does not disappoint in the slightest. So make the most important decision of your life - Join the Helldivers today!

It's easy to think this is just a Metroidvania platformer relying on its aesthetic alone. To some degree that is correct. Headlander wears it on the sleeve of its disco jacket. It mixes the style of old pulpy science fiction with a heavy 70s flair. The dialogue, the art, the jokes, the characters, they're all full of it. If that's not an aesthetic you like, don't buy it.
If it is, but you're still unsure, let me say that there's still a good game underneath it. Instead of a character, you play a disembodied head, floating around and taking control of cybernetic bodies that have different security clearances through different doors. Puzzles revolve around that and navigating obstacles like laser barriers, hostile robots, and weirdly designed levels. There's some puzzles that involve shot trajectory which isn't my favorite, but they're okay.
I won't spoil the plot here, but it is interesting to say the least. The protagonist certainly comes off like HAL from 2001, but there's more too it.

While The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a gorgeous looking game, seasoned hardcore pc adventure gamers will find the puzzles set to easy (like counsel gamer easy), the game mechanics easy to figure out, and a rather linear story once it's finished.  I had great expectations for this game and it started strong -  with the possibility that you can miss things easily in this game - and intriguing.  Unfortunately as I progressed I found few things to capture my attention (the puzzle in the Carter's house was good, but not tough once I figured it out) and the game makes no attempt for the gamer to give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about any of the characters: not even Ethan Carter.  The Astronauts should have concentrated more on character development which would of made for a much more deeper game and longer development, but think of the difference it makes in games such as The Last Us, which I consider to be the video game ever made to date.  Not to gloat about my favorite game of all time but when characters died in The Last Of Us you were left to ponder if you can emotionally continue the journey without those companions, especially Tess, I felt screwed after loosing her.  The Last Of Us forced you to go on, but here I was never shocked by the shear body count in the game.   All the characters could of hung themselves in a mass suicide and would be like: "heh."  In short the only real challenge in the Vanishing of Ethan Carter is locating a few items sprewn about the vast area, and while I'm on the subject it has to said that Ethan should get an award for most amount of dead world space in a video game.  I mean there's a building by the river that's as big as a high school building and only two rooms are accessible.  The rest is just painted decor with large windows and doors enticing the player to come in: only to find that its a giant blade of grass with no interactions.  Bummer.  However I did like the ending to this game, but felt it could of been made more effective if we gave a damn about anybody, but instead  watched completely unmoved.  In short the begining and ending are good, there was crazy stuff happening throughout the game which is explained by the surprise ending, however the middle could of has tougher puzzles and a more indepth story.  It did get a bit interesting in the tunnel where elements of HP Lovecraft's Cthulu Mythos seem to be introduce.  Teasers these game developers.

This was a game I bought around a year ago because it was on sale, I played it for an hour and then forgot about it. It sat there in my library for 11 months before I finally decided to pick it up and play.
Boy, do I sure regret letting this game sit unplayed in my library. It's not often that I come across a game that engrosses me into its world as well as Metro 2033. I was so fascinated by this game's atmosphere and story that I decided to get the novel, of which the game is based on: Metro 2033 by Dmitry Glukhovsky.
The game originally came out in March of 2010, but in 2014 both 2033 and it's sequel, Last Light (Which is also based on a Dmitry Glukhovsky novel) were both remastered and released together as Metro Redux for the next generation. The graphics still hold up amazingly, the scenery is gorgeous and the lighting is fantastic. The atmosphere for this game is bar none, If you love the setting for the Fallout, S.T.A.L.K.E.R., or any Post-Apocalyptic setting in general, I have no doubts that you'll be fully immersed in this game world.
My only complaints with the game are that the AI for monsters is a little wonky at times; for example, when you and a group of soldiers are defending against a horde of monsters, often, they will only attack you, and sometimes when fighting hordes of monsters it is easy to get pinned in a corner and get slaughtered. Also, the accents are pretty bad, they sound like something straight out of a b movie, which is pretty moronic seeing how the developement studio is located in Ukraine.
And, if you're wondering about the book. It's amazing. The game does a great job of adapting the novel into another medium. The only complaint is that they pretty much cut the entire first 2 chapters.

While this game is getting flooded with early negative reviews, I played it my first time expecting to play it maybe 20 to 30 minutes for an first impressions review.. and I ended up playing for about 1 hr and 45 minutes!
Watch my livestream here (my scoring is at 1 Hour and 43 minutes into this video):
Using my scoring system I use for all games, which is most heavily based on "value" and asking the question "are you getting a good gaming value for your dollar?".. this game scored an impressive 86% score from me.
The game, while being pretty simple, offers very decent 3D graphics and nice textures and very fluid movement and controls.  Timing is critical, and while I already see some reviews knocking the game for being impossible to jump across lava to get the keys or not being able to hit enemies.. it's all timing and skill based movement to succeed.   Every enemy has a different attack style and speed and method and weapon needed to best defeat them.  If you aren't patient enough (or smart enough) to try different strategies or weapons, then this game might not be for you, but don't knock the game because of your lack of patience or logic.
It's not a AAA game, but I think it's a very nice game for it's asking price, and it offers plenty of replay value as well with randomized dungeon layouts, multiple weapons to buy, and three levels of difficulty, as well as three attributes which can be increased with experience earned.
One note: If you buy this game, PLEASE start on the "easy" difficuluty level which will allow you to save your experience and gold progession and advance through the game without getting too frustrated early on.
Recommended to people who can appreciate a good old school type RPG game with simplistic controls and a game that will reward you if you go in not expecting a AAA game and if you are logical and patient.

This is still one of the best first person shooters available.  Almost a decade after it's release you will still be able to join multi-player games.  Graphically, it is starting to show it's age, true, but it isn't any worse than say, Skyrim which used the exact same textures as Fallout New Vegas.  The terrorist AI is adequate during the campaign.  The controls are really easy to use.  There is an excellent weapon selection, and plenty of maps in multi-player to use them all on.
Where the game is lacking is in small areas.
First, in the campaign your AI squadmates tend to get in the way.  Since this is very much a 1-shot and you die kind of game, you do not want to get stuck between them in a firefight.  Second.  The stats on the weapons are off.  By a lot.  Not to the point that selecting some of the "bad" weapons are unplayable, but it is noticeable.  Since real life weapons and gear are used, the game tries to make them as close to the real life variants as possible.  However, when you take the Commando 552 (what the game calls the M4) and compare it to the AK-47, it blows the AK-47 out of the water in every category.  This however, is not true to life, as any and every person who has shot them both will say they are very similar.  Most will have their preference.
Now, another thing to point out about the weapons is that you only get 1 attachment for each weapon.  HOWEVER, be careful with this, as some of the weapons make up for lackluster statistics by coming with attachments or modifications on them already!  The Tar-21 is a prime example of this as it comes with a reflex scope on it right out of the box.  Generally speaking, with the exception of pistols and sub guns, the first weapons you get in each category are the best.  The Commando 552 is the best Assault Rifle.  The 21E is the best Machine Gun.  The Spas-12 is the best shotgun.  This kind of annoys me, because I swear I've been sniped by more SPAS-12s than any other weapon in the game.  You don't snipe with a shotgun.  Shotguns in general, have this weird ability to hit targets at really long ranges even though they're full of buckshot and not slugs.  I digress.  The best sub gun is debatable, but I tend to stick with the Mac-11 since I use it as a joke, or when I get caught by 4 terrorists rushing me and I need a really fast way to dump a whole bunch of bullets at close range targets in a matter of less than 2 seconds.
The point with the weapons, if you're reading between the lines, is that they aren't flawed in a way that would annoy the casual (or even serious) gamer.  They simply annoy me as a matter of personal preference because I am a firearms enthusiast who knows things about them in real life.
Moving along.
The game has a pretty large cluster of multi-player maps.  Granted, the game is 10 years old, so for someone like me who has already played through everything there is to play, I just want more.  While I would like to have seen another map pack with about 4 or 5 more, or at least the ability to generate my own, it isn't at all necessary.  In fact, there is an official map pack that adds 3 more multi-player maps and some early bug fixes with sound.  So if this is your first play-thru, or if you have played before and simply not played the game in years, you'll be just fine.
The only REAL flaws this game has are...
-No modding support.  At least not to speak of.  It isn't like the old games where you can find and download a NATO mod to give yourself access to 65 more weapons.
-Some aspects of cover and concealment have a tricky learning curve because a lot of "cover" is actually concealment that can be shot through.  I routinely get kills in both multi-player and campaign modes by shooting through whatever another player (or terrorist) is hiding behind.
-There is one bug that was simply never fixed.  Over on my end, we call it "Machine Gun City" and it's an aspect with sound where if you get killed while firing your machine gun by a terrorist with a machine gun while somebody else is also firing a machine gun, you will get stuck with a constant machine gun echo going off through your speakers/headset.  This is rather annoying as it tends to drown out every other sound in the game.  Thankfully this ends as soon as the match is over.
Overall, I give this game a perfect 10 out of 10.  It is, by far, beyond the shadow of any doubt, better than anything Halo has made.  It's better than anything and everything Call of Duty past the first one.  It's better than Battlefield too.  It's better than those games even now, 10 years past it's debut.  Why?  Because as a shooter it still holds up graphically.  For replay value?  It's all there.  For the need to use tactics and strategy?  Yes.  Rainbow Six is the series that made FPS games.  It's the series that put tactics and strategy on the map.  And perhaps most importantly?  If you're like me and don't want to play a multi-player game with a bunch of impatient people or kids running around trying to give everyone a "teabag" or getting hit with a tomahawk in the ankle from halfway across the map, than this game is DEFINITELY worth few bucks and installation time.
Try it.
You'll like it.

To those who are pondering on whether or not to buy the game, let me ask you this before going any further: Have you watched Starship Troopers? If so, you'll find that this game has the same tongue-in-cheek comedy with an almost original Robocop-esque subtlety on overpatriotism and a government that has so many twists in it it can rival the #$%^ing Gordian Knot. However, we're not here to discuss social commentary, we're here for a random person's verdict on the game.
Objectively, the game runs superbly. The movement controls have tight responses and it feels like you're moving with actual friction as opposed to gliding around, the weapons are diverse and are as difficult to master as they are fun to use on your adversaries as well as the odd unwitting ally (Did I mention there was friendly fire in this?). The strategems, little goodies dropped from high orbit, can either aid you with the contents of it or kill you via crushing you, and don't think the enemies won't be obliged to smear your entrails across the ground. You may be scared at first from what I've just told you, but don't worry! You are not alone, and other players can jump in anytime to help you out of your spot of bother. I might also want to add that you can communicate to your brothers and sisters in arms efficiently without using voice chat.
In short, Helldivers is a hilarious, over-the-top Sci-Fi twinstick shooter that is the love-child of Starship Troopers and Arrowhead Studios, the makers of the Magicka franchise. It has transferred well on to the PC, and I am glad to say it does not disappoint in the slightest. So make the most important decision of your life - Join the Helldivers today!

Vegas 2 has to be my favorite out of the 'Rainbow Six' franchise. You play as Bishop, a Rainbow squad leader in charge of a small counter-terrorism unit. Your mission -- to track down the dangerous Cabrero cartel in possesion of deadly chemical agents through the city of Vegas. The fun and easy squad tactics combined with the unique environments and map layouts make for some interesting scenarios in taking out the bad guys. The graphics aren't too bad for its time, and the voice acting is exceptionally well done. One of the best parts about the game is its customizable elements. From your apparel to your combat loadout, you can tweak everything to your liking.
The only downsides are a limited arsenal, a drawn-out leveling process, and a boring playing experience once you've earned all the gear and acheived prestige level. The three difficulty tiers all feel the same, as well.
All other things aside, with campaign, versus mode, and the additional terrorist hunt mode, this game is quite a steal for $10. It's certainly worth your time.

Arguably the most important thing in any armed conflict is taking cover. How did a game that focuses on micromanaging troops in combat screw this up so badly?
First you have to click on the unit. Sounds simple enough, but for some reason I had a lot of difficulty with this. For some reason, units would not always select / de-select on the first click, sometimes it took two clicks or box selecting the unit to do so. That is just unacceptable. It lead to a lot of wrong orders, wasted time, and deaths. How can a game that is two years old not have that figured out?
Order the unit to take cover. The fact that I have to babysit each unit to order them to take cover blows my mind. How could they not code the most basic of human instincts of taking cover when being shot at? It would be one thing if the cover was far away, you did tell them to move to the open location, but if a stone wall is just 5 yards away and they are under machine gun fire, why do they wait for your command to take cover rather than just moving?
Now make sure they actually move. In addition to waiting for a command that should not need to be ordered, once it comes, they don't always follow it. Sometimes I had to repeat orders to take cover, not because they were being pinned down by supressing fire, but because they were so busy standing and shooting they ignored me.
Once they actually move, make sure they take the correct positions. For some reason, my units loved to hop over and "take cover" on the wrong side of the wall. W...t...f...? At first I thought I was clicking on the wrong side of the wall, but I was not. They take cover on the right side of the wall and then jump over to chase retreating units, a command I neither gave, nor desired because there were still enemy units holding the line that quickly targeted and killed them.
Even though they are now in cover, you still cannot relax. One of the great features of this game is the distructible environment. The infuriating aspect of this is that your idiot troops don't shoot around cover, they shoot through it. Yes, you read that correctly, when hiding behind a wall, your troops will attempt to shoot through the wall rather than around it. Judging by tracer rounds and riccochet / impact effects, about 33%-50% of all rounds hit the wall. If they are behind a tank or truck, it's more like 50%-75%. How can they be so stupid as to destroy their own cover and shoot their own allies? How can they not figure out how to shoot over the wall or around the vehicle? I wouldn't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥if they hid behind the wall, closed their eyes, poked the gun out, and blind fired the entire mag aimlessly and never even came close to the target, at least they wouldn't be aiming down the sights at the wall and still shooting it. Within seconds, the wall will crumble due to the combined friendly and enemy fire and your troops will be out in the open.
Now that your troops have destroyed their cover and are out in the open, return to step one and repeat the process. Don't forget about your 15 other equally stupid units, they all need micromanaging too.
If this seems like your game, go for it. It's not all bad, there are some great features like weather, map details, destructible environment, and the visual and sound effects, but they all sit on the core of the game, which is ordering troops to take cover. Whether they are advancing, retreating, defending, or supressing, they need to be in cover, and because that is broken, the whole game is.
Needless to say, I do not recommend this game and am grateful I never bought it and only played on free weekends.

We have seen many titles of Double fine so far, like Grim Fandango, Psychonauts and Broken Age. all of them were simple, and at the same time they had their own Traits which made them quite strong and memorable. We can say that the Headlander has succeeded in maintaining this particular way to become a good, amusing and memorable experience. if you felt the lust for science fiction stories recently, and you like to spend you weekends with a simple but engaging game, Headlander can be a good choice

I also covered this game on YouTube:
Headlander is a new Metroidvania style game with a big coat of 70s sci-fi art and music and a typical goofy Double Fine premise. You are a disembodied head that has both a fully functional brain and a jetpack. You're in a world where the majority of humanity has had their personalities digitised and attached to robot bodies, serving an evil AI overlord. Your goal is to try to free everyone from this oppression and make them truly human again. You do this by possessing other robots by pulling their heads off and sticking yours on their bodies. For freedom!
Most of the standard Metroidvania tropes are here, including doors that are restricted to certain weapons or robot types, a largely open area to explore and objectives that sometimes involve a degree of light puzzle solving. There's also some quirky combat and boss fights along the way.
It's not particularly challenging as it's very hard to die, harder still after a few upgrades and even when you do, you basically just respawn in the same room with no penalty. While the station you're in is vast, you also have a map system that makes it relatively straightforward to find where you have to go next and rarely laves you lost.
You'll also come across the occasional station goer who will have an optional side mission that can yield additional points to upgrade yourself, plus there are numerous hidden upgrades in the station, though the paths to them are often indicated on the map and aren't hard to find.
Double Fine is known for humour in their games and rightly or wrongly, there's always a heavy expectation of this from them. Headlander make me chuckle a few times but the humour is pretty understated compared to some of their past efforts. What really makes this game stand out for me is how gorgeous it looks and how well they nailed the vibe they were going for. Headlander is bright, colourful and doesn't take itself seriously, visually or in its writing. Those are good things to me.
After multiple crowdfunded titles that I all thought were poor, it seems Double Fine managed to put out quality stuff when they have a publisher keeping their legendarily poor money and project management skills in check. Headlander won't necessarily challenge you but it's a good Metroidvania in its own right and quite a memorable one too. Given that Double Fine's never made one of these before, it's a great first effort.

Quake Live is a game which is somewhat near and dear to my heart at this point because in my near 100 hours at the time of writing, the experiences I have had in this game have outdone those I have had in any other game besides LISA, which takes the cake for story and emotions. This game is the golden standard for online FPS, with everything being very straightforward and having very few, if any, randomized mechanics. Quite literally, this game has almost zero explaining to do except for item spawn timers and the fact that the lightning gun has a limited range and knockback. In other words, the popular phrase "no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t" applies here in the grandest sense. I have only but the grandest praise for this game. Its weapon roster is simple and iconic for those who have played this game, the only exclusion being the proximity mine launcher, a weapon you never see and never should. The music, for this game, is actually just SO GOOD. I didn't really realize how much I loved the music. It's never this uninvited, screaming track which just hurts the experience. Rather, they're all these sort of ambi-metal tracks which are just...ahhh. They fit so well. Next are the map layouts. Obviously, certain maps are better than others, but practically all of them provide a cohesive, well-built experience which will quickly be ingrained within your muscle memory due to just how complex but easy to grasp these maps are. For example, the map silence, one of my favorites, is a very tight, layered, vertical map which is comprised of three main areas which are somewhat further subdivided by the layers as stated. On one end you can find the red armor and in the main area there are columns which help to make fighting between the layers a more difficult but more rewarding and tactical experience. Another map, limbus, is all about space. There is an abundance of it which is added to by elevated blocks which make fighting an ever adapting experience, rather than being frustratingly intrusive. Next are the character models. This is a small touch in the grand scheme of things but they all have a distinct silhouette which, if you play on a server consistently, you will begin to attribute to returning players. Another thing is the skill curve, which is basically a "sky's the limit" situation. No matter how good you think you are, somewhere, there's always someone better. And more to the point, in this game, there is no space for complaining. No one weapon is outright unfair or random, they are all cold and calculated machines of destruction in the right hands. The cheating is non-existent and VAC is enabled, which says either credit to the system or just a general lack of cheaters. However, what I'd like to tell you most about is the community. This is my favorite part of the game, and while it is unquantifiable, I can definitely tell you that the lads who are playing in Chicago are some great people to just hang around with on a saturday night. Oh, another thing to mention is that I've been connecting to that Chicago server from California and the ping tolerance usually holds out pretty well. Very little lag for that distance in comparison to other games. Anyways, community. The community is usually a group of these eccentric stoners of quite literally every single age, from the young adult to a grandpa. Maybe they'll get on high or maybe they just have a good story to tell. Maybe they're in a good mood, maybe they're not. But unlike other games, where everyone is just an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ or just doesn't act like a social being, these people do. Those guys have said some of the funniest stuff I've ever heard. In fact, I have screenshots of a guy discussing how he orders toothbrushes and toothpaste online because he doesn't want to drive to Walgreens. Another story which I can tell you about is a sad one, but one of the regular guys on that Chicago server had a car crash and he told us about it, and after playing with that guy for a while, you feel it too. He then had to go down a desert highway for miles with hurt legs in order to get help for his friend, you couldn't move (I believe this was the case). Another time, one of the older guys on the server stopped appearing, and everyone began hoping and praying that he wasn't dead. After all, he was one of the best. On a better day, we had a person who had ping in the hundreds and some people wanted to kick him, but we kept the trooper in. Even with so much ping, he managed to pull his way up on the scoreboard despite tons of deaths. That man deserved a medal for his willpower. In a way, although nobody every acknowledges it, you all become friends, and it's wonderful. I would never trade my time in this game for all of the money in the world because I just love those people so much, and while it's a dumb thing to get teary eyed over a game, I kind of do. This game has no flaws to me and if you just want an excellent shooter game which you can't rage over without being irrational, buy this. It's the best FPS game in the world to me with no other game coming remotely close.

Headlander is a 70s style sci-fi Metroidvania game from “Double Fine Games” and published by Adult Swim.
During the current indie renaissance we are currently seeing a decent amount of Metroidvania games none of which from Castlevania or Metroid but that’s a conversation for another time.
A few videos ago we looked at the rather excellent Ghost 1.0 and actually Headlander is in many ways very similar so is it worth jumping in for some more Metroidvania loveliness yet again?
Headlander sees you in a futuristic Dystopia where mankind have replaced their bodies with robotic ones. The main premise of the game is you are the last human awoken from cryogenic storage and thus only your head has survived. So you find yourself as a floating head in a jar which can float around and attach yourself to other robots. The setting of the game is vaguely reminiscent of something like Logan’s Run in terms of style.
As you attach yourself to different robots they gain you access to different weapons and more importantly different security levels that allow you to progress. Now don’t get me wrong Headlander is a good quality game but I can’t help but feel a few small changes would have made it one of the best Metroidvania out there.
In terms of Metroid-i-ness this game is Metroid Fusion as opposed to Super Metroid. There is very little in terms of exploration which is a bit of a missed opportunity. Every door is coloured or a hatch and almost all sections are really clearly marked on the map. There are a few hidden secrets that involve jumping down gaps or smashing through walls but these are definitely in the minority. My first play though not going out of my way to find secret yielded a 92% completion rate with the 100% doable in little over an hour extra.
The game is split up into a number of zones which each have a specific challenge to the zone. My personal favourite was the Chess Zone which sees you take over robots that work in the same was as chess pieces that lead to the game’s most memorable boss… even though there are not that many bosses.
One thing that I did really like are the angle puzzles. In Headlander lasers generally bounce off of walls and this is used in a number of puzzles where you have to shoot multiple mirrors at once. The few of these puzzles that there are which tend to appear in the later stages of the game are fun and well thought out of these… An iOS game containing just these puzzles would be a welcome mini game.
Each zone has an extra quest that involves killing a mob or finding something specific but these are generally low key and definitely could have been made into so much more and that really sums up the game. It’s a fun, interesting and competent Metroidvania that is well worth playing through but it feels like everything could have been so much more. Maybe a little more development time, maybe a little more money who knows but as it is Headlander is a pretty good game as opposed to a jewel in the indie game crown. If you love Metroidvanias then this is a good one but it isn’t the absolute best of the genre.

I've played for 3 hours now and I'm about halfway through the second stage (there are three) with a couple of the hardest ones on stage one still unsolved. So far, there have been a couple of puzzles where you need to move quick to get out of the way, but usually you can just stay on the button and observe how the pieces move. If you don't get it right, you can replay the puzzle normally or in shadow mode where you can see your previous setup to help figure out what went wrong.
I prefer to play with a controller and the button mapping in this game is strange. A is cancel and B does the actions. Took me a while to realize that the controller does work once you find the right buttons. Also the difficulty levels aren't quite correct in my opinion. Some marked Normal are actually fairly tricky, whereas some marked Hard are not at all hard. However, that could be because I find it easier to solve hard puzzles with fewer pieces than normal puzzles with a lot of moving pieces. You usually have access to more than one puzzle at a time, so if you get stuck, just try another puzzle and come back later.

I absolutely love this game. As many have already have said, there are two characters to play as initially, with a third being unlocked after you beat the game with either of the first two. I recommend playing the game at least three times, once with each character. The order I played in was: Yunica (close/medium-range), Hugo (medium/long-range), then the secret character (very close-range). All three have interwining stories, and you only get the full picture after beating the game with all three.
The story itself is interesting, and makes you want to keep playing long after the credits roll. The good thing about Ys Origin is that you don't need any backstory from the previous games, due to this title being a prequel to the rest of the series. The combat is addictive, with the environments and enemies changing often enough so as not to get repetitive. The soundtrack is sublime, and will make you want to listen to it even outside of the game.
I played the game on Normal difficulty, and doing so will probably net you 8-10 hours of game for each character. However, I recommend playing on Hard, because grinding even a little bit on Normal will make the game obscenely easy. Overall, if you like action-RPGs, a great soundtrack, and a great story, you can't go wrong with this one.

Adding RPG stats to an action game always weakens the game, but despite that flaw Ys Origin has some of the best hack and slash boss battles on Steam outside of Ys Oath in Felghana and the bosses alone make the game worth playing. Each is a brutal brick wall requiring a lot of learning and retries to get all the patterns down, and, yes, unfortunately, a touch of grinding is required sometimes. There are levels you are meant to be at, as the boss time attack mode makes clear, and sometimes you don't get to those levels without going back and bashing mooks for a while. Still, at the right level, you can treat Ys like a real game and not yet another RPG grindfest.
Other problems, it's flatly worse than Ys Oath in Felghana. The mook combat is more interesting but the addition of multiple characters with different styles screws the balancing all up.
The story tells an "origin" that doesn't really ever justify itself. The priests of Ys had no grand mystery behind them and other than locking you in a dreary endless tower and throwing a lot of redone Ys 1 and 2 enemies at you, this story ends up offering no real insight to the Ys story, nor does it ever really get interesting enough to justify the freakishly long unskippable cutscenes.  Oath had a bloated tale too but at least it was a rollicking good adventure. Origin isn't even that.
Still, if you liked Oath and want another helping of those amazing boss battles, Origin is worth your time. Even if the balancing is off, the variety is here in spades. If you haven't played Oath yet, go get that.

HELLDIVERS is an incredibly fun game. If you recall Starship Troopers or Robocop (original) from Paul Verhoeven then you can imagine the exaggerated, ignorantly utopian world which is pretty much a satire for everything we know. This feeling has been delivered here by Arrowhead Game Studios in a game format, which is entertaining and addictive.
It's an isometric action shooter for 1-4 players where you are an Super Earth elite soldier battling 3 alien races throughout the galaxy sectors, with progress being accumulated by every player's contribution by completion of objectives. Which in turn leads to additional, major events.
Game has an incredible amount of weapons - from direct damage firearms, mechanized exosuits, APCs, tanks, to turrets, call-in airstrikes and technological gadgets. All of them can be upgraded by receiving research points from leveling or gathering special objectives (samples) in levels, opening new ways to use them or improve on weak points.
HELLDIVERS has 12 difficulty levels divided by planets in sectors. Every loadout slot is a tactical choice and can either compliment team composition to be able to deal with all manner of threats or strengthen individual divers.
Essentially it's an Alien Swarm meets Magicka game. Having very dynamic gameplay and challenges for all levels of skill and group compositions.
If you decide to get it - buy the full dlc version as it will save you money on individual dlc purchases where some really great items are provided (perk boots, tank, solid mid tier walker, etc).

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter was a video game that just popped out of nowhere for me, I hadn’t really read anything about it up to it’s release, or much after. It was only when I saw that one of my favourite Youtubers, Sips_ , uploaded a play-through of it that I decided to check it out. I quickly saw that it was a story driven game that I would not want to ruin my watching a video, so I didn’t.
The Vanishing of Ethan Carter was developed and published by an unknown developed called The Astronauts, but this team is made up of some well known people (including Adrian Chmielarz, who was the director of People Can Fly) It is really lovely to see a small team of developers get together like this and make a game extremely refreshing and delightful to play.
The story of The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is really one that you need to play for yourself, do not try and watch a few ‘Let’s Play’ videos of it because this game is a wonderful experience that will be ruined if you just watch someone else play it. The game starts of with the introduction of the character you are playing in this tale, and that is a supernatural detective called Paul Prospero. Paul received a fan letter from a young lad, Ethan Carter (who has…well…vanished) This letter described supernatural on-goings that no young boy should experience. Already knowing of Ethan’s disappearance, Paul has made it his mission to find out what is going on in the small town of Red Creek Valley, and to find the young Ethan Carter before it is too late.  Want to know more of the story? Well I am not going to spoil anything, play it yourself!
The Vanishing of Ethan Carter  is a first person detective game, with the events that Ethan Carter has suffered through have already completed. It is your job (well, Paul’s job) to find those clues scattered around and to put them into chronological order to how you believed it had happened – you will then see the story behind those clues. Each part to the story is split into different scenes, the clues are located in roughly the same area so that you won’t be trawling through the map trying to find clues that you may have missed – as long as you make sure you don’t just run through everything without paying attention, but you won’t have to run from one end of the map to the other because you missed one clue. Be sure to read all notes and stories that Ethan has left behind for somebody to read, they are all gems.
The story takes you through a few different locations in Red Creek Valley, and all these locations are as beautiful as the next.  The Vanishing of Ethan Carter may be the best looking game I have ever played, no over-reaction.  I spent the first couple of hours just wandering around taking screenshots to upload to my Steam profile, that is how beautiful it is – I even posted these screenshots onto websites and people would be astonished and ask what game it was!  I am amazed at the sheer effort The Astronauts went through to make these photo-realistic scenes, there is a wonderful article written by Andrzej Poznanski on The Astronauts website about how they achieved this,
it is a great read.
What is a great looking game with no atmosphere? The sounds in The Vanishing of Ethan Carter were as top notch as everything else. Just walking through the woodlands and hearing the wind gently whistling past with the steps my character made as he walked through some thick grass was nothing short of immersing, I really did feel like I was in the game – in the story. Gently playing in the background was the soundtrack to the game which was composed by Mikołaj Stroiński, who has also worked on the upcoming Witcher 3 Wild Hunt. The soundtrack was very peaceful, relaxing and something I would definitely buy and have on my iPod (in fact, I may check to see if they sell the OST now) Whenever I hear the music that was in the game, It instantly takes me back to the game and the great experience that I had – and in my opinion, that is what makes a good soundtrack.
The game ran very well on my GTX 980 and i7 4770k and I was getting constant 60 frames per second with only minimal drops from time to time. I was playing on the highest settings on 1080p, but there were plenty of alterations you could make to the quality of the game. If your PC is a bit older, drop a few of the settings and it will still look great.
All in all, I would highly recommend buying The Vanishing of Ethan Carter. If you are not much into story driven games where you are not running around shooting people – then this game may not be for you, but anyone who loves a good story with a sit back and relax nature to it (except one of the missions!) then definitely pick this up. The game spans around 5 hours, so if you are not sure if the game is for you, you may wish to wait until a sale or until it drops a bit in price – but at the current value, I would recommend it.

Metro 2033 is a game that I REALLY wanted to like. The story is great. Not outworldly, but still above average for a FPS. The game has a great atmosphere and is quite long for such a linear game. Oh, and looks amazing, even by 2016 standards.
Unfortunately, even after trying to stomach this game for three hours on PC, I just felt like I couldn't play it anymore. The game is just not FUN for me. The shooting is the worst part: you pump two shotgun cartridges into an enemy, and it doesn't even flinch! Takes a while for the shotgun to reload, so you decide to change to the machine gun, just to see one of the longest reload animations ever. Hell, all weapons take too long to reload. I take it that they tried to make the game more realistic this way but, TO ME, it just made the game more frustrating.
And there's the filter gimmick. Here's the thing: you are forced to use a gas mask when you are outside (and sometimes inside). The thing is: the filters for the mask are not infinite: you have to buy more, and replace them from time to time. And believe-me: this seems interesting at first, but gets boring way too fast. You have to replace filters too frequently, your mask gets dirty and you have to clean, your mask can break, and you have to find a new one, etc. That's NOT fun, just boring and repetitive.
The game has lots of good things going on for it, but it just didn't manage to make me have fun. They tried to make the game more realistic, while making you fight huge creatures that jump at you faster than you can reload your weapons. They tried to add realism, while also adding regenerating health. It's like they didn't know if they wanted this game to be realistic or not and then weit with neither.
Oh, and the enemies are bullet sponges sometimes, to make things even worse. ¬¬
If you have the patience of a Buddhist, go ahead. The game DOES have an interesting story that deserves to be experienced. I may be getting old, however, because I just couldn't have fun with this game.  It felt more like work, not like something that wants me to have fun.
I'm disappointed with this game, and sadly, I can't bring myself to even TRY the next game...
