Beatbuddy is a game that comes together musically, but in some gameplay areas falls short. For the first half hour roughly you'll learn what "Beat" can do and how the world works around him. There is some awkward, slightly whimsical story that surrounds everything but it's not always clear what is happening.
Gameplay is derived from moving around fluidly while creatures and things in the world all move to a beat. This is where I say musically the game shines. At some points you get an almost Fantasia feeling as a selection of sea creatures all make their own music, animating to the beat of the tune for the environment.
The music itself is catchy and immersive. My favorite moments in the game was when I would transition from just playing as Beat to navigating the watercraft vehicle. When this transition occurs, the levels music transitions to a chorus of sorts, making the song pretty powerful.
Unfortunately with all the cool rythmn actions happening, this is where gameplay tends to become awkward or constricted. Often times you'll struggly to effeciently pick up the object you need without spamming the mouse button. It just isn't a clean action, and since it's used heavily, you'll have moments of pure frustration sadly.
Movement is fluid as I mentioned, which once you learn the small nuances is easily adaptable. I was able to navigate almost all regions with ease.
The overall game is good and worth a play certainly, if not just to experience the cool music and beautiful 2d art and subtle animations. They definitely maximized the use of Unity for this game and it shows nicely. The overall game will feel repetitive after Environment 3 imo, but it'll be an enjoyable experience nonetheless.

Most people, if you ask them to name a 25-year-old game series in which you explore dungeons and fight monsters, will likely say “The Legend of Zelda”. Even though the Ys series is as old as Zelda and has enjoyed immense popularity in Japan since the first game, Ys 1: Ancient Ys Vanished (1987), the series has never been that popular outside the Orient.
A few entries did make it west on PS2 and PSP, either through Konami in 2005 with Ys VI: Ark of Napishtim (the first English release of the series in thirteen years) or XSEED’s masterful handling of translations starting with Ys: The Oath in Felghana. XSEED released Ys: The Oath in Felghana, a remake of Ys III: Wanderers from Ys (1989), on Steam in March. This is the first time most PC gamers get to experience what is (in terms of number of game releases) the largest Eastern RPG series second only to Final Fantasy.
Released on Steam in May, Ys Origin is the seventh game in the Ys series and a prequel. It takes place first in terms of chronology, 700 years before the events of “Ancient Ys Vanished” (Ys I & II). As you explore a huge vertical dungeon known as “Darm Tower”, the game elaborates on much of the series’ backstory, including characters, mystical artifacts and locations.
There are three playable characters (one is initially locked until you beat the game once with either of the other two), each has their own story and combat style. Yunica, a young knight, uses an axe and sword for close-range melee. Hugo Fact, genius magician and all-round ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, shoots bullets and is the easier of the two to play. We’re not going to spoil the third character for you.
Combat is fast and action-packed, with enemies having clear and recognizable patterns to their attacks. As you hack-and-slash your way up the tower, there are some mild puzzles to solve and mild platforming elements to jump through. There’s a kind of momentum system to keep you pushing forward: as you kill enemies without stopping, you gain a bonus to the rate at which you get experience points and “SP”. The “SP” points are spent to permanently buff your character, such as increasing resistance to negative effects like poison or confuse , or to upgrade your armour.
The boss fights are where the game (and series) really strut its stuff. While mowing through general enemies is pretty easy, boss fights require focus. You’ll need to learn their attack patterns, figure out which skills to use against them, and if you’re really into that kind of thing there are Time Attack and Boss Rush challenge modes.

I rarely finish games, but I finished Ys Origin twice and almost went for a third do-over.
The game as its core is quite fun. Mash Z at baddies. Baddies come straight at you, pushing you towards progress. Build that experience multiplier with every hit. Room emptied? Quick, rush to the next one, don't let it fade away! Mash, mash, hack and slash! Faster, Yunica, faster!
The part where the game forces you to essentially stop having fun mashing enemies to pieces are decidedly the least fun, and the very first chapter is probably the worst in this regard.
For the rest, however, the game doesn't look upon you for pushing recklessly forward: the game recognizes that there is nothing wrong with W+M1 (or, rather, Z+↑); it embraces the euphoria you get by building up your attack chain and going from monster to monster, building up buffs in the progress, leveling up without a break -- there is none of that "YOU JUST GOT ONE SKILL POINT STOP EVERYTHING YOU ARE DOING AND SPEND IT RIGHT THE HELL NOW" stuff, and the upgrades you CAN buy can wait in between flurries. Hell: the way NPCs in the game described Yunica in their fixed scripts matched perfectly the way I was playing -- accidental Z-mashing-based rolepaying has no right feeling this rewarding.
You spend 10 hours finishing the game, and you feel rewarded and spent and awesome. And then the game says you've unlocked a new character.
This is where I usually tune out; I don't really tend to do NG+s with rare exceptions. Ys Origin however was just so much fun it earned a chance for one, and oh boy. This new character's plot is completely different from Yunica's; it feels like the sequel to the story, or rather, a better version of it; and indeed my understanding is that it's this second version of the story that gets picked up in the next games.
The way he plays, also, is like Yunica squared: for a few boss fights, Yunica could rely on long range attacks to keep safe, but this second character has no ranged options at all. He must get in close and personal and it feels rewarding as hell, even though I've actually been playing on easy throughout -- it's still a game from Japan and I do NOT trust their sense of scale when it comes to difficulty.
I enjoyed Ys Origin a lot and it's almost a pit that the third character's plot doesn't seem different enough to warrant a third replay.

For over an hour this game was engrossing.  The environments are gorgeous, the soundtrack is lush without being overbearing, even the narration is enticing if a bit melodramatic.  Finding out so quickly that things are not as they seem is exciting, there's even an undertone of American decay the likes of which I haven't seen since the film Killing Them Softly.
Then, I completed the game, so it seemed.  Psychological horror games are among my favorite and I obsessively search every nook and cranny in any given area.  After I found several bizarre things which I presumed must be easter eggs, (the game is developed by "The Astronauts") there was nothing left to do.  I kept wandering around and found out that the path ahead is a circle, an island going nowhere.  Cutscenes repeated, puzzles I completed reappeared, I presumed I was in glitch hell.
Then, I skimmed an FAQ and found out what is meant by, "this game doesn't hold your hand."  No, I don't need hold handing, but when I complete a puzzle and it doesn't "finish," that is a flaw in the game.  There is an investigation in a churchyard that is "finished" when you are able to use the protagonist's metaphysical ability-- yet nothing happens.  I have completed the sequence multiple times and nothing happens but an incomplete "vision."
I moved on and it was more of the same.  Not realizing it, some of the other puzzles I had, "failed," but there was no notification of this.  Moreover, there was no way to restart certain puzzles.  I'm at the cusp of skipping the frustration of completing the game the "right" way and watching a playthrough video instead.
This is a shame because the bones of the game are unlike any I have played before.  Had they playtested the game or polished it further it could have been a classic story the likes of the second Silent Hill or Dead Space games.  Hell, I enjoyed Alan Wake for what it was.
Spoiler alert: there's an irritating maze with a monster that causes instant death toward the end.  There is more backtracking, too, including a requirement to backtrack at least twice through an area where the character walks in slow motion.  This game should be so good, the environments are fascinating to explore, certain gags like the "cold boiling" water were novel, what went wrong?

When I was ten years old and playing Myst for the first time, this is the game I wished I were playing. I just didn't realize it yet.
That's not to say that The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is very much like Myst, from a gameplay perspective. But it does present exactly the sort of open-ended, fully explorable, non-prerendered, gorgeous and mysterious videogame setting I could only fantasize about in my formative days as a young gamer. The game plays a bit like some sort of three-way polygamous marriage between (1) a minimally interactive narrative game like Gone Home, Kentucky Route Zero, or one of Telltale's newer titles; (2) a more abstract, mood-driven exploration game (or "walking simulator," if you prefer); and (3) a more traditional adventure game with actual puzzles, though the puzzles here are rarely as difficult or obtuse as the ones seen in most classic point-and-click adventures. If you enjoy any of those (admittedly loosely-defined) genres at all, Ethan Carter is definitely worth a look. If you hate them, chances are you won't love this game.
I'll avoid getting into any specifics regarding the plot or gameplay, and instead just say that a large part of my enjoyment of the game came from going into it relatively blind, and that I would recommend others try to do the same. More so than any other game I've played in quite some time, Ethan Carter's strange story developments and pervading sense of mystery left me genuinely wondering what in the hell was going to happen next (and this is something I really wish more games would do).
Also, the soundtrack ranks up there with my all-time favorites in a game.

While I could have skipped large amounts of the content and have been only satisfied by the gorgeous visuals and cinematic style, I instead took the time to solve every murder, and boy is it worth it.  This game is incredible.
As for who this game will appeal to, it is perfect if you enjoyed:
-Half life 1/2/e1/12
-Metroid Prime 1/2/3/Trilogy
-The Fall
-Portal 1/2
+The plot is perfect.  The writing is great, and is based on the premise of a family driven off the edge of madness, half due to paranormal influence and half due to the other half's insanity.  All the characters have well defined motivations, and they act in an incredibly believable manner given the premise.
+It's a movie.  A lot of people don't realize this, but there is almost nothing that you can do in the game that couldn't be rationalized in a movie.  This adds an enormous amount of value to the cinematic experience and deepens immersion to a ridiculous level.  Past its supernatural elements, this game just may be the most realistic game ever due to this fact.  For example, you don't get head bob if you hold forward and you would normally walk at a wall.  Nobody just continues walking when they hit a wall.  No one even hits the wall in the first place.
+The murder solving mechanics are flawless.  You actually feel Paul Prospero's thoughts as if they were your own, and the chronology mechanic makes it so you are literally piecing the mystery together.
+Did I mention this game is gorgeous?  With all settings maxed out, this game has the capacity to look even better than real life.  I showed this game to someone who sees VERY little value in video games, and even she said it looked like a watercolor painting.
+I won't spoil it, but the ending is about as satisfying as they get.
+I encountered almost no bugs.  This even further adds to the immersion.
+The dev artists must have a thing for the Bloom Effect.  It is used in spades.  You may think of it as a fetish, but I believe it does nothing but better the experience.
+/-You can't jump.  While this can make you feel more limited, at the same time it adds to the immersion exponentially, by preventing things like jumping in place  repeatedly or walking into a wall while jumping.  In real life, nobody jumps continuously in the direction of a rock just to hope that they will get on top one time or another.
+/-The game doesn't hold your hand.  While this means you will often get stuck without level cues to tell you what to do, it does mean that the game surpasses the tropes of level design and instead lets you immerse yourself fully.  If you get stuck, it's your own fault, because the game told you it wasn't going to help you.
-It is only pseudo open world.  While you can always visit earlier areas, there are very many barriers blocking you from falling off of cliffs or going to places where the devs don't have a fully fleshed out terrain map.
-This game needs a mammoth stacked on top of a dodo crammed into a pc to run.  Not to say that it isn't optimized or can't be configured to run at lower settings easily, but to get the full intended effect, you need an infinite probability drive to run it.
-There is occasional red flashes or blue flashes at certain settings.  I am not sure which settings cause this, but they barely detract from the experience.
-One section employs jumpscares.  This employs both stealth and horror elements, which don't belong in a game where these elements are employed nowhere else.  Had there been similar parts throughout the game, I wouldn't mind.  Instead, this became the only part of the game that broke immersion even slightly for me.  As it was also the only part in the whole game in which you could "die," being set back at the start of the section felt as if it would have been better as permadeath.  At least that way I could continue to justify everything that occurs in the game.
Overall, this game is a masterpiece.  Its pros heavily outweigh the cons, and the cons are negligible at best.  I doubt I will see anything quite as engaging, immersive, beautiful or as perfectly paced as this absolute opus magnum of a game.  While it may not be flawless, like a good movie it creates a perfect illusion that does more than enough to negate those minor flaws.
9.5/10

Slash It 2 is the sequel to Slash It. It is the same as Slash It in that there are multiple modes to play and you must type letters and/or numbers to score points. This game has 6 modes, but the Classic mode from the original Slash It game is gone. However, I think Slash It 2 does well without the Classic mode in which you must match different shapes. By dedicating itself to strictly matching numbers and letters, I think Slash It 2 is better than Slash It.
The game encourages you to hone your typing skills on the keyboard. The mode gets progressively faster as you correctly type the number or letter on the screen. A great addition to Slash It 2 is the Words mode. The Words mode is better than the Classic mode on Slash It. Words travel across the screen from right to left and the objective is to type the words correctly to score points. Eventually, more words will flow across the screen, causing the mode to be more challenging that at the beginning. The Words mode fits more into the Slash It franchise’s purpose of helping you improve your typing skills than the Classic mode from the original Slash It.
The soundtrack of Slash It 2 is outstanding. The music plays from the start of your playthrough and the screen flashes as you type numbers, letters, words, or a combination of numbers and letters. Thus, the music truly adds to the entertainment value of the game. You can buy the Slash It 2 – Electronic Music Pack for $0.99 to add to the already entertaining classic music that comes with the game.
I recommend Slash It 2 to anyone with and desire to improve their typing skills and for the entertainment that comes with type letters, numbers, and words. I firmly believe that it you liked Slash It, you will love Slash It 2. Kudos to Just1337 Studio for making a sequel that improves on the original.

This game is pretty epic, you're gonna die, someone on your team is gonna kill you, and then Bugs will teabag your corpse. this game goes from easy to WTF real quick. On the plus side the community is pretty friendly. Haven't run into many folks that rage due to friendly fire.

You drop in with your friends, kill a bunch of aliens from 1 of 3 factions (crustacean bugs, cyborgs that are a bit like Warhammer 40k's orcs, or the illuminates that are based on the trope of super-intelligent aliens with their gleaming white robots), call in drops called "stratagems" and kill everything.
The game works by generating a small map with several objectives (the number and type of objectives changes on higher difficulties). The objectives vary from just capturing an area to performing geological surveys to disarming minefields to escorting people from one point to another and so much more.
Singleplayer is completely viable, which is very nice. But the game really opens up with multiplayer (up to four people total). And all bullets flying through the air are capable of hurting you, be they from the enemies, you, your friends, your turrets, your friends' turrets, etc. Going prone puts you out of danger from all that, and even helps you survive explosions. One possible objective of the game is to blow up a structure using a massive explosive that you have to call in and activate; jumping to prone right before it goes off and surviving is incredibly satisfying.
At the end of every mission, after completing all the other objectives, you have to get to the extraction point, call it in, and hold out until the ship gets there. At this point, everybody pulls out their mechs and turrets and heavy machine guns, and all the enemies know you're there and you get swarmed. But it's incredible because everyone is firing like mad, and the guns feel powerful - it reminds me of how the Dawn of War games would be with big-scale shootouts and ridiculous firepower.
On top of it all, there's a huge number of unlockables - weapons, perks, stratagems, upgrades - that you'll go hunting for. Some of them you get from leveling up, other times you get them as a part of completing planets (each planet has 2-3 missions), and all the upgrades you get from research points that you find in the map or from leveling up. There's so much to get, and none of it changes the game so much to make you feel pointlessly invincible.
The DLC has some stigma because it was there on release. The thing a lot of people don't realize is that those were released slowly over time while this game was on the PlayStation, and it would be pretty unfair to get them for free when the PS players had to pay for them all. Also, none of the items are game-changers, and you can do without them. Furthermore, buying them supports the incredible Arrowhead.
That said, they've already released 3 free content expansions during its time as a PlayStation exclusive, and from what I understand, they intend to make more. That means all the meaningful content like new planets, enemies, or mechanics aren't lost on people who don't want to pay extra for the game. They don't want to split their community, especially because it plays such a pivotal part of the central game. All Helldiver players everywhere indirectly take part in a universe-wide war with the three factions, fighting for territory or defending planets.
The price might seem a bit steep at first, but then you realize that the game has so much there. There are no gimmicks or tricks, it's just plain fun. All in all, I have little to no complaints. The game is extremely replayable, fantastically fun, works well in singleplayer, and shines in multiplayer.
Edit:
There's some negative opinions about the game's keyboard and mouse controls. I've tried them, and I think they need a bit of getting used to but don't hinder the gameplay much at all. That said, the game does play better on a gamepad (it's called a twin-stick shooter for a reason) and even if the keyboard and mouse controls were 100% perfect it still would not be as good as playing with a gamepad. Gamepads are simply better controllers for certain kinds of games, and this is one of them. Just get a gamepad if you really mind the K&M controls :)

Half-Life 2: Episode One is yet another single-player FPS from Valve that came out in 2006 year. It's a direct continuation to Half-Life 2 and supposedly a start of episodic releases. If forget that it never got past Episode Two. Episodic releases of games just never work, unless you are Telltale.
It's quite similiar to Half-Life 2 and uses game design philosophy behind it, as well as gameplay. And assets. So there isn't much to explain. A fancy shooter with gravigun. Only this time you often has a teammate, Alyx, who doesn't die easily.
Plotwise it continues where Half-Life 2 ends, as you are found in rumbles of a citadel of City 17. Now it's your mission to get out from city and cause trouble for yourself in meanwhile.
It starts out quite weak, as you have to venture through some amount of storyline scenes and then left with super-charged gravigun. Super-charged gravigun was quite a nice surprise at the end of Half-Life 2, but here it overstays it's welcome, as it's the only weapon you can use, with no variety.
It gets better after first two chapter, as you slowly gain standard weapons, find much more creative uses for gravigun and will get to enjoy Alyx's fighting company much more, while you are exploring dark underground, ruins of a city and hospital. Hospital also featured some AI vs AI fights, something that me and many players love watching. And boss. Same old in new enviroment.
Episode One adds a big new feature in Valve games for first time: Developers commentary.
When activated, the flying icons will appear in the levels that you can use. Upon usage you will be listening (and reading in subtitles) to one of the developers talking about something related or unrelated to where the icon was placed. It could be Alyx's AI, or changes in lighting, or the way that scene came to be, or just how smart they count themselves.
It's quite a great addition and is much better than Developer Commentaries in later Valve games, which was more like Voice Acting Commentary: How Amazing It Is To Have No Script.
Overall, it's a decent FPS. Decent episode. Something that you will beat, have fun and then forget. Still nice.

So, what is it you want from a game? Pretty visuals? An excellent story? Intense action? A challenge? If the answer to the last two questions are "yes", you should try this game. The anime/JRPG style visuals may not be everyone's cup of tea, so take that into account. The story is by no means bad, but nothing that'll keep you at the edge of your seat. But there are some really good reasons why to play this game.
First of all, the gameplay. Fast-paced and fluid hack&slash action typical for an ARPG with the difference that it has a vertical dimension as well, adding some platforming to the whole concept. Initially you get to pick between two characters, and can unlock a third one. The story remains more or less the same (it's best described as 3 different points of view), but there are significant differences in how the characters are played, each of the 3 offers a unique gameplay experience. You can pick either a controller or the KB/mouse duo, both work just fine. The configuration tool is user-friendly and offers a lot of freedom in defining your desired configuration.
There are five difficulty levels, ranging from "very easy" to "nightmare". The game is quite challenging, don't be shy to try it on a lower difficulty if you just don't seem to move forward. The strongest point of this game are the numerous and intense boss-battles, which test your reflexes and wits alike. You won't get anywhere with the "hit it until it stops moving" idea even on "very easy". Expect to hit the retry button numerous times, sometimes it's not obvious what you need to do from the start. Explore and experiment, it's fun!
Finished story mode with all 3 characters? The game still has replay value! In the Time Attack mode, you can test your mettle against the game's bosses without having to replay the whole game again. And it doesn't end there. While Time attack can be played right after completing the game with one character, once you clear the story mode with all 3, you gain access to Arena Mode, where you fight waves of enemies from the level of your choice and collect SP (the game's currency) to unlock bonus content.
The soundtrack is simply amazing. Masterpiece after masterpiece, greatly adding to the enjoyment the game has to offer.
If "challenge" is your middle name, then you shouldn't miss this game.
The verdict: 8.9/10

This is only an issue because you don't know how the game is supposed to play regarding your "sense" until you complete your first scene, so you don't know that you actually missed something til it's too late. Overall 9/10. I had to dock that one point for the end game running and continuity break.

I cannot recommend this game, because it in my opinion doesn't qualify as a game.
It is more like an interactive story, but the interactivity does nothing to improve on anything.
Since there are no game elements - there is no way to "lose", for instance - the choice to not include a simple way to navigate between the "chapters" of the story, or something as simple as a map, mystifies me. Instead we are forced to wander back and forth across the albeit gorgeous landscape, searching for what to experience next. The fact that you can find these things in the wrong order and have to go back looking for the rest of them in order to "finish" the story only adds to the aggravation.
At risk of spoiling things, and you may not want to read any further if you don't want to be spoiled, it seems strange that the makers of this program didn't include a "fast travel" option that would let us instantly go back to places we had already visited. After all, one such fast-travel mechanism is introduced at the very end, when everything is pretty much over. Strangely it is only usable from the most remote part of the area, so once you have used it you are still forced to walk all across the landscape over and over if you need to use it again. The landscape is marvellously beautiful, but I still find myself permanently pressing the "run faster" button in order to get around at a reasonable pace. The mood of the story would have won a great deal if running wasn't always possible, but instant relocating was.
I suppose the puzzles in the story could be called a game, but since they can all be solved with brute force with little need to think or find clues, I don't know if I can agree. Once again, there is no way to "lose", which I think is a critical part of a game. Since nothing you do has any effect on the story whatsoever, the idea to wrap the story in a very pretty environment and sell it as a game is a bit strange. Presumably the market for barely interactive puzzle adventures isn't that great.

Headlander is just such a strange idea for a game. You play as a floating head that can take over robot's bodies. While it is not perfect, Headlander is a fun and enjoyable experience.
The gameplay for the most part is enjoyable. For some reason it is satisfying to rip off the robot's heads to take over their bodies. The shooting mechanics are interesting as well. The shooting mechanics work well but I liked them most when the game forced you to use ricochet shots in order to hit enemies. I wish the game had more areas like this rather than the situations where you get swarmed by enemies and just have to keep shooting to destroy all of them.
While I enjoyed the gameplay, towards the end of the game it started to feel repetitive. After you have developed a good strategy of defeating robots you pretty much just keep repeating it. While the gameplay is fun I was starting to wish there was a little more depth to it towards the end of the game.
Overall I am conflicted on Headlander's story. I think the game does a very good job creating an interesting environment. The problem is that I found the story itself is pretty average and not that memorable. The game is also not as funny as I have come to expect from Double Fine.
I enjoyed my time with Headlander. It is a unique and fun game. If you usually enjoy Double Fine's games I would guess that you would enjoy Headlander as well.

While Double Fine may bring a whole array of positive and negative feelings, there's always been a set of talent that you can see in all of their games. Headlander is no exception, but is a lot better then a lot of Double Fine's recent work in my opinion. A metroidvania game that focuses on exploration, Headlander oozes style from every pore, focusing on great art design and colorful storytelling over technical mastery. Cutscenes were always fun thanks to some great voice acting work, and the story is able to execute the standard dystopian sci-fi tropes rather well. Some good 70s/80s scifi music complement the action as well, and good sound design all around the board. Gameplay is where things get a bit more iffy, as the combat sections have the mechanics of a fun metroidvania game....they just don't have the difficulty that a veteran of the genre would want. It has trouble complementing its gameplay at times with its art design at times, and some of the control decisions at times don't make a lot of sense. The main vacuum mechanic is still fun as hell, and is one of the more unique mechanics in the genre. And when the game does get the combat right, it can be fun, especially in the boss fights. It just needed more oomph in the end. But Headlander is more about the journey and about the story that it tries to tell: and in that, it succeeds.

It's a very fun metroidvania-type game. Flying around as a disembodied head, and taking over all sorts of robotic bodies, many of which move and behave in very unique ways is awesome. There are also a lot of upgrades you can get by spending XP points found in the world, which actually give you useful abilities/boosts.
Not all is great though. The main issue with the game is, that the core gameplay isn't quite as satisfying as it should be. Shootouts are too chaotic for their own good and usually don't involve much in the way of strategic thinking. It's definitely not perfect, however that doublefine charme goes a long way to ensure it's an enjoyable romp throughout.
I'd recommend it to anyone interested in doublefine games and/or sidescrollers. There's a lot to like here, especially if you're a completionist type. There are many optional health,power and helmet-thrust upgrades to find in the environment if you keep your eyes open, and if you miss something you can always go back to get it. I actually enjoyed 100%ing the game. Attempting that with other games often severely bogs down the pacing, or it's just flat out boring, but in Headlander it's fun throughout as the map subtly helps you find all the upgrades.
So yes, definitely a recommendation from me!

EDIT:  Here is my amended review now that I beat the game (on Windows) - I left the original review at the bottom.
Turns out that Windows was the key to enjoying this game.  I loved the art style, the music was awesome, the level design was exceptionally well done especially considering how it could've been extremely easy to get lost (yet I never seemed to), the only issue I really had was the controls.  On the Mac side, the mouse controls were terrible and a 360 controller didn't function properly.  On the Windows side, everything worked great on the controller and it made the game enjoyable since the controls were so tight.  If you only have a Mac, avoid this game.  If you have a PC or dual boot (and have a good controller), it's absolutely worth a buy.
V.1 - I want to like this game.  The music seems cool, the art style is interesting and the concept is a fresh take on the genre, but technical problems (at least for the Mac version) are holding me back.  The game crashes more often than it runs and the menu navigates without fail via 360 controller, only to have none of the buttons work once actually in the game.  Mouse control feels supremely subpar compared to what a gamepad setup would allow.  I'll try this game again on the Windows side later, but as it stands now, I'd pass if on a Mac.

So, have you played
before? Well, this is pretty much the same game, but with better graphics.
There is always this hidden “rule” that all Triple A titles must have outstanding graphics on release and this one is no exception. The visuals are fantastic even at lower settings, I played this on the Medium pre-set and didn’t notice a single fault on the games’ visuals. This is essentially an ‘upgraded’ version of
if we’re just talking about the graphics itself.
It’s not good or should I say it’s “generic”, because that’s what the entire story is, it’s pretty damn generic from start to finish…even the ending (which I won’t spoil), but really you shouldn’t even consider buying this game if you’re looking for a good story.
The side quests? I only did 6 of them to increase my points, but they’re the same as most games…you talk to a person, you get a thing for them and you give that thing to get your points. So, nothing special in that department.
From the voices to the gunshots, it’s on-point 90% of the time. This game also has really nice surround sound that immerses you which most games lack. The only small issue is the soundtrack that plays in the background in some of the missions…they can get quite repetitive/annoying especially if you’re trying to concentrate on listening out for zombies, you can always lower these down or turn it right off in the settings if you want though.
Remember how I said this is like
? Well, it plays out similarly too, from the quest layout to the weapon blueprints. I’d say 85% of the gameplay aspects from Dead Island was transferred to Dying Light which isn’t to say it’s a bad thing, I’m glad they did it this way as it made everything very familiar and made the game layout easier to understand.
£39.99, that’s how much this game costs. That is a lot for a game that offers a terrible story and borrows a lot of gameplay mechanics from another game. But, if you can look past that, you get a game that has outstanding visuals, great all-round audio and a smooth gameplay experience.

Short, sweet, and definitely on point. I've been waiting to pick up A Story About My Uncle for some time now, and I'm glad to say that I finally did. For what you pay for, this game is immensely engaging and has tons of replay value. Anyone who enjoys perfecting platforming runs will be sure to be at this game for a while trying to gather all of the achievements for efficiency.
On top of that, it's got a good, heartfelt story that is a sharp contrast to the cookie-cutter narratives that plague Indie games nowadays. By the end of the game you love the characters and don't want to see them go.
And lastly, this game is downright gorgeous. Coffee Stain knows what makes a beautiful environment and they took that and ran with it when they published A Story About My Uncle. It is optimized and smooth, and won't disappoint you.
Overall, I highly recommend this game for fans of the indie and platforming genres. It's well worth the price you pay.

Still, the Redux gives more then it takes and in the end makes it worth your while.

Metro 2033 is not the game I expected it to be.  I had heard that it was a good horror shooter and that description gave me certain expectations.  I assumed that the game would play like a first person Dead Space or Resident Evil 4.  I figured I'd be fighting some crazy monsters with barely enough bullet to get by.  I figured I'd have to worry about inventory management as I constantly searched for life saving healing items to keep me from dying.  I expected to have the tools I needed to just barely get by, but never really feel like a badass.  So I start playing and the game gives me a revolver with hardly any ammo, so far so good.  I have limited healing items, but my health regenerates.  That takes the tension out of it a bit, but I'm still counting bullets and that's fine by me.  Then about a third of the way through the game I start to fight some human enemies.  After I took them out I looted them for ammo and never had to worry about running out of bullets for the rest of the game.
It was at this point that I realized that I wasn't playing a survival horror shooter.  I discovered that I was actually playing a FPS that just had some creepy parts in it.  The craziest part of it all is that I was enjoying Metro 2033 too much to feel betrayed.  It may not have been what I expected, but it was still a good game.  The game does a great job drawing you in and has a good sense of atmosphere.  On top of that the guns feel good to use and combat is fun.  The game does a good job mixing to combat up between human and monster enemies.  THis keeps things from getting stale.  When fighting agains human enemies the player usually has the option of using stealth to get kills instead of going guns blazing.  It's not exactly Metal Gear Solid, but the stealth gameplay is competent.
My only major complaint is that the player character is a silent protagonist in a story that doesn't really mesh with the whole silent protagonist thing.  Still, I guess if that's the biggest complaint that I have then that means the gameplay holds up.  I'd recommend this game, but just keep in mind that it's not a straight horror game.

Make no mistake: this is a “FIND THE HIDDEN OBJECT” game, in case it wasn’t clear by the game’s video trailer and description. (It wasn’t clear to me, anyway)  If these “hidden object” games are not your cup of tea, then you might want to pass this game by.
As far as “hidden object” games go, this one’s pretty decent, but with a VERY SHORT play time. It has nice “photorealistic” graphics, an interesting (although a bit melancholy) storyline, and a few mildly-amusing minigames. One twist in the gameplay/graphics was the “multi-plane” scrolling of each level; moving around shifts the perspective a little, possibly revealing a hidden object.
Another twist: hidden letters in the scene, often in the form of misspelled signs, often must be found.
The story is entirely linear (except the final level), so the “time-shifting” aspect is just part of the linear storyline; you can’t “time shift” on your own. This game has a psychological/meaning-of-life motif that seems to be in vogue these days, but I found the story intriguing enough to want to play the game to the end.
The game is very short, and can be beaten in about 2 or three hours.
So yeah, I liked it. It's a short but decent casual game. Consider the cost of the game versus the two/three-hour playtime, though.

The puzzle design is a low point for the game with many puzzles requiring preconditions to allow interactions despite having the correct items and ideas before the game allows them to work.  This flaw adds confusion to the adventure game formula which in general doesn't need anymore.

I don't understand why this game has so many negative reviews. I played it and I thought it was a really good game. It is sold at a great price and the graphics are really nice. I do have to agree that the bonus chapter is a little better, but I enjoyed the whole game.

Graphically beautiful scenes, great music, well-composed HOGs, varied puzzles, pretty good VOs, and decent character design, but the positives are somewhat marred by unintuitive gameplay, a terribly cobbled-together cliché storyline, and bad editing (in English at least). Still worth a play even without achievements or cards - but the wow factor is mostly in the visuals.
Your omg-so-close-we're-practically-telepathic twin goes missing and you set off to find her. Along the way you get pulled into playing detective to find a woman's missing kids, and ultimately get wrapped up in a conspiratory necromantic cult ritual that for some reason only you can stop (even though there are knights and friendly dragons and mythical birds just hanging around doing nothing). Save the kids, save your sister, destroy the cult, the end. Yawn.
It's the same old formula: Save [family/friend] by collecting [X number] pieces of [magic items] of different [colors/runes] to stop [evil person/group] before they do [evil ritual] to resurrect [evil being]. That about sums it up. It's a tired and overused plot, and in this case it's also not executed very well.
Many plot elements introduced in the first scenes are seemingly ignored for the rest of the game, and there's literally no way to know how the heck it all fits together unless you read the store page description. Really. In game you find a news article that vaguely hints at your origins, but that line of intrigue is dropped/forgotten almost immediately. A few things are touched upon in your journal, but not enough to answer questions like why there are dragons and harpies and golems and ghosts mucking about. Reasons.
The core gameplay is alright-ish, but the majority of point-and-click elements are very unintuitive. Many items you find make no sense for the situation, and make even less sense when you figure out what they're for. Why did I just find a monster's severed arm, and why is it only useful to burn a hole in a rock? Why can't I use paint unless I mix it with angel tears? And so on. Also, when you use tools you have to actually click multiple times to use them. Need to dig a hole with a shovel? Click to dig. Then click to dig. Then click to dig. Why can't the animation just play 3 times on its own? Ultimately the game is still playable and enjoyable, but you'll probably be making liberal use of the hint button or strategy guide.
This game is gorgeous. Amazingly artistic backgrounds for almost every location. I'm seriously impressed, and would even go so far as to say the game is worth playing for the visuals alone. (If you're also an artist, it's a goldmine of inspiration.) The lighting is very well done, proportions, angles, composition, mood, space, textures, just everything. Even the more 'drab' locations were drawn well - just not as "ooh, screenshot!" worthy. The art is on par with (or even better than) several of the top Artifex games, which is saying a lot. Though I honestly wish the game supported widescreen/1920x1080 res (it's 1024x768 windowed), because then I'd have a whole new bunch of desktop backgrounds to cycle through.
The character design is good, but the animation can get awkward. The lip sync is decent and movement isn't terrible, but in many cases the facial expressions turn from nice to creepy once they start talking (particularly the uncle and the two kids). The non-human characters are way more appealing. The dragon in the bar is one of my favorites, and I really appreciated the fact that the artist thought it through enough to plan out where the *rest* of the dragon would fit in the building. It was creatively done and quite amusing, and the kind of detail other fantasy games never really take into account.
Cutscenes are surprisingly almost as clear as the static art. Definite plus there too.
The music is lovely. The mood is a little "off" in a couple of scenes (mainly the bonus chapter), but overall I liked it enough to save the music files (the CE extras are in the game folder). SFX were great as well.
I don't know why there are complaints about the voiceovers, because they're pretty darn good for the genre. It may not be top dollar voice work, but it's far better than countless other titles. The only issue is that several spoken lines don't quite match the subtitles, but you can't really fault the actors for that.
HO scenes are just as pretty as the location backgrounds, but the actual clutter is a little jarring. Many items are placed/scaled oddly and there are a few repeated graphics. Hitboxes are also very precise, which can be frustrating. Still, overall they're well-constructed as standard HO scenes with an above-average difficulty.
Puzzles are also mostly above-average difficulty, with a toughie or two thrown in (the spiked gear puzzle in the bonus chapter is infuriating). I enjoyed them though, which is what counts. Unfortunately this is also one of those games where the puzzle window poofs the second you find the solution, so there's no way to see what you did correctly if you were just trying random things. On the plus side, there's an in-game strategy guide that shows all the solutions if you find yourself stuck.
The bonus chapter doesn't make sense as a bonus chapter. It just seems like they took out the section about saving the second boy and slapped it onto the end to further justify "Premium" in the title. Still, it was nice to have access to the artwork, sketches, screensavers, and OST.
Despite its weak storyline and no Steam extras, Sister's Secrecy is still worth playing, if only to appreciate the fantastic artwork. HOGs and Puzzles are standard fare, but the whole thing is bug-free, and the length is just right. If you got it in a bundle, by all means, do play it. If you're on the fence because it has no cards or achievements, keep it on your radar and wait for a good  sale.

Sister’s Secrecy: Arcanum Bloodlines is a generic Hidden Object game that doesn't do anything badly, or anything particularly well.
The Good.
I found the background scene graphics appealing, kudos to the artist.
Voice acting wasn't AAA but it was good for the genre for the most part.
Bonus chapter
Decent length, not too short or too long.
Lots of HO scenes that are well detailed, and the puzzles were on the easy side.
You can collect coins to unlock artwork which you can then save to your computer. I appreciated that because I liked the artwork.
The Bad.
Same tired old story line. Missing friend or family member/supernatural elements. Please do something original once in a while!
Minor translation errors for object descriptions (you are asked to find a "loop" but the object is a "noose")
Once again, the "bonus" chapter was ripped from the main game and added back in as "bonus content." In the main game, a mother asks you to find her two sons who have gone missing. You only find one of them in the main story but it's enough for the mother to thank you and complete the quest line. The "bonus" chapter is finding the other son, but there's no introduction or explanation as to what you have to do in the bonus chapter until you find the second son a few scenes in, it feels cut from the main game. I wish developers wouldn't do that ...simply to just put "Premium Edition" on the game to drive more sales.
The click detection is not the best, both in HO scenes and when trying to use/place objects in the real world, occasionally requiring multiple clicks before the object is found/placed.
Although fairly easy, sometimes there's a lack of clear direction and you find yourself wondering what to do next or what the objects in your inventory react with.
Overall, it's a very average game that HOG fans might find on the easy side. There's nothing here that sets it above the rest, and there are lots of games on Steam that are worse.

Amazing game. Many people complain that a specific army is too overpowered but the people on the other side fighting them tend to say the same thing. IE: People playing russians complain about germans. People playing germans complain about russians. It is all how you build your army and use your resources.
The game has an amazing cover system.
If you have squads behind a low wall, for example, they use it as cover and take less damage.
If they are a sniper or other specialized unit, they can stealth in certain cover and buildings. They are revealed when they shoot so they are not overpowered. Also a sniper (for all but the upcoming British) cannot affect tanks.
There is also negative cover. A group of conscripts walking in the middle of the row can AND WILL get gunned down by a german heavy machinegun.
Anyways just an amazing game try it out. Campaign is beautiful and there are many ways to win.

I loved the first game. The pacing, the intricacy of the puzzles, the cumulative clues - it was intuitive but still tricky. Beautifully rendered, and the story let you fill in a lot of the blanks on your own with its subtlety.
Not this one. Like another reviewer mentioned last month, I was sorely disappointed because it felt like the puzzles got diluted; you basically spread the same level of puzzle around a much larger area, and that's it. Solutions weren't intuitive.
I didn't use the hints at all in the first game because no matter how stumped I was, I knew there was a reason behind every placement and item. Nothing was superfluous. In this game, I had to resort to using hints frequently because some things were completely unrelated to one another. Cleverness doesn't help at all if you're in a different part of the room and you needed something from an entirely different part.

I recommend this game to the casual puzzle enthusiast.  It is not a very long game; however, the content that is there is great.  The graphics are a lot better than I would have imagined a remastered mobile game to have; and the lighting definitely helps set the eerie vibe that runs throughout this game.
The puzzles in this game have a good amount of difficulty and excel at challenging both your memory and ingenuity.  If they prove too difficult, however, there is a progressive help system that can save you from mindlessly clicking on every item in the room, hoping for a solution.  Not that I did that...  Anyway, the game is fairly episodic in its gameplay and can be tedious if puzzle boxes are not your thing.  This game is all about them.
Lastly, I read some reviews that were angry at the seemingly missing story.  Although it is sparse, there is definitely a story in this game.  It is the final puzzle that ties everything together.  If you can piece together everything you’ve experienced over the course of this game, you will start to unravel the mystery that is The Room.

I was very impressed by The Room, and my expectations have been exceeded with this second instalment.
A bit more spooky and mysterious than the first game, it features stunning, gorgeous graphics and more interesting environments. The game is much the same - several chapters of puzzle games - but a completely new experience nonetheless. The game is short, but it's well worth the small cost.
Definitely a masterpiece if you like puzzle games, very highly recommended! I'd love to see more of these, and will definitely buy any sequels they put out.

Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six: Vegas 2 is a tactical shooter video game and the sequel to Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six: Vegas. It was announced by Ubisoft on November 20, 2007. The game was released for the Xbox 360, PlayStation 3, and Microsoft Windows-based PCs on March 19, 2008 in North America and March 20 in Europe, except in Germany, where the game has been delayed. A world-exclusive first-look of the game appeared in the January edition of the Official Xbox Magazine. One of the biggest announcements of the game is that Logan Keller, the lead character from the previous game, has been removed in favor of having the player create his own character to play through the campaign. The player will assume the role of Bishop, a member of the Rainbow squad with a great deal more experience who is more deeply involved in the story. The game is billed as "part sequel, part prequel", as the events of the campaign run both before and concurrently to the story of Logan Keller and continue after where the first game concluded. Episode 1 is the nice, short and sweet sequel to Half Life 2 that essentially more or less gives us answers as to the sudden and very cliffhanger-esque conclusion of the second game in the Half Life series.  Besides perhaps some extra technical updages and level design not much new is seen in this sequel, however even when recycling their assets Valve managed to deliver in terms of story and fun gameplay, giving us another round with the overpowered uber gravity gun that marked the highlight of the game's finale as well as throw in some extra suspense.
One thing I will mention is how much I liked the short, episodic way they unveiled this 'sequel' of sorts.  It gave a relatively inexpensive means to continue the story without putting a lot of stress on the dev teams who likely also had other things to do.  Like the original Portal, it was short enough to be almost considered an intern project, but well developed enough that it had the nice spit and polish of a fully professionally-made triple A title (back when the term didn't just restrict to game price and graphic output and actually referred to the quality of the overall game).  In a way it's kind of like seeing an expansion pack of sorts to the original, and I like that.
Not much else to say.  If you were a fan of Half Life 2 and don't own this one yet (which I don't know why) it is definitely worth purchasing along with the next one.

My Experience with ASAMU is not the first time, as I remember playing the old free to play thing from their website. Due to the lack of any game that resembles ASAMU (at least that I know of), I'll compare it to the old ASAMU.
The first thing that I notice is the change of story and the cutscenes. They don't have that stuff back in the day, and I personally welcome the addition. The only thing that kind of disappoints me is the lack of emotion during the story-telling of main character to her daughter. I get it that story was never the strong part even in old ASAMU, but if they really want to take the game into storry-telling direction they can at least make the story-teller a little bit more... Expressive. This doesn't affect the natives as they are not human to begin with, so I give them a benefit of the doubt by assuming they have different culture.
The second thing that is noticeable is the change of maps, which is pretty minor. They also make the town a lot bigger and vibrant than the old ASAMU so there is that.
As far as music goes, I think they are hit and miss, the music in sanctuary is really good and fit the atmosphere while the city didn't.
The biggest upgrade is probably in the graphical and setting department. This is welcomed as setting is non-existant in the older one. As far as graphical update goes, it is really good. The saddest thing that comes to my mind are several graphical glitches, which are more prominent compared to old ASAMU.
The question now is should you buy this game? Yes is my answer. It brings something fresh to the whole first person gaming market and as one of the pioneer(?) it is pretty impressive.

Headlander is a sci-fi metroidvania style platformer where you play as a flying head that takes control of robots.
The story starts off with you waking up as the last known human in universe with no memories of what happened to you. On your journey to learn more, you move through a world inhabited by robots that are controlled by a mad AI. You get to rip off robots’ heads and seize control of their bodies as you see fit. Being a flying head is super silly, and I was curious to see how Double Fine would make this work. Needless to say, I’m impressed. The mechanic of taking control of robot bodies is pretty awesome, and the whole system of opening doors based on your robot body’s colour clearance is implemented well.
There’s a lot of combat, and it’s fun throughout the game. Vacuum sucking robot heads off bodies never gets old, and the constant need for body changing keeps things exciting. There is one section of the game though where the gameplay feels inconsistent with the rest of the game: instead of swapping bodies often, you have to download data with one specific body type and keep that same body alive, and upload it at another location without it dying. It felt weird to have to play more safely with the body you have, when normally bodies are disposable.
Combat gets more challenging later on, and laser beams ricochet like crazy, and it’s near impossible to avoid damage to your host body. You have to be careful, especially if you’re not attached to a body since you’re a lot more vulnerable.
The game took me about 8 hours to finish, and I only struggled on the final boss when I didn’t have enough upgrades. There are still some side quests, collectibles, and plenty of achievements that I can go back for if I want to. Overall, Headlander is a fun game with an interesting concept, and I have very few complaints about it. If you’re looking for a decent metroidvania game with nice graphics, unique mechanics, and a lot of collectibles, you will probably enjoy Headlander.

The detailed, memorable graphics of Sister’s Secrecy hide a game with flat story, bad voice acting, and incredibly good hidden object scenes.
It seems that during the development of Sister’s Secrecy: Arcanum Bloodlines, most of the effort went into the hand-drawn graphics and the hidden object scene design. Both feature very detailed scenery with lots of elements, but without making them feel crowded.
The hidden object scenes especially deserve praise: there are many items, but their placement is loose, everything is in sight and can be found easily. In other words, it’s really fun and enjoyable to play these segments. And there are many of them.
The other parts of the game… well, they aren’t even nearly as good. The puzzles just feel old and tired. The story initially has a great hook– the protagonist’s twin sister gets kidnapped, and it almost feels like a good mystery–, but it just descends into a “stop evil countryside cult from resurrecting Dark Lord” plot right after the intro. Also, the voice acting is terrible.
Still, the game is highly worth for its hidden object scenes alone.

This is a hidden object game, which actually does a lot of stuff quite right. You'll experiencing a good story which can be superficially described as a Steampunk/Fantasy crossover. You'll encountering Knights (some in ghostly form), Necromancers, Dragons and other Monsters of High Fantasy and on the same time steam engines, magic, gear driven machines and other stuff that is relevant to both settings.
The story actually creates some humorous aspects which don't feel artificial or set up, in the same moment the story is captivating like a fairy tale - with some twist and turns.
Technically the devs have taken care to create an inviting game environment, with some detailed and beautyful graphics, a good voiceacting (not overdone, not too shallow), and an atmospheric soundtrack to the game. The bonus Chapter is also quite well done - and it's really like in a fairy tale, where in the end the good ones always win. The hidden Object Games are also good, so good to the point that you don't need any hints - just patience to solve the HOS. The riddles are more on the easy side, just three riddles need more time to solve them - others are solvable in less than a minute.
This game is one that might sit well in a starters library. It's a perfect start for somebody who is unfamilliar with the Hidden Object Genre, or Adventure Light as someone called them more recently. The game has a lot of merrits, one of those is that it's very intuitive play, and very fair Hidden Object Scenes... As I already told the story is a mixture of High Fantasy, Steampunk and Fairy Tale - so that might get at times too much, the aimed audience for the game is young and adolescent women - but, who cares. It's a fun game with a sinister setting, which got so wide spread now.
If you have a chance to dig your teeth into this one, please do so - you won't be too disappointed. Though as with all HOG's - the replayability is very, very limited.

Ugh. I can forgive the low-rez graphics and clunky game engine, but there remain serious problems with this game.
First, forget about playing it in "expert mode": the game doesn't make enough sense to make that possible, unless you've played it before. Play it in "casual mode", and even then expect much bizarreness and frequent use of the "hint" button. "Well this definitely looks like a can of paint". And you need to moisten it using a goblet of angel tears. Of course, right?
Maybe it's my fault for playing in English? Maybe "viburnum fruit" means something more readily recognizable in other languages? Maybe. Well, my point is: expect the hidden-object scenes to be quite opaque (but still easy).
Other than the nonsensical gameplay, the other major flaw is the story and characters: they're there, but there's no chance you will care about any of that. The dialog is bad, and the voice acting (nice bonus!) is dialed in.
The graphics are fine, if inconsistent in style, despite the low resolution.
Fans of HOGs: unless you got this for free, spend your money and time on something better.

One could say that Headlander follows a formulaic pattern of Niche concept + Metroidvania = Profit. That formula isn't necessarily a bad thing though. Headlander is a game that feels familiar but different. Challenging but simple all at the same time. This is Headlander's strength as much as it is its weakness.
You're going to have fun and the entire ride is well crafted, from interface, design, and setting. The selling point atleast for me was the setting. Headlander takes place in this dystopian future where robots who were formerly human have chosen a cold metal exterior in exchange for immortaility. Its somewhere between Lost in Space meets a psychedelic episode of Twilight Zone. It keeps this tone of surreal robotic world with splashes of cheeky, colorful, and weird for most of the game, Throwing in humor as much as possible. Even after about 14 hours and completing the game, I still chuckled as I rocketed my head about and it bounced around like a ping pong sometimes. You're a floating head for petes sakes.
Gameplay is broken up into shooting and puzzle elements. Mostly its get from point A to B. There are a couple of sidequests but no major reward for completing them aside from achievements. The obvious draw here or "niche" part of the game features is the ability to replace the head of just about anything with yourself and possess its abilites and functions. From moving elevators, guards, tour guides, even an entire live action chess match,(which I should mention was FREAKING AWESOME.)
Headlander can do more as you progress through the game, from charging objects until they explode, to creating dummy bodies that fight on your behalf. All the tropes of a Metroidvania upgrade system are there and done very well. Progression and map design is not blocked by jumping or movement but by color. Robots each have a unique color or scheme and as the story progresses the security clearance of robots is raised more and more until you have access to everything. It's a cool idea and it works, although it does start to feel a bit of a  rinse and repeat nearing the end of the game.  Visually the game is astounding as color is used quite effectively and not once did the environments ever really bore me. The game keeps you moving along that no one area over stays its welcome.
The only gripe I have with the game is its combat. As you get access to more advanced robots with better mega-man-esque blasters. Shooting becomes more of a spamfest and less about accuracy and cover. There is a cover system but it really feels almost pointless as most of the time it was far easier to just suicide run into a buncha of robots and just simply get a new body, no consequences. This becomes almost a pivotal strategy later on as hordes of robots are thrown at you and keeping any one body is just simply not going to happen. PRO-TIP: Spam the headbutt and GG, you win. There are 2 boss fights in the game and each of them is varied and very entertaining. I felt they could've added more but think it would feel forced and out of place. The bosses that are there are there for good reason.
The little facets of the game are given a good amount of attention as well. From voice acting being fantastic despite the fact that everybody has that voice modulator thing going. It never got grading on the ears. The sound department did a fine good job of making everything sound impactful while maintaining its quasi-seventies space themes. Controls are a bit hit and miss as button spamming is required nearing the end game as you headbutt your way to victory. Sometimes despite my many presses my character just stood there and got shot in the face. Flying was sometimes tricky as you rocket your head about in hilarious fashion but this is hardly a gripe. It should be noted the game does feature controller support and rebindable keys so major props for that.
Replayability is probably where the game falls flat. Aside from seeking out all the games little upgrades there is no reason to continue playing. So unless you wanna do everything over again just for kicks. This is a play it and leave it type of game.
In all I enjoyed every minute of Headlander and think its a wonderful game. I wish there was more of a epilogue then what you get but perhaps this leaves room for a sequel? Headlander 2: More Head, More Action. Just an idea.
The game makes strides in being unique but anyone familiar with the genre will not find anything that blows the head off your shoulders. Pun intended. To wrap up, Headlander is another great addition in the library from a consistently delivering developer/publisher.

Okay, let's just get the obvious out of the way right now: The intro to this game is LONG. LOOOOONG. Like, possibly the longest intro to an RPG I've ever played.
HOWEVER, once you get past the intro, you're introduced to the meat of the gameplay, and holy hell is it satisfying! The combat in Ys: Origin is fast placed hack n slash that seems mindless at first, but if you just mindlessly spam attacks with no thought, you will die. A lot.
In fact, even if you're careful, you will most likely die a lot, because this game is HARD. The normal enemies are usually no trouble, though there are indeed cases where they can chump you if you're not careful, but the real meat of the difficulty lies in the boss battles.
If you're at all familiar with the Ys series, than you probably know that one of the series' most lauded aspects is the incredibly designed, incredibly difficult boss fights, and Origin is no exception. You will most likely die to a boss at least once before you learn how to deal with them. And each boss as their own styles, attacks, and strategies, so each boss feels fresh and exciting.
Also, did I mention the music? Because HOLY HELL the music is amazing. Quite possibly one of the best soundtracks I've ever heard.
All in all, if you're looking for an RPG with fast paced action, an interesting story, amazing bosses, amazing soundtrack, and a difficulty level that constantly keeps you on your toes, then Ys Origin is for you. In fact, give the whole Ys series a try. Its a great series, and Falcom and XSeed are great companies that deserve your support.

The Ys series is old, having started back in 1987. One of the first action-oriented JRPGs, and one of the few series that still sticks around today. There's a reason for that, it's a series that has evolved over time without losing it's roots. It's still all about running around, killing monsters, growing stronger, finding key items and fighting challenging bosses.
In that, it's pretty much a cousin to the Legend of Zelda.
It does have it's own style of combat, and it's own setting (generic by today's standards, but when the series was new it was one that helped build the stereotypes) and each entry tends to have it's own twists and tricks.
This is one of the later entries to the series, and uses 3d environments with good-looking 2d spritework for the characters. It mostly sticks to overhead view, but there's sections that twist the viewpoint along the way.
story-wise it's the prequel to the story. As such, the mainstay hero swordsman Adol is nowhere in sight yet, and instead you have 2 playable characters with their unique playstyle (with a 3rd one to unlock).
Each character has a different playstyle, and gets different special skills to use.
Pros:
- Game provides a good challenge on Normal difficulty, ramping up quickly but smoothly. Easier & harder difficulties are also available.
- Bosses are memorable, with fairly tricky attack patterns at times (and mostly references to the bosses from earlier games in the series)
- The playable characters do handle completely different, adding replayability
- Crisp high-res artwork, holding up well today even though the original Japanese version of the game dates back to 2006
- Pretty cool soundtrack
- One of the playable characters is a non-sexualized, non-stereotypical female protagonist. That seems to be a big deal in this day and age so I'll list it as a pro.
- Plenty of customization options. (if using a gamepad, you will want to remap the pause/menu button though - for some sillt reason it's not mapped to start button by default)
- Solid controls
- Update: Unlockable bonus modes, with leaderboards and all, which start unlocking once you complete the game
Cons:
- While good-looking, there isn't that much variety in the different environments you'll run through
- There's a couple of weird things, like a key equipable item not being in the equipment screen, but tucked away in between the usable items instead.
- No auto-saving. This being an old-school game it uses a savepoint mechanism, which works well. What's weird is that savepoints do work as checkpoints when you die, but don't auto-save to an actual save game.
- Non-skippable cutscenes. Which is annoying if you want to start a new game but can't skip the minutes-long opening movie to get into the action. Update: At least the long animated scenes become skippable after you complete the game once. So it's mostly annoying if (like me) you want to try both initial characters without beating the game first.

Ys Origin is an original JRPG/Hack & Slash game with really good fighting mechanics, a decend story and Metroidvania style levels.If that's not enough praise, let me say it's one of the best games I've ever played.
You first (first because you can unlock more characters) play as Yunica Tovah, a young woman who has sworn to protect the godesses of her world; a girl who is looked down upon by all the other guards because she possesses no magical powers whatsoever. A girl, that proves to be more than valuable and capable without magical powers in rescuing the godesses and the whole world in the course of the story.
The gameplay feels really slick, it's not simply a matter of button mashing but you have to react to what enemies do and figure out strategies to effectively kill each one of them. They have certain movesets that are predictable and thus can be learned - something I really appreciate. There is no buIlsh!t going on with the enemies. If you fail, it's your fault - it's quite Dark Souls'esque in this regard. Especially noteworthy are the bosses that are all very unique in their mechanics and that are thoroughly fun to fight. Each and every one of them has move-sets that are to be learned and understood if you want to defeat them. It's not too difficult to figure out what to do because each of their movements can be predicted by the animations they have - to me it seems that's one of the biggest strengths that Japanese/Asian games have over western games (the rules to beat the game are very clear - it's still tough).
The level design is great. There may be some backtracking involved but it's really only if you didn't check everything properly in your first run-through. Everything is connected in a consistent and logical manner and there are various styles of areas.
The sound design is great as well. The feedback you get for your actions is quickly ingrained into your brain, and helps you understand what's happening even if you can't take in all the visual information at the time - perfect. The soundtrack is pumping and very well done, suits the overall game.
The graphics are not top notch but they suit the kind of game Ys Origins is. They are probably even perfect for what the game tries to achieve. They are simplistic but nice to look at, everything fits together and there is nothing that sticks out as ugly or unfitting. Especially noteworthy are the character models that look very nice.
My one problem with the game is that if you are underleveled, you will have a really tough time against some of the bosses. An unnecessarily tough time that may force you to go back and grind 2-3 levels. Which doesn't take too much time but is tedious nonetheless and could've been circumvented by making levels count less and making items count more for the overall strength of your character.
All in all - who woulda thunk it after reading what I just wrote - Ys is one of my favorite games of all times.

The character sprites are well made and environments have clear and different themes and feels. The fast pace of the monster slaying is maybe a bit too often grinded into a halt when you have to sit through lengthy and uninteresting line exchanges between the monotone and cliche characters.
One interesting thing of note is the other main character of the game, Hugo. He should probably get an award for the most edgy video game protagonist ever. Most of the cringe material of the game comes from his teenage rebel attitude. The story might have been much less cringy had I picked Yunica for playable character, but I also think the edginess is kinda charming and memorable.
In conclusion the rock solid gameplay and soundtrack totally redeem this game from any negatives I might have towards it. It was a blast to play and a definite recommendation.

I originally played
on mobile a couple of years ago. The PC version updates the textures, but keeps everything else the same. This includes the control scheme, so you will end up doing a lot more clicking and dragging than you ever wanted to. Other than that, my original review holds up:
If
was a good proof-of-concept for what a premium game should look like on mobile,
took that concept and perfected it. Nearly everything about it improves on the foundation that the original laid down. In a lot of ways it reminds me of my impressions of the first two
games. We had never seen anything quite like the original, and I finished thinking it was a pretty good game; then the second comes along and suddenly I realized that it was the game the original should have been all along.
As in its predecessor,
tasks you with solving physical puzzles. The original was limited to opening various types of safes, but
takes it several steps farther. Most of the rooms you find yourself in contain several different objects to interact with. Each provides pieces that are required to solve different parts of the others. That addition alone makes the game five times more interesting. It also means that most chapters are longer than the chapters in the original. There are also several more chapters, so all told it takes about twice as long to complete.
The visuals are also vastly improved. Not only are the textures all high enough resolution to not be distracting, they added little touches like motion blur when zooming from one part of a room to another and little particle effects. I thought the particle effects were a little much, but they never got in the way of being able to solve the puzzles.
Speaking of puzzles, I thought they were better designed this time around. There were several times in
where I got so stuck that I had to read all of the hints to understand what was expected of me. It may have been the result of already being in the correct mindset, but I only ever had to read the first clue this time around. There were times when I struggled for a while, but otherwise it would have been too easy.
I mentioned the creepy vibe I felt in the original. In
they took that vague sense of unease and did the best they could to turn it into a horror game. There is only so much they could do given that the player only has the ability to look around a room (don’t expect any chase scenes). But they did an excellent job creating creepy environments and using jump scares to keep me on my toes. There were even a few times I thought I saw something out of the corner of my eye, but when I looked nothing was there.

I had a great time playing The Room and The Room 2. There were a few puzzles where I was pretty well stumpped and needed to look up some help, but usually because there was a way to rotate something or look under something and I just hadn't taken my exploration quite far enough to find what I needed. Things are challenging, but not so much so that you want to just give up. The graphics are beautiful and the controls are easy enough, especially considering it's a mobile port. I greatly enjoyed that there was an ongoing storyline behind all of the puzzles that actually made sense and was worth following.

This game is fantastic.  While I expected something more along the lines of S.T.A.L.K.E.R. series, I recieved  something that it comparable, which is a surprise to say the least.  This game delves far into story telling, but in a fashion that is pleasant as well as exciting.  The gameplay is action packed.  The delivery is a mixture of creepy, somewhat disheartening, and at the same time somehow bringing hope for humanity.
While it is a railroad RPG FPS, it still has enough options of game style to allow what you want out of the game.  It is difficult enough to challenge any skill level, as long as you aren't a little pansy and don't start off on some pathetic difficulty.  Once you start the game and learn the basics, do yourself a favor and up the difficulty to one of the Ranger modes.  Honestly, if you can't keep track of your own inventory from level to level, maybe survival FPS isn't for you.  You can choose between a more stealthy approach, to a more "OH DAMN, I JUST MUFFED UP!" level of gtfo.
While I can't say this has the replayability of the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. series, I can say that I'm glad I played it, and I will be playing it again when I get bored of all the other generic shooters I have stockpiled in my inventory.  There's something about the doom and gloom that makes me feel like, "Wow, so glad the world ended..."

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter gets past the trust issues a lot of games seem to have.
