is basically what happens when the developers of a visual novel decide to make stress on the 'visual' part. The game's surroundings are relatively small but almost any inch of the landscape can be a spot for a lovely screenshot. That part is adorable and the environment is very picturesque.
Unlike many other visual novels, this one has a first-person view and freedom of action. It involves you into the game's world yet more. Seeing a path is one thing, walking it yourself is quite another. Moving around slowly and quietly, exploring, pondering over matters, watching for details that need attention - and that's all as if you were there. Nothing threatens you. Nothing disturbs you. You have all the time in the world to go where you want to go and see what you would like to see. My explorer's nature was deeply satisfied.
The plot is curious. I won't say that it's entirely original - the basic idea around which all the events circle has already been seen in a certain game, - but it certainly doesn't mean that you will easily understand everything from the very first minute. There will be no instructions on where to go and what to do next, no maps, no journals with careful recordings of each step. If you want to rebuild the story then use your memory and look for hints in what you have already seen.
The bad part of it is that the game is painfully and heartbreakingly short. 4 hours of gameplay is the best you can get from it, and it generally looks more like an exercise in game building - like, "look what we could do with the engine". I was feeling like the developers had initially planned something bigger and more complicated but circumstances forced them to cut their ambitions short.
Small amount of gameplay time is in part based upon the lack of real content. The protagonist has come to the area for investigation but in fact he hardly investigates anything. When he actually does, the solution is often ridiculously simple, as if the game creators didn't want to bother their players with too much of intellectual business. It becomes more and more obvious as you progress towards the end of the game, and it often feels like the developers were getting tired of their product and were trying to get it finished as soon as possible.
You will like it if you are fond of walking meditatively around an area and exploring. For a couple of hours you will be living in a beautiful place with a touch of weird mystery about it.
You might also like it if you prefer visual novels and if you don't mind composing a story out of bits and pieces instead of following a predefined storyline.
If you want to feel like a detective who tries to solve a number of challenging cases, you will probably be disappointed.

I was going to wait for a Steam sale, but I threw caution to the wind nad picked this game up for 10 bucks (US.) I started playing and was instantly hooked. There's just enough content to keep things interesting, but not enough to become overwhelming. The music is fantastic, and every asset contributes to the peaceful-yet-uncertain atmosphere of the game.
It's also fun to name your crewmembers after your friends and watch as they are suffocated, infected, blown up, and/or shot.
You will die a lot in this game, and while frustrating, it doesn't make you want to stop playing like in other games. Unlike other games that send you back to the beginning where the difficulty is much lower than you're used to, this game doesn't really have a difficulty curve to send you back down, so dying is more like losing supplies rather than starting over.
TL;DR  This game is fun and you should play it right now.

Dying Light is a zombie infested open world action adventure game with RPG elements, a very fun combat system and a campaign story that drives it all forward. It has its frustrating faults but not enough of them to ruin the experience.
So, you are thrown into a zombie infested slum city and you need to survive. Do you pick up that tire iron on the floor there? Climb the tallest building, curl up in a ball and cry? Run like that one dude in that movie? It's up to you, Dying Light does not care how you play and just rewards you for doing anything but dying. There are three different progression systems: agility; level by running & climbing, power; points for killing things, survivor; helping people and progressing. All systems offer ability points to spend on passive and active skills that can sometimes be a hit and miss. Some improve the gameplay while others actually hinder your abilities (yay grappling hook, nay tic tac wall jumping).
The "agility" aspect of the game, a more passive approach, is all about running around zombies, climbing buildings assassin's creed style and general parkour shenanigans. While "power", a more aggressive play style, offers different ways to killing zombies such as ground pounding with heavy melee weapons or conjuring shrapnel explosives for maximum blood spray. While gunpowder based weapons exist and are plentiful later in the game, the meat of the action is melee combat. Light and heavy weapons weigh off speed vs damage and feel right when wielding. Katana swords swiftly cut through flesh and rotten bone whiles heavy axes bludgeon and crush skulls. Weapons do break and will have to be fixed (limited amount) and later replaced for better ones. Weapons can also be modified for extra damage, speed and conditional effects such as electricity, poison or fire.
Of course this would all be nothing without a zombie wonderland to explore. The campaign takes you around two different stylized maps: Brazilian-like slum ridden outskirts and a European styled old town. Both are large enough to get lost in and provide a handful of things to do. Quarantine zones - filled with lots of loot and zombies, different challenges based on the agility and power play styles mentioned earlier, safe houses to secure and side quests that can be fun (and some are fairly well written) but the majority revolves around fetch quests. A saddening fact considering the writers had such an unique world to play with. Luckily the main campaign story is more entertaining. You can of course forgot the story and play at your own pace. After all it is a sandbox at its core.

Ys isn't as bad as the first few hours make it seem.  There's enough about it that's bad enough to give it a thumbs down, but it's definitely done some things pretty well.  This review lists major points concisely with more detailed explanations at the bottom.
Here are the flaws I've seen so far:
-Character and item upgrade systems are pathetically bad.
-Uninspired levels.
-The 'puzzles' involve finding an item and backtracking to use it.
-Framerate issues with some graphical effects.
-Controls need autofire and autocharge.  Other control problems may be specific to me.
-Too many rpg text dialogs that can't be skipped.
-The difficulty curve isn't right.
-The rate of levelling needs adjusting, and the effect of gaining levels is not done well.  It increases damage done and decreases damage taken, altering boss fight difficulty too much.
Game's strong points:
+The bosses are very challenging with fully-avoidable attacks
+The action is fast-paced.
+The graphics are colorful, and I like the graphical style of the characters.
Regarding difficulty,
On Hard difficulty with the magic user, the monsters are a joke, unable to threaten the player.  The bosses are very challenging.  On nightmare difficulty with the melee character, the (skippable) trash monsters are about right, but the bosses are extremely challenging.
There is at least 1 boss fight that cannot be won without grinding due to its being a dps race.  It is not obvious that grinding is the intended (and only) way to win the encounter.  Grinding 5 levels for that fight also reduced the boss's attacks from 40 dmg/hit to 9 dmg/hit.  I do not know how hard those bosses are supposed to hit, and I suspect the developers don't either.
Without grinding, nightmare bosses can take 1-10 hours to beat, including the time to learn their moves.
Unskippable dialogs
are ubiquitous and boring.  Even if I were interested in reading the story of a hero who rescues princesses and saves the world, my replays through the game would not be.
The intro cinematic is well done, but it can't be skipped either.  It takes at least 15 minutes to start a new game due to the unskippable cut scenes and dialog.
The controls
desperately need an autofire button and a way to hold down the magic charge button.  Using outside configuration utilities creates some problems in the game such as menus opening and closing due to autofire.  Holding down the magic charge button while imtermittently holding down the attack button and periodically jumping has led to some hand soreness.  Without autofire, the repetitive button presses will cause a lot of repetitive stress.
Even after some configuration, there are still occaisional phantom axis motions, and recharging magic immediately after casting makes it cast twice.

I got this game on Humble Bundle for $6. I was skeptical whether or not it was worth the asking price of $20.
After playing through the game with the first character, I can say $20 is a fair price for what it gives.
The game isn't an "RPG" in the traditional sense that people are used to (i.e. Final Fantasy, Dragon Quest). There isn't much grinding (unless you want achievements) in this and it isn't slow turn based combat where you repeat a set of tactics. Combat is quick, fluid, and fun. Bosses are hard if your difficulty is on hard or above. I died quite a few times to each boss on hard.
Cutscenes aren't so long as to detract from the experience as some people have mentioned in negative reviews.
Cons: Now my primary complaint is that the initial control system is attacking with the keyboard and moving with the mouse. I would recommend inverting this to attacking with the mouse and using the keyboard to move. I.e. the traditional layout for PC games. I cannot understand why this wasn't the default, but it was a simple change in the configuration.

This game serves as my introduction to the world of Y's (pronounced EES). I've been wanting to play a game in this series for a while and I'm so happy I picked this one up. A Diablo-style action RPG, this game is hella fun. I'm several hours into my first playthrough and have really enjoyed it so far. Challenging boss fights, decent level design that rewards you for exploring while providing a decent story. It's all a very solid and polished experience that's worth your time. A lot of games like this have mecahnics that suffer or that are a bit loose. To me, this is a crucial part of enjoying a game's platforming sections. It's very frustrating when you feel like you told your character to jump from the platform they're on to the one on the right only to find that you were pressing every so slightly in an upwards/downwards direction which caused you to miss the platform and fall into the pit. Not so here. I felt like I had good control over the character and rarely if ever made such a mistake that felt all too common even in AAA titles that are top ranked in their class.
Overall I really can't find much to fault in this game. To nitpick I'd say the costumes are a bit plain when you're talking to others but this is also refreshing at the same time. It's simple, and practical. I would also say there maybe could have been more variety with the monsters but this doesn't really bother me at all either. It's just a fun game that's knows what it is and has fun being just that. If you like games like this I highly recommend giving it a try.

FTL is a very detailed strategy game; it became very enjoyable once I grasped the depth of the game mechanics.  In FTL, you assume command of a Federation fleet spaceship, the goal is to “run” to the other end of the galaxy and deliver data onboard your ship that is vital to the Federation fleet.  You must race across a randomly generated galaxy via a web of sectors; each sector is yet another web of interconnected quadrants.  The goal within a sector is to explore as many quadrants as possible, finding the exit, and not getting caught by the pursuing Rebel fleet.  Overall, FTL is a challenging space simulation game with detailed strategic gameplay.
The one initial hurdle for FTL is its steep learning curve.  The title does come with a tutorial but it only explains the basic game mechanics.  The learning process starts with the first game.  It took me about three games to fully understand all the features; I think anyone who plays this title must go through this process to get the full value of the game.  Furthermore, I believe this title will be “hard to swallow” for those players not familiar with the concept of permanent death.
I had no idea of what to expect from FTL.  I think I developed some expectations after playing the tutorial.  Once I played my first game and failed miserably, I thought the game was going to be a waste of my time; my expectations fell to the floor.  Like I said before, it wasn’t until two gameplays later that I fully understood the overall concept and goals of the game; after that I was hooked.  I truly believe FTL is just one of those titles that offer no grey areas; you like it or you don’t.
In my opinion, the graphics in FTL are of medium quality, offering a highly detailed 2D top-view perspective.  In FTL, the main character is the spaceship you choose to command; eventually, you’re able to unlock different types of spaceships as you accomplish certain achievements.  As you progress in the journey through the galaxy, you’re able to upgrade your ship.  The only objects FTL allows you to interact with are the individual crew members onboard your vessel; each member has a set of skills that can be developed throughout the game, i.e. a crew member that is always assigned to conduct repairs eventually becomes your repair specialist.  The menu system in FTL is simple and very user friendly.
FTL is mainly played utilizing the mouse; point, click, and drag depending on the interaction.  Other than the space bar to pause the game, FTL offers some keyboard commands in the form of shortcuts; in my opinion, they aren’t really necessary.  Overall, the game controls for FTL are simple and somewhat intuitive.
In FTL the story is short and simple.  The real immersion value of the game is the well balanced combination of exploration and tough decision making; FTL does not allow you to completely explore the entire galaxy, but when you add the random encounters along with the time constraints imposed by a pursuing enemy, FTL draws your attention and engages you by forcing the player to make life and death decisions.  I played the game for 9 hours, and at times I had to make some very tough calls to ensure the survival of my space ship and crew members.
The musical score in FTL, in my opinion, is very rich and augments the experience of immersion into the vast galaxy exploration theme; after all, the original musical soundtrack is available for purchase separately.  The sound effects in FTL are consistent with the high level of thrill and excitement during gameplay; especially when it comes to combat.  FTL does not offer any voice-overs, the random encounters are all text based.  Overall, FTL’s audio is a perfect match with all other elements in the game.
FTL is already a very detailed complex game, where critical thinking is of the essence.  One feature that would make this title better, is to allow for more diversity in the difficulty levels.  FTL currently only offers easy and normal gameplay, adding a “this is my first time” option would really bridge the gap on the learning curve.  Another feature that would make this title even better is to include an encounter editor; FTL has hundreds of encounters, but there have been numerous times where I found myself saying, “I’ve seen this already.”  Also, the ability to share player created encounters would fortify the community aspect of the game and pretty much guarantee infinite possibilities.
The one element that makes FTL exciting is the concept of permanent death; it provokes critical thinking and gives you the true immersion value of what it would be like to command a Federation fleet space vessel.  Every action a player takes is nerve racking, bad decisions only lead to failure; just like in real life.  The “permadeath” concept may not be popular with all types of gamers, but I think it’s worth experimenting with.

The Room Two, as the title self explains, is the second installment of the series, gradually being ported as PC version.
Be aware that there is no chronological succession, you can play them in any order as they take place in a different contextual environment.
I played the first episode, therefore my review will be highly influenced by both gaming experiences.
There are many similarity with the The Room One as well as differences.
The game mechanics are obviously preserved. You will need to find your way to solve the puzzles through levers, hidden mechanisms, and a lot of wit. The enthralling atmosphere of mystery with its beautiful soundtrack is very familiar, and it really helps to get in the mood of the game. The puzzles may appear to be a bit simpler than the first title, perhaps due to the fact that the player already knows what to expect and how to operate the mechanisms. However, here come the differencies.
The Room Two tends to be more story driven. While The Room One focused on puzzle solving, this episode has a very good story behind, and acts as a glue that keeps every level tied. This feature is translated into the game through the introduction of different types of puzzles that detatch from the original pattern; through the addition of numerous lore-based items; through a distinct division among the levels.
I will avoid any kind of spoiler, as part of the experience is the feel of awe when you discover how to progress in the game. What you may want to know is that every stage of the game presents a wider area of play, with multiple puzzle structures (if they can be considered such) entwined. Some puzzles could be hard to grasp or notice at first because they may not appear objects that require invisetigation. You are really required to lok out of your schemes!
Personally, I really liked it; I can't say I completely love it. My recommendation has a thumb partly up. The only small flaws I noticed are mere subjective opinions.
The recurrent hints given when you are stuck pondering appears to be too recurrent and too helpful. The best part of the game is trying to find every small detail and see if there is a small hidden button to press; sometimes the final hints clearly tell you what to do (thankfully hints are optional, so don't look up them unless strictly necessary!), rendering the game in a very linear experience if you decide to rely on them.
Another small observation concerns the game pace. At the very begin I perceived it was way too easy and it required a couple of levels before things actually started being interestingly complicated, and considering the few amount of stages, I can define it a slow start.
This title is a turn from the previous installment, therefore its perception could be welcomed either positively or negatively.
To everyone reading: Play it! That's the best advice I can give. Reviewers will either love this game to death or dislike it according to personal tastes. Even when not on sale (and it usually is) is extremely cheap. Fun is ensured, and even though it's a 2.5/3 hour experience, I can reassure that it is extremely worth it!

I really enjoyed Dying Light. Overall a great game with incredible graphics, a very polished interface, and a very interesting story. Graphically it is just amazing, and this is the only game I have ever played where I actually felt vertigo when climbing up on high structures.
You are dropped into a city filled with infected that are essentially zombies but instead of shooting thousands of them you pretty much have to stay away from then by keeping to the rooftops. I really enjoyed this part of the game and missed it sorely when in the later parts you are so overpowered you just run wherever you want to go or snipe the bosses from the rooftop. It took most of the tension out of it.
The game features a bunch of resources and things to craft but I have to admit I never made anything other than healthkits, I found stuff at a fast enough rate and the things I did enhance quickly broke, making that part of it fairly useless to me.
The single player story is really quite good and very tense and emotional, centering around trying to find a cure and helping the few surviving groups of uninfected people.
The negatives are pretty minor, mostly around wishes. Jumping to grab on was very frustrating until I learned to hit the spacebar at exactly the right time to make him grab the ledge. I don't remember that being shown in the opening tutorial and I wish they had, as it made the first 20% of the game a lot harder.
Another negative is around weapon breakage. I just don't understand it, quite literally your sledgehammer "breaks" after 30 or 40 swings and cannot be fixed more than a couple of times. It pretty much eliminated any desire to enhance weapons as they broke after an hour of gameplay and you had to move on to soemthing better anyway.
The other wish I have is around quests. There really isn't much to do other than the main quest. There are a bunch of contests and competitions scattered across the map, like how fast can you get across an area, but actual quests where you are doing something meaningful are very few and far between. I've noticed this carries over into the DLC as well. As of this writing there isny anything contentwise in the DLC, its all outfits and gun/vehicle enhancements. Not a single new area or campaign or anything.
Still, it is an amazing game and well worth the money.

A Story About My Uncle is a first-person sci-fi fantasy platformer that focuses on simple yet enjoyable mechanics: run, jump, grappling hook, and rocket boots. The player is placed in the shoes of a father telling his daughter the adventure he had as a young boy in search of his uncle, an adventurer who had gone missing. The young boy came upon a intriguing mechanical suit that fit him and a launch pad that propelled him into a world full of wonder, intrigue, and a lot of floating rocks.
The good:
The environemt is really well-made and offer enough variety to let you forget that you are in caves 80% of the time. There were standard caves, dark menacing caves with glowing plants, ice caves, caves of floating villages, and caves of artifacts from another time. All caves were enormous, big enough to contain a whole city and then some.
The art style leans toward cartoonish but fits quite well with the fantasy setting that requires a bit of suspension of disbelief (floating rocks, duh).
The sound and music were well-done and serve the mood of the game nicely.
The dialogue, though few, was quite decent and the voice-acting was excellent.
And the mechanics are very polished and together the setting, the art style, the music, the sound, and the gameplay made up a very immersive experience. It is hard not to feel the pounding of your heart as you run, jump, grapple and slinghshot yourself through various terrain with incredible speed. The rush is there, but gravity never did forget you. I remember countless times where I miss the right timing to connect my grapple then look up as all rocks around me shoot up, the wind swoosh by. and everything fade to black.
The bad:
While the mechanics were quite good. There were definitely a few places in the game where I felt there could be more  cues as to what can be connected with the grapple. In one instance I was supposed to connect to the stalacites on the cave ceiling to swing myself across, but no sound or environmental cues were provided. And I felt frustrated as I tried to super-jump myself across but inevitably fell to my miserable death every time. At another time, there were these glowing crystals where the player is supposed to use in mid-air to charge the grappling hook and further the swinging distance, but for a quite a few of them no matter how close I get no charging was possilbe. And so I had to plan my route not using them. Note that these frusrating intances are far and few in between, and the developer are still releasing patches, so I remain hopeful that they will be fixed in due time.
final words:
If you are looking for a neat game you can enjoy in an afternoon, and the idea of being Tarzan swinging in fantastical caves intrigues you, then consider "A Story About My Uncle." It is an atomoshperic, narrative-driven experience that takes you away to a different world one swing at a time.

A Story About my Uncle is an unpolished gem among the Steam Library. Though short, poorly textured, and horrible voice acting, the mechanics, scenery, and story outshine all it's flaws.
When I first played through the first level of this game, I was hooked on the grapple system. It was so similar to Spider-man's web-swinging, but it didn't feel as clunky or hard to control as it though. The way it works is you can click any surface within range and draw yourself to it. In addition, you can grapple multiple times before landing, which allows for some interesting parkour throughout the area. Each stunt I pulled with the grapple system /never/ failed to make me feel like I just did something impressive. In addition, the only way you can really die in this game is by falling into the abyss, which I thought made the game that much more relaxing. There were times in the game where it tried to feel a little more dangerous, and beckoned you to move quicker, but it offered nothing to back these claims of urgency up. Just move at your own pace and you'll be fine. Don't get me wrong though, this game has flaws, and lots of them.
The voice actors are hilariously awful. Hard to listen to at first, but then you start giggling at how terribly they deliver certain lines, and wonder to yourself how they even got into this game. Either the designer didn’t care, or they must have been personal friends of him/her. Either way, they were difficult to ignore throughout the entire game. In addition, the game’s graphics are not the best. Minimally-rezzed textures scatter this game’s landscape, which look really good from a distance, but up close you are painfully reminded this is still an indie game. In fact, some textures in certain parts of the game feel so out-of-place that you end up stopping to tilt your head at it before moving on. (you’ll understand what I mean if you play this game). Luckily, the player models and textures are alright, though some background characters aren’t even animated, which also makes you tilt your head as you pass them. None of the background characters have any sound either, which is a little creepy. (Or, should I say, none of the background characters have sound that you can understand).
The one thing that really saved this game for me though...was the story. A Story About My Uncle follows the nephew of an esteemed scientists and inventor named Fred (not the most appropriate name, but after remembering this is a children’s story, you eventually allow it). The nephew, or “protagonist” searches for his uncle who has been missing for months, only to be thrown into an interstellar adventure to another planet of some kind? What really perplexed me about the story was that the game itself couldn’t seem to decide whether the events that transpired actually happened... or were purely fictional. The story is told in a hilariously false manner, purposefully stretching the truth left and right only to cover its tracks later to try to pass itself off as a true story. Despite this though, the story was endearing, and left me with a fuzzy feeling inside as I reached it’s conclusion. The only character that sticks around long enough for you to care about (and the only one that sticks around for more than 90 seconds) is Maddie, who is relatable enough to get attached to through the story. In addition, the lore objects found throughout the game give all the main characters enough depth to care about as well, which I thought was a needed touch.
Overall, A Story About my Uncle is a game that you have to take the good and the bad with. It has just as many flaws as it does strengths, but I loved the grapple mechanic, I loved the concept, and I truly believe this is an indie game worth the money it’s asking. In addition, I happily await a sequel. (so long as they don’t use the same actors >_>)

One of the most visually stunning and thought provoking games currently available. The developers have really hit the story telling and immersion nails on their respective heads. The gameworld is borderline photorealistic, every intricate detail down to some roots at the side of a track or the cracks in a rock are realised to an unbelieveable level of detail. I looked up how they did it, they used a method called photogramming (I think?) and it works to perfection.
The story.. is at first difficult to get into, simply because you have literlly 0 idea what's happening. My experience was that I came across clearly relevant things (hello railcart with legs etc) but didn't find every little detail (TINY bloodied rock) and so left the area and had to later glance at a guide to actually realise I'd missed anything. That said, once you start realising the mechanic of the story telling, you realise it's a really good idea and you start putting things together in your mind. There are areas of the game that instill a deep sense of unease (Hello senor Graveyard) and the whole game has an increasinly dark atmosphere. It's a brilliant example of exactly the way narrative in a game should be handled, with sensitivity and inginuity. The climax is thoroughly thrilling, and the whole story is incredibly evocative and quite thought provoking.
To anyone thinking of getting this, DEFINATELY do, you won't regret it if you appreciate beauty in multiple forms. HOWEVER I would recommend NOT reading a guide if you can avoid it, just be sure to thoroughly search every area that you find something that looks like a clue to make sure you find all of the relevant things in the region. Otherwise it's pretty easy to miss stuff. I know the game 'doesn't hand hold' but yeah it might have been nice to know I'd have to search every inch of the rail track in order to find what I needed to progress the story. (The story is actually non-linear and you can do it in any order, but it does require that you complete every section.)
A SOLID 9/10, the -1 being just for the fact that you have literally 0 idea how the game works when you first enter the world and can consequently wander for hours not knowing what to do. (Honestly that might not be a bad thing, given how beautiful it looks.)

Set in the shattered subway of a post apocalyptic Moscow, Metro 2033 is a story of intensive underground survival where the fate of mankind rests in your hands. In 2013 the world was devastated by an apocalyptic event, annihilating almost all mankind and turning the earth’s surface into a poisonous
•	Metro 2033 is a gripping, atmospheric first person shooter experience powered by cutting edge technology, featuring full DX10 and NVIDIA PhysX support for high-end gaming PCs, to deliver incredible visuals.
•	Witness the everyday horrors of a broken society living in constant fear.
•	Brave the darkness of the tunnels, where mutants hunt their prey and ghostly spirits lurk.
•	Explore the desolate city-surface, trusting your gas mask and rifle to protect you from a poisoned world and the creatures that roam there.
•	Steel your nerve and prepare to face the terrors that await.
In terms of gameplay Metro 2033's gameplay, 2033 is a very linear, set piece littered game that is bursting with innovative ideas, and constantly has you doing things you've certainly never done in a game before; all the while setting itself apart through its distinctive setting. Your impression of the core-gameplay will be decided by the difficulty setting you play on though, as it will determine just how difficult and tense the moment-to-moment gameplay is. Elements of the gameplay include FPS combat, stealth, light exploration/looting, resource management, and even a little bit of survival-horror. The stealth is a perfectly crafted system as well, and requires you to always stay out of light to remain undetected, but there are some problems with the line of sight the AI has, because you can often walk right in front of their faces and be unseen as long as you are not illuminated. The stealth is very rewarding though, as slipping away without firing a shot or taking down enemies with backstabs and throwing knives is never not a compelling way to play through Metro 2033. As for the exploration, in some environments you are given a chance to stray off the beaten path in order to loot the area for supplies and gather collectables. Moving on to the resource management, depending on the difficulty you play, items you need such as ammo, med-kits, and gas-mask filters will always be in short supply. This forces you to choose your engagements carefully, and always think before you act. The last aspect of the gameplay is the survival horror element, which is brought up in key moments of the game, either for narrative importance or gameplay purposes. All of these elements combine to establish an immersive, amazing gameplay.
Set in the shattered subway of a post apocalyptic Moscow, Metro 2033 is a story of intensive underground survival where the fate of mankind rests in your hands.
In 2013 the world was devastated by an apocalyptic event, annihilating almost all mankind and turning the earth’s surface into a poisonous wasteland. A handful of survivors took refuge in the depths of the Moscow underground, and human civilization entered a new Dark Age.
The year is 2033. An entire generation has been born and raised underground, and their besieged Metro Station-Cities struggle for survival, with each other, and the mutant horrors that await outside.
You are Artyom, born in the last days before the fire, but raised Underground. Having never ventured beyond your Metro Station-City limits, one fateful event sparks a desperate mission to the heart of the Metro system, to warn the remnants of mankind of a terrible impending threat. Your journey takes you from the forgotten catacombs beneath the subway to the desolate wastelands above, where your actions will determine the fate of mankind.

Thats right, I'm writing a review for a game everybody with a penchant for being an argumentative poopsmear claims is dead.  I'm tossing one back to the baseline.

I jump into any random good-ping FFA server, and within one map, the thing is full. (And thats a 32 player server!
)

But the biggest question is, simply put;
How? Didn't Quakelive.. fail??
Because Quake Live tows a line like a rock star snorts cocaine. Sure, It's had it's rocky moments, back when somebody had the genius idea to 'modernize' the game with gloriously bad features like loadouts, universal ammo boxes, on screen item timers and simplified jumping physics. (okay so nobody really minds that last one.)
Oh, and they made all these settings standard on all public servers, none of these tracked any stats, and if you wanted classic mode/stats, you would need to run your own server on the website, which was fine, but then no noobs would play the 'hard' mode servers because thats not how the human brain pleasure/reward center works.
Nobody asked for any of it. Nobody wanted any of it. But we were told time and time again how it was 'good for quake' and would 'bring in more players' by 'lowering the skill gap' and such. (You know, This sounds familar..)

Sounds like a bunch of bull♥♥♥♥♥♥drummed up by a 'marketing research focus group' or something, doesn't it? It basically killed the game. Old schoolers hated it, newbs thought it was fun, until they realized spamming wildly and running around like idiots got boring after a few days.
Needless to say, after some months of having it crammed down their throats, people left. I personally went back to QW/Q3A, and Reflex, noobs evaporated because they had become bored with ez-mode spam and suddenly found themselves in a skill vacuum with no upper teir to try for.

started downsizing, and eventually it was announced it would be shut down.

Somebody up at Id, somebody with a spine, somebody with some functioning chunk of testicular fortitude sat up and did something I can only imagine was fueled by drugs, disregard for upper management and the fact they were being made fun of by everybody on the internet. They harked back to the age of Id before Bethesda, before Zenimax, Before focus group studies and marketing budgets and swaths of people in ties who's idea of 'hardcore gaming' was using a stock xbox controller with no custom grips playing skyrim at 30 fps.

And they cranked out the 'Apology update'. (If you just heard angels and chior voices mixed in with rocket fire, that is perfectly normal.)
And that is what you see before you right now. The apology update compiles everything everybody had been begging and asking for for YEARS together and makes them, all of them, a reality.

Are you ready for the bullet list? Lets do the bullet list, I like bullets.
See why I saved the bullet list? That was a good one.
It took the QL community a little time to find its footing again, this was all completely new.. it feels like QL, it plays like QL, but it's not free anymore. Yet it has everything they could have possibly asked for, and slowly but surely it started to lure people back in.
The itch, the need, that drive to white-knuckle the mouse and grit teeth while rocket jumping from flag to base, and tickle the risk-reward pleasure center of the brain Quake has always been so damned good at tickling like some hot porn star. Got fragged? Do better. Learn, adapt, evolve, FRAG.


Oh, and then Quake Champions happened. Which.. I'm not even sure if you can classify that as a Id title, or even a quake title at this point.


Ironically, one of the devs let it slip that Quake Champions, in terms of a 'time line', happens
, which I find hilarious yet perfect. Clearly it fits better as a prequel to Q3A/QL, QL is ultimately refined to a razors edge. QC is a kludgey slow mishmash of bad ideas and marketing spiel. It fits that time line perfectly.

QC comes across like low-grade blow scraped off a dirty table after you think the party is over and nothing is left. Then you find out the real party started back in the VIP area years ago, and somebody just introduced 'their guy' who showed up with a trunk load of some crazy blue stuff he calls 'Quad powder', and some skimpy dressed chick with a skull mask and feathers just started pole dancing with a rocket launcher while some giant green robot tries to get some gigantic eyeball thing to do a keg stand.

And then you start to wonder why the hell you even went to the other party in the first place.
Let the good times roll.

Clicker game with no rewards or other action than clicking

*Note: Even though I received this game for free, my review would be unaltered if I purchased it*
At first, I thought this would be a great cross between Pokémon and clicker style game... however I was quickly disappointed and here's why:
Pros:
♦ Graphics are decent (The units and enemies graphics are decent looking. However, there aren’t any graphics beyond these)
♦ Nice unit/enemy variance (When the enemies do end up switching and you end up getting new units this is great to keep the game exciting)
Cons:
♦ Nothing to do with Pokémon (The game claims you can capture creatures... you can't as you are just handed new creatures as you progress. Also, the creatures have no abilities like in Pokémon that you can use. You just buy the ability and it stays on permanently as a bonus. Could have been way better regarding the Pokémon element)
♦ Terrible UI (The game UI is so confusing that you'll click things you didn't mean to numerous times expecting them to do something different to what happens)
♦ UI Bugs (When trying to click on certain things it can click through them onto other things and then break the whole UI so you can't click on anything. For example, in the Craft menu when trying to craft items somehow it can open the Job Offer menu and then when you close that menu back to the Main Game screen, you won't be able to click on anything as it'll just register as you attacking enemies)
♦ Job Offers are too hard (I had one job offer that wanted 50 silver for 40k gold. That seems fine, but in 4 hours I've had max 15 silver and I've made over 245k gold just by killing enemies)
♦ No explanation of how anything works (There needs to be a tutorial. For example, I had no idea if the starting creature we get to choose does anything different based on the one we chose. I have no idea what I've got from a chest every time I open it. I have no idea what the trainer does or how they level up. I have no idea when bosses appear etc.)
♦ No idea when a new biome or enemies or units come or are unlocked (Nothing tells you or explains when you verse different enemies or the biome changes or you are going to unlock a new unit. Needs to be something to say new biome in x waves which will unlock new unit scorpion etc)
♦ Crafted items seem way to weak for the amount of resources (For example crafting an item gives 5-20 dps max depending on the item crafted. These items require almost all the resources found in the game. Hence, one of my units has 740 dps in the same time it's taken me to craft 3 items giving me +25 dps. There doesn't seem to be any incentive to craft items when I can save the resources for jobs and get gold to enchant my units which will give me triple the dps than crafting items will give me)
♦ No incentive to buy Empower over enchanting your units (I say this as 50k to unlock and then 75k for 20dps when I can for example enchant the Field Rat 10 times for 5k and get 20dps. At the stage you're at when you can afford to unlock Empower, 20dps is worthless to you)
♦ Can't idle to collect gold easily (This clicker can't easily be idled if you want gold. This is terrible as you must purchase a relatively expensive upgrade just to pick up gold automatically which seems to miss 90% of the gold dropped anyway. There should be an easier way to idle the game or make gold)
♦ Raid List seems ridiculous (I say this because they are almost impossible to kill unless you've played the game for years as each Raid List boss has too much health and not enough time to kill them. Also, there is nothing anywhere that tells you what the benefit of killing them is)
♦ Trainer isn't explained (What is the point of the trainer, how does it level up and what does its level do?)
♦ Can reset Wasp Loot Data and Job Settings but no idea what either of these are (What is Wasp Loot Data and Job Settings? Wasp doesn't seem to get its own loot and there doesn't seem to be any Job Settings?)
♦ Achievements galore (There is literally an achievement for everything, now the achievements are simple to get by idling the game... However, there is too many and it just gets grindy trying to unlock them all which takes the fun out of having achievements)
♦ DLC not worth paying for (I say this because you can easily get what the DLC gives you for free in under an hour of playing. I know this is a good way to support the Devs but I would have expected to get something unique from doing so that you can only get from DLC. For example, a new unit or something that is only obtainable through DLC etc. For now, there is no incentive to buy the DLC)
♦ No better or different to any of the free Clickers (I say this because this Clicker costs $2 USD which is expensive when you can play any of the free Clickers which are on Steam and the gameplay of them are either similar or better)
♦ No uniqueness (There is nothing that makes this clicker unique from any other)
♦ Bosses are few and far between (I've seen two bosses by wave 30 and have no idea when they appear. I assumed they'd appear every 10 or so waves, but this isn't the case. Plus, since you need Boss Souls to level up your units further, this is relatively annoying)
♦ Music seems to be generic one song and sounds like elevator music (This is annoying because the music never changes no matter what happens in the game whether you’re fighting a boss or what. I would have liked to see some variance in the music or at least be able to switch between a few songs to keep the game interesting)
♦ No unit/enemies sound effects or animations (By this I mean no effects when enemies die, no effects when your units are attacking. I would have liked to see some kind of unit attack animation and sound depending on which unit we have selected at the time. Also, depending on which enemy we are fighting I would have liked to see some unique death animation and sound effect rather than every enemies just fading in and out when they die)
♦ Unit upgrades don't seem scaled for cost (For example buying an upgrade is way more expensive for a small amount of dps when I can enchant them for a huge amount of DPS for a lot less)
♦ Fully levelling your starting unit to level 50 doesn’t seem to do much other than changing its graphical appearance (This is annoying as I thought something unique might have happened levelling it to 50 as it’s the only unit that changes its graphical appearance and seemingly evolves as it levels. However, all that happens is, it evolves and the graphical appearance changes. Nothing cool unlocks, is upgradable or happens. This essentially makes the unit pointless unless you want to upgrade your click damage)
Overall, since the game has way more cons than pros, is confusing as, tries to use Pokémon as a selling point when it has hardly any Pokémon similarities and the fact that it is no better than a Free to Play Clicker, I can't recommend this game for any price.

I realize this is in Early Access, so normally I would assume things will get much better down the road, but in its current state, I can't recommend it, and it's been 5 months since we last heard a peep from the developers.
First: I didn't encounter any bugs as others have, but the UI leaves a lot to be desired. When you hover on a button, no explanation is given as to what it does. Upgrades are hidden behind several of these mystery buttons, but so are game resets. Click with caution.
But on the topic of achievements: obviously that is mainly what a clicker game is for, right? But you can get all of the achievements except the ones for kitting out every creature with 100% epic items within the first few hours of gameplay. The veritably spam your screen with non-stop achievement pop-ups and then you reach about 85% and they slow to a trickle before petering out to nothing while you leave the game running idle to get the epic achievements, which still doesn't take much time for a clicker game (most of which have a long tail to keep you interested for weeks and months.) The reason for this? The game is completely unbalanced.
They made it possible to go back and grind lower levels rather than forcing you to progress with what you have, but it completely disincentivizes 99% of the game. There is no point to ever actively clicking the game because you can simply set it back to the lowest level and grind up again until you can no longer one-shot the enemies, and repeat. Boss souls can only be gained by defeating a boss for the first time and are encountered only every dozen or so levels, but the only point to boss souls is to ascend your creatures so they do more dps. Since you can simply set the level low, there isn't a lot of point to this. There isn't even an associated achievement. You get the same amount of money (which becomes virtually pointless later on in the game) and treasure boxes having your creatures one-shot level 5 monsters as you do having them 2-shot level 300 creatures. There's no point in wasting your time having them 2-shot creatures. The majority of the time you will spend in the game will be leaving it up, idle, then coming back, saying a prayer to RNGesus and opening up a pile of chests with a creature active that you want to upgrade, hoping they get that one last epic item so you can get your last couple of achievements and uninstall the game once and for all, then setting the level back to the minimum and starting all over again.

FTL is a very detailed strategy game; it became very enjoyable once I grasped the depth of the game mechanics.  In FTL, you assume command of a Federation fleet spaceship, the goal is to “run” to the other end of the galaxy and deliver data onboard your ship that is vital to the Federation fleet.  You must race across a randomly generated galaxy via a web of sectors; each sector is yet another web of interconnected quadrants.  The goal within a sector is to explore as many quadrants as possible, finding the exit, and not getting caught by the pursuing Rebel fleet.  Overall, FTL is a challenging space simulation game with detailed strategic gameplay.
The one initial hurdle for FTL is its steep learning curve.  The title does come with a tutorial but it only explains the basic game mechanics.  The learning process starts with the first game.  It took me about three games to fully understand all the features; I think anyone who plays this title must go through this process to get the full value of the game.  Furthermore, I believe this title will be “hard to swallow” for those players not familiar with the concept of permanent death.
I had no idea of what to expect from FTL.  I think I developed some expectations after playing the tutorial.  Once I played my first game and failed miserably, I thought the game was going to be a waste of my time; my expectations fell to the floor.  Like I said before, it wasn’t until two gameplays later that I fully understood the overall concept and goals of the game; after that I was hooked.  I truly believe FTL is just one of those titles that offer no grey areas; you like it or you don’t.
In my opinion, the graphics in FTL are of medium quality, offering a highly detailed 2D top-view perspective.  In FTL, the main character is the spaceship you choose to command; eventually, you’re able to unlock different types of spaceships as you accomplish certain achievements.  As you progress in the journey through the galaxy, you’re able to upgrade your ship.  The only objects FTL allows you to interact with are the individual crew members onboard your vessel; each member has a set of skills that can be developed throughout the game, i.e. a crew member that is always assigned to conduct repairs eventually becomes your repair specialist.  The menu system in FTL is simple and very user friendly.
FTL is mainly played utilizing the mouse; point, click, and drag depending on the interaction.  Other than the space bar to pause the game, FTL offers some keyboard commands in the form of shortcuts; in my opinion, they aren’t really necessary.  Overall, the game controls for FTL are simple and somewhat intuitive.
In FTL the story is short and simple.  The real immersion value of the game is the well balanced combination of exploration and tough decision making; FTL does not allow you to completely explore the entire galaxy, but when you add the random encounters along with the time constraints imposed by a pursuing enemy, FTL draws your attention and engages you by forcing the player to make life and death decisions.  I played the game for 9 hours, and at times I had to make some very tough calls to ensure the survival of my space ship and crew members.
The musical score in FTL, in my opinion, is very rich and augments the experience of immersion into the vast galaxy exploration theme; after all, the original musical soundtrack is available for purchase separately.  The sound effects in FTL are consistent with the high level of thrill and excitement during gameplay; especially when it comes to combat.  FTL does not offer any voice-overs, the random encounters are all text based.  Overall, FTL’s audio is a perfect match with all other elements in the game.
FTL is already a very detailed complex game, where critical thinking is of the essence.  One feature that would make this title better, is to allow for more diversity in the difficulty levels.  FTL currently only offers easy and normal gameplay, adding a “this is my first time” option would really bridge the gap on the learning curve.  Another feature that would make this title even better is to include an encounter editor; FTL has hundreds of encounters, but there have been numerous times where I found myself saying, “I’ve seen this already.”  Also, the ability to share player created encounters would fortify the community aspect of the game and pretty much guarantee infinite possibilities.
The one element that makes FTL exciting is the concept of permanent death; it provokes critical thinking and gives you the true immersion value of what it would be like to command a Federation fleet space vessel.  Every action a player takes is nerve racking, bad decisions only lead to failure; just like in real life.  The “permadeath” concept may not be popular with all types of gamers, but I think it’s worth experimenting with.

I read the reviews on this game, a lot made it sound like the best game ever. So when it went on sale for 23 dollars I bought it. Played the intro, which took me about an hour and fifty five minutes to get through, and was really unimpressed. I thought to myself, I should probably return this before the two hours is up for a refund. But I kept thinking about all those positive reviews, and thought it has to get better. Well. it didn't get any better, was just one meh moment after another. Why do I say it is just meh? Well, you look all over town for saw blades and batteries left in tool boxes, string and silly stuff like that. You do this to make weapons that break after killing 3 zombies... It's really repetitive work, with very little reward. What fun is putting a saw blade on a pipe, so you can kill 3 zombies? Very grindy for sure. And there are packs of zombies that can run, and climb like a mofo. Which would be fine, if your weapon didn't keep breaking over and over again. And I mean come on, how the f@#% do you break an iron pipe? I thought the story, from what I saw of it was weak, and kind of silly. And guess what? Just when we started to get our levels up so we could actually do something, the zombies leveled up as well....Making all that work a waste of time. You don't really want to use guns, or it will attract huge hordes of zombies that you probably can't get away from...Who wants a zombie game where you shouldn't really use a gun? You just run around with a club, which breaks easily, over and over again. I thought, wow, they dropped the ball on everything in this game, it's pretty much just like that other meh zombie game, Dead Island. Then i realized, it is from the same studio that made Dead Island, doh! Another thing I really hated was the camera. It is always rocking, rolling around, which really gave me a sense of motion sickness, and really made the game hard to play. And the parkour aspect everyone raves about made the motion sickness even worse, and really wasn't that impressive anyway. There are some funny moments in the game and the graphics are ok. The zombies are well done and have good animations. But unless you love a really simplistic grind of the same thing over and over, I would avoid this, especially at full price. And honestly, looking at all the positive reviews make me wonder if they were really legit, the game is just not that good. You were warned.

Half-Life 2: Episode One is the first story-driven expansion for the original Half-Life 2 by Valve. Taking play mere minutes after the end of the first game's campaign, it follows the effort of both Gordon and Alyx as they try to escape City 17, where the collapse of the Combine Citadel is about to set off a huge explosion.
As far as gameplay goes, nothing really changes from the main game, aside for new situations you have to face with the instruments you are given (one sequence, for instance, requires you to shine your flashlight on enemies to help Alyx killing them while you don't have weapons to speak of). Alyx will accompany you for the whole episode and fight alongside you.
As a downside, this time around Gordon isn't as effective as in the original Half-Life 2: you spend the first half of the game armed with your gravity gun only and generally you unlock other weapons at a slow pace. While this forces you to relay on the environment and your creativity more, it can get annoying during particularly hard sequences.
Half-Life 2: Episode One is roughly three or four hours long and takes places in environments you already got yourself familiar with, but still it expands nicely on the original story and keeps the gameplay fresh enough
Very nice episode.

"A Story About My Uncle" is an indie title that boasts a magical art style and a simple yet poignant bedtime story format, as told by a father to his daughter. You play as the narrator, a young man who traverses across space to find his uncle, who is presumably doing some sort of insane experiment. Throughout the story, you come across a race of alien people and use your uncle's space suit to explore worlds in a sort of parkour format.
While this game doesn't have so much in terms of puzzles, the challenge lies in being able to catapult yourself across vast spaces using a grappling device and some rocket boots that can be helpful in a jam. While playing through the story, you may find some hidden objects tucked away, which trigger more storytelling opportunities about the backstory of this  man's uncle.
As an indie game, this one fares very well. It has a short story, a handful of different environments, and new powers and tools are introduced in each one. Details are thoughtfully put into all the landscapes you come across, even if they serve no purpose aside from aesthetic appeal. That being said, the game can be a little glitchy. The problem with giving the player so much jumping power is the fact that you can sometimes skip necessary paths that are needed to trigger events, which can lead to some backtracking. Likewise, the freeroaming you are granted is sometimes overwhelming. Grapple points and ledges may be few and far between, leaving you with little knowledge about where to go or how to get there.
Overall a great concept with a solid execution. The sheer abundance of power the player has sometimes allows them to plow straight through important areas without even realizing this, and the development team should have fixed that. Voice acting sometimes gets lazy, but the budding complexity of the characters helps make that. I would really like to see how this game would be improved if it was made by a bigger developer. Would definitely recommend to anyone who likes casual games, adventure games, fantastic artwork, and heartwarming stories.

I haven't 100%'d the game yet, but I feel like I'm ready to review it after 120 hours of gameplay and 3 playthroughs on nightmare on all characters.
I have played three games from the Ys series so far (Ys I & II, Origin and Felghana) and each one of them clearly shows the extreme effort Falcom and XSEED put into every aspect of the game: super smooth gameplay with solid mechanics and very few bugs or inconsistencies, pretty challenging difficulty, excellent performance, very flexible settings that support even 120hz and up monitors and modern resolutions, the portings are very compatible with modern OSes even though these games are from 2006 and earlier, the anime graphics and the artwork are sweet and pleasant (but not necessarily ultra detailed) and the soundtracks are masterpieces.
In poor words, Falcom consistently does a great job in every aspect of the game and puts a great effort into making every detail perfect and solid. Both the engines of Ys I & II and Origin & Felghana have the perfect balance between graphics, performance and gameplay quality.
I won't talk too much about the plot because I usually don't care about that stuff.
Ys Origin is a prequel set 700 years before the events of Ys I & II and tells about the past of Ys, the twin goddesses, the black pearl and Solomon Shrine. Most of humanity fled to Solomon Shrine (which is on a floating island up in the sky), as the surface got taken over by demons. For the very first time we're not playing as Adol. We will be playing as one member of a group of adventurers (you can choose between 3 characters) sent to investigate on the disappearance of the twin goddesses, who seem to be inside the Darm tower.
Pro / Cons:
+ = pro
- = con
- no more "bump mechanics" from Ys I & II. In my opinion, this combat system was unique and kinda set Ys apart from other action RPG's, also it made boss fights a bit more challenging. Ys Origin & other newer Ys games ditched that system for more generic hack n slash mechanics + magic which is okay but nothing special.
- the game takes place entirely inside of the Darm Tower, so there is not that much variety environment-wise.
- while Ys I had very short but extremely fast & challenging boss fights (except for a few bosses with bugged AI's), the boss fights on Ys Origin are slow and long, and since the bosses heavily rely on RNG, defeating a boss on Nightmare difficulty is 50% skill 50% luck unless you overlevel to fight that luck factor. Either way, there is too much luck involved in boss fights, and sometimes it can become frustrating even if you can actually beat the boss 100% of the times. This also makes boss rush / time attack extremely tedious and frustrating especially on Nightmare where you will be barely equipped to beat the boss. In Ys I & II, on the other hand, the boss fights were 100% skill based and used nearly no RNG-based attacks, but they were so challenging that you had to practice for a bit to master them even if you memorized them, so the results of the boss fights scaled directly with the player's skill.
- there is a lot more grinding required, too much for my tastes. Leveling up for bosses takes much longer and filling the monster book is now random instead of having to kill each mob 31 times.
- the dialogue can be sped up but not skipped. this can be frustrating when playing through the game multiple times.
- the save system does not allow you anymore to save anywhere - you can teleport to save points, but you will have to save there so that adds some useless backtracking when saving before dangerous situations. On the other hand, the teleport system is handy to quickly teleport to every area of the game, but a system like the wings in Ys II would've been enough.
- Alt + F4'ing the game has a chance to corrupt your monster book
+ a playthrough takes about 10 hours if you kill all of the bosses first try and 20-30+ hours if you take a few tries to beat each boss, which is pretty optimal for multiple playthroughs or speedruns.
+ amazing soundtrack with lots of remasters of the original darm tower musics in Ys I
+ lots of references to Ys I & II: remastered bosses, lots of monsters in common, lots of remastered music, some key items in common and the plot is nicely linked and properly explains all of the backstory behind Ys I.
+ very high replay value: each character sees the story from an entirely different perspective, will encounter slightly different bosses and each character's boss fight is balanced differently. There's also an arena mode where you will be able to fight monsters from different areas of the game to gain SP you can use to unlock alternative versions of the characters and other bonus content, including a secret boss. Completing all of the achievements will take up to 6 playthroughs or more. There's also the usual monster book you have to fill by grinding all of the monsters in the game (some are missable), an upgrade system for your characters where you can spend SP earned from mobs, and various Roo's hidden around the game that will give you missable upgrades if you feed them Roda Fruits (also hidden & missable).
+ the achievements where you have to beat two "unbeatable" boss that you normally have to lose to are pretty interesting challenges even though they're heavily rng based
+ retrying bosses doesn't make you go through the dialogue all over again
+ perfect support for the 360 joypad and ps3 joypad + ds3 tool
+ the engine has a minimum guaranteed performance: for example, if there's too many effects on screen some of them will not display, that way there is always a guaranteed minimum framerate even in the worst scenario.
+ the bosses partially retain the "bullet hell on foot" feel that Ys I & II had.
It's not a masterpiece like Ys I & II, but it's an excellent game like most Falcom games and it's certainly worth the price. Highly recommended.

Beatbuddy's concept of fusing catchy music with puzzle/adventure gameplay is an appealing one. At first glance it looks like Beatbuddy does a good job of bringing that concept into reality. Unfortunately that just isn't so.
On the 3rd of 6 levels I ran into not one, but two different level breaking bugs that required a restart from the beginning of the stage. Exiting to the menu and continuing from last checkpoint did not fix either problem. I stopped playing the game after that. Normally I would persevere through these kind of issues but this brings up Beatbuddy's other fatal flaw: it's not fun to play.
At its core Beatbuddy is a pretty simple 2D exploration game. The environment moves to the music but your character does not. That detachment from the beat makes playing the game feel like any other average 2D adventure game. Couple that with collectable shards that are completely worthless unless you get every single one within a level (e.g., 411/412 won't cut it!) and you're in for a ho-hum experience.
Don't let Beatbuddy's snazzy soundtrack and visuals fool you; save yourself some time and money by just listening to the soundtrack on YouTube.

Beatbuddy is a 2D exploration game with the whole game universe based on Music. The presentation is really creative, and the art original. The worlds are varied (with the exception of enemies only two in the entire game...) the Musc is very enjoyable and the fact that it builds up as you explore further gives a really gratifying feeling.
However while the artsy part of the game is great, the "Game" part really doesn't keep up.
For starters the narator has a tendency to mimic DJ scratching when he speaks. While it is a very interesting idea the result of it are cutscenes that are painfully long because of him, delaying any sense of conclusion at each and every sentence. Thank god they appear only rarely in the game.
The whole game is underwater which makes it impossible to have granular control. You'll often find yourself restarting mutiple times parts where very precise tasks are required to be done in very little time. Furthermore as you don't gain short invulnerability when hit and enemies love to push you around when they hit you
find yourself being bounced about to your inevitable death. This happenning quite often it is one of the main reason while you will start cursing the game for not being forgiving.
Level design is not very well thought out either, you will often find yourself trying to find out why you can't go there, if you are actually supposed to be there and stuck because you went somewhere you weren't supposed to be.
All these issues lead to a hot mess of frustration and anger, powerless against a game that punishes you for being to curious.
And it really is a shame that the actual gameplay is the worst part of the game, leaving what otherwise would've been a enjoyable experiment.
Even though BeatBuddy has the looks of a fun rythm/exploration game, it's faulty game mechanics and ill conceived levels put an swift end to any enjoyable experience. Therefore I cannot recommend this game.

FTL is a very detailed strategy game; it became very enjoyable once I grasped the depth of the game mechanics.  In FTL, you assume command of a Federation fleet spaceship, the goal is to “run” to the other end of the galaxy and deliver data onboard your ship that is vital to the Federation fleet.  You must race across a randomly generated galaxy via a web of sectors; each sector is yet another web of interconnected quadrants.  The goal within a sector is to explore as many quadrants as possible, finding the exit, and not getting caught by the pursuing Rebel fleet.  Overall, FTL is a challenging space simulation game with detailed strategic gameplay.
The one initial hurdle for FTL is its steep learning curve.  The title does come with a tutorial but it only explains the basic game mechanics.  The learning process starts with the first game.  It took me about three games to fully understand all the features; I think anyone who plays this title must go through this process to get the full value of the game.  Furthermore, I believe this title will be “hard to swallow” for those players not familiar with the concept of permanent death.
I had no idea of what to expect from FTL.  I think I developed some expectations after playing the tutorial.  Once I played my first game and failed miserably, I thought the game was going to be a waste of my time; my expectations fell to the floor.  Like I said before, it wasn’t until two gameplays later that I fully understood the overall concept and goals of the game; after that I was hooked.  I truly believe FTL is just one of those titles that offer no grey areas; you like it or you don’t.
In my opinion, the graphics in FTL are of medium quality, offering a highly detailed 2D top-view perspective.  In FTL, the main character is the spaceship you choose to command; eventually, you’re able to unlock different types of spaceships as you accomplish certain achievements.  As you progress in the journey through the galaxy, you’re able to upgrade your ship.  The only objects FTL allows you to interact with are the individual crew members onboard your vessel; each member has a set of skills that can be developed throughout the game, i.e. a crew member that is always assigned to conduct repairs eventually becomes your repair specialist.  The menu system in FTL is simple and very user friendly.
FTL is mainly played utilizing the mouse; point, click, and drag depending on the interaction.  Other than the space bar to pause the game, FTL offers some keyboard commands in the form of shortcuts; in my opinion, they aren’t really necessary.  Overall, the game controls for FTL are simple and somewhat intuitive.
In FTL the story is short and simple.  The real immersion value of the game is the well balanced combination of exploration and tough decision making; FTL does not allow you to completely explore the entire galaxy, but when you add the random encounters along with the time constraints imposed by a pursuing enemy, FTL draws your attention and engages you by forcing the player to make life and death decisions.  I played the game for 9 hours, and at times I had to make some very tough calls to ensure the survival of my space ship and crew members.
The musical score in FTL, in my opinion, is very rich and augments the experience of immersion into the vast galaxy exploration theme; after all, the original musical soundtrack is available for purchase separately.  The sound effects in FTL are consistent with the high level of thrill and excitement during gameplay; especially when it comes to combat.  FTL does not offer any voice-overs, the random encounters are all text based.  Overall, FTL’s audio is a perfect match with all other elements in the game.
FTL is already a very detailed complex game, where critical thinking is of the essence.  One feature that would make this title better, is to allow for more diversity in the difficulty levels.  FTL currently only offers easy and normal gameplay, adding a “this is my first time” option would really bridge the gap on the learning curve.  Another feature that would make this title even better is to include an encounter editor; FTL has hundreds of encounters, but there have been numerous times where I found myself saying, “I’ve seen this already.”  Also, the ability to share player created encounters would fortify the community aspect of the game and pretty much guarantee infinite possibilities.
The one element that makes FTL exciting is the concept of permanent death; it provokes critical thinking and gives you the true immersion value of what it would be like to command a Federation fleet space vessel.  Every action a player takes is nerve racking, bad decisions only lead to failure; just like in real life.  The “permadeath” concept may not be popular with all types of gamers, but I think it’s worth experimenting with.

Headlander is a really far-out metroidvania with the main focus being you, as a floating head, (the headlander,)  pulling heads off bodies and headlanding (as the game calls it) into them to use 'em for yourself. Robots, not other humans.. After all, you ARE the last human around in this world... Anyway, this ability alone is used to solve many puzzles where you need certain bodies in certain places, especially for door opening since the doors can only be accessed if you're the right color. You're also able to explore hidden areas just like any other metroidvania and collect energy points to upgrade your head and body abilities, or upgrade your health, thrust power, or energy. To be honest, I just tried to collect nearly everything that was around before continuing, some of the later areas can get really spicy.
The areas that you travel in look really nice as well, heck, stunning even. I remembered myself purposely going slow just to take in the colorful environments I was traveling through. The dialogue was fun to hear too, whether it was a robotic map happily talking to you before you ripped its head off or a door you wanted to nuke open because it mocked you yet again for not being the right color. Made me giggle so much.
Welp, as a metroidvania, I guess the only replayability is finding Easter eggs if there are any or completing the game 100% or something like that. As of me writing this review, I have 100%ed the game in about 8.6hrs, not counting the 6 hidden achievements that I'll try exploring for. Despite the game being a little short, the experience that I had with it excuses the shortish time length (for me). As for the price? ..Meh. Preordered the game when it was coming out and I think a bit of a price drop from the $20 that Headlander stands at now would be good but if you can't wait, by all means, headland into Headlander.

Let me begin this review by saying I enjoyed my time with this game, but ultimately am conflicted about recommending it. This game is like candy, and that may sell it for you or not. It has a lot of visual flair, interesting gameplay, and decent sound design. What makes it like candy is that it's short (though 7.5 hours to complete a $20 game 100% is good bang for your buck, if that matters to you) and is entirely lacking in substance beyond its general gameplay concept and gorgeous visuals (which I have found to be the case with other Double Fine games of late, maybe their writing team doesn't know they aren't good).
The story tries to allude to ideas regarding what it is to be human in a post-corporeal world, but the few audio logs you find, what Earl and Methuselah say, and the world at large don't tell a complete story in my eyes. Even though it's only 7 hours long, you will begin to tire of repeated lines from the security doors (some of which were entertaining the first dozen times) and if you re-explore old areas after completing the game, you will get tired of the new lines added in after the first time you hear them.
The gameplay is compelling as you start out, with the main exception being aiming. When using a controller, it's a complete pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to aim reliably without getting killed pretty quickly in the process. If you play this anything like I did, you will end up avoiding combat and instead of shooting, rip heads off bodies. It's fairly fun to fly around, though, and see the sights. The general concept of "rip heads off, pick best color for security clearance, and avoid lasers" does not overstay its welcome. The best part of the game in terms of making you think spatially and about what you need to do to get somewhere is the Power Dome. The areas following it are a little bit more combat oriented and feature only small parts wherein you need to think. The puzzles about hitting markers nearly simultaneously are fun and brief, but I wish there were more of them.
Headlander is full of many gorgeous sights to see, and the visual effects they layer on top of well executed 2.5D make it all the better. 99% of the game is inside space station type areas, but it stays fresh in my eyes throughout the whole game. You will love shooting fractal laser beams, watching them bounce around everywhere, even if those lasers don't accomplish much. The single tiiiiiny negative I can give about visuals is overwhelming chromatic abberation after a certain point in the game where an area is slow motion for a good while. I think it might have been a bug, but my game went back to normal speed but still had a kind of glow around everything from that point on. Sound-wise, the game has an enjoyable soundtrack that I would probably never listen to outside of playing the game and excellent sound effects, with no faults I can remember, writing this just after finishing it. Having said the lasers look beautiful, I also think they sound beautiful.
If this game didn't look as good as it did, I wouldn't have purchased it, and if it didn't keep me interested as long as it did, I would have returned it. It's not great, it's just good. I recommend it only on two conditions: you like eye candy or it's on sale for less than $10.

Combine Just Cause 2's gameplay with Dear Esther's breath-taking environments and you get something like A Story About My Uncle.
The story isn't quite as spectacular as you might think, but it still manages to hold your attention throughout the length of the game. It's very simple and whimsical, like a children's fairytale.
It's incredibly satisfying to swing and leap from one platform to another at high velocity, like a mechanical spider weaving a complex web in the sky. Once you begin playing, you'll lose yourself, mesmerized by the game's beautiful environments and excellent pacing.
This game can be beaten in about 3 hours. There's a time trial mode you can unlock, but that's about it. $12.99 might be a little steep for how short the game is, but I feel that this is definitely a case of quality over quantity. The overall experience of this game is so finely tuned and well-crafted, that I'd find it difficult to justify spending any less for this gem.
If you're looking for a first-person adventrue game that's different and unique without sacrificing any of its gameplay elements (i.e. Gone Home, Dear Esther) A Story About My Uncle might be just what you're looking for.
