I picked this game up on sale after wanting a really good JRPG, or rather an action platformer. With a good combat system and a strong, responsive, gameplay methodology the game is a winner. You can complete the game inside of 10-20 hours depending on difficulty setting and past that there is a tonne of replay-ability through either doing it on harder modes or in playing the game again from another character's point of view (there are 2 characters to choose from at the start, a third being added at the end). It's well worth whatever price you pick it up for, though if you're not sure you'll like it (it grows on you), I would recommend at least snagging it on a sale. Basically, it's Zelda on the PC in 1080p, or rather a Zelda-esque game.
Story: 8/10
I played through the game on hard as 'Yunica Tovah', aka, Axe Girl. Being more of a agility-speed player it was my natural choice as I've never been that into mage characters, which is the other character model available as you start the game fresh. As a character Yunica is more or less your bumbling anime girl that has inner strength that expresses itself as impatience and immaturity, which naturally changes over time. I found her interesting - a little predictable at times, but as the plot progresses she does develop more facets and towards the end her angry side really is a welcome extension of her persona.
As for the overall story and setting, I found them engaging and enjoyable. It's definitely a fantasy game firmly within in the anime genre, and if you like that then you'll love the game. Me, personally, I can take it or leave it, so for me the it would be the gameplay that would swing me on this.
Gameplay: 9/10
The gameplay is fantastic. Fluid, sharp, and precise. Everything I like and enjoy. As a new player to this type of game it only took a quick control re-mapping to something more western - WASD as apposed to ZXCV - and then I picked it up pretty quickly. The gameplay is great because you have a really well thought out of mix of trash mobs, mid-level, high-level, then boss-level type enemies. And towards the end-game they start mixing in conditions and aoe gravity pulls to really start tripping you up if you haven't mastered how to pick off certain enemies. And that's what the gameplay really is at heart: you get thrust into a new situation and you have to adapt to these new conditions pretty quickly through piecing together enemy attacks, patterns, strengths, and weaknesses. This is especially true of the boss fights, which were always thoroughly enjoyable, challenging, and at times, a little frustrating. All of which are designations of a good game.
Difficulty is king here. If you have it on easy, you'll somewhat breeze through the game. Greater difficulties are just that in this game - it's not the western version of difficulty where 'Veteran' is what 'Easy' used to be in the late 90s, Nightmare literally means Hell.
I didn't give the gameplay 10/10 because of one reason: if you miss a chance to power up your weapon and you progress to the next stage, you'll suddenly hit a spike in difficulty. The same can be said if you don't more or less flatten the majority of enemies on contact (at first). So this can be a little infuriating as you suddenly can hit grind mode, unless you go back and find that missing upgrade. But, the good news is there's a transport system so it's not difficult at all. And, worse comes to worse, you can always use GameFAQs to trace your steps to that upgrade.
Game design: 8/10
This game is obviously Japanese in regards to design which naturally means that some inherent Western expectations aren't fulfilled. This takes the form of, or rather, a lack of:
A nice looking menu
The ability to map controls inside the game (instead of inside the launcher only)
The ability to skip cutscenes - even if you've already seen them
These are gripes that you get used to and they're only mildly annoying. If you're a JRPG fan, well, you're used to this kind of thing anyway.
Level design throughout is interesting and never repetitive; effectively think of the game as like a Mario or Zelda game: you're always in one 'general area' but as you go progress through the levels/stages the scenary changes etc, such as Ice to Fire to Sand and so on. It's classical and is nice to go through again if I'm honest. These different stages bring with them different unique challenges that do require a bit of trial and error occasionally, which I feel is a good thing. Not enough games punish you for messing up, this one does punish you; but never in an unfair way. I like that method of design.
Conclusion: 8.5/10
Highly recommended if you want an old school experience in 1080p that is reminiscent of Zelda and old school Mario. It's a great game with solid gameplay elements and the story is engaging and interesting. If you're an anime fan then I'm certain you'll find worth in this game. If you're not an anime fan then your opinion will likely differ, maybe drastically so. But regardless, the gameplay is super strong and rewarding, so if you want a challenge then this is it.
If you're in the unsure camp like I was, wait for a price reduction via sale then snap it up.

Beatbuddy: Tale of the Guardians is a short indie game that has emphasis on music quality. The music style is closer to electric, beatbox, and dubstep.  (Sorry dubstep fans, I didn’t hear any wub wub wub) The gameplay itself was more focused on solving puzzles.
There are two cinematic throughout the game, the beginning video and ending video, you  are the character “beat” who has been awoken from his sleep and must save the other two guardians and go back to sleep. The guardians are the ones who create the music for the world, so it’s of the utmost importance that they all go back to sleep soon.
The game itself plays to the music, everything is done in rhythm, if you’re boosting, you need to do it in rhythm, if you’re hitting a parasite, it’s in rhythm. There are two “play modes” that you experience in the game, one in a “beatbuggie” where you’re in a vehicle that bounces along to the music on its own, the other is when you’re just swimming through the water as Beat.
As I indicated in my quick review, the game is quite focused on the music quality, and but to me the gameplay was focused on rather simple fun puzzles. I had been playing the game A Virus Named TOM for the past week, so the puzzles were very simple and relaxed compared to my earlier game.
First time playing through I got the majority of the achievements (this pleases me, I want to get through my indie games sometime this year) There are the notorious “speed run the game” and “collect all the things”  achievements, but as a whole most of the achievements you will earn simply by playing through the game once.
Beatbuddy: Tale of the Guardians costs $9.99, that’s a consistent price for indie games on steam apparently, I’d suggest waiting for a steam sale, or purchase the game in a humble bundle. I noticed there is also a demo you can download and test out. As always; if you’re really interested in getting a game, checking out a demo is always a smart way to go.
For me on my personal value system (price divided by time equals value) I only played 5 hours of the game until I had It completely beaten, I do intend to go back and try to get tougher achievements, however 5 hours of entertainment for $9.99 would be too hefty for me. For most other people though, that’s a perfectly reasonable price.

This game is a swimmy platformer that excels at the gimmick of synchronizing environmental mechanics and hazards with the syncopation of the techno soundtrack. The music is great, the graphics are sharp and beautiful, and the engine is responsive with excellent player control. Other than the music gimmick it's a pretty run-of-the-mill platformer that doesn't seem to do anything other games in the genre haven't before. As such, I've played the first area twice and may never play more than that, but it was totally worth the price for just that brief experience.
One of the hardest things to do is to meaningfully synchronize gameplay with music and Beatbuddy does it better than just about any other game. It's obviously a lovingly polished game made by lovers of dance music.

While I found the trailer and reviews intriguing enough to try it, also given that I'm a fan of many music games and platformers I gave it a try. But my opinion is that too easy, the gameplay is way to repetitive only getting a bit interesting late game, and a lot of the difficulty, when it is there, is more due to annoying, imprecise/unpredictable controls, combined with high requirements exactly for precision. I tried both mouse and keyboard controls, both of which didn't work all that well.

I recommend this game because the mechanics are unlike any other RTS (save for CoH1) and make for a thrilling and enjoyable experience. In practice, however, it is only enjoyable sometimes, and I play it out of a gambler's scenario of never knowing when the big win will occur.
From the point of view of mainly an Allies player in 4v4 (although I have hundreds of games as Axis), most of the time matches are exasperating and brood a cynical disposition within me. The game has been out for years now, and still this game mode (as opposed to 1v1) has remained with a strong Axis favour.
It is a test of one's patience when the opposing player's basic infantry can force off your machine gun (the counter for basic infantry) by walking directly up in front of it and firing a long-range rifle-shot grenade. Or when your mortars (only Soviet, as the US do not get them), when they do hit something, are promptly nerfed while the Wehrmacht mortar hits targets dead-on with almost every shot, has been doing so since beta, and costs the same amount of resources to field.
Allies, particularly the Soviets, are forced to use cheesy tactics such as HMG spam, Sniper spam, or M3 scout cars with flamethrower units inside. This is because their units by themselves rarely can get the job they are supposed to do done, meaning the only option are high-risk succeed-or-lose strategies. These are successively nerfed as they are found by the players.
There is a significant disparity in effort required to manage Allied and Axis armies. This is to do with the number of clicks, abilities, and number of units and their synergy with each other. Allies are supposed to use more specialised units in combination to bring down powerful multi-role Axis units, which are fewer in number. This just means there is more to manage, and more moving parts which can go wrong for the Allied player.
Company of Heroes 2, from the 4v4 Allies player, has been and seems to always will be a game to do with how much you can entertain your opponent before he satisfyingly defeats you and messages "GG".

Headlander was a nice reprieve from my recent gaming trends.  Lately I’ve been drowning in MOBA's and YouTube.  While i wait on some projects i kickstarted, Double Fine has provided me with something that tickles my aesthetics.  Retro Future design, tied with clever dialog and animation.
Double Fine's Artistic team is one of the best in the business.  The environments are well put together and filled in with detail. The effects on the character are great and brought me to the days I saw all of the covers for Activision games on my Atari 2600. Electrical and Plasma looks great, and the color palate choice was appropriate for the setting.  Animation was top notch as well.  I laughed out loud when i got to the chess pieces that you will come across.
The enemies in the game work well, each bot carrying a different weapon, and each functions in the same way, but gives you different results.  Single shot, spread, fractal spread, etc.  I was not expecting the fractal weapon at all.  And strangely, as many shots as you could put into the air, it was not overpowered.  You must still play carefully in certain areas, or you will lose the robot body you worked so hard to keep alive.
The mechanics work well, but felt a bit lacking.  In most metroidvania games, your access to the map is mainly restricted to gaining abilities or equipment.  While that exists, the main means of restricted access is in the robotic body that you happen to be driving at the moment.  Since all your weapons and access is based on which one you have, the search for weapons and doing tricky moves to progress doesn't feel as satisfying.  For me, discovering the weapons in this genre was half the fun of backtracking the map.
The story and narrative are well done but a bit thin.  When I finished my initial run, I felt a bit let down for some feeling of ending.  It was more of a soft close, like the end of a chapter instead of ending a book.  But they story did have me engaged to see the progress as I played.
In Summary, Headlander is a excellent contribution to Double Fine’s library of projects.  I feel the average gamer may complete this in around 9 hours or so.  And I have blown more money on a bad steak from a restaurant.  A worthy buy.

It does have some problems, mostly due to being a phone/tablet game ported to the PC.
- The mouse-only controls can get annoying when viewing items; some sort of axis modifier/holder would greatly improve this
- What can be interacted, and how, is too often guessing/random clicking. As an example: one puzzle was started by rotating an existing knob, but the knob resembled previous puzzles where you had to find the missing half of it. Randomly trying to interact I somehow missed being able to turn it, and it took a hint for me to try again and move on.
- Some interactions were repeated multiple times in the same location and became tedious. One puzzle sequence requires you to type out words many times, and is made all the more annoying by forcing you to type with the mouse (rather than allowing you to just use your own keyboard to type it out)
If there's a Room Three, it would be great for these to be addressed.

I really enjoyed this game and I recommend it to anyone. This is why :
-There are no enemies to kill so hardcore gaming skill is not required. You play to enjoy the experience.
-The graphics are gorgeous and a joy to behold. You visit many varied and creatively built locations, like a dream.
-The controls are really good and easy to understand and learn. My girlfriend has almost zero gaming experience and she could easily play and have lots of fun.
-The game has good flow. It sees you flying through the levels with athletic jumps and swinging with a sci-fi grapple beam. You could build a racing game built around this. The game does slow down for some story though.
-The world really feels alive and its really fun to explore every nook and cranny. There's even secret collectibles that unlock extras! Its also very detailed and you'll be able to get up close to examine or read things.
-The story is good! Its a bit childish and unrealistic (its set up as a bedtime story, after all), but its heartwarming and cute. You can examine certain key objects and you'll get narration about it. The ending was also good and worth the travels.
-Goat mode. That's right! They made Goat Simulator after all... there's also other unlockables!
The cons :
-Pretty short. I finished the game in one night. However, if you're not used to first-person shooter games (you shoot rocks) it will take you longer.
-The characters are really creepy looking. This is of course a limitation of technology, but since they're like aliens the effect can be seen as intentional. You also cannot interact with any secondary character, breaking the immersion somewhat.
-Very linear. The only side-paths are for secrets. At least you won't get lost.
-Fake areas : in the distance you may see lights and houses, but often they are just decoration and try as you might, you won't reach them. Don't be fooled, this ain't no Skyrim, the world is much smaller than it seems, and its quite disapointing to leave so much unexplored.
Here's hoping that we can revisit this world again in a sequel.

This is one of the most hardcore co-op games I've ever played.
Be prepared for friendly-fire from your teammates, your teammates' turrets, your support drops, your teammate's support drops, etc... Everything deals damage to you, and the game plays like a couch co-op game when multiple people are in a game, where the camera is focused in on the host while everybody else moves around within the confines of that camera's field of view.
Helldivers is an absolute blast to play with friends, randoms online, or even yourself. The game is balanced well in singleplayer, where you're given more than one life, but it's still best played online so you can experience the various unique mechanics that make teamwork as necessary as it is. It's not anywhere near as simple as evading enemies and spraying bullets all over the place like most twin-stick shooters. Instead, you'll find yourself picking your targets before firing, and ensuring that no teammates are going to get caught in the crossfire. Leveling up also rewards you with upgrade points and new gear to spend them on, allowing for an even more diverse group of helldivers ready to take on the game's strongest foes. There's also a lot of time management and cover fire necessary to throw out the various abilities you can select from, as they're cast with unique button combinations, and required for necessary functions such as reviving teammates and supplying your team with more ammunition.
On top of the great looking visuals and audio, online voice chat quality is top notch, and there's text-based chat as well.
You're getting a ton of content for your money with the vanilla version of the game. It's well worth every penny.

The game takes place after the third game in the series & you've just been elected president of the United States.  Suddenly, the earth is invaded by aliens & destroyed because you wouldn't obey their demands.  You & your friends now reside in a virtual reality of Steelport with some minor alterations.  Your goal is to escape the virtual reality & make those alien a-holes pay for their crimes against humanity.
The gameplay is almost identical to the last game in the series with 3rd person shooting, driving, etc.  But now you have super powers because you've hacked the VR you're living in.  The downside is the way you unlock powers.  You don't unlock them from leveling up like you would in most games.  Instead, they went with some collectathon type system where you collect glowy objects spread throughout the city.  There are hundreds of these & you need a lot of them to level up.  This whole system of how you unlock powers becomes very tiresome early on & I found myself getting sick of it within the first hour of gameplay.  You don't need to collect them all but there are so many it just feels like the city is littered with virtual garbage & the only way to clean it up is by collecting them all.  Maybe I'm just a bit OCD about it but there are just too many of these things.
The other gameplay elements are basically the same as the third game.  Shoooting & driving are identical & the super powers are basically ripped from the DLC with added features such as Super Jump, Prototype-like Gliding, Air Dashes, etc.  If you enjoy the powers from the Prototype games you will feel right at home here.  The combat for powers is a bit different though.  You caan use different powers in different ways but the first one you get is basically a grenade of different varieties.  These recharge over time.  other powers include heavy stomp attacks & basic strong punches/kicks.  You also get super speed but that's mostly just used for traveling the city.  Super speed pretty much makes cars useless, especially once it's fully upgraded.
The city is littered with towers as well that unlock new areas.  When you have all the towers you basically control the city.  They feel similar to the towers in Assassin Creed games except instead of climbing up you're leaping & sprinting up them.  The more towers you control the more of the VR you control which basically makes the sky turn blue instead of black/red.  That's the only real change they make.
Instead of buying shops you hack them as well.  The hacking minigames are similar to ones you would find in the first Bioshock game with the pipes.  You get a limited amount of tokens & have to use them to solve a maze like puzzle.  It's pretty easy & you could spend your first few hours in the game just running around & unlocking shops to increase your cache flow.  And yes, the replaced cash with cache.
So the game takes place in a glitchy VR world & it seems like the devs decided to make the game glitchy on purpose or just leave glitches in the game because you're inside a game.  I dunno, but there are a lot of game breaking glitches in this game that have forced me to restart missions or flat out restart the game in order to fix.  Also, the game crashes a lot & seems to have performance issues which SR3 never had.  If you have a good PC you probably won't have any issues but if you're like me & have an old toaster then you'll probably see some FPS drops, crashes & some performance issues every now and then.
I first played this game during it's first FREE weekend & ended up beating it in co-op with a friend which was pretty fun.  Overall, I enjoyed it & ended up buying it later on during a good sale of the complete edition.  If you enjoyed SR3 this is basically more of the same but even crazier so you will most likely enjoy this one as well.  I'd say it's worth the price I paid but it does feel more like an expansion than a whole seperate game.  The city is 90% identical to the last game so it all just feels too familiar sometimes.  Still a fun game, regardless of how much copy/pastey it feels.

I had to reload my game, use a cheat, save & close the game to get it to unlock.  Honestly can't believe this glitch exists in the game because it haults your progress entirely.

PROS
- Wide variety of weapons to play with around each map. Some are patently better than others, but all weapons are useful at some point in the game.

CONS
- Would not suggest for NA players. A lot of the servers for this game are located in the EU, and you experience a ton of lag unless you have godly internet. If you live in Europe or Asia, however, I would suggest this game on the grounds that you'd have a decent connection.

Unless you get this game for free like I did, I wouldn't suggest getting it, especially if you live in NA. 5/10.

I tend to be weary of japanese game ports. The PC gaming market is small over there, and it's common for developers to misunderstand PC expectations. Moreover, these types of games attract a passionate fanbase, who will often overlook technical flaws in their reviews.
Good news: none of this applies to Ys Origin.
The game runs at 60 frames per second without a hitch. Widescreen resolutions are properly supported. There is minimal letterboxing on menus, but devs have added additional graphics on the sides (rather than black bars), a nice touch. 7 hours in, I haven't been able to spot a single bug or glitch. Keyboard controls are implemented and the various tutorial screens actually reference these keys rather than gamepad prompts.
As for the gameplay itself, other reviews give a good overview so there's hardly any need to expand on this. Personal recommandation, don't let your ego get in the way of a fun experience. As someone who finds the Dark Souls series' reputation for punishing difficulty to be largely overblown (and I love all Dark Souls games), Ys Origin's demo boss still handed my♥♥♥♥♥to me several times on Normal difficulty. Picking Easy for my real playthrough after buying the game, so far it has been appropriately challenging.
Also worth noting leveling seems to be important in this game. Sometimes, getting two extra levels can be the difference between hitting a boss for 1 damage per hit or 10 damage per hit (those numbers might seem paltry either way, but when you think about it, the latter hits ten times harder). On Easy there hasn't been any need to grind experience so far.
Overall, an excellent game. -75% discounts come and go on a regular basis, and at that price it's a steal if you're even remotely interested in the genre. Heck, I don't even like anime, but one can only stay grumpy for so long in the face of sheer fun.

So, I'm about an hour in writing this review and I've got to say, this is the most confusing clicker I've ever played. Expect to see "I don't know" a lot during this review.
Anyway, let's start at the start. Unlike most clickers, this one is paid. It's in Early Access, and already got some DLC. Not a promising start. Being paid, one expects it to be way better than the free ones, but while it may have a ton of different stuff to do, the lack of explenation and horrid UI-design completely wrecks it's neck.
Main menu you can't change full-screen. Or turn off music/sound. I've resetted my progress by accident, but since I didn't got any, not too bad. Promotes free DPS for facebook and twitter, another good first impression (not). So, let's start the game then, not much else on this menu.
First off you need to pick 3 eggs. No clue what is what or what's going on I picked the coolest looking one. And then you're in the game, which is very ugly.
Started around clicking various icons to see what they do, since, well, no explenations, and while clicking anything of the menu I also saw numbers appear. Damage click it turned out. Oh joy (yes, every menu click counts as a damage click, I've never seen that before, and it's not a good thing). In the first 5 minutes just exploring the menu's I got all gold-achievements (all 80 of them!). Infact, at this writing, 60m in I got 55% (270!). You get thrown to death with them, another sigh worthy. Got like 50 when my monster found it's first item, and similar happenings make it look even more amateurish.
Anyway, in one of the menu's you can select your icon. Or well, it has arrows but does nothing, great. There's also a raid icon here of all places, which is apparently a though monster you need to kill in a time-limit. Fair enough, but that's not much of a "raid", AND WHY HERE? There's also a skill-tree I think, with 2 skills. Thought I would get info on what it does, unlocks etc. clicking the "+click power" but nope, I just bought it (no confirmation). After gaining +15 I had a clicking power of... 7. Oh great, works juuuust great. You can also get jobs and first time I got one tried accepting, fail. Ignoring, German text suddenly, and still was on screen. Appears you have to leave with a tiny button in the top-left. Grreeeeat design again. Also some reset buttons here I didn't bother with, and had no idea what their text meant.
The main menu shows you have resources. Bronze, silver and gold. What they do? I don't know. How to get them? I don't know. You got bronze, silver and gold chests but apparently it would be TOO LOGICAL for them to drop there, instead, well... I don't know. The chests themselves I had no idea what they did, until I read other reviews saying they gave items. Great feedback game. The gear on monsters is a tiny icon with a lock and no overlay I only clicked by accident, and shows ILVL. What is that? I don't know. Eventually you get some of the things horribly hidden away in odd places, but by then one lacks the willingness to even care anymore. What does a farm do? No clue, guess one has to spend cash to find out. Boss essence (never noticed a boss, just getting an achiev for slaying one) apparently resets the monster level and increases a "stage". Why? Not a clue. Seems it allows more enhancements (+DPS for money).
Also since the menu is so unclear, I've had plenty of times I closed the game when I wanted to return since everything is seemingly randomly placed.
This is EA, so I'll let it installed (few MB anyway) to see if the dev can clean the mess that is the UI, since there seem plenty of options here just hidden away by bad design and UI. Perhaps clean up your base game before addition functions? Then we'll be back to check again. But for now it's just "Why? Eh, screw it, I don't care. I'll play a clicker that isn't a mess of unexplained systems."

I must admit, when I first purchased this game on sale for $30, being a huge fan of the original, I was really dissapointed with COH2. The single player campaign was not very interesting, and without finishing the campaign, this game began to accumulate dust in my steam account. Fast forward over a year, I decided to try to finish the campaign, which I did, then proceeded to play the multiplayer. This is where the game begins to shine.
While multiplayer is fun and addictive, server issues (Lag, drops, AI taking over, etc) and unbalanced game play may make COH2 a little hard to get into. Firstly, automatch games take forever to find a game, and when you do get into a game, some people drop at the very beggining. COH2 does not allow dropped players to rejoin games either, so you're stuck with AI bots for the duration of the game. The AI does not care about troop preservation, and would be buying useless units late game, but they do aggressively capture territory points. Currently there are much more players playing as Axis, so players playing as allies find games slightly faster.

So after many patches, the game is probably the most stable it's going to be. I say this, because Relic will not patch it again after this, so if something's buggered, it's staying that way.
Despite everything, the game is a solid RTS, but unfortunately, as it transitioned (i.e. was forced) into the Esports scene, it left behind its soul, what made the game fun. Flame Half-tracks were terrifying, T34s were driven by Kamikaze Russians.
There was no support for Theatre of War, despite it seeing several (costly) DLC packs that simply added more missions. The Ardenne Assault was a cash grab if I've ever seen one, full retail price for what was essentially a couple of campaign missions and two factions which could be bought seperately and nowhere near on par with the base game. Commanders also get nerfed, and then promptly abandoned, which is the worst thing devs can do to a game, striping variety in order to force a competitive scene.
As stated before, the devs tried to push this into the Esports, but the (relative) lack of developper support, coupled with their abandonment of it in order to focus on Dawn of War III sealed the fate of this game.
Fun with friends and to waste time, but would not recommend as a serious purchase, unless you play RTS games frequently.

'This Game Is A Narrative Experience That Does Not Hold Your Hand'.
The opening line of the game sums up the entire experience. Similar to 'Dear Esther' and 'The Old City: Leviathan', but with more user interaction than either, much better looking, and with far fewer loading screens (none, in fact). 'Much better looking' means, in this case, visually stunning and gorgeous.
This game will not be for everyone. There is no combat, and while not explicitly an horror game, it exhibits many of the overtones and atmospherics of the horror genre. While you can choose to walk past certain events, or explore them out of order, the game is very much a vehicle for the story, rather than a video game in the traditional sense.
On the topic of the story, you take the role of supernatural detective Paul Prospero, investivating 'The Vanishing of Ethan Carter', as the title suggests. Around 10 major self-contained events, puzzles and crimescenes, pertaining to the plot, are woven seamlessly into the environment, with assistance in piecing together the mystery provided in the form of Sherlock-esque floating statements showing Prospero's deductive reasoning, and eerie supernatural reconstructions of crimescenes.
It is worth mentioning, however, that some of the puzzles are easier to solve than others; without going into too much detail, I spent over an hour trying to reconstruct a burnt-out house only to discover that said puzzle was not required for story progression. Interesting, but not an hour's worth of interesting. I was somewhat annoyed at the time, as you can imagine. A little bit of hand-holding would have been appreciated here!
Recommended to anyone who enjoys games that do something different, like the aforementioned 'Dear Esther' and 'The Old City: Leviathan', for those of us who value quality over quantity, and if you're more competent than I am at the puzzle elements.
UPDATE - A new version has been released that, I am told, addresses some of the 'hand-holding' difficulty issues (and more frequent autosaving) I flagged up. It also makes the game EVEN MORE PRETTY, which means that my computer, when attempting to run it, transforms into a screaming death machine (reminiscent of the Xbox360's aeroplane turbine 'disc reading' noises) to push the framerate into double figures

I don't normally write reviews for games. But after playing this game for over a year, and finally getting to the boss on hard mode (which is really hard), I felt this game deserves it. And not only because the game is great, but because I have learned so much about the game itself and about life: 1. Life is a rogue-like. 2. Life has an easy learning curve, but is impossible to master thanks to the infinite possibilities on a single run. 3. Life is VERY RNG-dependent. 4. You can take frankly good or frankly bad decisions sometimes, but more than often, you'll be taking marginally good or marginally bad decisions. 5. On rare occasions will you be able to instantly see the total outcome of a decision you make; more than often you'll have to wait to see, i.e. every decision should be valued in retrospective (and then learn from it). 6. Giant alien spiders are no joke.
A must play, great roguelike, amazing execution, surprisingly detailed yet easy to learn, and you control a spaceship, what's not to like?
I recommend this game.

This is one of the most hardcore co-op games I've ever played.
Be prepared for friendly-fire from your teammates, your teammates' turrets, your support drops, your teammate's support drops, etc... Everything deals damage to you, and the game plays like a couch co-op game when multiple people are in a game, where the camera is focused in on the host while everybody else moves around within the confines of that camera's field of view.
Helldivers is an absolute blast to play with friends, randoms online, or even yourself. The game is balanced well in singleplayer, where you're given more than one life, but it's still best played online so you can experience the various unique mechanics that make teamwork as necessary as it is. It's not anywhere near as simple as evading enemies and spraying bullets all over the place like most twin-stick shooters. Instead, you'll find yourself picking your targets before firing, and ensuring that no teammates are going to get caught in the crossfire. Leveling up also rewards you with upgrade points and new gear to spend them on, allowing for an even more diverse group of helldivers ready to take on the game's strongest foes. There's also a lot of time management and cover fire necessary to throw out the various abilities you can select from, as they're cast with unique button combinations, and required for necessary functions such as reviving teammates and supplying your team with more ammunition.
On top of the great looking visuals and audio, online voice chat quality is top notch, and there's text-based chat as well.
You're getting a ton of content for your money with the vanilla version of the game. It's well worth every penny.

This game sounded like everything I could imagine and more- a story driven, relaxing, and touching first person platformer based on problem solving through movement puzzles in a violence free environment. It sounds phenominal, but... doesn't succeed.
Firstly, the game is not story driven, it's a rage game. Later levels are unforgiving and seem designed for the singular purpose of having you die multiple times so that your time in game expands from the hour of actual gameplay there is. That's right- four out of my five gameplay hours were me dying- and I couldn't even finish the end of the final level before shutting off.
Allow me to explain. You have three grapples- no more, and no less. You have to grapple to falling stalagtites- but once you're down to one grapple, you have to grapple one of the crystals on the walls of the hall- this will give you three grapples. However, this means that you fly free for a few moments before you manage to aim at the crystal- many of which are blocked from some angles by objects that'll take your last grapple attempt and allow you to fall and restart the section. After you've refilled the grapples, you have to continue. You have to do this with pinpoint accuracy six or seven times before you land on the ending platform. However, the challenge doesn't stop there. Stone walls lie in your path, forcing you to go higher or lower in relation to the ceiling. Finally, the stalagtites are far enough apart that, unless you launch yourself perfectly from the last grapple, you'll die.
That's the entire game in one paragraph. It's frustrating, and the story is overshadowed with frustration. Not recommended, sadly.

I'm going to give a honest review of Redux, as someone who played the original version on Xbox 360 (Don't do that, don't ever do that.) back when it was released and just finished a hardcore run on Metro 2033.
____
Gameplay - Metro 2033 was a bit rough on gameplay. It's stealth system was pretty crappy due to the fact that the map designers didn't a good amount of thought into placing broken shards of glass and cans in reasonable spots but rather put it in corridors and doorways intended for people to stealth (I'm looking at you Frontlines). It's combat wasn't well tuned because of the poor amount of weaponry available in the game, but hey! Redux gives you a huge amount of variety. (Use the Bidet if you buy this game, best thing I didn't try till late-game.) Enemies in combat are also smarter, and have different varieties whereas before they didn't. Russians and Germans are actually different looking and can actually be noticed by their outfits and faces (Before in 2033, everyone can kinda suffered from same-face and same-outfit, even different factions, but now in the Redux, you won't really notice that except for that one guy.)
Redux fixes a good amount of the maps to be longer and redone, have cover or to have other routes so that players can have a chance in combat as well with actual well done placed shards of glass and cans so that people still have to actually pay attention if playing stealthy. Enemies will actually hear you blowing candles out if you're behind them, they'll recognize the lights being shot at even if you use a silencer, and they'll actually go searching for you in this game.
(Redux uses the Stealth System from Last Light which made all Russian and German enemies with their heads stuck in their asses, you could essentially just walk in front of them as long as they didn't have a mounted spotlight in front of them).  TIP: Press E to knock out enemies, it was a thing added to the game but because the original 2033 didn't have it, they forget to tell you. So you're not going around knifing every ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and then complaining you couldn't get the good ending.
____
Story - If you played 2033, there isn't much to offer here because you essentially played the story. But, hey, the Story is pretty well done if you're into the post-apoc games, branching out into what a world would be like if the Russian culture had decided to preserve itself into the tunnels. Different areas have different reasons for the way they are. (A certain free market is called the Armory because all of the descendents came from workers who manufactered guns for the Military before the nuke, and then became the largest gun traders in the metro, all that sort.)
The game takes ahold of Artoym, the silent mute protagonist who has visions with these so called powerful mutants wtih superpowers called "The Dark Ones". The Rangers/The Free Metro believe that The Dark Ones are causing mutants inside of the Metro to be more aggressive and violent, Artoym decides to go on an adventure braving the Metro and the Surface to save his town, Polis, from the ever relentless Dark Ones. Artoym (You) will soon discover that there more than the Dark Ones and Mutants that danger not only Polis, but the future of the Metro.
____
Environment/Atomsphere - The game has a great atmosphere and environment. (However, I wouldn't purchase this with the mindset of that you're going to♥♥♥♥♥♥your pants of horror.) The game has some good ♥♥♥♥ing creeps, like some really good ones from time to time. The game captures the idea of a run-down Russia affected by nuclear warfare, markets and people who are deprived of resources and are constantly trying to survive on the brink of death.
____
Graphics -  This game is going to look nice, it's a thing these developers have had to do and keep up with ever since Metro 2033 was released. Why? Because people were using this as a benchmark if their chinese supercomputers were powerful, hell, it was competing against Crysis which was known for basically "Great Graphics, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ Gameplay, Can't run at all".
The game makes the overall decaying, ice-ridden and desolate environment filled with ♥♥♥♥ing beasts on the surface ♥♥♥♥ing beautiful. You'll take back saying "Russian places that were completely destroyed by radiation are never pretty" until you've seen the Dead City. Because Chernobyl is a ♥♥♥♥ing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ while the Dead City is an exotic latvian supermodel... with radioactive beasts and possible superpowered mutants, but still worth it.
____
Cons - I'm not going to do a pros because it's pretty obvious.
The game is short, it can be really ♥♥♥♥ing short. Even new players will have a decent record time of 5-8 hours if you're not even attempting to find collectables, moral points, achievements.
It's a Railway. Yeap, if you're looking for an open-world post-apoc, this isn't it. Metro 2033 is still an enjoyable good railway shooter especially if you're looking for something more so along the lines of gunplay and combat such as the Stalker series.
The game does auto-saves, a good amount of them will cause your frames to just stop and make it look like the game crash for a good 1 or 2 seconds. I hated it.
The game's replayability is heavily dependent on what kinda gamer you are. If you've never played a game like Stalker, you're probably only going to get one or two playthroughs out of this game.
____
TL,DR: Metro 2033 Redux gets a 8/10 from me, I personally give the original a 6.5 or a 7 because of how rough it was and Redux acutally polished the game and made the experience way more enjoyable. It's stealth was improved, the combat was improved, more variety of enemies, more weapons, redone and polished maps/levels, different character models and faces.

Slash It 2 is the sequel to Slash It. It is the same as Slash It in that there are multiple modes to play and you must type letters and/or numbers to score points. This game has 6 modes, but the Classic mode from the original Slash It game is gone. However, I think Slash It 2 does well without the Classic mode in which you must match different shapes. By dedicating itself to strictly matching numbers and letters, I think Slash It 2 is better than Slash It.
The game encourages you to hone your typing skills on the keyboard. The mode gets progressively faster as you correctly type the number or letter on the screen. A great addition to Slash It 2 is the Words mode. The Words mode is better than the Classic mode on Slash It. Words travel across the screen from right to left and the objective is to type the words correctly to score points. Eventually, more words will flow across the screen, causing the mode to be more challenging that at the beginning. The Words mode fits more into the Slash It franchise’s purpose of helping you improve your typing skills than the Classic mode from the original Slash It.
The soundtrack of Slash It 2 is outstanding. The music plays from the start of your playthrough and the screen flashes as you type numbers, letters, words, or a combination of numbers and letters. Thus, the music truly adds to the entertainment value of the game. You can buy the Slash It 2 – Electronic Music Pack for $0.99 to add to the already entertaining classic music that comes with the game.
I recommend Slash It 2 to anyone with and desire to improve their typing skills and for the entertainment that comes with type letters, numbers, and words. I firmly believe that it you liked Slash It, you will love Slash It 2. Kudos to Just1337 Studio for making a sequel that improves on the original.

This game surprised me to no end. I played Magicka a bit but it bored me after a few sessions, for this game I just keep going. Over 20 hours in 5 (working) days...
The game is frantic non-stop action with a high skill ceiling and varied gameplay.
What stood out to me the most (if I have to focus on one unusual thing) is the attention to detail in the animation department. E.g. how the Helldivers enter various vehicles. A lesser dev might have just made them pop in and out of the models but not Arrowhead! The Helldivers enter and exit through hatches on the models with a corresponding unique animation – which has a function from the gameplay standpoint too since the vehicles can burn up and explode and you have to take the escape time into account.
Or one could provide the example how they made all vehicles control differently on purpose – the motorcycle controls like something out of a racing game with the RT serving as the accelerator while the bastion tank destroyer controls, well, literally like a tank with each stick moving one tread (push both up to move forward, push them in opposite directions for quick turning).

Give a look see and maybe even a try before definitely buying as always, but I heartily recommend this game.

On the surface, Helldivers is your stereotypical twinstick shooter that's been brought over from PSN to steam after being out for 9 months. Set in a scifi environment, you are part of an elite squad of soldiers, the Helldivers, sent forth from your home planet of Super Earth to spread justice, liberty, and democracy, to alien scum, etc etc. Now, it sounds pretty generic and B-rated movie nonsense, but honestly it shines as a strong co-op game that hinges well on good teamwork and coordination, while not ruining it for people looking for more casual fun too with the different difficulty levels of missions.
However, the biggest point that stands out for the game is it's unique supply drop system, called "strategems". Basically, you can call down extra firepower or support by plugging in a set combination of directional keys and then waiting for them to arrive. While it seems simple, it can get very hectic to do so while under fire and being swarmed by the enemy, so it adds a fun challenging charm to an already amusing game.
The small quips your soldiers make while fighting are humerous, the guns feel nice when firing, the aliens die satisfyingly, and you get a good sense of accomplishment when completing missions, especially if you can manage to do so without dying.
Speaking of dying, this game was made by the same folks who thought up Magicka, so yes, there is friendly fire, and yes, you can in fact be crushed by the strategems you call in if you're not careful enough. so have fun with that, since it adds more to the teamwork dimension of the game.
Does the friendly fire take away from the game? Honestly, after playing the game for a bit with a mix of pubs and friends alike, I can safely say that it really doesn't. More often then not, you'll be killed by the aliens or the strategems you called in, not by your teammates, unless they're actively trolling you. If that's the case, you can kick people being problematic from your game and continue on your merry way of spreading democracy in the name of Super Earth.
I highly recommend the game to anyone looking for a good priced co-op shooter, and don't let the DLC fool you, you don't need all of them (or any of them for that matter) to enjoy the game. They just add some armor customization cosmetics and a few alternative versions of weapons you can already unlock by simply playing the game itself, only 2 or 3 actually make a noticeable difference and are "worth" getting (and I use the term "worth" loosely here)
As a whole, great fun, totally recommend it, grab it with some friends and get to shooting!

I must admit, when I first purchased this game on sale for $30, being a huge fan of the original, I was really dissapointed with COH2. The single player campaign was not very interesting, and without finishing the campaign, this game began to accumulate dust in my steam account. Fast forward over a year, I decided to try to finish the campaign, which I did, then proceeded to play the multiplayer. This is where the game begins to shine.
While multiplayer is fun and addictive, server issues (Lag, drops, AI taking over, etc) and unbalanced game play may make COH2 a little hard to get into. Firstly, automatch games take forever to find a game, and when you do get into a game, some people drop at the very beggining. COH2 does not allow dropped players to rejoin games either, so you're stuck with AI bots for the duration of the game. The AI does not care about troop preservation, and would be buying useless units late game, but they do aggressively capture territory points. Currently there are much more players playing as Axis, so players playing as allies find games slightly faster.

So after many patches, the game is probably the most stable it's going to be. I say this, because Relic will not patch it again after this, so if something's buggered, it's staying that way.
Despite everything, the game is a solid RTS, but unfortunately, as it transitioned (i.e. was forced) into the Esports scene, it left behind its soul, what made the game fun. Flame Half-tracks were terrifying, T34s were driven by Kamikaze Russians.
There was no support for Theatre of War, despite it seeing several (costly) DLC packs that simply added more missions. The Ardenne Assault was a cash grab if I've ever seen one, full retail price for what was essentially a couple of campaign missions and two factions which could be bought seperately and nowhere near on par with the base game. Commanders also get nerfed, and then promptly abandoned, which is the worst thing devs can do to a game, striping variety in order to force a competitive scene.
As stated before, the devs tried to push this into the Esports, but the (relative) lack of developper support, coupled with their abandonment of it in order to focus on Dawn of War III sealed the fate of this game.
Fun with friends and to waste time, but would not recommend as a serious purchase, unless you play RTS games frequently.

There are a lot of games in the Ys series, several of which are on Steam. This is actually a prequel, set hundreds of years before the main series games.
Yet... this is my favorite.
The Ys series are action RPGs. What makes them unique is that a level-up should not be underestimated - it makes the difference between getting served by a boss and dominating it. So grinding feels genuinely rewarding, and something you shouldn't have to do much of if you're not playing on higher levels. Plus, the soundtrack absolutely rocks.
There is a bit of a Metroid feel as you'll be backtracking and searching around for powerups to help you get further into the tower. There are three characters, and for me the game was never really boring enough not to replay with the other characters. Getting all achievements, however, requires beating the game a total of six times, and on the highest difficulty for three of them. Don't think I'm going for that.
The Ys series was never huge on story - you won't find anything revolutionary here. But it's not a problem, since the gameplay more than makes up for it.
In summary: Genuinely fun action, great music, and a great intro into the Ys series. GET THIS GAME.

I'm going to give a honest review of Redux, as someone who played the original version on Xbox 360 (Don't do that, don't ever do that.) back when it was released and just finished a hardcore run on Metro 2033.
____
Gameplay - Metro 2033 was a bit rough on gameplay. It's stealth system was pretty crappy due to the fact that the map designers didn't a good amount of thought into placing broken shards of glass and cans in reasonable spots but rather put it in corridors and doorways intended for people to stealth (I'm looking at you Frontlines). It's combat wasn't well tuned because of the poor amount of weaponry available in the game, but hey! Redux gives you a huge amount of variety. (Use the Bidet if you buy this game, best thing I didn't try till late-game.) Enemies in combat are also smarter, and have different varieties whereas before they didn't. Russians and Germans are actually different looking and can actually be noticed by their outfits and faces (Before in 2033, everyone can kinda suffered from same-face and same-outfit, even different factions, but now in the Redux, you won't really notice that except for that one guy.)
Redux fixes a good amount of the maps to be longer and redone, have cover or to have other routes so that players can have a chance in combat as well with actual well done placed shards of glass and cans so that people still have to actually pay attention if playing stealthy. Enemies will actually hear you blowing candles out if you're behind them, they'll recognize the lights being shot at even if you use a silencer, and they'll actually go searching for you in this game.
(Redux uses the Stealth System from Last Light which made all Russian and German enemies with their heads stuck in their asses, you could essentially just walk in front of them as long as they didn't have a mounted spotlight in front of them).  TIP: Press E to knock out enemies, it was a thing added to the game but because the original 2033 didn't have it, they forget to tell you. So you're not going around knifing every ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and then complaining you couldn't get the good ending.
____
Story - If you played 2033, there isn't much to offer here because you essentially played the story. But, hey, the Story is pretty well done if you're into the post-apoc games, branching out into what a world would be like if the Russian culture had decided to preserve itself into the tunnels. Different areas have different reasons for the way they are. (A certain free market is called the Armory because all of the descendents came from workers who manufactered guns for the Military before the nuke, and then became the largest gun traders in the metro, all that sort.)
The game takes ahold of Artoym, the silent mute protagonist who has visions with these so called powerful mutants wtih superpowers called "The Dark Ones". The Rangers/The Free Metro believe that The Dark Ones are causing mutants inside of the Metro to be more aggressive and violent, Artoym decides to go on an adventure braving the Metro and the Surface to save his town, Polis, from the ever relentless Dark Ones. Artoym (You) will soon discover that there more than the Dark Ones and Mutants that danger not only Polis, but the future of the Metro.
____
Environment/Atomsphere - The game has a great atmosphere and environment. (However, I wouldn't purchase this with the mindset of that you're going to♥♥♥♥♥♥your pants of horror.) The game has some good ♥♥♥♥ing creeps, like some really good ones from time to time. The game captures the idea of a run-down Russia affected by nuclear warfare, markets and people who are deprived of resources and are constantly trying to survive on the brink of death.
____
Graphics -  This game is going to look nice, it's a thing these developers have had to do and keep up with ever since Metro 2033 was released. Why? Because people were using this as a benchmark if their chinese supercomputers were powerful, hell, it was competing against Crysis which was known for basically "Great Graphics, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ Gameplay, Can't run at all".
The game makes the overall decaying, ice-ridden and desolate environment filled with ♥♥♥♥ing beasts on the surface ♥♥♥♥ing beautiful. You'll take back saying "Russian places that were completely destroyed by radiation are never pretty" until you've seen the Dead City. Because Chernobyl is a ♥♥♥♥ing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ while the Dead City is an exotic latvian supermodel... with radioactive beasts and possible superpowered mutants, but still worth it.
____
Cons - I'm not going to do a pros because it's pretty obvious.
The game is short, it can be really ♥♥♥♥ing short. Even new players will have a decent record time of 5-8 hours if you're not even attempting to find collectables, moral points, achievements.
It's a Railway. Yeap, if you're looking for an open-world post-apoc, this isn't it. Metro 2033 is still an enjoyable good railway shooter especially if you're looking for something more so along the lines of gunplay and combat such as the Stalker series.
The game does auto-saves, a good amount of them will cause your frames to just stop and make it look like the game crash for a good 1 or 2 seconds. I hated it.
The game's replayability is heavily dependent on what kinda gamer you are. If you've never played a game like Stalker, you're probably only going to get one or two playthroughs out of this game.
____
TL,DR: Metro 2033 Redux gets a 8/10 from me, I personally give the original a 6.5 or a 7 because of how rough it was and Redux acutally polished the game and made the experience way more enjoyable. It's stealth was improved, the combat was improved, more variety of enemies, more weapons, redone and polished maps/levels, different character models and faces.

This game deserves credit, for the following reasons:
*It is scary. But not Outlast scary, it´s sort of less horror than jump-scares and simply the sounds and visuals. Especially the sounds. They´re mostly the same all the time, but sh*t they are scary, every time.
*It has (fairly) good shooter mechanics. The weapons shoot realistically and the damage models are solid. What makes it interesting is that there are no specific damage points. You don´t know how much damage a weapon does, you just have to try it out. Makes the weapons choice just that much harder, and trust me weapons choice does matter in this game, depending on if you want to have a fun and entirely possible expirience or a difficult and far-less fun experience.
*It has puzzles. Well, not many and they aren´t really that difficult, but it make the game more challenging and makes this not just an ego-shooter, but also sort of a thinking game.
*The story is amazing. It is filled with plot-twists, creative levels and, most importantly, russian.
There are of course a fair share of bugs, or things the game does not tell you which makes it a lot harder. I experienced this myself. the game does not tell you that if you press (M) to hide your weapon Librarians (Monsters later in the game) will not attack you. This doesn´t spoil much as you can of course try to kill them, but it´s extremely difficult and takes up too much ammo. I wasted hours on that level and had to rely on outside help, even with normal mode on. I also had some other places where I required outside help, where the game was not explicit enough, but the main thing is that you acctually have to listen to dialogue, otherwise you are clueless.
Overall, I´d say that Metro 2033 is definitely a good buy, especially if it´s on sale as it is now, and it appeals to many genres. If you like FPS, puzzle and horror games, this is definitely the game for you. And let me also add that the fact that I even bothered to write this review, and make it so positive, just goes to show that this game is definitey worth a buy, just like its sequel, Metro: Last Light, which I am yet to play but will soon review too, if it impresses me as much as this game does

Rainbow Six Vegas 2 is a much needed improvement over the original game, and it improved aspects of the original game's design without changing very much of the overall gameplay.
The biggest addition Vegas 2 added was the ability to customize your character. Instead of playing as a gruff southerner named "Logan" you instead play as a customizeable character named "Bishop". Bishop can be male or female and his/her apperance can be heavily customized. You're given the option to pick between what clothing Bishop wears and what armor you wear. Which will impact how much damage reduction you get and how fast you move.
In addition Rainbow Six Vegas 2 helped start the trend towards unlock based multiplayer. Now you played as a character who was universal across Terrorist hunt and PVP. And your character would gain stats in both singleplayer and multiplayer, which would unlock new guns and cosmetics. This was really popular at the time and reminded me a lot of multiplayer games like Syphon Filter the Omega Strain. These were all great improvements and made the game feel very fresh and new. It made it feel more akin to an RPG despite leveling being automatic and the game fundamentally playing the same. The multiplayer was expanded to have many more gamemodes. And Terrorist hunt was expanded to be much more customizeable.
There's actually very little I can say that's negative about Rainbow Six Vegas 2 apart from how they didn't really change very much about the actual gameplay, so it still has the same flaws like the general stiffness to the combat. The storyline is also a bit weaker. And if you're a fan of older style Rainbow Six games, you're going to remain disappointed.
All that aside though, it's a very effective sequel. And there's little wonder why it's more fondly remembered than the first game.
